1. A Country Called Spain

1In Berga, citizens gather for a theatrical show during a festival. Spain occupies the Iberian Peninsula, in the southwest of Europe. The Pyrenees, pronounced PEER-uh-neez, stand along its northern side. South of those peaks, the country continues until the Strait of Gibraltar. Africa lies across that narrow passage of water. The northeast neighbor is France. The western neighbor is Portugal. East of the mainland, the Balearic Islands form a Mediterranean chain. Spain counts that chain as a province. Fine beaches are one reason people visit. Rich holiday customs are another. The Canary Islands sit near Morocco, on that country's west side. Spain counts them as a region. Holidaymakers go there for the beaches too. Berga's festival and the islands' holidays show the same love of gathering. The water at Gibraltar is a tight passage, not a broad sea. France meets Spain on land. Portugal meets Spain on land as well. The Pyrenees lie between Spain and France. Beach travel draws crowds to the Balearic group. It draws crowds to the Canary group too. A map marks the Bay of Biscay. It marks the Atlantic Ocean. It marks the Mediterranean Sea. Pamplona, Madrid, and Barcelona are among the cities shown. Valencia, Córdoba, and Granada are shown too. France and Portugal appear beside the borders. Morocco appears across the southern water. Ceuta is labeled as part of Spain, next to Africa. Melilla is labeled as part of Spain too. Corner insets show Europe, Africa, and Asia. The festival crowd in Berga is one face of public life. Island beaches are another. Both belong to the same country.

2Madrid is the capital, and it is also the biggest city. Roughly 3.3 million people live in the city itself. About 6.5 million live in the area around it. The city rests on a high plateau. That plateau stands about 640 meters, or 2,100 ft., above the sea. The Royal Palace there ranks among the grandest buildings in Europe. King Alfonso XIII was the last monarch to make the palace his home. In 1931 he departed from Spain. With the king gone, the state took charge of the palace. No royal has lived in it since that change. Today's royal family stays in a much smaller palace beyond Madrid. Spain's government is a constitutional monarchy. A prime minister leads the day-to-day government. A parliament makes laws, and voters choose its members. King Felipe VI stands as head of the government. Lawmaking and passing laws belong only to the elected officials. Builders finished the Royal Palace in the 1700s. It holds 2,800 rooms. State ceremonies use it now. Public tours use it too. Olive growers in Spain raise more than two hundred kinds. In 2014, Spain passed Italy and became the world's top maker of olive oil. Estimates keep the population under forty-eight million. City dwellers greatly outnumber people in the countryside. About three-quarters of the people live in Madrid, Barcelona, Valencia, or other smaller cities. Tourism gives work to about two million people. That industry matters a great deal to the economy. Making cars is still one of the biggest sources of jobs. Textiles, food, clothing, shipbuilding, and medical equipment are other industries. Spain also leads all rivals in olive-oil output, and it ships that oil to other countries.

3Spain belongs to the European Union, often called the EU. The EU started in 1951. Membership began with Belgium. Germany was in that first circle. France was in it. Luxembourg was in it. Italy was in it. The aim was joint work on shared problems. Trade was one of those problems. Security was another. The rights of citizens were another. Most members use the same money, the euro. By 2022, the EU included twenty-seven nations. Spanish, also called Castilian, is the official language. Most people speak it. Basque is spoken in some regions. Galician is spoken in some. Catalan is spoken in some as well. One photo shows textile workers getting clothes ready for shops. Another shows people at a sidewalk cafe in Palma. Spain's land changes from place to place. High plateaus fill much of the interior. The south has dry areas that seem like desert. Beaches and mountain chains around the country create very different settings. The Meseta Central is a plateau in the middle. It covers about half of Spain. In the mountains along that plateau, people mine silver. They mine lead. They mine copper. They also raise livestock there. The Sierra Nevada is a steep, rocky chain over the south. Mount Mulhacén, pronounced moo-lah-THEN, stands taller than every other peak in that chain. The range belongs to the Andalusian region, pronounced an-duh-LOO-zhuhn, in the southeast. To the north, the Pyrenees form a firm natural line between Spain and France. The Meseta Central lies in central Spain. As a plateau, it is high ground with a fairly level top. About half the nation rests on it. Mines in the bordering mountains yield silver. They yield lead and copper too. Herds of livestock use those slopes. Dry southern country feels unlike the high interior. Beaches feel unlike both. The mountain walls add still another setting.

4The Pyrenees run from Mediterranean shores in the east to the Atlantic coast in the west. Their length is 434 kilometers, or 270 mi. The western stretch is green, rolling, and thick with woods. Vineyards fill much of the east. Orchards do too. The center holds granite summits, deep canyons, and waterfalls. Hundreds of mountain lakes sit there as well. Several peoples call these mountains home. They include the Andorran, the Catalan, the Béarnese, pronounced bair-NEEZ, and the Basque. Farming has long been their living. Raising livestock has too. Wild animals share the slopes. The brown bear lives there. So does the chamois, pronounced sham-WAH, a kind of goat-antelope. The rare bearded vulture lives there as well. Fir, pine, and oak forests cover the hillsides. In Granada, the Moors built the Alhambra on a height that looks over the whole valley. It served as both a palace and a fortress. Settlers from Phoenicia, pronounced fi-NEE-shuh, reached southern Spain around 800 BCE. The lands of Phoenicia are Lebanon, Syria, and Israel now. Those settlers were skilled artisans. They were skilled sailors too. Ivory went out in their trade. Perfumes went out as well. Bronze came back to them. Silver came back too. Around 500 BCE, another group of traders arrived. They were Greek, and their home port was Carthage. Tunisia occupies that place today. Olive trees came with them. Grapes came with them too. Near 200 BCE the Romans took control, and their rule lasted about six hundred years. Towns were linked by the roads they laid. Bridges linked towns as well. Aqueducts carried water out of rivers and into cities. After Rome, Germanic people moved in from the north. In 711 CE, Muslim settlers known as Moors took charge. Moorish control continued until Catholic rule began. Their buildings can still be seen. One is the Alhambra, a palace raised in Granada in the 1300s. Another is the Great Mosque standing in Córdoba.

5Spain spent many centuries split into kingdoms. Aragon, Castile, and Granada were the main ones. King Ferdinand II of Aragon married Queen Isabella I of Castile. That wedding made two kingdoms into one. Both rulers were Catholic monarchs. They won a war against the Moors and took Granada. They set up a group called the Spanish Inquisition. The group pressed people to follow the Catholic faith. Jewish residents were driven from Spain. Muslim residents were driven out as well. The king and queen paid explorers. Christopher Columbus was one of them. The goal was fresh trade paths to Asia. He came ashore on Caribbean islands. Those islands were called the New World. Spain built colonies there. Homebound ships carried gold, silver, and spices. During the 1800s and the early 1900s, rich and poor lived worlds apart. An attempt to overthrow the elected government did not succeed. Open fighting followed. People call it the Spanish Civil War. It started in 1936 and ended in 1939. General Francisco Franco seized control once fighting stopped. He governed as a dictator. Only his death in 1975 ended that rule. King Juan Carlos I took the throne next. Adolfo Suarez was his choice for prime minister. Democracy in Spain grew under Suarez. Fiestas are local holidays people wait for. A fiesta may honor a harvest, a past event, or a saint. Dance, song, parades, and fireworks keep the days lively. April 23 is St. George's Day. Loved ones receive books and red roses. July brings Pamplona's running of the bulls, named for San Fermin. Runners try not to be caught as the animals charge the streets. October 12 is National Day. It marks the first Spanish arrival in the Americas. Spaniards also honor their country's place in the world. Once a year, La Tomatina honors a patron saint. Crowds hurl ripe tomatoes, and the aim is fun.

6Tapas are small finger foods. They may be served cold. They may be served hot. Small plates usually hold them. Along the coasts, shrimp and squid are common tapas. Inland, sausages are common instead. Daily meals usually come in a set of three. A morning drink might be coffee. It might be milk. It might be hot chocolate. A sweet roll can come with that drink. Cereal is sometimes added. The biggest meal is lunch, served near two in the afternoon. Lunch can start with soup. A salad can follow. A main course can follow that. Dessert can close the meal. The evening meal is smaller. It is served late, sometime between nine and eleven. Each region cooks in its own way. Seafood is typical where the ocean is close. Central kitchens often use beans. They use lentils. They use lamb and pork. Valencia's fame rests on rice. Paella is the known dish, and it can mix rice with fish, with meat, and with vegetables. Gazpacho, a soup many people love, began in the Andalusian region. Tomatoes go into it, along with other vegetables. Summer servings are often chilled, and the bowl feels refreshing. Antoni Gaudí designed a striking church that stands in Barcelona. Construction started in 1882. Workers are still building it. Pride in Spanish culture is common. Someone may identify first with a town. Someone else may identify first with a region. Festivals still draw those people into one nation. A few regions keep working to protect local customs. Even so, Spain has stood as one country for a long time. Among European Union lands, it is a lively center of culture. Arrivals from many distant places helped build that heritage. Their gifts included celebrations. They included food. They included architecture. The past is long, and it is complex. What Spain has done, and the culture it carries, has touched lands far away. Lovely landscapes are part of the gift. So is the friendly warmth people show. The wider world is a more interesting place because of both.

7Counts published for 2022 put the population at 46,785,909. Land area is 498,980 square kilometers, which is 310,052 square miles. Castilian Spanish is the primary language, and 74 percent of the people speak it. Roman Catholic faith is the primary religion. The euro is the currency people use. Aqueducts are built channels that move water between places. Heritage means customs, a manner of life, or a trait passed along by older generations. An archipelago means islands clustered as a group or a chain. Parliament means the officials who may write laws and revise them. Artisans are skilled in a craft or trade, and their goods are made by hand. A plateau is broad land that sits up high and stays mostly flat. Currency is accepted money that stands for what goods and resources are worth. Where a parliament exists, the prime minister is usually the person in charge of government. Democracy means the people run the state by voting in free elections. A strait is water squeezed into a narrow lane that links two bigger waters. Economy means how money circulates among industry, buying and selling, and finance. Urban refers to towns and cities, and to people who live in them. These 2022 counts and these word meanings close the portrait of Spain.

2. A Country Called Ukraine

1Kyiv Pechersk Lavra is a major landmark of Ukraine. Another name for it is Kiev Monastery of the Caves. A welcome to Ukraine opens this book. The land comes next. The people come after the land. History follows the people. Landmarks follow the history. Celebrations follow the landmarks. A conclusion ends the book. Independence came to Ukraine in 1991. Few countries on Earth are younger. The past, though, stretches a long way. That past is full of interest. Rich soil let an early farming culture take root there. The start was over 5,000 years back. Visitors today can still walk in castles that have stood for over 1,000 years. Some cities are that old too. The place where Ukraine sits made empire after empire fight to hold it. Those struggles lasted for centuries. Art in Ukraine still shows those empires. Cooking still shows them. Buildings still show them. Good meals wait for visitors. Medieval castles wait for them. Lively music festivals wait for them. There is a great deal to see and to do. A march moves through the city of Kyiv. The marchers wear clothes in the old Ukrainian style.

2Farming uses a large share of the land in Ukraine. No larger country lies entirely inside Europe. Russia is bigger. Russia reaches into Europe and also into Asia. Italy would fit into Ukraine twice. Texas is only a little larger than Ukraine. Seven countries touch Ukraine. Belarus is one. Hungary is one. Moldova is one. Poland is one. Romania is one. Russia is one. Slovakia is one. The Black Sea meets Ukraine along the south. The Sea of Azov meets it there too. The longest river is the Dnieper. Say that name NEE-pur. The river runs down the center of Ukraine. It comes down from Belarus in the north. It ends in the Black Sea. The Crimean Peninsula lies south of the mainland. A narrow link of land joins the peninsula to that mainland. The link measures 8 kilometers. That is about 5 miles. No country produces more sunflower oil than Ukraine. Cooks like that oil. The Carpathian Mountains rise in the west. The Crimean Mountains rise on the peninsula. Flat land covers most of what remains. Summer days are often warm. They are often humid. Winter days are cold. They are dry. Soil on the plains is fertile. Weather there is mild. Wheat grows well on that land. A nickname for Ukraine is the breadbasket of Europe. Wheat is among the main crops. Corn is among them. Sunflowers are among them. Potatoes are among them. Sugar beets are among them. Visitors often go to Synevir Lake.

3Ukraine holds about seventeen million fewer people than Italy. Over two-thirds of Ukrainians make their homes in cities. The capital is Kyiv. Say it KI-yeev. No city in the country is larger. Close to three million people live in Kyiv. Native Ukrainians are most of the people. Russians are the next largest group. An ethnic group called Slavs includes Ukrainians. Slavs come mainly from the center and the east of Europe. Their languages are Slavic. Eastern Europe has few cities older than Kyiv. The founding year was 482 ce. More than 1,500 years have passed since then. Young students in Ukraine practice reading at school. Ukrainian is the language most people speak. Other languages are common too. Russian is spoken. Polish is spoken. Yiddish is spoken. Some Jewish people in Europe use Yiddish. Ukrainian is the official language today. That was not true in every era. Schools were at times forbidden to use it. Churches were forbidden to use it. Theaters were forbidden to use it. Other public places were forbidden to use it. Printing a book in Ukrainian was even against the law for a time. Giving a baby a Ukrainian name was against the law too. The year 1989 made Ukrainian official once more.

4Human life in Ukraine goes back to prehistoric times. In the 8th century bce, settlers arrived from the land now called Iran. They settled on the plains. About 2,750 years have passed since then. Later centuries brought Greek colonies. Those colonies lined the Black Sea. They also lined the Sea of Azov. In that same era, Slavs moved out of lands lying north of the Carpathians. They spread through the region. They built settlements. Business centers grew from those settlements. Political centers grew from them too. One early settlement became Kyiv. By the 11th century ce, Slavs and Viking raiders had united. The Vikings came from Scandinavia. Together they formed the kingdom called Kyivan Rus. No empire in Europe was larger then. Mongol attackers ended that reign. The Mongols came from central Asia. The attack came in the 1200s. Control of most of Ukraine passed to Lithuania in the 1300s. Ruins in a photo are the old city of Tauric Chersonese. Builders raised it around 422 bce. People date Kamianets-Podilskyi Castle to the 1200s or the 1300s. Poland invaded in the late 1500s. Most Ukrainians were forced to live as serfs. A serf was a farmer tied to land owned by someone else. Wealth was scarce for serfs. Power was scarce too. Anger at that life sparked a rebellion in the 1600s. The fighters called themselves the Cossacks. They asked Russia to help defeat the Polish. Freedom from Poland followed the Cossack victory. By the late 1700s, Russia held nearly all of Ukraine. In that period, people were barred from using Ukrainian. The year 1922 placed Ukraine inside the Soviet Union. No country that has ever existed was larger. Lands inside it are now separate countries. Lithuania is one of those lands. Belarus is one. Russia is one. Moldova is one. Many other lands were inside it too. The Soviet Union split apart in 1991. Ukraine declared that it was independent. The first president was chosen that same year. His name was Leonid Kravchuk.

5In April 1986, explosions at a nuclear power station in Chernobyl sent radioactive material into the air. Say that name chair-NOH-bil. Materials that are radioactive give off radiation. Radiation is a form of energy. Living things can be harmed when the amount is high. Wind moved the material west. France lay in its path. Italy lay in its path. Hundreds of thousands of people were exposed. Millions of acres of land were exposed. Thousands of people had to leave home after the accident. The law then barred anyone from coming within 30 kilometers of the station. The distance is 18 miles. Land there had become radioactive. Water had become radioactive. Air had become radioactive. Animals born near the site showed deformities. A deformity is a body part with a misshapen or abnormal form. Nobody lives there now. The land is still radioactive. The animals are still radioactive. Landmarks in Ukraine are many, and they are striking. Some were shaped by nature. Some were built by people. National parks number more than forty-five. Carpathian National Nature Park is one of them. The park was established in 1980. Its job is to protect Carpathian Mountain scenery. Mount Hoverla stands there. Say it hoh-VAIR-lah. No mountain in Ukraine is taller. Oleshky Sands National Nature Park is another place people like. It lies in the south. Sand dunes there cover 1,620 square kilometers. That area is 625 square miles. Kyiv would fit into those dunes twice. Morning mist and a rising Sun fill a photo of the Carpathian Mountains. Castles stand across Ukraine. Palaces stand there. Monasteries stand there. Cathedrals stand there. Visitors often choose Kyiv Pechersk Lavra. Say it peh-CHAIRSK LAHV-rah. People also call it Kiev Monastery of the Caves. Seven places in Ukraine are World Heritage Sites, and this monastery is one. Such sites matter to the history of the world. The founding year was 1051 ce. Caves lie under the monastery. Catacombs lie under it too. A catacomb is an underground place of burial. Important religious relics are kept there. Bodies of monks are kept there too. The bodies were mummified. Glass coffins hold them. Khotyn fortress is another landmark of high importance. Say Khotyn as HOH-tin. The fortress stands in the town of Khotyn. That town is among the oldest in Ukraine. Wood was probably the first material. The early 11th century was the likely building time. Later rulers added more. Few forts still standing in Eastern Europe are older. A fortification is a structure made to hold off an attack. A wall added in the 1400s is nearly 6 meters thick. That thickness is about 20 feet. The wall rises over 40 meters. That height is about 130 feet. Cannon fire could not break a wall that strong. Fortifications in Ukraine number more than five thousand, and this fortress is one.

6Tunnel of Love draws huge numbers of visitors in Ukraine. The tunnel is natural, and it runs 4 kilometers. That length is 2.5 miles. The tunnel covers a railway. The city is Klevan. Planters set trees along both edges of the rails during the 1940s. The goal was to hide trains. Those trains were bound for an army base. Branches later arched over the tracks. Beauty there now pulls visitors from every part of the world. Celebrations fill the Ukrainian year. Independence Day, on August 24, is among the most important. It marks the 1991 break from the Soviet Union. Concerts fill cities across the country. Festivals fill them. Parades fill them. Marchers carry the national flag of Ukraine on that day. A girl in old-style Ukrainian dress sets a wildflower crown on her head. Season holidays are part of life here, as in many countries. Ivan Kupala Day marks the start of summer. Dancing circles a bonfire. Wreaths are made from wildflowers. People bathe in lakes. Masliana lasts a full week. It greets the end of winter. It greets the start of spring. Cheese goes into many foods that week. Butter goes into many of them. Varenyky and pancakes are two favorites. Say varenyky as vah-REH-nih-kih. A varenyky is a dumpling. Old belief said a merrier week brought a better year after it. Music is plentiful. Entertainment is plentiful. Food is plentiful.

7Landscapes in Ukraine are incredible. The architecture is beautiful. The cities are vibrant. Millions of visitors come each year. History here is long. Parts of it were hard. Empire after empire ruled for centuries. Independence came at last. Through all of that, people held on to their language. They held on to their culture. Yearly festivals still keep traditions that are centuries old. National parks stun the eye. Festivals bring joy. Ukraine has a great deal to offer. A woman holds the national flag of Ukraine. Banned means something is not allowed. Mummified means a body was prepared and wrapped in cloth for burial. An empire is a set of nations, or of peoples, under one ruler or one government. Native means tied to a place by birth. An ethnic group shares traits such as background, faith, language, or customs. Prehistoric points to the time before people wrote history down. Prohibited means a law or a rule forbids it. Fertile soil can grow a great many plants or crops. A reign is the stretch of time one ruler holds power. A landmark may be an important old building or site. It can also be a land object used to show where you are. A settlement is a new place where people make a home. It is where a community gets its start. The mainland is the chief mass of land of a country or a continent.

3. A Disguise on the Road to Freedom

1Portraits on this page show Ellen Craft and William Craft. The table of contents comes first. Introduction is listed on page 4. Born into Slavery is listed on page 5. A Decision Fueled by Love is listed on page 6. Slavery in States and Territories, 1860 is listed on page 7. Preparing and Planning is listed on page 8. The Great Escape Begins is listed on page 10. Setting Sail for Freedom is listed on page 12. Across the Ocean to Safety is listed on page 13. The Long Trip Home is listed on page 15. Glossary is listed on page 16. Introduction. Dressing in costume as someone else can be entertaining and fun. Imagine if your life depended on how well you played the part. In the nineteenth century, William and Ellen Craft lived that case. They were enslaved. They changed their appearance so they could leave the South.

2Born into Slavery. During the middle of the 1800s, many Black people in America began life already enslaved. William and Ellen Craft were among them. William's birth year was 1824. His home was Macon, Georgia. The man who owned William's family enjoyed gambling. Debts from that habit were paid by selling the family. He sold them one person after another. William's own sale came when he was sixteen. By then he had trained as a carpenter's apprentice. His skill was high. That training later proved to be a real asset, and so did his talent. A bank cashier became his new enslaver. The cashier saw that William could bring in steady money. He set William to work as a cabinetmaker. The wages went to the cashier. Ellen was younger than William by two years. Her father was a white man. He kept Ellen's mother in slavery. Ellen's skin was light. It was so light that people did not guess her mother was Black. At eleven, Ellen was handed to a half sister who had just married. Ellen's job was a servant's job. She moved to Macon with that sister's family. In Macon she later met William. A Decision Fueled by Love. Love grew between William and Ellen. They wanted a shared life. Marriage for enslaved people was full of trouble. Law treated them as property. Freedoms held by white people were not theirs. A wedding required an enslaver's permission. Even a permitted couple could not share a home if two different enslavers owned them. Permission finally came in 1846. For the next two years they kept separate homes. Meetings happened only now and then. Living apart wore the Crafts down. Either one might be sold at any moment and sent far off. Ellen refused to have children for that reason. She could not stand the thought of a child pulled away and sold.

3In time the Crafts saw only one path to a real family life. They would have to flee toward the North. In the Northern states, Black people were able to live in freedom. The hard question was how to leave without capture. A plan, luckily, was already in their minds. Free States and Slave States. The United States contained thirty-three states in 1860. Slavery was lawful in fifteen of them, the Southern states called slave states. It was unlawful in eighteen Northern states called free states. Inside a slave state, an enslaved Black person held none of the rights a white enslaver held. Inside a free state, a Black person could live as a free citizen. The slave states broke away and formed the Confederacy. The South then lost the Civil War. After that loss, the Thirteenth Amendment to the Constitution ended slavery in the United States. Every state became a free state. A map titled Slavery in States and Territories, 1860 marks free states, slave states, and territories where slavery was still allowed.

4Preparing and Planning. Fear held Ellen back at the start. She was unwilling. Capture would bring harsh punishment. A beating was certain. Their lives might be at risk as well. She agreed once the details of the disguise were settled. On the night they left, William would cut Ellen's hair until it was short. Special clothing worn underneath would hide the shape of her body. A bandage would wrap her face. Green spectacles would cover her eyes. Together, those pieces would hide skin with no beard, and features that looked feminine. One arm would rest in a sling, and the costume would be complete. Ellen had never been taught to read. She had never been taught to write. Travel papers of that time required a signature. The sling gave her a reason not to sign. Glasses, a bandage, and a sling would also make her look ill. William's presence would then make sense. He would seem a careful servant looking after the person who enslaved him. Suspicion would stay low, and the pair could move. The Great Escape Begins. December 21, 1848, was the day they chose. Money for the journey had been hidden by William. It came from his cabinetmaking. The couple asked their enslavers for days away so Christmas could be spent together. Giving enslaved people a short holiday break was a custom. Those days would cover the escape. Nobody would notice the absence until the Crafts were far ahead. When the morning came, William cut Ellen's hair. He helped her dress in the costume. They prayed. Then they walked to the train depot in Macon and bought tickets. Savannah, Georgia, was the destination. Because travel kept the races apart, they entered different cars. They waited there for the opening stretch of the trip. A map titled The Crafts' Escape Route covers December 21 to 25, 1848. Labels include Boston in Massachusetts, Pennsylvania, and Maryland. The Atlantic Ocean is marked. So are Washington, D.C., and North Carolina, plus a note dated December 1850. The map also shows South Carolina, Liverpool in England, and Macon, Georgia.

5A known face suddenly appeared on the platform. William recognized the owner of the cabinet shop where he worked. That man suspected William might be running away with his wife. He started down the train, looking for the pair. William bent low in his seat and shook. The man had just reached William's car when the bell for departure rang. He got off. William breathed out in relief, because he was safe. Ellen faced a fright of her own in a different car. The person who sat beside her was a close friend of her enslaver. He had known Ellen for years. She held still. She would not speak, and she would not raise her eyes. The costume fooled him completely. He greeted her without looking twice, then took his seat. Ellen acted as if she could not hear. Silence kept her from giving the secret away. Setting Sail for Freedom. Savannah was reached without capture. There the Crafts boarded a steamer bound for Charleston, in South Carolina. After landing, they tried to purchase tickets onward to Philadelphia, in Pennsylvania. A clerk would not sign those tickets. Ellen's seeming injury did not change his mind. The captain of their earlier boat walked past at that moment. He offered help. His word stood behind the couple. Soon the journey north continued. Odd meetings filled the rest of the trip. Other riders scolded Ellen for thanking William. Thanking an enslaved person was not something people did. One man asked to purchase William from Ellen. Other riders told Ellen to watch out for abolitionists in the North. Those abolitionists, they said, would urge William to run. Baltimore, in Maryland, brought the last barrier. Slave states that touched free states posted border patrols. The patrols searched for people who had escaped. Officers in Maryland demanded proof that William was owned. The Crafts feared freedom was lost. Pity moved the officer instead. He told the conductor to allow them aboard. Christmas Day of 1848 found them safe in Philadelphia. An abolitionist gave them shelter in a home.

6Across the Ocean to Safety. Three weeks in Philadelphia came to an end, and the Crafts moved on to Boston, in Massachusetts. Cabinetmaking became William's work again. Ellen took up sewing as a seamstress. For a time, their days were good. The calm did not hold. Congress, in 1850, passed the Fugitive Slave Act. Helping a fugitive became a crime, and free states were not exempt. An officer of the law could earn a large reward. The reward came from catching escapees and sending them back to enslavers. The Underground Railroad. Once Philadelphia was reached, how did the Crafts know the next step? A network for messages and travel gave them direction. People called it the Underground Railroad. The name sounds like a subway. There were no tracks. Nothing about it was under the ground. It was a web of escape paths and safe houses. The people who ran it helped escapees reach freedom. Paths crossed the free states of the North and continued into Canada. Abolitionists watched for Black travelers arriving from the South into a free state. Shelter, food, and directions then guided the newcomers onward. Two bounty hunters came to Boston from Georgia. Their names were Willis Hughes and John Knight. Money was their aim. They planned to carry the Crafts back to Georgia. Boston's people fought them hard. The city knew the Crafts' journey and how brave it had been. Residents warned William and Ellen. They also harassed the hunters. Friends hid the frightened couple while the hunt went on. A life of fear was more than they could accept. December 1850 opened a new journey. This time the destination was England. The Bloodhound Law. The Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 set a fine of 1,000 dollars. That was a huge amount then. The fine fell on anyone who helped an enslaved person escape. A payment called a bounty waited for the person who brought an enslaved captive back to a Southern enslaver. People named the act the Bloodhound Law. Hunters used bloodhound dogs to follow people who fled. The act was a federal law, so free states felt it along with slave states. Many officials in free states who opposed slavery refused to obey. They would not actively chase escapees. They would not chase the people who helped them. A poster in Boston warned Black residents. Under the new act, a person could be seized with no fair trial and forced into slavery.

7The Long Trip Home. West London became the Crafts' home. Five children were born there. Across Great Britain, they gave talks against slavery. William put their escape into a book in 1860. Teaching became one way they supported the family. They also kept a boarding house. They ran a business as well. Slavery in the United States had already been ended for several years when 1870 arrived. The Crafts went back to the country of their birth. A farm outside Savannah, Georgia, became theirs. They also opened two schools for Black people. Freedom from slavery did not end the fight against an unfair society. A white terrorist group, the Ku Klux Klan, burned those schools. Another school opened in 1873. This one stood in Woodville, Georgia. Anger from white people, and harassment by them, forced the school to shut. The farm was lost next. No bank would lend the money the land required. In 1890 the Crafts moved into their daughter's home. They stayed with her until death. What they had wanted most, they gained. They raised a family that slavery could not split. They loved each other. They lived out their years side by side. Glossary. Abolitionists are people who worked to make slavery against the law. Escapees are people who have gotten free from something. Bounty hunters follow others and seize them in exchange for a reward. A fugitive is a person running from something, often from officers of the law. Harassment means treating people in a way they do not welcome, often through pressure or fear. Complexion is the color and look of the skin on a face. A conductor takes tickets from riders on public transportation. To harbor someone is to shelter that person, or to hide that person. Segregated means held apart because of a group difference, such as race. Disguised means changed one's looks in order to seem like someone else. Vouched means stated that something was true, or spoke up for another person's good character. Enslaved means held in slavery, owned by another person, or forced to work for that person.

4. A Jail Cell Full of China Tales

1This book starts with a story told in a prison. Then it describes a far land called Cathay and a trade road. Next, Mongol fighters take China. Then the book follows Marco Polo and his family. A long trek toward China comes after that. His years inside China come next. Then the family heads home. War and a prison cell follow. The book asks if his tales were truth or lies. A word list and a topic list come last. A prison cell held a man in 1298. His name was Marco Polo. The cell was in Genoa, Italy. His thoughts turned to the remarkable life behind him. As a young man, Marco left Italy behind. Italy was the land of his birth. The places he reached were far away. Great adventures filled more than 20 years of his life. After he came home, he was held as a hostage. Two Italian cities were at war. One city was Genoa. The other was his home city, Venice. The name Venice sounds like VEN-is. A man in the same prison became his friend. That man was a writer named Rustichello. The name sounds like rus-ti-KAY-loh. Rustichello said he had heard talk about Marco. The talk said Marco had been to Cathay. The talk said Marco had seen many amazing things. People in Italy used the name Cathay for China. People in other parts of Europe used it too. The name sounds like ka-THAY. China was a mysterious land. Few people knew much about that land. Marco said that yes, he had been to Cathay. He asked if Rustichello wanted the story. Rustichello nodded. He said that he did want it. Marco leaned back. He began telling about his fantastic journey. Month after month, he told one story and then another. Rustichello kept a pen in his hand. He wrote down every word. He told Marco the stories would make a wonderful book.

2An engraving shows Marco Polo. Marco was not the first European to see Cathay. A few travelers had reached it before him. Those travelers never put out popular books about their trips. That is why the Asian land stayed little known. Even so, traders had carried Chinese goods for hundreds of years. The goods went to Europe. They also went to other parts of the world. The traders came from distant lands. People in Europe had wanted Chinese things for a long time. They wanted beautiful pottery. They wanted carved jade. They wanted silk. Silk is a beautiful cloth with a shine. Workers make it from silkworm cocoons. Before the ad 500s, the silk method stayed inside China. Ancient Romans valued silk at a very high price. Their time was around ad 100. They would trade gold for silk. The gold had to weigh the same as the silk. A great share of the China trade used one long path. The path ran from east to west across the continent of Asia. It was really several paths joined together. About 4,000 miles lay along it, which is 6,400 km. The path went through deserts. It crossed mountain ranges. For centuries, camel caravans used it like a highway. A caravan is a long line of camels loaded with goods. The caravans hauled many valuable things. From Europe they carried gold toward China. Other western lands sent goods on those same lines. The loads included ivory. They included wool rugs. They included precious stones. They included other wares. On the way back, the caravans hauled Chinese goods. Those goods went to people in Europe. They also went to other parts of the West. Silk was only one item among many from China. It was probably the item people wanted most. That is why the caravan path received a special name. People called it the Silk Road. A picture shows a silk pillow made in modern times.

3People set up the Silk Road in about 200 bc. At that time a dynasty ruled China. A dynasty is a line of rulers from one family or one group. This dynasty was called the Han. The name sounds like HAHN. In later centuries, travel on the Silk Road rose and fell. Sometimes the trip turned dangerous. Warring groups caused the danger. Bandits caused it too. When danger rose, few caravans dared to use the route. In ad 907, the road fell into a serious decline. In the early 1200s, danger on the road grew even larger. The Mongols were the people who spread out then. They left their home region of Mongolia. Mongolia sits on the Asian steppe. Steppe means grassland. The Mongols began conquests across Asia. They were fierce warriors. They showed enemies little mercy. Whole cities were sometimes wiped out by Mongol armies. They killed every person in those cities. One picture of an Asian battle is titled Fighting with the Mongols. A man named Timujin led the Mongols. In 1206, his people gave him a new name. They proclaimed him Genghis Khan. The name sounds like JENGgihs KAHN. The name meant Universal Ruler. Later ages remember him by that name. Genghis Khan took over a huge area. Later Mongol rulers took more land. People called that huge area the Mongol Empire. A picture shows Genghis Khan. Genghis Khan wanted China inside his empire. He died in 1227. Death came before he could finish that plan. His grandson finished the plan for him. The grandson's name was Kublai Khan. Kublai took northern China in 1264. Then he took the rest of China. In 1279 he began the Yuan dynasty. The name sounds like yoo-WAHN. Once the Mongols held Asia firmly, peace came back. Camel caravans could use the Silk Road safely again. Safety returned even before Kublai finished taking China. A picture shows Kublai Khan.

4A map shows the Mongol Empire around the year 1260. Japan is on the map. Korea is on the map. Karakorum is marked as the capital of the empire of Genghis Khan. The China Sea is marked. The Indian Ocean is marked. Mongolia is marked. Cambaluc, also called Beijing, sits in China. Tibet is marked. China is marked. Lake Baykal is marked. Lake Balkhash is marked. India is marked. Siberia is marked. The Golden Horde is marked. The Aral Sea is marked. Moscow is marked. The Caspian Sea is marked. Baghdad is marked. Arabia is marked. The Black Sea is marked. Africa is marked. The birth year of Marco Polo was 1254. Kublai Khan's rule over northern China began only ten years later. The city of his birth was Venice. Venice is a city in northern Italy. The city had grown rich through trade. The trade was with lands far away. Marco's father was named Nicolo. His uncle was named Maffeo. Both men were merchants. When Marco was only a baby, the two older Polos left home. They left on a trading trip. Marco's mother stayed in Venice. She raised Marco by herself. She probably made sure he received a usual education. Sons of merchant families got that kind of schooling. The boy most likely learned reading. He learned writing. He learned arithmetic. He learned about money from other lands. He may also have had lessons about a cargo ship. The lessons would have covered how to handle one.

5A picture shows the city of Venice in Italy. Marco lost his mother at age 13. An aunt then cared for him. An uncle cared for him too. The family surely asked when the travelers might return. They wondered if Nicolo would ever return. They wondered the same thing about Uncle Maffeo. Venice saw Nicolo and Maffeo Polo again in 1269. They had been away about 14 years. They explained a surprise about the trip. China itself had been the surprise end of their trip. In China they met Kublai Khan. The great Mongol ruler treated them very well. He asked them to come back. Almost right away, Nicolo and Maffeo started getting ready. They would go to China again. This time they chose to take Marco along. Before leaving, the Polo brothers gathered letters for Kublai Khan. They gathered gifts too. The new pope supplied those letters and gifts. The pope's name was Gregory X. On the first trip, the brothers had told Kublai about the Christian religion. The Mongol ruler grew very interested in Christianity. He wanted the brothers to return with missionaries. He also asked for information. Late in 1271, Marco left Venice with his father. His uncle went too. Marco was 17 years old. This was the family's second trip to China. Two missionaries traveled with the group. Pope Gregory had chosen those missionaries. Hormuz was the port they planned to sail from on the way to China. Hormuz is in the country of Persia. Persia is the land now called Iran. Every ship at Hormuz was built very poorly. So the group chose to go by land. They got camels. They started east. For a large part of the trip, they followed the Silk Road. The journey was very hard. It crossed deserts. It crossed mountains. At times they rode camels. At other times they rode horses. Early on, the missionaries would not go any farther. They turned around. Marco kept going. The two older Polos kept going with him. A picture shows Pope Gregory X, who lived from 1210 to 1276.

6A route map shows the Silk Road of Marco Polo. One line is the way he traveled toward China. Another line is the way he traveled back to Venice. The map marks Venice. It marks Constantinople. It marks Acre. It marks Hormuz, Kerman, and Kashgar. It marks the Gobi Desert. It marks Karakorum. It marks Cambaluc, which people also call Beijing. It marks Amoy. It marks Sumatra. Sri Lanka is on the map. Europe is on the map. Mongolia is on the map. China, Arabia, and Africa are on the map. The China Sea is on the map. The Indian Ocean is on the map. A picture shows the Gobi Desert beside a camel caravan of today. Crossing the Gobi was one of the hardest parts of the journey. The Gobi is a huge desert in western Asia. Most of it is rock. Summer there gets hotter than 45 degrees Celsius, or 113°F. Winter cold drops to -40°C (-40°F). Marco and his companions felt glad once the Gobi lay behind them. By then they had entered China. Three and a half years of travel lay behind the Polos. Kublai Khan's court was the place they finally entered. The Mongol ruler gave them a warm greeting. After they had rested, they went with him to the capital. The capital was called Cambaluc. People also called it Ta-tu. Today that city is Beijing. In the capital, Marco stared at the palace of Kublai Khan. Its size amazed him. Its beauty amazed him. He said no palace anywhere had ever been greater.

7A picture shows Marco Polo on his knees before Kublai Khan. While Kublai ruled, blue and white porcelain grew more refined. The quality impressed people in Europe. The Dutch were impressed most of all. Written language came into wider use. Tibetan Buddhism grew strong in those years. Figures such as Guanyin stand for that faith. Soon the Polos held posts that carried real power, given by Kublai Khan. Those posts let them grow rich. Kublai did not like putting Chinese people in his government. He and the other Mongols treated the Chinese as lesser people. Mongols held every top government job. Foreigners from other lands held those jobs too. Marco joined an important government group. People called it the Privy Council. For three years he served as a high tax official. His city was Yangzhou. The name sounds like yang-JOE. As he moved among China's people, Marco watched them closely. Hatred of the Mongol rulers was plain among the Chinese. He said the people felt they were nothing more than slaves. Kublai Khan did not care about that deep sadness. The other Mongols did not care either. They felt sure of their power.

8China kept surprising Marco. So did its culture. In that age, China was further along than the lands of Europe. China was richer too. Marco talked about several things above the rest. One was a mail system. Runners carried the messages. Riders on horses carried them too. Paper money impressed him even more. He watched people in China use it. In that age, Europe's only money was coins. A government can give plain paper the worth of silver. It can give that paper the worth of gold. Doing so shows the power of the government. China's rulers simply announced that their paper bills had worth. Nearly all paper money works in that way today. A picture shows Chinese paper money from modern times. Marco was also surprised by a fuel. People burned stones that burned the way logs burn. They used those stones to make heat. The stones were coal. Coal was easy to find in Europe. People in Europe had not yet learned its use. Home called to the Polos once 17 years in China had passed. They had gathered a fortune. Part of it was gold. Part of it was jewels. Part of it was other treasure. Kublai Khan was then in his mid-70s. The Polos feared he might die soon. If he died, the next ruler might refuse to let them leave. That ruler might keep their wealth. Kublai liked the Polos. He did not want them to leave. At last he said they could go. First they had to do him a favor. He asked them to take a Mongol princess to Persia. Marriage to that land's Mongol ruler was her purpose. The Polos said yes. In 1292 they left for Persia by ship. The princess sailed with them. After they brought her there, they went on toward home. Part of that last trip was by land. Part of it was by sea. In 1295 they reached Venice. They had been away for 24 years. Marco told about Chinese ships that had four masts. A crew of 300 people worked each ship. Those ships were more advanced than ships in Europe.

9A small painting shows Venice in the late 1200s. Marco Polo reached home at a bad moment. Venice was in a contest with Genoa. Genoa was a rival city in Italy. Both cities wanted control of the Mediterranean Sea. War started between them. Marco was then in his early 40s. Even so, he joined the navy of Venice. Officers put him in charge of a war galley. A galley is a ship that many people row. Genoa beat Venice in the war of 1298. Genoa took about 7,000 prisoners. Marco was among them. Guards put him in a prison in Genoa. The writer Rustichello met him in that prison. That writer appears at the start of this book. Marco and the other men from Venice stayed in prison for a year. By the time they got out, Rustichello had finished a large task. He had written down every China tale Marco told. He was about to make the name Marco Polo famous. Marco's account of his China years first appeared in 1298. He was still in prison at that time. Europe did not yet have printing. Every copy of the book was written by hand. The book came out in several languages. It also came out under several titles. One title is The Travels of Marco Polo. People use that title today. Marco's memoir caused a sensation. He became well known across Europe. People called him Il Milione. In Italian, that name means about this. One meaning made him a man with a million stories. Some hearers said the name meant something else. Other people heard the name as a man with a million lies. Most readers treated the book as a pile of tall tales. They would not accept one idea. They would not accept that China was so far ahead of Europe.

10A small painting comes from one of the many copies of Marco's book. The copies describe wonders he said he saw in China. Marco Polo and Kublai Khan are shown trading in this scene. The Great Wall of China sits at the center of a later argument. Even now, some people doubt the book. Most historians think it is a true report of his travels. Other historians do not agree. They say he probably traveled no farther than Persia. In Persia he could have learned China's wonders from someone else. Persia's Mongol rulers could have told him. Why do some people still say Marco Polo lied? His book leaves out things that seem hard to miss. He never writes about drinking tea. He never writes about Chinese writing. He never writes about the Great Wall of China. The doubters also look at Chinese records from the 1200s. Those records never mention the Polo family. Marco Polo always swore that his words were true. In 1324 he lay near death. He was 70 years old. A priest came to see him. The priest urged Marco to save his soul. He wanted Marco to say the whole book was lies. Marco refused. He answered that he had shared less than half of what he saw.

11Ancient describes something that comes from long ago. Astonished means very surprised. Authority means power to make laws. It also means power to give orders. Caravans are lines of vehicles or animals moving over land. Conquests are acts of entering other lands and then ruling them. A dynasty is a group of relatives who rule for many years. An empire is a nation that rules lands it has conquered. Famous means well known. Foreigners are visitors who come from another land. Journeys are long trips. A memoir retells what one person lived through. Merchants are people who trade goods. They may also sell goods. Mysterious means strange and hard to understand. A steppe is a wide stretch of dry land. Trees do not grow there. Topics in this book include Genghis Khan. They include Kublai Khan. China, also called Cathay, is a topic. Beijing is a topic. Yangzhou is a topic. Christianity is a topic. The Mongols are a topic. The Han line of rulers is a topic. The Yuan line of rulers is a topic. Marco Polo is a topic. Maffeo Polo is a topic. Nicolo Polo is a topic. Europe is a topic. The Gobi Desert is a topic. The Romans are a topic. Pope Gregory X is a topic. Rustichello is a topic. Hormuz is a topic. The Silk Road is a topic. Iran, also called Persia, is a topic. Timujin is a topic. Genoa is a topic. Venice is a topic.

5. A Leader Who Would Not Quit

1A map shows German domination of Europe in 1940. On August 19, 1941, Winston Churchill stood outside his office and greeted a crowd. He was prime minister of Great Britain. A meeting with King George VI came next. In October 1941 he spoke at Harrow, the school he had attended as a boy. A dark time faced the nation. World War II was being fought. Most of Western Europe had been conquered by Germany. Britain stood alone against German power. Danger did not daunt him. Victory, whatever the cost, was the only goal he would accept for Britain. He told the listeners never to give in. He said never, and he said it three times more. Those words guided his whole life. He did not give in to the enemies of Great Britain. He did not give in to political opponents. He did not give in to his own personal challenges.

2Birth came for Winston Leonard Spencer Churchill on November 30, 1874. The place was a family estate near Oxford, England. An aristocratic family was his start, with a long history of government service and military service. Randolph Churchill, his father, stood out in conservative politics. Jennie Jerome, his mother, came from America. At age 20 he became a cavalry officer. School was a struggle when he was a boy. Low grades in some classes kept him out of Oxford. They kept him out of Cambridge University. Those were the best universities in England. Sandhurst, the Royal Military Academy, took him instead. Graduation in 1894 made him a cavalry officer. Duty then sent the young officer to India, an important part of Britain's colonial empire. While there, he published a book on the Mamunds revolt against British rule. The revolt was in a northwest province of India. Many nonfiction books would follow that first one. The army was behind him in 1899. Writing for the London Morning Post came next. South Africa was his assignment. He reported on the Boer War. Descendants of Dutch settlers, called Boers, were rebelling against British rule. Boer soldiers soon ambushed an armored train, not long after his arrival. Churchill was aboard with more than one hundred British troops. Capture followed. Churchill and several dozen British soldiers were imprisoned. He refused to give up. A night in December was when he climbed the prison wall and got away. Nine days of evasion followed. Then he fled to freedom. Home in 1900, he was a British national hero. Louis Botha, the man who had captured him, later led what is now South Africa as its first prime minister.

3Two of Churchill's paintings appear on the page. Inspired writing came from him very quickly. Great energy often filled his work. Forty-three books were the lifetime total. In his forties he took up art and pursued it with equal energy. More than five hundred paintings were made across forty-eight years. Terrible depressions often followed the bursts of creative energy. He called those depressions my black dog. The black dog returned many times in his life. Away from depression, he had a reputation for wit. The wit could bite. He spoke of a political opponent, Clement Attlee, as a modest man whose life offered plenty to be modest about. Ambition marked his political career. The highest levels of government were where he wanted to work. Parliament elected him soon after the 1900 return from South Africa. Five years of service followed. In 1908 he married Clementine Hozier, a young aristocratic woman. Five children would be born to them. Important government posts filled the years before 1911, when he was picked to lead the Royal Navy. World War I ran from 1914 to 1918. In those years he urged an attack plan in Turkey. Great Britain and its allies suffered a major defeat because of that plan. The navy post was lost. To repair his reputation, he rejoined the army. He led troops who were fighting the Germans in France. A picture shows him with his wife, Clementine, in 1914.

4One year before the war ended, he returned to the government. Weapons production was put in his charge. Help in developing the first combat tanks was part of that work. After the war he served on and off in Parliament. High office was denied by one prime minister after another. They did not agree with his thinking on many important issues. He opposed independence for India from the British Empire. British rule, in his view, was the better path for India. In the 1930s he argued that Britain should expand its military. Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party had come to power in Germany. The argument did not succeed. His fears about Nazi Germany were well founded. Hitler strengthened Germany's military. An alliance with Italy and Japan was formed. It was called the Axis. Demand followed demand for more territory in Europe. In 1938 Hitler threatened to invade Czechoslovakia. Britain's prime minister, Neville Chamberlain, flew to Germany. A deal gave Germany part of Czechoslovakia's territory. Peace was the promised exchange. Back in Britain, Chamberlain said he believed the result was peace for our time. A picture shows him in the late 1930s, when his attempt to avoid war with Germany did not succeed. Churchill opposed the deal in public. In a speech before Parliament he said Chamberlain had been offered war or dishonor. Dishonor was the choice, Churchill said, and war would still come. Six months later Germany broke the agreement. The rest of Czechoslovakia was seized. In September 1939 Germany invaded Poland. World War II was ignited. The first months went badly for Britain. Chamberlain resigned as prime minister. On May 10, 1940, King George VI named Churchill to replace him. Churchill was the man who had long argued for a larger military.

5Three days later he addressed Parliament. He warned that hard days were coming. He said he had nothing to offer but blood, toil, tears, and sweat. Those serious words soon became real. German planes began bombing in July. The attacks lasted nearly four months. The period is called the Battle of Britain. Airfields were hit. Factories were hit. Ports were hit. In time, London was hit. A picture shows Churchill inspecting London damage after a German air raid in 1940. Hitler wanted to invade England. The Royal Air Force, the RAF, stood in the way. Crossing the English Channel was impossible for the German navy while the RAF could still fight. England's skies filled day after day with RAF pilots against German fighter planes and bombers. Terrible losses hit the RAF. Its ability to fight was never destroyed. Hitler had to call off the invasion. Churchill thanked the RAF fighter pilots for the nation. He said that never before had so many people owed so much to so few. A 1942 picture shows a meeting with Franklin Delano Roosevelt, president of the United States. Over the years the two formed a close relationship. Churchill asked for help. Military supplies went from the United States to Britain. Ships were included. Tanks were included. Supplies also began to reach the Soviet Union. A German invasion of Russia in June 1941 had thrust the Soviet Union into the war. Japan struck the United States naval base in Hawaii on December 7, 1941. The United States entered the war. Britain entered the Allies. The United States entered. The Soviet Union entered. Other foes of the Axis entered too. Throughout the war, Churchill inspired his nation. Long hours were spent in an underground command center. Speeches rallied the people. He visited parts of London that bombs had damaged. He never backed down.

6The war's direction began to change late in 1942. November saw the German army driven from North Africa by the Allies. At the same time, Germany faced the Soviet army on the eastern side of the war. Allied bombers pounded German targets. Joseph Stalin, the Soviet leader, pressed Roosevelt and Churchill for an attack from the west. They finally did. June 6, 1944, is called D-Day. A huge Allied force came ashore that day on France's coast. Nazi control of France ended in August, when Allied forces freed the country. On May 7, 1945, Germany surrendered at last. Churchill told a London crowd that the victory was theirs. He called it a victory for the cause of freedom in every land. President Roosevelt was already dead when Germany went down to defeat. A stroke had killed him the month before. Japan surrendered four months later. The second world war had ended at last. Widespread rejoicing was mixed with reflection on the terrible costs. Deaths around the world numbered more than 40 million. A picture shows Churchill giving the V for victory sign while Europe's war ended in celebration. One of his most famous wartime speeches came on June 4, 1940. French and British forces in France had just suffered a crushing defeat from the German military. The mood across the country was grim. He said Britain would not weaken and would not fail. He said the effort would go on to the end. He said Britain would fight in France. He said Britain would fight on the seas and oceans. He said confidence and strength in the air would grow. He said the island would be defended, whatever the cost. He said Britain would fight on the beaches and on the landing grounds. Fields would be a battleground, he said. Streets would be too. He said Britain would fight in the hills. He said Britain would never surrender. The speech helped unite the country. People grew more willing to continue the war effort. War was over, but 1945 brought an unexpected political turn. In July, war-weary Britons rejected Churchill's Conservative Party. They voted the Labor Party into power. He was no longer prime minister. Depression followed. In 1947 another development alarmed him. India won independence from Britain. India's wish to exit the British Empire was something he had said Britain must never accept. The end of that empire was now in sight.

7A picture shows Churchill working on a painting during a 1946 visit to Florida. In 1953, during a last term as prime minister, he received the Nobel Prize for Literature. Ill health forced him to resign from the government in 1955. Writing continued. A History of the English-Speaking Peoples, one of his best-known works, was finished in 1958. Four volumes span many centuries. Caesar's invasion of Britain opens the story. The start of World War I closes it. In 1963 an act of Congress named him an honorary citizen of the United States. He was the first person ever to receive that honor. Few honors came after that one. He died on January 24, 1965. He was ninety. Words in this book have clear meanings. Ambitious means having a strong desire to succeed or to achieve. Politics means activities that have to do with government. Aristocratic describes a society's highest social class, usually wealthy and powerful. Where a parliament exists, the prime minister is usually the person who leads the government. To rally is to inspire or encourage people during hard circumstances. Depressions are periods of unhappiness and hopelessness. An empire is a collection of nations or peoples ruled by one person or one government. Toil is difficult or unpleasant work. Undaunted means unafraid of going on despite dangers or difficulties. A Nobel Prize is one of six yearly prizes. The fields are chemistry, economics, literature, medicine, and physics, or work that advances world peace. Wit is a talent for clever and amusing use of words and ideas. In the United Kingdom, Parliament is the body that makes the laws.

6. A Shoshone Guide on the Western Trail

1A route map follows the Corps of Discovery from 1804 through 1806. St. Louis is the departure point on that map. The Missouri River carries the line away from that town. Farther west, the line meets the Columbia River. Fort Clatsop is marked near the ocean. The Mandan village is marked along the river lands. One line shows the outbound route. Another line shows the inbound route. In 1806, states did not stand west of the Mississippi River. Borders used for states today were not the borders of that western land. The opening years of the 1800s hold this story. A teenager of the Lemhi Shoshone people joined a journey then. That journey was difficult. It was dangerous as well. American history has few trips that were harder. She was the only female traveler in the party. Isolation came with that place in the group. Hunger came on the trail. Illness came too. Severe weather struck the travelers. The terrain was challenging from day to day. A baby needed her care through all of it. Her name was Sacagawea. A common way to say it is sah-kah-gah-WEE-ah. She is one of the famous Native women in the story of the United States. Writers do not spell her name in a single form. Speakers do not all use one pronunciation. Many choose the sound sah-kah-gah-WEE-ah. Some people believe Bird Woman is what the name means. In Shoshone, Boat Launcher is another meaning it may carry.

2A map can show the Louisiana Territory. Fifteen states of today lie inside it. Some of those states lie fully inside. Some lie only partly inside. British land is north of the territory on the map. Oregon Country is on the west side. Spanish land is on the south side. The Atlantic Ocean is on the east side. France sold this land to the United States. The sale year was 1803. People called the land the Louisiana Territory. It sat on the west side of the Mississippi River. The area measured 820,000 square miles. It also measured 2,123,800 square kilometers. The country grew to twice its old size. Native nations already lived on that land. Their history there went back thousands of years. The United States still wanted the land. It wanted to claim the land as its own. Many countries in Europe had wanted land in that way. A team of explorers went because President Thomas Jefferson ordered the trip. The team was named the Corps of Discovery. Corps is said KOR. Meriwether Lewis led the team. He served as a captain in the United States Army. William Clark shared the lead. He served as a second lieutenant. Jefferson ordered a search. The search was for the Northwest Passage. People believed a waterway was there. They believed it linked the Atlantic Ocean to the Pacific Ocean. Some thought of it as a trade route that existed only in imagination. Boats in that picture would travel up the Missouri River. Later those boats would travel down the Columbia River. The team had to learn about the new lands. The team had to build relations with Native nations. Many of those nations lived in the territory. The Corps started on May 14, 1804. The boats left St. Louis. They traveled up the Missouri River. Sacagawea was born in the year 1788. The year 1789 is also possible. Today that birthplace is called Idaho. Her father was a chief. He led the Lemhi Shoshone. Lemhi is said LEM-hy. Nearby Native nations had firearms. Her people had none. Enemies could overpower them for that reason. Fear of the Blackfoot made them move. Fear of the Hidatsa made them move too. They fled to low hills. Those hills sit by the Rocky Mountains. Capture came in the fall of the year 1800. Sacagawea was about twelve. A Hidatsa group took her. The place is now called Montana. She went to live with the Hidatsa. She did not think she would see her own people. About two years later, the Hidatsa sold her. Toussaint Charbonneau was the buyer. Say his name too-SAN sharbuh-NO. He worked as a French-Canadian trapper. He made her his wife. Their home was with the Mandan. It was with the Hidatsa as well. Today that home is called North Dakota.

3Six months on the Missouri River brought Lewis and Clark to Sacagawea's home ground. November 1804 was when the Corps of Discovery built its fort. The fort stood near the Mandan village. Winter lessons came from the Mandan. They also came from the Hidatsa. The lessons were about lands farther west. Horses would be needed later. The Rocky Mountains had to be crossed. Interpreters would be needed too. The captains would meet Native nations and had to speak with them. They heard news of the Shoshone. That was Sacagawea's nation. Shoshone homes sat where the Rockies begin. Horse herds were large among those people. Lewis and Clark chose to hire Charbonneau. They asked that Sacagawea come. Her work would be interpreting. The arrangement was wonderful luck for both sides. An unknown region waited for the captains. Sacagawea already knew the area. She knew the Shoshone language too. For her, the trip meant a return to her homeland. She joined the expedition. No other member was female. She was pregnant when she joined. A son was born before the travelers left. Lewis helped at the birth. The son was named Jean Baptiste. Clark grew fond of the boy on the trip. He used the name Little Pomp. He also used the name Pompey. Long afterward, on the homeward journey, Clark carved his name and the date beside animal carvings on a sandstone rock in present-day Montana. The rock is called Pompeys Pillar today. His carved name is all the physical evidence that remains from the journey. The boy was the youngest person in the Corps of Discovery. A cradleboard on Sacagawea's back carried the baby. She carried him for most of the journey. Hardships hit her the same way they hit the men. Her son stayed alive. He stayed healthy. April 7, 1805, was the day they left the Mandan village. The spring thaw had opened the river. The party had thirty-three people. Sacagawea and the baby were in that count. Two large rowboats carried them. Sails were fitted on the rowboats. Six canoes came along. The territory ahead was new to all of them. It was new to Sacagawea too. May 14 brought a sudden danger. Charbonneau was at the steering place of one large rowboat. A high wind tipped that boat. Journals began to float off. Navigation instruments began to float off. Medicines began to float off. These were the most valuable things the expedition had.

4Those floating items mattered. The group would have faced disaster if those items had been lost. Jean Baptiste stayed on his mother's back. Sacagawea put out one arm. She pulled in almost every item. She was faster than the current. Lewis wrote the story in his journal. He gave her courage equal to any person on the boat. The moment was the accident. He gave her the same determination. She caught most of the light articles. Water had washed them off the boat. She kept them safe. She helped in more ways. She found plants. The plants put important nutrients into the meals. Deer meat was the usual food. Buffalo meat was the usual food too. Lewis was not impressed by Charbonneau. His journal gave the man no particular merit. The Rockies came closer. Sacagawea recognized the ground. It was the place of her kidnapping. The Shoshone could not be far away. Lewis went forward with three others. They went to meet the Shoshone. Clark followed with the rest of the group. He arrived a few days later. The chief made Lewis a guest in the Shoshone village. Sacagawea spoke for Lewis and Clark. The talk was a negotiation for horses. She suddenly hugged the chief. She cried. The chief was her brother. She had just recognized him. Horses were traded at that meeting. The horse count was twenty-nine. The chief received tobacco for them. He received knives. He received beads. He received clothing. September 1, 1805, was the day the expedition left that village. Sacagawea did not stay with her people. She went on with the Corps. The goal was the Pacific Ocean.

5No other stretch was as hard as the rugged Rocky Mountains. Nothing else came close. There was no trail. Snow made the crossing a struggle. Getting lost made it a struggle. So did the search for enough food. Range after range of the Rockies went by. The travelers then understood a hard fact. The Northwest Passage was not there. No link joined the waterways of North America from east to west. Three weeks passed before they could see beyond the mountains. They wanted to ride the rivers again. Canoes were needed. Food was needed. Sacagawea's people had described another nation. The name was Nez Perce. Say it NEZ PURS. That nation lived just to the west of the Rockies. Help could come from them. The Nez Perce gave food to the group. They helped build the canoes. They gave the way to go. November 7, 1805, brought the Corps to where the Columbia River ends. Tides made the river rise. Tides made it fall. The water started to taste of salt. The Pacific Ocean had to be close. The group felt relief. The weather was still terrible. A winter home was needed. Lewis and Clark asked for a vote. The vote would pick the fort site. Every person voted. Sacagawea had a vote. York had a vote. York was a Black man who was enslaved. Clark claimed York as his property. Sacagawea chose a place with wapato roots. The roots could feed the group. The captains accepted her idea. They built Fort Clatsop there. The spot is near present-day Astoria, in Oregon. Snow would block the Rockies until spring. The mountains would be too harsh for travel. Winter went to mapmaking. It also went to notes about the area. Sacagawea is the best-known Native helper of Lewis and Clark. Many other Native people helped. Historians have noted that help. That help hardly ever stopped. Without it, failure would have come to the Corps of Discovery. Corn came from the Mandan. Buffalo meat came from them too. That food lasted through the bitter cold. The place of that winter was North Dakota. The Hidatsa described landmarks on the route. The landmarks told the explorers the track was right. Horses were traded by the Shoshone. Horses were traded by the Salish too. Those horses carried the Corps across the Bitterroot Mountains. Salmon was a gift from the Nez Perce. Camas roots were a gift too. The group had nearly starved once the mountains were behind them. The gifts helped them recover. On the Columbia Plateau, Native communities supplied food that was badly needed. They supplied it on the way out. They supplied it on the way back. The Chinook lived on the Pacific Coast. The Clatsop lived there too. They gave food. They gave information. That information helped the travelers toward home.

6The end of winter sent the expedition away from Fort Clatsop. The return went up the Columbia River. Horses were bought from the Nez Perce on that stretch. The horses were for the Rockies. The two captains later divided the party. Lewis led one part. Clark led the other part. Sacagawea traveled with Clark. Jean Baptiste traveled with him. Charbonneau traveled with him. Their travel was by land. They aimed for the Yellowstone River. Shoshone lands were around them again. Sacagawea recommended a route. Clark accepted it. He wrote that this Native woman had served him greatly. He wrote that she piloted him through the country. She recommended a gap. The gap was in the mountain, and it lay more to the south. He wrote that he would cross that gap. Lewis's party met them again later. The whole expedition then reached the Mandan village again. Parting came on August 17, 1806. Clark's offer was a place for Jean Baptiste in his group. The city would be St. Louis. An education would be arranged. Sacagawea said the boy was too young. She said a year must pass before he could go. Clark later sent a letter to Charbonneau. The letter gave thanks for Sacagawea's service. Clark wrote about the journey's length. He wrote about its danger. He wrote that she deserved a greater reward. The reward at parting was too small. Washington, D.C., greeted Lewis and Clark as heroes. Congress gave extra pay. Each party member received it. Congress also gave land. Charbonneau learned about the rewards. In the fall of 1809 he went to St. Louis. Sacagawea went with him. Jean Baptiste went with him. The boy was four. Clark lived in that city. Jean Baptiste stayed there with Clark. Two years passed. Charbonneau and Sacagawea then left. They joined another expedition. The region is now South Dakota. August 1812 brought a birth. The baby was a daughter named Lisette. Four months after that, Sacagawea died. A fever was the cause. Her age was about twenty-five. Summer of the following year, a clerk from the fort carried Lisette into St. Louis. She joined Clark. She joined Jean Baptiste. Clark became legal guardian for both children. His adoption of them seems to come from real respect. The respect was for their mother. Later, white control of Native children turned into a tool. The tool pushed Native people away from their culture. In the closing years of the 1800s, boarding schools stood across the country. The government backed those schools. The schools separated Native children from parents by force. A child's own language was forbidden. A child's religion was forbidden. Traditional clothing was forbidden. Traditional hairstyles were forbidden. Anglo American names were forced on the children. As grown people, many went back to their homes. Life there was often a struggle. Family ties were hard to rebuild. Reconnecting with communities was hard.

7American history includes an important role for Sacagawea. Her story is still sad. Her story is still complicated. The expedition of Lewis and Clark succeeded. That success laid ground for settlers. The settlers came in huge numbers. They invaded Native lands. Those lands were west of the Mississippi River. Conflict followed. War came at last. It was war between many Native nations and the government of the United States. Traditional ways of Native life were disrupted. Many Native people were forced onto reservations. A dollar coin of the United States shows Sacagawea. People of her time could not see the decades ahead. They could not know the world would change so much. She was strong. She was brave. She made the best of each situation she met. People still remember her for those reasons. People still honor her. A time line can hold her dates. She reached the Pacific Ocean in January 1806. She died on December 20, 1812. She was around twenty-five. The place was Fort Manuel. It is in present-day South Dakota. Birth came in 1788 or 1789. The county was Lemhi County, in Idaho. Departure of the Corps of Discovery from the Mandan village came on April 7, 1805. She was back at that same village on August 17, 1806. In 1800, a Hidatsa group kidnapped her. A few words help the story. The Corps of Discovery was an army unit of the United States. Meriwether Lewis and William Clark led it. From 1804 to 1806 it explored land gained in the Louisiana Purchase. An expedition is people who travel together on a long trip. Fortitude means strength. It also means endurance. Inhabited means people live in that place. An interpreter turns one language into a different language. Kidnapped means taken by force. Money for a release is the usual aim. The Louisiana Territory was the big region France sold in 1803. The buyer was the United States. The region lay west of the Mississippi. Navigational describes steering. The steering aims at a destination. Negotiations are talks. The talks try to make a formal agreement. The Northwest Passage was a hoped-for trade path across North America. It was not a real path. A waterway is water that ships can travel. A Shoshone person belongs to a Native people of the Northwest.

7. A Special Day for the Circle Number
