1On Pi Day, some students shape their own bodies into the symbol for pi. What kind of pie do you like best? Would you pick apple? Would you pick pumpkin? Would you pick lemon cream? A mathematician might choose a very different favorite. So might someone who uses math in daily work. The word pi sounds just like the word pie. Pi is not a food. A special number carries the name pi. People all over the world use that number to do many interesting things.

2More than two thousand years ago, a Greek mathematician named Archimedes measured circles. His name is said ark-uh-MEE-deez. He was experimenting with shapes when he noticed something strange. He measured the length around a circle, a length called the circumference. Then he measured straight across the circle, through the middle, from one side to the other. That distance is called the diameter. He divided the around-the-circle length by the across-the-circle length. The answer came out the same every time. The size of the circle did not change the answer. A soup can, some string, and a marker or a pen are enough to test the idea. Loop that string once along the can's outer side. Cut it so the two ends just meet. Set one end of the string at the rim of the can and stretch the string across. Mark the far side at the place where the string touches. From that new mark, measure the same across-distance again. Keep measuring until three marks show that across-distance. A short piece of string will still be left after the third mark. That leftover piece is only the bit past three. It is not pi itself. In 1706, a math teacher in England became the first person to call this number pi. His name was William Jones. Pi is also the name of a Greek letter. Mathematicians and teachers now use that letter whenever they talk about the number. William Jones taught math to sailors on navy ships. He also taught math in coffeehouses. A short problem can use the number. Take pi as 3.14. The rule says the distance around a circle equals pi times the distance across. If the distance across is 2 inches, the distance around is 6.28 inches.

3People often write pi as 3.14, which is read three point one four. That writing is only an approximate value. The digits to the right of the decimal point continue without end. No method of figuring the number ever reaches a last digit. More digits always remain to be found. Computers have worked out pi to at least eight quadrillion digits beyond the decimal point. If someone tried to write every one of those digits, the paper would be enormous. That paper would loop around Earth more than a million times. Even then, the digits would not be finished. One student wrote the digits of pi out to 1,120 places. Farm machines show why the number matters. Agricultural sprinklers use long pipes set on wheels so crops get water in an even way. Pi begins with the shape of a circle, and it has many jobs. One job is finding the area of a circle. Area is the amount of space inside a shape that is flat. Landscapers use pi when they need that area. They figure how much lawn one sprinkler can cover. The answer tells them how many sprinklers are required if the whole lawn is to get water evenly.

4Pi can also find the volume of a shape like a ball. It can find the volume of a shape like a tube. Volume is the amount of space inside an object that has three dimensions. Farmers put the number to work in the storage yard. They use it to learn how much grain will fit inside a silo. That result tells them whether they have enough grain to feed their animals. Pi helps with other kinds of math and with science too. Airline pilots use it when they figure the fuel a flight must carry. Astronomers use it while they search for planets beyond our solar system. They also use it when they work out the shape of the universe. Galaxy Messier 81 belongs in this account. Johann Elert Bode was the first person to discover it, in 1774. Memory champions belong here as well. Chao Lu of China holds the world record for memorizing pi. In November 2006 he recited the digits from memory out to 67,890 places. Marc Umile set a record for the United States late in 2006. He memorized 12,887 digits. The next year he beat his own record by repeating 15,314 digits. Chao Lu later received an award for the reciting.

5Computers often have to generate numbers that are random, meaning the numbers cannot be predicted. A computer cannot create numbers that are truly random all by itself. It turns to pi for help. Pi lets the machine produce numbers that seem random to the person using it. Many computer games depend partly on luck. When you play one of those games, the machine is probably using pi. The number stands in for the roll of a pair of dice. March 14, 1879, was Albert Einstein's birthday. That birthday falls on Pi Day. March 14 is Pi Day for mathematicians and for many other people worldwide. The date was chosen because of the way people in the United States write dates. The number of the month comes first. The number of the day comes next. The year comes last. March is the third month, so March 14 can be written as 3-14. Those figures are the opening three digits of pi.

6Some people like to begin the Pi Day party at a very exact moment. They begin at 1:59 in the afternoon and 26 seconds. That clock time marks the first eight digits of pi, which are 3.1415926. Once in every century a special Pi Day arrives. Its date is written 3-14-15. On that day, people can claim a sort of extra credit. They start the party at 9:26 in the morning and 53 seconds. The earlier start adds two further digits, making the string 3.141592653. In 2009 the Congress of the United States voted to name March 14 as National Pi Day. One representative who supported the vote shared a hope. He hoped students would discover a real liking for math. He hoped they would discover a real liking for science. In 2010, students in an elementary school in Florida made a chain for pi. The chain contained 5,904 links. The earliest Pi Day celebration took place in 1988. An American scientist named Larry Shaw arranged a huge gathering at the San Francisco Exploratorium. People marched around a room that was circular. They sang songs, and they ate pie. News stories carried the idea outward. Schools took it up. Museums took it up. Communities took it up. In time, events for Pi Day were held in places all over the world. In 1988 Shaw walked at the front of the parade. Behind him, people carried the digits of pi. Many families and friends celebrate the day together. The favorite way to celebrate is to eat foods built around the pi idea. Many people make pizzas, and they make them round. They bake pies filled with fruit or with cream. Some people own a special pie pan cut in the shape of the Greek letter π. Anyone ready for one more joke can drink pineapple juice and call it pi-neapple juice. If the sweet foods are too much, dinner pies are waiting. Shepherd's pie is one of them. Chicken potpie is another.

7After the meal, some people walk off the food, and some people run it off. They take part in a pi marathon. One course measures 3.14 miles, which is 5.05 kilometers. Another course measures 3.14 kilometers, which is 1.95 miles. Moving in a circle, either walking or running, is another choice. Other people celebrate by decorating a room or by decorating themselves. They use objects that point to pi. They cut out the shape of π and place it on walls and on tables. Some wear T-shirts printed with π. Some wear jewelry made in the shape of π. Mathematicians celebrate this number because it is useful. It is important to a great many projects in math and in science. Everyone else can celebrate Pi Day too. The day is a reminder that science can be fun and that science can be useful. Some people like the number so much that they wear it. A few meanings help a reader. Square units measure area, the space that could cover a shape or a region. To calculate is to work out an answer with mathematics, or to estimate that answer. Circumference is the distance around the outside of a circle. A decimal point is the dot inside a number such as 1.47. Digits to the right of that dot stand for tenths, hundredths, and smaller parts. Diameter means how long a straight line is when it crosses a circle or a sphere through the middle. Digits are the numerals from 0 through 9, and they can be used to write any number. Divided means a number was found by division, by seeing how many times one number fits into another. Pi is a constant value. It stands for the ratio between the circumference of a circle and the diameter of that circle. Volume is the amount of space an object takes up, measured in cubic units.

8. A Step from the Edge of the Sky

1Felix gets ready to set records. The descent is just beginning in one photo. Millions watch live. Some watch on the Internet. Some watch on television. White boots push out past a round capsule door. Earth's curve hangs in the background, grand and wide. Legs of the suit show next. A body shows. A helmet shows. Felix Baumgartner sits on the lip of the door. He unhooks the oxygen tube. He unhooks the helmet strap. He pulls forward. He stands on the capsule's outer step. The camera looks down over the helmet. Earth spreads out below. Viewers hold their breath. He edges forward. A small salute comes next. Then he steps off into space. Four seconds later, the white pressurized suit is only a white dot. Another record has his name on it.

2Birth year: 1969. Birthplace: Salzburg, Austria. High air was what he always loved. Skydiving as a teenager felt like the work he was meant to do. He joined Austria's military. Five years went to its skydiving team. The team did demonstrations. The team also competed. Discipline from those years mattered later. Work ethic from those years mattered later. A 2005 photo was taken at an awards show for stunts. The show is called the World Stunt Awards. In his twenties he trained for BASE jumping. The sport is dangerous. A jumper leaves a cliff or a tall structure. A building can be the structure. A bridge can be the structure. A parachute brings the jumper down. Skydiving practice paid off in 1999. That year brought his first world record. BASE is a set of initials. B is for building. A is for antenna. S is for span, meaning bridges. E is for Earth, meaning cliffs. One photo shows him ready atop Taipei 101. Malaysia was home to the Petronas Towers. No buildings anywhere were taller then. Officials would not allow a jump from them. He dressed like a businessman. A parachute hid in a briefcase. He got in anyway. Window washers use a long boom. He climbed out on it. The drop was 1,479 feet, or 451 meters. The mark held only until 2007. He beat his own mark that year from Taipei 101. Taiwan is the country. That building was the world's tallest at the time. Security was slipped past again. He reached the top. The drop was 1,670 feet, or 509 meters. The new record lasted until 2010.

3Another 1999 record was the lowest BASE jump. On a low jump, timing is everything. A fraction of a second can decide the ending. Open the parachute in time, or hit the ground. Before dawn, he climbed a rope. The rope hung over the right arm of Christ the Redeemer. The statue looks over Rio de Janeiro, in Brazil. He left from the hand. The fall was 95 feet, or 29 meters. That record still stands. The parachute had to open almost at once. The year 2003 brought a flight, not only a fall. He left an airplane over Dover, England. A carbon-fiber wing was on him. The wing was 6 feet long, or 1.8 meters. No engine powered him. No vehicle carried him. He was the first man to cross the English Channel that way. Landing was near Calais, in France. About 14 minutes passed. BASE jumping is extremely dangerous. It is often against the law. The people who ran a site often never gave approval. Sometimes permission is impossible to get. Arrest and criminal charges can follow. Baumgartner faced many charges. He paid fines. He spent time in jail. One jump brought six days in jail. The span he left was called the Bridge of the Americas. Panama is the country. One photo shows a cave jump in Croatia. The depth was 623 feet, or 190 meters. He kept pushing limits. The world's tallest bridge was one launch point. Pitch-black caves were another. Skydiving plus BASE jumping gave him over 2,500 jumps. He once said he did not see himself as a thrill seeker. Planning was the point for him. Every scenario was thought through with his team. The goal had to be met. Nobody was supposed to get hurt.

4A 2010 press conference shows him shaking hands with Joe Kittinger. Kittinger was a friend and a mentor. The biggest jump began as a project in 2005. A sponsor joined him. Science was one aim. Records were the other aim. Speed was one record. Altitude was one record. Free-fall time was one record. Joe Kittinger had set those marks in 1960. Excelsior was the project name. The United States Air Force ran it. Kittinger left a capsule hung from a high-altitude balloon. The fall was 102,800 feet, or 31,333 meters. He wore a pressurized suit. Time in free fall was 4 minutes plus 36 seconds. Speed passed 600 miles each hour. That is 965 kilometers each hour. Then he opened his main parachute. Felix believed he could go higher. He believed he could fall faster. He believed he could fall longer. Easy was not the word for it. Seven years of work followed. The team passed one hundred people. Every piece of gear had to be designed with care. Every step had to be planned down to the last detail. Survival high up needs special gear. Mount Everest's peak is 29,029 feet, or 8,848 meters. Even there, people need oxygen tanks. They need extremely warm clothes. Felix planned to jump from above 120,000 feet, or 36,576 meters. That is more than four times Everest's height. Cold at that height is extreme. Almost no air is there. Almost no air pressure is there. Without protection, liquid in his body would become gas. Death would be nearly instant. Engineers built the suit and the helmet to hold temperature steady. They built them to hold pressure steady. Sensors in the suit collected data during the jump. Scientists and engineers would study that data later. More time in the suit brought a new fear. Closed space began to terrify him. Claustrophobia was the name of it. Panic attacks followed. Breathing failed. He felt he might pass out. The whole project was at risk. He refused to let fear stop it. Doctors worked with him. He learned ways to handle the fear.

5Thin plastic sheets built the balloon. Spread flat, the plastic could blanket close to forty fields made for football. Helium fills it. Filled, it is thin, and taller than fifty-five stories. Rising lowers the outside air pressure. Helium then expands until the balloon looks full. One photo shows the balloon being inflated. The capsule it lifts weighs 2,900 pounds, or 1,315 kilograms. Comfort and safety on the way up are the capsule's job. Four main parts make the capsule. One part is the pressure sphere. One part is the cage. One part is the shell. The last part pairs a base with pads meant to crush on impact. Each part has its own protective job. High altitude can kill. A crash can kill. One photo shows Felix inside the capsule. March 15, 2012, brought the first test with a person aboard. Seven years of work sat behind that day. Tests had been countless. Delays had happened. Launch was from desert ground. Roswell was the nearby town. New Mexico was the state. The ride up lasted 1 hour and 40 minutes. Altitude reached 71,615 feet, or 21,828 meters. Time in free fall was 3 minutes plus 40 seconds. Speed hit 365 miles each hour. That is 587 kilometers each hour. Success was complete. July 25, 2012, was the second test. Altitude before the jump was 97,146 feet, or 29,610 meters. Time in free fall was 3 minutes plus 38 seconds. Speed hit 537 miles each hour. That is 864 kilometers each hour. Overall, the jump worked. Landing damaged the capsule. Repairs were required. The first 1,000 feet of the climb, or 305 meters, is called the Death Zone. The name fits. If balloon or capsule fails there, parachute time runs out before the ground arrives.

6Many people still remember that date. It was October 14 in the year 2012. He boarded the capsule for a last climb. Height reached 128,100 feet, or 39,045 meters. Kittinger's old mark was beaten by 25,300 feet, or 7,711 meters. The door opened with the world watching. Final safety checks came first. He disconnected from the capsule. He stood. He saluted. He jumped. Speed climbed to 834 miles each hour. That is 1,343 kilometers each hour. He beat the pace of sound by over 70 miles each hour. The metric gap is 113 kilometers each hour. Nobody had traveled that fast outside a vehicle. A chart lines up record speeds. The unit is miles in an hour. Zero is the bottom. Marks rise by 100 miles. Bars run from the smallest at the top to the largest at the bottom. A land animal sits on the first bar. The animal is the cheetah. The speed is 70 miles each hour, which is 112 kilometers. A bird sits on the next bar. The bird is the peregrine falcon. The speed is 200 miles each hour, which is 320 kilometers. A boat sits on the next bar. Its name is Spirit of Australia. The speed is 317 miles each hour, which is 511 kilometers. A rail machine sits on the next bar. Its name is Sonic Wind No. 1. The speed is 635 miles each hour, which is 1,017 kilometers. A land machine sits on the next bar. Its name is ThrustSCC. The speed is 763 miles each hour, which is 1,228 kilometers. The longest bar is free fall. The person is Felix Baumgartner. The speed is 834 miles each hour, which is 1,343 kilometers. Numbers along the chart climb by hundreds, from zero up to nine hundred. Team members watch from the control room in one photo. He was in free fall for 4 minutes plus 22 seconds. That is 14 seconds less than Kittinger's time. Near the end he began to spin in a dangerous way. Uncontrolled spin pulls blood away from the body's center. That problem can kill. He straightened out. He opened the parachute. The team cheered. Joe Kittinger was among them. Alan Eustace took one record away from Felix. The date was October 24, 2014. Eustace jumped from 135,890 feet, or 41,419 meters. Alan was 7,790 feet higher than Felix. That is 2,374 meters higher.

7The whole jump took under ten minutes. Two world records broke in that time. Scientists and engineers gained huge amounts of data. Safer high-altitude travel can come from that data. Safer space travel can come from it too. Astronauts benefit. Space tourists benefit. Others benefit. A paragliding accident killed Felix Baumgartner on July 17, 2025. His age was fifty-six. People mourned him. People also celebrated what he had done. Memory keeps his bravery. Memory keeps the record jumps. Memory keeps what he added to the science of flight. Word meanings finish the book. Altitude is height above a surface. Pressurized means inside pressure is higher than the air around it. A BASE jumper leaps from a cliff or from something people built, then comes down by parachute. A building can be the launch. A bridge can be the launch. A sensor notices a signal. It also notices when conditions shift. Then it responds. A capsule is the detachable cabin on a high-altitude balloon. People ride inside it. Their instruments ride inside it too. Skydiving is a sport. A person leaves a flying aircraft and uses a parachute to come down. Claustrophobia is intense fear caused by places that are shut in or tiny. Specialized means made for one particular task. Deploying means moving, spreading, or placing something for a reason. The speed of sound is how fast a sound wave travels. At sea level it is about 750 miles per hour, or 1,200 kilometers per hour. Discipline is the ability to keep working toward a hard goal. Free fall is a fall with nothing slowing the faller down. In a parachute jump, it is the part before the parachute opens.

9. A Sweet That Starts on a Tree

1Ontario, Canada, has a chocolate shop in the opening picture. That shop buys cocoa beans from the people who grow them. Some growers live in Central America. Some growers live in South America. Topics in this book follow a set order. An introduction is first. The origin of the sweet is next. Bean preparation follows. The path from bean to bar follows that. History follows the path. Chocolate in the present day follows history. A closing comes after that. Special words come last. Name a favorite sweet and most people pick chocolate. The love is worldwide. Year by year, no other sweet is eaten in a greater amount. This book answers two questions. One question is where chocolate comes from. The other question is how people make it.

2A surprise waits at the start. Trees are what chocolate grows on. You still cannot pick a finished piece off a branch and eat it. Tree chocolate does not look like candy-bar chocolate. The taste does not match either. The smell does not match either. Cacao is the tree's name. Say it kah-KOW. The tree stays green all year. Its height can pass 40 feet, or 12.2 meters. Heat and wet weather suit it. The equator is where most of them stand. A young tree must be shielded from wind. It must be shielded from sun too. An older tree can take full sun. One map shades the growing lands. Those shaded lands hug the equator. Asia appears on the map. Europe appears. North America appears. Africa appears. Australia appears. South America appears. The Atlantic Ocean appears. The Pacific Ocean appears. The Indian Ocean appears. Home for the cacao tree was the Amazon River region. That region is in South America. Later the tree reached other South American places. It also reached Central America. It also reached Mexico. People carried it farther. Africa received it in 1870. Western Africa now grows more than two-thirds of all cacao. Brazil ranks next as a producer. Large farms hold most cacao trees today. Leaves are big. Leaves are smooth. Leaves are a shiny green. They do not drop off for winter. Small flowers open through the year. A bad smell comes off those flowers. Flies follow the smell. The flies pollinate the trees. A few flowers become pods. Most flowers never do. About one flower out of ten becomes a pod. Sometimes the share is one out of twenty. Pods do not start until a tree is four to five years old. Beans inside the pods are what chocolate is made from. Many trees bloom from their branches. Cacao does not. Its blossoms come out of the trunk.

3All year, pods form on the trunk. They also form on the bigger branches. Trimming branches helps workers get the largest pod crop. Green is the color of a young pod. Gold or red-brown is the color of a ripe one. Picking waits until the pod is ripe, or mature. Cacao roots lie near the soil surface. A step can hurt them. Workers stay off the roots while they pick. Pictures show the pods that hold the beans. Open a pod and the beans show. Step one is getting the pods off the trees. The pod shell is not the useful part. The useful part is the seeds, 20 to 50 in each pod. One kilogram of chocolate, about 2 pounds, takes many beans and much labor. The bean count is about 800. The pod count for those beans is 20 to 40. Gathering comes before opening. A worker opens each pod with a machete, a big blade. Say machete mah-SHET-ee. One hard hit can do it. Sometimes it takes two hits. Skill lets a person open up to 500 pods in an hour. Scooping follows the cut. Brown is what you might expect. Cream is the real color. Soft pulp coats each bean. The candy you know is still a long way off.

4Piles or boxes hold the pulp-coated beans. A cover goes over them. Air touches the beans and the color shifts. Cream gives way to purple. The inside changes as well. Fermentation is the name of that inner change. A week may not be long enough. More than a week is possible. Chocolate taste is still missing. Chocolate smell is still missing. Drying is the next job. Outdoor drying uses big mats in sunlight. Indoor drying uses hot, dry air that pipes blow over the beans. Turning the beans is part of drying. Cloth sacks, large ones, hold the dry beans for the trip to chocolate makers. A picture shows beans spread out to dry once fermentation ends. From fermented dry beans to a finished bar is slow. It is also complex. Cleaning strips off leftover pulp. It strips off pod bits too. Then makers mix bean types. The mix is how they lock in the flavor they want. Roasting follows, and that is what wakes up the chocolate taste. Smell changes at this stage. A chocolate smell starts to rise from the beans. Heat makes the thin shell easy to crack. A machine breaks the shells. Fans carry the shell pieces off. Giant drums at a candy plant are where the roasting happens in one picture.

5Shell off, the meaty center is left. Nib is its name. Crushing the nibs makes them liquid. Molds receive that liquid. Cooling in the molds makes bars. The bars taste bitter. No sugar is in them yet. Pressing comes next. Out comes cocoa butter, the key part, as a yellow liquid. A screen lets that liquid drain. Workers save it for the chocolate people eat. Powder is what the leftover solid becomes after grinding. Dairies receive the powder. Bakeries receive it too. Baked foods get flavor from it. Dairy foods get flavor from it too. Two spellings need a note. English speakers turned cacao into cocoa when the products arrived in their countries. Cacao is still the word for the tree. It is still the word for flowers, pods, and beans. Cocoa is the usual word for things made from the beans.

6Step 4 is mixing. Step 5 is conching. Step 6 is pouring. Step 7 is cooling. Step 8 is wrapping. Historians place the first chocolate use almost 2,000 years back. The place was Mexico and Central America. The drink was called xocoatl. Say it shoh-coh-WAH-tuhl. Roasted cacao beans made the drink. A sip today would not taste like modern chocolate drinks. Bitterness was the main flavor. Coffee is a fair comparison. Europe did not value the beans until one voyage ended. Hernan Cortes was the traveler. He was a Spanish conquistador. His trip had been to the place now called Mexico. Montezuma ruled the Aztecs. Montezuma gave Cortes a bean drink. The Aztecs called it the gods' drink. They said the beans added wisdom. They said the beans added strength. An Aztec man is shown with his chocolate.

7Beans were precious enough to spend like coins. Cortes cared more about that coin use than about drinking them. He set out cacao trees for the beans' money value. Chocolate was not his goal. Growing money on trees was his plan. At first Montezuma welcomed him as a guest. Later Cortes and his soldiers seized the Aztec ruler. Many Aztec people were killed. Gold was what Cortes wanted from the Aztecs. Chocolate was not. He still carried the drink method home. Lands outside the Americas did not take to it yet. Spain later stirred in sugar. Spain stirred in cinnamon. Spain stirred in vanilla. Spain served the cup hot. Nobles wanted it. Rich families wanted it. Spain hid the method from other European lands for almost a hundred years. Colonies in South America and Central America got many Spanish cacao farms. The farms were there so beans would not run short. Enemies of Spain sometimes captured Spanish ships in those years. Cacao beans filled those ships. The captors smashed the beans. They thought the cargo had no use. They did not know the beans' purpose. A common story gives the credit to monks in Spain. They were the people who at last shared the method. Other Europeans learned it. The world changed because of that. Through the 1600s and the 1700s, only luxury buyers had chocolate. Kings and queens had it. Strong church leaders had it. Mills in the 1600s ground beans in large batches. Output rose. Price fell. Someone invented smooth milk chocolate. Popularity rose again. London, England, saw the first chocolate shop in 1657. A steam-powered grinder arrived in the 1700s. Factories could turn out tons of chocolate fast. Ordinary people could pay for it. Many countries now treat chocolate as a favorite sweet. The price stays within reach. Every age group enjoys it with gusto.

8A timeline lines up later and earlier moments. Beside the first chocolate use in Mexico and Central America, the timeline shows 200. Beside money use in those same lands, the timeline shows 900. Cortes reaches Spain with beans. He also reaches Spain with the drink method. A shop in London, England, is the first of its kind. A Frenchman opens it in 1657. The cocoa press appears in 1828. A solid bar goes on sale for the first time in 1847. Milk chocolate is first made and sold by a Swiss man in 1875. The year 1894 is when Milton Hershey founds a company in the United States. The company is the Hershey Chocolate Company. Another invention lets makers put other sweets inside chocolates. Cacao-bean use worldwide passes 4,000,000 metric tons. Newer medical studies find real benefits in eating chocolate. Dark chocolate is the kind linked to those benefits. Milk chocolate is not the kind they point to. Heart disease can be reduced. Blood pressure can be reduced. A few special shops sell nothing but chocolate treats. Factory chocolate today mostly becomes candy. Ice cream gets some of it. Chocolate drinks get some of it. Cakes get some of it. Doughnuts get some of it. Mexico has a sauce called mole, said MOLE-ay, and chocolate is in that sauce.

9Tons of chocolate are eaten around the world every year. Per person, Switzerland eats the most. Plenty of other countries in Europe love it too. A yearly, per-person ranking follows. Do not change this order. Place 1 is Switzerland: 22.4 pounds, which is 10.1 kilograms. Place 2 is Austria: 20.1 pounds, which is 9.1 kilograms. Place 3 is Ireland: 19.5 pounds, which is 8.8 kilograms. Place 4 is Germany: 18.0 pounds, which is 8.2 kilograms. Place 5 is Norway: 17.9 pounds, which is 8.1 kilograms. Place 6 is Denmark: 17.7 pounds, which is 8.0 kilograms. Place 7 is the United Kingdom: 17.5 pounds, which is 7.9 kilograms. Place 8 is Belgium: 13.2 pounds, which is 6.0 kilograms. Place 9 is Australia: 13.0 pounds, which is 5.9 kilograms. Place 10 is Sweden: 12.9 pounds, which is 5.8 kilograms. A world map can sit with that ranking. Cocoa supply is a different map. West Africa sends out more cocoa than any other region. Children do much of the picking there, and that is a sad fact. The 2015 count was above 2 million children. Poverty is widespread there. School is often more than parents can pay for. Farm work takes the place of school for some children. Danger and hard labor are common in that work. One photo shows a young child collecting pods. Another shows Moahe, age nine, drying beans at a cocoa farm. Ivory Coast is where both children are working.

10Big chocolate companies have started to change. They want less dependence on children's work. The deep cause is poverty. Poverty does not yield easily. Daily pay for most West African cocoa farmers is under one dollar. A plain fix exists. Give farmers a higher price for the crop. Small companies already pay that higher price. Their product is called fair-trade chocolate. Families can then earn a living. School becomes possible, and farm work does not have to replace it. The higher bean price raises the shop price. Buyers cover much of that raise. A high price may turn some buyers away from fair-trade bars. Two campaigners spoke up in London in 2006. One was Raphael Agyapong. One was Isaac Owusu. Both come from cocoa-farming families in Ghana. They asked people to support fair-trade chocolate. Pause on your next bite and consider the making of it. Fame outside the first growing lands took a long time. Those lands were Central America and South America, where the trees were first grown and first used. Sugar joined the long, hard process over the years. Milk joined it too. Beans remain the start. Millions of kilograms are eaten worldwide now. No sweet is more popular.

11Try a batch of tasty chocolate brownies. Hot pans and knives need an adult helper. Collect the foods before you start. Butter or margarine: 1 cup. Unsweetened chocolate: 4 squares. Each square weighs 1 ounce. Baker's chocolate is another name for it. Eggs: 4. White sugar: 2 cups. Vanilla extract: 2 teaspoons. All-purpose flour: 1 1/2 cups. Baking powder: 1 teaspoon. Salt: a pinch. Set the oven at 350 degrees Fahrenheit. That equals 180 degrees Celsius. Choose a pan 9 inches by 13 inches, also called a 15-cup pan. Grease it by rubbing fat over the inside. Warm the butter in a pot on the stove. Keep the burner at medium. Once the butter is liquid, move the pot off the burner. Stir chocolate into it until the chocolate is liquid and blended. Drop in a single egg and stir hard. Do that again until all four eggs are in. Sugar goes in after the eggs. Vanilla goes in after the eggs. Stir to a smooth mix. A second bowl is for the dry items. Those items are flour, baking powder, and salt. Stir them together. Tip the wet mix, butter and sugar included, onto the dry flour. Stir gently. Stop when every bit of flour is wet. Scrape the batter into the pan. Smooth the top so it is even. Leave the pan in the oven for 25 to 30 minutes. Look for the edges starting to shrink back from the pan walls. Cooling happens in the pan. Cutting waits until the brownies are cool. Twelve brownies come from this batch. Meanings of special words finish the book. Cacao names the tree chocolate comes from. Conching names the smoothing step for a chocolate mix. A conquistador was a sixteenth-century man who seized American lands for Spain. To consume is to eat something or to buy it. Fermentation is a natural shift that shows up in many foods and in many plants. Ingredients are the separate foods a recipe uses. A machete is a knife that is long and thick. A mill is a grinding machine powered by animals, by wind, or by steam. Mole is a hot-spiced sauce from Mexico that uses chile plus strong chocolate.

10. A Tiny Drifter Feeds the Whole Sea

1This book moves through these parts. A speaker introduces itself first. The food web comes next. Life in the sunlit zone follows. The twilight zone comes after that. The midnight zone comes next. A return to the top closes the story. Word meanings come at the end. The ocean is a huge feast. It feeds everything in it. It feeds many land animals too, including humans. When you think of the ocean food web, you might picture a hunt. Great white sharks devour their prey. Enormous blue whales eat tons of krill. Here is a surprise. More than 90 percent of all sea creatures end up being eaten by other sea creatures. That means almost every organism in the ocean ends up as food. Another sea creature eats it at some point. Some little organisms almost always get eaten. They do not actually eat anything themselves. They are the most microscopic species in the ocean. Even so, they form the center of the ocean food web. Some people might think that role is a raw deal. Being food for everybody else sounds hard. The speaker finds it to be quite a powerful job. No animal on Earth is larger than the blue whale.

2The name for these microscopic phytoplankton is diatoms. Let the speaker introduce itself properly. Phytoplankton is its name. Say FY-tow-plank-ton. It is an alga. An alga is almost like a very tiny plant. Unlike plants, it has no roots. It is free to float around with the ocean currents. It prefers to remain near the surface of the sea. Sunlight is there. It can be found in every ocean on Earth. Like plants, it makes its own food. The process is called photosynthesis. It uses chlorophyll to capture the Sun's energy. It changes nutrients from seawater into food. Chlorophyll makes it green. Chlorophyll makes plants green in the same way. Phytoplankton is so tiny that the color is hard to see. You can see the color only when billions upon billions gather in one place. One cup of seawater can hold thousands of phytoplankton. Phytoplankton photosynthesis does a giant job for the air. It provides Earth's atmosphere with more than half of its oxygen. These tiny living things are also a good indicator of the ocean's health. From space, scientists can see phytoplankton gathered in large groups. They can get information about pollution in the water. They learn this when they see the groups struggling. They learn it when the groups die off. The most important job is still the center of the food web. Phytoplankton feed all ocean life forms. They feed the smallest creature. They feed the largest. A phytoplankton and zooplankton bloom shows up as light streaks. A photo taken from space shows those streaks.

3The food web can be seen in a simple tuna fish sandwich. Tuna are large fish. They eat smaller fish called mackerel. To make 1 kilogram of tuna flesh, the tuna had to eat a lot of mackerel. That mass of mackerel is about 10 kilograms. One kilogram is 2.2 pounds. Ten kilograms is 22 pounds. Those 10 kilograms of mackerel had to eat an even smaller fish. The fish is called herring. The herring mass was 100 kilograms, which is 220 pounds. Those 100 kilograms of herring devoured zooplankton. The zooplankton mass was a full 1,000 kilograms, which is 2,200 pounds. Zooplankton are microscopic animals. They include tiny animals such as krill. Krill look like little shrimp. Zooplankton also include larvae and babies of crabs. They include babies of jellyfish, shrimp, and other fish. To support those 1,000 kilograms of zooplankton, a huge mass of phytoplankton was eaten. That mass was 10,000 kilograms, which is 22,000 pounds. The chain runs in one direction. Tuna eat mackerel. Mackerel eat herring. Herring eat zooplankton. Zooplankton eat phytoplankton. A cross section shows the different zones of the ocean. To show how much life phytoplankton support, the speaker will take you through the ocean. The trip starts at the surface, where phytoplankton live. It goes down to the ocean floor.

4Life in the sunlit zone fills the top of the sea. This zone is called the euphotic zone. Say yoo-FOE-tic. It is the top level of the ocean. It extends about 200 meters down from the surface. That depth is 660 feet. There is lots of sunlight here. Most ocean animal species live in this zone. Humans get almost all their seafood from the euphotic zone. Clams live on shallow ocean floors. Mussels live there. Oysters live there. Lobsters scuttle about in coral reefs. Crabs scuttle among seaweed beds. Most species of fish stay up in the sunlight. Salmon stay there. Tuna, mackerel, cod, and swordfish stay there. There is plenty to eat. There is good light for hunting. The euphotic zone is also home to coral reefs. Those reefs hold most of the ocean's plant and animal species. These areas are fragile. They are beautiful. They are formed by the skeletons of small animals. Those animals are called coral polyps. Sea fans live on the reef. Brain coral lives there. Angelfish, sharks, shellfish, and crabs live there. Together they make the coral reef a colorful and busy place. Anemones are animals that look like beautiful flowering plants. They catch zooplankton with their stinging tentacles. Jellyfish swarm in massive numbers. They attract the sea turtles that love to eat them. Coral reefs also provide shelter for young creatures. Those young will live in the open ocean as adults. In the sunlit zone, the most popular areas are the colorful coral reefs. Humans come to the euphotic zone because coral reefs are so beautiful. They take thousands of tons of fish. Some fish are for food. Some are for pets in tropical aquariums. This human activity threatens the well-being of coral reefs. Pollution threatens them too. Pollution kills coral polyps. Boat motors break them. Divers crush them. All the other reef life suffers too after the corals die. One nondestructive way to see ocean life in the euphotic zone is a tide pool. A tide pool is a small pool of water. It remains on land when the tide goes out. Here you can find mussels. You can find sea stars, urchins, clams, barnacles, and snails. You may spot a hermit crab. It scurries about in another animal's shell. All of this sea life depends on phytoplankton. The link may be direct. It may be indirect.

5A visit to a tide pool may show a spiny sea urchin. Below the euphotic zone, the water begins to change. It gets darker. It gets colder. It gets heavier. You are now entering the twilight zone. It is also called the disphotic zone. Say dis-FOE-tic. It begins at about 200 meters, which is 656 feet. It goes to a depth of about 1,000 meters, which is 3,280 feet. The pressure in this zone would crush a person. The life forms that live here have adapted to this environment. The twilight zone does not have enough light for photosynthesis. It does not have enough light for plant life. Some animals do make their homes here. Others visit from the euphotic zone. Whales are visitors. Permanent residents include strange-looking hatchet fish. Viperfish live here too. The fish that live here often have huge mouths. The mouths have big, curved teeth. It is too dark to see well. The fish do not actively hunt. They simply hold open their frightening mouths. They wait for something to swim in. Many of them are black. Others are dark red. Those colors blend in with the dark water. Both the euphotic zone and the disphotic zone are home to octopuses. Squid live here as well. The famous giant squid is one of them. A living giant squid was not seen until fairly recent times. Few people have seen it at the surface. A handful of scientists have seen it in the disphotic zone. The giant squid is still mostly a mystery. Many animals in this zone depend on a strange diet. Scientists call it marine snow. Dead phytoplankton and zooplankton get this gentle name. When phytoplankton die, their bodies drift slowly down. They pass through the ocean layers. They go to the bottom of the ocean. The drift is like snow falling through the air. So even where phytoplankton do not live, they are eaten.

6The midnight zone is a totally dark region of the ocean. It contains 90 percent of the ocean's water. It holds little life. This zone is also called the aphotic zone. Say ay-FOE-tic. It extends from 1,000 to 5,000 meters and below. That range is 3,280 to 16,404 feet. The pressure is so great here that it can crush almost anything. It can crush most submarines. The water is very dark. The water is very cold. If you look closely, there is some life in the midnight zone. Many of the tiny animals that live here have glowing bodies. The lantern fish is one. The light comes from a special process. The process is called bioluminescence. Fireflies make light by this same process. Jellyfish are bioluminescent in this zone. Squid are too. Fish are too. Even bacteria are too. There is no sunlight. This light makes it possible for animals to see. It lets them communicate with each other. The light also helps them find mates. It helps them find food. Tiny bioluminescent animals glow in the pitch-black depths. Some oceanographers divide the midnight zone into two more zones. One is the abyssal zone. The other is ocean trenches. No light reaches the abyssal zone. It covers much of the ocean floor. That floor includes vast plains. It includes mountains, valleys, and canyons. Ocean trenches are found along faults. Large plates of the Earth's crust come together there. The colliding plates create canyons and cracks. Those cracks can be up to 10,000 meters deep, which is 32,808 feet. You would think that nothing could survive at the bottom of a trench. The darkness is extreme. The cold is extreme. The pressure is extreme. Openings at the bottom of the trenches spew hot water. They spew minerals from deep within the Earth. Animals living in this zone rely on the warmth. They rely on the nutrients. Special kinds of bacteria can use these nutrients. They use them in the same way that phytoplankton use sunlight. Tube worms can be found around the openings. Shrimp can be found there. Giant clams can be found there. They feed on these bacteria. The openings are called chimneys. Discovery of these chimneys came only recently. Only a few submarines have been built strong enough for the bottom of a trench. They must withstand the enormous pressure.

7Back on top, the speaker sums up the web. Phytoplankton are only at the top of the ocean. Even so, they are at the center of the food web. They support all other life in the sea. You might enjoy the ocean for the beauty of coral reefs. You might enjoy the mystery of the abyssal zone. You might enjoy some tasty fish and chips. In each case you have phytoplankton to thank. These words help with the book. The euphotic zone is the top ocean zone. It contains almost all of the ocean life. The abyssal zone is the part of the aphotic zone that includes the deep ocean floor. Faults are cracks in Earth's crust along which movement occurs. Anemones are plantlike marine animals. Their tentacles often look like flower petals. Photosynthesis is the process by which plant cells absorb sunlight. They use the Sun's energy to transform water and carbon dioxide into food. The aphotic zone is the bottom ocean zone. It receives no sunlight. Bioluminescence is the light created by a biochemical process within a living thing. It can also mean the emission of that light. Phytoplankton are single-celled algae that live in a body of water. Trenches are cracks in the seafloor. They are long ditches. Chlorophyll is the green substance in plant cells. It absorbs the light energy plants use to make food during photosynthesis. Zooplankton are microscopic animals that live in a body of water. The disphotic zone is the middle ocean zone. It receives very little sunlight. It contains no plants and few animals.

11. Abraham Lincoln: From a Kentucky Cabin to the Presidency

1Washington, DC, is home to the Lincoln Memorial. Americans love this monument deeply. It is among the nation's best-loved monuments. Introduction. The Early Years. Law and Politics. America Divided. The War Years. Glossary. Introduction. Few presidents matter more in the story of the United States than Abraham Lincoln. He led that nation through the Civil War. States in the North fought states in the South. They fought about what the country would become. People call him the Great Emancipator. What he did set enslaved people free. The freedom reached across the South. When the war ended, the states stood as one country again. They have stayed one country ever since. Pictures usually show three things about him. He is tall. He is thin. His face is solemn. People remember him as a common man. His beginnings were humble. He was born in Kentucky, inside a cabin built of logs. Later he became a great lawyer. He became a great speaker. He became a great leader in politics. He spoke about freedom. He spoke about justice. He spoke about bringing all Americans together. Those words were cut into stone. The stone is part of the Lincoln Memorial. Find that memorial in Washington, DC. A picture shows Lincoln in his younger days. What he believed was plain. He would not be held as a slave. He would not act as a master. He said that pair of choices was his idea of democracy.

2The Early Years. February 12, 1809, was the day Abraham Lincoln was born. Thomas Lincoln was his father. Nancy Hanks Lincoln was his mother. Home was a small farm in central Kentucky. The house was a cabin of logs. Later the family shifted to a town nearby. Abe went to school in that town. His older sister Sarah went too. Only short periods in winter were for school. The family left for Indiana when Abe was seven. A better life was their hope. Tom built a new cabin of logs. Two years after that cabin, Nancy grew ill. Then she died. Abe mourned his hard-working mother. Sarah mourned her too. She had been a loving mother. The father soon wed Sarah Bush Johnston. She entered as a widow. Three children came with her. Tom had known her in earlier Kentucky days. Her love made a warm home. Her care did too. Abe lived in that warm home. Sarah lived in it too. Encouragement from her followed Abe while he grew up. He grew into a tall youth. He was awkward. Friends noted his moody quiet. His stories were homey. The stories made people laugh. A cabin on view today is built of logs. Those logs are believed to come from the Kentucky cabin of his birth. Abe's main teacher was himself. He borrowed books from neighbors. He borrowed newspapers from neighbors and travelers. Daniel Boone appeared in pioneer stories he heard. Johnny Appleseed appeared in them too. The stories showed a world past the backwoods. The books showed that too. Days in school were rare. His love of learning was not rare. As a teen he reached 6 feet and 4 inches. That height equals 2 m. At nineteen he traveled on the Mississippi River. The journey ended at New Orleans. New Orleans was a busy port. Black men in chains were a new sight to him. Black women in chains were a new sight. Black children in chains were a new sight. White enslavers bought those people. White enslavers sold them. At twenty-two he settled in New Salem, Illinois. One job was storekeeper. One job was land surveyor. One job was builder. People knew him as a wrestler. They knew his speaking skill. Debates of the New Salem Debating Society showed that skill. In 1832 he ran for a seat. The seat was in the Illinois state legislature. He lost that year. He won two years later. John Todd Stuart was a lawyer. Stuart was a fellow legislator. Stuart urged a course of law study. Books of law became Abe's reading. He passed his exams during March 1837. He joined Stuart's practice. The city was Springfield. The Illinois legislature met in Springfield.

3Law and Politics. Lincoln held one strong belief about people. Each person was important. Wealth did not change that. Privilege did not change it either. He became respected inside the Whig Party. The Whigs wanted a strong government in the center. That government sat in Washington, DC. The Democrats were the other leading party. They wanted each state to control its own affairs. Lincoln was thirty when he met Mary Ann Todd. She became his wife later. The wedding was three years after they met. The year was 1842. Their first son was Robert. He was born the following year. Robert was a toddler when Lincoln won a post. The post sent him to the US Congress. He represented Illinois. Washington, DC, became home for every person in the family. Mary Todd Lincoln, 1846. Lincoln served in Congress as a split grew worse. Northern states and Southern states pulled apart over slavery. Paid workers kept the North running. Factories used that labor. Small farms used it too. Northern people wanted a strong government at the center. States of the North had already banned slavery. Cotton was the crop the South relied on. People named that crop King Cotton. It grew on large plantations. Enslaved people did the labor. Owners kept them as property. Daily life for most of them was very poor. Personal rights were denied. Civil rights were denied. Laws in Southern states allowed slavery. Those same laws protected it. The United States kept growing. Western territories asked to become states. Would a new state be free? Would it allow slavery? Lincoln was against slavery. He represented Illinois in Washington. He believed state laws in the South kept slavery safe there. He still fought so slavery would not spread. The western territories were the places he defended. After two years he went back to Springfield. For the next few years a partner shared his law work. The practice did well. Lincoln was known for honesty. He was known for skill in the law. He was known for wit. He was known for excellent speeches.

4America Divided. Groups that wanted slavery struggled for power. Groups that opposed slavery struggled too. A law from Congress arrived in 1854. Its name was the Kansas-Nebraska Act. Residents of each territory could decide. They might pick a free state. They might pick a slave state. Lincoln felt he had to speak. He spoke so slavery would not spread. He wanted a political office again. He joined a party that was still new. It was the Republican Party. The party opposed slavery. In 1858 the party nominated him for senator. The opponent was Senator Stephen Douglas. The campaign brought a famous set of debates. People know them as the Lincoln-Douglas debates. The country paid attention. Stephen A. Douglas. Lincoln said rights belonged to Black people too. One right was life. One right was liberty. One right was the pursuit of happiness. He said white people had those rights too. Douglas said the Constitution promised equality to white people only. He said each state had its own choice. The state could be slave. The state could be free. Lincoln said slavery had caused a national crisis. He warned with the picture of a house. A house at war with itself cannot remain standing. He did not think the government could endure one condition. It could not stay half slave for good. It could not stay half free for good. Lincoln lost the election for the Senate. The debates still spread his fame. He became popular. That was especially true among Republicans. In 1860 the party selected him as its choice. He would run for president. In that race they called him Honest Abe. They saw a homespun man. He seemed to belong to ordinary people. He stood for equality. He stood for freedom. A beard was new for Lincoln. He first grew it after the win was his. He grew it before he went to live in Washington, DC. A girl who was eleven years old gave the idea. The beard was her suggestion. November brought the result. He won. The North felt joy. The western territories felt joy. The South felt outrage. Inauguration day had not come. Even before it, seven states in the South held a vote. They chose to secede. They would exit the union called the United States of America. Slavery states then set up a government. They gave it a name. The name was the Confederate States of America. President Jefferson Davis was the leader. He got the Confederate states ready to fight a war.

5The War Years. Hope of avoiding war still lived in President Lincoln. Events moved faster than that hope. By April 14, troops of the North had surrendered Fort Sumter. Cannons of South Carolina had fired on the fort before that surrender. The Union hurried to prepare. The Confederacy hurried too. Volunteers were called. Arms were collected. Supplies were collected. The first big fight was at Bull Run. The South's military leaders were better then. They defeated the Union forces. Through the whole war, Lincoln looked for strong leaders. The leaders were for Union troops. General George B. McClellan brought some successes. The year 1862 stopped that progress. Confederate General Robert E. Lee halted the Union troops. Union forces did control New Orleans. They controlled the Mississippi River. Few victories came with that control. The North demanded action. More army plans moved into Lincoln's hands. War moved into a second year. Great numbers of young soldiers died. The losses hit both sides. Many were wounded. Many were missing. A picture is set at Antietam. In it, President Lincoln talks with General McClellan. Both sides suffered terribly there. No fight in the war was bloodier. A new order came in November 1862. McClellan was taken out of command. Strong senators from the Republican Party pressed the president. They wanted a war goal added. The goal was abolition. Abolition would end slavery. They argued that victory required a hard step. They said the fight's cause had to be taken away. Lincoln at last became convinced. As president he could order an end to slavery in the South. A proclamation went into effect on a famous day. That day was January 1, 1863. The proclamation's name was the Emancipation Proclamation. It freed all enslaved people held in the Confederacy. Free Black men had wanted to enlist sooner. They rushed forward after Fort Sumter fell. In the early months they were refused. The proclamation changed the rule. They could join Union forces. Men newly freed from the South could join too. When the Civil War closed, Black men who served as soldiers came to nearly two hundred thousand. They served in the military of the US. One record names Company E. That company belonged to a regiment. The regiment was the 4th. Its title was US Colored Infantry. Part of the company was newly freed men. The other part was Black men who were already free.

6Freedom for Some. Many people who were enslaved received freedom from one order. The order did not free everyone. Its name was the Emancipation Proclamation. It acted on the opening day of January 1863. Freedom was granted inside enemy territory. All enslaved people there were included. Black men who had just been freed got a new chance. The chance was in areas the Confederacy held. They could fight on the side of the Union. The North had a deep need for those soldiers. The order changed the war's main aim as well. That aim became the ending of slavery. Four border states were not included. Delaware was a border state. Maryland was a border state. Kentucky was a border state. Missouri was a border state. Why leave them out? They did hold people in slavery. They never seceded. They had remained in the Union. Lincoln feared what freedom there might cause. Those states might join the Confederacy. He believed the country would then lose the war. The South would be lost too. Ending slavery across every state would then slip away. Enslaved people still in the country had to wait. Two more years passed before they were free. Border States in 1863. A map carries four labels. One label is Union Free State. One label is Union Slave State. One label is Confederate Slave State. One label is Territory. Maryland is shown. Delaware is shown. West Virginia is shown. Missouri is shown. Kentucky is shown. West Virginia has a note beside it. No other state was formed the way it was. It formed by leaving Virginia. Virginia was a Confederate state. The years 1863 and 1865 bracket a slow change. In that span this new Union state brought slavery to an end. Summer of 1863 brought a Union win. The place was Gettysburg. The win turned the path of the war. President Lincoln spoke at a dedication. The place was a cemetery. It honored soldiers who had died in great numbers. The speech lasted two minutes only. Its name is the Gettysburg Address. People still remember the simple beauty. They remember the eloquence. Lincoln said the war tested the nation. The test was whether a democracy could survive. He spoke to those who were still alive. He asked them to complete work left unfinished. The dead had started that work. He asked the living to save a kind of government. Government of the people must not be lost. Government by the people must not be lost. Government for the people must not be lost from the earth. Another Oppressed People. Lincoln is widely called the Great Emancipator. Many Native peoples remember a harsher record. His effect on them was less positive. He was president during a great move west. The move is called westward expansion. His policies did harm. Native peoples already on those lands suffered. A railroad was laid across the continent. It is called the transcontinental railroad. The work forced many Native peoples onto reservations. Land was taken. Natural resources were taken. Their whole way of life was taken. The year 1864 names a Navajo chief. The chief was Manuelito. That year the Navajo were driven from land they called home. The land lay in northeastern Arizona.

7General Ulysses S. Grant led Union troops to new wins. Some wins were in the West. Some wins were in the South. Late in 1864, Confederate troops lost in Georgia. They lost in Virginia. Lincoln began to hope the war would finish. He was elected president once more. Early in 1865 he had cause to cheer. Congress passed an amendment. The amendment was the Thirteenth. It was joined to the US Constitution. The amendment outlawed slavery. The ban covered the United States. Four years was how long the war lasted. The dead numbered six hundred thousand. The Union survived. Slavery was no longer legal. Only six days after the war ended, President Abraham Lincoln was killed. An assassin fired the bullet. The killer was John Wilkes Booth. Booth supported the Confederacy. Lincoln was attending a play. Booth shot him at the play. The building was Ford's Theatre. That theatre stands in Washington, DC. A funeral train took the body home. Home was Illinois. He had loved that state. Mourners stood silent along the way. They saluted a great American hero. February 1865 dates a late photograph. It is one of the final photographs of Lincoln. Glossary. Abolition means the ending of something. In this book it means making slavery no longer legal. Equality means a condition. In it, everyone has rights that match. Homespun means humble. It also means a simple life away from cities. A campaign is a series of actions. The series is planned. It is designed to reach one goal. A legislature is a group of officials. Voters elect the group. The job is to make laws. The job is also to change laws. Civil rights are rights in three areas. One area is law. One area is society. One area is the economy. These rights guarantee freedom. They guarantee equality. They do so for all citizens. A privilege is a special benefit. Set conditions decide who enjoys it. It can also be an honor. Eloquence is a skill. It is clear speech that works well. It is also clear writing that works well. To secede is to withdraw on formal terms. A person or a state leaves a group. The group may be an organization. An emancipator is someone who lets other people go free. Solemn means serious. It can also mean sad. Enslaved means kept in slavery. Another person may own the enslaved one. That person may force work from them.

12. Amelia Earhart and the Last Flight

1A photograph shows Amelia in the year 1937. The flight told here came on another day. The date was May 21, 1932. A small red plane jolted through cloud. It flew 12,000 feet above the North Atlantic. That height is 3,658 meters. Ireland's coast still lay past towering dark clouds of a storm. Far underneath, icebergs rose out of a cold sea. Amelia Earhart was the pilot. Americans already counted her among their best-known fliers. In 1928 she had crossed as a passenger, the earliest woman to travel that ocean by air. Wilmer Stultz was the man who flew the earlier plane. A success now would mean she herself had taken an airplane across. No one, woman or man, had made a second airplane crossing of that ocean. She would be first to do it.

2The success was not yet won. Most attempts failed, and danger was the reason. Planes built in the 1930s were little. Pressurized cabins were rare. Tools that today's fliers trust were largely missing. Sight was her guide. The feel of the aircraft was the other guide. For hours at a stretch, her grip on the controls had to stay firm. Skirting the dark cloud mass was impossible. She aimed the Lockheed Vega straight into it. Ice followed the rain. Frozen controls threw the Vega into a spinning dive. Frigid water came closer as she fought to recover. Beneath the clouds, warmer air loosened the ice. She brought the nose up and ended the spin. Tiredness pressed on her too. Fuel leaked from a tank. A cracked manifold sometimes spat flames. Londonderry, in Northern Ireland, was the landing place, a grassy field used by farmers. The Atlantic lay behind her, flown by her own hands. Photos there show the plane beside her. Reporters crowd another photo taken after the landing. Flying and adventure had already made her famous. This crossing would lift her into legend. Memory, though, would cling hardest to a journey many people call her greatest miss. She vanished during a try at circling the globe.

3Amelia was six when people first flew an airplane. Wilbur Wright and Orville Wright built the craft, a machine with wings, using spruce and ash. The launch site was Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. The day was December 17, 1903. A picture keeps that moment. In 1936 the Douglas DC-3 entered passenger work. It stood among the earliest machines made to carry travelers. Plenty of onlookers called the brothers foolish. Others felt excitement at the very idea of flight. The danger was plain. Wood frames and canvas skins left planes easy to break, slow, and close to the ground. Cold wind and storms were a bad match for them. Crashes took many pilots' lives. By 1937 the machines had grown much better, because materials and building methods had advanced. Early airlines moved passengers on brief routes. Land lay under most of those routes. Daylight was the usual time to fly. Engineers drew stronger designs. Pilots, Amelia among them, learned safer habits. Mishaps did not stop.

4People who watched her grow up were unlikely to be shocked by later feats. She was determined from early on. Atchison, Kansas, was her birthplace. July 24, 1897, was her birthday. School months were lived at the house of her mother's parents, among cousins and friends. They scrambled on the banks beside the Missouri River. Cave trips had Amelia at the front. Horses were a joy. Sleds were a joy. Trees were a joy. Her grandfather's barn was where she invented games for the other children. Muriel was her sister. Both girls were so lively that bloomers were sewn by their mother. A dress kept a girl from running, riding, or climbing in a boy's way. Bloomers did not. The society of that time disliked girls who were so active. Amelia refused to quit. One photo shows the two sisters. The bright years closed at age eleven. Her grandmother's death led the parents to shift the family. Iowa became the new home for Amelia and for Muriel. Their father struggled to find work, so more moves came across the next few years. At twenty-one, Amelia saw the family settle in California. An air show one day filled her sight with loops and stunts. College was left unfinished. She already knew flying was her aim. Mixed jobs, and money from her parents, paid for lessons. She saved until a plane could be purchased. A license followed. Air-show crowds then praised her as a young woman at the controls. In a photo she stands at the right, next to Neta Snook, who gave her the first lessons.

5Boston was home in the stretches between flights. Denison House employed her to teach English. Students came from Syria and from China. People who were poor, children most of all, could get help there. She loved that teaching. She loved the social work beside it. Both were done well. Helping children was often part of the day, and a picture shows that work. A public reputation was starting to form. Then a chance unlike any other arrived. George Putnam, who promoted public figures in New York, wanted a woman for an Atlantic ride that no woman had taken. Danger was high. In the year before, three women had died while attempting the ocean. Every earlier success had been flown by a man. The chosen person would need a will as hard as iron. Extreme weather, real peril, and deep fatigue would all have to be borne. Putnam judged Earhart the right fit. She was ready to leave. Across her life the jobs were many, in a period when women rarely held jobs at all. She nursed. She did social work. She piloted. She designed clothes. She edited a magazine. She wrote. She helped lead an airline. She served as a professor. She also helped found the Ninety-Nines. Women pilots made up that group, and the group continues today. A 1918 picture shows her dressed as a nurse.

6She felt purposeless, and she likened herself to a sack of potatoes. Headlines spread worldwide after the ocean trip. A ticker-tape parade greeted her. A photo sets her in Southampton, England, once that flight was over. Writing about flight filled the years after. Speaking about flight did too. Funds for later projects came from clothing she designed, and from luggage aimed at women as active as she was. Two airlines were launched with her help. Transcontinental Air Transport was the first, and it would later be called Transworld Airlines, or TWA. Northeast Airlines was the second. She married George Putnam and kept on flying. She tried out new aircraft on journeys between coasts. Contests included her. Distance records were set by her. An autogyro moves forward by a powered propeller. Lift comes from a rotor up top that is not powered. With just fifteen minutes of teaching behind her, she flew one, and no woman had done that before. Two long tours of the country followed in the new machine. At thirty-nine, fame and respect were hers for work most people reserved for men. A fresh test was what she wanted. One major flight was still missing from her list. A path around the planet was the largest test remaining. Wiley Post alone had already taken an airplane around the globe. He kept to the Northern Hemisphere. He skipped the equator, which is the longer line and the harder one. Amelia picked that equator line. Whether she would finish was unknown. One photo catches her giving a speech to the public.

7Doubt about her skill was gone. A photo shows her posed on the Lockheed before the world trip's takeoff. March 1937 brought a first try, headed west toward Hawaii. The takeoff crashed, and the damage to the plane was severe. She changed the plan. The next attempt would run east around the planet. Navigator Fred Noonan went with her. The date was May 21, 1937. A new silver Lockheed Electra flew from Oakland, California, to Miami, Florida. That segment opened the world route. Brief landings came at Burbank, California, at Tucson, Arizona, and at New Orleans, Louisiana. A map of the 1937 path labels Asia, Miami, Africa, and South America. It also labels the finished portion, the zone where the plane was lost, and the portion never flown. The new plane had crossed North America from one side to the other. Mechanics in Miami then prepared the ship for longer hops. George Putnam had drawn the near-equator track with care. Amelia and Fred set out on it. Water would lie under long stretches, because the line stayed near the equator. Several small islands in the Pacific would have to serve as landing spots. The journey reached South America. Africa came next, then India, then Asia, then Australia. Senegal, Khartoum, and Karachi were stops on the way. At Bandung, Indonesia, monsoon weather delayed them while some long-range instruments were repaired. Apart from that pause, the flying stayed calm.

8A second map labels Asia, India, Hawaii, Lae, Howland Island, and Australia. Fred Noonan and Amelia appear in a photo from a late stop in Indonesia. Another clean historic success seemed close. Lae, on New Guinea, received them on June 29, 1937. New Guinea's Lae sits just above Australia, out in the Pacific Ocean. Familiar tasks filled the visit. Fuel went into the tanks. Maintenance was done. Maps were studied. Telegrams were sent homeward to the United States. Departure from Lae came on July 2. No warning of trouble showed. A U.S. Coast Guard cutter, the Itasca, was part of the support. Radio notes grew strange as Howland Island came closer. That small island was planned as the last pause before Hawaii, with California after that. The Itasca waited offshore, listening for the Electra. Two further ships of the United States had orders matching the cutter's. Every light was to be switched on. The glow would trace a path and help the fliers locate the island. Signals arrived in patches. Static broke them up. Amelia did not seem able to hear the cutter. She mentioned stormy weather. Above the island, conditions were clear. More than twenty hours had gone by since Lae. She reported the plane running on a north-south line. The time was 8:45 in the morning. The day was July 3, 1937. Nothing more was heard from her.

9What became of Amelia is a question that still haunts people. The Itasca at once joined a U.S. Navy hunt for the plane. Naval thinkers suspected a storm had brought her down, somewhere northwest of Howland. Searching lasted weeks. In the history of that navy, no air-and-sea hunt has been larger. The aircraft left no sign. Amelia left none. Fred left none. After twelve months, George Putnam, her husband, decided she had died in the ocean. Might that fail to be the whole account? Eight ships went out from the U.S. Navy. Among those ships was the USS Lexington. A scrap of airplane turned up on an island close to where she vanished. Some people think the scrap was hers. Explanations have multiplied. Broken gear is one idea. Faulty navigation, or faulty flying, is another. Being held prisoner is another. One view says the pair lived through a forced landing and a Japanese ship collected them. Prison on a Japanese island followed, and disease later killed them. A different view says they reached some other island. Foods of that place sustained them for a while. In the end, disease or old age took their lives.

10Many people call those ideas invented. Neither island account has proof behind it. A ditching on the water is the more likely end. Waves over 10 feet high would have torn the plane apart in a hurry. Those waves stood about 3 meters high. The life raft may never have been blown up. Drowning may have come before that chance. Her fate does not erase her rank. She stands with the greatest Americans of the twentieth century. She died inside the activity she loved most. She made plain that a woman's life need not be fenced in. She made plain that flight was open to any person. A legend, she changed the world. A picture shows the work she loved best: flying. An aviator is a person who flies an aircraft. A navigator charts a path meant to reach a chosen place. Disappeared means no longer in sight. Perilous means full of danger. Endeavors are serious tries. Pilots are the people who fly aircraft or spacecraft. Fabrication means the making of a product. Static is a crackle of electricity that muddles messages sent by phone, by radio, or by television. Inclement weather is cold, windy, and stormy. A tailspin is a fast fall in which a diving aircraft spins. A legend is a famous person remembered for a rare skill or a rare deed. A manifold is the piped chamber that moves gases and fuel into an engine and back out.

13. Attila, the Huns, and Rome in Decline

1The chapters run in this order. First comes the Roman Empire. Then come the Huns. Next comes the rise of Attila. After that comes his link with Honoria. Then comes the last great Roman general. A meeting with the pope follows. The fall of Hun power comes after that. A word list closes the book. Around 27 BCE, Roman armies were spreading across western Europe. They took control of much of the ancient world. From that expansion, the Roman Empire was born. Its rule lasted close to five centuries. That is nearly five hundred years. By about 350 CE, the empire was old. It was also very large. Age and size made it hard to govern. The land was so vast that two emperors were needed. One ruler could not manage all of it. The western ruler sat in the city of Rome. In the east, the ruler was Valens. He was based in Constantinople. That city is the place now called Istanbul, in Turkey. Bad news reached Emperor Valens in 376 CE. A messenger reported huge numbers of a Germanic people, the Visigoths. They were entering the empire. They wanted protection. They feared a new enemy from the east. That enemy was the Huns. Romans had never heard of the Huns before that report. A statue shows Flavius Julius Valens. His years as Eastern Roman Emperor were 364 to 378 CE. A map set around 450 CE names the Danube River. It also names the Franks, the Visigoths, the Ostrogoths, the Burgundians, and the Sueves. Western and eastern empires both appear. The Atlantic Ocean, the Mediterranean Sea, and Africa appear too. By the Hun invasion, the empire was already huge. Trouble with peoples along many borders was already there. The map helps show how wide that land had grown.

2For six years, the Huns had been moving toward land around the Black Sea. Their campaigns succeeded. Those campaigns shifted whole populations. The Visigoths were among the people set in motion. Great movements of people followed the fighting. Some Visigoth refugees received permission to settle inside the Eastern Roman Empire. The Romans treated them badly. Anger grew. The Visigoths rebelled. Their violent sweep lasted two years. It tore through a section of that eastern realm. The destruction was great. Villages and fields suffered as the rebels moved. An army under Emperor Valens tried to stop the uprising. His army was wiped out. Valens died in that defeat. The Visigoth king Alaric I headed the struggle. His target was the Eastern Roman Empire. A picture shows him in that role. He led his people in the fight against Rome. Losing Valens left the Roman Empire weaker. With no central leader, Roman defense of the territories failed. In 410 CE, the Visigoths sacked Rome. They took the city and stole from it. From that defeat, a long decline of the Roman Empire began. The loss of the emperor and the later sack of Rome were heavy blows.

3Bands of warriors made up the Huns. Rome had never faced a deadlier enemy. Where the Huns first came from is something historians do not agree on. The tribes that formed them were Eurasian. Their backgrounds were diverse. Leadership among them spoke Turkic languages. By 380 CE, the Roman army was already hiring Huns. The Huns learned siege warfare from that army. A siege is a long attack that also cuts a city off from food. Later, the Huns used that skill to destroy whole cities. A map set around 526 CE names the Danube River, the Franks, the Burgundians, the Ostrogoths, and the Sueves. The Atlantic Ocean, the Visigoths, the Mediterranean Sea, and Africa appear too. Nearly one hundred years after Rome was sacked, Visigoths and other Germanic tribes held the old western lands. Those lands had once been under the Western Roman Empire. A statue of Attila stands in Macka Park in Istanbul, Turkey. Land and power drove the Huns, as they drive every empire. In battle, Roman fighters could not match the Huns. By the 420s CE, a new eastern emperor was paying them. His name was Theodosius II. People say it thee-uh-DOH-shee-us. A large yearly gift of gold bought peace. In 433 CE, rule of the Huns passed to Attila. His name is said AT-uh-luh. It is also said uh-TIL-uh. He also ruled Germanic people already conquered by the Huns. A treaty with Theodosius kept the Roman gold payments going.

4Among Hun leaders, Attila is the most famous. He was born into a noble family. He could speak Gothic and Latin. He may have been able to read them as well. He became leader in his late thirties. People who met him spoke of very simple tastes. He ate in moderation. He joined feasts in moderation too. He did not go to extremes. His soldiers liked to show their wealth. They decorated horses and armor. Attila wore plain clothes. He used wooden cups. He saved gold cups for guests. No earlier leader had unified the Hun fighting force as he did. Exceptional horse archers filled his armies. Their whirlwind attacks were feared because the archers seemed to vanish. They moved fast in battle. A confusing pattern kept enemies running. Defeat of the Huns under Attila was almost impossible. They crushed nearly every army sent against them. A picture shows him at a feast with his warriors. In 441 CE, Roman armies were busy elsewhere. Sicily and North Africa were the scenes of that fighting. Attila broke the treaty made with Rome. He destroyed Roman cities as he drew near Constantinople. Ruin followed ruin, and thousands of people were killed. Theodosius accepted a doubled gold payment to halt the killing and the ruin.
