Each year the gold sent to the Huns would weigh about 950 kilograms, which is 2,100 pounds. Theodosius died in 450 CE. Marcian, said MAR-shun, was the new eastern emperor. He stopped further payments. Attila left the eastern empire alone because its wealth was already drained. His attention turned to the richer Western Roman Empire. Walls around Constantinople had been built for a reason. Invaders such as Attila were not supposed to take the eastern capital.

5A letter reached Attila in 450 CE. The writer was Justa Grata Honoria. Her name is said ah-NOR-ee-uh. She was sister to Valentinian III, who ruled in the west. Honoria was smart. She wanted the power held by her brother. She had a secret romance with a servant. People believed her plan was a coup. They believed the servant would remove Valentinian III and rule instead. The servant was put to death. An engagement was forced on Honoria. Her brother picked the man. She wanted freedom in a desperate way, so she begged Attila for help. Her ring went with the letter as proof she had written it. A picture shows the Danube crossing made by Attila. That river helped set the northern border of the empire. Another picture puts Honoria beside Valentinian III. Their mother, Galla Placidia, stands with them. Attila read the letter and the ring as a marriage proposal. He agreed to marry the young princess. In his view, she had done nothing wrong. The dowry he named was one half of the western realm. Valentinian III refused. Attila then threatened him. He said he would take that western realm with soldiers. About 100,000 men were gathered. Huns and Germanic allies both served in that army. Early in 451 CE, the army crossed the Rhine and entered Gaul. Gaul is the land now called France. For several months, conquered cities were sacked and burned. Men, women, and children were killed without mercy.

6One great general was left to the Roman Empire. Flavius Aetius was his name. People say it AY-tee-uhs. He served at the court where Valentinian III ruled. People usually call him Aetius. While the Western Empire crumbled, he did everything he could to hold it together. Those efforts are why memory calls him the Last of the Romans. Attila was moving through Gaul. Aetius hurried to gather soldiers. He argued that Attila was an enemy of humanity. Some Germanic tribes living in Gaul agreed to join him. A large Visigoth force was among the new allies. King Theodoric commanded that force. The army under Aetius was then about as large as the army under Attila. Aetius had needed a bigger force, and men from Gaul were the ones he convinced to join. The march began late in spring, in the year 451 CE. Aetius took his soldiers toward Attila and the Huns. The Battle of Chalons came next. The season was late June. The place was near Orleans, a city in the France of today. There Aetius caught up with Attila. Attila saw the Roman forces and pulled back. He chose a flat open stretch beside the town called Chalons-sur-Marne. Those two vast armies clashed on that stretch. People count the clash among the greatest battles ever fought. Afternoon was the start of the Battle of Chalons. Arrows flew first. Then the sides fought close in, with swords, spears, and axes. By evening the fighting had stopped. Tens of thousands from both sides lay dead. Theodoric was one of the dead. Who had won was not in doubt. The army of Aetius had defeated Attila. The Visigoth king died in the battle, yet the Roman and Visigoth armies still beat the Huns.

7People knew Attila, and the soldiers with him, for violent acts. On the next day, Aetius let Attila leave with the rest of that army. Scholars think Aetius held back from a full defeat for a reason. A total Visigothic victory worried him as much as his own loss would have. For him, the result that followed was the best one. Theodoric was dead. Attila was retreating. Romans looked like the winners. Aetius chose that outcome instead of crushing every remaining Hun. The story then turns to Attila and the pope. In June of the next year, Attila led his army over the mountains into Italy. Plenty of men were still with him. He still claimed marriage to Honoria. This time Aetius could not raise an army big enough for a fight. The Roman side had no force large enough to meet him. Destruction spread over the north of Italy, through both small towns and larger cities. The army moved ever closer to Rome. Fear grew as the Huns came nearer to the city. Aquileia was destroyed so completely during the Italian attack that the city never recovered. Nothing of that city rose again in the same way.

8A picture shows Pope Leo I, who stopped Attila from pushing the Italian attacks any farther. Aetius and Emperor Valentinian III chose diplomacy instead of another battle. Pope Leo I led the Catholic Church. They asked him for help. They wanted him to meet Attila and request that Italy be left behind. The meeting took place at the Hun camp. No record remains of what the two men said. Attila agreed to halt the attacks. Some historians think his position was weaker than many people knew. Recovery from the Battle of Chalons was not complete. A plague was killing many of his men. Food and other supplies were running short. Whatever the reasons, he left Italy and never came back. A map of his empire around 450 CE shows Europe, the Danube River, the Atlantic Ocean, the Mediterranean Sea, and Africa. After his death, rebellions rose inside that empire. Germanic peoples took part. Turkic peoples took part too. By 452 CE his realm reached into lands that are now Russia. It also reached Hungary, Germany, and France. In 453 CE he took a new bride named Ildico. A wedding day of feasting ended with the couple going to bed. Morning came, and Attila did not leave the bedroom. Worried servants went in. They found him dead. During the night a blood vessel had burst, in his nose or in his throat.

9Under Attila, Hun armies became the most powerful military force in Europe and also the most feared. His death did not leave a lasting empire. His sons fought one another for leadership. They split the Huns apart. They wasted the wealth. By 469 CE, the unified empire he had built was gone. Little written record remains of the realm he ruled. Even so, the story of the man himself has stayed alive through the centuries. He was fearsome. Memory still ranks him with the greatest generals. It also ranks him with the greatest political leaders. Many people think Hungary took its name from the Huns. That belief is wrong. Scholars link the capital name Budapest to his brother. That brother was Bleda, a man also called Buda. Words in this book can be explained this way. Allies are partners who join for one shared aim. Humanity means humankind, taken as a single kind. Moderation means staying reasonable and avoiding extremes in words, acts, or feelings. Conquered describes a takeover, most often a forced one, of people or of a place. Diplomacy means talks between leaders of separate countries. Rampaged describes a furious, violent advance. Refugees are people escaping danger such as war, hunger, persecution, or a natural disaster. Often they have no fixed place to go. Property or money given by the family of a bride to the family she marries into is a dowry. A collection of nations or peoples under one person with total authority is an empire. To destroy a city and steal its wealth after taking it from an enemy is to have sacked it. Germanic describes people who spoke a family of similar languages across northwestern Europe. A long surrounding attack that also cuts off food and supplies is a siege.

14. Beautiful Stones from Underground

1An introduction opens the book. Later parts explain how gems form, a try-this activity, and the path into jewelry. Value, the Mohs scale, kinds of gems, a conclusion, and a word list follow. Many people call gems the loveliest things Earth makes. Even a tiny piece of that beauty can cost thousands of dollars. Around the world, sparkling stones are worn on fingers, on necks, and on wrists. Families hand them down over the years. Crowns of royalty carry them. Sacred religious objects carry them too. The finest and costliest jewelry is often decorated with gems.

2Any beautiful stone fit for jewelry can be called a gem. Beautiful color or sparkle is common. Three major groups exist. Crystals are the first. Stones are the second. Both are minerals, the natural nonliving materials in ordinary rock. A crystal is a very pure mineral. Its shapes are tight, and its patterns are neat. A stone mixes minerals. Color and pattern can be beautiful, yet the shape is not strict. Organic gems are the third group. Living things make the substances they come from. A picture can place garnet, a crystal, at the top. Turquoise, a stone, can sit in the middle. A natural pearl, an organic gem, can sit at the bottom. Formation is the next topic. Fame and high cost belong to many crystals. Diamonds, emeralds, and rubies belong in that group. Every mineral is built from atoms, and those particles number in the millions. Ordinary rock mixes many kinds of atoms with no pattern and no order. In a crystal, the arrangement is very precise and orderly. Flat sides, called faces, build the shapes. Each kind of crystal has its own shape. Cubes are one form. Long columns with six sides are another. Names for those shapes include trigonal, cubic, tetragonal, monoclinic, and hexagonal.

3A picture can show diamonds born deep in the mantle. Eruptions carry them up to the surface. Labels can include magma, pressure from gravity, crust layers, the mantle, and heat. Special conditions deep underground produce most crystals. Diamonds are one example. Layers of rock squeeze the mineral. That squeeze packs the atoms into the smallest possible arrangement. Sapphires are another example. The mineral grows so hot underground that it melts. Slow cooling lets the atoms settle into a regular pattern. Opals form in a third way. Minerals dissolve in water. Very slow evaporation leaves the mineral behind as a crystal. Here is an activity. Make crystals of your own. Halite, also called rock salt, forms when salty seas dry up. A much smaller version of that process needs only water and ordinary salt. First, take one tablespoon of salt. Stir it into warm water filling one cup. Stop when you cannot see the salt. Second, keep adding small amounts. Stop when fresh salt sits undissolved. Third, stand a clean toothpick in the cup. Fourth, leave the cup in a warm sunny place. As the water dries, crystals grow on the toothpick and on the cup walls. Fifth, study them with a magnifying glass and ask what you see.

4Minerals inside stones lack an orderly pattern. Other minerals may be mixed in. Layers are common. The streaks and lines from those layers are the grain. Beautiful patterns and surfaces come from grain. Pearls, amber, and coral are organic gems. Living things produce them. A pearl starts when a grain of sand is trapped inside an oyster shell. Smooth nacre is laid over that grain in layers. The oyster builds its shell from the same material. Coral is the skeletons left by millions of tiny sea animals. Amber began as tree sap millions of years ago. Insects or spiders caught in the sap often remain as fossils. Pictures can show a spider in amber and oysters making pearls. Jewelry is the next step. Most mineral gems lie deep underground. Mines have to be dug. Because the stones are small and rare, much of the digging is still done by hand. Miners chip and cut the rock, searching for stones set inside it. A related fact follows. Opals grow when mineral-rich water dries out of underground cracks. A streak of crystal is left in the rock. That streak is a vein. The finest opals in the world come from veins underground. The town is Coober Pedy, in the Australian desert. Speakers of the Australian Aborigine language explain the town name this way. A white man in a hole is what it means. The mines are simple holes.

5A gem just found by a miner does not look like the stone in a ring or a necklace. Edges are often rough. The surface looks dull. The shape is bumpy. Flaws are common. They include cracks, dark spots, and bubbles. Cutters shape the gem into regular forms. Those forms display the best qualities and hide the flaws. Saws and polishers edged with diamond were once the tools. Lasers are a newer tool. A picture can show an uncut diamond, uneven and flawed. Flat faces, called facets, are cut on most crystal gems. Color and pattern show more clearly. Reflected light makes the gem sparkle. Several cutting styles are used. A picture of a cut diamond can show strong sparkle. Seen from above and from the side, the styles are step, brilliant, carving, rose, and cabochon. Each style brings out a gem's best features. Diamonds, which sparkle more than they show color, often receive the popular brilliant cut. Many facets bounce light off the stone. Deep green emeralds often receive the step cut. On that cut the top is wide and flat. The color there is pure. The facets are rectangles. The rose cut has a rounded top and triangular facets. Older gems are the usual place to see it. Oldest of the styles is the cabochon. It is said KAB-uh-shon. It is only rounded and polished. Opaque stones and patterned stones are its usual use. Small sculptures can be carved from jade. Coral can be carved that way too.

6Value has two roots. Beauty is one. Rarity is the other. Price also depends on hardness. Another guide is known as the four Cs. Cut is one part. Carat weight is another. Color is a third. Clarity is the fourth. Cut means how well the gem was shaped and polished, or how lovely it is in nature. A poor cut can look dull or uneven. Carat weight is size. One carat is about as heavy as one kernel of unpopped popcorn. The word carat comes from carob seeds. For centuries, jewelers used those seeds as weights. The seeds grow in pods. Their weight stays incredibly similar, no matter the tree or the pod. A modern carat is about as heavy as one of those seeds. Color is the next C, and a major reason gems seem beautiful. Ordinary rocks lack the bright, pure, strong colors of gems. Purer and stronger color means higher value. One mineral can yield gems of different colors. Red rubies and blue sapphires share a mineral. The color shift comes from other chemicals mixed in, only in tiny amounts. A single different atom in a thousand is enough to change the color. Clarity means how free of flaws the gem is. Dark marks, cracks, and bubbles lower the value. A cloudy gem is worth less than a clearer one. Size and rarity often matter more than clarity. Emeralds commonly carry many flaws. Rarity still makes a flawed emerald worth more than a diamond with no flaws. A picture can show an uncut emerald full of cracks and other flaws.

7Hardness on the Mohs scale is the next idea. It shows how pure and tightly built the mineral is. It also shows how well a gem survives daily wear. Friedrich Mohs, a geologist, made the scale. His test was simple. He scratched one gem with another. Only a softer gem can be scratched. Talc is the softest mineral. It can scratch nothing. Its number is 1. Diamond is the hardest substance on Earth. It can scratch anything. Only another diamond can scratch it. Its number is 10. Jewelry usually needs a gem at 5 or above. The list runs this way. Talc is 1. Gypsum is 2. Calcite is 3. Fluorite is 4. Apatite is 5. Orthoclase is 6. Quartz is 7. Topaz is 8. Emerald is 9. Diamond is 10. A fingernail measures 2.5. A penknife measures 5.5. Names that appear with the scale are sapphire and diamond. Turquoise, emerald, and quartz appear too. So do opal, pearl, ruby, and jade. Africa is one region where they occur. North America is another. South America is another. Europe, Asia, Australia, and the South Pacific are others. Diamonds come next among the types. They are the hardest natural objects in the world. They can cut metal and stone, so flawed or unattractive ones often go onto saws and drill tips. Most are almost colorless. Very rare ones are yellow, red, or blue. South Africa, Russia, and Australia are the most common sources. Engagement rings use them extremely often.

8The Hope diamond is among the most famous. It is not the biggest. Its color is a rare sky blue. Theft is part of its long story. So is ownership by royalty and by rich people. A legend of a curse grew from that story. The Cullinan diamond is the largest ever found. South Africa was the place of discovery. Its weight was over 3,100 carats. Its size matched a pineapple. Nine gems were cut from it. One piece is called the Greater Star of Africa. That piece weighs 530 carats. A picture can show the Hope diamond. Graphite, also called pencil lead, is the same mineral as diamond. In graphite the atoms sit in loose layers, so the material is very soft. Rub it on paper and atoms break away, leaving a pencil mark. In a diamond those same atoms are squeezed extremely tight. Nothing but another diamond can scratch them loose. Rubies and sapphires share one mineral. A ruby is always blood red or pink. Every other color of that mineral counts as a sapphire. Deep blue is the color sapphires are most famous for. A picture can show a red ruby beside a blue sapphire and a yellow sapphire. The Middle Ages were the first time birthstones were worn. A birthday was often linked by astrologers and by fortune-tellers to stars. Planets, flowers, and gems were linked as well. The stone was supposed to bring luck, protection, and wealth. Lists differ from place to place. A current list in the United States runs like this. Garnet belongs to January. Amethyst belongs to February. Aquamarine belongs to March. Diamond belongs to April. Emerald belongs to May. Pearl belongs to June. Ruby belongs to July. Peridot belongs to August. Sapphire belongs to September. Opal belongs to October. Topaz belongs to November. Turquoise belongs to December.

9Quartz is the most common crystal family. It is found worldwide, in every color of the rainbow. Most of it is common enough for anyone to afford. Length of the biggest quartz crystal on record was about 6 meters. That is 20 feet. Its weight was more than 44,000 kilograms, or 48 tons. That is heavier than a loaded truck with 18 wheels. Opal, a multicolored quartz, is the most valuable kind. White, blue, and red-orange often appear together. Australia is the most common source. A picture can show quartz. These crystals are common. They can grow very large. Green is the color emeralds are known for. Gem-quality pieces are rare and usually small. People prize the color so highly that emeralds outrank diamonds in value. Colombia yields the finest ones. The same mineral also makes aquamarine, a blue-green stone. Few stones are valued more highly than jade. Lavender, white, and nearly every shade of green occur. Green is the most valuable shade. The stone is very tough, yet it carves easily along the grain. Many civilizations, especially in Asia, carved beautiful knives, swords, and axes from it. Pictures can show a jade figurine and a person carving jade.

10Black speckles and stripes often mark turquoise. The blue-green stone comes from deserts in Iran, in Tibet, and in the southwestern United States. Pretty spots and streaks often run through it. Much of the world's supply is set in silver. That silver setting follows a Navajo tradition. Their belief was that sky itself had dropped these stones onto Earth. Natural pearls have strange shapes, and they are very rare. Building one from a speck of sand takes an oyster many years. Jewelry stores sell lovely round pearls that are almost all cultured. People helped make those pearls. A farmer places a round bead of shell inside an oyster. Nacre covers the bead. The pearl that results is perfectly round. Every color of the rainbow appears. Creamy white, pink, yellow, green, and even black are among them. Natural pearls stay rare and oddly shaped. Cultured ones are round.

11A picture can show a strip mine clearing an immense stretch of land. Gems of beauty occur around the world. Many stand for power and for wealth. For centuries, people have killed for them and died for them. Blood and violence still fill the trade in some regions. West Africa is one. Colombia is another. Digging with dynamite and with strip mines is often dangerous. People are harmed. Earth is harmed too. Scientists can grow gems in a lab. Those gems match the finest natural ones. The cost is a thousand times lower. Created gems may one day satisfy the wish for that beauty. They may also help protect Earth and the people on it. Words in this book can be explained this way. Atoms are the tiny particles that build every substance. Crystals are minerals grown in regular, tight patterns. Cultured means made with human help. Embedded means buried inside or surrounded. Facets are the flat faces of a cut gem. Grain means the lines and patterns left by mineral layers. Nacre is the material an oyster uses for its shell and for pearls. Opaque means you cannot see through it. Organic gems are made from substances living things create.

15. Boats That Opened the Seas

1An introduction opens this book. Early boat years come next. The Polynesians follow. The Vikings follow them. The Age of Discovery follows the Vikings. The Chinese follow that age. Later years come after the Chinese. A conclusion comes next. A glossary ends the book. Rivers often drew settlers. Lakes drew them. Seas drew them. Fresh water was there. Soil full of nutrients was there. Fish were plentiful. People beside wide water wondered what waited past the horizon. They also thought a water route might beat a land route. Some materials stay up on the water. Wood does. Reeds do. A skin stuffed with air does. From those thoughts came the first plain boat. Practical boats and ships let people go farther from home. New kinds of boats came as technology advanced. Cargo space grew. Safety often grew. Speed often grew. Comfort often grew. Commerce used boats as tools. Exploration used them. Defense used them. This book looks at boats that helped people explore. It also looks at how boats changed.

2Egypt holds the oldest record of travel on the sea. Earlier sailors may have existed. Written proof starts with the Egyptians. They left images of their own journeys. Stone carvings show them on the water. Those carvings are more than 6,000 years old. Life in ancient Egypt followed the great Nile River. Skill on the water followed from that. The first boats were tree trunks hollowed into a simple shape. Tree boats were not only an Egyptian idea. In the Americas, Indigenous peoples made dugout canoes the same way. They hollowed trunks. The boats were strong. They held little cargo. A picture shows an Egyptian boat. Larger loads became the next wish. Boats had to carry many people. Voyages were long. Food had to come along. Animals had to come along. Trade goods had to come along. One oak, carved into a canoe and pushed with a pole, could cross a lake. It could go down a river. Bulky goods did not fit. Imagine six sheep crowded into a narrow canoe on a wide lake. Room ran out. A picture shows a dugout canoe. People keep trying to perfect what they invent. Ancient builders wanted bigger boats. They wanted faster boats. They wanted safer boats. Far places would stay out of reach without better boats.

3A picture shows a canoe of birch bark. Builders next made a frame of wooden beams. Planks covered some frames. Tree bark covered others. Some cultures pulled animal skins over the frame. That outer shell is the hull. These boats were larger than older ones. Their shape was more streamlined. Cargo room grew. Paddles were invented for deep water. Oars were invented too. A pole cannot touch bottom there. Egyptians were first to sheathe a wooden frame with long flat boards. Some boats reached 21.3 meters. That length is 70 feet. Sails were an Egyptian first as well. Wind did the pulling. Rowing became less needed, or not needed at all. Some boats kept both rowers and sails. Large sailboats soon appeared among the Greeks. The Phoenicians built them too. Peoples of the Mediterranean Sea built large sailboats too. About 3,000 years ago, ships carried two masts. Each mast held a sail. Steering grew easier with the second mast. Speed grew too. Five hundred years after that, Greek builders made a ship with four sails. The ship could safely exit the Mediterranean Sea. Its route could follow Africa's western shore. The quickest ships of that age were made for war. Rowers often sat on three levels along each side. Tiers stacked that way put great power into a small space. Greeks called a three-tier ship a trireme. Distant shores opened to travelers. Trade and exploration moved past the Mediterranean Sea in this age. Danger on the ocean remained. Brave explorers still took the chance. Traders took it too.

4Pacific Island peoples in the South Pacific built boats for the open ocean. Eastward travel was underway more than 3,500 years ago. They went far past the island chain, or archipelago, where they lived. They also ranged off the mainland of Asia. Open boats later carried them thousands of miles. Those journeys came over 1,000 years back. Their design was an early form of today's catamaran. Two canoes were lashed together with large wooden poles. A deck crossed those poles. Length was usually 15 to 18 meters. That is about 50 to 60 feet. Masts and sails stood on the center deck. Several people could ride there. Supplies for a long trip fit there too. A picture shows a Polynesian catamaran. A map labels the Pacific Ocean. It labels Asia. It labels the Hawaiian Islands. It labels Easter Island. It labels Australia. It labels New Zealand. It labels routes of Polynesian expansion. Island-to-island trips were safe on these boats. New islands became new homes. By 1000 ce, Polynesian settlers lived on nearly all the Pacific islands fit for people. Hawai‘i was one home. New Zealand was one. Rapa Nui, also called Easter Island, was one. These sailors knew their work. Wave size told them where they were. Wave shape told them too. Stars guided them. Great distances were a chain of island stops. Life on the sea became ordinary for them.

5Over 1,300 years back, a separate people in another region started larger boats. They were the Vikings. Home was northern Europe. Warrior was a name they carried. Conqueror was another. Water travel was familiar work. By 700 ce their boats outclassed every other boat on the ocean. Trading boats were called knarrs. Say it kuh-NARS. Length reached 16.5 meters. That is 54 feet. Width reached 4.5 meters. That is 15 feet. Flat bottoms let a knarr take a very heavy load. Width made room for lots of cargo. The ride was stable. Open ocean was safe enough for them. Most sailors of that age hated to lose the coast from sight. Vikings did not share that fear. They found their way with a sun compass, a dial made of wood. New lands fell to them. No Europeans had visited North America before them. War boats were called longships. Front and back looked alike, so coming and going were hard to tell apart. Attackers could reverse course with ease. Speed could reach 15 knots. A knot measures how fast a boat moves on water. One knot is a bit faster than one mile in an hour. The biggest longships could hold 200 warriors. Speed, size, and easy handling met a fierce will to fight. Beating the Vikings was hard. They ruled the ocean for close to three centuries. The longship design stayed as it was. Other nations later built stronger ships. A picture shows a Viking knarr. A picture shows a Viking longship.

6Before the 1400s, explorers by sea mostly stayed near home waters. The Age of Discovery broke that habit in a dramatic way. Each European nation with ships wanted unknown lands. A race began. The prize was the Americas. Builders hunted for more speed. They hunted for more safety. The ships of the 1400s and 1500s were caravels. They were small. They were quick. They were sturdy. Three masts carried the sails. Steering improved. Speed improved. Square sails stood on the fore mast and the main mast. A three-sided sail called a lateen stood on the rear mast. A picture shows a caravel. What did these landings do to people already living in those places? The result was tragic far too often. Christopher Columbus led some voyages. Hernan Cortes led others. More Europeans led them too. Land they met was often exploited. People they met were often exploited. Money was the usual motive. Ships were soon used to haul people across oceans. Those people were enslaved far from home. Columbus sailed three caravels. Santa Maria was the biggest. Length was 27.4 meters. That is 90 feet. Width was 9.1 meters. That is 30 feet. A modern ocean liner dwarfs them. A modern cargo ship dwarfs them. Night brought no cabin for the crew. Sleep was on the deck or down in the hold. Small as caravels were, Ferdinand Magellan took five of them to circle the world. Sailors aboard numbered 260. Nearly three years passed before the crew returned. A single ship completed the circle. Eighteen sailors completed it. The rest of the ships were lost. The rest of the sailors died. Magellan did not survive. His death came in the Philippine Islands. Another person killed him.

7Chinese sailors were also at sea while Europeans crossed the world. By the 1400s their skill was high. The magnetic compass was a Chinese invention, made long before others had it. The rudder was theirs too, a thousand years before Westerners. Rectangular sails were stiffened with bamboo strips called battens. Sails grew tougher. Furling and unfurling grew easier. A sailor could climb a sail as if it were a ladder. From 1405 to 1443, Zheng He made seven long voyages. He is the best-known explorer of China from that age. Treasure ships in the fleet numbered sixty-two. Chinese sailors called them junks. Inside, the hull was cut into many sections. Watertight walls, called bulkheads, sealed each section. Damage stayed smaller that way. A hole in the hull could flood only one section. The whole ship did not have to sink. European ships were much smaller than Zheng He's junks. His largest deck could have held all three ships of Columbus. Length was 121 meters. That is 400 feet. Width was 45.7 meters. That is 150 feet. Support boats, smaller than the main traders, numbered over a hundred. The fleet reached Africa. Trade was one aim. Showing the power of the Chinese empire was another. A giraffe went home with Zheng He as a gift for the emperor. War against Asian neighbors pulled China away from exploring. The emperor outlawed ocean voyages. Every treasure ship was destroyed. A picture shows a Chinese junk.

8Spain took the lead as ocean trips continued. European yards had improved a great deal by the 1500s. The new ships were galleons. They were bigger than before. They were faster. They were more comfortable. One galleon ate two thousand oak trees. Length reached 42.7 meters. That is 140 feet. Chinese ships were still larger. Officers at least had pleasant rooms. A galleon did two jobs. It carried trade. It fought as a warship. Size let it mount many cannons. Battle turned dangerous. A picture shows a galleon. Late in the 1700s, British captain James Cook led some of the great explorations of his day. His first ship was Endeavour. He sailed it around the world. Earlier captains often sailed for war. They often sailed for treasure. Cook sailed for knowledge. He sailed for science. Three scientists came with him. One astronomer studied the night sky. Two naturalists studied plants and animals. Artists came to record the finds. Cook watched stars while he sailed. Each new land taught him about its plants and its animals. Europeans understood more of the world because of his work. Limes and cabbages were foods he made the crew eat. Health followed. Before his time, as many as half the people on a long voyage might die. Scurvy was one cause. Other diseases were causes too. A sick crew would have ruined his success. British sailors soon learned that vitamin C kept them alive. The late 1770s brought Cook to Hawai‘i three times. The last visit was in 1779. A fight broke out. Hawaiians and Cook's crew were the two sides. Cook was killed.

9Most coastlines of the world had been explored by the mid-1800s. They had been mapped. Clipper ships were very fast sailboats. A crossing could take only days. Sir Lancelot, a clipper, made a record run. The route went from Australia to England. The time was three months. Sail counts on some clippers reached thirty-five. Light wind was enough to move them. By the 1870s, steam engines had mostly replaced the wind. The Industrial Revolution was running at full strength. Machines mattered more to daily life. Ships bigger and faster than anyone had pictured became possible. Steam is out of date now. Other engines push ships. Nuclear power runs some submarines. It runs some aircraft carriers. A cruise ship can hold thousands of people at once. It is like a city that floats. Early ocean ships still earn our respect. The designers showed real ingenuity. Sea exploration did not help every person it touched. Sailing into the unknown still helped shape the world we know. An archipelago is a group or chain of islands. Buoyant means able to float. Commerce means buying and selling. It is trade. A galleon was a heavy Spanish sailing ship used from the 15th century into the early 18th. War was one use. Trade was the other. Habitable means life can be supported there. A hull is the main body of a ship that sails. Indigenous means belonging to a place from the start. Ingenuity is clever skill at solving a hard problem. Scurvy is a deadly illness of early sailors. Too little vitamin C causes it. Speculated means a person guessed from ideas that were not yet proved. Streamlined means shaped so air or water slips past. Tiers are levels placed one above the next.

16. Building a Small Greenhouse

1The parts of this book are an introduction, the history of greenhouses, how greenhouses work, finding a good location, building a cardboard box greenhouse, tips for care, a conclusion, and a glossary. Gardening was one of the most popular hobbies in the United States for many decades. Even difficult winter weather did not stop many people from tending their gardens. Heavy rain, harsh wind, fierce hail, and deep snow were all part of that winter. People have been interested in gardening indoors for hundreds of years. Indoor gardening can keep plants growing when the outdoors is too hard.

2One type of indoor gardening uses a greenhouse so plants can grow through the whole year. Harsh weather and extreme temperatures stay outside. Inside, the conditions for growth are ideal. The roof and walls are usually made of glass or plastic. Humidity is kept fairly high, and natural light is kept at a maximum. Carbon dioxide stays trapped so plants can breathe it. Some gardeners raise a whole crop inside. Others germinate plants there, then move them outdoors. The history of greenhouses reaches back to ancient Rome. A legend says the emperor Tiberius fell ill in 30 CE. His doctor told him to eat one cucumber every day to regain his health. Gardeners then had to keep that green vegetable growing all year. Large clay pots were their answer. A thin mineral called mica, clear like glass, covered the pots. The cover gathered sunlight, kept the soil moist, and held temperature changes off the cucumbers. Much later, in the sixteenth century, Europeans explored distant places and traded across the world. New plants came home with them. Colder European weather killed many of those plants. A shelter was designed so the rare plants could live through winter. Italy was first to build what we now call a modern greenhouse. Holland and England followed. Interest in botany, the study of plants, grew from those shelters.

3Colleges and universities tried to collect every kind of plant. Ordinary gardeners tried as well. They worked to classify the plants, grow them, or at least keep them alive. In France, people fell in love with the orange tree. They built orangeries to protect this fruit, which is native to warmer parts of Asia, from frost. In the seventeenth century, new technology and better glass let the French redesign greenhouses to be bigger and fancier. The grandest example of that age stood at the Palace of Versailles. It was more than 500 feet, or 152 m, long, 42 feet, or 13 m, wide, and 45 feet, or 14 m, high. Because the trees sit in pots, people can move them. Cold months are spent in the orangerie. Warm months move them into the gardens. Today, stores in many countries receive food and flowers from greenhouses in every season. Grocery stores can stock fruit and vegetables all year. Florists can sell spring flowers in the middle of winter.

4How a greenhouse works comes next. Plants inside can grow larger and faster than plants left outdoors in the weather. A simple structure of glass or plastic can do that job. Light travels in different wavelengths. Short waves from the Sun pass through the glass. Plants use that light to turn carbon dioxide and water into food, and that food lets them grow. This process is called photosynthesis. Once the light is inside, plants and other materials absorb it. They release the extra energy as heat. That heat has a longer wavelength, so it cannot pass back out through the glass. It acts like a blanket and raises the temperature and the humidity. The result is ideal growing conditions. A good location must be chosen before tools and supplies are picked up. The greenhouse in this book works best indoors. Sunlight, heat, and ease of use matter most. First, seek a window facing south or southeast. If none exists, use one facing east so morning sun can start photosynthesis. Second, keep the window away from furnace vents and other heat sources. With the right sunlight, the greenhouse will already be warm enough. Third, choose a spot that is easy to check and is not disturbed by daily activities.

5Why make a model? A model greenhouse is fun, and it teaches. You can watch how sunlight, water, and warmth help a plant grow. Many designs can be finished over a weekend at a fairly low cost. Some are simple, and others are complex. All of them require patience, focus, and a willingness to have fun. The project encourages creative thinking and gives a hands-on way to explore science. The cardboard box plan is on the smaller side. A parent or another family member can share the build. Common materials keep the job simple, affordable, and easy. The finished box still protects plants from cold or wind, just as big, expensive greenhouses do.

6Gather these materials. You need seeds, water, potting soil, and small plant pots. You need one cardboard box, 12 by 12 by 16 inches, or 30 by 30 by 40 cm. You need ten wooden clothespins or small binder clips, a utility knife or scissors, a ruler, and a pencil. You need enough small rocks for a layer 1 inch, or 2.5 cm, deep. You need 2 square feet, or 0.2 square m, of aluminum foil, craft glue, and gray duct tape. You need two sheets of clear plastic film, each 24 by 36 inches, or 61 by 91 cm, from 1.75 mm to 6 mm thick. Construction starts here. Step 1. On the 12-inch, or 30 cm, side, mark 4 inches, or 10 cm, up from the bottom. Draw a straight line through the marks. Carry it about an inch or two, or 2.5 to 5 cm, past each corner onto each long side. Step 2. On the long sides, draw a diagonal from that line to the top corner across from the start. The box should look almost like two triangles. Cut along every line you drew.

7Step 3. Spread craft glue on the bottom and the sides. Work quickly so the glue stays wet, or glue one section at a time. Step 4. Line the inside with aluminum foil. Tear or cut it to fit, then press it onto the glue. The shiny side must face into the box. Step 5. Line the bottom with one plastic sheet and tuck it deep into every corner. Where the plastic meets the foil, fasten it with duct tape. Let the foil glue dry before the tape goes on. Step 6. In each plant pot, pour rocks in a layer one inch, or 2.5 cm, deep so the roots can drain. Pour potting soil on top until it sits within one inch of the rim.

8Step 7. Plant the seeds by following the package directions. Different kinds of seeds may share the box only if they need the same sunlight and the same water. Different conditions would be hard to keep in one box. Step 8. Use the clothespins to hold the second plastic sheet across the top. The greenhouse is now complete. Put it in a sunny place inside the house and watch the seeds sprout. Care comes next. Check the greenhouse about once a week. Keep the soil moist, but not wet. After the first watering, mist the plants with distilled water from a spray bottle. Distilled water has been heated into steam and then cooled back into water. Drops may form on the inside of the plastic. That is normal. If the soil gets too wet, pull the plastic back, let the inside dry somewhat, and cover the box again. After germination, remove the weakest plants so only the strongest remain. Plant food or compost can strengthen them later, but only if a move outdoors is planned. Rich food plus a full life indoors could push them past the box too soon.

9You now have a place for year-round gardening, as gardeners around the world do. The protected cardboard box can hold plants, fruit, vegetables, seedlings, or flowers, even when snow is outside. Maybe cucumbers can keep growing in the heart of winter. Keep the outside dry. Check the cardboard from time to time, including the bottom. Water on the outside may mean the plants must be moved into another box. Words in this book can be explained this way. Botany is the study of plants. Classify means to assign things or people to categories. Climate is the weather in an area over a long period of time. Conditions are the circumstances needed for something else to happen. Germinate means to begin growing from a seed. A greenhouse is a building, often of glass or plastic, where plants get heat, light, and cover from harsh weather. Hobbies are pastimes people choose for enjoyment and rest. Humidity is how much moisture is in the air. Photosynthesis is the process in which plants turn sunlight, carbon dioxide, and water into food. Wavelengths are the distances from one crest of a wave, or one low point, to the next.

17. Caesar and the Making of an Empire

1A map covers the Roman Republic from 200 bce to 100 bce. It names the Atlantic Ocean, the Black Sea, and the Mediterranean Sea. Lands marked include Gaul, which is France, plus Macedonia, Rome, Spain, Greece, and Africa, and Asia on the map is Turkey. One view shows the republic in 200 bce, while another shows it in 100 bce, so a reader can compare the earlier reach of Roman power with the later one. At Caesar's birth, Rome was expanding fast, and that growth would stir turmoil among Romans. Trouble filled the world that met Julius Caesar at birth. The Roman Republic was vast and powerful, for it stretched across great distances and held many provinces, yet widespread corruption troubled it anyway. Tension between social classes led into civil war, and the war tangled the republic for years. Danger lived inside Rome too, especially for anyone in politics. Set into that world, Caesar came to dominate both armies and public life, though his years were relatively few. Cleverness marked him. So did enormous energy. World history counts him as an important leader, which is hardly surprising once the scale of the republic and the danger of its politics are held together in one view. Many languages, many cultures, and some governments can follow their roots back to ancient Rome, and that long reach is part of why the troubled world of his birth still draws attention. The map therefore does more than name seas and lands. It places a rapidly expanding republic beside the turmoil that expansion was about to cause, and it prepares the story of a leader whose cleverness and energy would carry him into both armies and public life before a relatively short span of years had ended. Expansion, corruption, class tension, and civil war were already waiting when he was born. Public life in that city was dangerous for politicians.

2Rome began as a city-state, meaning a city plus the countryside that supplied it, and neighboring city-states largely shared one language, one culture, and one religion, yet they often fought. By 250 bce, Rome was the strongest city-state and controlled the whole Italian Peninsula, although kings ruled it then. Legend says that in 509 bce the people rose up, drove out their last king, and created the Roman Republic, after which hatred of rule by a monarch became a very important thread in their history. Citizens of the republic elected their own leaders, called consuls, and each year two consuls were chosen to govern. Those consuls then picked the people who would sit as representatives in the Senate, the lawmaking body. Wealthy landowners were called patricians. People with less land and less wealth were called plebeians. The two groups argued often, because a plebeian could not serve as a senator, although a plebeian could be elected to the assembly, which held no official power in Rome yet did hold influence. Growth brought new provinces, and a governor was placed over each one, so that food shipped into Rome could make a province's governor very rich, as could the sale of enslaved people in the city. Corruption, unfortunately, spread through provincial government. Under that system the rich patricians grew richer still, while Rome's economy lay in ruins. Lower-class people and peasants struggled, and the government offered no help, until patricians and plebeians pressed against each other so hard that the strain snapped. Civil war followed, and it was bloody. His birth fell inside that turmoil, on July 12 or July 13 in the year 100 bce, into a family that was patrician but not especially wealthy or influential. His parents still gave him a strong education. Father's death came at Caesar's sixteenth year, after which the son led the family, and in that same year he married Cornelia, daughter of an important politician among the plebeians. Power soon gathered around a man called Sulla, who was powerful and a patrician, and who commanded the young husband to dissolve the marriage. Caesar refused. The refusal made his bond with the plebeians clear.

3He stayed loyal to his wife and to his allies, but the loyalty put him in danger, because aggression marked how Sulla led and force was the tool he used to seize Rome. Disobeying him could bring arrest, or even death. To escape threats in the city, Caesar joined the army and fought in distant provinces, and a patrician family background made him an officer. War thrilled him, and the men respected his leadership. Word that Sulla had died in 78 bce brought him back, so that he resumed political work in Rome. A picture shows him in a crown of laurel leaves. Cunning served him away from battle as well, and he climbed fast through a political world full of traps. He linked himself to Pompey the Great, a popular hero of the army and a politician. After Cornelia died in 69 bce, he married Pompeia, Pompey's daughter, and the marriage strengthened their political tie. His rise continued. The vote of 63 bce made him Pontifex Maximus, so Rome's religion then had him as its high priest. Two years after that vote, a large province received him as governor, the land now called Spain. By 59 bce he had left Spain, and voters then made him consul, a result that senators from the patrician class found frustrating. One year was the length of that consulship. An appointment then sent him to govern Gaul across five years, and Gaul, now northern Italy and France, gave him room to enlarge the army and to push the republic outward. Beyond Gaul, a frontier ran as far as any Roman knew. He knew little of that land. Gallic tribes and Germanic tribes who lived there loomed large in Roman imagination, and famous legionnaires, Rome's soldiers, both respected and feared those peoples as masterful warriors. Leaders before him had taken armies past the frontier, with little success. Slavery sat at the center of Roman society, and important tasks fell to enslaved people. Farms depended on them. Mines depended on them. Houses depended on them for cooking and for keeping the rooms. Some were highly educated and held special skills, including work as doctors, accountants, and even soldiers. War supplied most of them through capture, after which buyers in Rome purchased them into slavery. They were treated as property. The people who enslaved them could buy them and could sell them.

4Northern tribes were strong fighters, yet Roman legions were organized far better, because a chain of command let them move quickly and with effect. In Gaul the better-equipped Roman army held one more large advantage, and that advantage was Caesar. Training in that region, under his lead, produced an army the world had rarely seen stronger. He earned his soldiers' respect and their loyalty. Intelligence and bravery marked him, and he insisted on fighting beside his own men. As a powerful speaker, he stirred the troops to fight harder and with greater strength. Rome knew Caesar and his legions as skilled soldiers, and also as brutal ones. People liked the victories. They did not like the cruelty. Three major successes came in Gaul. First, he brought all of Gaul under Roman control, so that money systems, government, and engineering would strongly shape Europe's later growth. Second, he won a loyalty from his legions that would not fade. Finally, the campaigns left him very wealthy. After a defeat, invading armies commonly looted their enemies, and generals commonly enslaved people taken in war, a custom that Caesar followed. Men were included. Women were included. Children were included. Profit came from selling them inside Rome. A picture shows Pompey and Crassus, with whom Caesar stood on good terms, so that he could smooth the differences between them and build a powerful alliance. Command of soldiers was only one side of him. Public politics was the other. Even while fighting in the provinces, he had to stay alert and active to survive political danger back in Rome. Ten years among the Gauls kept him far from the city, and paid agents watched his interests there through that whole stretch. For a time he and Pompey remained close. When he wanted that alliance kept, he offered the hand of his daughter Julia to Pompey, and the marriage became another link between the two men. Crassus counted as another ally in those days. Few men in Rome held more wealth.

5Pompey and Crassus had been rivals in politics, yet Caesar found a way to pull them onto one side, and together the three grew even stronger in Rome. The alliance carried so much weight that people called it the First Triumvirate, a group of three men who held power. Time passed. Victories among the Gauls stirred jealousy in his two partners. Julia's death in 54 bce cut the family bond between Caesar and Pompey, and the next year Crassus died in battle, so the last strands of the triumvirate snapped. Pompey turned against Caesar and joined wealthy patrician senators who hated Caesar and felt threatened by him. Reforming Rome's calendar stands among his greatest achievements. The old count followed the moon. It was lunar, tied to monthly cycles of the moon, and it held 355 days, whereas a common year today holds 365 days. In the years before he acted, leaders picked where ten extra days would be placed, and that choice let them shift important dates for elections and for holidays. Working with astronomers, he built a calendar based on the way Earth moves around the Sun. Such a calendar is called solar. Extra days were set into particular months. The idea of a leap year was introduced. When the time in Gaul ended, he wanted to come back to Rome, but rivals in the Senate demanded that he give up command of the army first. He knew Pompey, now an enemy, had troops and would be waiting, and he suspected that a return without his own soldiers would mean arrest, and possibly death. In 49 bce he marched with the army to the Rubicon River, the border of Gaul and Italy, knowing the march would be read as an act of war. He hoped to take control of the state. He also hoped to repair a government rotten with corruption. The move opened a terrible civil war against Pompey's men, and experienced troops under Caesar defeated Pompey's forces quickly. Pompey fled the city and was killed soon after. A picture shows Caesar leading soldiers across the Rubicon into Italy. He came back a triumphant hero, yet government stood in crisis, and he named himself dictator for life. Growing power deeply upset many senators, who feared he would not stop until he wore a king's title.

6His time as head of state was short, yet within it he set up many policies meant to ease debt and money trouble for lower-class citizens. He also tried to meet unemployment by paying people to labor on many public buildings. He widened the Senate so it included individuals from cities other than Rome, and many supporters of Pompey were forgiven. Some even received important posts in the city. Support for the plebeians had been his aim. Repair of the republic had been the other aim. A circle of patrician senators answered with a plan to kill him. March 15, 44 bce, was the day, and Romans knew it as the Ides of March. The plot ended in his killing. A German painter, Karl Theodor von Piloty, made a picture in 1865 and called it Caesar's Murder. Murder made him a martyr at once, and Romans placed him among the gods, a declaration that came in 42 bce. The killing brought chaos, and further civil war followed. When the fighting ended, the Roman Empire had been born. He had been brutal and cunning, yet victories in war laid the base for that empire, while Greek knowledge and Roman knowledge, including military organization and law, would spread into many new lands. The empire would last for centuries, reaching from North Africa to Western Asia, so his leadership played a key part in shaping modern Europe and much of today's world. A map of the republic in 45 bce shows it at the time of his death, and that later view belongs to the close of his life rather than to the years of early expansion. Debt relief, paid public labor, a wider Senate, and forgiveness for former opponents were therefore crowded into a brief rule that the plot cut short. The painting keeps the memory of the killing, while the empire that followed the renewed civil war carried organization and law across a vast span for centuries.

7A life timeline for Julius Caesar lists these moments in order. Birth came in 100 bce. In 84 bce his father died and he married Cornelia. From 83 to 82 bce, Sulla gained control of Rome. In 78 bce Sulla died, and Caesar returned. In 73 bce he was elected Pontifex. In 69 bce Cornelia died. Pompeia became his wife in 67 bce, and Pompey, an ally, was her father. In 63 bce he was elected Pontifex Maximus. In 62 bce he divorced Pompeia. From 60 to 59 bce he came back to Rome, won election as consul, married Calpurnia, and formed the First Triumvirate. In 58 bce he became governor of Gaul and defeated tribes to the north. In 55 bce he defeated Germanic tribes that invaded Gaul, led legions across the Rhine River, and invaded Britain. In 54 bce his daughter Julia died, and she had been married to Pompey. In 53 bce Crassus was beaten in battle and killed. In 49 bce he crossed the Rubicon, and civil war began. In 44 bce the Ides of March brought the assassination. Allied means joined with others for a shared cause. To be assassinated is to die in an attack arranged beforehand, and the motive is often political. Campaigning means carrying out a planned series of military actions. Chaos means confusion, a lack of order. Corruption means dishonest or criminal behavior by people who hold power. A dictator is a leader ruling with total power, usually by force. Embroiled means caught deep in a conflict or a hard problem. Legislative names the section of government charged with writing the laws. A martyr suffers or dies because of beliefs or actions. A monarchy is rule by one person who was not elected, such as a king or a queen. An orator speaks before the public, and eloquence is what sets the best of them apart. Once Rome took over a territory, or an entire country, that land was called a province.

18. Calgary's Great Outdoor Show

1A map places Calgary in Alberta, and Alberta in Canada. The Pacific Ocean lies to the west. The United States lies to the south. North America is the continent. Topics follow this order. The parade comes first. Farm life and animals come next. A camp on the Elbow River follows that. Rodeo events and chuckwagon races follow the camp. A look ahead to next year comes last. Prairies stretch across this part of Canada. The Rocky Mountains rise beside them. Calgary grew up where those two landscapes meet. It began as a cowboy town. It is a city now. More than one million people live there. A picture shows a cowboy herding horses outside the city. Every summer, for more than a hundred years, the city has staged a huge rodeo and show. The point is to honor Western history. The show lasts ten days. Its name is the Calgary Stampede. Its nickname calls it the top outdoor show anywhere on Earth. Parades fill the city. Horse shows fill it. Carnival rides fill it. Barbecues fill it. More events fill it too. From the start, the rodeo was the biggest attraction. Many people condemn those events because animals can be harmed. History is another argued-over part of the Stampede. During the 1800s, settlers moved onto that land. Indigenous people had lived on that land for thousands of years. Cowboy culture, the thing the Stampede celebrates, is tied to that painful past. Indigenous people were not always allowed to take part. As time passed, many Indigenous nations started offering pieces of culture at the show.

2The year 1886 was the start, but the name was not Stampede yet. The local fair was called the Calgary Exhibition. Farmers showed crops. Ranchers showed animals. People showed crafts. More exhibitions followed over the next several years. An American cowboy and entertainer noticed how popular Calgary's fairs were. His name was Guy Weadick. In 1912 he staged the first event under the Stampede name. A parade was part of it. A rodeo was part of it. Riding demonstrations were part of it. Ranching displays were part of it. Animal displays were part of it. Those pieces are still in the show. The first one was a huge success. Weadick organized more stampedes in 1919. He organized another in 1923. Then the Stampede joined the Calgary Exhibition. The combined show was larger. It became a yearly event. A picture shows big crowds at the Opening Day Parade in 1930. Another picture shows the mayor greeting those crowds while on horseback. Opening day is a summer Friday, and it starts in the morning. Downtown streets are lined with people. Most of them wear cowboy hats. The packed crowd feels a rush of excitement. Horns blast. Drums beat. The Stampede Show Band starts down the street. People shout their best cowboy yell: Yee-haw! Opening Day shirts are the brightest ones the riders own. Cowboys wear them. Cowgirls wear them too. They brush their horses so the coats shine in the morning sun. Painted wagons roll behind huge draft horses. Two full hours pass before the whole parade has gone by. Music leads the crowd. The walk ends at Stampede Park. That is where they watch the events.

3Ranchers and farmers bring their best animals. They also enter old-style contests. One contest is blacksmithing. Another is sheep shearing. Giant barns hold hundreds of animals. Horses are there. Beef cattle are there. Dairy cows are there. Woolly sheep are there. Chickens are there. Piglets are there. Skilled herding dogs are there. Tiny horses are a crowd favorite. They barely reach an average adult's waist. They still have the full spirit of a large horse. Children race wild ponies. A picture shows a young rider trying to catch a pony in that race. At the other end of size is Draft Horse Town. Some of these horses weigh over 907 kilograms, or 2,000 pounds. On old Alberta farms they did the work tractors do now. Factory loads were part of their old work too. The Heavy Horse Pull shows their strength. It shows their beauty too. Teams strain as they drag huge sleds. Massive blocks load those sleds. A top team can drag more than 4,537 kilograms. That weight is over 10,000 pounds. Nations take part in the Stampede at the Elbow River Camp. One nation is the Siksika, said SIK-sik-a. One is the Piikani, said pee-KAN-ee. One is the Kainai, said KY-ny. One is the Tsuut'ina, said tsoo-TI-na. One is the Stoney Nakoda, said na-KO-da. When the Stampede was new, the Indian Act was already a law. The year of that law was 1876. It limited the freedoms of Indigenous peoples. That Act has not been erased. Some parts of it were later repealed. In one picture, an Indigenous woman sews. The design she sews is traditional. The 1876 law kept Indigenous people from leaving reserves. Reserves were small lands. Officials had already taken ancestral homelands. Then they forced people onto those small lands. Children were taken away from their families. They were sent to schools far from home. Breaking the Act could mean fines. It could mean forced labor. It could mean jail. Traditional clothes were illegal. Speaking and singing in Indigenous languages was illegal. Dance was illegal. Celebrating Indigenous cultures and religions was illegal. Temporary exceptions let some people join the Calgary Stampede. Decades passed before wider freedoms came. Many Indigenous peoples say the Act still gets in the way of their ways of life.

4The year was 1912. Weadick brought a plan to people who spoke for Indigenous nations. His Stampede vision needed Indigenous people in it. He worked with politicians. He arranged a pause in the Indian Act. The pause let Indigenous people travel off the reserves. It let them practice some parts of their culture in public. Communities did not all agree. In the end they said yes. The reason was a chance to practice traditions freely, even for a short time only. Two years later the federal government tightened the rules even more. Public performance was forbidden. Traditional clothing in public was forbidden. For years after that, Indigenous people could not join the Stampede. Today they help run it. They sit on the organizing boards. They help plan the event. In 2018 the gathering place got a new name: Elbow River Camp. In many Indigenous languages, the word for Calgary points to a bend. That bend is in the Elbow River. Each year the Stampede lets Indigenous communities share parts of their culture with visitors. Many families put up tipis. They stay on the festival grounds. Visitors are invited inside. Families teach traditions. They teach history. They teach culture. Opening ceremonies include dancing. They include drumming. Flags go up each morning. Flags come down each evening. Each Indigenous nation has a flag. Alberta has a flag. Canada has a flag. All of those are flown. Daily powwows matter too. A picture shows the Canadian flag flying high at the camp. The Nakoda flag flies there too. Traditions differ from tribe to tribe. Traditional regalia is usual. Dance contests happen sometimes. Outdoor cooking lessons teach visitors about foods that matter to each tribe. Meat-cutting contests show how to slice meat thin without leaving holes. Beadwork is on display. Storytelling is on display. Games are on display. Those parts teach and entertain.

5Rides and the big stage show look forward, not only backward. Follow thrilled screams and laughter. Bright lights of the midway are there. Few midways anywhere in North America are bigger. People fill it day and night. Rides and attractions fill it too. Concerts bring the biggest names in rock music. They bring the biggest names in country music. A juggler seems to stand on nearly every street corner. A mime does too. A magician does too. The biggest production is the Grandstand Show. It feels like a rock concert. It feels like a Broadway play. It feels like a circus. Training lasts the whole year. Some of those students are only eleven. A school for stage skills is where they prepare. The stage is huge. Lights cover it. Smoke covers it. Giant screens cover it. Platforms float far above the audience. Performers in fancy costumes fill each place on the stage. They sing. They dance. They do amazing acrobatic tricks. Some midway rides give visitors spectacular views. The Championship Rodeo is the biggest and most famous Stampede event. Eager fans pack the Grandstand. Anyone who steps into the center ring must wear Western clothes. A typical match puts one person on an animal. That animal might weigh ten times what the rider weighs. Bareback bronc riding has no saddle. The rider tries to last eight seconds on a bucking horse. A single hand grips a strap. The strap is fastened around the horse's belly. The horse leaps. The horse jumps. The horse twists. It is trying to throw the rider. A full eight seconds is required to qualify. The winner's prize is $100,000. A picture shows a bareback rider hanging on.

6Saddle bronc riding is similar. This time the cowboy sits in a saddle. Reins and stirrups are how he tries to control the bucking horse. Bull riding comes next. The basic rules match. The animal does not. The cowboy is on a huge bucking bull. The bulls jump and spin. Picture oversized rubber bands. Eight seconds is the hold time. The next move is a leap down from that animal. A chase can follow. Rodeo clowns run in before the rider gets hurt. They are skilled handlers of bulls. Their job is to distract the animal. They herd it away. The rider escapes. Steer wrestling matches its name. A rider on a horse chases a running steer. The rider jumps onto the steer. The rider pulls it down by the horns. Barrel racing is a timed test of horse control. Highly trained horses loop several barrels. The turns are tight. Balance is tested. Speed is tested. Skill is tested. A picture shows a rider and her horse rounding a barrel. Last comes the wild chuckwagon race. Earlier in the Stampede, crowds already saw a small version. Those were miniature chuckwagon races. Four horses make a team. They pull a chuckwagon with a canvas cover. Outriders are cowboys on their own horses. They line up behind the wagons. An outrider stands behind a wagon's tailgate. Poles are flung into the wagon bed. A rubber stove is flung in too. Wagon teams blast off at a gallop. Outriders leap onto their horses. They race after the wagons. The wagons bounce, rattle, and clang. Their path around the barrels is a risky figure-eight. Then they race the track at full speed. Hooves pound. Wagons rattle. Grandstand seats shake. First place pays $100,000. Many fans rank it as rodeo's roughest contest. The year 1923 is when these wagon races joined the Stampede. In those early years, winning meant something extra. Victory went to the first driver who got his stove burning after he crossed the line.

7Children get many chances to join the Stampede each year. Ten days at the show can leave you tired. They can also open your eyes. Thousands of workers take part each year. Thousands of volunteers take part. Thousands of participants take part. A show this large is hard work. Calgary is proud of the Stampede. In more recent years, Indigenous perspectives have been included. That inclusion has added even more cultural value. The show is a rare way for a city to mark its history. It is a way to think about that history. It brings people together. The wider world gets a picture of the Canadian West. Word meanings finish the book. An attraction is someone or something people like to see or do. Repealed means ended, removed, or reversed, when the thing is a law or a policy. Bucking describes an animal that jumps while kicking, with its back arched. Restricted means limited, controlled, or confined. Inclusion is the act of bringing someone into a group. A rodeo is a show or contest of skills with cattle and horses. Indigenous refers to a land's original people. Settlers make a lasting new home on a frontier. A powwow is an Indigenous gathering. Dance belongs in it. Music belongs in it. Arts belong in it. Crafts belong in it. Food belongs in it. Straining means showing great effort. Provisions, in the word list, means supplies, especially supplies for a journey. Vast means great in size, in number, or in amount.

19. California's Race for Gold

1A picture shows prospectors digging in California around 1852. The contents list Keeping a Secret on page 4, Panning on page 6, and The Forty-Niners on page 7. By Ship appears on page 9, By Wagon on page 10, and Equal Opportunity? on page 12. The Golden State is on page 15, and the Glossary is on page 16. Keeping a Secret. On the morning of January 24, 1848, James Marshall made an inspection of a water ditch. The ditch carried water from the American River through a new sawmill that his crew was building in California. Workers had deepened the outgoing stretch so the water would run faster. At the far end, something bright sat about six inches below the surface. Marshall gathered several bits and held them out for the crew to see. The crew ran tests, and the bits were gold. Marshall carried the gold to John Sutter, the man who owned the mill. Sutter held forty-eight thousand acres in California and named the land New Switzerland, after the country of his birth. He had purchased the acres from Mexico's government, yet the true owners were the Indigenous people known as the Nisenan. His bargain with Mexico said he must not harm any Nisenan people in the area. Even so, he drilled many Native people to serve in a private army of his own. He also seized other Native people and forced them to work the land as enslaved laborers. Sutter pressed everyone to hide the news because he wanted the riches kept for himself.

2A map shows territory the United States gained in the Mexican-American War. The treaty included land that now forms California, Nevada, and Utah, most of Arizona and New Mexico, and parts of Colorado and Wyoming. Many Native peoples had their homes on these lands. Mexico had claimed ownership, and after the war Mexico turned the lands over to the United States. Labels on the map include the United States, Sutter's Mill, San Francisco, the Pacific Ocean, the Rio Grande, Mexico, North America, and the Atlantic Ocean. Six days after the find, Mexico signed the paper that ended the Mexican-American War, and under that treaty California passed to the United States. Gold's discovery was still unknown to both governments. Sam Brannan kept a store close to Sutter's Mill and soon let the secret out because profit was what he wanted from the news. Digging for gold did not interest him. In San Francisco, the city close by, he bought up every shovel, put gold dust into a bottle, and raced through the streets shouting about the discovery. The city held 850 people, and it nearly emptied out. Brannan sold each person picks, axes, pans, and shovels, and he charged very high prices. Panning. Gold in California did not match gold in most other places, because it was not sealed deep under the ground. Long before, erosion had washed the metal down from the mountains, and rivers then held it. Miners used placer mining. A shallow, flat pan let them sort gold out of the riverbed, because gold is far heavier than gravel. Prospectors stood in the current, scooped gravel into the pan, took big rocks out first, and swirled the pan with care. Dirt and gravel washed over the edge with the water, while bright flakes stayed on the bottom. On most days a miner found only a little gold. In money of today, a usual day's find came to somewhere from 10 dollars to 15 dollars. Word Wise. A prospector is someone who moves to a place where gold might lie. The prospect is the chance of a find, and the dream is to strike gold and become rich.

3The Forty-Niners. Talk of western gold raced through the states in the East. An official in California mailed a report to Washington, D.C., and a sample of the metal traveled with the report. Congress heard about the find from the president during December 1848, and the story was true. A picture from 1852 shows a California miner lifting gravel. A mood called gold fever then seized many people. The phrase means greed, plus excitement that spreads from person to person, after gold is found. In those years a worker often earned less than one dollar for a day's labor, so the mines looked like the chance of a lifetime. Around ninety thousand people joined the rush in 1849 and became known as forty-niners. Women made up about 10 percent of them, and that share was nine thousand women. Forty-niners set out from every region of the United States. Mexico sent people as well, and so did Central America and South America. Asia sent travelers, and so did Australia and New Zealand. The crowds also included Black people. About 200 to 300 of them were enslaved, and enslavers had compelled them to make the trip to California. Free Black people headed west too, hoping the rivers held gold. By 1852, about 2,000 Black people were living in California, about 1 percent of all the people there. Reaching the mines could take months, and the cost was high. Travelers paid for transportation and for supplies that had to last until they arrived. Many forty-niners walked away from jobs and from families, planning to grow rich fast and then go home. Others welcomed whatever adventure waited. The first people at the rivers near the mill came from California, Oregon, and Mexico, and locals had only a short way to travel, with pack animals carrying their loads. People coming by boat from distant countries needed more time, and crossing the full width of the United States took longer still. In that era, a traveler could reach California from China more easily than from the East Coast. A route map labels North America, Saint Louis, Missouri, New York City, Sacramento, the Atlantic Ocean, San Francisco, Panama, the Pacific Ocean, South America, and Cape Horn. A key explains three paths. Travel over land took five to eight months. The path across Panama took one month, but only if a ship could be caught on the Pacific side. The path around Cape Horn took five to eight months.

4By Ship. About half the forty-niners picked a sea voyage, hoping to stay off land held by Native peoples. A ship needed from five to eight months. It left the East Coast, rounded the southern tip of South America, and sailed north to California. The cheapest ticket cost 75 dollars, about 2,300 dollars in money of today. Sleeping space was a tiny bunk low in the ship. Food was dried meat, plus hard biscuits that contained weevils, and the drink was water. Shipwreck, seasickness, and disease brought suffering. Many riders said the crush of people was among the worst trials, and boredom ranked with it. Printed posters offered passage, and each notice promised a ride that began in New York City and finished in San Francisco. Some riders tried to save days by cutting across Panama. They could paddle a canoe and then walk 60 miles through jungle, a stretch of 97 kilometers, hoping a second ship waited on the far shore. The land was extreme. Bad weather was a hazard they did not know well, and wild animals were another. Illness struck many of them. Even after a successful crossing, the next ship might not appear for weeks, and sometimes the wait lasted months. A drawing made around 1900 shows people on the move together, and their line of wagons was called a train. By Wagon. A wagon journey lasted about as long as the voyage by sea. Native peoples still held much of the ground that lay between East Coast travelers and California. Newcomers heading west often hunted where they had no permission, took goods from Native peoples, and attacked them as well. Native peoples therefore met the newcomers with hostility. Most departures began at Saint Louis, Missouri, at the time the farthest west of any city in the United States. Wagons rolled along the California Trail, which covered 2,100 miles of flat prairie, a distance of 3,380 kilometers. On a good day a wagon might cover about 15 miles, or 24 kilometers, but the day had to go well. The wagon could not break, rain could not be heavy, and the oxen had to stay healthy. Drivers still had to ford rivers, climb mountains, drop down cliffs, and cross deserts.

5Rain hammered the travelers, and so did wind and snow. Sickness was another threat, and so were hunger and accidents. Arrival in California did not ease the load. Prospectors slept in mining camps built from tents and rough shelters, and each workday ran for twelve hours. Illness was common, often caused by bad living conditions and a poor diet. Giving up was still difficult, because any fresh pan might hide enough gold to make a person rich. Around 1850, a picture caught miners in a California camp named El Dorado. Far away, the original El Dorado is a South American legend, and stories describe it as a place heaped with riches. A Fair Chance? For Native peoples, the rush for gold was a disaster. It opened a road into the West, and crowds of adventurers and settlers poured onto Native land. California was home to many different Native groups. As forty-niners pushed west, violent attacks drove Native peoples off much of that land. Thousands were killed, and disease killed thousands more. Statehood arrived for California in 1850, and the government of the United States then took charge of the land, including gold-bearing ground. Fear and hatred soon caused thousands of Native peoples to be killed. Fresh laws let settlers arrest Native people for small offenses, and payment of the fines was forced in the form of labor on ranches. California's Native population, before the rush began, stood near three hundred thousand. Twenty years later, more than one hundred thousand of them were dead. Strong Starts, Empty Endings. Several men tied to the first discovery finished with nothing they could show. John Sutter lost the property that glittered with promise, because the United States would not honor the land grant Mexico had given him. In the end, Sutter's fortune was gone. Sam Brannan's fortune was gone too, and James Marshall lost his fortune as well.

6As prospectors filled the hills, white miners turned against other groups who hunted gold, and Chinese miners faced the strongest opposition. At times, white prospectors used force to drive miners from outside the United States off the diggings. Almost three thousand Chinese people arrived in California in 1851. A ruined harvest in China lifted the count, and more than twenty thousand came the following year. California taxed any miner who had come from outside the United States. Some miners who were already citizens wanted the work to be so hard that newcomers would quit and leave. A picture shows Chinese miners searching California gravel around 1850. Of the miners who reached California in 1849, one in five died before six months had passed. Finding gold did not always keep it. Robbers took shares of it, gambling took more, and everyday goods, sold at steep prices, took still more. A few early prospectors did well, but most of the wealth flowed to large companies. Those firms could blast hillsides with powerful jets of water, and they could also sink deep shafts. Prices Out of Control. A forty-niner could buy almost anything, if the price was no object.
