The list below gives San Francisco costs in 1849 and the matching costs in 2021 dollars, after a change for inflation. Edward Dolnick gathered these prices in a history of the rush. The book's title is The Rush, and its subtitle is America's Fevered Quest for Fortune. The years it covers run from 1848 to 1853. A can of peas was 6 dollars then and 206 dollars in 2021. An egg was 1 dollar then and 34 dollars in 2021. A breakfast was 43 dollars then and 1,479 dollars in 2021. A pound of coffee, about 0.45 kilograms, was 3 dollars then and 103 dollars in 2021. A mule was 360 dollars then and 12,384 dollars in 2021. A pair of boots was 96 dollars then and 3,302 dollars in 2021. Sellers who supplied the miners built fortunes, and such sellers are entrepreneurs. Sam Brannan was among the earliest people in the country to reach a million dollars. Sturdy work pants were the product Levi Strauss sold, and people knew those pants as blue jeans. Women, more than others, found fresh openings in the West. They launched businesses. Some cooked meals, some kept boarding houses, and some washed clothes for the men in the camps. One owner of businesses was Mary Ellen Pleasant, a Black American, and she also worked with the Underground Railroad. Women were not treated as serious gold seekers during the rush. Some accounts say Pleasant took jobs as a cook and as a housekeeper for a hidden reason, because the work put her near people who had money and she could listen to their private talk. During the Gold Rush she bought buildings and businesses, then sold them, and that trade made her a millionaire. A portrait shows Mary Ellen Pleasant.

7One view shows San Francisco in 1851, and a second view shows the same city in the present day. The Golden State. The greatest gains from the Gold Rush went to white settlers, to the government of the United States, and to investors who already had wealth. For Native peoples, the rush was devastating. Settlers swept into California in numbers around three hundred thousand, and most of those settlers were white. During the 1860s, the country started to join the East with the West by a railway that crossed the continent. That transcontinental line brought still more harm to Native lands. The search for gold altered the western United States in a lasting way. Today California holds more people than any other state, and its economy is enormous, bigger than the economy of most countries. Almost two centuries after the rush, California still fits the name people gave it, the Golden State. Glossary. Devastating, an adjective on page 15, means causing severe harm to a body or to feelings. Hatred, a noun on page 12, means a fierce feeling of dislike or disgust. Hazards, a noun on page 9, means possible sources of danger or of risk. Economy, a noun on page 15, means the movement of money through industry, trade, and finance inside a country or a region. Hostility, a noun on page 10, means deep anger joined with an unfriendly spirit. Entrepreneurs, a noun on page 14, means people who launch businesses and keep them running. Settlers, a noun on page 12, means people who build a permanent new home along a frontier. Transcontinental, an adjective on page 15, means reaching across a whole continent. Erosion, a noun on page 6, means rock or soil carried off by water, wind, or ice in a natural way. Wealthy, an adjective on page 15, means in possession of a great deal of money or of goods. Greed, a noun on page 7, means a selfish hunger to hold more of something than a person needs. Gravel, a noun on page 6, means loose chips and fragments of rock mixed together.

20. Cities That Stand on Water

1A map titled Water Cities Around the World marks oceans and continents. The labels include Asia, Europe, North America, the Atlantic Ocean, and the Pacific Ocean. Africa, the Indian Ocean, South America, and Australia appear as well. Twelve places are numbered on the map. Venice, Italy, is number 1. Amsterdam, in the Netherlands, is number 2. Reine, Norway, is number 3, and Singapore is number 4. Palm Jumeirah, in Dubai, is number 5. Ganvié, in Benin, is number 6, and Fadiouth, in Senegal, is number 7. The Uros Floating Village, in Peru, is number 8. Mexcaltitán, in Mexico, is number 9. Auckland, in New Zealand, is number 10. Sausalito, in California, is number 11, and Manarola, in Italy, is number 12. Living Near Water, page 4. Europe, page 5. Asia, page 7. Africa, page 9. South America, page 11. North America, page 12. Oceania, page 14. People and Water, page 15. Glossary, page 16. Venice's main waterway is the Grand Canal. Living Near Water. Travelers from many parts of the globe visit Venice, in Italy. They come to see a famous city of canals and bridges. The city stands on more than a hundred islands. Venice is the water city that most people know first. It is not the only one. A water city is a place built on water, or built beside it. Some are tiny communities. Others are huge urban areas. They sit near oceans, seas, bays, lakes, and rivers, or they sit in those waters. Every continent has them except Antarctica. Each one exists for its own reasons. Each one has a story worth hearing.

2Europe. Amsterdam, in the Netherlands. Canals made this European city famous as well. It is the capital of its country. Roughly one-third of the Netherlands lies under the level of the sea. People have taken back about one-sixth of the land. They pumped water out of lakes and out of the North Sea. The city itself sits about 2 meters under sea level. That depth is 6.6 feet. Amsterdam began in the late twelfth century. It started as a village of fishers. By the seventeenth century it had become an important seaport. Today it ranks among the largest seaports in Europe. A map of Europe places Amsterdam beside the Atlantic Ocean. More than 1,200 bridges cross the city's canals. A moat ringed Amsterdam from 1480 until 1585. During the 1600s the number of people shot upward as the city spread. Workers emptied swamps of their water. They dug three more canals around the downtown. With the older canal, that made four waterways. People used them to move goods, to defend the city, and to manage water. Beyond those main canals, 161 more canals wind through the city. Together they stretch over 100 kilometers, or 62 miles. Nearly 100 small islands appear because of the way these canals slice through Amsterdam. More than 1,200 bridges tie the islands together. For centuries the canals were the chief routes for getting around. Smaller boats are the main users now. Even so, the canals still shape the character of the city. Reine, in Norway. Norway's tiny fishing village carries a bold nickname. People call it The Most Beautiful Place in the World. It lies more than 100 kilometers above the Arctic Circle. That distance is 62 miles. Reine sits on the coast of one island in the Lofoten group. Visitors can fish, paddle kayaks, ski, watch whales, hike, and walk gorgeous beaches. The village is also a fine spot for striking views of the northern lights.

3A map of Asia shows Singapore beside the Pacific Ocean. Singapore. This port city is one of the busiest in the world. It is the only island city-state on Earth. That means the island is a city and an independent country at the same time. Sixty-three islands make up the country. Resources supplied by nature are scarce in Singapore. Goods from elsewhere have to fill that gap. Nearly every needed item is brought in from outside. From the 1960s onward, dry land has grown by almost 25 percent. Amsterdam gained land by taking seawater away. Singapore did the opposite. It poured rocks and sand into the water to build new ground. A project that started in 2016 will copy Amsterdam's method. The goal is still more land. The United Arab Emirates, or UAE, is the country that holds Dubai. The city has a modern look. Many building projects fill the city. One of the largest is Palm Islands. The plan calls for three artificial islands. Each island is shaped like a palm tree. Workers pile huge amounts of sand and rock along the coast. The new shores will add hundreds of miles of coastline. They will also hold homes for many thousands of people. Building started in 2001. The first island was finished late in 2016. A curved seawall wraps the island. The wall shields it from strong waves and from storms. A map marks Dubai in Asia, next to the Indian Ocean. Palm Jumeirah ranks among the largest artificial islands anywhere.

4People sometimes call the village of Ganvié the Venice of Africa. A map places Ganvié in Africa, near the Atlantic Ocean. Africa. Ganvié, in Benin. Modern Singapore and modern Dubai stand in sharp contrast to Ganvié (GAWN-vye). Ganvié is the largest village on stilts in Africa. The water beneath it is Lake Nokoué, said NOHK-we. Benin is the country. About twenty thousand people live there. About three thousand buildings stand there. Only the school sits on solid land. A cemetery is the other place on land. The village began in the seventeenth century. In that era, people in West Africa were being captured. Europeans then sold them as slaves. A powerful group called the Fon took people from other groups as well. The Fon sold those captives into slavery. Fon religion did not allow the Fon to chase anyone who lived on the water. A group called the Tofinu fled to Lake Nokoué so they would not be captured. They built the stilt village. They shaped a way of living that still goes on. Their success shows in the village name. The name means we survived. Fishing is the main way villagers earn a living. Underwater fences let them keep fish and raise more. Chickens live there, and so do goats. Their ground is grass that pushes up through the lake. Travel is by long, narrow canoes. Those canoes are called pirogues. Fadiouth, or Shell Island, in Senegal. The people of Fadiouth (fad-YOOT), in Senegal, live on an island made only of clamshells. For more than three centuries they have eaten clams. They reuse the shells. Shells form the buildings, the streets, and the ground itself. Roots of trees and of reeds hold the shells in place.

5South America. A map shows the Uros islands, with the Atlantic Ocean marked nearby. The Uru people build canoes from reeds so they can travel. Uros, a floating village in Peru. The people of Uros moved onto the water to stay safe, much as the people of Ganvié did. More than five hundred years ago, the Uru fled to Lake Titicaca. The Inca people and the Colla people had taken their land. About two thousand Uru now live on the lake. Their home is about seventy islands that float. Reeds are the building material. Each island is from 1.2 to 2.4 meters thick. That is about 4 to 8 feet. The bottom of an island slowly breaks apart. Fresh reeds must be laid on top all the time. Reeds also become canoes, houses, and furniture. Fishing brings in a living, and so does the sale of crafts. Daily life still follows traditional ways. Even so, some modern tools are present. Uros runs a radio station of its own. Solar panels power some homes. Some residents use motorboats. North America. A map places Mexcaltitán beside the Pacific Ocean. The town sits on a sandbar off the coast of Mexico. The sandbar is 400 meters long, or 1,300 feet. Mexcaltitán, in Mexico. Between the fourteenth century and the sixteenth century, the Aztec people ruled wide parts of Mesoamerica. A legend places their first home on an imagined island set inside a lagoon. Their gods told them to search for a new homeland. The search lasted two hundred years. They then founded Tenochtitlán, and that city was their capital. Spanish forces conquered the city in 1521. After that conquest, Tenochtitlán took the name Mexico City.

6Say the name as mes-kahl-tee-TAHN. Mexcaltitán is a small island that people made. It lies near Mexico's Pacific coast. Some historians believe Aztec civilization started in this place. Old records show that early Aztecs paddled small canoes. Residents of Mexcaltitán use canoes of that same kind. A map drawn in 1579 puts the mythical island and Mexcaltitán in one spot. The island measures about 350 meters by 40 meters. Those lengths are 1,150 feet and 130 feet. About eight hundred people live there now. Their houses are built of adobe, of brick, and of cement. Many earn a living by catching shrimp. Local restaurants buy the catch. People sometimes call this water town the Mexican Venice. Summer is the rainy season. In those months, a boat is the only way to move through the streets. The island has a single soccer field, and floodwater covers it. Children play a game they call water soccer on that field. During flood season, local people boat in the streets and swim in them too. Oceania. Auckland is the largest city in New Zealand. A map of the South Pacific shows Auckland near Australia. Auckland, in New Zealand. This modern city holds 1.5 million people. It stands on the North Island, in the South Pacific Ocean. Two large harbors border the city. Between them is an isthmus. At the narrowest point, the isthmus is less than 2 kilometers wide, or 1.2 miles. One harbor opens east into the Pacific Ocean. The other opens west into the Tasman Sea. Residents call Auckland the City of Sails. Boat owners account for about one-sixth of the people. The city has held the America's Cup yacht race two times. Beaches number in the thousands. Water activities include kayaking and parasailing. They also include swimming, surfing, fishing, diving, and riding horses on the beach.

7Pictures for this closing page suggest California, Italy, and an aircraft carrier. People and Water. Water cities come in more kinds than the ones already described. Italy, for instance, has a tiny town of fishers. Brightly colored homes there stand on steep cliffs of rock. Northern California has a floating community. The homes are houseboats of several kinds. Members of the military may live for months on aircraft carriers. Water means different things to different people. For someone who lives in a water city, it may mean play. It may mean work, safety, or a whole way of living. It may also mean a tie to nature. It may mean a tie to the rest of the world. These cities are proof of something large. People can make a home in almost any setting on Earth. Glossary. adobe (noun), page 13: sandy clay mixed with straw and dried so it forms bricks. reclaimed (verb), page 5: taken back, or improved, so that people can use it. artificial (adjective), page 8: made by people, rather than found in nature. residents (noun), page 9: the people, and sometimes animals, who dwell in one spot. drained (verb), page 6: made a liquid, or energy, run out of something. seaport (noun), page 5: a town or a harbor where ships from the sea come and go. stilt (noun), page 9: a post that holds a building above ground or above water. The word also means one of two long poles that lift a walker high up. import (verb), page 7: to bring goods in from another country, or another state, so they can be sold. isthmus (noun), page 14: a thin strip of land that joins two bigger masses of land. transportation (noun), page 6: the moving of things, or of people, from one place to another place. lagoon (noun), page 12: a shallow, quiet body of water. It may lie between a reef and the shore, or in the middle of an atoll. urban (adjective), page 4: having to do with cities or towns, and with the people who live in them.

21. Climate Change: What the Evidence Shows

1The parts of this book are what climate change is, the evidence, the causes, possible results, what is being done, a closing set of questions, and a word list. What is the day like outside? Warm or cold? Sunny or rainy? A single day is easy to judge. Climate is the harder question. Over long stretches, weather follows patterns. Those lasting patterns are climate. The patterns can shift. Europe from 1400 to 1800 was colder than Europe from 1100 to 1300. The weather pattern changed between those eras. Many scientists think another shift is underway, back toward warmth. Global warming is their name for it. Some people fear harm to communities of plants and animals, and harm to human societies. Other people see little cause for worry. This book reports what scientists have found. Read with care. Then decide what you yourself think.

2Evidence is required when scientists offer an idea, including the idea that the planet is warming. What have they found? Weather scientists, called meteorologists, have kept surface-temperature records from the mid-1800s onward. Those readings include air near the ground, the kind an outdoor thermometer shows. Ocean surface temperatures are included too. The world average has climbed since the late 1800s. The climb is roughly 1.0 to 1.8 degrees Fahrenheit, or 0.6 to 1.0 degrees Celsius. That recent rise was compared with clues about climate thousands of years earlier. In 2006, a group of scientists in the United States reported a conclusion. Probably no point in the last twelve thousand years had a warmer surface. Old photos add more evidence. Mountain glaciers photographed from the early 1900s into the middle of that century look larger than the same glaciers today. Some are melting, and the shrink is speeding up. The sightings include Alaska. They include South America, Europe, and Asia. Many scientists blame rising global surface temperatures. The ice shelf is called Larsen B. It lies in Antarctica. Its age was four hundred years. Melting helped it break into smaller pieces.

3Ice near both poles is melting too. Much of the proof comes from satellite cameras over the polar regions. From the 1970s onward, sea ice has shrunk in the far northern ocean. That ocean is the Arctic, around the North Pole. Between 2004 and 2005, a loss the size of Texas was measured. Melting ocean ice may put polar bears at risk. In winter they hunt seals from ice floes, which are floating ice platforms. A 2005 report said the Arctic Sea has fewer floes than before. Many bears are not eating enough. Some may drown. Near the South Pole, satellites show melting of sea ice and of ice sheets, the ice that covers land, in western Antarctica. In 2002, an ice shelf bigger in area than Rhode Island broke into small pieces and drifted away. Where an ice sheet sticks out over the sea, that extension is an ice shelf. Meltwater from land ice, as on Antarctica and on Greenland, flows into the ocean. Over time, extra water could lift sea level. Scientists working with the United Nations report a worldwide average rise. Since the early 1900s it is at least 4 inches, which is 10 cm. More evidence exists than this chapter lists. Scientists also point to shifts in how certain birds migrate. They point to bleaching, an unhealthy state of coral reefs. They point to possible growth in extreme weather, including hurricanes. When you meet a claim, ask whether it makes sense. Reports from government agencies, from universities, or from scientific organizations are usually the safest. Many other reports contain mistakes.

4Causes are the next question. Ideas fall into two groups. Human activity is one. Natural causes are the other. Burning fossil fuels is the main human activity blamed. Coal, oil, and natural gas are those fuels. Cars, factories, and electric plants use them. Burning them for fuel or energy releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere, the air. Other gases are released too. Over time the gases collect. Sunlight energy mostly passes through and warms the surface. The surface then sends heat back out. Much of that heat drifts into space. Some of that heat is caught near the surface and aimed back down. Carbon dioxide does this. Certain other gases do it too. The surface grows warmer. The process resembles a greenhouse, a building whose special glass holds heat for the plants inside. The name greenhouse effect comes from that likeness. Carbon dioxide, methane, and other heat-trapping gases are greenhouse gases. Their sources can be sorted this way. Carbon dioxide comes from fossil fuels, from forests that are burned or cut, and from volcanoes. Methane comes from burning forests and from microbes in wetlands and in the intestines of cattle. Nitrous oxide comes from fossil fuels, from burning forests, and from chemical reactions in soil and in the ocean. Halocarbons come from old spray cans, from some cleaning fluids, and from other products. Aerosol particles come from fossil fuels, from burning forests, and from volcanoes. Ozone comes from cars and from power plants. Water vapor comes from evaporation and from plants. Earth uses this effect as a natural part of its working. Take it away and Earth would match the cold of Mars. Liquid water could not exist. Life could not exist. Many scientists think carbon dioxide from burned fossil fuels is strengthening that warming.

5What links that carbon dioxide to the warming? Large-scale burning began when industrialization spread. Industrialization means the use of machinery driven by power. The mid-1800s were when it became widespread. Since then, carbon dioxide in the air appears to have risen about 25 percent. Meteorologists say surface temperature rose in the same period. Deforestation, the cutting of forests, is another human act that adds carbon dioxide. Trees and other plants take that gas out of the air. They use it in photosynthesis. That chemical process is how they make food. Fewer plants mean more of the gas left in the air. Some scientists note that people are not required for warming. Warm spells and cold spells repeated long before fossil fuels were burned in quantity. Several ice ages came and went over a few hundred thousand years. In an ice age, ice covered much of the surface. Warm intervals sat between those ages. About 11,500 years before now, the most recent ice age finished. Geologists place us in a warm gap. An ice age sits on either side of that gap. European records show a cooling. One era is called the Medieval Warm Period. It ran from about 1100 to 1300. The colder era after it is called the Little Ice Age. It ran from about 1400 to 1800. Warming has continued since that little ice age ended. Those earlier shifts had natural causes. The present warming may have natural causes as well.

6Careful temperature records go back only to the mid-1800s. Earlier climates have to be read another way. Growth rings in very old trees are one way. A wet, warm climate grows more wood than a dry, cold one. Thicker rings mark greater growth. Ring studies reveal temperature trends hundreds of years back. Older trends need other methods. Ice cores are one. They are long cylinder-shaped samples drilled from Antarctica and from other frozen ground. Chemicals in a core record the air at different times, reaching back many thousands of years. Deeper ice formed farther in the past. Large amounts of carbon dioxide, among other chemicals, tell scientists the climate was relatively warm when that ice formed. A library of cores can be studied. One core can show volcanic activity under a glacier. These methods reveal past natural climate shifts. The natural causes are not fully understood. Several factors are suspected. Heat from the Sun changes from time to time. The shape of the path Earth takes around the Sun changes too. The tilt changes too. Earth spins on an imaginary line called its axis.

7Results may follow whether the cause is human, natural, or both. Scientists ask how to forecast the changes, what they might be, and what they would mean for you. Computer models are a common tool. They are programs built on mathematical equations. The inputs include sunlight and heat. Rainfall and wind are included. Ocean currents and further climate factors are included too. Scientists alter the equations to imitate real-world changes. The program then estimates the most likely effects. Models are most useful for laying out several possible outcomes. The forecasts are not certain. They might happen. They might not. Some models foresee very serious effects if warming continues at the present pace. Other models foresee far milder effects. One serious forecast says average surface temperature could rise by as much as 10 degrees Fahrenheit, or 5.5 degrees Celsius, by 2100. Habitats of many plants and animals could change enormously. Wetlands might become grasslands. Grasslands might become deserts. Species that could not adjust would die out. Vast ice on Antarctica and on Greenland could melt into the sea. Sea level could rise several feet. Some models look at a Greenland with no ice left. They say sea level might then climb past 20 feet, which is 6 m. A public warning is part of this story. In 2007, Al Gore, a former vice president of the United States, received the Nobel Peace Prize. The award honored his warnings about possible dangers. A book was written by him. A movie included him as well. Both used the title An Inconvenient Truth. Possible disasters in them included the loss of many animal species. Deadly floods in many countries were included. Much stronger hurricanes were included too. Those disasters are not certain. They are only the worst of many possibilities.

8Computers help map pollutants in the air over major cities. If seas rose high enough and fast enough, ocean water would flood many coastal cities and cities on small islands. Those cities could be destroyed. New York City and Boston might be among them, along with other large cities in the United States that hold millions of people. Surface temperature affects weather in complex ways. Models say continued warming would not treat every region the same. Some places could grow drier, and crops could become harder to raise. Shortages of water and of food could follow. Other places could gain a longer growing season from warmer, wetter weather. Crops there could become easier to raise. Extra storms are also possible. Hurricanes, tornadoes, snowstorms, or droughts could increase. The mix depends on where a person lives. In March 2008, Rio de Janeiro in Brazil faced an epidemic of dengue fever. Mosquitoes help spread it. Illness could increase if the weather stays warmer. Viruses spread more readily in warmth than in cool air. Bacteria and other germs do too. Malaria is one such disease. Dengue, which brings fever and pain, is another. Lung infections belong in this group too. Personal effects might include these. You might need to save electricity. One way is less time with television. Another is less time with a computer. Dangerous weather might show up more often. Tornadoes are one kind. Hurricanes, heat waves, and other kinds are possible too. Water or food might run short. The chance of certain diseases might rise. Wild animals you like to see, including some birds and butterflies, might grow less common.

9Action is the next topic, because climate change may seriously affect human society and wildlife habitats. Governments around the world are at work. Plans aim to limit possible effects. Most countries support the Kyoto Protocol. The name comes from the Japanese city where the first version was written, in 1997. Under the plan, industrialized countries cut releases from power plants, from cars, and from other sources. Carbon dioxide is one gas they cut. Other greenhouse gases are cut too. An industrialized country uses machinery and fossil fuels widely. Cuts must be large enough to hit set levels by set dates. The dates differ by country. An Indonesian student plants a tree. As of 2010, the United States government had not approved the plan. Some officials feared harm to the economy of the United States. Federal and state governments are still cutting emissions, which are releases of these gases, in other ways. Some laws order power plants and factories to release less carbon dioxide. Scrubbers are one method. These filters catch carbon dioxide. They also catch other pollutants. The catch happens before anything reaches the air. Newer systems can then store that carbon dioxide underground. Other laws order cars to emit less of the gas. Some factories in the United States have cut their greenhouse gases. Others have not.

10The United States government also pays scientists to study renewable ways to make energy. Most of those sources skip fossil fuels and do not emit greenhouse gases. The name renewable marks a difference from fossil fuels. The supply is not used up. In New York, a wind farm called Maple Ridge makes enough energy for about 160,000 homes. The renewable group includes hydropower, geothermal power, wind power, and solar power. A river, or other moving water, can yield energy. That method is hydropower. Heat from underground water, or from steam down there, is geothermal power. Wind power takes moving air. Solar power takes sunlight. Nuclear power also makes energy without emitting these gases. It does produce dangerous wastes. Gases can also be removed from the air, not only cut at the source. Planting more trees is the best way. Now the questions are yours. What do you think? What evidence supports your answers? Do you believe Earth is getting warmer? If you do, what is the reason? Might more than one reason be at work? What results might plants, animals, and humans see? Which results seem most likely, and which seem least likely? Should any action be taken, and if so what action? Will you change any of your own habits to help? If so, which habits? How will you learn more? Less fossil fuel means less greenhouse gas. You can use less electricity. You can recycle cans made of aluminum, and you can recycle paper and plastics. You can walk, or ride a bicycle, to places you must go. You can choose solar-powered electronics, such as calculators and watches. You can plant trees and gardens.

11Words in this book can be explained this way. The atmosphere is the gas layer around a planet, a star, or a moon. An axis is an imaginary line an object such as Earth turns around. Climate is the weather of an area over a long time. Computer models are program pictures of real things or ideas, built with mathematical equations. Fossil fuels are energy taken from Earth, including coal, oil, and natural gas. Geothermal refers to heat made inside Earth. Glaciers are large bodies of piled ice and packed snow that last all year and creep downhill. Global warming is a rise in the average temperature of the air and oceans, especially a rise big enough to change climate. The greenhouse effect is heat held in the air by gases. Greenhouse gases are the gases that trap heat and add to that warming. Hydropower is electricity from moving water. Ice ages were times when ice sheets covered wide areas of land. An ice shelf is a piece of an ice sheet that reaches into the sea and floats. Industrialization is a shift in how a group lives. Machines, automation, and technology become the common way to make goods. Meteorologists study the air, the climate, and the weather. An orbit is the route a smaller body follows around a larger one. A planet or a moon can be the smaller body. The Sun can be the larger one. Photosynthesis is how plant cells, using chlorophyll, make food. Sunlight, water, air, and nutrients are the inputs. Pollutants are dirt or debris that make air, water, or the ground unclean. Renewable energy is energy that use does not use up.

22. College Basketball's Wild March

1A 1950 photo shows City College of New York holding the NCAA Division I men's trophy. Another night matters even more to this story. It is April 4, 1983. Houston is the strong favorite in the national title game. The opponent is NC State, short for North Carolina State. NC State comes in as the underdog. Even so, the players are giving the game everything they have. The clock shows only seconds. Both sides have 52 points. An NC State guard still has the ball, but almost no time remains. His only choice is a throw toward the basket, with hope doing the rest. The ball does not reach the rim cleanly. It falls short. Then a teammate appears, as if from empty space, and catches the ball before it drops. He dunks. The clock hits zero at that same instant. Celebration rolls through the crowd. People there have watched an upset that still ranks among the thrilling peaks of college basketball. The dunk is the last score. NC State finishes on top, 54-52. That night is a picture of March Madness itself. The draw is excitement. The other draw is how little anyone can predict. Sixty-eight teams take part. The format lets a single loss end a team's run. With a rule like that, any club can spring a surprise. The 1950 trophy shot is a reminder that title night is an old tradition. The 1983 finish is why the tradition still feels electric. A tie, a short miss, a catch in midair, and a dunk at zero are the whole last sequence. Houston had looked dominant. NC State had looked unlikely. One basket flipped the night. A field of sixty-eight, with one loss ending the run, keeps creating nights of that kind.

2In the United States, the body that coordinates college sport is the National Collegiate Athletic Association. People shorten that name to NCAA. Its Division I men's basketball tournament opened on March 17, 1939. Another name for it is March Madness. Back at the start, just eight teams were invited. Over later years the championship became a roaring national event. Every March, it spreads across the country. Since that 1939 beginning, fans have met some of the greatest legends the sport has known. College is where many future professionals polish their skills. So the route into professional basketball passes straight through this tournament. The National Basketball Association, shortened to NBA, rosters many alumni of March Madness. Shaquille O'Neal first drew wide notice in the tournament. Magic Johnson did too. Larry Bird did too. Stephen Curry did too. Others belong on that list as well. Simon Fraser University is the one Canadian member of the NCAA. On March 20, 2016, Wisconsin won on a shot at the buzzer. A photo shows a Xavier guard reacting in the moment after. From the whole NCAA, the NBA drafts only a handful of players each year. College, for the rest, is the end of the basketball road. Their shot at glory is now, or it is never. Passion shows in how they play. When the horn sounds, a player may fall to the floor and sob. Happiness can be the reason. Disappointment can be the reason. Under both feelings sits love for the game. The tears, the legends, and the eight-team beginning all belong to one idea. For a few athletes the tournament is a doorway. For many more it is the last bright stage. Simon Fraser shows the event can reach beyond the United States. The names O'Neal, Johnson, Bird, and Curry show how far a college stage can launch a career.

3The championship road is long. It is also difficult. Eligible schools in 2016 numbered 351. By region, they sat in 32 conferences. The conferences differed in size. A tournament bid is what every team wants. Each year, though, the invitations stop at 68. Selection works in two waves. First, every conference runs a tournament of its own. There are 32 of those conference titles. Each winner qualifies with no further vote. A committee of ten people fills the remaining 36 places. People call that voting day Selection Sunday. During 2015, a bid reached the University of North Florida. The pep band celebrated at once. The mascot celebrated too. A printed chart for the 2016 men's Division I championship shows the shape of the weeks. Opening games lead into a second round. Regionals follow. National semifinals follow those. Four regions feed the last stage, called the Final Four. The regions are labeled South, East, West, and Midwest. Whoever wins a region moves on. In 2016 the South champion was Villanova. Villanova was the national champion too. The title game on that chart also names North Carolina. Add the 32 automatic bids to the 36 chosen bids and the field equals 68. That arithmetic is the whole door into the bracket. From there, a region must be won before a team can stand in the Final Four. South, East, West, and Midwest are the four roads. In 2016 those roads ended with Villanova on top, opposite North Carolina in the title game.

4Inside the United States, few sporting events pull in a wider mix of fans than March Madness. Plenty of the fans do not follow sports the rest of the year. Filling out a bracket is a large part of the fun. The bracket is a grid, and every tournament team has a spot on it. People mark who they think will win each game. They also mark who will advance. Looking at the grid, you can trace the path one team would need if it hopes to reach the title game. Across the nation, millions complete a grid every year. Some pick from statistics. Some choose the safe side and take the best-ranked teams. Others love the thrill of backing underdogs. Almost everybody is trying to beat another person's picks. The rival might be a relative or a friend. The rival might be a coworker. The rival might be someone met only online. Barack Obama, the former president of the United States, is a well-known fan. Television showed his grid in all eight years he served as president. His picks, at least during those White House years, did not go very well. During 2015, a girl who was eleven wrote him a letter. She wanted him to know her grid had won the comparison. She told him he was a great president. She also told him he was not the strongest person at filling a bracket. A letter came back from him. He included a signed photo of himself beside his grid. His message was that he would consult her before the next try. Duke's head coach, in 2010, gave Obama a copy of the men's bracket. The Blue Devils of Duke won the tournament that year. The champions later stood with Obama inside the White House.

5During the 2007 women's championship, the Tennessee Lady Volunteers attack the rim against the Rutgers Scarlet Knights. A photo freezes that drive. Women's March Madness began when the NCAA started it in 1982. The Division I women's field opened with 32 teams. It has since grown to twice that number, which means 64 teams. Connecticut's Huskies became the commanding women's program across the event's history. Eleven national championships belong to them. Head coach Patricia Summitt finished her career with 1,098 wins. No coaching total in NCAA basketball history is higher. Her seasons with the Tennessee Lady Volunteers ran from 1974 to 2012. Qualification never slipped away from the Volunteers, not once. Funding at the beginning was another story. It failed them. Uniforms for the players were bought with money from a donut sale. Some viewers make a case for Breanna Stewart. They see her as the finest player women's college basketball has produced. Her squad won the championship four straight years, 2013, 2014, 2015, and 2016. She took Most Outstanding Player honors in every one of those seasons. During the 2016 Final Four, a picture catches her controlling the ball. Eleven titles explain why the Huskies sit at the top of the record list. Summitt's 1,098 wins explain why her name sits at the top of the coaching list. A donut sale at the start shows how little money the Volunteers had. Four straight titles, plus four Most Outstanding Player awards, show why Stewart's name keeps coming up. The 2007 photo of Tennessee against Rutgers, and the 2016 photo of Stewart, are two pictures of that same women's tournament.

6Upsets and surprise starters supply the tales fans love best. People call them Cinderella stories. A Cinderella team is an underdog. Good odds are not on its side. Because a single loss removes you, any club can scratch its way to a shocking win. The 1985 championship final looked bleak for Villanova. Almost nobody gave that team much of a chance versus Georgetown. Georgetown came in as defending champion. It had also been handed the year's top ranking. Villanova's rank was eighth. A lot of people believed a miracle was the only path to victory. The miracle never had to show up. Villanova only had to play the finest game of its life. In basketball, any made basket other than a free throw is called a field goal. The shot counts two points, or it counts three. Distance from the hoop decides which. A separate figure, field goal percentage, tells how many tries go in. The higher that share, the better the shooting. Villanova made 22 baskets out of 28. The share was over 78 percent. No Final Four game had ever posted a higher field-goal share. The final score was 66-64. With it, Villanova claimed a first men's national championship. Joy shows on a Wildcat player after the Georgetown win. In the 2016 opener, Michigan State carried rank number two. Its nickname is the Spartans. Middle Tennessee carried rank number fifteen. Its nickname is the Blue Raiders. Lots of observers call what followed the biggest one-game upset in the history of this tournament. Fans were stunned when the Blue Raiders won 90-81 and sent Michigan State home. The Blue Raiders did not win the whole event. In the first round, though, they ruined a great many filled-in grids.

7A flawless bracket is what everybody hopes to build. Billionaire Warren Buffett, during 2014, teamed with a loans company. Together they put up a prize of 1 billion dollars. It was for the person who called every game correctly. Nobody collected. The miss is easy to understand. One figure for the odds is 1 in 5 billion. A wider figure is 1 in 135 billion. The true chance lies between those two. Nobody, as far as records show, has ever handed in a perfect sheet. March brings the same rush to millions of viewers. They come for Cinderella teams. They come for stars on the rise. They come for baskets that win as time expires. Some dreams land. Other dreams fade and do not return. Call it passion. Call the month March Madness. Good luck when you mark your own grid. Duke is shown rejoicing after a victory against Wisconsin in the men's 2015 championship. Maryland is shown beating Louisville in 2014, a win that carried Maryland into the women's Final Four. Names for the ideas help at the end. The bracket is that grid of paired opponents. Dominant describes a side that is more powerful or more effective than others. Drafted describes being picked from candidates to play professionally. Legends are widely known for one remarkable talent. In a single-elimination tournament, losing once means you cannot continue. Statistics are number facts that get collected, arranged, and examined. Underdogs are the competitors people expect to fall short. Unpredictability is the quality of a result that cannot be known early. Upsets are sports results that break those expectations.

23. Copying Living Things to Solve Problems

1This book moves through these parts. An introduction comes first. A definition of biomimicry comes next. Then come surprising sources of ideas. A hook-and-loop fastener comes from burrs. Reflectors come from a cat's eyes. Screens that cut glare come from a moth. Self-cleaning paint and roof tiles come from a lotus. A fast train nose comes from a kingfisher. Swimsuits come from sharkskin. Cooling systems come from termite mounds. Building materials come from coral. A chapter asks why biomimicry matters. The future of biomimicry covers artificial leaves, fish antifreeze, spider silk, and medicine. A conclusion and word meanings close the book. A peacock shows his feathers to get the attention of mates. Did you know that a peacock's feathers have little color of their own? The colors we see come from the shape of the feathers. That shape causes light to bend. The bend makes the feathers look colorful. Have you ever noticed flying locusts? They never seem to run into each other. One part of their tiny brains notices things in front of them. It reacts much faster than our brains can. Nature is filled with many plants and animals. They have special ways to live. They have special ways to survive. For years, humans have studied these ways. They want to learn more about how the ways work. Now a science called biomimicry teaches a next step. It teaches us how to use what we learn from nature in our own lives.

2In Florida, a scientist is shown studying a manatee. That study is one picture of this science. What is biomimicry? The word biomimicry comes from two words. Bio means life. Mimic means to copy. Biomimetics is another name for this new field of study. Both names mean the same thing. They mean the science of copying life. A simple idea sits behind this science. Scientists study how living creatures deal with the challenges of life. Researchers do that study too. Engineers do it too. These experts then look at human challenges that are similar. They ask if people can adopt the same approaches. Biomimicry does not involve using living things. It involves learning from them. The idea of biomimicry is nothing new. For hundreds of years, people have looked to nature when a problem needed a fix. One famous copy came from a burr. A picture shows the fastener under a microscope. A burr is shown close up. A boy wears a suit of the same fastener and hangs from a wall covered with it. The story starts with Swiss engineer Georges de Mestral. In 1941 he was on an autumn hike. He walked through a meadow with his dog. Burrs, which are prickly seeds, caught in the fur of his pet. He later studied the burrs with a microscope. He saw that parts of each burr had little hooks. Those hooks would catch onto cloth. They would catch onto fur. They would catch onto hair. After his discovery, de Mestral invented a fastener that copies the burr. It temporarily attaches two things together. It uses the same method as burrs. He designed two pieces of fabric. One piece has hooks. The other piece has loops. The hooks catch the loops. They hold the pieces of fabric together. People have used this system at home. They have used it at work. They have even used it in space.

3Reflectors on a dark road came from a cat. A picture shows a cat's eyes reflecting light. Another picture shows a road marker in Yorkshire, in the United Kingdom. Traveling in a car at night, you may have noticed a glow. Light reflects off small plastic bumps lining the road. These reflective bumps were Percy Shaw's invention in 1933. He was driving one foggy night. Shaw saw the eyes of a cat. The eyes reflected the beams from his headlights back at him through the mist. He had an idea. If he could mimic the way a cat's eyes reflected light, drivers could stay safer on dark roads. Shaw invented highly reflective spheres. He set them into the center of roads. He called the design a cat eye. Over the years, the design has not stayed the same. The idea remains the same. Reflected light guides people safely home. Some animals have eyes that reflect light. Other animals' eyes absorb light. A picture shows the antireflective surface of a moth's eye under a microscope. A moth's eyes are designed to reduce reflection. The eyes do not shine. That helps keep them from catching the attention of predators. Researchers copied this design. They made computer screens that absorb light. The screens reduce glare. This design helps prevent eyestrain. It helps people who work on computers. It helps people who play on computers.

4Self-cleaning paint and roof tiles copy a leaf. Microscopic views show the paint. They show the surface of a lotus leaf. They show water beading and rolling off. Lotus plants grow in ponds and rivers. They are surrounded by mud. Even so, their leaves appear clean most of the time. Look to the leaves' surface to find the secret. The surface looks smooth. It actually has tiny bumps on it. The bumps cause water to bead up. The water rolls off. It carries bits of dirt and dust with it. Engineers studied lotus leaves. They found a way to use this idea in house paint. They used it in roof tiles too. House paint and roof tiles copy the bumps on the lotus leaves. Every time it rains, a cleaning happens. The outsides of houses with these paints and tiles are washed clean. A kingfisher gave a shape to a fast train. A picture shows the bird. Another picture shows the bullet train pulling into a Tokyo train station. Japan's Shinkansen train is known as the bullet train. It is one of the world's fastest trains. It zips over the rails at speeds up to 320 kilometers per hour. That speed is 199 miles per hour. The train's rounded nose created a problem in tunnels. Air pressure built up around the train because of that shape. The pressure let go as the train came out of the tunnel. A very loud boom was the result. To fix this problem, the train designers looked to a small bird. The bird is called a kingfisher. The shape of the kingfisher's beak lets it dive for fish. It enters the water without making a big splash. The designers thought about the train's nose. They wondered if the same shape would help. Perhaps the train would move through tunnels more smoothly. Air pressure might not build up. The new nose shape solved the noise problem. It also helped the train run even faster.

5Swimsuits copied sharkskin. A picture shows a swimmer in a suit made to work like that skin. Shark scales are shown. A great white shark is shown. Sharks have been swimming in the ocean since before the time of the dinosaurs. Moving through water is something their bodies are well adapted for. Shark skin has tiny grooved scales. Those scales help these animals glide smoothly. They help them glide quickly. Competitive swimmers wanted to swim faster. They tried swimsuits that mimicked the design of sharkskin. Those new suits did appear to make a difference. Eighty percent of the swimmers who wore those suits won medals. They wore them at the 2000 games in Sydney. Cooling systems copied a termite mound. The Eastgate Centre lets out hot air through vents. The vents run along the sides and the top of the building. The cooling system works like a termite mound. Termites are small insects with big appetites. Huge living mounds are built by some kinds of termites. The mounds are climate controlled. No matter how hot it gets outside, the air inside the mounds stays cool. The mounds have a complex system of tunnels and vents. The tunnels and vents run from the bottom to the top. Hot air rises up out of the top of the mound. Cooler air from the ground enters from below. Engineers designed the Eastgate Centre in Harare, Zimbabwe. They copied the termite mound system. The copy helps keep the building comfortable. It does this without using costly air-conditioning. The building was made with heat-resistant materials. It has special vents at the top. Because of this design, the structure uses little energy. It uses only 10 percent of the energy another building of the same size would use.

6Building materials can copy coral. The Moss Landing power plant in California was one of the first to turn carbon dioxide into cement. It uses a process like one used by corals. Some living things can recycle waste into something useful. Coral is one of them. This gas, carbon dioxide, is a form of waste. In small amounts, it is usually harmless. In large quantities it can hurt the environment. When carbon dioxide in the air mixes with ocean water, it becomes a mineral. That mineral is calcium carbonate. Coral reefs are built by corals from this mineral. Calcium carbonate is also an important ingredient in a building material humans use. That material is cement. Scientists found a way to pump carbon dioxide through seawater. The gas turns into carbonate. Now people use it to make things. Coral does the same kind of making. Why is biomimicry so important? Biomimicry is a great way to help people solve problems. It helps them make the things they need. People do not have to figure out every fix from nothing. They can look to nature to find ways that already work. Most of nature's designs are surprisingly simple. They are easy to imitate. The hooks on a burr are one example. The bumps on a lotus leaf are another. Natural designs are not just simple and effective. They are also good for the environment. People often forget a cost. Discarded materials affect other living things. Products that are made to last do not decompose quickly. Many are of little use to other living things. They may in fact harm them. Near a small village in the United Kingdom, a truck dumps garbage in a landfill.

7In nature, nothing is wasted. A fallen tree is a place where mushrooms and moss grow. Another organism can use any waste as a resource. A dead tree becomes food for hundreds of living things. It becomes shelter. It becomes energy. One species' trash is another species' treasure. Everything discarded contributes to the well-being of the ecosystem. People can take their cue from nature. They can do their part by being careful about the resources they use. They can consider what happens when they are finished with those resources. A beach is littered with plastic bottles and other trash. The future of biomimicry includes artificial leaves. A tree turns sunlight into energy. A wall of solar leaves acts like real leaves and does a similar job. Solar panels turn sunlight into electricity. People see them as a cleaner source of fuel than fossil fuels. The panels produce no harmful gases. Even so, they are costly to manufacture. Making them creates waste products. Those waste products are hard to dispose of safely. Scientists have turned to green plants for a better way. They want a better way to change sunlight into energy. Green plants use chlorophyll to absorb light. They then turn that light into food. A new type of solar cell uses natural dyes. The dyes mimic how chlorophyll works. These new cells may perform just as well as the old cells. They may do it without the cost and the waste.

8Fish antifreeze is another future idea. An Antarctic ice fish is the model. Freezing temperatures can be hard on machines. They can be hard on living things. Chemical antifreeze keeps engines running in cold weather. It keeps machines running too. Some kinds of ice fish use natural antifreeze. It lets them survive chilly temperatures in Antarctic waters. Chemical antifreeze can harm living tissue. Fish antifreeze does not. Scientists are trying to learn more about the fish. They want to know how the fish make natural antifreeze. They want to know how the fish use it. This information can help researchers. They hope to create a safe way to keep living tissue warm and healthy. Spider silk is strong as well as sticky. A funnel spider and its web show the material. Spider webs are made of sticky silk. The silk is also quite strong. A thread of spider silk has a surprising strength. It is about three times as strong as a steel thread of the same size. Scientists have analyzed spider silk. They want to create a similar material. The human-made silk could be used for all sorts of durable materials. Bandages are one use. Fences are another. Medicine is a third future path. Animals that live in the wild sometimes get ill. People do too. Unlike humans, wild animals cannot go to a doctor. They cannot go to a clinic. Instead, they have found ways to treat themselves. Some eat certain plants. Some apply minerals. Many people around the world have used plants to treat illnesses. They have used minerals too. They have done this for thousands of years.

9Chimps stay healthy with help from certain plants. That is one lesson from the wild. Nature provides important lessons for humans. There is still much to be learned. Scientists can study the living things around us. They can find inspiration for solutions to important problems. The best answers may be right under our noses. They may be waiting to be discovered through the science of biomimicry. These words help with the book. Adapted means changed to fit a new or specific situation or environment. An ecosystem is a community of living things together with their habitat. Antifreeze is something added to lower the freezing point of a substance. Fossil fuels are energy sources taken from the ground. Coal, oil, and natural gas are examples. Chlorophyll is a substance in green plants. It can turn water, air, and sunlight into food. Glare is a bright light, usually reflected off something. Grooved means having long, narrow cuts or channels. Decompose means to decay, rot, or break down into small parts. An organism is a living thing. Discarded means thrown away or rejected. A resource is a supply of something valuable or very useful. Durable means sturdy and able to last for a long time.

24. Countries Joined for Peace

1World War II, as of June 1945, was nearly finished. One month before that June, Nazi Germany had fallen. Japan had not stopped fighting. Closing in were the Allies. The United States stood on that side. Russia stood on that side. Great Britain stood on that side. China stood on that side. Other nations stood with them. Roughly 50 countries sent delegates to San Francisco, California. The number of delegates was about 850. They came as international representatives. The question in front of them was what should happen after the fighting stopped. Their hope was an organization built for the big changes still to come. A final gathering took place on June 25, 1945. Anyone who accepted the charter was invited to stand. The document was the charter written for the United Nations. Work on it had already lasted years. All of them rose. The hall rang with applause. Fighting from 1939 through 1945 had been the gravest conflict humans had known. Out of it, countries shaped a body they hoped would protect peace. The new body opened its doors in October of that year. Delegates from around the world are shown meeting as the United Nations is founded. The standing vote, the applause, and the October opening are the birth of the organization. San Francisco was only the meeting place. The aim reached far past one city. Peace after the worst war people had lived through was the point of every speech in that hall.

2News reports mention this organization often these days. Where food is scarce, white UN trucks may arrive with supplies for people in need. Where fighting continues, UN Peacekeepers may be trying to hold order. Where an earthquake has flattened a town, UN workers may be putting up tents for shelter. Food is handed out by a UN-run center inside a Gaza Strip refugee camp. More than seventy years after it began, the UN still pushes countries to cooperate. Membership now stands at 193 countries. New York City is where the headquarters stand. Staff serving the UN around the world number about 44,000. Population and complexity have grown. The main aims have not. The UN tries to help people in trouble. It tries to promote human rights. It tries to deal with problems that cross the globe. Missions do not always succeed. Even so, the UN often takes on disasters nobody else will touch. Six main departments, called organs, make up the body. They are the Secretariat, the General Assembly, the Security Council, the Economic and Social Council, the Trusteeship Council, and the International Court of Justice. An international body like this was not a brand-new idea. After World War I, fought from 1914 to 1918, countries formed the League of Nations. Keeping world peace was its core purpose. Woodrow Wilson, the U.S. president, failed to get the U.S. Congress to accept the membership treaty. Congress chose to remain outside. The fear was that joining would strip the country of control over its own affairs. Successes did occur for the League. It slowly came apart anyway. It was dissolved in 1946, once the United Nations had started work. Day-to-day leadership sits in the Secretariat, which works as the executive branch. Its headquarters is a famous landmark in New York City. From there, executives watch the day-to-day work. Members elect the secretary-general. That person guides UN tasks. That person is often the main spokesperson. A secretary-general does not hold powers like the leader of a country. The role is closer to a top diplomat, urging others to help when a crisis hits. Eight secretaries-general have served. Each came from a different country. The Secretariat Building lately went through a renovation. It lasted five years. It cost 1 billion dollars.

3The General Assembly, or GA, is the UN's main body for decisions. All 193 member countries sit in it. There they discuss important questions. Sometimes they vote. Official languages number six. They are English and French. They are Spanish and Russian. They are Arabic and Chinese. An interpreter is often used. In some cases members vote yes or no on recommendations. Those recommendations are called resolutions. In 2010, for example, the GA agreed to send aid to Haiti, a Caribbean country, after a huge earthquake. Countries cannot be compelled to obey a resolution unless it deals specifically with UN matters. A photo shows the GA voting on a resolution. Smaller committees inside the GA give advice on set subjects. One committee works on international security. It builds programs meant to reduce violence across the world. Keeping peace and safety between nations is the Security Council's main job. Seats that never rotate number five. They belong to the five main Allies of World War II. China holds one of those seats. France holds one. The Russian Federation holds one. The United Kingdom holds one. The United States holds one. Any one of them can reject a resolution. They can do so even when the other countries are lined up against them. The council has to be ready to meet quickly if an international crisis breaks. Peacekeepers from Lebanon and from Italy are shown preparing for the International Day of Peace. Armed peacekeepers drawn from different countries are sometimes sent by the council to watch over a truce. Those soldiers may fight only in self-defense. If violence starts again, they must not take a side. Rwanda, in Africa, received about 2,500 UN Peacekeepers during the 1990s. Bloodshed between the Hutu and the Tutsi, two ethnic groups, was what they were sent to halt. They could not stop it. Hutu fighters killed more than 800,000 Tutsi people. Many regard that outcome as perhaps the worst failure the Security Council has ever had.

4ECOSOC is the short name of the Economic and Social Council. It handles economic issues that affect the world. It handles social issues too. One mission is support for vulnerable groups. A project, for example, works to improve women's rights in many countries. Another effort tries to protect local cultures that might die out. Aboriginal groups in Australia are one case. ECOSOC also tries to balance economic growth with care for the environment. Growth can bring new jobs. It can bring new technologies. It can also use up forests and lakes, or harm them. Those are important natural resources. Healing in Earth's ozone layer is a clear UN success. High in the atmosphere, that layer works like a filter. It shields all life from harmful radiation. During the 1980s, scientists found holes growing in the layer. People faced a much higher risk of skin cancer. Nations were urged by the UN to release less of the chemicals that had been opening those holes. Since that call, the holes have been shrinking. The episode showed countries could cooperate on a global environmental problem. A purple area on one image marks the world's largest ozone hole, over Antarctica, at its biggest. The Trusteeship Council is an organ that paused its work in 1994. The plan was to gather again if a need returned. Its duty had been to help colonies ruled by other countries move toward independence. It guided African lands, including Rwanda, Burundi, and Tanganyika. Tanganyika is now Tanzania. Other lands were guided too, toward governing themselves. Operations were suspended by the council in 1994. Palau, its last trust territory, had gained independence. Palau lies in the Pacific Ocean. Judges of the ICJ, the International Court of Justice, meet inside the Peace Palace. That palace is in The Hague, in the Netherlands. Fifteen judges serve. No two come from the same country. A judge from each permanent Security Council member is always seated there. There are five such members. Legal questions arrive from member states. Opinions come back from the ICJ. Rulings come back too. It decides border disputes. Fishing grounds are one example of the natural-resource rights it can decide. It decides cases about fighting between countries. People also call the ICJ the World Court.

5In Nigeria, a health worker gives a child a polio immunization. The World Health Organization, or WHO, is the UN's health arm. It promotes healthier habits worldwide. It teaches about cleanliness. It teaches about healthy eating. It teaches about other factors that can help stop disease. A worldwide push to end smallpox was led by WHO starting in 1967. Smallpox was a deadly disease. Workers taught the public in places where it was common. They taught how to keep it from spreading. Vaccination programs began across the world. Smallpox was announced as extinct by WHO in the year 1980. WHO also gathers data so members can see where health emergencies are. Plans were drawn to slow COVID-19's virus, as one example. That virus was deadly. Respiratory droplets spread it. The result was a worldwide pandemic. The Sphinx stands in Egypt, and so do the Pyramids of Giza. They are among the oldest and largest structures on Earth. The letters UNESCO name a body of the United Nations. Its longer title continues as Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization. The work covers education. It covers science. It covers culture. Its aim is cooperation among countries in education, in science, and in culture. Guarding World Heritage Sites is one of its best-known jobs. A World Heritage Site may be famously beautiful in nature. It may instead matter deeply to a culture. UN help protects it. The Sphinx and the pyramids rank among the world's most familiar monuments. Egypt, in 1995, wanted a fresh highway built near the pyramids. UNESCO persuaded the government to shift that highway farther off.

6About sixty-five million refugees are in the world today. War forces them from home. Violence can force them. Natural disasters can force them. During the middle years of the 2010s, Syrians leaving a war-torn homeland numbered close to five million. Many now live in camps run by the UN. A stark comparison comes from the UNHCR. That office is headed by the High Commissioner for Refugees. Not since World War II has the refugee count been this high, the office says. During a refugee crisis, the UNHCR supplies food. It supplies clean water. It supplies shelter and health care. The final hope is a safe return home. When return is impossible, the agency looks for countries willing to receive people. A chart lists registered Syrian refugee totals. One figure is 8,000. Another is 493,423. Another is 2,581,767. Another is 3,977,504. Another is 4,595,198. Another is 4,850,957. Another is 5,116,057. Another is 5,479,998. Another is 5,556,192. The highest figure shown is 5,667,026. Scale marks on the chart step by the million, from 1,000,000 through 2,000,000, 3,000,000, 4,000,000, and 5,000,000, up to 6,000,000. Some totals come from UNHCR rolls in Egypt. Others come from Iraq, from Jordan, and from Lebanon. They also count people registered by Turkey's government. They count people registered in North Africa. Hardly any corner of the globe sits outside UN programs. The organization is still controversial. Some critics say the work costs too much. They say money is wasted. Others point to Security Council failures to prevent war. They also point to failures against genocide. Genocide means civilians killed in huge numbers. A further complaint says too much power sits with the nations named in the charter. What helps one country can be pushed aside so that another country's wishes win. At the same time, more than seventy years of work have done a great deal of good. Over ninety million people receive UN food that may be all that stands between them and starvation. Child vaccination by the UN covers more than half the children on Earth and helps halt outbreaks. It seeks human rights for every person. It gives leaders a place to talk through differences instead of fighting over them. During 1948, UN members adopted a rights text. Its name is Universal Declaration of Human Rights. What every person deserves is written out in that document. Race does not change the list. Religion does not change it. Social status does not change it. Economic status does not change it. The listed rights include life, liberty, and security. They include privacy. They include an education. They include freedom of opinion and of expression. They include the right to own property.

7In 2007, in Marjayoun, South Lebanon, Lebanese children play beside a Spanish UN peacekeeper. The news people hear is usually bad news. Since the founding, though, there has been plenty of good news to share. Extreme poverty now holds under 10 percent of the world's people, a first. That finding comes from the World Bank. A study called the Human Security Report finds that deaths caused by war have fallen steeply after World War II. Average life span has grown, WHO says. Deaths of children younger than five have become less common, WHO also says. Improvements like these have many causes. One cause has been the UN. Hard challenges wait in the years ahead. Whether the United Nations can meet them is still a large question. A short word list closes the account. Committees are groups that consider a course of action or decide on one. International means involving two or more nations. Natural resources are useful things found in nature, such as minerals and forests, or things used to make a product. Controversial means causing a lot of disagreement. A crisis is a dangerous or unstable time that demands attention. Call something an organization when people or a system act together for one stated purpose. A diplomat represents one government to another government. A refugee has fled. The cause may be war. It may be famine or persecution. It may be a natural disaster. Often no firm destination is waiting. The environment is the natural world. Human rights are claims most societies say every person holds from the start. Justice is one of them. Freedom is one of them. Equality is one of them. Vaccination is a medical treatment made from weak or dead microbes. It teaches the body to fight a particular disease and become immune. Vulnerable means easily hurt.

25. Daily Life Without Gravity

1Astronaut Robert L. Curbeam Jr. smiles for the camera aboard the ISS. The smile comes after a successful space walk. The book covers weightless living and the race to space. It covers space stations and an astronaut's life. Sleeping, eating, and using the toilet each get a turn. So do bathing and teeth cleaning, free time, and exercising. Return to Earth follows. A word list ends the book. You wake just as the Sun is rising. A moment is needed to untangle yourself from the sleeping bag in that small space. You open the door, grab a handle, and flip yourself over. One gentle push carries you the full length of the room. Another crew member floats by and hands you some coffee. Good morning, he says, in Russian. You thank him and yawn. Tiredness comes because sleep has been short. Your stomach is not used to the lack of gravity yet. Excitement is huge. A picture shows a space shuttle docked with the International Space Station. Your first full day of work aboard that station is about to start. Years of training are behind you. Eating is still complicated without gravity. Bathing is complicated. Using the bathroom is complicated. It feels as if each simple act must be learned all over again. Six more months will pass before you head back to Earth. You may as well get started.

2The human race into space began in the 1950s and the 1960s. The first person in space was the cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin. His country was Russia, which then belonged to the Soviet Union. He orbited Earth one time. A safe landing came after 108 minutes on April 12, 1961. That August, a second Soviet cosmonaut circled Earth over 17 times. The trip lasted about 25 hours. Technology moved ahead quickly. People went farther. They stayed longer. In 1968, U.S. astronauts aboard Apollo 8 orbited the Moon with success. Apollo 11's crew set foot on the Moon on July 20, 1969. Vehicles for stays of days or weeks kept coming from space programs. Scientists were also building toward a more permanent structure. People might live there for months. They might live there for years. The Soyuz spacecraft were first created in the 1960s. Trips to the International Space Station and back still use these craft. The first space station was launched by the Soviet Union in 1971. It spent 175 days in space. Then it fell out of orbit. It burned up while reentering Earth's atmosphere. In 1973 the United States launched Skylab. Three missions were supported. Abandonment came in 1974. The fall back to Earth came in 1979. A picture shows a space shuttle docked with Mir. The Soviet Union launched the Mir space station in 1986. Say that name MEER. It was the first space station to last more than a few years. Fifteen years in orbit followed. That was three times longer than the original plan. Scientists from many different countries stayed there. Russian scientist Dr. Valeri Polyakov spent 438 days in a row in space during 1994 and 1995. He lived on Mir. He orbited Earth 7,075 times. His record still stands.

3Work on a new and larger space station began before Mir fell to Earth in 2001. The United States took part. Russia, Japan, Canada, and other countries took part too. The opening piece of the ISS went into orbit in 1998. The full name is the International Space Station. Further sections joined it as the years passed. More are planned. As of 2012, the ISS was 357 feet long, or 108.8 meters. Its weight was almost 1 million pounds, or 453,592.3 kilograms. A telescope is not needed to see it in the night sky. Visitors so far number more than 240, and they have come from nineteen countries. Living space inside is greater than in the average five-bedroom house. Time aboard the ISS is not the same for every astronaut. Many stays last about three to six months. A stay can last half a year of work and life with no gravity. The space is small. Three to six other people share it. Crew members may come from different countries. They may speak different languages. They are still a team. Stress can run high. Length of the ISS matches a football field. A picture shows an astronaut practicing a repair on an underwater model of the ISS. Underwater work helps them get ready for space walks. School for astronauts lasts many years before training begins. Physical training includes weightless flight in an airplane. Underwater practice in a space suit can last as long as seven hours. Life-size models of space vehicles sit in a huge pool. The pool holds 6.2 million gallons, or 23.5 million liters. Even after arrival, the lack of gravity still takes adjustment. Bodies and minds need time when astronauts first reach the ISS. Weightlessness can make some people ill. Special bags are kept on the station. A cloth side can be used for cleanup. An extra sealable bag is attached so disposal is easy.

4Six small sleep pods are on the ISS. Each holds a sleeping bag with armholes. Each bag is tied to the wall. That tie keeps the astronaut from floating away. Sixteen sunrises and sixteen sunsets pass each day because of the station's orbit. People are used to night sleep and daytime waking. Serious sleep problems can follow. A shades-down period makes the station dark and quiet. Astronauts can then get the sleep they need. A picture shows astronaut Alvin Drew getting ready to sleep on the ISS. Another picture shows coffee beside a tortilla holding eggs and sausage. Early astronauts ate gels, pastes, and freeze-dried food. The meals held the nutrition they needed. The taste was not very good. Today the menu includes foods most people enjoy. Chicken is one. Fruits, peanut butter, and brownies are others. No refrigerator is on the ISS. Food must be packed so it will not spoil. An oven is available. Some food can be eaten as it is. Other food, such as spaghetti, needs water added. Salt and pepper are used in liquid form. Regular grains would float away. They could damage station equipment. Swallowing still takes practice after the food is ready. Astronaut Piers Sellers compared it to eating while lying on one side.

5Floating objects make the bathroom tricky. Special training is required before an astronaut uses the toilet. Two parts make up each ISS toilet. Liquid waste goes into a tube that ends in a nozzle. Solid waste requires foot straps and handles so the body stays in place. The person must line up over an opening 4 inches wide, or 10 centimeters. A toilet on Earth usually opens 12 to 16 inches, or 30.5 to 40.6 centimeters. Light suction moves the waste from the opening or the tube. Storage is in another part of the station. Liquid waste goes into the tube hung on the wall. Solid waste goes into the base set on the floor. Two toilets are on the ISS. They have stopped working more than once. Repair parts must be sent from Earth. The wait can take months. On the ISS, astronaut Karen Nyberg demonstrates a hair wash. Body washing uses water and special soap on a cloth. Hair washing uses a shampoo that needs no water. Tooth cleaning uses a toothpaste that can be swallowed at the end.

6Free time on the ISS may include cards, reading, or writing, among other things. Contact with loved ones matters too. Calls are possible. Video chats are possible. Students around the world sometimes get answers to their questions. Video tours of the station are sometimes given. Many astronauts simply look out the windows. Many take photos. The view is pretty amazing, so the choice is easy to understand. A guitar is in the hands of astronaut Chris Hadfield aboard the ISS. That last visit even included a music video. A treadmill on the ISS is where astronaut Sunita Williams works out. On Earth, bones and muscles work against gravity, and that work makes them stronger. In space, very little strength is needed to move a thing. The same thing might be extremely heavy on Earth. Ease of movement lets bones and muscles weaken over time. A workout of at least two hours is required every day. Resistance in the special gym equipment helps astronauts stay strong. A daily workout still does not stop the loss. A six-month stay costs most astronauts 20 to 30 percent of their muscle.

7Japanese astronaut Soichi Noguchi gives a thumbs-up. He has returned to Earth. The year is 2021. He is aboard a SpaceX Crew Dragon capsule. Coming home from the ISS does not end the work. Recovery after months in space takes a long time. A six-month stay calls for six weeks of workouts. Those workouts help lost muscle return. A full year can pass before bones recover completely. The effort is hard. Living and working in space is still worth that effort. Scientists keep watch on physical health. They keep watch on mental health. Information already gathered has helped astronauts live healthier lives. It has helped them live happier lives. Farther goals in space may take months to reach. Some may take years. Some may take decades. This vital information might decide success or failure. It matters for future space exploration.

26. Eight Billion Humans and Still Rising

1Soon, India will have a larger population than any country on Earth. What Is Inside. A Huge Puzzle 4. When Is the Number Too High? 5. Did This Start Lately? 7. The Fast Rise 8. New Tools That Helped 9. A Better Sign 12. A Future We Cannot Be Sure Of 13. Food Enough for All 14. A Small World in Space 15. Glossary 16. A Huge Puzzle.
