People settled on Rapa Nui in the Pacific Ocean. Easter Island is its other name. Trees were cleared for homes. Trees were cleared for fields. There was plenty of fish. There was plenty of wildlife. There was plenty of crops. The population grew. They carved moai (MO-eye). Each moai is a huge human figure of stone. The figures were raised along the coast. Around the year 1680, carving came to a stop. The population dropped. One theory explains why. The Rapa Nui had used up many resources. Their population had grown too large. A resource is a natural thing around us that helps us live. Food is a resource. Clean water is a resource. Energy is a resource. A small population could once get food from the island. Water was available too. Wood for building was available too. The huge stones had to be moved. Tree trunks may have worked like wheels to roll them. Later, the population was too large for the island. Not everyone could get what they needed. The forests were gone. Many people died. The resources had been used up. Eight billion humans now live on Earth. Many people think the planet's resources are being used up in a similar way. Will our ending match what happened to the people of Rapa Nui?

2These giant statues on Rapa Nui were far too heavy to carry. How were the statues moved? When Is the Number Too High? A look around may show an Earth that does not seem crowded. Empty houses are still there. Open fields are still there. Forests are still there. A typical square mile in New York City holds 29,729 people. Parks still fit in that city. Overpopulation is not about running out of space. It is about too few resources. It means people have passed carrying capacity. Carrying capacity is the top number of people a place can support. Those people must survive without losing the resources they need. Scientists give Earth a wide range. Carrying capacity falls between two billion and forty billion people. The width comes from how much each person uses. A Growing World Footprint. The global material footprint is all raw material taken out for human use. Experts expect this footprint to rise faster than the population. The 1990 total was 43 billion metric tons. The 2060 estimate is 190 billion metric tons. The rise is 442 percent. The 190 billion figure is an estimate. The source is the UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs, 2019. The chart shows 92 billion as well. It shows 43 billion as well. Two billion people is the limit if everyone lived as most Americans live. Most of the world's resources go to high-income countries. The United States is one. Countries in Western Europe are others. A small share is all that low-income countries use. Of all people on Earth, three-quarters have homes in middle-income countries. Resource use in those countries keeps going up. China is upper-middle. India is lower-middle. Each country has more than a billion people. Forty billion people could live here if each person used only enough to stay alive. Other species would be pushed aside. Life would be hard.

3Did This Start Lately? Experts suspect many civilizations fell in a way like the Rapa Nui. Farming began in the Middle East about ten thousand years ago. Irrigation watered the crops. More food followed. Populations soared. Irrigation can erode soil. It can leave salt behind. Enough salt will kill the crops. People called this land the Fertile Crescent. The name fit because food grew there in such large amounts. The land wore out. The theory says the land could support less over time. Carrying capacity fell. The ancient civilizations disappeared. A population past carrying capacity can face starvation. Disease can spread. The environment can be destroyed. Wars can start over scarce resources. Some people leave if they can. They look for new resources. The people of Rapa Nui had no way to leave. Thousands of miles of ocean separated them from any neighbors. No wood remained for canoes. Clearing trees can cause erosion. Plants can die when soil contains too much salt. Here, trees were cleared so people could farm. Salt was left in the soil. The land was ruined. The Fast Rise. In the year 1800, Earth's people numbered one billion. Getting there took humans 120,000 years. By 1927 that number had doubled. Only 127 years had passed. The year 1960 came thirty-three years later. The number had tripled. Three billion people lived then. The eight billionth person arrived in 2022. More than 200,000 people are added every day. New technology in the Industrial Revolution started the population explosion. The years were 1760 to 1850. New farming practices changed daily life. Manufacturing changed it. Railroads changed it. There was more food. Distribution was better. More children survived. People were healthier. Cities gained people who had lived on farms. Factory jobs were the draw. Scientists found the causes of many diseases. They found ways that saved thousands of lives. More children reached adulthood. More adults could then have children. The human population boomed. A baby breathes penicillin as a vapor. This medicine has saved a countless number of lives.

4New Tools That Helped. Human numbers might have grown faster than food. The Green Revolution got its start during the 1940s. Scientists developed special seeds. Farmers could grow more food with them. Scientists developed chemicals. The chemicals controlled insects. The chemicals controlled plant diseases. Land once unfit for farming could grow food. Chemical fertilizers made it possible. Irrigation made it possible too. The new way of farming spread across the globe. Low-income countries grew more food. Food production rose threefold. Some people thought invention would allow growth forever. New problems arrived with the technology. Irrigation needed more water. Chemicals on crops polluted food. They polluted water. They poisoned the environment. Some people realized the danger. We were destroying the planet that life depends on. Some resources are renewable. Replacement can happen. People can plant new trees. The Sun offers a huge supply of energy. Wind offers a huge supply of energy. The water cycle renews water all the time. Only a 2.5 percent share of water on our planet is fresh. Two-thirds of that fresh water is frozen in glaciers. Usable fresh water is under 1 percent of Earth's water. Fresh water is not in every place. One quarter of people have no safe drinking water. Most of them are in Africa or in parts of Asia. Irrigation uses seventy percent of the fresh water on hand. In the West of the United States, pumps pull underground water onto fields. The pumping is faster than replacement. The mighty Colorado River ends before the sea. People take the water for irrigation and for cities. Water is growing scarce. Much farmland that feeds the world will turn to desert. Nearly 40 million people get their water from the Colorado River. The river now ends in a trickle. The sea is still out of reach.

5Some resources on Earth cannot be renewed. Coal is one. Copper is one. Other metals are too. Millions of years go into their formation. Once they are used up, they are gone. China uses far more coal than any other country. The United States uses the most oil. That use is more than its share. World population living there is less than 5 percent. Its share of world oil is 20 percent. An ecosystem cannot be renewed. Planet health depends on work that ecosystems do. Swamps clean water. Swamps reduce flooding. Grasslands form rich soils. Forests balance the atmosphere. Heavy use of wood is destroying many important ecosystems. Heavy use of farmland is doing the same. Tropical rainforests are the most diverse ecosystems. Losses have taken nearly two-thirds of them. Each year, extinction takes thousands of plant species. Each year, extinction takes thousands of animal species. We cannot bring those species back. Our planet is warming. People burn fossil fuels. Oil is a fossil fuel. Coal is a fossil fuel. Burning them lets carbon dioxide enter the atmosphere. More heat is trapped at the surface. Ecosystems around the world are changing. Polar ice caps are melting. Deserts are spreading. Weather is growing wilder. These trends will not turn around easily. A Better Sign. Global population growth had slowed by 2010. A rate of 2.2 percent a year fell. The lower rate is 1.1 percent a year. In many high-income countries, growth of population has stopped. In some countries, it has reversed. Births are under the replacement rate. Replacement means 2.1 children for each woman. Over time, that average of births for each woman holds a population steady. More people see that resources on Earth are limited. Wind power is being developed. Solar power is being developed. These sources are renewable. Many countries passed laws so air would be cleaner. They passed laws so water would be cleaner. They passed laws to protect ecosystems. Forests have grown in some places. Ecosystems from old forests are often still lost. New trees do not always save them. World Population Projections, 1990-2150. The figures come from UN Long-Range World Population Projections, 1991. Three estimates trace the world population ahead. Each one begins at 5 billion. The estimates pull apart in later years. Across sixty years, fewer births change the total by a great deal.

6A Future We Cannot Be Sure Of. The good news did not stop growth. Most new growth is in low-income countries. The United Nations predicts that 2050 will have nearly ten billion people. Most estimates say that count is almost twice a sustainable population. You can believe any estimate. Everyone now agrees on one limit. Growth of the human population cannot go on without an end. The planet would be destroyed. Lower birthrates are critical. High-income countries could share Earth's resources more fairly. Fairer shares can bring the global birthrate down. How would that work? Women need education first. With education, women can choose family size. They usually have fewer children after that. Children need better health care second. They need clean water. They need good food. Families have fewer children when they believe the children will live. Governments can help third. They can help elderly people. They can help sick people. Parents then know care will be there in old age. Food Enough for All. Look at the United States. It has moved beyond its carrying capacity. Americans must bring resources from other countries. Their standard of living depends on that. Eight billion people live on Earth. Many more planets would be needed for all of them to live as most Americans do. Everyone can still have enough to eat. High-income countries must eat smarter. They must waste less. Grain is the main food the world depends on. Meat production has boomed in high-income countries. It has boomed in middle-income countries. A third of the world's grain goes to livestock. Meat of 1 pound (0.45 kg) uses a lot of grain. Low-income countries gain grain when people eat less meat. Valuable grasslands gain protection from that choice. In 2009, China passed the United States in total energy use. An average American still eats more food than survival needs. An average American still uses far more water than survival needs. No other people consume as much. Wise choices about how life is lived could change that. Those same people could be the most efficient consumers on Earth.

7How Many Planets Would We Need? Numbers in the chart come from National Footprint and Biocapacity Accounts 2022. Think of one country shown there. If every person lived as a resident of that country, the chart shows the planets required. A Small World in Space. Carved tablets still keep records from the Rapa Nui. That ancient language has no reader today. We can still learn from their experience. Their little island gives a warning. The warning is to protect limited resources. Earth is a small island of our own, out in space. On page 12, birthrate (n.) means how many babies a population gains in a set time. On page 5, carrying capacity (n.) means the full population an environment can support without a stop date. On page 14, consumers (n.) means people who pay to own or borrow goods or services and then use them. On page 8, distribution (n.) means getting goods and services out to people or out to stores. On page 11, ecosystem (n.) means a habitat plus the living things that form a community in it. On page 14, efficient (adj.) means good at using time and good at using resources. On page 11, fossil fuels (n.) means coal, oil, and natural gas taken from the ground for energy. On page 6, middle-income countries (n.) means a mixed group of countries with average incomes that are not very high and not very low. On page 5, overpopulation (n.) means an area with more people than it should hold, or more other living things than it should hold. On page 4, resources (n.) means supplies of a thing people value or find very useful. On page 14, standard of living (n.) means the comfort and wealth a person, a community, or a country can reach. On page 13, sustainable (adj.) means used in a manner that leaves a resource in place and does not harm it forever.

27. Empires Clash over a Continent

1Ships fill this artwork. It shows the Battle of Quiberon Bay, a sea fight from 1759. Opening Shots. Two Empires, One Continent. Plans and Battles. William Pitt Takes the Lead. A Road That Led to Rebellion. Opening Shots Serious trouble found colonial soldiers and British soldiers on July 3, 1754. The ground is in today's Pennsylvania. George Washington, an officer of twenty-two, had been sent that spring toward Fort Duquesne. Say the fort's name as doo-KAYN. Pittsburgh stands on that spot today. He was told to warn the French. They were on land Britain claimed, and they were to quit the fort. The warning did not work. Later he struck a small French party by surprise. Seneca people went with him. Twenty-one fighters became his prisoners. Ten were killed. A larger force arrived to settle the score. French soldiers in that force numbered more than seven hundred. Fighters from seven Native tribes came as allies. The Huron were one of those tribes. Another artwork shows Washington on his way to Fort Duquesne. The date of that departure is April 1754.

2Workers later rebuilt Fort Necessity. Visitors can still see it in Farmington, Pennsylvania. About four hundred colonial and British men made up the force. At Great Meadows they put up a small fort and named it Fort Necessity. The walls did them little good. French troops and their allies closed in and struck. Death or wounds took many of the British. Night had not yet fallen when Washington gave up the fight. A long war began with this battle. Its prize was control of North America, and either France or Britain might win that prize. Two Empires, One Continent Through the 1700s, Britain and France each reached for power across the world. Each nation was an empire that kept growing. Each planted colonies in lands far from home. Furs were something the colonists claimed. Land was something they claimed. In some colonies they also claimed people, and those people were forced into slavery. Wealth poured into both countries from these resources. Strong armies and strong navies were built with that wealth. The leader of New France, in 1749, sent 270 men out to mark where the colony ended. New France was the French territory. Quebec and Ontario, provinces of Canada today, lay inside it. Those men posted the French claims. British settlers found inside those claims were driven off. About two thousand French soldiers set out in 1753. Their job was to raise forts so the British could not settle the Ohio River Valley. Trade made the country around the Ohio River valuable. A drawing shows a French fort from 1701. It stood in the land that is now Michigan.

3Places and groups that mattered in the fight for North America appear on this map. By then, land held by France sat above the British colonies and also off to their west. British numbers in North America rose much faster than French numbers. New France, in 1754, held only about eighty thousand colonists. About 1,160,000 people lived in the British colonies. Enslaved people there added three hundred thousand more. Britain wanted fresh land, and New France blocked the way. Both empires wanted Native nations on these lands to side with them. That support was a way to gain the territory each empire wanted. Over many years, French ties with Native peoples were stronger than British ties. Native land was treated with respect by the French, and trade between them went well. Britain took Native land as its own. Native peoples were pushed to live under British rule. To guard their land and stay independent, many Native nations joined France. The Huron joined. The Shawnee joined. The Native nations did not act as one. The Iroquois, said EER-uh-kwoi, tried to keep clear of both sides. Later they had to choose, and the side they chose was Britain. A painting from 1755 shows Native fighters beside the French.

4Plans and Battles Several attacks on the French in North America began from the British side in 1755. The aim was to wipe out French forts that stood on the border between the two lands. French fighters knew the frontier well, and their Native allies knew it too. Forest and rough country worked in their favor. Again and again they caught the British by surprise and beat them by clever movement. Britain had far more colonists and far more supplies. The opening years of the war still went badly for Britain. A clear French edge appeared in 1756. On Lake Ontario, in today's New York, Britain had raised Fort Oswego and Fort Ontario. Deeper raids into French land were supposed to start from those forts. France attacked the forts instead. August 1756 brought their capture. The win was a large one. British plans fell apart. Native leaders also read the win as a sign that France was likely to come out ahead. Many of those leaders wanted friendship with the winner, so their nations could remain free. More Native nations moved to the French side. A War across the World Americans remember the fighting in North America under the name French and Indian War. Those battles also belonged to the wider Seven Years' War, from 1756 to 1763. Europe's strongest powers took part, and so did their colonies. Britain's partners included Prussia. Prussia was a kingdom whose land lies in today's Germany and also in today's Poland. Portugal stood with Britain, and other partners did too. On France's side stood the Russian Empire. Spain stood there too. Sweden did as well. Fighting reached Europe and the seas around it. West Africa saw battles. The Philippines saw battles. India saw battles. North America was another field of battle. Historians often call this the first war that spanned the world. One map lays out the main powers and the alliances of that European struggle.

5William Pitt Takes the Lead May 1756 was when the French and British empires each announced, in official words, that they were at war. The Seven Years' War dates its start from that announcement. It was a fight across the globe among Europe's strongest nations and the colonies they held. What happened in Europe mattered more and more to the contest in North America. William Pitt, a politician in Britain, gave himself to making the British Empire larger. He held that the Seven Years' War would be won only if France was beaten in North America. Changes he made lifted Britain's chances. He first sent money to Prussia, the ally fighting France on European ground. France then had to leave soldiers in Europe, and leave supplies there too. Next he moved extra British troops across the ocean, and extra ships as well. He also pressed for more pay and better training for troops raised in the British colonies. France, at the same time, had trouble finding the money its war required. Weapons of the War During the years Americans call the French and Indian War, a foot soldier's usual weapon was a flintlock musket. Loading it took work. A shooter with long practice could still get off only two shots in a minute, or three. Hits were reliable out to 175 yards, a distance of 160 meters, and good conditions stretched that range. Bayonets, which are long knives, fixed onto the muskets and turned them into stabbing tools. Artillery means the cannons. They weighed a great deal, and rough ground made them slow to haul. A blast from one of these guns could break fort walls and other defenses. Grapeshot, a load of small metal balls, could also be fired. One spray was enough to halt a charge by infantry. Pictures here show a flintlock musket and a bayonet. Pitt's North American plan aimed at Louisbourg, said LOO-iss-burg, a French fortress beside the St. Lawrence River. That river was the way to Quebec, capital of New France. British ships put about fourteen thousand men ashore near the fortress in July 1758. Eighteen days of siege brought it down. Quebec then lay open to British ships and British soldiers. The war turned in a major way with this win. In October of that year, Britain signed a treaty with the Shawnee. Fourteen other Native nations signed as well. France, lacking those allies, had to abandon Fort Duquesne. The Ohio River Valley passed into British control.

6Britain looks back on 1759 and calls it the Year of Miracles. Quebec fell in September of that year. People call the fight the Battle of the Plains of Abraham. A blockade by British ships then shut the St. Lawrence River. Men and supplies from France could barely reach New France after that. November 1759 brought another big British win, this one thousands of miles off. France's navy, in a desperate plan, meant to invade Britain itself. Along the French coast, twenty-three British warships found the French fleet. The fight is called the Battle of Quiberon Bay, said kee-buh-ROHN. The attack was bold, and the French navy was badly hurt. Command of the Atlantic Ocean passed to the British fleet. Damaged French ships, at the close of that bay fight, appear in a painting. Montreal fell to the British the next year. No other major city in New France was still unconquered. That capture finished the French and Indian War. The larger Seven Years' War closed in 1763. Peace terms, set down officially, came in the Treaty of Paris. Claims France had made to North American land were given up. Among European powers there, the British Empire now stood first. Native nations suffered a disastrous result, even the nations that had sided with Britain. No rival European power remained to block the way. British colonies pressed west, deeper into Native lands. French Life after the Loss France had lost, yet French culture did not vanish from North America. Montreal and Quebec City both lie in Quebec. Quebec is the largest province in Canada. The language officials use there is still French. British soldiers, in 1755, forced out a French people called the Acadians. Their home province was Nova Scotia, also in Canada. Some of those Acadians moved on to Louisiana. The name they took there was Cajuns. Music, food, and culture of their own are still part of Cajun life. One picture shows British soldiers telling Acadians to depart from Nova Scotia.

7A Road That Led to Rebellion North America took much of its later shape from the Seven Years' War. New France, once Britain ruled it, grew into the country of Canada. Canada keeps strong links to French culture and to English culture. The United States was shaped by the war as well. Britain, in 1765, put higher taxes on its colonies in North America. The extra money was meant to pay debts from the war. Britain also stopped American settlers from spreading farther west. The limit was meant to mend ties with Native nations. Colonists grew angry at both steps. By 1775 the anger had broken into the American Revolutionary War. Leaders of that war included many veterans of the French and Indian War. George Washington was among those leaders. France treated the American Revolution as a way to strike back at Britain. Supplies and ships from France let the Americans hold out. They then beat a British military that was stronger than their own. Independence from Britain came to the United States in 1783. A hard lesson followed. Britain lost much of the very land the French and Indian War had been fought to win. Soldiers take shelter in a fort, a strong building or a set of buildings. Allies are people, or groups, who join together for one shared cause. Invading means going in by force to conquer, to weaken, or to injure. A claim is land that someone, or some group, says it has a right to hold. To be outmaneuvered is to be beaten by skill, or put at a disadvantage by skill. Colonial refers to a colony. In U.S. history it often means the years before the thirteen colonies broke free of Britain. A siege is a long surround of an enemy, and attacks often go with it. Food and other supplies are kept from getting in. Disastrous describes harm, loss, or damage that spreads widely. Expansion means a growth in size, in amount, in volume, or in scope. Someone who has surrendered has stopped fighting in order to live. Territory is land or water that a state, a country, or a group controls. A fleet is ships that sail together and follow one command.

28. England's First Lasting Town in Virginia

1The founding's 400th anniversary was marked in 2007 with copies of three ships. Those ships had carried colonists to Jamestown. Godspeed stands at the left. Susan Constant stands in the middle. Discovery stands at the right. The Earliest Colonists. The Land Called Tsenacomoco. Hard and Hungry Months. A Crop Called Tobacco. A Captive Who Made Peace. Who Gained from the Success. The Earliest Colonists Massachusetts is where the Pilgrims came ashore at Plymouth Rock. Thirteen years before that landing, three ships from Britain reached another coast. The modern state there is Virginia. May 1607 was when the ships found a place on the James River. Going onto land waited until the day after arrival. England's first settlement in the Americas that lasted began on that ground. Jamestown was the name chosen for it. A Secret Kept from Spain One drawing shows a triangle. That was the fort's first outline. Earlier English tries at colonies in North America had not succeeded. Spain, by then, had started many colonies across the Americas. Spain's navy was a known danger to the people at Jamestown. Fear centered on the Spanish king. News of the town might move him to order the place destroyed.

2King James I of England gave the settlement its name. In 1606 the king gave Virginia Company of London a charter. Exploring was allowed. Conquering was allowed. Colonizing was allowed. The reach ran from today's New York State as far as North Carolina. Gold in North America was what the investors hoped to locate. Silver was another hope. A river shortcut toward the Pacific Ocean was a third hope. Trade with Asian countries would be easier if that river existed. Labels on a small map include Jamestown and Virginia. Maryland and Delaware are labeled too. Men and boys from England made up the first group, and they numbered 104. The site was picked for several reasons. Supply ships could come close, because deep water was nearby. No people were seen there. Defense looked easier because of the land's shape. Regret came later. Marsh covered the ground. Mud and salt were in the river water they drank. Do You Know? Two women from England, the first to arrive, reached Jamestown in 1608. Further years brought more women. Men still outnumbered women for most of the century. The Land Called Tsenacomoco Tsenacomoco also contained the site. Say it seh-nah-koh-MOH-koh. Tribes gathered under that name. Population stood near fifteen thousand. Camping on the Jamestown ground was a habit of one tribe. Surprise followed. A lasting town was going up, and nobody had asked them. The year 900 CE is when Tsenacomoco began. Life in the low country along today's Virginia coast went back even further for these tribes. Towns stood beside rivers. Yehakin was the name of a house. Local trees were carved into canoes. Stone and bone supplied the tools. Hunting and fishing were men's work. Farming was women's work. Powhatan and His People Powhatan is a name sometimes used for the people of Tsenacomoco. Say it POW-uh-tan. Their leader is the source of the name, and so is his own tribe. Control of numerous tribes in the region came to Powhatan by inheritance. The time was the middle and later 1500s. Tribute reached him from roughly thirty tribes by 1607. Tsenacomoco was the sum of those tribes plus the land they shared. Historic Jamestown, the archaeological site, yielded a copper medallion. Chief Powhatan is the person it is thought to portray.

3Practical farming was something the first colonists hardly knew. Storing food was another weak point. So was organized labor. Business leaders, not laborers, made up most of the grown men. London's investors wanted gold, the kind Spaniards had taken in South America. Day after day, many colonists hunted for gold. Nothing came of the hunt. Farming received little of their time. Completion of the fort came on June 15. Food still was not gathered in enough quantity, and it was not stored well, because the group lacked skill. Jamestown's earliest church went up in 1607. The next year, 1608, fire wiped it out. A drought was already in its second year when the English got there. The dry spell would not end until 1612. Food was scarcer at the very time these strangers needed the land to yield more. August 1607 brought sickness. Too little food was one cause. Drinking water was bad. Mosquitoes carried disease. Death took many. Burial sometimes depended on only 5 men still well enough to do it. The first year closed with 38 survivors out of the original 104. Leadership passed to Captain John Smith in September 1608. A rule of his was new to the town. He said, "No work, no food." Farming had to fill four hours of every colonist's day. A link with Powhatan, the powerful leader, was something Smith managed to form. Chief Powhatan was the colonists' name for him. Smith and the town, Powhatan hoped, could be brought inside Tsenacomoco. Peace held, but only briefly. Virginia's Jamestown Museum displays a statue of Chief Powhatan. Trade pleased the Indigenous peoples in the beginning. Food was what the Powhatan brought. Metal tools were what they wanted back, along with other copper goods. A better stretch of land was also offered to the English. Game and seafood lay within easier reach there. Failure of the whole settlement was the likely end, in those first years, without Powhatan aid. Powhatan tools dating from the 1600s are pictured too.

4Hard and Hungry Months Conflicts grew once new officers showed up, along with more colonists who had little experience. Chief Powhatan had marked lands for the English. They spread past those lands anyway. Fresh settlements appeared farther along the James River. By 1609 a poor reputation clung to the colonists among many tribes. Fear of Smith was common among Indigenous peoples. Villages saw him walk in, set guns against chiefs' heads, and insist on food and supplies. October 1609 was the month he stopped being leader. Injury was part of the story. Treatment required a return to England. Discouragement deepened in Jamestown once he was gone. Health was poor, and the struggle was heavy. Extra food for trade was something the tribes did not have, yet the colonists were desperate for food. The Powhatan and the English grew more hostile. Raiders from the English side burned Indigenous villages. They took food. Captain John Smith appears in one picture. A yehakin housed a single Powhatan family. Saplings were bent and tied together at the top, making an arch. Mats that had been woven covered the frame, or bark did. Bringing the settlers into Tsenacomoco was Powhatan's aim, and it failed. War followed in 1609, the First Anglo-Powhatan War. Five further years of fighting lay ahead. The Powhatan answered English violence by besieging the fort at Jamestown. Months passed under that siege. Food supplies could not be gained. People call the winter of 1609–10 the Starving Time. Anything at hand was eaten. That included rats. That included leather from shoes. Early 1610 found as many as 90 percent dead. The causes were starvation and disease.

5A Crop Called Tobacco Spring of 1610 found the remaining colonists finished with sickness, hunger, and death. England was where they decided to return. Another English ship met them as the coast fell behind. New colonists were aboard. Supplies that could keep people alive were aboard. Baron De La Warr was aboard, and he was the colony's new governor. Jamestown, he ordered, was where the tired colonists must go back. Eating was possible again. Profit for the Virginia Company was still required. Small industries were attempted. One was glass. One was silk. One was wine. Success came to none of them. Failure still described the settlement. Around 1612, tobacco entered the story as a cash crop, brought in by John Rolfe. Virginia farmers raise tobacco even now. Rolfe's own arrival had been in 1610. Long, warm summers in Virginia struck him as ideal for the crop. Moisture was the obstacle. A leaf just picked is green, and it is too wet to burn. Curing has to happen before anyone can smoke it. No good curing method was known to Rolfe. The Powhatan knew one. He wanted their techniques. Sharing was refused. The practice was sacred, and it was not for the English. A clearer view had formed among the Powhatan. Trade was not why the English had stayed. Land was what they wanted. Forest fell so tobacco fields could expand. Worn-out soil, after several years, pushed them farther into Tsenacomoco. More trees came down. Fights between the groups were frequent. De La Warr's time did not heal the relationship. Villages were raided by his troops. Houses burned, and cornfields burned. Food was stolen. The Powhatan struck back in kind. Delaware, the state, takes its name from Baron De La Warr.

6A Captive Who Made Peace Samuel Argall, an English captain, chose a plan that same year. Indigenous attacks were what he meant to stop. Chief Powhatan's favorite daughter would be seized and held until a ransom was paid. Matoaka was her true name. A flower between two streams is what the name means. Pocahontas is the nickname the world uses now. Her age was about sixteen. A husband and a young child shared her village when Argall arrived. Hand her over, he told the village, or face violence. She placed her baby with the village women before she went. Jamestown was where she was taken. She did not know the fate waiting for her husband. On his return to the village, the English would kill him. Corn was one ransom demand. Prisoners and stolen goods were to be given back. A treaty of peace was demanded too. Immediate agreement covered some demands. Negotiation was Powhatan's answer for the rest. Captivity still held her a year later. Argall brought her to Powhatan, and 150 men with weapons came along. The unpaid part of the ransom was what he insisted on. Fighting started again. Indigenous villages were burned by settlers. Indigenous men were killed. Pocahontas spoke to her father about a wish to marry John Rolfe. She may have seen the marriage as a road to peace. Captivity was where she had met Rolfe. Artists have pictured her many times. Only one portrait is thought to be truly authentic. English clothes are what she wore for it, during a London visit. Consent came from Powhatan. April 1614 was the wedding month. That wedding closed the First Anglo-Powhatan War. Colonists and the Powhatan were at peace again, though it would not last. The Peace of Pocahontas is what people still call it. A few years of calmer conflict followed the marriage of this Indigenous woman and this Englishman. In those quieter times, Pocahontas stood as the symbol.

7Rolfe gained something besides peace from the marriage. Curing methods for tobacco were now shared with him. The sharers were Powhatan spiritual leaders, and they were Pocahontas's family. England soon treated his tobacco as a sensation. A profitable venture, at last, seemed to be in Jamestown's hands. Leaves of Virginia tobacco are hung until they dry. Drying is the visible part of curing. How the tobacco finally turns out depends on this crucial step. Who Gained from the Success Tsenacomoco did not gain from the demand for tobacco. Land in large amounts was required to grow it. Labor in large amounts was required too. The tobacco trade now reached for Powhatan tribal lands. More colonies, past Jamestown, kept being planted by the growing English population. Seizure of Tsenacomoco land continued. Cheap Labor Work was scarce for some Europeans. A fresh chance, as indentured servants, drew them to Jamestown and to other North American settlements. Passage aboard a ship was the usual offer. Room, board, and a place to sleep followed arrival. Service ran from four years to seven. Freedom came at the end, and land was often part of the reward. Servants sent out from England under indenture are estimated at 80,000 to 85,000. Virginia and Maryland were the destinations. The period was the 17th century. Tobacco farms in Virginia received some of them. The Jamestown economy soon could not do without them. Colonies received their first African people in 1619. Indentured service was the work they were brought to do. Ndongo was their kingdom. Today that place is Angola, on Central Africa's western coast. Capture had come during a war against the Portuguese. Chances to become free matched, for a while, between Black indentured servants and white ones. Laws about slavery arrived soon after. Mid-century was when colonists started holding Africans enslaved for life. The main labor supply shifted. Indentured servants gave way to enslaved people.

8The tobacco industry succeeded. Money for the colony did not. Bankruptcy of the Virginia Company was declared by the king in 1624. A British colony replaced the company, and Virginia was the first such colony in the Americas. Lost money was the investors' price. Lives were the price for many colonists. Six people might cross the Atlantic, and only one of them would survive. Disaster also struck the Powhatan. People beyond counting were lost. So was most of the land their families had held for centuries. England was where Pocahontas died in 1617, while she was visiting. Suspicion surrounds the circumstances. The next year brought the death of Chief Powhatan. Peace between his people and the English settlers ended with that death. Gravesend, England, has a statue of Pocahontas outside St. George's Church. Another war, the Second Anglo-Powhatan War, opened in 1622. More than ten years passed before it ended. A peace treaty in 1646 had the agreement of the new Powhatan chief. The Third Anglo-Powhatan War, the final one, ended with that treaty. Indigenous peoples here now lived under the English king. Tsenacomoco, the Indigenous chiefdom, was gone. The Powhatan Today Eight separate Virginia tribes make up the Powhatan now. Culture and traditions are still kept, and still taught, by all eight. Reservations remain for two tribes. Banks of the Mattaponi River hold the Mattaponi Indian Reservation. The Pamunkey River is the line of the Pamunkey Indian Reservation. The Pamunkey Tribe included Pocahontas and Chief Powhatan. A traditional chant is performed by Rev. Nick Miles. Another name for him is Tecumseh Red Cloud. The Pamunkey are his tribe. NASA, in Washington, D.C., is where he performs in the picture. A 2019 ceremony named a celestial body, and Miles was part of it. The Hubble Space Telescope had found that body. Arrokoth was the name given. Algonquian languages of the Powhatan are the source of the word. Sky is the meaning.

9Timeline The 1570s are when Chief Powhatan inherited a chiefdom. Six tribes were in it at the start. About 25 further tribes were his by conquest as of 1607. London saw three ships depart in 1606. The planned town was meant to sit at a latitude from 34 degrees to 41 degrees. Jamestown was settled by the English in 1607. John Smith sailed for England in 1609. The Starving Time killed many settlers at Jamestown. That same year opened the First Anglo-Powhatan War. Homeward sailing began in 1610. A supply ship met them, and they turned around. Tobacco planting by John Rolfe began in 1611. Jamestown found the crop highly profitable. Pocahontas and John Rolfe married in 1614. The First Anglo-Powhatan War stopped. Chief Powhatan's death came in 1618, one year after Pocahontas died. Baron de la Warr died in that year as well. The Virginia Company was declared bankrupt by the British king in 1624. Virginia's status became that of a British colony. Fighting in the Second Anglo-Powhatan War ran from 1622 to 1632. Fighting in the Third Anglo-Powhatan War ran from 1644 to 1646. An official document that sets out rights and duties, for a person or a group, is a charter. A ransom is what is demanded, or what is paid, to free someone or something from captivity. Colonizing means going to a place and living there because your country claims it. Forcing out the people already there is common. Great excitement is a sensation. A person or a thing that stirs that excitement can be called a sensation too. People living in a new place form a settlement. A community has been set up there. Designated means picked out, given a name, or selected for one special use. An investor may be a person, a company, or an organization. Money goes into a purchase or a business in the hope of profit. A symbol stands in for something else. It may be a person, or it may be a thing. Thwarting means blocking a plan, or standing against a hope. Labor is hard work done with the body. The word can also mean the people who do that work. A venture is an undertaking that carries risk. Negotiating means talking in order to reach an agreement that is formal.

29. Enormous Beasts of the Deep Past

1A portrait at the top left shows Georges Cuvier. He set the ways scientists decide an extinct animal's looks. Megatherium is drawn at the top as one example. Geologist William Buckland stands in the left foreground. A magnifying glass sits over his find. The find is a tiny jaw bone from a mammal. A dinosaur toe bone was with that jaw. From those two bones, Buckland and Cuvier made a choice. Mammals had lived in times older than people had believed. What Giants Lived Long Ago? Giant Invertebrates. Giant Fish and Amphibians. Giant Reptiles. Giant Birds. Giant Mammals. A World Without Giants? Glossary. What Giants Lived Long Ago? Dinosaurs were not the only giant animals of prehistoric times. Other reptiles grew giant in that age too. Some shellfish were giants. Some insects were giants. Some centipedes were giants. Some fish were giants. Some amphibians were giants. Some birds were giants. Some mammals were giants. An ape grew to giant size as well. Old adventure tales still show an ape almost that huge. Paleontologists are the scientists who do this work. They learn about animals of prehistoric times by studying fossils. A fossil can be a bone. A fossil can be some other remain. A fossil can be a trace left behind. One fossil can reveal when an animal lived. It can reveal where that life was. It can reveal the size of the body. It can reveal the food the animal ate. It can reveal how the animal moved. Do You Know? Species kept changing all through the history of Earth. Old species became extinct. New species showed up after them. Take every animal species that has ever lived. More than 99 percent of them are extinct now. Scientists break Earth's history into periods. A period is one length of time. Periods are gathered into eras. A chart later in this book names each animal's period. The same chart names the era. Imagine a time machine. Enjoy a prehistoric trip among these giants.

2Giant Invertebrates. Point the time machine at the Paleozoic era (pay-lee-ah-ZO-ik). An invertebrate is an animal with no backbone. Some of the giants fly in the air. Others swim through ocean water. Cameroceras, the Scariest Shellfish. Begin at 470 million years ago. End at 440 million years ago. Every animal lives in the ocean. A giant shellfish goes by the name Cameroceras. Pronounce it cam-er-ah-SAIR-us. It looks much like a squid. A shell shaped like a cone covers the body. The head pokes out of the shell. Eight tentacles poke out too. The shell may reach 36 feet. That is 11 m. Cameroceras hunts animals of the sea. Tentacles grab the prey. A sharp beak tears that prey into pieces. Do You Know? Small relatives of Cameroceras left fossil shells. People long ago found those shells. They thought the shells were horns of unicorns. Meganeura, a Dangerous Dragonfly. Now leap forward more than 100 million years. A swampy forest is around you. The opening date is 311 million years ago. The closing date is 282 million years ago. Down swoops a huge dragonfly. Its name is Meganeura (meh-guh-NYUR-uh). Most birds you know are smaller. The distance from wing tip to wing tip is 2.5 feet. That distance is 76 cm. No insect known since has been larger. Today's giant insects set next to Meganeura. The air feels heavier than air you know. More oxygen is the reason. Heavy air can hold up this giant flyer. Extra oxygen lets Meganeura become truly giant. Other animals become giant for the same reason. One living giant insect is the atlas moth. Another is the goliath beetle. Another is the desert centipede. Arthropleura, the Biggest Bug. A crawler comes toward you on the forest floor. No land arthropod has ever been larger. Its name is Arthropleura (AHR-throw-PLOOR-ah). It looks like a centipede. The leg count is 60. Length can pass 8 feet. That length equals 2.5 m. Swampy forests are where it lives. One boundary is 340 million years ago. The other boundary is 280 million years ago. Oxygen makes that air heavy. That is why this bug can grow so large.

3Giant Fish and Amphibians. These next giants lived in separate periods. The era is called Mesozoic. Pronounce it MEZ-uh-ZO-ik. Pack a snorkel. The water ahead is the sea. Next is the biggest of all fish. Its name is Leedsichthys. Pronounce it leeds-ICK-thiss. It grew larger than any other fish. Its years open at 165 million years ago. They close at 155 million years ago. Length can reach almost 55 feet. That is 16.8 m. It swims while gulping huge amounts of water. The rear of the mouth holds the teeth. There are more than forty thousand teeth. Each tooth is long. Each tooth is thin. The teeth work like a screen. Shrimp stay in when the water leaves. Jellyfish stay in too. Other small animals stay in as well. The fish then pushes the water back outside. This eating method is called filter feeding. In your time, many whales feed this same way. Leedsichthys later becomes extinct. One possible cause is a fall in the seas. The seas grow smaller too. A smaller sea means less food for this giant. Do You Know? Fishermen in Thailand made a catch in May 2005. The catch was a Mekong giant catfish. It was almost 9 feet long. That is 2.7 m. Scientists wanted time to study it. They never got that time. The fishermen ate the fish. Friends who were with them ate it too. Koolasuchus, a Slimy Giant. Jump farther, but stay in the Mesozoic. The jump may be 40 million years. It may be as long as 60 million years. Koolasuchus (KOOL-ah-SOOK-us) waits there. It is a salamander. It is slimy. It is giant. Length is about 17 feet. That is 5 m. The head is wide. The head is flat. Swampy forests are home. Home begins 137 million years ago. Home lasts to 112 million years ago. The big head holds long teeth. The count is more than 100. Those teeth capture fish. They capture crabs. They capture turtles. They capture other prey. Eyes rest on the top of the head. The body can bury itself in muddy water. The eyes can still watch for prey. Koolasuchus will disappear. Other giant amphibians will disappear too. Climate will change. That change drives them to extinction. These are animals from the Mesozoic era.

4Giant Reptiles. Dinosaurs walk the land in the Mesozoic era. Giant reptiles of other kinds swim the ocean. Some are as gigantic as certain dinosaurs. Some are every bit as dangerous. First is a reptile with a fishlike body. Cymbospondylus lives early in this span. Pronounce it sim-bow-SPON, then di-lus. The span opens at 240 million years ago. It closes at 210 million years ago. Length is 33 feet, which is 10 m. It is one of the sea's biggest animals. The head is huge. The snout is long. The snout is pointed. Many rows of small teeth sit in the jaws. The teeth are for catching fish. They are also for holding other animals. The hunts take place in deep water. Liopleurodon of the Ocean. Move forward in time. Stay with the salt water if you feel brave. The animal swimming here is named Liopleurodon. Pronounce it LIE-oh-PLOOR-oh-don. Its bite invites a comparison with T. rex. The jaws are large. The jaws are powerful. Any animal of the sea could be killed by them. This hunter's neck is short. Life starts at 160 million years ago. Life ends at 155 million years ago. The body can grow to 49 feet. That is 15 m. Elasmosaurus, Long-Necked Hunter. Try a later time in the water. Start at 85 million years ago. Stop at 65 million years ago. Elasmosaurus is easy to miss. Pronounce it eh-LAZ-mo-SAWR-us. It still grows to 49 feet. That is 15 m. The neck holds most of the length. The tail holds much of the rest. Most of the body can stay far from the fish. Those fish are what it hunts. The long neck can slip under a school of them. The fish may never know a giant is below. This reptile swam with the neck straight out in front. It had four flippers. Each flipper was shaped like a diamond. Ornithocheirus, a Flying Reptile. Look up to see Ornithocheirus in flight. Pronounce it or-NITH-oh-KY-rus. It lives near coasts of the sea. It lives near lakes too. The years open at 140 million years ago. They close at 70 million years ago. Wing tip to wing tip can measure 40 feet. That reach is 12.2 m. Body length is about 11.5 feet. That is 3.5 m. The animal is gigantic. Its weight may still be close to yours. The bones are hollow. Hollow bones help it fly. These giant flyers form large groups. They build nests. The nests sit on tops of cliffs.

5Giant Birds. Terror birds are huge. They cannot fly. Spotting them is easy. Gastornis, a Ton of Terror. Look in forests. Look in swamps. The years open at 56 million years ago. They close at 41 million years ago. Gastornis (gas-TOR-nis) lives there. Height is about 7 feet. That is 2.1 m. Dinosaurs are already extinct by then. This bird may be a top predator in North America. It may be a top predator in Europe. Modern scientists are not sure of its food. The beak is sharp. The beak is powerful. That beak could rip flesh. It could crush the bones of a small animal. The bird would have to catch the animal first. Weight may pass 1 ton. That is 0.9 metric tons. Speed and Danger in a Later Terror Bird. The bird is Phorusrhacos (FOR-us-RAH-kus). Height can reach 10 feet. That is 3 m. It hunts small animals. Some hunts are on plains. Some hunts are in woodlands. The years open at 27 million years ago. They close at 2.5 million years ago. It weighs less than Gastornis. Lower weight lets it move much faster. It may chase prey at 43 miles an hour. That speed is 69 kmph. A car on a city street is usually slower. Giant Mammals. Giant reptiles had already died away. Giant mammals then began ruling the land. Many scientists share a thought about terror birds. The birds died out at a later time. That time sits in the Cenozoic era. Mammals were better at hunting. They left nothing for the birds to eat. Plants are the only food of the giant mammals that follow. An eater of plants alone is called a herbivore. Indricotherium, a Rhino of Dinosaur Size. Climb a tree if you want a clear view. Indricotherium stands below. Pronounce it IN-drik-oh, then THEER-ee-um. The rhinoceros of today is a relative. The neck is long. A giraffe feeds with a long neck in the same way. Leaves high in the trees are food. Branches high in the trees are food. The years open at 30 million years ago. They close at 25 million years ago. Height is at least 15 feet. That is 4.5 m. A one-story house is not as tall. Weight is 16 tons. That is 15 metric tons. Very few mammals grew larger than this one.

6Gigantopithecus, a True Giant Ape. Gigantopithecus is a real ape of giant size. Pronounce it jeye-GANT-o, then PIHTH-uh-kuhs. The years open about 8 million years ago. They close 100,000 years before the present. Some males stand on their hind legs. Height then is 10 feet. That is 3 m. Weight for those males passes 1,000 pounds. That is 454 kg. A female reaches only half of that size. Call this ape a gentle giant. Bamboo is food. Fruit is food. Seeds are food. Other plant foods are eaten too. The home forests are tropical. They grow in Asia. Do You Know? People still ask if this ape could be alive. Hundreds of people say they saw a creature. It was huge. It was hairy. It looked like an ape. Some reports come from the northwestern United States. Other reports come from Canada. Footprints in those places can measure 16 inches. That is 41 cm. The footprints led to a common name. The name is Bigfoot. Asia has reports of a creature of a similar kind. The name there is Yeti. Most scientists do not believe these animals are real. An early human may stand near you in this time. The human is called Homo erectus. Homo erectus shares these years. Homo erectus shares these places. The Woolly Mammoth and Other Mammuthus. Move forward into the last ice age. The age opens at 4 million years ago. It closes at 10,000 years ago. A woolly mammoth may appear. It is a species inside Mammuthus (MA-muh-thus). Picture a huge elephant. Hair covers it. Tusks leave the face. The tusks are long. The tusks are curved. The tusks push snow aside to open a path. The likely goal is a search for plants. Woolly mammoth height is almost 12 feet. That is 3.6 m. A different Mammuthus species grows taller. It can reach 14 feet. That is 4.3 m. Mammoths become extinct once the ice age ends. The weather turns warmer than they can live through. A drawing puts an African elephant on the left. The woolly mammoth stands there too. Three ancestors stand with them. Those ancestors are close kin. Another huge mammal shares that ice age. Its name is Megatherium. Pronounce it meg-ah-THEER-ee-um. It is a ground sloth. The years open about 2 million years ago. They close at 8,000 years ago. Length is almost 20 feet. That is 6 m. Tree sloths still live in South America. They are much smaller. Megatherium is related to them. People today have found footprints that turned into fossils. The sloth could stand. The sloth could walk upright.

7A World Without Giants? The giants in this book once walked Earth's land. They once swam in the ocean too. We cannot look at them today. That is a sad loss. Many other giant animals are alive now. You are able to see them. A threat of extinction hangs over many. The reason is population size. The populations are very small. Protecting them is important. The main path is to preserve habitats. Then we need not face a world with every giant gone. Chart of Eras and Periods. Each line gives the era, the period, when it began, and the animals in this book. Era Precambrian. No period name. Began 4.5 billion years ago. No animal from these pages. The earliest known animal shows up in this stretch, about 600 million years ago. Era Paleozoic. Period Cambrian. Began 543 million years ago. No animal from these pages. Era Paleozoic. Period Ordovician. Began 490 million years ago. Animal: Cameroceras. Era Paleozoic. Period Silurian. Began 443 million years ago. No animal from these pages. Era Paleozoic. Period Devonian. Began 417 million years ago. No animal from these pages. Era Paleozoic. Period Carboniferous. Began 354 million years ago. Animals: Arthropleura and Meganeura. Era Paleozoic. Period Permian. Began 290 million years ago. No animal from these pages. Era Mesozoic. Period Triassic. Began 248 million years ago. Animal: Cymbospondylus. Era Mesozoic. Period Jurassic. Began 206 million years ago. Animals: Leedsichthys and Liopleurodon. Era Mesozoic. Period Cretaceous. Began 144 million years ago. Animals: Ornithocheirus, Koolasuchus, and Elasmosaurus. Era Cenozoic. Period Tertiary. Began 65 million years ago. Animals: Gastornis, Indricotherium, Phorusrhacos, and Gigantopithecus. Era Cenozoic. Period Quaternary. Began 2 million years ago. Animals: Mammuthus and Megatherium. Glossary. Amphibians are cold-blooded animals. They have backbones. They generally spend part of life in water. They also spend part of life on land. An ice age is one of several spans in Earth's past. During it, broad sheets of ice lay over much of the land. Invertebrates are animals. They lack a backbone. An arthropod is one kind of invertebrate. The body is made of segments. An exoskeleton covers it. The limbs have joints. Insects are in the group. Arachnids are in the group. Crustaceans are in the group. Paleontologists are people. They study fossils from plants. They study fossils from animals. Prehistoric describes the time before history was written down. Eras are large pieces of time. They divide the long story of Earth. A species is a group of living things. Members of the group look much alike. Members can reproduce. Extinct means the group is gone. It is not in existence anymore. It has been fully wiped out. Habitats are natural homes. Plants live in them. Animals live in them. Tentacles are animal limbs. They are long. They bend. The word fits an invertebrate most of all. Herbivores are animals. Their food is plants and nothing else.

30. Fighting Fires in the Wild

1An introduction opens this book. High points and low points of the job come next. Causes of fire follow. Life with the crew follows the causes. Tools of the work follow. Who fights fires comes next. Protection and prevention follow. A conclusion follows that. A glossary ends the book. A photo shows a mobile home park in Arizona ruined by the Rodeo/Chediski Fire. Wildfires belong to nature. Scientists have found that some plants and some animals need fire. Fire clears dead matter. Fresh growth then has room on the forest floor. The lodgepole pine is one tree that needs fire. Heat melts the waxy seals on its cones. Seeds can then fall. People use wild land too. They live near it. They raise crops and livestock in the country. They visit places such as national parks. Homes can lie in the fire's path. Farms, ranches, and parks can too. Wildland firefighters try to save those places. Many wildfires are simply too big to put out. Firefighters then try to steer the fire. They clear fuel from its path. They may move the fuel aside and make a firebreak. They may burn the fuel off with a small, controlled back burn. Humans start most wildfires.

2Todd Cupell fights wildland fire out of Tucson, Arizona. He gave this interview in 2002. Asked what he loves about the job, he talks about scenery. Hiking into remote fire country shows him some of the finest views on Earth. He sees green, lush land turn into flame and burned ground. Flames and smoke fascinate many people. He also likes the variety. No two days match. Asked about the worst part, he names more than one thing. Destruction is one. Property and homes are what hurt to see. Saving things people value takes hard work. Feeling short of time is painful. Feeling that the work was not good enough is painful. He sometimes thinks one more action might have saved a house. That feeling may be the hardest part of the job. The other hard part is mop-up. Crews flip every rock and every pile of ash. Gloves come off. The backs of hands test the ground for leftover heat. The work is long, hot, and tedious. Gear rides on their backs. A bladder bag is a pump that sprays water. Hand tools come too. The job is hot, heavy, and dirty. A picture shows a bladder bag.

3A photo shows firefighters lighting small back burns that are carefully controlled. The burns remove fuel a wildfire could use. Asked about his scariest moment, Todd says scary moments are common. Danger is always nearby. Entrapment is among the worst. Fire burns all around a crew and cuts off the way out. Crews deploy their shelters. They hope that cover will be enough to save them. Entrapment is the greatest fear because it is how many firefighters die. Lightning fires often start far from people. They are usually bigger than fires people start. Asked how wildfires begin, Todd gives two main causes. The first is nature. Lightning is the most common natural cause. A rare windstorm can knock down a power line. A spark then starts a fire. Even so, lightning starts most wildfires. Nature's fires are often in the middle of nowhere. Nobody sees them in time to report them. Control comes too late.

4People are the second cause. In the year of this interview, people started almost every major wildfire in Arizona. Embers blow from campfires that are illegal and left alone. The ground catches. Some fires are set on purpose. The Rodeo Fire was set by a firefighter. Work had been scarce that season. He wanted a fire so he would have a job. The fire escaped his control. Other firefighters were put in danger. Homes were put in danger. The Madera Canyon Fire began when a helicopter flew too low. It clipped a power line. Vehicles start fires too. A blown tire throws sparks into dry brush or grass beside the road. That happened more than once that year. North of Tucson, Arizona, the Bullock Fire was blamed on a campfire. Smoke jumpers are special firefighters. They reach the most remote parts of large wildland fires. They parachute from planes into the middle of the flames. Asked how he feels about people who start wildfires, Todd calls it a shame. That year, two fires were set on purpose by firefighters. Whatever their reason, it stains the name of crews who work hard and love the job. Those crews risk their lives for homes and property. Arsonists light fires on purpose. They are not well liked.

5Asked about life with the crew, Todd says a lot of time is spent at the station. The crew feels like a family. One man put it cleverly. Fifty years earlier, firefighting was a brotherhood. So many women now do the work that it feels more like a family. Everyone pulls toward the same goal, controlling fire. Camaraderie is strong after a shift. Lunch is shared. Dinner is shared. On a fire, these families stay together. Firefighters rest in a photo. They had just worked 16 hours. The fire was Rodeo/Chediski. Crews from several cities may share one fire. They still usually eat with their own team. Fights among firefighters are not seen. On the fire line, trust is required. The person beside you must be competent. Shared training helps. Shared fires help. Shared experience helps. Your life depends on that person. That person's life depends on you. A typical day depends. The station is often quiet. The first days of the Rodeo Fire were brutal. The crew stayed 43 hours on the line without sleep. Todd rose about five each morning. A briefing with the forest service told him the plan and where people were going. The day then went to the fire lines. Houses were cleaned up around. Back burns were set. Whatever the fire needed, they did.

6Asked about gear, Todd starts with Personal Protection Equipment, or PPE. PPE is the clothing. It includes a Nomex shirt and Nomex pants. Boot soles must resist fire. Boots are leather. Boots cannot include cloth that might ignite. Cloth that might melt is banned too. Todd appears in full gear. A radio is with him. A head lamp is with him. Safety goggles are with him. Asked what Nomex is, he calls it a special fabric that resists fire. A match will not set it alight. Sparks are everywhere. Ordinary clothes could catch. Nomex is a lifesaver. A folded fire shelter must also be carried. It looks like a tent for one person, made of aluminum and fiberglass. It is the last chance to live. If you are entrapped and fire will burn over you, you open it and climb in. Inside, heat can reach 190 degrees Fahrenheit. That is 88 degrees Celsius. A person can survive that. Outside, flames can hit 2,000 degrees Fahrenheit. That is 1,093 degrees Celsius. Those flames would kill at once. Breathing the gases and the superheated air would burn the lungs. That can kill too. People still die inside shelters. The shelters also save many lives. A hard hat is required. Dead trees can fall on you. So can branches. Firefighters call those hazards snags. Many things can fall.

7An IA pack is an Initial Attack pack. It is basically a backpack that holds a lot of water. Other items ride in it. Usually there is one change of clothes. Fusees ride in it. A fusee is a very hot flare used to start a fire. One escape from entrapment is to light a new fire and burn the fuel in a spot. The firefighter then moves into the black, the ground already burned. That ground is called a safety zone. An IA pack holds a surprising amount of gear. A partial list includes a fire shelter that opens fast. It includes several hand tools. It includes reference books for every kind of fire. It includes a fastener strip for mending clothes and packs. It includes extra socks and bandannas. It includes extra Nomex pants. It includes extra shoelaces. It includes lip balm. It includes earplugs. It includes goggles. It includes fusees. It includes matches. It includes electrical tape. It includes MREs, meals ready to eat. Gloves are always required. Heat, flame, and wood demand hand protection. Each firefighter usually carries one hand tool. It may be a Pulaski, which joins an ax and a hoe. It may be a pick. It may be a scraper. Todd says there are too many tools to name. The basic needs are a fire shelter, a helmet, water, and Nomex. Other gear depends on the job. The load is at least fifty pounds. That is 23 kilograms. A photo set shows gloves, a helmet with a Nomex neck shroud, a Pulaski, and a McLeod rake. Heavy clothes and heavy gear meet hot conditions. Body temperature can climb to a dangerous level. In twenty minutes, sweating can cost a firefighter as much as one liter of water. Drinking water all the time is vital. Carrying that water adds weight.

8The photo shows crews in mop-up. The flames are already gone. Asked which traits matter, Todd puts teamwork first. You must take direction. You must give direction. A whole group must work well together on the line. Everyone must share the same plan. Cooperation matters. Helping others matters. Leading others matters. Team spirit has to live in the personality. A plane drops chemicals that slow fire, ahead of a wildfire. Asked what a person needs in order to qualify, Todd lists good fitness. Long hours are required. Orders must be taken well. Orders must be given well. Love of the work is required. Without that love, a person will not last. Hard work can open the job if it is truly what you want.

9Wildfires can start in forests. They can start in deserts. They can start in neighborhoods. Climate change has made wildfires more frequent. It has made the season longer. More fires now cover larger areas. Families can prepare. Keep an emergency kit ready in case you must evacuate. Pack plenty of fresh water. Pack a battery radio and spare batteries. Pack blankets. Pack food that will not spoil. Pack medicines and supplies your family needs. Obey every evacuation order. If the neighborhood is cleared, do not stay to guard the house or your things. Do not return until officials say it is safe. Leave the fire to the firefighters. Before you leave, close every window. Ask an adult to shut off gas lines. Ask a parent or guardian to keep the roof and the gutters free of debris. Ask if a fire-resistant layer can be added to the roof. Large sparks travel far. They can ignite a roof miles away. In very dry times, when danger is high, keep flammable piles away from the house. Firewood, brush, and garbage are examples. Ask a parent or guardian if plants and trees touching the house can be taken away. Plants are easier to replace than a home. In wild country, follow posted campfire rules. Skip the fire when the rules forbid one. A feeling of safety is not enough. A grownup should build the fire and watch it. Never leave it alone. Build it safely. Clear debris from the pit or fireplace. Rocks should ring the fire. Use two layers or more. Keep extra wood away from the flames. A big bucket of water should sit close to the fire. Keep a shovel nearby. Drown stray sparks with water or with a shovelful of damp dirt. Put the fire out with lots of water. Stir the ashes so water reaches every burning bit. Feel the ground with care. No heat should remain.

10Wildland firefighting is not easy. A wildfire is unpredictable. It can jump from a low brush fire to a firestorm in the treetops in seconds. Rough ground can block escape. Many firefighters lose their lives. The work can also reward you deeply. Homes are saved. Jobs are saved. Beautiful wild places are often protected. Hard work plus excitement may make this the job for you. The photo catches the Rodeo Fire moments before Pinedale, Arizona, was burned through. Several homes were destroyed. The local fire station was destroyed. An arsonist is a person who starts a fire on purpose. Crews work the fire line, which is a wildfire's outer edge. A bladder bag is a water bag carried on the back. Fire-retardant means able to slow a fire. A briefing is a meeting that updates everyone. A fusee is a very hot flare used to light a back burn. Mesmerized means fascinated. Brutal means harsh or vicious. Nomex is a fire-resistant fabric known by that name. Camaraderie means friendship. A Pulaski combines two tools. An ax forms one end. A hoe forms the other. It is named for its inventor. Competent means the person can handle the work. Entrapment means being trapped with fire all around. Tedious means boring and slow.

31. Forests That Time Left Standing

1Four old-growth forests around the world appear on these pages. Shirakami-Sanchi is in Japan, and it is named twice. Great Smoky Mountains National Park is in the United States, and it is named twice. Sequoia and Kings Canyon National Parks are in the United States, and they are named twice. The Western Caucasus is in Russia, and it is named twice. The book begins with a look at great age. The United States comes next, then Japan, then Russia. The future of old-growth forests follows. A word list ends the book. Imagine a dark, lovely forest around you. Trunks wider than cars tower overhead. Almost every bit of sunlight is blocked. Small ferns and other plants take in the little light they can find. Pine needles cover the ground. Other dead leaves cover it too. Wonder and mystery belong to an old-growth forest. A fairy tale might feel the same.

2Truth would not be far from that scene in some old-growth forests. A very different look belongs to others. A single tree type fills some of them. Many tree types fill others. Sky-touching height seems true of some trees. A height shorter than a house is true of others. Scientists therefore share no one definition. Features in common have still been noticed. At least 150 years of age is required by many scientists. The age of each tree may still vary widely. A complex structure is required as well. Varying layers must make up the canopy. Large trees stand in those layers. Some are living. Some are dead or dying. Fallen trees leave holes in the canopy. Young trees can find sunlight there and grow. Snags are the name for upright dead trees. Food comes from fallen trees and from snags. Shelter comes from them too. Animals depend on that help. Plants depend on it. Fungi depend on it. Earth offers no second home to some of these species. Forest levels can be named. The canopy holds tall trees like pines, maples, and oaks. The understory holds small trees and bushes. The forest floor holds grasses, mosses, ferns, and logs. Beauty marks old-growth forests. Scientific interest marks them too. They rank among the finest places of both kinds on Earth. Humans have made many of them shrink. Humans have made many disappear. Study of the ones that remain, plus protection, can teach us. The ecosystems they create are complex and delicate.

3California is the home of Sequoia and Kings Canyon National Parks. Together they cover more than 1,353 square miles, which is 3,504 square kilometers. Old-growth forest inside them covers more than 300 square miles, which is 777 square kilometers. A variety of tree species grows there. Most of those trees are coniferous. Deciduous trees grow there as well. The giant sequoia is one of the most amazing. It is found only in California. Few living things match these huge trees for age. Life can last more than 3,000 years. One giant sequoia is known as the General Sherman Tree. It is the planet's largest tree. It is not the tallest tree. Thousands of creatures live in the park. One is the Pacific fisher, a relative of the weasel. It lives under the thick canopy of old-growth forest. Birds are part of its hunting. Small mammals are part of its hunting. Porcupine is its favorite meal. Old-growth forest is the limit of its habitat. That limit has made it rare in California, in Oregon, and in Washington. Pictures are labeled fisher, sequoia, and redwood. California grows both the giant redwood and the giant sequoia. Both have bark of one color. Both are huge, yet they differ. Giant redwoods are the world's tallest trees. They can reach 378 feet, or 115 meters. Giant sequoias are the largest. Diameter can reach 40 feet, or 12 meters. A sequoia can reach nearly double the width of a redwood. Fog is the best setting for redwoods. Dry heat is what lets sequoia cones open. Redwoods grow near sea level. Sequoias grow from 5,000 to 7,000 feet, or 1,524 to 2,134 meters.

4Autumn color fills Great Smoky Mountains National Park. North Carolina and Tennessee share the park inside the Appalachian Mountains. It covers more than 800 square miles, or 2,072 square kilometers. Almost all of the park is forest. Old-growth makes up only about 25 percent. Deciduous trees make up most of that old-growth. Species include dogwood, Carolina silverbell, and magnolia. American beech grows there. Yellow birch grows there. Maple grows there. Other kinds grow there too. The Carolina northern flying squirrel is endangered. These trees are its home. These small mammals do not actually fly. Skin attached at the front paws and the back paws lets them glide. Fungi and lichens are most of what they eat. Fruits and nuts may be eaten as well. These animals would vanish without the old-growth forest. Towering trees are not a feature of every old-growth forest. Fierce and frigid winds strike some harsh places. Pines, spruces, and other coniferous trees then become stunted and twisted. People call them Krummholz. The German word means crooked wood. They live near the Arctic. They live near timberline, the mountain boundary where the trees stop growing. They never grow much over 6 feet, or 1.8 meters. Some are one thousand years old. Do not let their size fool you.

5Sunlight draws a Siebold's beech upward in Shirakami-Sanchi, Japan. Northern Japan is the setting of Shirakami-Sanchi. East Asia has almost no untouched old-growth forest left, and this place is one survivor. Siebold's beech trees make up most of it. The area covers just 65 square miles, or 170 square kilometers, of the Shirakami Mountains. Forests like this once covered most of northern Japan. Many have been cut down. Humans have left Shirakami-Sanchi almost completely untouched. It has no trails. It has no structures. Steep slopes are why no trees have been cut. Wildlife in the area is protected. Bear hunting is sometimes permitted for the Matagi, a group of hunters. The hunt is part of their religion. The Japanese serow lives in the forest. Besides this forest, Japan has only two other small areas where this goatlike animal lives. More than 2,100 insect species live in the forests. So do 87 bird species. The black woodpecker is one of them, and it is endangered in Japan. Pictures show a Japanese serow and black woodpeckers.

6A fallen fir can help other plants grow. This one stands in an old-growth forest of the Caucasus region of Russia. Russia's Western Caucasus stretches about 1,062 square miles, or 2,750 square kilometers. The Black Sea is one end. The Caucasus Mountains are the other end. Caucasus State Biosphere Reserve protects the area. Sochi National Park protects it too. Great diversity is on display. Most of the forest trees are coniferous. Pine, cedar, fir, and spruce grow in different areas. Beech and oak grow there too, and both are deciduous. Different elevations suit different species. Snow leopards appear in a picture. Endangered animals of many kinds make these forests a home. Some scientists think a very small number of snow leopards still survive. No sightings have been reported for years. Paw prints are still found. Scat is still found. Those signs come from the large cats. People have also put the wisent back into this forest. That animal is the European bison, and it is endangered. The year 1927 saw the killing of the final wild wisent in the Western Caucasus. Captive wisents were set free in the area in 1940. A picture shows wisents.

7Very complex ecosystems often fill old-growth forests. Life there has been supported for hundreds of years. For some forests the span is thousands of years. Governments protect many of these places. National parks protect many. Organizations protect many. Other old-growth forests are still in danger, whether they are small or large. Human actions can damage these delicate ecosystems. Human actions can destroy them. Once they are gone, their beauty may be lost forever. The scientific information they hold may be lost forever too. Logging is blocked by law in certain old-growth forests. Laws do not prevent it in others. People still argue about the right amount of protection. Words in this book include the following. The canopy is the leafy upper layer made where the crowns of many trees crowd together. A coniferous plant, usually a tree, grows cones and has leaves like needles or scales. It belongs to a large plant group. A deciduous plant drops its leaves in the fall and grows them again in the spring. Diversity means lots of different things are present together. An ecosystem is the living community plus the habitat those living things share. Endangered means a living thing could die out completely. Old-growth describes a forest of very great age. A reserve is land kept so wild plants and wild animals stay safe. A species is a group whose members are alike in body and can have young.

32. From a Weaver's Cottage to a Steel Fortune

1A Man of Great Wealth Buyers paid $480 million in 1901, the year Carnegie parted with his steel firm. After that payment, few men anywhere were richer. The climb is more striking when you look at the start. He reached America from Scotland as a boy who owned nothing. The years after the sale are the part people find hardest to believe. He used those remaining years, and nearly all the money, so that other lives would improve. Death came in 1919. Nine-tenths of the fortune had already gone out as gifts. Libraries he helped raise now stand in many countries. Universities received millions of those dollars. Some of the schools were in the United Kingdom. Others were in the United States.
