New York City is where he built Carnegie Hall. People count that concert hall among the most famous in the world. He also set up the Carnegie Institution for Science. Another foundation was Carnegie Mellon University. So were the Carnegie Museums of Pittsburgh. Further projects followed those. He belongs with the richest people who have ever lived. He also belongs with history's great philanthropists. A philanthropist is someone whose aim is help for humanity. He named what he thought a noble motive should be. Leave the world improved, even in a small way, compared with the day you arrived.

2A drawing from 1850 already shows factory smoke over Dunfermline, in Scotland. Early Years Andrew Carnegie was born in 1835. Dunfermline, Scotland, was the town. At first the family lived in a cottage, and that cottage had a single main room. Living, meals, and sleep all happened in that one room. Weaving on a hand loom was his father's trade. Jobs like that grew hard to find once the Industrial Revolution arrived. Factories took over work that families used to finish at home. Margaret, his mother, started a small food shop so the household could manage. Making shoes brought her more pay. Her sisters were already in the United States, in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. She wrote and asked them for advice. Their answer was to leave home and settle in Pittsburgh. Friends and relatives there would be able to help. Pittsburgh sat on the Ohio River, and that site had turned it into a fast-growing industrial center. The family moved nearby in 1848, in the middle of that boom. Also in 1848, the parents sold every possession they had. The money paid for the sea journey to the United States. Andrew was twelve on that trip. His parents came, and so did a younger brother. Allegheny, just outside Pittsburgh, was the new home. A cotton factory hired him when he was thirteen. Machines there needed their thread spools changed, and that was his task. A day at the factory ran twelve hours. The week ran six days. The wage was $1.20 for each week. Children at Work Look at 1820 in at least three states of New England. Children were more than 40 percent of the people those states employed. Ten was the age of some of those children. Others were younger still. Dangerous shops and long hours were expected, because families needed the pay. Factory owners wanted to hire children. A child's wage could be set below an adult's wage. A union was something children rarely formed. Demands for better pay were rare as well. Once work began, more schooling usually did not. Pennsylvania acted in 1848. It was the first state to name a youngest allowed age for factory jobs. The age it chose was twelve.

3Where His Rise Began A telegraph office hired him the following year, as a boy who carried messages. Each week the office paid $2.50. He gave the work close attention. Running the equipment was a skill he picked up. He also stored in memory the locations of businesses nearby. A promotion arrived before a year was out. The new post was telegraph operator. School had to stop, because the job filled his days. Reading stayed a love of his. Colonel James Anderson lived in the town and owned a personal library. He let boys who worked borrow those books. Gratitude stayed with Andrew. He decided something for later. If wealth ever came, other poor boys would receive the same chance Anderson had given him. One picture shows a boy inside a telegraph office. A message has just arrived on the wire, and he is collecting it. Around 1853, a job offer arrived from Thomas Scott. Scott's firm was the Pennsylvania Railroad Company. Carnegie was about eighteen. Railroads were growing fast, and he learned every part of the work that he could reach. Superintendent was his rank by age twenty-four. With Scott's help he learned how a business should be managed. He also learned how to keep spending low. His first investments came in that period. Companies linked to the railroads were the first place he put money. Oil came later. Before long, those investments earned much more than his pay did. The railroad also brought him together with other people who could sway business. Those links served him through the rest of his working life. Scott himself kept rising. In the end, that same firm made him its president.

4July 1863 brought a riot of men in New York City. They were protesting a draft that pushed them into military service. Black men died in large numbers during those protests. Someone with money could hire another person to serve in a war in his place. War between the States The Civil War started in 1861. The Union Army drafted Carnegie. Fighting was not the path he took. Another man received $850 from him and reported for duty in his stead. Law allowed the practice. Many people still called it wrong. Thomas Scott, his boss, received a wartime post. The post was Assistant Secretary of War. Scott then gave Carnegie work inside the war department. On the Union side, Carnegie helped the telegraph service stay in operation. He helped the railways stay in operation too. He came to see how large the need was for materials. Weapons had to be built. Armor had to be built. Buildings had to be built. Near the war's end he moved his business interests. Railroads were no longer the center. Iron and steel were. His largest wealth would come from iron and from steel. A Steel Leader Takes Shape The iron business grew one piece at a time. Keystone Bridge Works was the firm he formed in 1865. Iron went into railways in great amounts. It went into bridges and into buildings. It went into weapons and into tools. Steel is an alloy. That word means a mixture, here of iron plus other metals. Beside iron alone, steel is harder, and it is stronger. Producing it was costly, and it ate up time. A quicker, less costly method appeared in the 1850s. It started with pig iron, meaning iron in a raw state, and turned that iron into steel. Carnegie put the new method to work at the Edgar Thomson Works, his first plant for steel. Braddock, Pennsylvania, is where the plant opened, in 1875. Two decades later, a large share of the steel sold in the world was under his control. Owning each step of steel-making was one reason he succeeded. Mines that yielded iron ore became his. Coal mines became his, so the factories would have fuel. Railroads and ships became his as well. Raw materials could ride to the mills. Finished goods could ride away from them. Wages at his mills stayed low. Unions were banned. Those choices cut what he spent and raised what he kept. Rival firms could barely match such advantages.

5Horseback rides in Manhattan's Central Park were how Andrew and Louise Carnegie met. The wedding came six years later. A Belief about Riches Age changed where Carnegie put his attention. Louise Whitfield became his wife in 1886. Twenty-one years separated their ages, with Louise the younger. One child followed, a daughter they named Margaret. Two places shared their time. New York City was one. Skibo Castle, their house in Scotland, was the other. In his fifties he stood as the most powerful person in the steel industry. Millions of dollars came in every year. Business was not the edge of his interests. Books came from his pen. So did magazine articles, and the topics ran from travel across to politics. Gifts to charities were common among wealthy business people then, and he gave them too. He wanted the habit of giving to go much further than that. Business and wealth were subjects of many books and essays he wrote. An essay of 1889 carried the title "The Gospel of Wealth." Its idea was that people with riches should avoid heavy spending on themselves. Giving the fortune away, so society would get better, was a duty. His line on the point was sharp. Die while still holding riches like that, and the death is a disgrace. Dunfermline's Free School had been his school as a boy. Adam Rolland, a Scottish judge and a philanthropist, was the person who had founded it. That schooling may have made one belief stronger. Improving other lives, he felt, worked best through education. Teach people until they can stand more on their own, and until they produce more. He held that this was how the world would get better.

6Giving on a Grand Scale J. P. Morgan bought Carnegie Steel in 1901. Carnegie stepped away from business and turned to philanthropy. Big gifts had already gone to Dunfermline, Scotland, the town of his birth. The year 1883 saw the first Carnegie Library open there. Early Carnegie Libraries inside the United States were all put up close to the Pennsylvania home of his childhood. Step by step, the library plan spread. By 1929 the count of Carnegie Libraries stood above 2,500. Forty-seven U.S. states had them. Canada, Britain, and Ireland had them. Australia and New Zealand had them. South Africa had them. The West Indies had them, and Fiji had them too. Carnegie Hall hosts musical performances at a world-class level. The hall stands in New York City. Large sums from Carnegie also backed projects aimed at peace among nations. His 1910 creation was Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. The Peace Palace, which he funded, opened in the Netherlands in 1913. It is a building where international law is administered. Carnegie Corporation of New York began in 1911, and he was its founder. Among grantmaking foundations in the United States, it is now the oldest. Help from it has reached thousands of projects. Finding insulin was one of those projects. Creating Sesame Street was another. That program is a well-known television show for children. J. P. Morgan Hartford, Connecticut, was the 1837 birthplace of John Pierpont Morgan. Wealth and influence marked his family. Banking and business had gone well for the Morgans across several generations. Unlike Carnegie, Morgan did not raise his firms from the ground up. Other people's businesses were what he took over, and trouble at those firms was often the moment he moved. U.S. Steel was the company he created once the Carnegie Steel Company was his, in 1901. No firm before it had been valued above a billion dollars. During the peak of his career, he was the United States' most powerful banker.

7What Remained after Him August 1919 was the month Andrew Carnegie died. His age was 83. Gifts by then totaled more than $350 million. Across the United States, his mark as a business pioneer is easy to see. Carnegie steel went into buildings, railroads, and bridges that still stand. Looking ahead, and giving freely, also changed life for millions of people. A hundred years after his death, children in cities and towns worldwide can walk into a Carnegie Library. Books wait there for them. Colonel James Anderson's library once opened that same world to Andrew, when Andrew was a boy. A Newer Wave of Giving Other wealthy people have taken up Carnegie's thinking and used money to fund resources the public can use. The Giving Pledge gathered forty signatures in 2010. Every signer ranked among the richest people on Earth. Each one promised to give up more than half of a personal fortune. The causes are ones the signer picks. Millionaires and billionaires who have signed now number more than two hundred. Bill Gates is on the list, and so is Melinda French Gates. Warren Buffett is on it. Mark Zuckerberg is on it, with Priscilla Chan. Jeff Bezos is on it, with Mackenzie Scott. Not everyone is comfortable with money that comes from very rich individuals. The worry is that such funding gives them too large a say in the country's policies. A different duty is what the critics want. Raise the wages of workers, they argue, and pay the government more in taxes.

33. Gandhi's Peaceful Struggle

1A map names places touched by Gandhi's life and work. The labels include Asia and Pakistan. They include Africa and India. They include the Indian Ocean and South Africa. The book opens with the name Father of India. Early life comes next. South Africa follows. Then come his years as a leader in India, the Salt March, and the start of change. Death and legacy come after that. A word list ends the book. A picture shows Mohandas Gandhi. Say his name moh-huhn-DAHS GAHN-dee. He was a lawyer. He was a civil rights leader. India's independence from British colonization owed much to the part he played. Fairness, freedom, and peace were beliefs he held strongly. Years of struggle did not break those beliefs. Nations were changed by them. People called him the Father of India. Long after his death, he still inspires people around the world.

2A picture shows Gandhi beside his older brother. Birth came on October 2, 1869, inside a large Hindu family in India. Nonviolence was a strong family belief. Caring for others was another. His mother set a good example. Daily prayer was her habit. Sick people often received her care. Poor people did too. His father served as a local government leader. Disagreements between local people and the British rulers of India were often settled by him. Respect for other people, and for their beliefs, was a lesson Gandhi took from his father. Marriage was arranged by his parents when he was very young. That custom was common in India. He was thirteen when he married Kasturba. She was the same age. At eighteen, Gandhi sailed to England so he could study law. School in London led him to study different religions and their texts. He learned about the Bible. That sacred text belongs to many faiths, including Christianity and Judaism. He also learned about the Bhagavad Gita, a sacred Hindu poem. Say that title BAH-gah-vahd GEE-tah. A picture shows Gandhi in London in 1908. A few years of study brought him a law degree. He returned to India. Shyness still marked him. Work was hard to find. A post in South Africa finally came. A picture shows Gandhi and Kasturba in 1913.

3British rule also covered South Africa, and life there was very different. Laws discriminated against Black people. They discriminated against coloured people, the South African term for mixed-race people. They discriminated against Asian peoples. Gandhi felt he had to act. A proposed British law would have denied Indians the right to vote. He stayed in the country to help protest. Speeches were one tool. Letters were another. He even tried to file a lawsuit so the law would not pass. Success did not come. Attention did. People noticed him, and they noticed the struggles in South Africa. Indian people began to unite under his leadership. Equality for everyone was not yet his goal. In his view, Indians stood above the Native African peoples. Equal treatment from the British, he argued, should come because Indian heritage was similar to British heritage. Discrimination by the British government against Indian people still went on. A picture shows a police officer confronting Gandhi. He is leading a protest in South Africa in 1913. Racial superiority was a common idea when Gandhi was a young man. Anti-Black views influenced his early work. Age changed those views in a major way. Once he was a leader, most of his years went to fighting every kind of discrimination. A few years later, every Indian was forced to register with the British government. The aim was to limit rights to trade and to land. At a protest, Gandhi explained satyagraha. Say that word suh-TYAH-gruh-huh. It means holding firmly to the truth. He used it for his form of nonviolent protest. He asked Indians in South Africa to disobey unjust laws. He asked them to accept the punishments. Beatings and jail came from the British police. Many Indians suffered, and Gandhi was among them. News of the protests and the punishments traveled around the world. Shock led people to speak out against the government. A compromise with the protesters was forced on the government at last. Twenty years was the length of Gandhi's stay in South Africa. Western clothes were given up. A kurta shirt and a sarong took their place, as a sign of his heritage. Later he became known for a simple dhoti, or loincloth. Say that word DOH-tee. He wore it in solidarity with people who lacked wealth.

4By his return to India in 1915, people already saw him as a leader. He joined the Indian National Congress, called the INC. Freeing India from British rule became his work. Support grew quickly. The year 1919 brought the Rowlatt Acts. Authorities could arrest people who caused political trouble. They could hold those people without a trial. A strike was the answer from Gandhi and his supporters. Staying home from work was the plan. Staying home from school was part of it. Violence against the British broke out, so Gandhi canceled the strike. A few days later, thousands gathered in the city of Amritsar. The protest was peaceful. It was also illegal. British troops stood around the crowd. They opened fire with no warning. Ten minutes of shooting left between 400 and 1,500 Indians dead. Many others were wounded. A picture shows Gandhi on his return to India in 1915. Working with the British government had been his aim up to this point. The Amritsar Massacre changed everything. Soon his call was noncooperation. That was one more way to protest without violence. Indians were asked to stop buying British goods. They were asked to stop working for British people or companies. Jobs in the British government were to be quit. British honors were to be refused. Some success followed these efforts. Violent clashes still happened between Indian protesters and the British military. People saw Gandhi as the leader of the protest movement. Violence led to his arrest. A sentence of six years in prison followed. Release came after two years. He went back to the work at once. Gandhi and Kasturba had not known each other at first. In time they supported the same ideas. She worked alongside her husband. She even stood in for him while he was imprisoned. Four sons were born to them. The marriage lasted until her death in 1944. A picture shows Kasturba with her sons.

5A picture shows Gandhi and some followers marching toward the shore. One of his most successful protests came in 1930. Only British companies were allowed to produce salt. Only they were allowed to sell it. A large tax sat on any salt that was sold. Gandhi believed the charge was unfair. The salt came from Indian lands, yet Indians had to pay the British for it. Large salt flats line India's coast. Seawater evaporates there. Salt is left on the ground. Gathering that salt and using it had been free until British law made it illegal. A map marks India, the salt march route, the starting point, and Dandi. A picture shows the salt Gandhi lifted when the long march was finished. On March 12 he set out with a few dozen followers. The walk lasted 21 days. It covered 240 miles, or 386 kilometers, across India to the sea. Along the way he spoke to people. He made speeches to large crowds. By the time the coastal town of Dandi came into view, followers numbered in the tens of thousands. Early on the morning of April 6, he went down to the shore. British soldiers stood around him. From the ground he lifted one grain of salt. His followers did the same. Arrest took Gandhi and more than sixty thousand others.

6A picture places Gandhi beside Mohammad Ali Jinnah. Jinnah led the Muslim League. Anger spread through the world after the arrests of Indians. Voices against the British grew louder and more numerous. Independence talks were interrupted when World War II started in 1939. Gandhi and the INC told the British in 1942 that India must be left. All of them were arrested. Violent protests broke out all over India. The war ended in 1945. British and Indian leaders began to discuss a British departure. Conflict between Hindus and Muslims had often marked India's history. A united India, Gandhi believed, could hold both religions in peace if the people learned how. Muhammad Ali Jinnah did not share that belief. Say his name muh-HAH-muhd ah-LEE JI-nah. Later people would call this Muslim leader the Father of Pakistan. Protection for Muslim rights, after a British exit, was something he did not trust. He wanted two states, one Muslim and one Hindu. A picture shows a Pakistan-bound train with Muslims climbing aboard. British rule ended under an agreement signed in 1947. The country was divided. Pakistan was the new country formed by Muslim people. The move between the two countries involved more than ten million people. The division was done too quickly. The British left too soon. A great deal of violence followed. Hundreds of thousands of people died. Talks and nonviolent protests brought Gandhi a number of temporary peace agreements. Fasting means going without food. Many religions practice it, including Hinduism. Religious practice often included a fast for Gandhi. Fasting was also a tool he used in politics. In 1947 he fasted to protest the riots in Calcutta. The riots ended. He fasted again in 1948. Peace in Delhi followed after he persuaded the people there.

7A memorial to Gandhi was built in 1950. On January 30, 1948, he was holding a prayer meeting. About five hundred people had gathered to hear his prayers. A young Hindu man in the crowd rejected Gandhi's work for peace with Muslims. The man came up to the stage. He pulled out a gun. He shot Gandhi three times. People all over the world were affected by that death. An estimated 150,000 people attended the funeral. Indians called him Mahatma, which means Great Soul. After death he continued to inspire leaders. Martin Luther King Jr. was one. Nelson Mandela was another. The world felt a major impact from his influence. Words in this book include the following. Political means having to do with government, with politics, or with politicians. A compromise is an agreement reached after each side gives up part of what it asked for. A protest is an action that shows strong disagreement or disapproval. Discrimination means unjust treatment of a person or a group. The reason may be gender, race, age, religion, or another difference. To have been sentenced is to have received a formal punishment from a court of law. Hindu relates to the major religion in India, with many gods and a belief in reincarnation. A struggle is a hard goal, or the hard effort to reach it. It can also mean a fight or a conflict. To inspire is to encourage a person to act. A tax is a fee a government collects so it can pay for services, functions, and operations. Muslims are people who follow the religion of Islam. Nonviolence is the refusal to answer with physical force or with violence. Unjust means unfair, undeserved, or dishonest.

34. Home in the World's Dry Lands

1Bedouin friends embrace in the Sahara in Morocco. Demanding deserts open the book. Later parts visit the Tohono O'odham in the Sonoran Desert, the Bedouin in the Sahara, and Mongolian nomads in the Gobi. A way of life and a word list close the book. A Tuareg woman prepares a meal outside her home in the Sahara in Mali. Dictionary definitions usually call a desert a barren land. Little life, or none, can be supported there. Some desert regions match that picture. Others look very different. Trees, shrubs, and cacti grow on mountainsides. Many kinds of creatures live in these places. Some deserts look like endless seas of sand, with rolling dunes like waves. Streams and rivers cross some regions. Those waterways can stay empty for long periods.

2Shared traits still exist. Compared with other lands, deserts are arid. Yearly rain or snow is usually under 25.4 centimeters, or 10 inches. Soil tends to be dry. Vegetation tends to be scarce. A few deserts grow very cold. Most are sunny and hot. Pictures can show palm trees beside an oasis. That scene is the Sahara of Egypt. Flowers in Australian dunes can be shown. Flowing water in the Sonoran can be shown. They can show the largest salt flat on Earth, in Bolivia. Children run together in the Thar Desert of India. Nearly one-fifth of the land on Earth is desert. Hot deserts occur on five of the seven continents. Europe does not have them. Antarctica does not have them. Size varies. Some deserts are small. Others are huge. A trip around the world can teach more about these lands. Indigenous peoples are part of that lesson. These lands have been their home across thousands of years. Desert people survive as other people do, by adapting to what is around them. Food, water, and shelter still have to be found, as in any hard place. For the people who live there, survival is not the whole story. The desert is home. It is a way of life.

3The Sonoran Desert is hot and dry. The area is 310,800 square kilometers. That equals 120,000 square miles. The span crosses the southwest of the United States and the north of Mexico. Months can pass with no rain. Summer days can reach 49 degrees Celsius, or 120 degrees Fahrenheit. Winter nights can fall below freezing. Rain here is greater than in any other desert. Summer monsoons often soak the whole region. Shade trees grow. So do large cacti, including the saguaro (suh-WAR-oh). Summer flowers grow too. The Tohono O'odham are Indigenous people of this desert. Their name means desert people. A map can show California, Arizona, New Mexico, the Pacific Ocean, Mexico, and North America. Native plants here number more than 2,500. No other desert has a higher number. During recent centuries, newcomers arrived from Europe. Others arrived from the United States. Piece by piece they took ground. The O'odham had lived on it for thousands of years. Today that land is split among four tribes. The Tohono O'odham Nation is one. One place the O'odham language is spoken is a community on the Gila River. Another is the Ak-Chin community. Another is the community at Salt River, also called Pima Maricopa. Each of those is an Indian community. Differences exist from tribe to tribe. Sells, Arizona, is the capital. It is also the largest community. People live on reservations. They also live off reservations, in towns and in cities. Francine Jose is shown with baskets her relatives made long ago.

4Water came from the desert. Food came from it. Shelter came from it. This lasted thousands of years. Floodwater irrigation, including water diversion, was one tool. Planting sites were chosen with care. They became masters of dryland agriculture. Corn, squash, and beans were among the crops. More land was taken over time. The government of the United States pressed them to adopt its ways. They still fought to keep their traditions. Many now weave those traditions into modern life. Farming, cooking, and basketmaking are examples. The saguaro is central to the culture. Beautiful flowers open on it each spring. Large red fruit ripens in the middle of June. Special tools take the fruit from the tops. The giant plants can reach upward of 22 meters, or 75 feet. The fruit is made into wine. Early July brings their New Year. The wine is important to that celebration. A picture can show Bedouin children getting ready to race camels. The Sahara is the next desert. Northern Africa is where it lies. The area is 8.6 million square kilometers, equal to 3.3 million square miles. Heat and dryness are extreme. So little rain falls that few plants flourish, and few animals do either. The Bedouin (BED-oo-in) live there. Arabic supplies the word Badw. People of the desert is what Badw means. The group name comes from that word. A map can show Morocco, Tunisia, Western Sahara, Algeria, and Libya. Egypt, Mauritania, Mali, Sudan, Niger, and Chad can be shown too, along with the Atlantic Ocean, Europe, and Africa. In some parts, yearly rain is under 25 millimeters, or 1 inch.

5Pictures can show a Bedouin village in the Egyptian Sahara. Dry vegetation is the building material. Another picture can show the colorful inside of a tent in Oman. Herding was the traditional work. In the rainy winter they roamed the desert. Dry summer sent them back to farmland. Camels came with them. Sheep and goats came too. Scarce resources forced a nomadic life. Travel went from oasis to oasis. Wells were dug for water. Ancestor ways are still followed by some families. Today a nomadic family can also buy supplies at markets, from sellers, or in other places. Homes were low black tents called bayts. Goat hair or sheep wool was the cloth. Sun, wind, and blowing sand were kept out. Some families still use bayts. A camp can be taken down and packed in a matter of hours. For about the past hundred years, countries have been taking the land these people traditionally used. Many are no longer nomadic. Life may be seminomadic, or fully settled. Herding is no longer the only work. Many kinds of jobs exist now. Umm Sayhoun is a village near Petra, in Jordan. A picture can show a mother smiling with her son inside a home in Oman.

6A map can mark Asia, the Indian Ocean, Mongolia, China, and the Gobi Desert. This desert is a rain shadow. Rainy weather was stopped by mountains. Without that rain, plants could not flourish. The Gobi covers 1.3 million square kilometers, or 500,000 square miles. It runs from southern Mongolia into northern China. The land is rocky. In the language of the Indigenous Mongolian people, Gobi means large and dry. It can also mean the waterless place. For thousands of years, nomads have roamed this cold, windy desert. Horses, sheep, goats, and cattle are herded. Two-humped Bactrian camels are herded too. A Mongolian woman herds her animals in the Gobi. A Mongolian boy runs outside his family's ger. A traditional home is a yurt. People also call that round tent a ger. A wooden frame covered in felt makes it. Harsh weather can be withstood. Extreme heat and extreme cold are kept off the people inside. Animals can still suffer. Many families have given up nomadic desert life. Winters of unusual harshness, and summers with little rain, have hit thousands of families. Some lost part of a herd. Some lost every animal. Government changes have also hurt herders. Earning a living grew difficult. The year 1989 began a large move. More than half a million nomads left for the capital. Food and work were what they sought. The capital is in Mongolia. Most bring the ger along. Districts of these tents have grown in the city.

7Deserts have been home for thousands of years. Each one sets different challenges. Indigenous peoples have always found answers, using local resources for houses, food, and water. Much has changed. Many dwellers now live modern lives. Some still live in traditional ways, as ancestors did. Many still celebrate the traditions of their communities. Desert life is demanding, and it is also rewarding. People who make it home have always respected their surroundings deeply. They honor what the land offers, and they use it. They also recognize its great power and its beauty. A picture can show a man and a camel. They walk a busy street. The country is the United Arab Emirates. Words in this book can be explained this way. Arid means very dry. Barren means without vegetation. Districts are areas that share features inside them. Dwellers are people or other animals living in a particular place. Indigenous means native to a place. Irrigation means bringing water to fields or crops to help them grow. Monsoons are storms of a season. They drop heavy rain. An oasis is a fertile, watered spot in a desert. Tribes are groups that share a culture and land.

35. How Japanese Animation Grew

1Hayao Miyazaki wears many hats. Animation is one of them. Directing is another. He also produces films, writes scripts, writes books, and draws manga. Reporters heard him speak in 2014. The place was Studio Ghibli, a studio he co-founded. His talk sits inside a much older habit. People told stories with pictures long before his films. Pictures existed long before anyone wrote words down. The earliest people told stories by making images. Paintings from prehistoric times cover cave walls. Small figures were carved with care into clay. In those pictures, artists showed their view of themselves. They also showed the world around them. Later, language gave people symbols and words. Ideas traveled that way more often than before. Storytelling still needed art. Paintings and illustrations are not the only images now. Cartoons can move. Video games can move. Japan, an island country in Asia, made one style of moving art that spread widely. People call that style anime. It is liked in many countries. Ancient stories survive in the cave paintings of Lascaux, a site in France. They also survive on clay tablets that come from Mesopotamia. The French caves are the large picture. The tablets are the smaller picture beside them. Both remind us that pictures carried tales before anime existed. Miyazaki's 2014 talk sits at the modern end of that long line.

2The story of anime starts more than two centuries back. Scrolls, large ones, held most Japanese art before the 1800s began. Scroll methods were exact. They also ate up time. Painting could be done in one long stroke of the brush for each image. A second method cut the picture into a block of wood. Ink went on the block. A press then transferred the picture. Owning such work cost so much that rich families were nearly the only buyers in Japan. Each color on a print needed its own block. Twenty blocks might build a single finished picture. A famous piece of manga art shows a well-known fable. The fable is about blind men and an elephant. Manga as a new art showed up in 1814. Sheets of paper held sketches drawn in a free hand. Katsushika Hokusai taught with those sketches. He asked students to draw their own. The students passed the pictures around. Funny images pleased the public and spread. Compared with scroll art, manga was quicker. It was also cheaper. Because the price was low, anyone could have it. Two Japanese words sit inside the name. Man is the word for curious. Ga is the word for sketches. Side by side, they equal what English calls a cartoon. Hokusai used that name first, for the comical drawings in his own sketchbooks.

3By the late 1800s, manga in Japan had become fully itself. The country had kept apart from others up through the mid-1800s. Ports had to open after a United States naval expedition arrived in 1853. The pressure was for trade with other nations. Merchants from Britain came next. Merchants from America came too. Newspapers from their home countries came with them. Cartoons about politics, and comics, filled those Western papers. Manga artists in Japan took lessons from that style. They started using story boxes set in order, called sequenced panels. Faces in manga grew more expressive, in the Western manner. Around the year 1900, lots of Japanese newspapers carried manga. Cartoons on politics mocked the news of the day. Strips of comics offered simple jokes to children. Adults enjoyed them too. The lively drawings won more fans all the time. A manga strip in a paper resembles the Western strip it grew from. Movies were another medium, and the new century delivered them. Film production began at American studios. Western studios outside the United States joined in. Crowds packed theaters to watch. The new entertainment then reached theaters abroad, Japan's included. Early films did not last long. They had no color. Nobody's voice was recorded, so they were silent. Musicians played in the theater as the reel turned. Screen text told viewers what was happening. It also gave the lines the characters spoke. With no way to record a voice, actors showed feeling by other means. The acting was silent and still highly dramatic. Faces were pushed past real life. So were the movements of hands and bodies. The 1917 movie Patria shows actors doing that. Their gestures are larger than life so viewers can read the emotion.

4The new medium fascinated cartoonists in many countries. Walt Disney, an American illustrator, figured out how drawings could move. Max Fleischer figured that out too. Comic characters people already loved seemed to leap onto the big screen. Sound was still missing, just as in live-action films of that time. A band or a piano supplied music. Storytelling used motion, faces, and hand signals, the same tools real actors used. Running time was under ten minutes, so the films were called shorts. Both children and grown-ups were delighted. A short played first. A full-length feature followed. Live musicians were required, because films and cartoons had no recorded dialogue and no sound track yet. One pianist might follow the action. A whole orchestra might play instead. Two purposes sat behind the music. Projector noise was loud, and the music drowned it. The music also held the crowd's excitement. Seitaro Kitayama and other manga artists soon built Japanese shorts of their own. Strong manga features suited the big action and the big expressions a silent story needed. The Japanese name for these cartoons was animēshon. It was based on animation, an English word. Later the name shrank to anime. Better machines brought color to Western cartoons. Recorded speaking arrived too. In the 1930s, cartoonists in America worked to make human figures look closer to real people. Walt Disney's first movie at full length shows that effort. Snow White is the start of its title. The Seven Dwarfs is the end of its title. Multiplane animation was another tool in that film. Background and action were both meant to look real. Different background pictures were painted on glass panels. The panels were stacked. Filming moved the stack forward and back. Depth of field improved, and so did the sense of motion. Cameras built for multiplane work gave animated films their depth.

5Sound entered Japanese anime. The realistic Western look did not. Filmmakers instead used a trick from long Japanese movies. A shot could stay still for a while. Then it could snap to a close view for drama. Artists kept using anime's ink look, with no color in the drawing yet. That manner told viewers the work was Japanese. The look is easy to recognize. Detail fills the backgrounds. Energy fills the characters, along with expressions and gestures pushed past ordinary life. Angles are often extreme, and Western cartoons rarely use those views. Eyes carry a special job. Trust and a childlike quality go with large eyes. A squint, with the eyes made smaller, points to sneakiness. Evil shows up when the eyes are tiny. Size and shape need not stay fixed. A blush over the nose means embarrassment. The feeling looks stronger if the character scratches the back of the head. Anger has several signs. Blue lines may cross the face. Eyes may narrow. Veins may bulge. Sweat may appear in drops. Hair is part of the style. Bright color is common. So are unusual shapes. The hair can shift to show motion or a feeling. A face may be drawn happy. It may be drawn sad, angry, or embarrassed. Cost was one reason the style held still. Backgrounds are important, yet tools like multiplane animation cost too much. War was the other reason. World War II began in 1939. Leaders in Japan wanted the public behind them. Pride in the nation was the goal, so films and cartoons from abroad were banned. Foreign-looking work was not allowed. Only art that praised certain Japanese values could be made. Some animators would not obey. They left the country. Others put work out secretly. Capture meant punishment. Posters asked the public to support the government against enemy nations. Japan's ending to the war was terrible. Surrender came in 1945. By then, nearly two million Japanese people had died. Atomic bombs had destroyed Hiroshima and Nagasaki, both the cities and the people there. Art changed because the people had changed. Serious themes replaced light fun. Government rules were gone. Manga artists and anime artists then argued, through their work, for peace. They argued for justice. They argued for freedom.

6Television, new in the 1950s, often carried those messages. Home viewing widened the audience, because a cartoon no longer required a theater. Osamu Tezuka drew a manga comic called Mighty Atom, and a very popular show was based on it. Mighty Atom was a boy and a robot. His feet were rockets. Episode by episode he crossed the world and rescued it from danger. In Japan the show became one of television's favorites. New Year's Day of 1963 was the premiere date for Astro Boy. Early in the 1960s, American viewers got the same series under that name, and it was a hit. More anime shows followed that success. Mecha was the name for cartoons about teens, giant robots, and battles to protect the world from monsters. Japan in the 1970s loved Mazinger Z, one of those mecha stories. The star robot was built from a special metal. The metal had been discovered on Mount Fuji, in Japan. Like manga, newer anime aims at narrower groups. A story line and its characters fit a chosen audience. The Japanese word shonen means young boy. Action and comedy are what those plots stress. Dragon Ball Z is a favorite shonen title. Japan saw it first in 1989. Stations around the world still air it. Its own run lasted from 1989 until 2003. The Japanese word shojo means young girl. Early plots stayed with feelings and with relationships. Later plots added heroines who act, inside romance and inside adventure. Naoko Takeuchi's 1990s series Sailor Moon is a classic of that kind. A girl in middle school receives special powers. She turns into a guardian of Earth. Evil forces are what she holds off. At least three films use the character. Thirty-nine video games use her too.

7Worldwide hits began leaving Japanese studios in the 1980s and again in the 1990s. Hayao Miyazaki released a 1984 film whose name begins with Nausicaä. Valley of the Wind is the rest of that name. Viewers embraced it. A young princess has to rescue her planet. That is the plot. Spirited Away, a Japanese anime from 2001, followed a young girl into the spirit world and put that tale on a large screen. Hayao Miyazaki directed it and earned strong praise. An Academy Award went to the film. The prize category was Best Animated Feature. Earnings since the 2001 opening have passed 396 million dollars. This century's media carry anime as well. Video games let favorite characters move again. One is Astro Boy. Another is Digimon. Fighters out of Dragon Ball Z join them. A player steers a character and, with one press of a button, sends that character on a mission. Old pictures once acted out daring adventures. Screen images still do. What anime adds is a cast so lively that modern story art reaches further than before.

36. How Plastic Entered Everyday Life

1page 16. Bottles made of plastic weigh little. They are strong, and they cost little. Why Plastic Feels Easy. During 2016, buyers around the world purchased more than 480 billion drinking bottles made of plastic. That total is almost 70 bottles for every person on Earth. Sales do not pause. Each minute, more than a million of these bottles are sold somewhere in the world. Throwaway bottles are only one way plastic is used. The material shows up everywhere. It is light. It is cheap. It is strong, and it can still bend. Makers can form it into nearly any shape. The uses number about a million. Look around. A computer keyboard may be plastic. A pen may be plastic. The wrapper on a candy bar may be plastic too. Many other goods are some kind of plastic as well. This era belongs to plastic. The material is a wonder of modern life. It is also a rising worry. People have to decide what to do with all the plastic they throw away.

2A Brief Past. Plastic is not ancient. Not very long ago, it did not exist at all. The 1850s were the decade of Alexander Parkes. This inventor worked in Britain, and he was the earliest person to produce the material. He named his material Parkesine. He saw it as a way to keep cloth dry. John Wesley Hyatt lived in America. He improved on the work of Parkes. He ran experiments meant to improve the material. The year 1869 brought his own version. He called it celluloid. It replaced elephant ivory well. It also replaced animal horn and tortoise shell. Factories shaped it into combs. They shaped it into teeth that were artificial. Keys on pianos used the material. So did the balls used in billiards. Photographic film used it. So did film for movies. Toy makers took up plastic almost as soon as it could be had. A picture shows toys from that early period. In 1907, Leo Baekeland made something new by accident. He was a chemist, Belgian by birth and American by life. His find was the first plastic that was fully synthetic. The name was Bakelite. Heat let workers shape it into almost any form. Cooling then locked it into a hard, stiff piece. Later materials followed its lead, including plexiglass, polyester, nylon, and vinyl. Telephones were made from Bakelite. Radios, kitchen tools, and parts for cars were too. Thousands of other goods joined the list. Household objects became a normal place for plastic because Bakelite made the idea popular. The word plastic itself stayed uncommon until the 1930s. Greek supplies the root. Plassein means to mold or to shape. Almost any object can be molded from plastic. Chemists and engineers of materials are still discovering fresh forms and fresh jobs for it. A Surprise in the Lab. Baekeland had been hunting a new chemical to coat furniture. Bakelite appeared instead, by accident. Other scientists have stumbled onto important substances in the same way. Charles Goodyear, the story says, left a chemical mix on a hot stove by mistake and got rubber that stood up to weather. Stephanie Kwolek, a chemist, was trying to make a fiber that was strong and light, for use in tires. What she found was Kevlar. Bulletproof vests use that fiber.

3Cotton is a natural polymer. Wood is one too. So is latex taken from rubber trees. A Material That Seems Like a Wonder. Plastic stands apart because of its atomic structure. Atoms join into molecules. Every kind of matter is built from those tiny blocks. Plastic belongs to a group of substances called polymers. A polymer is a substance whose large molecules repeat, link by link. The bonds in those long chains are very strong. Breaking them is hard, so the material is very durable. Plants build cell walls from cellulose. Cellulose is one kind of natural polymer. Most plastic made today does not come from nature. It comes from synthetic polymers. Scientists build those polymers from oil or from natural gas. They can also start with chemicals drawn from oil or gas. Carbon atoms pack those chemicals. The carbon forms strong bonds with other atoms. Plastic falls into two types. One type is the thermoset. The other is the thermoplastic. A thermoset is hard, and it is brittle. Heat does not easily damage it. Once it has been shaped and cooled, melting it again is impossible. Bathroom tiles can be thermoset plastic. Countertops and baking dishes can be too. Tiles of this kind on a counter stay strong, and they resist heat. A thermoplastic can stretch. It can be melted, shaped again, and recycled with fair ease. Milk jugs are one example. Storage boxes of plastic are another. Most toys are another. More than 90 percent of the plastic goods people know and use are thermoplastics. Storage containers made this way stay light, and they stay strong.

4Athletic shoes once relied mainly on leather and on cloth. Plastic has largely taken that place. The Argument for Plastic. Over the past century, plastic became the changeable wonder that manufacturers dreamed of. Wood can be fragile. Metal can break more easily than people expect. Stone can too. So can glass, and so can ceramics. Those materials can be hard to shape. Plastic can be molded with great exactness. Businesses can get the form they need. Consumers can get the form they want. Making plastic is easy, and changing it is easy. It has come to stand for convenience. People drink from a plastic bottle. They clean teeth with a plastic toothbrush. They eat outdoors on disposable plates, then throw the plates away. A picture shows how plastic parts lighten a car and cut the fuel it burns. Energy saved is another benefit, one people may not notice. Builders place plastics in the walls of homes. Schools and office buildings get the same treatment. The material insulates. On a cold day, heat stays inside. When the thermometer rises, heat stays outside. Either way, energy is saved. For packaging, plastic weighs less than glass. It weighs less than other materials that might wrap the same goods. Lighter loads burn less fuel while goods are shipped. Plastic pieces have trimmed the weight of cars and of trucks. Aircraft and other transport have grown lighter too. A lighter vehicle needs less fuel to move. Shoppers then pay less, because making goods costs less and shipping them costs less. Most plastic items can also be produced in huge numbers. That mass production is more efficient, and cheaper, than making the same item from other materials. Consumers pay less again. Food waste drops as well. Plastic wrap keeps meat fresh longer. Bread stays fresh longer, and so do vegetables. Manufacturers gain. Retailers gain. Customers gain. Plastic has been good business for all three.

5Walk into a hospital or a doctor's office and plastic's value to health care is plain. An operating room is full of plastic gear. Monitors are there. Tubes are there. Surgical instruments are there. The surface cleans easily. It resists contamination. Supplies meant to be thrown away keep costs down. Syringes, gloves for exams, and gowns for patients are examples. They also lower the chance of infection. Low price, light weight, long life, and many uses explain why plastic fills so much of daily life. A picture shows disposable medical supplies of plastic. They help protect doctors and patients. They also leave a large pile of plastic trash. A Sea of Plastic. The plastic that reaches the ocean each year weighs above 9 million metric tons. Think of a truck packed with garbage. More plastic than that reaches the sea with every passing minute. The amount doubles every 11 years. Big pieces hurt fish and other wildlife. An animal may eat the plastic. It may choke on it. It may become tangled in it. Plastic does not vanish. As time passes, it only breaks into smaller bits. A single bottle can split until the tiny fragments number past 10,000. Shellfish eat those pieces. Other life in the sea eats them too. The tiny bits also climb the food chain until they reach people. Someone who eats a usual share of seafood swallows about 11,000 plastic fragments across a year. Researchers, including teams at the University of Georgia and at CSIRO, have measured these flows. The Trouble with Plastic. Plastic has acted like a miracle material. Its drawbacks, though, are easier to see all the time. Look into a full dumpster. Plastic trash is the problem staring back. The material is becoming an environmental disaster. Water served from a plastic bottle can feel cool and refreshing. A cost comes with that bottle. Four centuries, and then some, could pass. The same bottle would probably still be somewhere on Earth. It may lie buried in a landfill. It may rest on the seafloor.

6Because plastic lasts, the environment faces enormous challenges. Food usually breaks down as time passes. Wood, paper, and other plant materials do too. Nature can use them again. Plastic does not follow that pattern. Petrochemicals supply the raw matter for most plastic. Wind, water, and living things have trouble pulling that matter apart. Often they cannot pull it apart at all. A plastic object may crack into smaller and smaller bits. Those bits are called microplastics. The material still never fully disappears. Cheap manufacture makes the trouble worse. A new bottle, or another new product, costs less to make than to reuse or to recycle. Recycling programs exist in many communities of the United States. Even so, under 10 percent of plastic is recycled. Another 15 percent is burned to produce energy. More than 75 percent goes by truck to landfills, or it ends up dumped in the ocean. Ugliness is not the only harm. Biologists have shown that plastic hurts wildlife and kills it. Dead whales have come ashore with stomachs packed with plastic bags. The whales had swallowed the bags. They had mistaken the bags for jellyfish or for other food. Many seabirds die after swallowing bits of plastic. Researchers also find microplastics in fish. They find them in oysters and in other seafood people eat. As the piles grow, more people try to help. Some communities forbid stores to hand out disposable plastic bags. A few countries try charging a modest fee in advance on every drink bottle made of plastic. The buyer gets that money back when the bottle comes back. Norway runs a program called the Deposit Return Scheme. Under it, 96 percent of the country's plastic bottles are recycled instead of becoming garbage. Children sometimes lead. Milo Cress was nine years old in 2011 when he began a campaign called Be Straw Free. He asked restaurants to stop offering plastic straws. He asked customers to stop using them. His group estimates a daily total for the United States. Americans use half a billion straws each day. Straws rank among the most common pieces of plastic trash. Paper straws can take their place. Metal straws can too. Those choices do less harm to the environment. Even so, plastic pollution is still a large problem waiting for a solution.

7A Different Future for Plastic. Plastic will remain, and the reasons are many. Daily life grows easier because of plastic goods. It grows more affordable. Convenience increases as well. Creative genius belonged to the chemical engineers who did this work. Inventors shared in that genius. Together they worked hard to build a material with so many helpful uses. Minds of that same kind now need to take up a new task. They need to invent forms of plastic that injure the environment less. Until then, ordinary people can act. Plastic habits can be watched with more care. No rare talent is required. No special knowledge is required. People can use less plastic. They can reuse it when they are able. They can recycle it whenever a chance appears. The benefits can still be enjoyed. Plastic That Breaks Down? Makers are trying to produce biodegradable plastics. The design lets weather break them down in a natural way. Chemicals released by microorganisms can do the work too. Engineers of materials and chemists have not yet succeeded at one goal. They have not made plastics that break down under ordinary conditions outdoors. One fork is formed from a special plastic based on corn. It can break down in as few as forty-five days. Glossary. atomic structure (noun), page 7: the way the most basic parts of an element or a substance are arranged, including protons, neutrons, and electrons. molded (verb), page 4: shaped, or formed, into a chosen form. petrochemicals (noun), page 13: chemicals that result when workers process petroleum, or when they process natural gas. chemist (noun), page 6: a scientist whose subject is the elements, and how one chemical affects another. synthetic (adjective), page 6: made by people, by joining two or more substances, and not found in nature. consumers (noun), page 9: people who pay for goods or for services, whether by purchase or by rental, and then use what they paid for. thermoplastics (noun), page 8: materials that turn rigid once they cool, and turn soft and flexible again when heat returns. disposable (adjective), page 4: made to be thrown away after use. thermosets (noun), page 8: materials that heat makes permanently rigid. durable (adjective), page 7: strong enough to remain useful across a long stretch of time. manufactured (verb), page 5: turned from raw materials into finished goods. versatile (adjective), page 11: able to be used in many different ways.

37. How the Colonies Turned on Britain

1A map for 1750 shows land claims in North America. It marks New France. It marks British Canada. It marks Louisiana. It marks the British colonies. It marks a disputed area. It marks Florida. It marks New Spain. The Atlantic Ocean is on the map. The Pacific Ocean is on the map. This book first tells how Britain held colonies. Then it tells about a war for land in North America. Next it tells about taxes when people had no voice. Then it tells about angry acts and payback. After that, the fighting starts. A word list comes at the end. More than 200 years ago, colonists began a war against an empire. They won that war. Those colonists lived in the land that is now the United States. They fought Great Britain. Great Britain was already a strong country. It had been powerful for a long time. Britain wanted land in a place Europeans called the New World. That name meant North America. It also meant Central America. It also meant South America. Other countries in Europe wanted land there too.

2The New World had more land. Growing populations in Europe needed that land. Indigenous peoples already lived in the New World. They had lived there for thousands of years. Millions of Indigenous peoples had been killed by European colonizers by the 1700s. The colonizers had also claimed Indigenous land. Great Britain set up thirteen colonies. The colonies were in eastern North America. Colonists was the name for people who settled in Britain's colonies. Great Britain sat far from the colonies, with a wide ocean in the way. That distance let colonists form their own ideas. It also let them form their own ways of doing things. A map shows London in Great Britain. The Atlantic Ocean lies between London and the thirteen colonies. Florida is on that map too. Europe is on it as well. A scale on the map can help a reader judge the distance. An independent spirit helped start the Revolutionary War. Friendship had once joined the colonists and Great Britain. In the 1700s, they worked together against a shared enemy. That enemy was France. In the 1750s, France and England both wanted the same land. The land was in North America. Hundreds of years of rivalry lay between those two countries. They each wanted more power in Europe. The same contest continued in North America. The French had explored land around the Great Lakes. They had explored the Ohio River Valley. French fur trappers had set up trading posts in those areas. England claimed to own the same areas. Colonists settled there. Indigenous nations in the region got along better with the French. They traded with the French. They did not get along as well with the British. Leaving the East Coast, British colonizers headed west. They claimed land where Indigenous peoples lived. Indigenous peoples had also hunted there for centuries. Indigenous peoples wanted their lands back. Many nations took the French side. They hoped to protect their trade. They hoped to protect their lands. They hoped to protect their independence.

3France and Great Britain got ready for war. Great Britain was the choice of some Indigenous nations. Other Indigenous nations sided with France. Fort building in the Ohio River Valley was started by both sides. Each side wanted to protect its rights to the land. Fort Duquesne was a French work of 1754. The name sounds like doo-KAYN. The fort stood where Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, stands today. People thought that spot was the key to the Ohio River Valley. Both sides wanted the fort. A map marks Fort Duquesne near three rivers. The rivers are the Ohio, the Allegheny, and the Monongahela. Britain sent a young surveyor to the fort. His name was George Washington. He was sent to talk the French into leaving. The French refused. A band of French scouts was attacked by Washington and his men. Indigenous allies joined that attack. The attack killed 10 men. Washington's men built Fort Necessity. It stood not far from Fort Duquesne. The French captured Fort Necessity. Washington and his men surrendered. Then they escaped. Washington next fought beside a British general. The general's name was Edward Braddock. Braddock wanted to drive the French out of the Ohio River Valley. He planned to start with Fort Duquesne. The French hid soldiers in the woods. Their Indigenous allies hid there too. The woods ran beside the marching British columns. The hidden fighters shot at the British. The British panicked. They ran. General Braddock was killed. Over half of the men under him died as well. Many people treat this fight as the opening real battle in a long conflict. That conflict is the French and Indian War. The 1756 fight at Fort Duquesne appears in a painting.

4Another map pictures who held the land once the Seven Years' War ended. British Canada is on it. The thirteen colonies are on it. Some British land was reserved for Indigenous peoples. New Spain is on the map. Florida is on it. The Atlantic Ocean and the Pacific Ocean are on it. France and Great Britain entered an official war in 1756. Official fighting began in that year. Plenty of fighting had taken place already. Some were in North America. Some were in Europe. Extra British troops went out to the colonies. France sent more troops too. A French victory looked likely in the early days. Then the British attacked Fort Niagara. They attacked at Lake Champlain. They attacked Quebec. More Indigenous allies helped them. The Ohio River Valley was shut off from the French. They were cut off from the Mississippi River. They were cut off from the port at New Orleans. The French needed supplies from those places. The French could not stay in North America once supplies were gone. Great Britain won the war. The Treaty of Paris was signed in 1763. North America no longer held any claim by France. British colonists could now move into land France had controlled. That land included Canada. Disaster for Indigenous nations followed that change. More of the land of Indigenous nations went to British colonists. For a brief time, belonging to Great Britain pleased the colonists. Many had fought beside British troops. Both had faced one enemy while the French and Indian War was fought. After France lost, many colonists changed their view. British protection no longer seemed needed. British oversight no longer seemed needed. Only about a decade after the war, feelings flipped. Gratitude and friendship turned into distrust. They also turned into revolution. King George III became king of Great Britain in 1760. He was only 22 years old. He wanted the colonies to stay loyal to Great Britain. What Britain did once the war ended stirred colonial anger. King George III and Parliament raised the colonists' taxes. The extra money was meant to shrink Britain's war debts. Then Britain placed soldiers in the colonies. The soldiers were there to defend the larger empire. Colonists were expected to house those soldiers. They were expected to feed them too.

5In 1764, Parliament passed the Sugar Act. Only one year had passed since the Treaty of Paris. The act taxed molasses from Spain. It taxed molasses from France. It taxed sugar from those countries when colonists bought it. Colonists had been buying cheap Spanish sugar. They had been buying cheap French sugar. Prices climbed until British sugar was what they had to purchase. The tax brought in money. Britain could use the money to pay war debts. In 1765, Parliament passed the Quartering Act. The act said colonists must house British troops. About 10,000 troops were still in America. Those troops were still there when the French and Indian War was done. The housing was in private homes. The soldiers lived with colonist families. The soldiers did not have to pay rent. The host family could expect no help from them. A picture shows Britain's soldiers living with colonists. The Stamp Act came in that same year. That act caused the loudest outcry. It said colonists must buy a British stamp. Any printed paper they used called for that stamp. They would pay a tax on newspapers. They would pay a tax on calendars. They would pay a tax on playing cards. They would pay a tax on other paper items. Colonists were angry about the taxes. No voice was given to them by the government collecting the taxes. Their cry said there should be no taxation without representation. A speaker of their own inside Parliament was their wish. Colonists giving him orders did not please King George. He thought about how to strike back at the rebels. At the same time, colonists started working together. They worked together to fight the taxes. Over the years, colonists had learned to rule themselves. Voters in Virginia chose an assembly. That body made the colony's laws. That assembly argued about whether the Stamp Act was fair. Patrick Henry was a young lawyer. He stood up in the assembly. Only Virginians, he said, could place a tax on Virginians. The assembly accepted his position. Some people called Henry a traitor. They said he spoke against King George. A picture shows the Virginia Assembly.

6Samuel Adams spoke out for revolution against the British. He opposed Britain's taxes. Independence was a subject he raised before most others did. Newspapers reported Patrick Henry's position. Soon, people across the 13 colonies protested the Stamp Act. Samuel Adams joined Henry. He also spoke against the tax. Patriots was the label for colonists such as Adams and Henry. Loyalists was the label for colonists who stood with King George. Some Patriots formed the Sons of Liberty. Some formed the Daughters of Liberty. These groups urged colonists to refuse British trade. They urged colonists not to buy British goods. Some colonists even attacked British stamp agents. More acts from Parliament were still to come. More attacks were still to come. In the 1700s, women were largely kept out of politics. They still helped the patriotic cause. The Daughters of Liberty organized boycotts. They took part in the boycotts too. Many women bought the goods for their households. Many women ran small shops. The boycotts hit British merchants very hard. Sewing circles became one way women backed the cause. In October 1765, nine of the thirteen colonies sent people to New York. Those people joined the Stamp Act Congress. The congress asked Parliament to repeal the Stamp Act. Repeal means to cancel. In 1766, King George said yes. The Stamp Act was canceled. The Townshend Acts arrived in 1767. Those acts taxed glass. They taxed paint. They taxed lead. They taxed paper. They taxed tea. Colonists were furious about the new taxes. They boycotted British goods. To boycott means to refuse to buy. By 1770 Britain had dropped every Townshend Act but a single one. British merchants were losing money. Patriots and Great Britain grew steadily more tense. British soldiers spread through the colonies. They were there to enforce the taxes. More taxes brought more resentment. One night in Boston, that tension turned violent.

7Many British soldiers made homes in Boston once the French and Indian War had ended. For a time, life there was fairly peaceful. Colonists still resented the soldiers. For years the two groups shared the town without open war. A noisy Boston crowd started a fight on March 5, 1770. They picked the fight with some British soldiers. The trouble grew. The soldiers began to shoot. They killed five colonists. Samuel Adams was a Patriot. He saw the Boston fight as a chance. He wanted more colonists to choose independence. His friend Paul Revere was asked to create a picture. Revere was a silversmith. Adams wanted him to engrave what happened in Boston. Many people believe Crispus Attucks died first in the Boston Massacre. He lived in Boston. He worked as a whaler. His ships sailed in Boston Harbor. Freedom from Great Britain was a cause he held dear. Speakers at the memorial honored the bravery he had shown. Adams gave the fight a name. He called it the Boston Massacre. The fight had been started by colonists. The engraved picture showed something else. In the image, British soldiers shoot at a group that looks peaceful. The picture was printed in newspapers. It was printed in other places too. The events did not happen the way the picture claims. Adams still received the outcome he was after. The picture made many colonists furious. A picture on this page shows Revere's engraving as it looked in print.

8By 1773, one Townshend tax was left. It was the tax on tea. The Tea Act said colonists must buy tea from only one seller. That seller was Britain's East India Company. Colonists still had no representatives in Parliament. They were angry that some taxes remained. A frustrated group showed how much they hated the tea tax. They climbed onto a British ship. Into Boston Harbor went tea from 342 chests. Their clothing copied the dress of the Mohawk Nation. They hoped the costumes would keep the blame off them. The British were not fooled. The British were not amused. People called the act the Boston Tea Party. King George and Parliament answered with punishment in 1774. They passed the Coercive Acts. Colonists renamed those laws the Intolerable Acts. Those acts aimed punishment at the rebellious colonists. One act closed Boston Harbor. No ships could come or go. Many Boston colonists lost their work. They worried that they would starve. Colonists in other places felt sorry for Boston. They were furious with Great Britain. General Thomas Gage got Britain's appointment as Massachusetts governor. Boston was the city he was ordered to bring under control. The number of troops who came with Gage was 4,000. Colonists then had to house those troops. They had to feed them. The Intolerable Acts pulled colonists together against Great Britain. The Stamp Act had done that earlier. Delegates of twelve colonies gathered in Philadelphia in September 1774. A delegate is a representative. They met as the First Continental Congress. The delegates insisted that the Intolerable Acts be repealed. No tax law should pass, they insisted, unless colonists had a say. Parliament refused those demands. Parliament said the colonies were in a state of mutiny. Patrick Henry is pictured during the First Continental Congress.

9The Continental Congress delegates urged Massachusetts colonists to gather weapons. They also pushed for an end to every kind of trade with Great Britain. The Congress began to train soldiers for the fight ahead. Those soldiers were called militiamen. They were also called minutemen. Colonists were getting ready to fight for independence. Many of them no longer believed the old country. Many no longer trusted it. Patriot soldiers got the nickname minutemen for a reason. A minute was enough time for them to seize weapons and get outdoors. Most Patriot soldiers did not even wear uniforms. In Boston, General Thomas Gage commanded the British troops. He grew alarmed by reports he heard. The reports said colonists stored weapons at Concord. About 20 miles east of Concord lay Boston. British soldiers went out at night on April 18, 1775, under his order. The stored weapons were what they were sent to seize. Gage also planned to arrest two leaders of the rebellion. The leaders were Samuel Adams and John Hancock. They were in Lexington. Lexington and Concord were towns only a short way apart. A picture shows General Thomas Gage. Samuel Prescott was a Patriot doctor. He learned about Gage's plans. His warning told the militia of British troops on the way. On the road to Concord, the British met a group of militiamen. There were 70 militiamen. Lexington's village green was the place of their wait. The British soldiers attempted to pass by the waiting men. Then a shot rang out. Nobody had ordered that shot. Nobody is sure which side fired first. With that shot, the Revolutionary War had its start. People later gave that first shot a famous name. Its famous title is shot heard round the world. Eight militiamen lost their lives as the fight went on. Ten militiamen were wounded. The British went on to Concord.

10A warning story made Boston's Paul Revere famous. The story claims he carried a warning to fighters at Lexington and at Concord. They say he told them the British were coming. That story is a tall tale. One part is true. A spy watched the British soldiers because Revere sent him. The spy was to hang lanterns in a church tower. The lanterns would show which way the British marched. One lantern meant the soldiers were traveling by land. Two lanterns meant they would cross the Charles River. Revere looked at the church tower that night and counted two lanterns. He rode a horse out of Boston. William Dawes rode with him. They headed toward Concord to warn people about the British. Samuel Prescott came along with the pair. British officers stopped Revere. They stopped Dawes too. Prescott got away. It was Prescott who got the warning through to the militiamen. A picture shows the famous midnight ride of Revere. Some of the supplies in Concord were ruined by the British. Most American weapons were already in hiding. Hancock and Adams, the Patriot leaders, avoided arrest. Militiamen reached Concord in large numbers. They attacked the tired British soldiers. The attack was at Concord's North Bridge. On the following day the British set off toward Boston again. The militiamen kept attacking. The fight was behind the British soldiers as they fell back. Militiamen hid behind trees. They hid behind stone walls. From there, they fired on the lines of British soldiers. The British soldiers were professionals. They were humiliated by the defeat. They had lost to a rough group of colonists. Those colonists had been trained quickly. British deaths from the two towns totaled 273. In those same fights, 93 militiamen died. The Revolutionary War had begun. A picture places the Patriot line and the British line on Lexington's green.

11Allies are people or groups that join others for a shared cause. A colonist lives in a colony. Starting a new colony can also make a person a colonist. A debt is something a person owes. The thing owed is usually money. Delegates are people who are chosen or elected. They represent others and act for them. A militia is an army of ordinary citizens. These fighters are not trained soldiers. A mutiny is a refusal to follow orders. The orders may come from a government. They may come from another authority. Parliament is the lawmaking body of the United Kingdom. It has the House of Commons. It has the House of Lords. Protesting means showing strong disagreement. It can also mean showing disapproval. Rebellious describes a person who tends to fight a government. That person may resist another authority instead. Force that removes a government is a revolution. Another government takes its place. Rights are freedoms that people can justly claim. Powers people may fairly claim are rights as well. Taxes are fees a government collects. The money pays for the government's services. It pays for its functions. It pays for its operations.

38. Ibn Battuta's Years on the Road

1A map of the astonishing travels of Ibn Battuta labels Europe, Asia, China, India, Africa, and the Indian Ocean, plus the years he spent moving. Today, countries and cultures can be explored in many ways. Modern transport carries people from country to country. Written works, along with technology, open easy paths to a huge store of knowledge. People can meet and learn from one another with no trip at all. None of this existed in the Middle Ages, the years from 500 ce to 1500 ce. Very few people could travel far, so knowledge of other cultures stayed limited. Even then, one man covered 75,000 miles, or 120,701 km. He saw nearly every land of the Islamic empire, and places beyond it. Those remarkable journeys pushed him to write an important book about travel. His name was Ibn Battuta. Say it I-buhn bah-TOO-tah. He was the greatest traveler of the Middle Ages who saw the wider world.

2He set out soon after the Islamic Golden Age, the years from 750 ce to 1258 ce. In that age, mathematics, science, art, and culture grew enormously across the Islamic empire. Muslims worked beside people who were not Muslims. Together they made scientific inventions, translated books, and produced art. Sea routes, and caravans over land, slowly opened long-distance travel. More people began to move. Ideas, goods, and services were traded through the empire. Windmills at Nashtifan, built between 500 and 900 ce, are still working today. The traveler's full name was Abu Abdullah Muhammad Ibn Battuta. Tangier, in Morocco, was his birth city. The year was 1304. While still young he took up the study of law. He meant to continue those studies with other scholars of the Islamic empire. Before that, one journey mattered more. Being a Muslim, he wished to complete the hajj. Pronounce it HAJ. That duty is a pilgrimage whose goal is Mecca, inside Saudi Arabia. Islam's founder, the Prophet Muhammad, was born in Mecca. Across his life he would return to Mecca again and again. This trip was only the start. In 1325 he began a journey of 3,000 miles, or 4,828 km, and that journey took sixteen months. Stops fell in many lands of the Dar al-Islam. That phrase means the world of Islam. Islamic law was the ruler there. Muslims there could follow their faith without fear. Other parts of the world did not offer that safety. Five duties, called the Pillars of Islam, fall on every Muslim. One duty is to declare belief in Islam. Another is prayer, five times daily. Another is charity, a gift of money. Another is a fast through Ramadan, the sacred month. Fifth comes the pilgrimage called the hajj, and Mecca is its aim. Each year, followers from every region make that trip. The stay in Mecca lasts five days or six. Prayer fills those days. Rituals at several sacred places fill them too. Sickness can block a Muslim from the journey. A lack of money can block the journey too. In either case a Muslim may ask a friend, or a relative, of the same faith to go instead. About two million Muslims make that pilgrimage each year.

3North Africa's shoreline was his path, and Egypt lay ahead. The road from Egypt led toward Syria. Along it, his hunger to see further lands grew stronger. Cultures, people, and places unlike his own were what he wanted to study. Mecca received him in 1326. More than three weeks passed in prayer. He also went to places held sacred. When the hajj ended, he still was not ready for home. He still wanted to explore marvels inside the Islamic empire. Marvels beyond its edge called him too. New lands came in 1326, in the regions now called Iraq and Iran. Both were recovering from invasions by the Mongols. Those warriors were nomads out of eastern Asia. Their push ran westward. Many cities inside the Islamic empire were ruined as they tried to stretch their power. Among the losses was the House of Wisdom. It had been a great library. It had also been a place where people learned. Ibn Battuta still found beauty in cities the attacks had spared. The years 1327 to 1330 took him out of Mecca. Jidda, a city close by, was the next stop. He crossed Yemen by land. Aden was the port where he boarded a ship. Coastal towns of East Africa waited at the end of that sail. Trade centers along that coast held many local residents. A large share were outside the Muslim faith. Arabic was not their language. Languages of those places reached his ears, and they were new to him.

4A welcome met him in every place he traveled. Admirers included Muslims and people outside that faith. Sultans invited him to stay in palaces. They gave gifts. They honored him with parties. Judge was a job several rulers gave him. The wages paid for the next stage of travel. On these travels he heard about Sultan Muhammad of India. High wages for scholars of Islam were part of that ruler's reputation. Delhi, a city in India, became his goal. He wanted a meeting with that well-known sultan.
