Once Muslim lands had been conquered, a large number of Mongols joined Islam. Slowly they began to shape local culture. Their influence on art in Persia was strong. Persia was a region covering roughly what is now Iran. Persian writing art still shows pieces of their style. Paintings show them too. So does pottery. They also worked with Persians on science. The Maragheh Observatory, now closed, stands in present-day Iran. There they studied the stars together and built important scientific tools. Persian pottery often carries very fine detail. On the way to India he visited the land now called Turkey. Followers of Islam, Christianity, and Judaism lived there peacefully, along with different ethnic groups. Everyone treated him kindly. The year 1334 brought him to India. From the sultan came a dwelling. Money came too. So did presents. A judge's post was added, and the salary was generous. The work in India lasted several years.

5Muslim rulers held most of India, yet the sultan often distrusted people near him. After an unsuccessful battle he returned to Delhi and believed his power was slipping. Suspicion spread until he treated each person near him as disloyal. In time he suspected Ibn Battuta of that crime. The scholar did know people who disliked the sultan's policies. No proof ever showed that he had betrayed the ruler. Even so, the sultan banished him for five months. The banishment ended, and a summons returned him to the ruler's court. A new task arrived in 1342. The sultan made him an ambassador whose destination was China. He would join Chinese messengers going home and carry gifts for the emperor. The road to China was hard. An attack separated him from his companions. More than once he nearly lost his life. Reunion with his companions led to a sail. A port held three ships prepared for the voyage toward China. The ships had not yet left when a storm wrecked two of them. Sultan Muhammad's presents went down with the wrecked ships. The remaining vessel departed. Ibn Battuta was left on shore. Unable to find that ship, he decided to continue to China alone. The Maldives were a stop on that solo route. He stayed two years and worked as a judge. Sri Lanka came next. A local sultan there offered a new ship so the trip could go on. China was finally reached in 1346. Mongols ruled it. China surprised him. Important posts were held by people from many faiths and many ethnic backgrounds. He judged the country safe and welcoming.

6China held him for under a year. Then he had seen enough. He chose to return home to Morocco. Arrival came in 1349, and he learned his parents had died. After a few days he set off again. Granada, in Spain, was first. A young writer lived there, Ibn Juzayy. Say the name I-buhn zhoo-ZAY. Years afterward that writer would help the stories of the journeys reach other people. He next chose Mali, in West Africa. Eight months there let him watch cultural practices and admire architecture that was elegant. The year 1354 brought his final journey. He was going home once more, and this time he would stay. Writing had begun in 1353. With help from Ibn Juzayy he started a book about the travels. The title was the Rihla, said RIH-hlah. In Arabic the word means journey. Readers received a broad picture of how people lived in the Middle Ages. No earlier writer had laid that picture out. His life ended in Morocco. The year was about 1368, or perhaps 1369. Little is known of his life after the traveling stopped. The Rihla may not have struck readers hard when it was new. Its first translations into other languages came in the 19th century. Historians then recognized an important travel book. Politics of that era fill its pages. So do social life and culture, both inside the Islamic empire and in lands beside it, all during the Middle Ages. Exact features of the period appear with a care for accuracy. Other history written then seldom matches that care.

7A well-known traveler from the Muslim world is a common label for him. Plenty of readers say that label is too small. Cultures unlike his own interested him. So did other religions. So did unfamiliar ideas. That curiosity made him a world traveler in an age when few people could claim the name. Travel plus writing let other readers look in on the Middle Ages. The people there were fascinating. The cultures were too. Places tied to his story include Tangier in Morocco, Istanbul in Turkey, Tehran in Iran, and Granada in Spain. Readers met astonishing places through his pages. They also met the cultures of the Islamic empire. An invasion means crossing a boundary in order to conquer, weaken, or injure. An ambassador is an official who travels to a new place, or lives there, to represent a country or its people. A nomadic life keeps moving. No lasting home is part of it. Appointed means chosen for a job. Pilgrimage names a trip whose aim is a holy site, or another place set apart, a shrine for example. To banish someone is to force that person to leave. Elegant means dignified or graceful. A sultan rules. The land is often Muslim. The role resembles a king, or an emperor. Ethnic marks a group sharing cultural heritage or nationality, set apart by customs, traits, language, and a common history. To suspect is to believe a person is lying or disloyal, even when proof is thin. A traitor betrays a home country by aiding an enemy. Governed means made laws for a country or an area and enforced them.

39. Inside Your Thinking Brain

1The book starts with the brain itself. Three brains in one come next, along with the brain stem, the cerebellum, and the cerebrum. Right brain and left brain follow. Then come studying the brain, brain mapping, and seeing brain activity. Mind control, keeping the brain in shape, brain training, and protecting the brain come after that. A word list ends the book. Only 2 percent of body weight sits in one organ, yet that organ burns more than 20 percent of your energy. That part is the brain, the most complicated piece of the body. About 86 billion neurons need plenty of energy. These brain cells carry electrical signals. Thoughts depend on those signals. Memories depend on them. Feelings depend on them. A bike ride is possible because of neurons. Remembering a teacher's name is possible because of them. The network they form has more than 125 trillion connections. Neuron links in your head outnumber the stars in 1,500 Milky Way galaxies. This complex wiring lets the brain act as the control center for the whole body. Signals move through neurons toward different parts of the brain. They also move toward different parts of the body.

2Neurons tie the brain to the rest of you. Muscles receive instructions. Sense information comes back. The same cells link the three main brain parts. Those parts are the brain stem, the cerebellum, and the cerebrum. Each part controls specific body activities. Some people give the brain stem the nickname lizard brain. In a lizard it does nearly the same job it does in you. Survival depends on the body processes it runs. Day and night, breathing stays steady because of it. Digestion stays steady. The heartbeat stays steady. Other automatic processes do too. Every body movement brings the cerebellum into the work of coordinating muscles. Other brain parts may send a movement signal. The cerebellum adds targeting instructions. It uses facts such as current speed and current position. A smooth touch of your own nose is possible with that guidance. Without it, the motion would be jerky. You might miss your nose completely. Muscle-movement memories are stored there as well. Repetition makes those memories stronger. Practice is why some motions become automatic. Playing guitar can feel that way. Skateboarding can too. The cerebrum is the largest brain part. Most high-level activity happens there. Thought is included. Speech, learning, and emotions are included. Sense information is interpreted there too. Senses arrive as electrical signals. The cerebrum reads them as sounds, as images, and as other sensations. Stored memories are the comparison. Meaning gets attached. A stream of electrical impulses can become a purple bus. It can become a crowing rooster. Ignoring things is a real part of this job, which may surprise you. Pause and notice everything your senses are sending. A flood of information never stops. Screening some of it out lets you focus on what remains.

3A diagram names the cerebrum, the corpus callosum, the cerebellum, and the brain stem. It also names the left hemisphere and the right hemisphere. A look inside the head would show the cerebrum split into two halves. Those halves are called hemispheres. A nerve bundle called the corpus callosum joins them. Messages travel between them on that bundle. Opposite sides of the body are controlled by the hemispheres. The signal to raise your right hand comes from the left hemisphere. Shaking your left foot is work for the right brain. Some tasks can be done by either half. The two halves are still not identical. Creativity usually sits with the right brain. Artistic skills sit there. Interpreting what you see sits there too. Speech is generally a left-brain job. Writing is too. Math skills are too. Four sections, called lobes, divide each hemisphere. Each lobe has specific jobs. Scientists did not realize this until the 1800s. A doctor then recorded the strange story of Phineas Gage. Injury came in 1848. A blast that no one planned drove an iron rod three feet long clean through his head. Survival was amazing. Memory was not harmed by the hole. Thinking ability was not harmed. Personality was changed. He became rude. He became thoughtless. He became stubborn. Friends said he was no longer Gage. A portion of his frontal lobe was lost. That cerebrum region governs emotions and attention. Scientists received one of their first clues from his injury. Specific brain regions control specific brain functions. A picture shows Phineas Gage holding the iron rod. The rod had passed through his left eye and his frontal lobe.

4Lobe jobs can be listed. The frontal lobe handles problem solving, attention, speaking, and emotional control. The parietal lobe handles movement, plus recognition and categorization of objects. The temporal lobe handles hearing, memory, and understanding speech. The occipital lobe handles vision and shape recognition. Doctors studied the Gage case for many years. Then 1914 brought the start of World War I. Brain injuries struck large numbers of soldiers. The same symptoms kept appearing when the same regions were hurt. Maps of brain regions and their functions could begin. Learning the brain only from injuries was like learning cars only from broken engines. Essential regions could be identified. Little more than that could be learned. Healthy brains had to be studied for a clearer picture. A German scientist built a machine that measured electrical activity in the brain. The machine is called an EEG. It was only a partial solution. Running begins with tiny electrical signals in the brain. Singing does too. Thinking does too. Other actions do too. Electrodes on the surface of the head let an EEG measure those signals. Researchers can see activity while you walk, talk, read, and more. Signals near the surface are all an EEG can detect, unless electrodes are surgically implanted inside the skull. Deeper activity was hard to watch. It was potentially dangerous to watch. A test called an fMRI changed that. An EEG measures electrical activity. An fMRI finds active regions by measuring blood flow. The measurement of brain activity is indirect. Electrically active neurons need more oxygen. Blood is the body's oxygen delivery system. More blood flow generally means more electrically active neurons.

5Two medical professionals review an fMRI in a picture. Blood-flow changes, unlike electrical signals, can be detected deep inside the brain. Precise regions show up on an fMRI when you sing. They show up when you laugh. They show up when you startle. The detail goes far past what an EEG can provide. Detecting brain signals raised a new question. Could the signals be decoded? A computer that could decipher those electrical signals might let a person control an artificial limb. A robot might be controlled through a brain-computer interface. EEG is short for electroencephalogram. Say that word ih-LEK-troh-en-SEH-fuh-luh-gram. The short form fMRI means functional magnetic resonance imaging. The idea may sound like science fiction. Think again. Experimental devices already exist that the mind can control. Electrodes detect the brain signal. A computer decodes it. A mechanical device can then be controlled. Researchers hope the technology will help people with disabilities move better. They hope it will help them communicate better. Brain signals might also be sent from one person to another. In early experiments, a brain signal for finger movement left one person. It traveled over the Internet into another room. The second person received that signal from a special device. His finger moved. The instructions had come from another brain. At the University of Washington, one researcher sent a brain signal over the Internet. A second researcher received it. The receiver's finger moved on the keyboard. The picture places the sender on the left and the receiver on the right.

6Different activities turn on different parts of the brain. A 3D MRI picture catches a brain at work on a problem. A puzzle is one example. Yellow marks the active area. The brain is an amazing machine. Proper care lets it operate best, as with any machine. Using it is the first step toward top condition. Brain exercise helps it grow. Physical exercise helps muscles grow in a similar way. The left hand of a violin player must learn finger motions that are complicated. Most people have a smaller brain area for that hand than these players do. Brain changes usually stay in regions directly involved with the activity. Some mental training may cause broader changes, research suggests. Harvard Medical School studied people who practiced meditation for eight weeks. Changes appeared in regions used for learning. Changes appeared in regions used for memory. Changes appeared in regions used for emotional control. Physical exercise has benefits across the brain. Exercise that raises the heart rate does this most of all. Dr. Arthur Kramer directs the Beckman Institute for Advanced Science and Technology. That institute is at the University of Illinois. He studies how exercise affects the brain. Exercising helps the body, he says, and it helps the brain. Research has shown a pattern in children who exercise regularly. Their memories are better. Their attention is better. School tests often go better too. Healthy brain work also depends on sleep. Dr. Ken Paller directs the Cognitive Neuroscience Program at Northwestern University. Evidence suggests that memories are replayed during sleep. Skills may stick because of that replay. Information may stick too. However the process works, too little sleep clearly lowers the ability to learn. It lowers the ability to think.

7Children in a picture wear helmets so their brains stay protected. Dr. Ann Mckee's research names protection as the top key if a brain is to stay healthy. Shock-absorbing fluid guards the brain. A hard skull guards it too. A fall of only two or three feet onto concrete can crack the skull. It can bruise the brain. Blood to the brain is cut off quickly if the inside of the skull swells. Only a few minutes without oxygen can be survived. A properly fitted helmet during sports gives extra protection. It may save the brain. It may save a life. No body part may matter more than the brain. Exercise helps it operate smoothly for years to come. Enough sleep helps. Protective headgear helps. Words in this book include the following. The brain stem sits at the top of the spinal cord. Basic jobs under its control include breathing. Heart rate is included. Blood pressure is included. Electrodes are points where electricity flows into a device or out of it, as in a battery. A hemisphere is one half of a sphere, or of something mostly round. A planet can be split that way. A brain can too. The cerebellum is the lower back part of the brain. It coordinates sensory information with muscle movement so the body can balance and move smoothly. To interpret is to tell, explain, or understand the meaning of something. A lobe is a rounded section of an organ or of the body. The ear has lobes. The brain has them. The lungs have them. In many mammals, no brain part is larger than the cerebrum. Thinking is under its control. Feeling is too. Communicating and emotions are too. Some senses are too. A network is a group of connected things that communicate with each other. The corpus callosum is a group of nerve fibers in the middle of the brain in some mammals. It connects the two hemispheres and lets them communicate. Neurons are nerve cells. They carry information inside the brain and between the brain and the rest of the body. To decipher is to make out the meaning of something hard to understand. A signal sends a message by an action, a sound, or an object.

40. Ireland's Years of Hunger

1During the Great Hunger, a map shows the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland. A second map shows that region today. Scotland is labeled. Northern Ireland is labeled. The Republic of Ireland, England, Wales, Ireland, and Great Britain are labeled too. One scale uses miles, marked at 0, at 120, and at 240. Another scale uses kilometers with those same marks. Europe is where the maps belong. The parts of this book come in order. First is the Emerald Isle. Then come hard times and a horrible discovery. The first winter follows. Hope, disaster, and relief come next. Going to America follows them. The aftermath, a conclusion, and a word list finish the book. Dublin, Ireland, has a popular spot for visitors called the Liffey River Bridge. The picture shows that bridge. The Emerald Isle is a name for Ireland. Off northwestern Europe sits this beautiful island. Rolling hills there are green. Castles on the land are ancient. Shores there are windy. A colorful history belongs to Ireland. Fame has come from its music. Fame has come from its literature. Fame has come from its folklore. Elves, leprechauns, and faeries fill the magical land some people imagine. Hard work marks the country as well. Most of Western Europe has economic health like Ireland's. Tourism stays a prime industry. Yearly travel to Ireland tops six million people. Beautiful countryside draws them. Places of historical interest draw them too. It has not always been that way.

2From 1800 to 1840, Ireland added over 50 percent to its population. The count reached 8.5 million people. Industry was too small for a crowd that size. British rule on the island had already lasted over a century. The United Kingdom included Ireland. Equal rights with people in Britain were denied to the Irish. A vote was impossible for most. Public office was impossible for most. Land ownership was rare. Factories gave Britain many jobs. Ireland had few factories. Leased land was what most people farmed. Wealthy landlords held that land. Those landlords made their homes in Britain. Only a few acres made up many farms. Rent was paid with wheat or with other grains grown by tenant farmers. Family meals came from potatoes. A foggy day in fall 1845 led farmers into their fields. The discovery waiting there was horrible. Smell from decay filled the air. Black marked the leaves of the potato plants. Wilt marked those leaves too. Desperate diggers went beneath the plants. Mush was what they found instead of firm potatoes. Night was when the change struck. Unusually wet and cool weather was blamed by some. Tribes of faeries, said others, had been at war and had ruined the crop. A different blame came from some British Protestants. They called the loss God's punishment on Irish people for holding the Catholic faith. One picture is a potato turned black and mushy. Potato blight is what destroyed it. A link between potatoes and Ireland is common. Original growth of the plant was in South America. The 1500s were when the Spanish carried potatoes into Europe.

3Dependence on the potato crop was nearly total. Almost no other food reached three million Irish people. One acre could supply a farm family with enough potatoes. Storage through a whole winter was possible. Milk, cabbage, and fish turned that food into a nutritious diet. Rot then claimed a third of the crop underground. Worry filled struggling families. They did not know how to survive until spring. Grain left the farmers' hands because landlords took it for rent. Little food remained once potatoes were gone. Livestock was sold so food could be bought. Furniture was sold. Clothes were sold. Large workhouses were opened by the government. Desperate families could live inside if they worked. Help of that kind was wanted by nobody. Long hours filled each day. The bed they got was ragged. The food they got was little. Leaving was forbidden unless permission came first.

4Indian corn was bought in America by the government. The hungry population was supposed to eat it. Grinding the hard, dry kernels into cornmeal was impossible for the people. Poor cooking of the corn made some of them sick. Higher prices hit food. A way to earn money became a desperate need. Public works were started. Roads were one project. Bridges were another. Jobs came from that building. Hard work was required. Low pay was offered. Nearly five full days of labor bought cornmeal for only three days. That amount was for a family of six. Men still walked many miles. They still stood in long lines. Any work they could find was accepted. The long winter did end at last. Eagerness for a new potato crop filled the farmers. August brought disaster once more. Failure took three-fourths of the plants. Nothing remained that desperate families could sell. Crowding filled the workhouses. A long winter without food loomed. No choice remained for families like that of ten-year-old Michael O'Kane. His father labored on farms and could find no work. A walk of hours carried Michael with his parents. Two brothers and three sisters walked too. The start was Killylea Village in September 1847. The village name sounds like kih-lee-LAY. Life with the boys and men was required. A separate area held his mother and sisters. Morning was for school. Afternoon was for whitewashing walls. Cleaning pigpens filled that time as well. Bridget, the youngest sister, died over the winter. Easy travel marked the diseases. Workhouses made the spread worse. More deaths came from typhus and cholera than from starvation. Obvious need did not move many officials in Britain. Landowners there ignored pleas for help. They ignored relief plans. Export sent grain to other countries. Irish farmers were not allowed to keep it.

5Wanting to help was true of other people. Relief money was raised by the British Relief Association. It was also raised by the Society of Friends, known as Quakers. Irish immigrants in America sent money for family and for friends. Soup kitchens began to serve. As many as three million people stood outdoors each day. Men were in the lines. Women were in the lines. Children were in the lines. A bowl of soup was handed out. A piece of bread came with it. Nearly enough, it was not. Every penny went to food. Overdue rent on the farm could not be paid. Some landlords offered money or grain. Their tenants were starving. The offer was only a temporary help. Eviction was the act of other landowners. Empty homes were then torn down. Some were burned. The goal was to avoid taxes on those houses. Hopeless conditions drove people off the land. Ships filled with Irish crowds bound for the United States. Other ships were bound for Canada. Hundreds of thousands left the Irish homeland forever.

6Crossing the Atlantic Ocean took a ship forty days. Good weather did not make the journey easy. Coffin ships was the grim name for many boats full of Irish emigrants. Packing below deck was severe. Overcrowding and filth let disease spread. Food was often lacking. Water was often lacking. Blankets were often lacking. Death took many passengers. Sickness and weakness marked many who lived to reach America. A time line records the potato blight and the famine in Ireland. Population increase fills the span from 1800 to the 1840s. A rise of 50 percent hit between 1800 and 1840. Employment stayed limited. Potatoes remained the main food for struggling rural families. August 1845 brought the first report of blight. By September the blight had moved into Ireland from southern Britain. Scotland, Belgium, and Holland were on that path as well. The year 1846 is when relief efforts began. Workhouses were expanded. Work projects of the government began. Three-fourths of the year's potato crop was lost that fall. The year 1847 is when mass evictions began. Daily meals from soup kitchens reached over 3 million people. Tenant farmers were evicted. Homes were burned so taxes could be avoided. Full workhouses and spreading disease mark 1848 to 1849. Cholera reports climbed, above all in workhouses that were overcrowded and filthy. Two-thirds of the 1849 potato crop was lost. A gradual end arrived in 1852. The blight was finished by then. Death had claimed over one million people. Emigration had claimed another million. Ireland was changed forever after the blight ended in 1852. A million people were dead. Over a million had emigrated. Homelessness and joblessness marked many who stayed. Landlords could not make money from the fields. Some sold the land for other purposes. Some abandoned it rather than pay high taxes. Decades of further emigration followed for people with no land and no jobs. In 1861 only 5 million people remained, after a fall from a total once over 8.5 million. Gone was more than every third person. Another drop, down to 4.5 million, came ten years later. Britain took the blame from many Irish people. It was the most powerful country in the world then. They believed more help should have come. Bitterness from that failure helped fuel the revolution. The split of Ireland into two countries finally came in 1922. Two countries have shared the island since 1922. South of the divide is the independent Republic of Ireland. The United Kingdom still includes Northern Ireland.

7Scientists in time learned the name of the potato disease. It is late potato blight. A funguslike organism called Phytophthora infestans was the cause. Spores of that organism rode the wind. Rain then washed them down into the soil. People in Ireland called the famine the Great Hunger. Immigration from Ireland to the United States kept going afterward. The years 1850 to 1920 brought more than five million arrivals. Some of those people ran for political office. Others opened businesses. Famine-era ancestors stand behind famous Americans. President John F. Kennedy is one. Inventor Henry Ford is another. Pride in Irish roots is claimed by forty million Americans today. Folk traditions and holidays of Ireland are part of that pride. Irish literature stays widely known because of them. Irish music and Irish film do too. World culture now counts those arts as an established part. Cobh Harbor in Ireland holds a statue of Annie Moore and her brothers. Every famine emigrant is represented by that statue. A better life was the reason they left Ireland. Words in this book include the following. Blight is a plant disease that can damage a plant or destroy it. A landlord rents out land, an apartment, or a building. Decay is the process of rotting, or the state that rotting brings. A population includes every member of one species inside one area. An emigrant leaves a country or a region in order to settle elsewhere. Starvation is hunger at its most extreme, or death caused by too little food. A famine is a major shortage of food spread over a large area. A tenant pays a landlord for land, for an apartment, or for a building. A homeland is the birth region or the birth country of a person. A workhouse takes in people who are poor or dependent. They live and work there in return for shelter and for food. An immigrant comes into a new country to live, often in order to settle. Ireland is the northwestern European island that holds both the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland.

41. Joy in a Mountain Kingdom

1page 16. Introduction. Happiness is not simple to name. Does the word mean only a quick laugh or a sudden feeling of joy? Or does it point to something larger? In Bhutan (boo-TAHN), people treat happiness as contentment or satisfaction. Leaders there hold that happiness matters more than wealth. Because of that belief, this small mountain kingdom asks citizens how happy they feel. The questions go out every few years. Officials then use the answers to make daily life better. A nickname grew from that aim. People call the country The Kingdom of Happiness. Four quick facts about Bhutan follow. First, the Himalaya Mountains hold the country, with China on one side and India on the other. Bhutan covers about as much land as Switzerland. Second, children grow up speaking Dzongkha (ZOHNG-kah). English is also spoken by many citizens. Third, bows and arrows guarded the borders for centuries. Archery is now the sport of the nation. Fourth, the year 2008 brought a new kind of rule called a constitutional monarchy. In that system, a parliament watches over the power of the king. A map of this part of Asia labels China, Bhutan, Nepal, India, and Bangladesh. The map also marks the Great Himalaya Range, the Lesser Himalaya Range, and the capital, Thimphu.

2Low plains fill the south of Bhutan. Towering peaks of the Himalaya Mountains rise in the north. One famous building is the Tiger's Nest Monastery. It grips a high cliff. The Paro Valley lies thousands of feet below that cliff. Growth and Happiness. Bhutan's first survey of happiness took place in 2007. The wish to follow the nation's happiness had begun long before that year. The throne passed to Jigme Singye Wangchuck in 1972. Bhutan's new king was sixteen years old. He wanted the country to prosper. He also wanted Bhutan to stay true to its own values. He felt that other nations pictured prosperity in a way that did not fit Bhutan. Most other nations follow growth with a measure called Gross Domestic Product, or GDP. GDP adds up the value of every good and service a country produces. Leaders use that total to steer growth. Trade was not what pushed Bhutanese culture forward. Farms and villages are common across the land. Factories are scarce, and so are cities. Bhutan is mainly a Buddhist nation as well. In that faith, reaching happiness is an important step on the way to a fulfilling life. For Buddhists, happiness is not a matter of money. A person must study several sides of life and improve them. One side is spiritual. Another is physical. A third is social. The last is environmental. King Wangchuck was sure the whole country should care for those same sides. A focus on money alone did not make sense to him. He believed Bhutan would grow and thrive if people's happiness rose, not only their wealth. A portrait shows King Jigme Singye Wangchuck.

3Happiness on Four Supports. The Bhutanese government shaped an idea called Gross National Happiness, or GNH. GNH became a guide for how the country should be run. The young king, who was popular, spoke with his ministers. Together they asked how large decisions could support happiness. They chose four key areas. People call those areas pillars. The pillars connect to the Buddhist view of happiness. The first pillar looks at how people are governed. It matters because policies and laws shape the way citizens live. The second pillar looks at how people work and play side by side. Shared work and play can change a person's mental state. They can change happiness too. The third pillar concerns keeping Bhutanese culture alive. That culture is critical to who the Bhutanese are. The last pillar explores the link between people and the land around them. Four Bhutanese values hold up the GNH measure. The first value is good governance. The second is sustainable socioeconomic development. The third is preservation and promotion of culture. The fourth is environmental conservation. Leaders believed these four supports had to stay in balance. Only then, they said, could citizens reach happiness in life. At the start, the pillars were only simple suggestions. Nothing was measured. No records were kept. Bhutan was a secluded land. The huge Himalaya Mountains kept the modern world at a distance. Trade with Western nations was small. Visitors were rare. Then the pattern changed. Tourists began to arrive, eager to learn about the quiet kingdom. Giant prayer wheels stand in many places across Bhutan. Some sit near bus stops. Others stand at monasteries.

4In schools that follow the GNH plan, morning meditation is part of the day. In 1999, television was allowed inside the country for the first time. The Internet was allowed in that same year. Citizens started learning about lands beyond their own. People outside started learning about Bhutan. Visitors were drawn by scenery that still looked wild. They were also drawn by a calm way of living. Guests found that the hours felt less hurried. Traditional Bhutanese clothes were worn in classrooms. The same clothes were worn on the job. Signs beside the roads asked citizens to spend time in nature. Quiet sitting was part of each day. During that time, a person stays with his or her own thoughts. Families also spent hours together. All of these habits fed a shared sense of well-being. Here is a surprise. No traffic signal hangs over a Bhutanese street. One signal was set up in the capital, Thimphu. People felt it was too modern, so it came down. An officer now guides cars through the downtown streets. At a monastery in Paro, young monks lean in around a single cell phone. A Measure of Happiness. A new century brought fresh changes. Machines and new tools slipped through the mountains. Those peaks had once held outside influences back. The kingdom that had stood apart now kept one foot in older ways. The other foot stood in the modern world. After quiet meditation, children watched television. They also played video games. People dressed in old styles carried cell phones. Leaders feared that long-held customs and values would fade. If that happened, the older reasons for happiness might fade too. Bhutan needed an orderly plan to prevent the loss. Checking happiness on a regular schedule would show what was changing. The government could then look for ways to answer the worry.

5Finding a way to measure happiness for a whole country was a hard task. The Bhutanese Ministry of Planning took up the work. First the ministry named nine areas. Those areas are called domains. They grew from the four pillars. Each domain was then split into dozens of smaller categories. Viewed as one set, the domains and categories make a full picture of happiness. That picture is called the Gross National Happiness Index, or GNH Index. The index works as a scale. People can use it to judge happiness inside the kingdom. The next step turned the categories into many questions. The questions ask about a person's own satisfaction. One question asks how fully a person enjoys living. Nine domains make up GNH. They are well-being, living standards, and health. The set also holds time use, the environment, and community vitality. Education is on the list. Good governance is on it too. Cultural resilience completes the set. The GNH Centre Bhutan supplied these names. Gross National Happiness sits in the middle of the nine domains. The questions went into a survey for citizens. Every answer received a number. The numbers were added into a score for each person. Teams carried the survey into far-off mountain villages. They also visited farms in the valleys. They visited the main cities as well. The teams explained why the questions were being asked. They said the answers would help make Bhutan better. During 2007, a trial of the survey ran in selected districts. By 2010, the survey was ready for every part of the country. In that year, over 7,000 people gave answers. The nation held more than 700,000 residents. Workers studied the answers with the GNH Index. A higher number means a higher level of happiness. The results showed that some groups were the least happy overall. Women were among them. Farmers were among them too. So were older people, and people without schooling. After the survey, health care got better. Standards of living got better as well. A later survey took place in 2015. Its numbers were set beside the 2010 numbers. Officials learned that happiness across the country was 1.8 percent higher. Deep happiness described more than 43 percent of the people.

6Was Every Person Included? One group inside Bhutan was left out of the survey. The missing group has a name, Lhotshampa, said loh-TSUHM-puh. These citizens trace their families to Nepal. Their homes are in the south. Many of those families left Nepal during the nineteenth century. They came to farm rich soil. The Lhotshampa follow Hinduism. That faith is not the same as Buddhism. In the middle of the 1980s, the government opened a campaign. Every citizen was told to dress in Bhutanese clothing. Every citizen was told to speak Dzongkha. Every citizen was told to follow Buddhism. Through the 1990s, Lhotshampa left in the tens of thousands. Some reached Nepal and made homes in camps. By 2015, the number of those refugees who had reached the United States was close to 85,000. Many still hope to go back to Bhutan one day. A picture shows a Lhotshampa woman with her child in her arms. She does heavy physical work on a road project in Thimphu. Happiness fell in other areas too. Scores dropped for mental well-being. Community strength dropped as well. Cultural variety dropped too. People gave less time to unpaid help than before. Fewer people felt that old customs mattered. The government plans to use the survey to lift happiness. Leaders may set dates for festivals, for example. Those gatherings would invite communities to take part in ancient customs. The aim is a day when 100 percent of the people are deeply happy. Happy People in Other Lands. Countries far from Bhutan have paid attention to the GNH Index. Some have used the idea to learn about happiness at home. In 2007, Thailand built a national index of happiness in a similar style. South Korea made a scale of its own from Bhutan's index. Great Britain did so too. In 2009, a large survey firm in the United States asked people there about happiness. Each of these countries saw real worth in the effort. They hoped happiness would keep growing among their citizens. A 2016 report on world happiness names ten leading countries. Denmark stands first. Switzerland is second, and Iceland is third. Norway is fourth. Finland is fifth, and Canada is sixth. The Netherlands is seventh. New Zealand is eighth, and Australia is ninth. Sweden is tenth. Figures in that report show the same ten countries stayed at the top in every year that was surveyed. Their places on the list may have shifted. The United States stood at number 13. Bhutan stood at number 84. Each place comes from an average score. Residents scored the quality of their lives from 0 to 10.

7In far-off Bhutan, a person's happiness comes ahead of economic growth. In 2011, the United Nations carried out its first study of happiness around the world. The United Nations is a body of countries from across the globe. The first World Happiness Report came out in 2012. The report placed countries in a ranked list. The ranking used factors much like the ones in Bhutan's GNH Index. In that same year, March 20 received a special name. It is the International Day of Happiness. On this date, the Sun lines up with the equator of Earth. Day and night last the same number of hours. The date stands for a belief held by King Wangchuck. He taught that well-being and happiness depend on balance. Glossary. Analyzed means studied with close care, and the word is on page 7. Secluded means set apart, with few people near, and the word is on page 3. Surveys means putting questions to a group so the answers can be studied, and the word is on page 5. Buddhist means belonging to Buddhism, a faith that follows Siddhartha Gautama, who taught in ancient India. Spiritual means concerned with the inner spirit, the soul, or a divine being. Critical means of the highest importance, or linked to a turning point. An index is a number used to measure something, or to show that a level rose or fell. Thrive means to grow in a strong and healthy way. Prosper means to gain success with money, or to become healthy and strong. Traditional means linked to a custom people have kept for a very long time. Remote means far away, or cut off from other places. Contentment means a quiet feeling of being satisfied. Pillars means strong supports that hold an idea up. Domains means areas of life that people measure.

42. Landforms on a Long Drive

1I live in Boston. A road trip will take part of my summer. My parents and I will share the drive. Our route follows Interstate 90. That highway runs all the way to Seattle. Mom says amazing landforms wait along the way. Mountains are one kind we will pass. Plains are another kind. Rivers are on the trip as well. Lakes are on the trip too. Still more landforms will show up before Seattle. In class we study our planet. We also study the forces that build different landforms. Real landforms will be exciting to see at last. Only one week of school is left. After that week, we leave. A map of major landforms can ride along on a drive like ours. Canada lies to the north of the United States. Mexico lies to the south. Monterrey is marked in Mexico. The Pacific Ocean borders the west side. The Atlantic Ocean borders the east side. The Gulf of Mexico meets the southern coast. Seattle is marked in the northwest. Boston is marked in the northeast. New York is marked on the map. Philadelphia is marked there. Detroit is marked near the lakes. Chicago is marked in the north. Saint Paul is marked in the north too. Houston is marked near the Gulf. Los Angeles is marked in the southwest. The map key uses four land types. Those types are hills, mountains, plains, and plateaus. The Cascade Range is marked near the northwest coast. The Columbia River is marked in that region. The Columbia Plateau is marked beside that river. The Coast Range follows the Pacific side. The Sierra Nevada Range stands inland in the west. The Central Valley lies in that western area. The Mojave Desert lies in the southwest. The Sonoran Desert lies near that desert. The Chihuahuan Desert lies farther south. The Great Basin Desert lies inland in the west. Great Salt Lake lies in that basin region. The Rocky Mountains form a long chain. The Colorado Plateau stands near those mountains. The Grand Canyon cuts into that plateau. The Colorado River runs through that country. The Rio Grande River runs farther south. The Edwards Plateau stands in the south-central land. The Gulf Coastal Plain spreads beside the Gulf of Mexico. The Mississippi River Delta spreads where the great river meets the Gulf. Lake Okeechobee lies in the far southeast. The Atlantic Coastal Plain follows the eastern shore. The Appalachian Mountains rise in the east. The Ozark Plateau rises inland from the central country. The Great Plains cover a wide middle. The Central Lowlands lie near those plains. The Missouri River crosses the middle of the country. The Mississippi River crosses that middle too. The Ohio River runs through the east-central land. The Badlands stand on the northern plains. The Great Lakes fill part of the north. Lake Superior is one of the lakes on the map. Lake Huron is one of them. Lake Michigan is one of them. Lake Erie is one of them. Lake Ontario is one of them.

2My teacher is Mr. Lopez. He compares Earth to a hard-boiled egg. The core sits in the middle, the way the yolk does. The outer core is liquid. Solid metal forms the inner core. Both parts of the core are incredibly hot. The mantle is like the white of the egg. Weak rock makes up the mantle. The mantle moves very slowly. The mantle is very hot. It is almost hot enough to melt. It is not quite hot enough to melt. The crust is like the cracked shell of that egg. Thicker parts of the crust are usually continents. A continent is a huge landmass. Most of the thinner crust makes up the seafloor. That seafloor lies under oceans and seas. Both the thick crust and the thin crust hold different landforms. The surface of Earth is always changing. Some changes happen very slowly. Some of those changes are peaceful. We might not even notice the slow ones. Other changes happen really fast. Fast changes often come with violent force. Slow changes can alter landforms that already exist. Slow changes can also create new landforms. Fast changes can alter old landforms. Fast changes can create new ones too. Separate pieces of the crust fit together like puzzle pieces. The Eurasian Plate is one piece. The Pacific Plate is one piece. The North American Plate is one piece. The Indian Plate is one piece. The African Plate is one piece. The Indo-Australian Plate is one piece. The South American Plate is one piece. The Antarctic Plate is one piece. Movement of these many separate pieces is one force that creates landforms.

3Earth's crust is built from huge pieces of rock. Those pieces are called tectonic plates. The plates float on the mantle like rafts. A shifting mantle drags the plates along on top of it. Two plates can bump against each other. Two plates can slide past each other. Two plates can move away from each other. Landforms owe more to these underground movements than to any other hidden force. Heat in the mantle can make the mantle move. An ocean plate can move under a land plate. Heat from that ocean plate can cause magma to form. Sometimes a small area high in the mantle gets hot enough to melt. The melted rock is called magma. Magma can push up toward the surface. It can erupt there as lava. Lava can cool and then harden. Hardened lava can build upward over time. That buildup can form a volcano. A volcano is a type of mountain. Erosion by water and wind carved the Grand Canyon. Weathering formed a rock arch in another place. Tectonic plates change Earth under the ground. Magma changes the underground Earth as well. Other changes happen on the surface at the same time. Weathering breaks rock apart. Weathering also shapes the rock that remains. The broken pieces are called sediments. Erosion carries sediments away. Later, those sediments are deposited in a new place. Wind is one main tool of weathering and erosion. Water is another main tool. Ice is another main tool. Mr. Lopez handed our class a list of different landforms. I will carry that list on the trip. I will try to see every landform on it.

4Some landforms on the list are right here in Boston. I started with those. Castle Island was the place Mom and I visited. Castle Island is in Boston Harbor. From there, Mom and I saw a group of islands. Castle Island is not a real island. Water does not surround it on all sides. One side joins the mainland. That join makes Castle Island a peninsula. Massachusetts Bay includes Boston Harbor. Massachusetts Bay is a body of water joined to the Atlantic Ocean. The eastern shore of North America is where Boston stands. A continent is an incredibly huge piece of land. My list asks me to spot an island. It asks me to spot a harbor. It asks me to spot a peninsula. Out on the road, Boston's terrain is rolling. The ground goes gently up and down. Heading west on Interstate 90, we watch the hills get bigger. Valleys grow larger on that same stretch. The road feels as if it is taking us higher. Dad says we will soon reach the Berkshires. The Berkshires are part of the Appalachian Mountains. I have read about the Appalachian Mountains before. Even so, I do not see tall mountains while we drive. Dad says those mountains are very old. Erosion has worn them down into big hills. To me, the Berkshires look more like big hills. They do not match the mountains I had pictured. The list also asks for a mountain. It asks for a hill. It asks for a plateau.

5Across New York State, some land is low and hilly. Other places in the state stand higher. Dad says the higher places are part of the Allegheny Plateau. Allegheny is said al-uh-GAYnee. Plateau is said pla-TOH. The Allegheny Plateau is a huge, high area of land. Sediments built that high land over a long time. The sediments were deposited because of erosion. A map of this stretch shows Canada to the north. It shows the Adirondack Mountains. It shows New York and the Catskills. It shows the Allegheny Plateau. It shows Buffalo and Pennsylvania. The key on that map marks plains, plateaus, hills, and mountains. North America has no plateau bigger than the Colorado Plateau. Part of it lies in Colorado. Part of it lies in Utah. Part of it lies in Arizona. Part of it lies in New Mexico. We stop overnight in Buffalo, New York. In the morning we continue west. Along the south shore of Lake Erie, the land is much lower. The land is flatter there as well. One member of the Great Lakes is Lake Erie. The lake is much too wide for us to see the far side. A glacier carved the basins that hold the Great Lakes. The carving happened about fourteen thousand years ago. These lakes are Earth's largest group of freshwater lakes. Mom says we will see Lake Michigan when we get near Chicago. Another map of the lakes shows Canada. It shows Lake Michigan and Wisconsin. It shows Buffalo, New York, and Boston. It shows Michigan and Lake Erie. It shows the Ohio River and Chicago. It shows Pennsylvania, Ohio, Illinois, and Indiana. The landform to check off here is a lake.

6We stay overnight in Chicago. Then we return to the highway. After we enter Wisconsin, we drive past Madison. Madison is the capital city of Wisconsin. An isthmus is where downtown Madison stands. Isthmus is said IS-muhs. A thin band of land with water on both sides is called an isthmus. Lake Mendota is one of those bodies of water. Lake Monona is the other one. Wisconsin's state capitol building stands on Madison's isthmus. I grin at the sight. I check isthmus off the list. After more driving, we stop to see the Wisconsin Dells. The Dells is a gorge. A gorge is a steep, narrow valley. The Wisconsin River carved this gorge. Canyons lie along its sides. A canyon is similar to a gorge. A canyon is not as steep as a gorge. A canyon is not as narrow either. The Mississippi River will not be far ahead. Few rivers on Earth stretch farther than this one. Glaciers carved most of this part of the Mississippi. A river is another landform I can check off. A gorge is one I can check off too.

7After we cross the Mississippi, we are in Minnesota. Soon we will officially be on the Great Plains. A plain is a large area of flat land. A plain does not have many trees. Two tectonic plates once smashed into each other. The two plates joined together. That joining formed the Great Plains. Some parts of the Great Plains are flat. Other parts are hillier. The wide grasslands were once home to huge herds of bison. Huge herds of horses lived on them too. Western Minnesota is where we stay for one night. The next morning we drive into South Dakota. The land stays pretty flat for a while. The view changes near Badlands National Park. We hike in the park. We see amazing rock formations there. Deposited sediments helped make those formations. Wind erosion helped make them. Water erosion helped make them. The park holds many fossils. One fossil is the skull of a mammal. That mammal lived from 38 million years ago to 16 million years ago. After another night's stay, we drive through a corner of Wyoming. The Bighorn Mountains pass on our left. Snow rests on some of those peaks. Mom says even bigger mountains are still ahead. A map of this part of the drive shows Montana and North Dakota. It shows the Mississippi River and the Missouri River. It shows South Dakota and Minnesota. It shows the Bighorn Mountains. It shows Wisconsin and Badlands National Park. It shows Madison, Wyoming, Iowa, and Nebraska. It shows Chicago. The landform to check here is a plain.

8We cross into Montana and pass the city of Billings. Dad tells me to prepare for a sight that will impress me. Not long after that, I let out a whoop. A row of high peaks stands ahead. Snow covers those peaks. The peaks are the Rocky Mountains. Among the chief mountain chains of the West, the Rockies stand out. White snow lies on the tops of a Rocky Mountain range in Montana. Two small tectonic plates once sat beneath the Pacific Ocean. Those plates slid under the North American Plate. That movement formed the Rockies. A map of the western drive shows Canada and Washington. It shows Seattle and Montana. It shows the Missouri River and Mount Rainier. It shows North Dakota and the Columbia River. It shows Billings and South Dakota. It shows Oregon, Idaho, and Wyoming. We drive across Montana, then across Idaho, then across Washington. I am excited to see water again. I am even more excited to see Mount Rainier. Rainier is said ray-NEER. Mount Rainier is a huge volcano. Dad says hardened lava piled up in layers. Ash piled up in layers with it. The layers grew over a long time. That is why the volcano stands so tall. We drive into Seattle. Seattle sits beside Puget Sound. Puget Sound is an arm of the Pacific Ocean. People also call that arm an inlet. We have reached the end of Interstate 90. Our search for landforms is nearly finished. Glaciers cover the top of Mount Rainier. A glacier is a large field of ice and packed snow. The ice and snow remain through the whole year. A mountain range is on my list here. A glacier is on the list. A volcano is on the list too.

9One landform is still left on the list. For the last stop we travel one hour north. We go to the delta of the Skagit River. Skagit is said SKA-jit. This landform formed where the river flows into Skagit Bay. Sediments built up at that meeting of river and bay. Over time, the buildup made the river split. The river split into many smaller branches. Those branches spread through the area between the dotted lines on a drawing. I have seen amazing landforms on this trip. I have learned a great deal about how Earth's surface changes. I am eager to share the summer with Mr. Lopez. A few trip words are worth keeping. A basin is a low place in Earth's surface. People also call that low place a depression. An isthmus can also be the narrow land that links two larger landmasses. A delta is ground at the mouth of a river. Sediment builds it. The shape is like a triangle. Landforms are natural formations on Earth's surface. Valleys, plateaus, mountains, plains, and hills are examples. To deposit means to set a material down on a surface. Sediment is one material that can be set down. A peninsula is a long piece of land. Water goes almost all the way around it. Erosion means nature carries rock or soil away. Water can do that work. Wind can do it. Ice can do it. A plateau is a wide stretch of flat land that stands raised above nearby ground. A gorge is a deep valley that runs a long distance. Higher land stands around it. Tectonic plates are the huge rock sheets that form Earth's crust. An interstate is a major highway. It runs through two or more states. Terrain is the natural character of a piece of land. The word also means the ground itself.

43. Learning the Craft of the Camera

1An introduction opens this book. A history of photography follows. A project for a pinhole camera follows the history. Modern photography comes next. The art of aiming and shooting comes after that. Lighting tips follow. Fun projects follow the lighting. Ways to explore more come next. A glossary follows. An index ends the book. Picture a vacation morning. A parent pulls you from bed at 5:00 am for a whale watch by the ocean. A huge tail then rises from the water. A camera in your hands saves that moment. Photos of whales at dawn can hold a memory. Photos of old landmarks can hold one. Photos of family members doing silly things can hold one. Taking a photo is easy now. A cheap single-use camera can do it. A basic compact camera that you point and shoot can do it. A digital camera can do it. Aim, then press. Early photography was not like that. Gear cost a lot. It was heavy and awkward. Chemistry knowledge was required. Patience was required. Most people now use digital cameras. Film skills still help anyone who wants strong photos.

2The Latin root of camera means a chamber. It can also mean a dark room. A camera is a dark box. The back wall holds film that reacts to light, or it holds a chip. A click opens a shutter at the front. Light enters for a very short time. Light that bounces off a subject forms the picture. The picture lands on the film or on the chip. A lens gathers that light. It focuses the light, much as the lens of an eye does. A diagram labels film advance and the film itself. It labels a flash and a viewfinder. It labels the shutter. It labels an image that is reversed. It labels the lens. It labels the aperture, which adjusts light. It labels the subject and the film roll. The first rough camera appeared around the year 1500. All it could do was cast a picture onto paper or onto a screen. The pinhole project on the next page works in that spirit. You can build a pinhole camera. Punch a hole the size of a pencil point in one side of a shoebox. Cut a square 2 inches, or 5 centimeters, on the opposite side. Cut tracing paper a bit larger than that opening. Tape the paper over the opening. Tape the lid shut so light cannot leak in. Ask a person to stand still in bright light. Point the pinhole toward the person. Watch through the tracing paper. A small image of the person should appear after a few seconds. Look for something unusual about that image. Try to trace it on the paper.

3Early cameras demanded that people hold very still. A small move blurred the shot. The woman's face at the left of a photo shows that blur. Centuries of science passed before a picture could be made to last. Certain chemicals darken in light. That was the first discovery. Other chemicals could then stop the image from fading. The earliest cameras needed hours for one blurry picture in black and white. Louis Daguerre, an inventor from France, found a sharper method during the 1830s. A picture could be ready in under thirty seconds. Those pictures are daguerreotypes. Say dah-GARE-oh-types. The name honors the inventor. They became the first popular kind of photography. Setup and shooting once took half an hour for a single photo. Children grew restless. Even a tiny move ruined the picture. Photographers often held up a metal bird. They told people to watch the birdie. Just before the shot, air blown into the bird moved its tail or made a tweet. Children looked, and they held still.

4A simple box camera in 1888 turned photography into a hobby ordinary people could afford. The camera was light. It did not cost much. It was easy to use. Best of all, amateurs no longer had to develop the film themselves. That old process was long and full of careful work. Like later film cameras, the box camera stored pictures on a roll. People sent the roll and the camera back to the maker. Prints were made there. The camera came back with a fresh roll inside. Early box cameras look large now. For their own time they were small. The cameras you will likely use while learning come next. A disposable, or single-use, camera has automatic focus. A flash is built in. A button releases the shutter. A basic compact camera has an automatic flash. It has a viewfinder. Film advances and rewinds on its own. Focus is automatic. A zoom lens is included.

5An SLR camera is a single-lens reflex. A flash can be attached, though the drawing does not show the flash itself. Film rewind is manual. Film advance is manual. A lens is on the front. Focus is manual. A digital camera can zoom in and zoom out. It can delete a shot. It can review a picture. An upload jack is on it. A video display is on it. Many simple cameras still use film. Film is a plastic strip coated with a silver substance. Light makes that coating react. An image forms. Finished pictures need several steps. Developer, a chemical bath, makes the image visible. A second chemical bath is the stop bath. It halts the developer so the picture does not grow too dark. The result is a negative. Light things look dark. Dark things look light. A drawing shows a positive image beside a negative image.

6A print, also called a positive, is a larger copy made from the negative. The steps run backward. Light is shone through the negative onto photo paper that reacts to light. The paper flips the negative back, so you see the scene as it was captured. A chemical fixer then locks the image on the paper. Many pros print in their own darkrooms. You will probably send film to a local photo lab. Machines do the work there. Numbers on a film roll tell three things. They tell width, or format. They tell length. They tell speed, which matters most. Width for most film is 35 millimeters. Length, often 24 or 36, is how many pictures the roll holds. ISO is the speed rating to notice. It depends on when and where you will shoot. Speed is how fast the film reacts to light. A higher number needs less light. Film at 400 is better in dim light. It is better when the subject is moving. Film at 100 is better outdoors in full daylight. Film at 200 is a good all-purpose choice. Match the film to the pictures you want.

7Two photos show the same dog. A computer has changed the one on the right. A digital camera follows the same idea as other cameras. Film is not used. Reusable chips that sense light store the shots. The screen shows a shot at once. A bad shot can be deleted. You can try again. No film is wasted. Chosen shots can move to a computer. You can change them there. That is when digital work becomes the most fun. Colors can grow richer. One photo can sit inside another. Something, or someone, can be removed. Retouching and airbrushing once belonged only to skilled darkroom workers. A computer can do those tricks now. An artistic eye is still required. Patience is still required. You know how a camera works, so it is time to shoot. Pick a subject first. Your subject might be someone. It might be a place. It might be an object. It can be all three. Framing, also called composition, is the way you set up what is in the shot. For a person, fill the frame. Allow a small gap around the head. Allow a small gap around the shoulders. Keep the person inside the viewfinder lines, or the top of the head may be cut off. That crop can look artistic. It can also look unkind. Too close, and the image may turn fuzzy. A bad frame cuts off the head and whatever the person is looking at. A good frame includes the whole person and the action.

8Bunch people near one another. Closeness should run across the row and from front to rear. Each person should stand at a similar distance from the lens. Faces closer to the lens can turn pale and bright. People in back may look dark. Try ideas. Mistakes are allowed. Put the subject in the middle. Then put the subject off to one side. Shoot through a window. Shoot through an arch. Look for contrast in shapes. A jagged fence set against curving hills is one example. Think about angle. Kneel and shoot upward to make the subject look more important. Hold the camera tall for a portrait. Stress the foreground, the front of the scene. Then stress the background in a similar shot. Scenery often looks richer with a person in front. The person gives a sense of scale. Watch the background. Keep it simple. Make sure nothing odd seems to stick out of a head. Clear clutter in front that steals attention. You can also step to a fresh viewpoint. Ignore the background, and a cactus may seem to grow from someone's head.

9A dark photo and a light photo can both miss the mark. Exposure is how much light falls on the film. Photography comes from Greek words that mean to draw with light. Light is a photographer's best friend. It is also the worst enemy. Too much light is overexposure. The picture looks washed out. Too little light is underexposure. The picture looks too dark. Pros use light meters, flood lamps, and screens that bounce light. A flash can throw a sudden burst into a dim scene. Simple cameras often have a built-in flash. Some flashes turn on by themselves when light is low. Do not shoot straight into the light. A person in front of a bright window can look shadowy and dark. Side light makes a picture half bright and half in shadow, unless that is what you want. Put the light behind you. On a sunny day a person facing the sun may squint. Keep your own shadow out of the frame. Use the flash even when light seems like enough. It can fill dark spots and even the light. Shoot the same outdoor scene at sunrise, at noon, and at sunset. Sun direction changes the look and the mood. Glowing red eyes are common with cheap cameras. Turn on more room lights. Ask people to glance aside. They should not look straight into the lens.

10Focus is how sharp the image is. It depends on distance from lens to subject. It also depends on distance from lens to film or chip. A lens can focus only at certain distances. Most simple cameras do best at about 5 feet. That is 1.5 meters. Advanced compact cameras have motorized zoom lenses. A button pushes the lens out for a close view. It pulls the lens in for a wide view. Cameras are sensitive machines. A tiny shake can blur the shot. Hold the camera with both hands. Keep fingers and hair off the lens and the flash. Tuck your elbows against your sides. Stand with your legs a little apart so you feel balanced. For more steadiness, crouch on one knee. Or sit cross-legged with elbows on your knees. Press the camera against a table or a wall. Squeeze the shutter button slowly and evenly. A panorama is one long picture of a very wide view. It might be a city skyline, a mountain range, or a beach. Even the scene outside your own front door can work. Pick an open spot without too many objects in front. Imagine the scene split into three to five sections. Practice sweeping the camera from left to right without moving your feet. That sweep is called panning. Let each new frame cover about one-third of the frame before it. What sits on the right of the first shot should start the left of the next. Begin at the left and work right. Several shots of each section are a good idea. Four overlapping photos of a city mural made one panorama.

11Lay the prints so the right edge of one meets the left edge of the next. Glue or tape them into one continuous picture. Other projects are fun too. Colored cellophane in front of the lens blocks or reduces that color in the photo. What might happen if a yellow car is shot through a yellow filter? Aim through the lens of sunglasses that are polarized. Shine from bright sun and from glossy surfaces is cut down. Cut shapes from black construction paper and tape the paper over the front of the lens. Try stars, keyholes, or arches. Use your own ideas. This frame filter changes the edges of the shot. Choose your best shots. Arrange the album so the pictures tell a story. Put the date under the photo. Put the place under it too. Name the people. Say what is happening. A sample note might recall a happy trip and a pair of 3-D glasses. Do not throw away the weak shots. Make a collage. Cut pieces from unwanted photos. Arrange them as you like. Paste them on a poster. Make a line of greeting cards. Glue on a photo of yourself, of family, or of friends. Use places you have been, sights you have seen, or shots of wildlife and nature. Fold the paper in half. Write a personal note inside.

12A library or a bookstore holds many books on photography. They teach pictures of people, of scenery, and of odd and interesting things. Ask a librarian for instruction books written for kids. The art shelves hold books of famous photographs. Studying pro work teaches a lot. On the internet, search for a subject you want to learn. Digital cameras are one search. Photography is another. Adding the words for kids can turn up more useful pages. Read the results and open one that looks interesting. Step back to earlier results when you want another page. The best exploration is taking many pictures. Carry a camera wherever you go. Notice what around you might make a good photo. Try to make art from people, places, and objects nearby. Mistakes are fine when you are having fun. Amateur means not professional, a person who does the work as a hobby. Composition means the way objects sit inside the frame. Crude means plain, and the design is rough. Cumbersome means heavy and awkward to carry. Daguerreotypes are old photographs invented by Louis Daguerre. A darkroom is shut off from daylight. Dim red light lets a photographer turn film into prints. Exposure means how much light reaches the film. Multipurpose means one item serves many uses. Painstaking means work that is precise and takes a long time. Panning means you sweep the camera sideways. Your feet stay put. A shutter is the camera part that, when triggered, lets light into the lens for a brief moment. The index lists daguerreotype and darkroom. It lists film speed and flash. It lists negative and panorama. It lists pinhole camera and zoom lens.

44. Leaving Home to Find Safety

1Made to Leave. Who Counts as a Refugee. Rights That Protect Them. On the Journey. After the Border. Beginning Again. In 2019, refugees from Guatemala crossed a river into Mexico. They used a raft they had put together themselves. On March 24, 2022, refugees from Ukraine crossed into Poland. They were leaving because Russia had invaded Ukraine. Imagine having to quit your home, and your country, carrying only what your hands can hold. Imagine that familiar things must stay behind, since safety for you and your family is gone. Ahmed's departure was sudden. A civil war brought fighting into his city. Noorkin had to leave with her son. Officials had started persecuting anyone who shared their ethnicity. Yoshie had no choice but to flee. Foreign rulers had seized the island that was her home. All three stories are true. All three people are refugees.

2Who Counts as a Refugee. One agency defines refugees in a clear way. They are people who fled war, or violence, or conflict, or persecution. They crossed a border between countries so they could be safe in another land. That wording is the one used by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees. The short name is UNHCR. Its purpose is to help and protect refugees around the world. The United Nations, or UN, is the body that runs UNHCR. The UN's main purpose is to reach peace in the world. When people are displaced, meaning they are forced to flee, persecution is the cause more often than any other. Danger may come because of race. It may come because of religion, nationality, or a social group. It may come because of political beliefs. The dangers can include violence. They can include discrimination. They can include jail that is illegal, or arrest without a good cause. A key part of persecution is what a government does. It may be unwilling to protect its citizens. In some cases it takes part in the persecution itself. People who are forced to flee do not trust that help exists inside their own borders. Do You Know? The UNHCR reported about 32 million refugees worldwide as of May 2022. Persecution and conflict force about 45,000 people to flee on a single day. Each minute, that pace equals 30 people. A photograph from 2022 shows a woman cooking in front of her tent. The camp is in Afghanistan, and she is internally displaced. War is another common cause of displacement. People flee death and injury. They also flee the chance that bombing will destroy a home. War threatens survival in further ways. Crops cannot be grown or harvested. Food and water run short. Earning a living becomes impossible, and poverty follows. Care for illness and for injuries is often limited, or missing entirely. Living in constant fear disturbs sleep. It disturbs mental health. It disturbs any sense of safety. A normal life cannot continue in these conditions. Fleeing is often the only choice left. Terrorism can create the same kinds of conditions. Terrorism means groups use violence, or threaten it, in a planned way, to reach their goals. Whatever the cause, refugees cannot go home unless the conditions that drove them out come to an end. Only then can they be safe and well. Many never get to return.

3Some people travel straight to the country where they will ask for safety. The name for them is asylum seekers. Protection in that country has to be requested. Proof is required that the refugee label fits them. Other people flee to a second country for protection right away. They wait there for a chance to settle in a third country. The name for this second group is refugees for resettlement. UNHCR helps many of them settle for good. They then go through the steps to become citizens. Once they are citizens, they are no longer counted as refugees. A 2022 map names leading countries people left, and leading countries that received them. Counts printed on the map include Poland at 3,200,000 and Ukraine at 6,000,000. Afghanistan is marked at 2,600,000. Turkey is marked at 3,700,000. Syria is marked at 6,800,000. Pakistan is marked at 1,400,000. South Sudan is marked at 2,200,000. Venezuela is marked at 4,100,000. Colombia is marked at 1,700,000. Uganda is marked at 1,500,000. Oceans on the map include the Arctic, the Atlantic, the Pacific, the Indian, and the Southern. Continents labeled include Asia, North America, Europe, Africa, South America, and Australia. The source of the map is UNHCR. Other groups are sometimes mixed up with refugees. Their challenges are different. Internally displaced persons, or IDPs, leave home for reasons much like the ones that move refugees. They do not leave their country. Their own government still protects them. UNHCR also gives them help. Stateless people are helped by UNHCR as well. No country counts them as citizens. No country, therefore, protects them. Discrimination can make a person stateless. Certain other situations can do it too. Immigrants choose a permanent move to a new country. Nobody forces that move. Better jobs are a common reason. Chances for education are another. Returnees are former refugees. Improved conditions let them go back to the country they had left. Sometimes the word refugee is used for people who must flee because of climate change. Names people use include "climate refugees." They include "climate change refugees." They include "environmental refugees." UNHCR suggests different wording for these cases. It suggests the phrase climate change and disaster-related displacement.

4Belongings travel with people leaving the Democratic Republic of Congo. The next country they enter is Uganda, in Central Africa. The name is said yoo-GON-duh. Rights That Protect Them For centuries, people have fled persecution, and countries have taken them in and protected them. Laws of the modern kind, however, start only once World War II had finished. The war ran from 1939 to 1945. The United Nations was founded in that closing year. The year 1948 was when the UN adopted a document. People know it as Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The document describes thirty separate rights. They belong to people everywhere. One right is to seek asylum in other countries, and to enjoy it, when persecution is the cause. UNHCR itself was founded soon afterward, in 1950. The key UN document on refugees came in 1951. People call that treaty the Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees. The treaty defined who counts as a refugee. It also set a practice. Refugees are not to be expelled, or sent back, to a country where life or freedom is in danger. The danger may rest on race, religion, or nationality. It may rest on a social group, or on political beliefs. The treaty followed World War II and was meant to help Europeans the war had displaced. It applied only to events in Europe that happened before January 1, 1951. A newer treaty in 1967 widened the area. The rest of the world was included. Countries also write their own refugee laws. The United States Refugee Act, passed in 1980, is one example. It set up a system for admitting refugees and for resettling them. Over its history, resettlement admissions by the United States have been larger than those of all other countries combined. The yearly total is a joint choice. The president takes part, and so does Congress. The number can change. Political events around the world can change it. A newly elected president can change it too. In 1980, the number admitted was 207,116. In 2016, the figure was 84,994. In 2018, it dropped to 22,491.

5On the Journey Laws and totals sit in the background. The personal experience of a refugee is distressing. A few have time to fill a bag with possessions they value most. Most leave in a hurry. They drop everything and run. Food may be missing. Money may be missing. Warm clothes may be missing. Even shoes may be missing. No object is left that can call up the life they are leaving. They cannot carry much anyway. The trip is often on foot, and the distance is long. Weeks may pass. Months may pass. Many do not know how they will reach safety, or when. A family may escape together. Another person may have to escape with nobody beside them. Children are sometimes in that second group. Staying alive may depend on strangers who choose to be kind. Parents may have been separated from the child. The danger may already have killed the parents. Desperation pushes refugees into unsafe travel. Storms or fierce heat meet some of them, and they lack decent food, water, clothes, and a roof. Some ride in a boat that is dangerously overcrowded. Some pay strangers to sneak them across a border. Food and water may be absent for a long stretch of that hidden trip. Sadly, the journey kills some of them. After the Border Counting someone as a refugee requires a crossing of at least one border between countries. The new country is called the asylum country. There, a request for protection can be filed with UNHCR. After an interview, UNHCR may send people back to the country they came from, if that country is safe. It may instead let them stay where they are. A further choice is settlement in some other country. Resettlement is considered only in a further case. In the asylum country, threats must also reach life, safety, freedom, health, or further basic rights. Worldwide, UNHCR estimates the share who need resettlement at about 8 percent. The share who actually move on is under 1 percent. Each country that accepts refugees for resettlement sets a yearly limit. The need is far larger than the number of open places. A photograph from 2019 shows a Venezuelan refugee in a camp in Colombia. A child rides on the man's shoulders.

6Children from Myanmar sit in class at a makeshift school. Thailand is the country, and the school sits in a camp for refugees. Most refugees end up in camps. A camp is a temporary settlement built to cover basic needs. Camps are not comfortable. They are still far better than staying on the run. Crowds are heavy. Space is lacking, and so is privacy.
