Sleep happens in tents, in shacks, or in trailers. Volunteers supply food and clothes. They supply medical care. Sometimes they supply schooling for children. Electricity is often missing. Running water is often missing. Summer heat and winter cold have little protection against them. Camps can be dangerous. People are sometimes attacked, especially at night. Years in a camp may pass before a new country says yes to someone selected for resettlement. Another picture shows refugees of various backgrounds in class. They are studying English as a Second Language, called ESL. The class is in Lancaster, Pennsylvania. Beginning Again Refugees want what all people want. Feeling safe is one thing they want from a place to live. A home that is comfortable is another. They want work that pays the rent, buys food, and covers other needs. They want their children kept safe. They want those children to have a better life. Arrival in a new country is hopeful. It is also full of challenges. Most refugees carry personal histories of trauma and of tragedy. The new country may be one whose language they do not speak. Bringing up children where daily life is so unlike home can be hard. Pay that covers housing, when that housing is safe and not too costly, can be hard to earn. Someone who had a successful career at home may not find similar work.

7Outside a house in Rutland, Vermont, a Syrian family poses in 2019. They fled a civil war before they reached that house. Gratitude is still what most refugees feel. A safe home and dependable work matter, even when the new life looks very different from the old one. Many meet the new chances with energy and with enthusiasm. Many become successful. They pursue education. They find jobs and build professions. They buy homes and raise children. They become members who contribute to their communities. They hold tightly to the chance of a better future, both for the adults and for the children. At the same time, they honor the place they came from. They honor what they have lived through. Persecuting means mistreating a specific person, or a specific people, or oppressing them. Asylum is protection, or safety, that a government gives. The person has left home to escape harm. A refugee flees war, or famine, or persecution, or a disaster in nature. A clear destination is often missing. Desperate describes an extreme need, or a willingness to use extreme measures. Systematic describes something done by a planned method, or by a formula. Discrimination means someone, or a group, is handled in a way that is not fair. The cause may be race, age, sex, religion, or a further difference. Temporary means lasting only for a limited time. Distressing describes what brings pain, or worry, or deep sadness. Trauma is severe emotional distress. An upsetting event or experience is the usual cause. Ethnicity is belonging to a group that shares a culture, or shares a nationality. Violence is a force that hurts, or a force that destroys. Expelling means officially forcing someone to leave. The place left may be a school, an organization, or a country.

45. Lewis Latimer and a Brighter Bulb

1The Lewis H. Latimer House stands in Flushing, New York. Latimer lived in it from 1903 until 1928. Visitors now find a museum there. On view are his inventions, plus work by other inventors who were Black Americans. Lewis Latimer was a Black American inventor. Enslavement was what his parents had escaped. In 1879 a technical drawing was in his hands, and that was the moment his chance came. Into the Bridgeport, Connecticut, machine shop walked a visitor. Latimer's job was in that shop. The man wore a bushy beard, and he wore a mustache. He was Hiram Maxim, inventor and chief engineer for the U.S. Electric Lighting Company. Latimer's drawings excited him. Maxim had found a draftsman with real skill. The hire happened on the spot. Drawings of Maxim's ideas would be Latimer's work. So would the duties of a personal secretary. Only one year had passed since U.S. Electric Lighting began. Latimer started at once and learned electric lighting from every side he could. Before long he ranked with the leading experts. Bulbs and electrical technology were getting better at speed. A span of little more than ten years would alter their place in life. What had been a novelty would turn into an everyday convenience. In the technological change that followed, his part was an important one.

2A Family's Freedom Virginia still held George and Rebecca Latimer in slavery in 1842. They risked death to flee. Lewis was their son. A northbound ship was their hiding place. Hunters, paid to chase people who had escaped, were on their trail. Only when Boston, Massachusetts, came into reach did the constant danger ease, and freedom begin. Safety there was still incomplete. Massachusetts law forbade slavery. Even so, a visitor from Virginia knew George's face. Friends concealed Rebecca. Officers arrested George and locked him in jail. A return to Virginia looked likely. People called abolitionists took notice of the case. An abolitionist was someone who stood strongly against slavery. Protests were organized for George's sake. A letter demanding protection gathered signatures from more than sixty-five thousand people. The protection was for anyone who had fled enslavement. Boston printers, in 1851, put out a poster of warning. Escapees who were Black Americans could be grabbed. Carelessness could mean a return to bondage in the South. Four hundred dollars changed George's case. A Black minister paid that sum to the Virginia man who had held George in slavery. The payment made George free. Rebecca's danger did not end. Years afterward, both of them still feared capture and a forced return. Courage on the parents' part meant four children could be born free. The youngest was Lewis. Chelsea, Massachusetts, was his 1848 birthplace. Boyhood work included his father's barbershop. He also helped hang wallpaper, and he attended school. He had turned twelve when the Civil War's first shots were fired. That war ran from 1861 to 1865. Southern states, calling themselves the Confederacy, had broken from the United States. Keeping their system of slavery was the reason. Both of Lewis's older brothers entered the Union Army. The navy's legal age was eighteen. In 1864 Lewis said he was that age. He was sixteen. His service was on the USS Massasoit, a gunboat of the U.S. Navy. Defeat of the Confederacy ended the war in 1865. With that defeat, slavery stopped being legal in the United States. Pride in that service stayed with Lewis Latimer for life. He had fought in the struggle that sought freedom for Black Americans.

3Learning to Draw for Patents Boston was home again after the war. A patent law firm took him on as an assistant in the office. Inventors treat a patent as a key step. Plans go to the U.S. Patent Office so the inventor can show something important. The invention really is new. The idea is original, or it improves an earlier one. Money can then be earned from the invention. Copying it, or stealing it, is blocked. Use by others requires permission, and it requires payment. From the first day, this work held Latimer's interest. Mechanical drawing was a needed skill, and he taught it to himself. Promotion followed. He rose to head draftsman of the firm. His earliest patent came in 1874. The invention improved the toilet compartment used on trains. Nobody ever built it. Washington, D.C., housed the U.S. Patent Office, and the late 1800s kept that office busy. Latimer had expected something from the end of chattel slavery. Black Americans, he hoped, would meet greater equality and wider chances. Prejudice remained, and so did discrimination. Schools, organizations, and businesses run by white people seldom treated them as equals. Most professions shut them out. Skilled work shut them out too, above all when the job meant working face to face with white people. Set beside those barriers, his rising success looks still more unusual. The telephone's patent, in 1876, was a project he helped. Alexander Graham Bell is the person who received that patent. Bell's students included people who struggled to hear. Latimer pictured a small electric machine. It would improve what those students could hear. A meeting with Bell was where he explained the idea. Technical drawings came next, from his own hand. Bell's patent for the revolutionary technology rested in part on those drawings. Similar inventions and designs were appearing from many other inventors at about the same time. The first patent, though, was Bell's. Bridgeport, Connecticut, became Latimer's home in 1879. The hire came from Hiram Maxim, at U.S. Electric Lighting. Lighting systems that really worked, powered by electricity, were the effort he joined. He arrived as a young draftsman who was also an inventor.

4A Stronger Bulb Practical incandescent bulbs were the aim of many inventors by the 1870s. Maxim shared that aim. Latimer shared it too. Electric current becomes light inside an incandescent lamp. Any electric appliance, a bulb included, needs the current to travel a full loop. That loop is called a closed circuit. Turn a light on, and the wires connect, which closes the circuit. Turn it off, and the circuit breaks. Early Black American Inventors Elijah McCoy's years were 1844 to 1929. Fifty-seven patents from the United States were his. Among them was a system of lubrication. Steam engines ran more efficiently because of it. Granville T. Woods's years were 1856 to 1910. Many different talents fed his inventions. Electronics were his specialty, along with devices that made railroads safer. Madam C. J. Walker's years were 1867 to 1919. She opened a field of products meant for the hair of Black Americans. No Black American woman before her had become a millionaire. Garrett Morgan's years were 1877 to 1963. One invention was an early gas mask. Another was a traffic light with three directions. Both conductors and resistors matter inside an incandescent bulb. Electricity passes readily through a conductor. Copper wire does this well. Water does too. A resistor slows electricity down. Carbon behaves that way. Rubber and glass are insulators. No current gets through them. Conductors in a lamp bring electricity from the power source as far as the filament. Usually the filament is a thin strip. Metal is a common material for it, though other materials are used. Because it is a resistor, electricity struggles to cross it. Heat builds until the strip glows, and the glow is light. Late in the 1870s, the unsolved need was a filament that cost little and lasted long. Thomas Edison, famous already, led a team on that problem across several years. Carbonized bamboo was the filament his team produced in 1879. It could be afforded, and it held up. Twelve hundred hours was not the limit of its life.

5Joseph Nichols worked with Latimer, and in 1881 the two of them developed an incandescent bulb of their own. The next year brought Latimer a patent. It covered a fresh method for making filaments out of carbon. Edison's method was less efficient than this one. A Timeline of Light Bulbs Humphry Davy, a British inventor, introduced the arc lamp in 1802. Power came from an early kind of battery. James Bowman Lindsay, a Scottish inventor, gave a demonstration in 1835. He showed the first electric light that stayed constant. People see it as an early version of the incandescent bulb. Thomas Edison, in 1882, proved a further point. Electricity could be shared out from one central source of power. The first utility company for that power was his, and he placed it in New York City. Carbon filaments lost their place in 1904. Tungsten filaments lasted longer and wasted less. Fluorescent lamps reached the United States in 1939. Set beside incandescent bulbs, they need much less electricity. The light emitting diode arrived in 1962. Its short name is LED. Earlier bulbs needed much more power than an LED needs. Homes gained compact fluorescent lights in 1985. The short name is CFL. Energy use drops by 75 percent compared with an incandescent bulb. Life of the lamp stretches to ten times as long. Home buyers could get energy-saving LED bulbs in 2008. Those bulbs cut energy use by 50 percent next to a CFL. They also last six times as long. With the Early Builders Electric lighting was catching on, and Latimer proved himself a strong solver of problems. Streetlights and other systems grew common in the 1880s, especially inside cities, and his knowledge was worth a great deal. Lighting work took him to New York City. It took him to Philadelphia, in Pennsylvania. It took him to Montreal, in Canada. French was a language he learned in Canada. He needed it for talk with French-Canadian crews. Mornings began at the factory at seven. Night work followed the day shift. He stayed out installing wire and lamps until midnight. Mary, his wife, traveled with him to London, in England. A lamp factory for U.S. Electric Lighting was launched there with his help. One illustration, set in 1883, shows New York City under new electric streetlights.

6A photograph from 1881 shows Thomas Edison outside an office in New York City. Edison Electric Light Company used that office. Edison stands at the left, at the top of the stairs. Skill and knowledge carried Latimer into Edison Electric Light Company during 1884. Chief draftsman became his title. He was also the patent specialist inside the legal department. When people argued over the use of Edison's technology, Latimer's experience helped settle the fight. Encouragement from Edison led Latimer to write a book. Its title was Incandescent Electric Lighting: A Practical Description of the Edison System. Publication came in 1890. Readers found a description of technology that was remaking the United States. The same technology was remaking the wider world. Latimer treated electric lighting as a high point in human history. He said so in the book. What Latimer Left Behind Invention and making things never stopped for him. An early form of air conditioning earned him a patent in 1886. A safety elevator was his design in 1894. A rack that locked, for hats and for coats, was patented in 1896. Music was another talent. Poetry and plays came from him as well. Art and science, he often said, sit close together. Creativity was the tie he named. The Edison Pioneers counted him as a founding member in 1918. No other Black American was named in that founding group. Inventors belonged to it, and so did engineers and other specialists. All of them had worked on Edison's team in the early years. Because of the Pioneers, electric light became an ordinary fact of life. People of every walk of life gained it. One photograph lines up the Edison Pioneers. Lewis Howard Latimer is in the front row. He is the second person from the left.

7Racial equality was a cause he kept standing up for, alongside everything else he achieved. Time and energy went to volunteer teaching. Young people of color learned job skills from him. Mechanical drawing was one of those skills. A public letter in 1895 set down his hope. Faith, he wrote, told him the nation would answer a plea. The plea asked for equality in front of the law. It asked for safety that the law would protect. It asked for a real chance, kept open by respect for the law. That chance was to enjoy a blessing side by side with fellow citizens. Those citizens included every race and every complexion. He said the Constitution had already guaranteed the blessing. Inside the Lewis H. Latimer House, an early incandescent bulb stands on display. The year 1928 was when he died. Flushing, New York, was the place. The house he left is a museum now. The museum covers what he achieved. It also covers inventions by other Black Americans who broke new ground. In 2006, National Inventors Hall of Fame added him as a member. The honor covered the work of his whole life. He had helped the world grow better. He had helped it grow brighter. Carbonized means turned into carbon, or into charcoal. Heating can cause that change, and so can fossilization. An innovator creates a new change, a new idea, or a new invention, or brings one in. A convenience is useful. Daily life feels easier because of it, or more comfortable. The word mechanical points to machines. It also points to tools. A novelty is new, and it is interesting, and it is often unusual. Discrimination means treating a person, or a group, in a way that is not fair. Race can be the basis, or age, sex, religion, or some other difference. A patent is the document that gives someone the right to earn money from an invention. A dispute is an argument, or a disagreement. Technical refers to the knowledge or the methods of one field. Science is often that field, and so is mechanical work. A draftsman draws detailed technical plans. Machines, buildings, and other structures are typical subjects. Technology means using scientific knowledge, or using tools, so a task can be finished or an object can be built. When something is efficient, time is not wasted, and resources are not wasted.

46. Olympic Games From Long Ago to Now

1Being the best in the world is the first topic. Ancient Olympic Games come next. A revival of the Olympics follows. Change in the Olympics follows that. Today's Olympics come after the changes. A glossary ends the book. María Colón, from Cuba, won the women's javelin in 1980. The throw measured 68.4 meters. It was a world record then. It was an Olympic record then. Three Latin words are Citius, Altius, Fortius. They mean Faster, Higher, Stronger. They are the Olympic motto. A strong athlete wants to beat the people in the contest. Olympic victory means still more. Gold at the Olympics marks the best in the world. Where did these Games begin? Ancient Greece is the start. Peaceful contest has a long history there. Cities still compete to host, even though the cost is high. A Summer Games host joins a rich tradition. A Winter Games host joins it too.

2Old writings place the first Olympics at Olympia, in Greece, in 776 bce. Many historians think the real start was earlier. Greeks of that age held four athletic meets. One meet came each year. Each meet honored a different god. The Olympics was only one of the four. Summer and Winter Games now trade places every two years. Zeus, king of the gods, was the Olympics' honor. His home was Mount Olympus. Importance followed from Zeus. The Olympics soon outranked every other athletic meet. A map shows ancient Greece near the time of those first Games. Labels mark the Black Sea. They mark Italy. They mark Mount Olympus. They mark ancient Greece. They mark the Ionian Sea and the Aegean Sea. They mark Delphi, Asia Minor, and Eretria. They mark Thebes, Athens, and Olympia. They mark Corinth, Argos, and Sparta. They mark Greek areas and the Mediterranean Sea. They mark Rhodes, other lands, and Crete. They mark Greek city-states. Only short footraces filled the earliest Games. Other contests were added over the years. Fourteen events stood at the end. Some events used the stadium. Some used a racetrack. Stadium events included footraces, boxing, and the discus. They included the javelin, wrestling, and jumping. Chariot races, which were dangerous, used the track. Soldiers made up many early athletes. Some events looked like army training for the Greek city-states. Rules existed. They were looser than rules now. A wrestler could kick, punch, or pull hair. A wrestler could break bones. A chariot racer could topple another chariot. Horses could be knocked down. Serious injury was common. Death was possible. Inside the temple at Olympia stood a statue of Zeus. People counted that statue among the Ancient World's Seven Wonders.

3An artist pictured the old Olympic grounds. A stadium connects toward the horse-racing track. A gymnasium is marked. So is a living area for athletes. So is the Temple of Hera. So is a swimming pool. So is the Temple of Zeus. So is a bank and market. So are spaces for boxing and for wrestling. Spectators came by the thousand from every part of Greece. Training lasted months. For some athletes it lasted years. Winners were treated as heroes. The only official prize was an olive branch cut from a sacred tree. Fame still followed. Honor followed across Greece. Hometowns often paid champions so the victory could be celebrated. Taxes were dropped for the rest of a champion's life. Business boomed for many Greeks. Visitors needed food. They needed supplies. They needed beds. Meetings of business fit the crowded days. Family reunions fit them too. Visitors found many services on the grounds. Sport buildings were there. A hotel was nearby. A pool was nearby. A sauna was nearby. A market was nearby. A bank was nearby. Religion mattered to some visitors. A temple held a huge Zeus made of gold and ivory. Public ceremonies drew others. One was the parade, also called a procession, of athletes and officials. A large rite for Zeus drew many people. A feast drew them. Peace mattered most. A truce, strictly kept, stopped fighting among the Greek city-states. City-states could rival one another without war. Travel across Greece was safe from war while the Games lasted.

4Other gaps separated the ancient Games from Games today. Early contests allowed only men. Women could not enter. They could not even look on. Girls were allowed to watch. A women's festival was added in 470 bce. It honored Hera, wife of Zeus. Popularity lasted hundreds of years. The Roman Empire took Greece in 146 bce, and the Games still went on. Theodosius, emperor of Rome, halted the Games in 393 ce. Say thee-uh-DOH-shee-us. He was a Christian. Festivals for the old Greek gods were banned. The Olympics was one of them. Olympia was left empty. Neglect, war, quakes, and floods piled up for hundreds of years. Rubble buried the grounds. Memory faded. A picture shows women athletes at the Heraean Games. Historians still cared about the stories more than a thousand years later. Archaeologists began the search in the 1700s. By the 1890s most major buildings at Olympia were uncovered. Pierre de Coubertin, a Frenchman, cared about the old Olympics. Say duh coo-bair-TAHN. He liked that Greeks had used sport instead of war. He wanted a new Olympics for the whole world. People loved the plan. He formed the International Olympic Committee, the IOC, in 1894. A photo shows the ruined stadium entrance. Olympia, Greece, is the place. Builders raised it near 200 bce.

5Coubertin wanted the new Olympics to honor love of sport. Money was not to be the prize. A simple award would replace cash or goods. Pros were barred. A pro was someone paid to compete. Amateurs were the first field. Later the IOC eased the ban on pros. Before that easing, Jim Thorpe lost the gold medals of 1912. He was American. His nation was Sac and Fox. Pentathlon gold was his. Decathlon gold was his. The two added up to fifteen events. Officials learned he had played paid baseball for a short time. The medals were taken. They were never returned. Many people still rank him among the greatest athletes. A picture shows Jim Thorpe. Greece, home of the ancient Games, hosted the first modern ones in 1896. Proud citizens packed the rebuilt stadium. Athletes numbered two hundred. Countries numbered fourteen. Women were barred, as in the old Games. Track and field covered running, jumping, and throwing. Tennis was on the program. Weightlifting was on it. Cycling was on it. Wrestling was on it. Swimming was on it. Gymnastics was on it. Each winner received an olive branch. A certificate came too. A silver medal came too. A photo shows men in the marathon at the 2008 Summer Games. The city is Beijing, China.

6The photo shows the close of the 2008 Summer Games in Beijing, China. The Olympic flag comes down there. The next two Games struggled. Paris hosted in 1900. St. Louis hosted in 1904. Neither city built Olympic grounds. Neither built a village for athletes. Housing was poor. Equipment was poor. Bad weather delayed many outdoor events. Some events were canceled. No official women's events were listed. Women still competed on an unofficial basis starting in 1900. Advertising was weak. Few people noticed. Crowds stayed small. Organizers studied the failures. Slowly the Games became the popular Olympics known now. In 1906, during a year off the normal cycle, an opening procession returned. Athletes marched behind national flags before play began. Every Olympics after that had a colorful opening ceremony. The Olympic flag debuted in 1920. The cloth is white. Five rings of different colors lock together on it. The rings stand for five settled continents working in peace. Every nation's flag shares at least one of those colors. Posters advertised the 1900 Summer Games in Paris, France. Other posters advertised the 2004 Summer Games in Athens, Greece.

7France hosted the first Olympic Winter Games in 1924. The town was Chamonix. Say sham-oh-NEE. Athletes numbered more than 250. Nations numbered 16. Women and girls numbered 11. Events included speed skating. They included cross-country skiing. They included ski jumping. They included ice hockey. Success was large. Norway's Sonja Henie was twelve that year. Say SOHN-yuh HEN-ee. She fell. She finished last. Failure at twelve did not end her path. She became one of the great early Winter athletes. Fame later placed her among history's best-known athletes. Gold came in 1928. Gold came in 1932. Gold came in 1936. Ice shows came later. Films came later. A picture shows Sonja Henie. Amsterdam, in the Netherlands, hosted the 1928 Summer Games. Women could officially compete there for the first time. Sports open to women kept increasing after Amsterdam. An Olympic torch was lit for the first time in 1928. A relay of runners began in 1936. Sunlight, strengthened through a lens, lights the torch in Olympia. That place is honored as the origin. Runners carry it to the new host city. They pass it through countries. They pass it over oceans. At the opening, the last runner hands it to a special guest. The guest is often a past Olympic champion. The guest lights the Olympic flame. The flame burns until the Games end. Cathy Freeman, an Australian sprinter, lit the flame at the 2000 opening. She later became the first Aboriginal woman with an individual gold medal.

8At London in 2012, North Korea's Un Guk Kim broke a world record in weightlifting. Some Olympics have fallen during worldwide conflict. Athletes have used the Games to challenge bias by race. They have challenged bias by gender. Raven Saunders used the 2020 Games podium for a protest. She crossed her arms into an X. She is a Black woman. She belongs to several communities that face discrimination. The X was her symbol. The crossing stood for a meeting point of groups that suffer different unfair treatment. A worldwide pandemic touched some Games. The 2020 Summer Games were put off for a year. COVID-19 kept spreading, yet the 2022 Winter Games stayed on schedule. A positive test during the Olympics ended many athletes' chance to compete. Berlin, Germany, hosted in 1936 during a major world conflict. Adolf Hitler led Germany. Supporters belonged to the Nazi Party. The group was racist. Its actions later caused World War II. The 1936 Games were used to spread those racist ideas. Eighteen Black American Olympians then humiliated the Nazis with stunning performances. Jesse Owens, a runner, was among them. A photo places him at the far right. He had set several world records. College track had already made him famous.

9Paralympic Games display contests among athletes who have a range of disabilities. Italy hosted the first in 1960. Athletes numbered 400. Nations numbered 23. The 2021 Paralympics gathered more than 4,400 athletes. Nations numbered 162. From 1988 onward, after those Summer Games, the Paralympics have shared the calendar with the Olympics. Shared cities and shared venues needed a partnership. The International Paralympic Committee joined with the International Olympic Committee. Runners who cannot see get help from guides. The guides wear vests of bright yellow. A rope called a tether joins the pair at the wrist. Much has changed since the 1896 revival. The show is huge. The contest is fierce. Training to meet the world is a full-time job. The body tires. The feelings tire. Most early gold winners could not qualify now. In 1924 the men's cross-country ski race of 50 kilometers took the winner 3 hours and 45 minutes. The distance is 31 miles. The 2022 winner needed only a bit more than 1 hour and 11 minutes. Giorgio di Centa of Italy won that 50-kilometer race in Turin in 2006. The distance is 31 miles.

10Olympic-level sport now demands harder training than ever. Medal hopefuls need the newest equipment. They need the best trainers. They need the best sponsors. Many athletes start young. Huge amounts of time go into skill. Special training centers in many countries support that work. Chloe Kim won halfpipe gold at the Winter Games of 2018. She won it again in 2022. Pressure to win pushes some athletes to cheat. They want an edge past what training gives. Recent years have seen secret drug use. Trainers or doctors have often helped. Banned substances have hurt how people see the Olympics. Tests for performance-boosting substances have been routine since the mid-1970s. A failed test can strip a champion's medal. Lance Armstrong, a cycling star, had to give his medals back. Steroids and growth hormones were found. Fights over judging have hit figure skating. They have hit diving. A judge may have gifted points to athletes from the judge's own country. Judges may have traded points. The IOC must keep the Games honest. The IOC must keep them fair. Size and popularity keep rising. World records fall at most Games. Jamie Salé and David Pelletier, a Canadian pairs team, received gold only after a judging scandal came to light. Fair play remains the ideal, as in the ancient Games. Peaceful contest among nations remains the ideal too.

11Ancient means very old, from long ago. Archaeologists study what ancient cultures left behind. An athlete trains for sports or games that need strength, speed, and skill. A ceremony is a formal act or ritual. A city-state is a country built around one major city and the land beside it. A competitor is a person or a team in a contest. A controversy is a disagreement about an issue. A motto is a short line that states a guiding idea. A procession is a formal parade kept in order. To qualify is to prove enough skill for a hard event. A sauna is a room built for steam bathing. A truce is a promise not to fight.

47. One Day inside the Nation's Attic

1Charles Lindbergh flew an airplane alone across the Atlantic Ocean. Nobody before him had made that ocean crossing alone. He named the airplane Spirit of St. Louis. The name honored his supporters. Those supporters lived in St. Louis, Missouri. Picture a family parking the car. Excitement is hard to keep inside. The plan today is the Smithsonian Institution. People call it the Nation's Attic. Last year a best friend took a trip to Washington, D.C. The friend said the visit was amazing. The family wants to see many sites in the city. Little time is left for the Smithsonian. You will still see as much as the day allows. The car is parked. It is time to go.

2The National Mall lies under your feet as you cross it. Monuments famous across the nation stand in that open ground. Several museums of the Smithsonian stand there too. You are headed to the Castle. It is the original museum. The building is red brick. James Smithson's remains are kept inside. He was a scientist from Britain. He worked as a chemist. He worked as a mineralogist. The institution is named for him. A friendly volunteer explains more once you are inside. The year 1829 was Smithson's death. A nephew received his fortune. The nephew was Henry James Hungerford. The will carried strict instructions. Hungerford might die and leave no children. Then the entire fortune would go to the United States. The collection would go too. The gift would establish the Smithsonian Institution. Scientific notes were in the gift. Minerals were in it. His whole library was in it. Smithson wanted a place for knowledge of all kinds. He wanted everyone to experience that knowledge. Founding of the Smithsonian Institution came in 1846. Alexander Graham Bell invented the telephone. In 1904 he carried Smithson's remains into the United States. The volunteer explains the next part. Smithson's money and the first collection started something vast. It became the largest complex of research and of museums anywhere. Museums and galleries number nineteen. Artifacts number more than 138 million. The institution studies historical items. It works to preserve them. It makes new discoveries. It shares resources. It also hosts the National Zoo. Museum of Natural History is only a short walk from here. So much information is hard to hold at once. A side note tells about Smithson's books. The collection has 126 titles. They sit in the Smithsonian vault now. Most titles are journal articles. History books are there. Memoirs are there. Political pamphlets are there. Travel books are there. Museum guides are there. A few cookbooks are there. Travel took a large share of Smithson's days. He collected different minerals. A special cabinet kept them. His chemistry work examined chemical compounds. He also studied how to improve coffee making. He studied how to improve tea making.

3A green dome rises on Museum of Natural History. Fancy columns stand there too. The outside suggests a government office more than a museum. Opening came in 1910. You go up the stairs and push the doors open. A huge rotunda waits inside. Henry stands in the center. He is a huge African bush elephant. His native home was Angola. That country is in southern Africa. A sign in front of Henry explains the display. It shows scientists from different fields working as one team. They study animals. Habitats are part of what they study. Real elephant skin formed Henry. That animal's age was nearly a hundred years. A map shows many choices. Mammals are one path. The origins of humanity are another path. Geology is another path. Days would be needed to see everything. Sant Ocean Hall is the room that draws you before the others. You leave Henry behind and step in. You look up. A model of Phoenix floats overhead. It looks as if it is swimming in the air. Phoenix was a North Atlantic right whale. The model is a replica. It is bigger than a school bus. The length is 45 feet. That length is 13.7 meters. The weight is 2,300 pounds. That weight is 1,043 kilograms. Something that large can still look graceful. A sign explains right whales. Hunters pushed them nearly to extinction. The prize was their oil. People used the oil for light. People used it as machine oil. Among all the large whales, these are now the rarest. Scientists estimate a small North Atlantic population. It is fewer than five hundred. The real Phoenix has been tracked since birth. She was born in 1987. The place was off the coast of Georgia. Each exhibit adds a lesson. You learn about coral reefs. You examine skeletons of other ocean creatures. You explore life in ancient oceans. You even see a giant squid that has been preserved.

4One photo shows the Hall of Bones. Visitors there can see skeletons. The skeletons come from many creatures. Another photo shows the Hope Diamond. A king of France once wore that diamond. Stories say the diamond is cursed. The Hall of Bones comes next for you. Skeletons stand in the cases. The creatures in those cases number in the hundreds. You see primates of different species. You see cats. Some of the cats are big. Some of the cats are small. You see deer. You see other mammals. You see snakes. You see turtles. You see crocodiles. You see other reptiles. You see birds. You see ocean animals. No skeleton matches another. The diversity is amazing. You must move to the next museum soon. Before leaving, the Hope Diamond gets your visit. After a brief stroll along the mall, another building appears. The name is National Museum of American History. Its facade looks like huge boxes. Those boxes look set one beside another. A cool, squiggly sculpture stands before the door. It moves slowly. It seems to change shape. Inside, you face the same choice as before. Where should you begin? Just inside the door is the exhibit for the Star-Spangled Banner. You walk into a dark room. A huge flag is on display. The flag is tattered. This exact flag gave Francis Scott Key his idea. He wrote a poem from that idea. The poem became the national anthem of the United States. The flag's age is past two hundred years. Some kinds of light can harm the cloth. A special room holds the flag for that reason.

5One photo shows a light bulb. It comes from the workshop of Thomas Edison. The shop was in Menlo Park, New Jersey. Another photo shows a marshmallow toaster. Electricity gained uses beyond light. That change sparked small appliances. This toaster is one example. Your family wants the exhibit called Lighting a Revolution. You head there. Light bulbs crowd every shelf. Gadgets crowd them too. Old appliances crowd them as well. One early bulb made by Thomas Edison is on view. That bulb dates from 1879. Changes in bulbs over the years fascinate most of the crowd. You love the inventions that failed. The electric marshmallow toaster is your favorite. A chart lists museums by the numbers. Opening year for National Museum of Natural History was 1910. About 8 million people visit in an average year. Opening year for National Museum of American History was 1964. About 4.9 million people visit in an average year. Opening year for National Air and Space Museum was 1976. About 8 million people visit in an average year. All nineteen museums together draw 30 million people in a year. Julia Child's kitchen is the next stop. A huge wall holds pots and pans. Cooking tools are arranged in a neat way. Many kitchen appliances stand there. This is the famous television set where Child cooked. She cooked on that set for years. She invented new dishes. She helped people learn more about food. The counters were made for her alone. Her great height was the reason. Next you reach displays of the American presidency. You stop at a uniform of George Washington. He was the first president of the United States. You also see a lap desk. Thomas Jefferson used it while writing the Declaration of Independence. The hours are nearly gone. You hurry to a pair of ruby slippers. Dorothy wore them in the movie The Wizard of Oz. Much more remains. You still want the next museum. A volunteer explains a limit. Seeing every object is impossible. The museum keeps changing its displays. Millions of artifacts wait for a turn. A return next year could show a completely different set of rooms.

6The Wright Flyer spreads its wings 40 feet and 4 inches. That span is 12.2 meters. It is a little wider than a school bus measured end to end. You make your way into National Air and Space Museum. The building is huge. Aircraft of many kinds fill it. Spacecraft fill it too. You then learn about a second site. A whole other museum of this kind stands in Virginia. This time you start at the beginning. You go to the Wright Flyer. It was the earliest airplane with a motor that also carried a pilot. Beside modern airplanes it looks tiny. It does not look very sturdy. The year 1903 was the year of the flight. Orville Wright flew with Wilbur Wright. They stayed in the air for 12 seconds. They covered 120 feet. That distance is 36 meters. They reached a height of 9 feet. That height is 2.7 meters. The engine had less power than most lawn mowers a person can ride. Milestones of Flight Hall is only a few steps on. Apollo 11's command module is waiting there. It carried astronauts toward the Moon in 1969. Nearby, your hand touches a real Moon rock. Amelia Earhart's airplane is next. The paint is bright red. In this airplane she crossed the Atlantic Ocean with no other pilot. No woman had crossed it alone before her. Black Wings is the exhibit you enter next. It tells about Black pilots. They flew even when unfair treatment followed them because of race. Bessie Coleman's life holds you. The year 1921 was when she earned a pilot's license. No Black woman had earned one earlier. She performed in aerial shows. Those shows traveled across the country. Her dedication to flying inspired many people. Her passion for flying did the same. Many went on to pursue aviation. A note explains Apollo 11. A crew landed on the Moon for the first time on that mission. The Moon rock feels smooth. It feels cool. In another area a real airplane engine sits open for you. You can explore it. You can use some mechanic tools made for airplanes. You have only started to look inside the engine. Then it is time to go.

7The walk back to the car is long. You ask whether the family can come back next year. They say they will think about it. Until that visit, they will explore the Smithsonian Institution with you through a computer. Cool things pack the online site, tons of them. It has things to learn. Some of those things are not on display inside the museums. You cannot wait to tell your friends. You will describe the displays. You will describe what a person can discover online. You pass the Castle once more. It was among the earliest buildings raised on the National Mall. You wave at it. A puzzled look comes from your family. You explain. The wave is a thank-you to the Smithsonian. It is a thank-you to the staff. The day was a wonderful gift.

48. Our Star at the Center

1A picture shows a solar eclipse. An introduction opens this book. A chapter treats the Sun as one more star. Energy comes next. Action on the surface follows. The path from Sun to Earth follows that. The Sun and people come next. The Sun's death comes near the end. A conclusion follows it. A glossary follows. Ways to explore more follow the glossary. An index ends the book. Burning gas forms the Sun, and the ball is huge. Our solar system has this star in the middle. Billions of stars fill the galaxy, and the Sun is one of them. Life on Earth could not last without it. Heat on Earth depends on the Sun. Light depends on it. Weather depends on it. Scientists know a great deal about the Sun. They know how it affects Earth's inhabitants. They keep learning. They keep finding new ways to use its power. The Sun is a violent storm of activity.

2A diagram names Uranus, Jupiter, Earth, and Mercury. It names Neptune, Saturn, Mars, and Venus. Those planets orbit the Sun. Room inside the Sun could hold 1.3 million copies of Earth. Gravity from the Sun reaches far. That pull holds Earth on its oval path. It holds the other seven planets too. They do not fly off into space. One full circuit of the Sun takes Earth 365 days. That trip is one year. A slower orbit would turn Earth into a doomed fireball. Earth would crash into the Sun. Speed the orbit up, and Earth would escape the Sun's gravity. Earth would become a block of ice drifting in space. Take the Sun away and Earth turns dark. It would freeze. Life would be gone. Our solar system is only a tiny piece of the Milky Way. The Sun is one star among billions in that galaxy. The Milky Way is a huge gathering of stars. Beside billions of other stars, our Sun is small. Yellow runt is a nickname some astronomers use. Color, size, and brightness sort all stars, including the Sun. The biggest are hypergiants. A hypergiant may dwarf our Sun by over 1,500 times. The smallest are white dwarfs, and they are very hot. Yellow stars sit between the giants and the dwarfs. Our Sun is one of them. Yellow stars are the most common kind in the Milky Way.

3Earth's Sun began making energy soon after it started to form. Scientists put the start near 4.5 billion years in the past. A vast cloud, made of gas plus dust, was the start. Gravity pulled the cloud into a huge ball. More dust and gas packed in. Pressure rose around the hydrogen at the center. Temperatures became extreme. A reaction started in the core. A diagram labels parts of the Sun. It shows a solar flare. It shows the radiation zone and the core. It shows the convection zone. It shows the corona and the photosphere. A fusion diagram shows helium at about 30 percent. It shows hydrogen at about 70 percent. It shows extreme heat. It shows helium, and metals made from hydrogen by fusion, at about 0.1 percent. Fuel has kept the reaction going ever since it began. Scientists call the core's energy reaction thermonuclear. Hydrogen, a gas that can burn, is about 70 percent of the Sun. Most of the rest is helium. Hydrogen is the fuel. In the reaction, tiny hydrogen atoms join into larger helium atoms. That joining is fusion. Fusing atoms release small bits of energy. Trillions upon trillions of atoms do this. The total is a huge release of energy. Surface heat can reach 6,000 degrees Celsius. That is 11,000 degrees Fahrenheit. Boiling water is only 100 degrees Celsius. That is 212 degrees Fahrenheit. The Sun's surface is 60 times hotter.

4Energy creeps from deep in the core out to the surface. Particles of energy need hundreds of thousands of years to cross more than six million miles. That distance is 9.7 million kilometers. Much of the energy is lost on the way. What remains at the surface is visible light. From Earth, that leftover energy is the light in our sky. Solar telescopes let scientists look closer. One stands on Kitt Peak in Arizona. Viewed from Earth, the Sun may seem calm and softly bright. Scientists know the surface is actually raging. Energy keeps rising to the top. The motion resembles soup at a boil. The surface is always stormy. Some times are stormier than others. Activity seems to run in cycles of eleven years. The surface is called the photosphere. Action shows there and in the corona.

5A drawing places the Sun and Earth apart. Energy streams outward in all directions because the Sun is round and huge. Only a tiny share reaches Earth. Most of it goes into space. In active times, dark spots move across the surface. Those spots are sunspots. They are cooler than the gases around them. They appear where magnetic energy bursts outward. Other activity peaks with the cycle. The most violent events are solar flares. A flare is a huge loop of energy high above the surface. Some loops rise more than 100,000 miles. One of the largest on record erupted in 1946. It arched 140,000 miles high. A picture shows a solar flare. While flares shoot outward, the corona grows very active. The corona is the Sun's bright outer glow. The corona sits high above the surface. Strangely, it is hotter than the surface below. It passes two million degrees Celsius. That is 3.6 million degrees Fahrenheit. An active corona throws out huge masses of radiation. Waves of high-energy particles sweep toward Earth. The radiation can disable satellites. Those satellites run radio, television, and cell phone links. They also relate to electrical power. A huge solar blast in 1989 shut down a power grid. Electricity failed for nearly seven million people. The outage hit the United States and Canada. Solar explosions can cause massive blackouts.

6Earth lies 150 million kilometers away from the Sun. That is 93 million miles. Traveling that far equals over 3,700 trips around Earth's equator. A drawing again shows the Sun and Earth. Many people think solar heat travels here and warms the ground. Heat must move through matter to go from place to place. Space is a vacuum, so the energy does not heat space as it crosses. On the way here, the energy is radiant energy, a form of electromagnetic wave. It turns into heat only when matter absorbs it. Visible light is one kind of radiant energy. Infrared light is another. Ultraviolet waves are another. Visible light makes up roughly half of the radiant energy that reaches us. The rest is infrared and ultraviolet, which people cannot see. A diagram starts with 100 percent of the energy leaving the Sun. The atmosphere reflects 6 percent. Clouds reflect 20 percent. Clouds and atmosphere absorb 19 percent. The surface reflects 4 percent. About 51 percent is absorbed by the atmosphere and the surface together. Radiant energy moves at 300,000 kilometers each second. That is 186,000 miles each second. One second at that speed could loop you around Earth close to eight times. Even so, the trip from Sun to Earth takes eight minutes. Atmosphere and clouds bounce much of the energy away before it hits the ground. What gets through is partly absorbed by the air, and the air warms. Land, water, and other matter also absorb it. Absorbed energy becomes heat. Visible light or infrared waves stir the molecules they strike.

7A test asks which cup grows warmer. Land and water do not heat the same way. Land absorbs radiant energy better than water. Dark surfaces absorb energy. Light-colored surfaces reflect it. You need flat black paint. You need two tin cans of 16 ounces, with labels off. You need a thermometer, a small brush, and water. Cover one can's outer surface with black paint. After the paint dries, fill that can about halfway. Fill the bare can with the same amount of water. Set both cans in sunlight for two hours. Then use the thermometer to see which water is warmer. Nearly all the energy people use can be traced to the Sun. Food energy comes from plants that grow by sunlight. An apple carries the Sun's energy. A plate of spinach does too. Coal, gasoline, and oil also come from the Sun. Those fuels were plants that grew long ago on solar energy. Even wind energy comes from the Sun. Uneven heating of the surface makes the air move. In that sense the Sun pushes sailboats. Wind-generator blades turn because of that same push. A picture shows windmills turned by that wind.

8A picture shows solar cells gathering sunlight. Scientists can catch that energy. They use it to heat homes. They use it to make electricity. A solar cell absorbs sunlight and turns it into electricity. Calculators use solar cells. Large panels of cells ride on satellites. During colder months, solar energy heats cities and houses. A solar power plant in Germany can supply almost 2,000 homes. The site is bigger than 37 football fields. It holds 33,500 large solar panels. Only solar energy runs it. Air and water stay unpolluted. Solar collectors make heat. They are black pipes full of water. The black surface absorbs radiant energy. The energy becomes heat and warms the water. The warmed water is piped indoors. Heat radiates from that water and warms the indoor air. Solar furnaces make very high temperatures. Curved mirrors focus sunlight onto a tiny spot. The concentrated energy becomes heat of thousands of degrees. Those temperatures make new materials. They destroy harmful waste. A future solar furnace might hang in space. It would beam focused energy down to Earth. A 1000-kilowatt solar furnace stands in Odeillo, France.

9You can build a solar cooker at home. Gather black construction paper and scissors. Gather a white foam cup and two rubber bands. Gather a shoebox and a sealable plastic bag. Gather two or three apple slices, aluminum foil, and newspaper or foam packing. Cut a strip of black paper to fit inside the cup. Seal the apple slices in the bag. Cut a hole in the shoebox lid big enough for the cup. Set the cup in the box. Surround it with shredded newspaper or pieces of foam packing. Use the rubber bands to hold the lid. The foil should form a funnel. Place that funnel around the cup, matching the picture. Keep the foil smooth. The shiny side faces in. Line the cup with the black paper. Put the bag of apples inside. Aim the foil funnel at the Sun. Wait one to two hours. Take the cup out and eat the baked apple. Ask what made the cooker hot. A house in a photo uses solar energy through windows that face south. Passive solar homes are built to collect sunlight. Large windows face south in places north of the equator. They face north in places south of the equator. In colder months the Sun sits lower. Light passes through the windows. Walls inside absorb it and it becomes heat.

10The Sun keeps us alive, and it can also harm us. We keep learning how solar energy damages skin. Melanoma is a skin cancer. Too much ultraviolet light from the Sun causes it. Years in the Sun, and bad sunburns, can damage skin cells. Wear sunscreen when you are outside. Wear clothes that cover skin, especially for long periods. Never look straight at the Sun. The rays can burn the cornea. The cornea is the sensitive part of the eye that lets you see. A burned cornea can cause blindness. Sunglasses cannot fully protect the eyes. Fusion turns more hydrogen fuel into helium every day. The fuel still left is estimated near five billion years. Then the Sun will cool and, in time, die. The Ring Nebula shows what our Sun might look like at the end. We depend on the Sun to survive. Daily life draws most of its energy from this star. Scientists work to understand it better. Orbiting satellites gather Sun data for scientists. New solar telescopes on the ground point toward the Sun. Their job is to gather data. As understanding grows, and as new uses appear, we will depend even more on the Sun's power.

11A solar flare is a sudden burst of energy. It looks like a large bright loop on the surface. Fusion is atoms blending in a way that releases energy. A sunspot is a cooler, dark spot that throws out magnetic energy. Matter is stuff that fills space. It also has weight. An orbit is the path one body takes around another, such as Earth around the Sun. A thermonuclear reaction releases energy when hydrogen atoms combine into helium. Radiant energy moves as electromagnetic waves. Infrared is one kind. Visible light is another. Radio waves are another. Ultraviolet waves are like light, but people cannot see them. Radiation means energy leaves as rays. Light is one example. Heat is another. A solar cell is made from silicon or plastic. It absorbs the Sun's light and turns that light into electricity. To learn more, search the internet with words from this book. Glossary words and index words work well. Useful search words include solar energy. Sunspots work too. So does thermonuclear reaction. The index lists the Sun's beginning and the corona. It lists dangers and energy. It lists electromagnetic waves, infrared, magnetic energy, and radiant energy. It lists ultraviolet light and visible light. It lists fusion, the galaxy, and gravity. It lists heat, helium, and hydrogen. It lists light and matter. It lists orbits and passive solar homes. It lists radiation and the thermonuclear reaction. It lists satellites and solar cells. It lists solar collectors, the solar cooker, and solar furnaces. It lists the solar system and stars, both size and type. It lists surface activity, sunspots, and solar flares. It lists temperatures and weather.

49. People Who Came to Make a New Home

1A photograph shows Ellis Island Immigration Station as it looked around 1905. Arriving in a New Land. Looking for a Better Life. Gold Farther West. Making Homes in Cities. Doors into the Country. Anger against Newcomers. Fewer People Allowed In. A Different Set of Rules. Children leaving Austria wave toward the Statue of Liberty as their ship reaches the United States. Arriving in a New Land Emma Lazarus wrote a poem called "The New Colossus." Famous lines from it are carved into the stone under the Statue of Liberty. The statue stands in New York City. Those lines ask that tired people be welcomed, and poor people too. They speak of crowds packed close, people longing to breathe as free persons. The year of France's gift was 1886. The gift was meant to honor the friendship of the two nations. As years passed, the statue came to mean something larger. Millions of immigrants saw it while their ships entered New York Harbor, bound for Ellis Island. Seeing the statue gave them a sign of hope. It is still a strong symbol. The symbol stands for freedom, and it stands for immigration.

2Looking for a Better Life People were moving to this land long before the United States was a country. Thousands of Europeans arrived in the 1600s, headed for what would later be the United States. Taking land that was not theirs was the usual pattern. They pushed out Native peoples who already lived on it. Land and wealth drew many of the newcomers. Some wanted a place to practice religion in freedom. Others were getting away from war or from violence. For centuries the number of arrivals stayed steady, and it stayed low. A change began in the 1830s. Immigrants then started coming in much larger numbers. Affordable land was one promise that pulled them. High wages were another. For some people, this country was the only way to stay alive. A chart tracks immigration from the 1830s through 1939. It counts people in millions. The chart credits its figures to the Department of Homeland Security, a U.S. office. Decades on the chart include the 1840s, the 1900s, and the 1910s. They also include the 1930s, the 1920s, the 1830s, and the 1870s. The 1860s, the 1880s, the 1890s, and the 1850s appear as well. Ireland's potato crops were destroyed by a blight in the years 1845 through 1849. A blight is a disease. Irish farmers needed those crops both for pay and for food. Failed potatoes left people without food. Starvation and disease then killed over a million people in Ireland. More than one million others left for the United States. By 1850, New York City held more citizens born in Ireland than Dublin did. Dublin is Ireland's largest city. A picture shows immigrants packed onto a ship as they reach New York City. The potato disease was not only an Irish problem. Germany and other parts of Europe suffered it too. Food ran short. Poverty and conflict pushed many Germans to leave home. Across the 1800s, newcomers from Germany totaled five million. Most chose the Midwest. Soil and climate there resembled Germany's. Catholics were the majority among both German and Irish arrivals. Their religion and their culture differed from those of most people already in the United States. Because of that difference, opposition to them spread more widely than it had against earlier immigrants.

3The Homestead Act European immigrants were drawn to the Midwest by the Homestead Act of 1862. A citizen of the United States could receive 160 acres. An immigrant could receive the same amount. That area is 64 hectares. The cost was a small fee, plus a promise. They had to promise five years of farming on that land. Native peoples had held this land. The U.S. government forced them from ancestral homes and moved them elsewhere. Officials hoped the law would help the country spread toward the west. One photograph shows a homesteading family in front of a house. The house is built of sod, which is dirt mixed with grass. Gold Farther West Gold turned up in California in 1848. A large wave of immigration toward the West Coast followed. About one-third of the people seeking gold came from other countries. Mexico sent many of them. France sent many. The West Indies sent many. China sent many. Before this wave, few immigrants had come from those places. A picture from 1877 shows Chinese immigrants laying railroad track. The mountains are California's Sierra Nevada. Railroad building across the West depended on thousands of workers from China. Some people thought gold mining should be limited to citizens born in America. As open land and gold grew scarce, feeling against immigrants grew. California's government, in 1850, passed the Foreign Miner's Tax. An immigrant miner had to pay $20 each month. That sum equals about $660 today. Lawmakers later repealed the tax. A replacement tax aimed specifically at Chinese miners. Discrimination was a regular part of life for Chinese immigrants. Companies paid them much less than they paid white workers. White Americans feared losing jobs to workers from China. Rivalry over jobs fed resentment. It even fed hatred. Congress answered that anti-Chinese feeling with a law in May 1882. The law was the Chinese Exclusion Act. Most Chinese workers were barred from entering the United States. No earlier U.S. immigration law had singled out one ethnic group in this way.

4Making Homes in Cities Another huge wave of immigration opened in the 1880s. This time most people came from Southern Europe and from Eastern Europe. Italians, starting in the 1880s, left for America in large numbers. Poverty pushed them. High taxes pushed them. Italians who moved to the United States from 1880 until 1920 numbered more than four million. Most of them had lived in southern Italy. Jewish people from Europe formed another large group, beginning late in the nineteenth century. From the 1880s, feeling against Jews in Eastern Europe turned into violent attacks. Towns of Jewish people were destroyed. Thousands of people were killed. Jewish newcomers in those same years, 1880 through 1920, numbered more than two million. They were escaping persecution tied to religion. In New York City, a neighborhood called Little Italy had Mulberry Street as its main road. New York City was where most people from Southern Europe and from Eastern Europe remained. Small communities grew up there, tightly knit, of people from one home country. They set up churches, or they set up synagogues. They set up businesses and social clubs. Many customs and traditions from home stayed alive. Nicknames grew up for these neighborhoods. "Little Italy" was one. "Little Russia" was another. Inside them, people could live beside others who shared a language. They shared religious beliefs. They shared a culture. Life in a Tenement Newcomers often shared low buildings packed with many tiny apartments. People called the buildings tenements. Rent stayed low. The quality of life stayed low too. Light and fresh air were often scarce. An indoor bathroom was often missing. Privacy was often missing. Coal stoves heated most of the apartments, and the air turned dirty and dark. By law, twenty residents were supposed to share one outhouse. Nobody enforced that rule. Crowding let diseases spread fast. One room often held ten immigrants, or even twelve.

5Doors into the Country The federal government opened Ellis Island, an immigration station, in 1892. New York Harbor was its setting. For an arrival, this kind of station came before anything else in the United States. Officials there decided a question. Would the person be allowed to stay, or be sent back home? No immigration station in the nation was bigger than Ellis Island. A picture shows an immigrant family arriving there. Before anyone could leave the island and start a new life, two tests waited. One was a health exam. The other was an interview. Fear of being refused earned the island a nickname. People called it the "Island of Tears." Ellis Island closed in 1954. The total who had gone through it was above twelve million. Angel Island, inside San Francisco Bay, was the biggest West Coast station. Doors stayed open from 1910 to 1940. Estimates put the number who went through it, over those years, near one million. Most came from China, Japan, India, Mexico, or the Philippines. Anger against Newcomers A sudden rush of immigrants in the 1800s fed a rise in nativism. Nativism is the belief that citizens born in America should hold more rights than immigrants do. Both nativists and officials in the U.S. government split newcomers into two groups. Some were called "desirable." Others were called "undesirable." Race could decide the welcome. So could wealth, nationality, and beliefs about politics or religion. An immigrant who was not white and Protestant often met discrimination. An immigrant who did not speak English often met it too. Laws were passed to cut the number of people the government called "undesirable." Two laws built a quota system. One was the Emergency Quota Act, from 1921. The other was the Immigration Act, from 1924. A quota limited how many people could come from each country. People from Northern Europe could enter with relative ease. People from Western Europe could too. People from Eastern Europe found entry much harder. People from Southern Europe found it harder as well. From many countries in Asia, immigrants were banned entirely.

6Fewer People Allowed In Several events in the twentieth century changed how many people immigrated to the United States. Early in that century, Europeans crossed the ocean by steamship. World War I began in 1914. The military took over most steamships. Travel across the Atlantic became very hard. After the war, suspicion fell on people from lands that had been enemies. Entry was refused to many of them. High unemployment struck the United States in the Great Depression, during the 1930s. It brought poverty too. Both facts discouraged people from moving here. Some Americans worried newcomers would fill every job that was open. That fear led to repatriation of at least one million people who were Mexican or Mexican American. Repatriated means they were forced to go back. Mexico was where they were sent. Immigration numbers did not climb again until the 1950s. People then began leaving Cuba to escape political turmoil. They fled it in Southeast Asia as well. During the Great Depression, farm workers often lived in camps made of tents. A Different Set of Rules A new law passed in 1965. Its name was the Immigration and Nationality Act. The quota system set up in the 1920s came to an end. The act had two aims. One aim was to bring families back together. The other was to make entry easier for workers who were well educated, or whose skills the country judged useful. A picture shows President Lyndon B. Johnson signing that 1965 bill. A person who had gained U.S. citizenship could now sponsor relatives. A sponsor promises money support if the relative is given a visa. A visa is a document. It allows someone to remain in a country, but only for a stated period. After this change, arrivals from Latin America climbed fast. Mexico was the source of a particularly large share. In 2016, relatives of citizens made up close to half of everyone who immigrated here. Today, Asia and Latin America are the home regions of most people who enter. Joining family is one reason. Others come for jobs. Others come to get away from political instability at home.

7Becoming a Citizen A Permanent Resident Card is what a person applies for when the goal is to stay and hold a job in the United States for good. People sometimes call it a "green card," because that is its color. A visa is a different document. A green card holder has most of the rights a U.S. citizen has. Not every right is included. After five years, the card holder can apply to become a citizen. A picture shows people at a ceremony where they become U.S. citizens. Closing Words Immigrants now meet many of the same obstacles that earlier generations met. Moving to a new country brings many challenges. Work must be found. A new culture must be learned. Sometimes a new language must be learned. Prejudice may appear. Discrimination may appear. Even so, diversity and energy in the United States grew from these arrivals. The reason is the people who chose it as home. Birthplace does not change the shared hope. Differences do not change it either. Nearly everyone who moves here wants the same thing. A better future, for the mover and for the family, is the hope they share. Discouraged means someone tried to keep another person from doing something. Persecution is unfair treatment of a group. Religion, politics, or race is often the reason. Discrimination means a person, or a whole group, is treated in a way that is not fair. Race may be the basis, or age, sex, religion, or some other difference. Quotas are fixed numbers. They can limit how much of something is allowed, or they can set a goal. Ellis Island sits inside New York Harbor. It used to be the main port where immigrants entered the United States. A sentiment is a feeling, or an opinion. Suspicion is a belief, a feeling, or a thought about something. Ethnic describes a group that shares a culture, or shares a nationality. Turmoil is a condition of disorder, confusion, or agitation. Unemployment is the state of being without work. Immigrants are people who decide to make a home in a country they did not come from. Opposition means acts or views that express a no, or that express a clash of opinion.

50. Quiet Water Held by the Land

1Water That Heals Being near water can heal a person. Recent research in science backs up what people have likely sensed from the earliest times. A calm feeling comes from water. A busy mind grows quieter. Creativity gets a spark. Wonder rises. Healing can come from any water. Lakes and ponds still feel different from other water. Stillness is usual in them. Ocean waves, by contrast, are wild. A flowing river rushes. Picture a landscape mirrored with perfect clarity on a lake. That sight is one way people meet the calming power these waters hold. Fog at morning rises off a lake. The lake is in Vermont, inside Green Mountain National Forest.

2Earth's surface is covered by different kinds of environments. Scientists group a region with its living communities and call the whole thing a biome. Deserts belong on the list of biomes. Rainforests belong on it. Rivers belong on it. Lakes belong on it too. Making a biome takes many factors. Land biomes take up over a quarter of the surface of this planet. Latitude matters a great deal for those land biomes. It tells the distance, northward or southward, from the equator to a place. Elevation matters too. Elevation is how high the place sits over sea level. Warmth and coolness depend partly on those two measures. Water biomes take up close to three quarters of Earth's surface. Whether the water is salty or fresh is one of the biggest factors for them. Lakes and ponds are the subject of this book. Fresh water is what most of them hold. Land wraps all the way around them. The water stands in place. It does not race along as a fast current. Nobody can point to one exact difference that splits a lake from a pond. Size is usually smaller for a pond. Depth is usually less. Waves tend to stay gentler. Light from the sun has a better chance of touching every part of the bottom. Heat in a pond is generally even from one spot to another. One picture shows water lilies resting on a pond. Lakes turn up on each continent. They turn up inside each land biome. Millions of them exist, and size and depth vary a lot. First in size is the Caspian Sea. Salt water fills that lake. People long ago called it a sea. Huge size and salty water were the reasons for that name. Scientists, in general, still treat it as a lake. Among freshwater lakes, Lake Superior is the largest. It belongs to the Great Lakes. Canada and the United States share the border where those lakes lie. Calm is the picture many people have of a lake. Big lakes break that picture. The Great Lakes are an example. Currents in them are strong. A few ocean-like traits show up in them as well. Famous lakes include Great Bear Lake. They include Great Slave Lake. They include Lake Baikal and Lake Winnipeg. They include the Caspian Sea. They include the Great Lakes. The Great Lakes include Lake Superior. They include Lake Huron. They include Lake Ontario. They include Lake Erie. They include Lake Michigan. Other famous lakes include Great Salt Lake. They include Lake Pinatubo. They include Lake Victoria. They include Lake Tanganyika. They include Lake Titicaca. These lakes lie in North America and Europe. They lie in Asia and Africa. They lie in South America and Australia.

3The Philippines hold Lake Pinatubo. The year it formed was 1991. Youth is one claim to fame: it is among the youngest crater lakes anywhere. Depth is another claim. At 2,000 feet, no other lake in that country goes deeper. Ways a Lake Begins Low ground, once it fills with water, is a common start for a lake. The low ground is a basin. There is more than one way to shape a basin. About fourteen thousand years have passed since the Great Lakes formed. Many other Northern Hemisphere lakes share that age. The last ice age was ending then. Glaciers of huge size crept forward. Basins were carved out. Land was worn away. Rock and sediment underneath were crushed as the ice moved. The tiny pieces that resulted are called glacial flour. Later the ice melted, and that water filled the basins. A volcano can shape a basin as well. Rain may collect in the crater once eruptions stop. Snowmelt may collect there. A caldera can hold water too. That word means a large depression. Violent eruptions sometimes collapse a volcano's top, and the depression is what remains. Croatia is home to Plitvice Lakes National Park. Say the park's name PLEET-veet-suh. Waterfalls there link sixteen solution lakes. Underground rock of certain kinds can dissolve when water works on it. A lake may follow. Limestone is the rock most ready to dissolve. Rock made of salt is ready too. Support for the ground above disappears after the rock is gone. The ground falls in. A lake occupies the hole. Soluble is the word for rock that can dissolve. The word means able to be dissolved. Solution lakes are the lakes that form from this process. Deep under the surface, enormous pieces of crust can shift. Basins can open because of that shift. Faults, which are deep cracks, can open when the pieces move. Southern Russia holds Lake Baikal, and this is how it formed. No lake on Earth is deeper. An estimate puts the depth at 1,637 meters. In feet, that is 5,369.

4Not every lake begins as an empty basin waiting for water. River currents, for example, build what is called an oxbow lake. A winding course is how some rivers run. Faster water on the outside of a bend wears the bank away more. Slower water on the inside lets sediment pile up. Those piles, given time, pinch a loop shut. The river finds a fresh course. What stays in the pinched-off loop is an oxbow lake. A landslide can block a stream, and a mudslide can too. Hill or valley slopes shed rocks, soil, and mud. The pile dams the flow. A lake of this sort seldom lasts. A beaver dam can stop a small stream in a similar way. People build lakes on purpose. Those artificial lakes are reservoirs. Hydroelectric dams on rivers are how people make them. A human lifetime can make a lake seem lasting. It is not. Fewer than twenty thousand years is the age of most lakes we see today. Wetland is the next stage. After that, the lake can vanish altogether. Movement in the crust also made a few very old lakes. Lake Baikal is the oldest of them. Twenty-five million years is the least that can be claimed for its age. Salt Lakes Open and closed are the two groups scientists use. Most open lakes lose water by sending it onward. A river may receive it. Another body of water may receive it. Most closed lakes lose water in only one manner. The water evaporates. Salt remains, so these lakes are salty. Saline is another word for that. Salt flats often ring a saline lake. Every drop of lake water has dried away in a salt flat. Ground there wears a thick coat of salt. A freshwater lake's salt share is tiny. It is 0.05 percent at most. Writers also say 5 parts per thousand, or 5 ppt. Sea water sits near 3.5 percent salt. That figure is 35 ppt. A saline lake may go past 30 percent, which is 300 ppt. The figure changes a lot from lake to lake. Great Salt Lake, in Utah, ranks first for size among saline lakes of the Western Hemisphere. Salinity there runs between 6 and 30 percent. The same span is 60 to 300 ppt. Middle Eastern salt water includes the Dead Sea, itself a saline lake. Salt makes up 33.7 percent of it, or 337 ppt. Antarctica's Don Juan Pond ranks with the saltiest lakes anywhere. Its salinity can hit 44 percent, or 440 ppt. Freezing waits until the air nearby falls under −50 degrees Celsius. The Fahrenheit reading is −58. A picture shows how easy floating is in salty water. Utah's Great Salt Lake is the example. Add more salt, and the water grows denser. Denser water holds a swimmer higher.

5Shallow lakes and ponds often let sunlight travel clear to the bed. Deep ones do not work that way. Light, wind, and temperature change from one zone to another. Closest to shore is the littoral zone. Water there is shallower than anywhere else in the lake. It is also warmer. Sun reaches the water in plenty. It reaches the soil under the water too. Plants can live, and so can algae. Cattails root in the bed and rise past the surface. Reeds do the same. Pondweed roots in the bed and stays fully under the water. Floating leaves on rooted plants may be the plants people know best. Water lilies are that kind. Duckweed does not root. It floats free. Animals use these plants as homes. The list includes insects and frogs. It includes crayfish and snails. It includes sponges, worms, and small fish. Eggs are laid on the plants by many of those animals. Fish are the prey of a great blue heron hunting in this zone. Middle-of-the-lake water, near the top, is the limnetic zone. Sunlight is plentiful there, as it is by the shore, so plants can grow. Phytoplankton live in that open water. Zooplankton live there too. Those names mean organisms too small to see without help. Fish are numerous. Oxygen in the water is high. Under the limnetic zone sits the profundal zone. Cold is its character. Sunlight does not arrive, because the water is deep. Fish numbers drop. Oxygen is low in some seasons, and that is why. Bottom sediment is the benthic zone. Cold and dark describe most of it. Worms live in it. Clams live in it. Other animals live in it, and some fish eat them. Organic matter that has died in higher zones sinks to this floor. Bacteria take that matter apart.

6Strictly aquatic is not a fit for every animal a lake supports. Land and water together are required by frogs. Salamanders and turtles need both. Muskrats, otters, and beavers need both. Alligators need both. Loons, ducks, geese, and herons need both. Visitors come to eat. Moose are among them. Raccoons are among them. Birds on migration are among them. Breeding for many organisms happens in ponds. Hidden corners in lake plants give a place to raise young. Winter ice grows from the surface downward. A solid block of ice is rare. Deep water therefore lets many organisms last until spring. Kenya, in East Africa, draws flamingos in hundreds of thousands every year. Two lakes host them: Bogoria and Nakuru. Algae is their food. Chicks are raised there. How People Use Lakes Ancient times already made lakes and ponds important to people. Travel and trade sent ships across the large ones. Crop irrigation used water from lakes and from ponds. Drinking water today comes in large part from lakes. Cooling water comes from them too. Power plants use it. Steel mills use it. Chemical plants use it. Drought plans rely on reservoirs, which hold water until it is needed. Fun draws people as well. Each year, thousands come to fish, to boat, to swim, or to water-ski. Campers come. Hikers come. Photographers come. People who watch wildlife come. Winter adds ice-skating and ice fishing. Wyoming's Bighorn Mountains are the setting of one picture. A mother and her daughter are fishing.

7Day's last light bounces off Maligne Lake. Say the name muh-LEEN. Among lakes of the Canadian Rockies, this one is longest. It is also deepest. Calm and Beauty Lake origins remind us of a planet that never stops changing. A hidden lake with a glassy face shows a second truth. Serene is a word that fits nature too.
