Wild beauty is something lakes ask us to trust and enjoy. They also ask for a slower pace, and for attention to the surroundings. Henry David Thoreau, a writer from America, answered that call by stepping out of regular life. Concord, Massachusetts, had been his home. Walden Pond is where he lived by himself. Two years was the length of the stay. Simple living filled those years. Nature was his study, and his writing grew from that study. He described a lake as a landscape's finest feature, the one with the most to say. Earth's eye was his name for it. Look into that eye, he wrote, and you measure how deep your own nature goes. Aquatic has to do with plants and animals whose lives are in water or beside it. Freshwater has to do with fresh water: water that is not salty. It can mean made of that water, or living in it. A current is water or air moving along one path. Reservoirs are big tanks, or lakes, that gather water and keep it for human use. A depression is lower than the ground around it. Saltwater has to do with salty water. It can mean made of that water, or living in it. Dissolving is a breaking apart, usually after a liquid touches something. Sediment means bits of dirt and of rock. Water can carry the bits, and so can wind or ice, then set them down in a new place. An environment is the full set of conditions acting on organisms in one area. Those conditions include plants, animals, weather, and the shapes of the land. Still describes what does not move. A volcano is an opening in the crust of Earth. A cratered mountain is a common form, and gas, ash, and lava burst out onto the land. Eroding is the wearing down of rock or of soil. Water can cause it, and so can wind or ice.

51. Seabirds with Bright Beaks

1Landing is what a horned puffin attempts on a rock inside the Alaska Maritime National Wildlife Refuge. If you have ever seen a puffin, you are not likely to forget the sight. Even if you have never seen one, you probably know the look of these appealing birds. The look is impossible to mix up with another bird. They have plump bodies. They have feathers that are black and white. They have huge beaks full of color. People also recognize the way they stand, which is upright, and the determined way they walk. With traits this unusual, these sturdy little birds have captured the imagination of many people. Their amusing colors earned them a nickname. People call them the clowns of the sea.

2Puffins are seabirds, members of a group that spends most of life on the open ocean. They are skillful swimmers, and their bodies are perfectly shaped for ocean living. They zoom through the water by using their wings as flippers and their feet as a way to steer. They can dive 100 feet or more, a depth of 30 meters. They can remain underwater for about half a minute. You might suppose that such strong swimming would spoil their skill in the air. That idea is a common myth. In truth they are quite capable when they fly. They also walk with ease across rocks and across other surfaces. In flight, the wings can flap as fast as 400 beats in one minute. Underwater, the swimming looks as if the bird were flying. From the middle of spring through summer, puffins gather in nesting colonies. The colonies sit on islands and on coastal cliffs of the North Atlantic Ocean and the North Pacific Ocean. One of the largest colonies of Atlantic puffins is in the Labrador Sea, near Canada. In this season the beaks are large and full of color. Patches of bright white feathers show. Extra feathery decorations help attract a mate. The webbed feet turn a bright orange. During the rest of the year the birds are far out at sea, and they look much plainer. Black, white, and gray replace most of the brighter breeding colors at that time of year. Four types of puffins live in these oceans. Each type has features that let people tell the birds apart. The scientific name of the Atlantic puffin is Fratercula arctica. The Latin words mean little brother of the north.

3An adult Atlantic puffin stands 10 to 12.5 inches tall, which is 25 to 32 centimeters. Both shores of the North Atlantic Ocean have these birds. In the breeding season, more than half of them live along the coast of Iceland. No other puffin type is smaller than these birds. They are also the least fancy, even when they are dressed in breeding plumage. Bright orange colors the tip of the beak. A blue-gray section sits behind that tip and is trimmed in yellow. The feet are orange. The face, the chest, and the belly are white. Adult males and adult females look alike, though a male may be a bit larger. Young puffins look similar to adults that are not in breeding plumage. An adult horned puffin averages 15 inches tall, which is 38 centimeters. South of the Arctic Circle, in the North Pacific Ocean, is the main home of horned puffins. During breeding they look roughly like Atlantic puffins, with a white face and a white underside. A spike of black feathers above each eye gives them away. Those feathers look like eyelashes, so the birds seem to be wearing makeup. A black line also runs from behind each eye to the back of the head. A large yellow patch where the beak begins is a further clue. An Atlantic puffin has blue-gray on the beak in that spot instead.

4An adult tufted puffin averages 15 inches tall, which is 38 centimeters. Tufted puffins live in more places than the other types do. Both shores of the North Pacific Ocean hold these birds. The range reaches as far north as Alaska. It reaches as far south as Japan and as far south as central California. Unlike the Atlantic puffin and the horned puffin, the tufted puffin has a black chest and a black belly. In winter the bird is black and carries a large red-orange beak. The breeding season brings a different look. A white mask appears. An olive-yellow section appears on the beak. Long tufts of gold feathers grow above the eyes. Orange feet and orange rings around the eyes finish the summer look. Rhinoceros auklets are less famous than the other puffins, and they look very different. That difference is why some people treat them as close cousins rather than as actual puffins. An adult averages 13.8 to 15 inches tall, which is 35 to 38 centimeters. These birds live along the Pacific coast of North America. They also live along the coast of Asia near Japan. In the breeding season the thin bill is yellow-orange, and a short horn grows at its base. Brown covers most of the feathers, darker along the back and paler on the chest and belly. Two narrow stripes of white feathers mark each side of the head.

5Puffins usually come back from the sea in late March or in early April. Through the breeding season they often live in colonies that may hold several thousand birds. A pair usually stays together, and the pair returns to the same nesting site each year. Once they are back, the pair prepares a burrow, and the female lays a single egg in it. Tufted puffins usually dig that burrow in soft soil. European Atlantic puffins usually dig in soft soil too. Rhinoceros auklets usually do the same. Horned puffins often choose a different nest. North American Atlantic puffins often choose that same different nest. They use openings between rocks on coastal cliffs. A puffin that has just hatched is called a puffling. The parents take turns keeping the egg warm. Both parents feed the chick for one month or for two months, until the chick can fly. Some reports say the parents stop caring at a certain point. The truth is kinder. The chicks leave by themselves when they are ready. A puffin becomes an adult around the age of five. It can live for twenty years or even longer. Every type of puffin mainly eats small fish. In winter, when fewer fish can be found, other foods appear. Puffins may then eat squid, shrimp, crabs, and other small creatures. Adults eat while they are still underwater. They also gather fish to carry home to the chicks. One beak can hold fifteen fish or even more at a single time. A rough tongue helps keep the fish in place. Spines on the roof of the mouth help as well. A puffin can stack dozens of fish in that beak at one time.

6For hundreds of years, humans have hunted puffins for meat, for eggs, and for feathers. In some places the hunting still goes on. People also take too many of the particular fish that puffins need. Those fish are caught far faster than they can reproduce. Warmer temperatures in the sea, caused by climate change, are leaving puffins with fewer fish. Chicks cannot eat some fish that are common now, because those fish are too big. Other kinds are less nutritious. Puffins get tangled in fishing nets. Pollution harms them. People have disturbed many of the places where they nest. Other predators are a serious threat as well. The list includes gulls, eagles, rats, and foxes. People who share the puffins' homes are trying to fix these problems. They want these amazing seabirds to go on living. Puffins are unique members of the natural community of Earth. They are also important signs of how healthy the oceans are. Healthy seas and healthy puffins go together. Eastern Egg Rock is a small island off the coast of Maine, in North America. Dr. Steve Kress is a wildlife scientist and a puffin expert, and his full name is Dr. Stephen Kress. His interest in nature began in fourth grade. He watched suburbs spread near his home and wipe out natural habitats. As he learned more, he decided on a career in wildlife. In the early 1970s he visited Eastern Egg Rock. Atlantic puffins had lived on that island one hundred years earlier. He wondered whether the birds could be brought back. He founded Project Puffin. He used imaginative methods, including the method of thinking like a puffin. Those methods brought the seabirds back to Eastern Egg Rock. As of 2014, the island held 148 breeding pairs. The National Audubon Society sponsors Project Puffin. The society works to protect birds, other wildlife, and the places they inhabit.

7Outside a den on a coastal cliff in Iceland, an Atlantic puffin stands. If you want to see puffins in the wild, remember where they spend the year. For many months they are out at sea. They come onto land only in the breeding season. You will mainly find them on cliffs and on islands that are difficult to reach. The trip is worth the effort if you can make it. Choose a place that allows people to view wildlife. Take care not to disturb birds that are nesting. Hikers may walk many miles and still catch only a glimpse of one puffin or of two. A boat tour can make the viewing easier. From the boat you will probably see the birds at a closer distance. Tour companies know the best areas, and they share interesting information about the birds. Wherever you travel to see them, bring binoculars and bring a camera. These little clowns are sure to amuse you, and they are sure to fascinate you. A few meanings help with the words. Breeding season is the time of year when animals of a particular species reproduce. An animal digs a hole in the ground and lives in it, and that hole is a burrow. Climate means the long-term, lasting pattern of weather for Earth or for one region. Coastal means related to the coast of a sea or of an ocean. Colonies are groups of animals that live together. To inhabit a place is to occupy it or to live in it. Offspring like the parent appear when a living thing reproduces. Tufted means feathers, hair, or grass growing together in a tight bunch. Webbed describes fingers or toes that are joined by a thin skin.

52. September 11, 2001

1Emergency crews stand before the ruined Twin Towers. The look on their faces is awe. Book topics run in this order. An introduction is first. The attack comes next. The towers' fall comes after that. Heroes come next. Clearing the wreckage comes after the heroes. Responsibility comes next. The country's quick answer follows. A replacement trade center follows that. Word meanings come last. One photo is a crossing in New York City. The avenue is 5th Avenue. People on foot are crossing it. The date was September 11, 2001. The morning in that city looked ordinary. Roads were jammed with cars. Sidewalks were crowded with people rushing to work. Horns blew. A siren sometimes sliced the noise. Two towers stood at the south end of Manhattan Island. Their name was the World Trade Center. They seemed to watch the city below them. Thousands of workers stepped out of taxis. Others stepped out of buses. Others came up from subway trains. Work waited in those towers. The stacks rose 110 floors. Speedy elevators lifted people from the street to their floors. A jet engine then roared above the streets, with no warning. Canyons of skyscrapers hear plenty of strange noise. They had never heard this. Walkers looked up. A big jet, full of passengers, was overhead. It flew much too low. It headed right for the trade center.

2Wonder did not last. Horror replaced it. Disbelief replaced it. The jet was American Airlines Flight 11. Eighty-seven people, passengers and crew together, were aboard. High floors of the northern tower took the blow. Seventeen minutes passed after that. United Airlines Flight 175 hit the South Tower. Sixty people, passengers and crew together, were aboard that second jet. Fuel filled both planes. Each strike became a giant ball of fire at once. One photo shows the towers burning that morning. Another photo is dated five days later. Sunrise lights the U.S. Capitol in the back. The Pentagon, already struck by a jet, sits in front. While tower news was spreading, a fresh report arrived. A passenger jet had struck the Pentagon. Washington, D.C., is across the Potomac River from that building. United States military offices fill the Pentagon. Flames took hold immediately. All fifty-nine people on the plane were killed. That count includes passengers and crew.

3Attack had come to the United States. Hijackers had taken the planes. The crashes were on purpose. The planes were being flown as missiles at well-known American sites. The full number of taken planes was still unknown. Others might still be flying. Planes already in the air were ordered down. Incoming foreign flights were turned toward Canada. They were also turned toward Mexico. Military planes were the exception. Everything else was kept on the ground. Silence fell over the American sky. United Airlines Flight 93 was the other hijacked plane. Cell phones linked passengers to people on the ground. Those people at home described three earlier crashes. The targets had been the two towers and the Pentagon. Crew and passengers refused to let their plane be a weapon. They struck back at the hijackers. The hijackers flipped the aircraft. The clock read 10:03. The crash site was outside Shanksville, in Pennsylvania. A likely target, many believe, was the United States Capitol. The White House is the other place many name. Both stand in Washington, D.C. That attack never arrived. The people on the plane stopped it. Forty died, every one of them. LeRoy Homer Jr. is remembered as a Flight 93 hero. His job was First Officer. United Airlines was his employer then. Before that, active duty in the Air Force lasted seven years. The branch was the U.S. Air Force. Reserve service came next. He reached the rank of major. His age was thirty-six on the day of the hijacking. He joined the fight to block the hijackers' destination. The Shanksville crash killed him. He stands among several heroes from that flight. George W. Bush was president. He was visiting a Florida elementary school. The first tower strike happened while he was there. The second strike happened while he was still there. Staff hurried him onto his own aircraft. Six fighter jets flew as escorts. By evening he had returned to the White House. A televised talk to the nation lasted five minutes. He said the attacks can break steel. He said they still cannot break American resolve. One photo catches the moment he hears about the second strike.

4A map follows four routes. Flight 175 belonged to United Airlines. It departed Boston Logan International Airport at 7:58 a.m. Los Angeles International Airport was the planned stop. At 9:05 a.m. it hit the trade center's south tower. Flight 11 belonged to American Airlines. It also departed from Boston's Logan airport. The time was 7:59 a.m. Los Angeles was its planned stop too. At 8:45 a.m. it hit the trade center's north tower. Flight 93 belonged to United Airlines. Newark International Airport was the start, at 8:10 a.m. San Francisco International Airport was the plan. The map marks a crash at Shanksville, Pennsylvania, at 10:10 a.m. Flight 77 belonged to American Airlines. Dulles International Airport was the start, also at 8:10 a.m. Los Angeles was the plan. At 9:40 a.m. it struck the Pentagon's west side. A dotted line means the track after the transponder went off. Emergency teams were called in New York City. They were called in Arlington, Virginia, the Pentagon's home city. Police and firefighters began clearing the towers after the North Tower was hit first. Worker numbers in the two towers were above 14,000. Most people on floors under the impacts got out fast. Collapse of the South Tower came at 9:59. By then, fifty-six minutes had gone by since the second jet hit. Floors pancaked, one onto the next. The North Tower came down at 10:28. That was twenty-nine minutes after the south tower. A diagram marks floors 77 through 85. It also marks floors 93 through 99. Story count for each tower was 110. Below the impact, 99 percent survived in each tower. Above the impact, and in it, survival was tiny. Only a handful lived, and only in the South Tower.

5Dust and broken pieces blanketed New York City. Fifty-six minutes was the South Tower's time after impact. One hundred two minutes was the North Tower's time. Nearby buildings were hit by the debris. Fires broke out. Two neighboring buildings were ruined completely. Heavy damage hit many others. Demolition was later planned for some of them. Firefighters move through the rubble in one photo. Death came to many firefighters inside the buildings. Death came to many police officers there too. They had been trying to reach hundreds of trapped people. Fire held those people. Thick smoke held them too. Deaths tied to the tower attack total 2,753. More than seventy-five countries lost citizens. The dead included young people. The dead included old people. The official toll still climbs years afterward. Lung disease and other illnesses from the destruction keep adding names. A chart lists how many people died. For the trade center, the figure is 2,753. The Associated Press is the source of that figure. Pentagon: 184, with PBS as the source. Shanksville, Pennsylvania: 40, with USA Today as the source.

6Heroes numbered in the thousands. The list includes firefighters. It includes police. It includes emergency medical workers. It includes everyday citizens. It includes people who worked in offices. It includes ironworkers. It includes others who dug through rubble looking for victims. Some of those heroes died in the effort to save someone else. First responders march at the Pentagon in one photo. The ceremony remembers 9/11. Among emergency crews, the New York Fire Department lost the most. Firefighter deaths there numbered 341. Paramedic deaths there numbered two. Falling towers trapped most of them. A fire helmet turned up at the trade-center site. Leaders knew the towers might fall. They tried to call the rescuers back out. Broken communications blocked the message. Chaos blocked it too. Police deaths totaled sixty. Private ambulance crews lost eight medical workers. The story from United Flight 93 may be the one people feel most strongly. Dozens aboard showed courage. Because of them, the plane did not hit a further target. Because of them, more deaths were prevented. Every detail will stay unknown. The passengers' heroism is known. One photo shows a girl who is eleven. She is straightening a ribbon. She stands at a temporary memorial just outside Shanksville. Pennsylvania is the state. Her father died on Flight 93. He was one of forty.

7Work crews moved in the moment the towers fell. The date was 9/11. Smoke still rose from the rubble. Searchers looked for living people. They looked for the dead. They also hauled wreckage out. Ground Zero became the site's name. Pentagon crews did related work. They pulled debris from the hurt building. They searched for bodies. Clearing there finished, and repairs finished, inside one year. Visitors could enter a memorial beside the Pentagon on the seventh anniversary. Benches fill that memorial. Washington, D.C., is the city. The benches number the Pentagon dead. The number is 184. Trade-center clearing took far longer. Ironworkers stayed on the job day and night. So did operators of heavy machines. So did other laborers. They sliced apart bent steel. They trucked it away. They combed the pile for remains. Almost nine months removed 1.8 million tons. The material was steel and concrete. Nothing of the towers' footprint remained but a vast hole. People named that hole The Pit. A new trade center was planned. A victims' memorial was planned too. One photo shows the clearing work. Shanksville's wreckage came up quickly. A temporary memorial stood five hundred yards from the impact. A permanent Flight 93 memorial came years later. Black granite forms a walkway at the Memorial Plaza. Visitors can walk a piece of the plane's route. The Wall of Names runs along that walk. Marble panels number forty. Each panel is inscribed with names from the flight. Passengers are named. Crew members are named.

8Who was behind the surprise attack? Eyes turned fast to Al-Qaeda, a terrorist network. The name is said al-KY-duh. Formation came about twenty years before 2001. Afghanistan was being invaded then. The invader was the Soviet Union, as it was called at the time. Washington sent money to many groups that fought back. Other support went too. The aim was to halt the invasion. Civil war followed inside Afghanistan. Al-Qaeda could form in that war. It could grow there. By 2001 its aim was clear. It wanted U.S. influence gone from the Middle East. It wanted Western Europe's influence gone too. Hours after the crashes, the FBI listed nineteen men. Hijacking was the suspected crime. A suitcase of the group's leader was found. All nineteen names were in it. More evidence was in it too. Tora Bora is a cave area in Afghanistan. A photo shows those caves. In 2001, belief held that Al-Qaeda's leader was hidden there. More evidence surfaced before midnight. It pointed to Osama bin Laden. He led Al-Qaeda. Investigators tied him to the attacks. U.S. forces began planning a hunt that same period, right after September 11. Afghanistan was not the home country of any hijacker. It was still the base of Al-Qaeda's work. Bombing started in under a month. American forces took part. Allied forces took part. Targets were camps thought to belong to Al-Qaeda. The Taliban, then ruling Afghanistan, was attacked too. That group is a fundamentalist Muslim movement. Some members had sheltered Al-Qaeda inside the country. Bush and Congress approved a 2002 law called the Homeland Security Act. A new department came from that law. People know it as Homeland Security, a federal department. A second law also passed Congress. That law is the USA Patriot Act. Finding terrorists was one goal. Arresting them was another. Prosecuting them was another. Phone listening was allowed. Email reading was allowed. Online activity of U.S. citizens could be tracked. Critics called this a blow to personal freedom. One photo shows the department's sign. The city is Washington, D.C.

9March 2003 brought a claim from President Bush. Iraq was the country. Saddam Hussein was the ruler. Bush said they were building weapons of mass destruction. He called those weapons very dangerous. U.S. troops entered Iraq. Hussein was later executed. Proof afterward said the weapons were not there. Proof also failed to show a clear tie from Iraq to the 9/11 attacks. Security grew tighter in hopes of blocking later attacks. U.S. borders were part of that tightening. Shipping ports were part of it. U.S. airports were part of it. Countries elsewhere took similar steps. Daily life was not the same after 9/11. One photo is from 2003. A TSA employee, from the Transportation Security Administration, checks a girl with a wand. The check is gentle. The girl is three. Her family is heading home to Boston from Denver. Denial from Al-Qaeda lasted more than three years. Bin Laden denied a role too. Public responsibility came in 2004. He stated a reason. U.S. troops had stayed in Middle Eastern countries in the 1991 Gulf War. He wanted to punish that. He also named American support for Israel. Soon after the attacks, Bush asked Americans to show respect. He meant Muslims who live in this country. Hate crimes against Muslims still soared in the following weeks. FBI figures put anti-Muslim hate crimes at 28 in the year 2000. The 2001 figure was 481. Islamophobia was the driver. The word means dislike, or prejudice, aimed at Islam. It can also be aimed at Muslims. Harassment hit Muslims. Beatings hit them. Killings by fellow citizens hit them. Police stops singled them out more often. So did random searches. Worship sites called mosques were damaged on purpose. Other faiths were targeted too. Middle Eastern descent raised the risk. South Asian descent raised it too. Arizona was where Balbir Singh Sodhi was killed. The killer sought revenge for the attacks. Sodhi's faith was Sikh. A turban and a beard caused a wrong identification. He was not Muslim. Between 2000 and 2009, anti-Muslim hate crimes climbed 500 percent.

10One map sets the United States between two oceans. One ocean is the Atlantic. One ocean is the Pacific. The Indian Ocean is marked as well. The hunt for bin Laden lasted years. Eastern Afghanistan was where capture nearly happened. He crossed into Pakistan. May 1, 2011, was the day President Barack Obama spoke. Navy personnel from the United States carried out the raid. Their training was special. The place was a compound in Pakistan. Hiding there was the belief about bin Laden. Entry was swift. Bin Laden was killed. Another map marks several places. Afghanistan is one. Israel is one. Pakistan is one. The Indian Ocean is one. Africa is one. India is one. Iraq saw its last American soldiers leave in 2011. August 2021 was when President Joe Biden withdrew U.S. troops from Afghanistan. War deaths reached the tens of thousands. Afghan people forced to leave home number at least 2.2 million. Iran is one place they went. Pakistan is another. About $2.3 trillion is the cost to the United States. Plans for a replacement building started soon after the towers were gone. Argument over the design lasted a long while. Construction of One World Trade Center began in 2006. Height puts it among the world's tallest buildings. Completion came in 2014. More towers are still rising there. The finished tower measures 1,776 feet if the antenna counts. Metric height is 541 meters. The feet match the year the United States declared independence. Great Britain was the country it left.

11Ground Zero gained a memorial and a museum as well as new buildings. People killed in the attacks are the ones the memorial honors. Two broad reflecting pools sit among trees. Bronze edging on the pools carries every victim's name. Artificial waterfalls there are the largest in North America. Old tower footprints are where the pools sit. The twin falls sit there too. Visitors learn the 9/11 story in the museum. They also learn what led to that day. Victim portraits hang inside. Objects saved from the first site are inside. Millions visit yearly, and teaching them is the museum's purpose. The teaching aims at a kinder future shared by everyone. Stopping another tragedy like this one is the other hope. Meanings come last. Chaos is confusion, order gone missing. Hijacked means an outside force took over a vehicle. A compound is a cluster of buildings inside a wall. Invaded means forced entry aimed at conquest, weakening, or harm. Debris is the scattered leftover after something is destroyed or removed. A memorial keeps the memory of a person, a place, a thing, or an event. Demolition is total destruction, often by explosives. Resolve is determination. A sacrifice is something given freely, an act or an object, to help others or a cause. Evacuating is shifting people away from danger. Fundamentalist means following a belief set in a very strict way, often a religious set. Terrorists use terror as a tool of politics.

53. Seven Great Builds of the Modern Age

1A world map marks seven great works. The North Sea Protection Works are marked. The CN Tower is marked. The Golden Gate Bridge is marked. The Channel Tunnel is marked. The Empire State Building is marked. The Atlantic Ocean and the Pacific Ocean are marked. The Panama Canal is marked. The Itaipú Dam is marked. This book moves through these parts. Picking wonders comes first. The Channel Tunnel comes next. The Netherlands North Sea Protection Works follow. The Canadian National Tower comes after that. The Empire State Building and the Golden Gate Bridge come next. The Panama Canal follows. The Itaipú Dam and a closing thought come after the canal. Word meanings and a word list close the book. Long ago, scholars selected the seven greatest works built by human beings. They called them the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. These wonders honored courage. They honored the power to do things people thought could not be done. Of the Ancient Wonders, only the Great Pyramid of Egypt still stands. Hundreds of years later, a group of engineers asked a question. They asked experts around the world to select seven new wonders. The Modern Wonders on their list honored the same ideas as the older list. The seven modern works are these. The Channel Tunnel links England and France. The Netherlands North Sea Protection Works stand in the Netherlands. The Canadian National Tower stands in Toronto, Canada. The Empire State Building stands in New York City, in the United States. The Golden Gate Bridge stands in San Francisco, in the United States. The Panama Canal runs through Panama. The Itaipú Dam stands on the border of Brazil and Paraguay.

2The Channel Tunnel is the first stop. Let us start in England and France. Imagine traveling 31 miles through an underwater tunnel. That distance is 50 kilometers. The speed is close to 100 miles per hour, which is 161 kilometers per hour. The Channel Tunnel is also called the Chunnel. It provides speedy travel between England and France. About 20 minutes is all the trip takes. A cutaway shows the sea and the seabed. It shows a service tunnel. It shows a westbound tunnel. It shows an eastbound tunnel. People had dreamed of this tunnel for years. The work was hard. The work was risky. It took about 13,000 people to build it. The work ran from 1987 to 1994. They built three tunnels. Together the tunnels are a total of 95 miles long, which is 153 kilometers. First, workers dug huge chunks of chalk from the bottom of the English Channel. They dug clay too. The tunnels were then built beneath the water. Cars drive off a Channel Tunnel train. Passengers can now ride through the Chunnel in buses. They can ride in cars. Those vehicles are loaded onto the widest trains ever built. One tunnel allows train travel from England to France. A second tunnel allows travel in the opposite direction. The third tunnel is a service tunnel. It is used for repairs and emergencies. Safety was a top priority. A couple of years after the Chunnel opened, a fire started. It started in one of the tunnels. A fire could have killed many people. The Channel Tunnel had plans for emergencies. People were taken off the train. They were led to the tunnel used for repairs and emergencies. Some people became sick from the smoke. They were taken to the hospital. No one died. No one was seriously hurt. Those safety plans kept the day from ending in disaster.

3The Netherlands North Sea Protection Works come next. Travel north from France to the Netherlands. Much of the land there is below sea level. During storms, floods destroyed homes. Floods destroyed farmland. In the early 1900s, the Dutch suffered the effects of war. They suffered terrible storms. Food shortages were a problem. They decided to find new ways to protect the land from the sea. They wanted to protect the people too. The people began building the North Sea Protection Works in 1927. They dammed areas along the coast. The dams created lakes. They created farmland. A picture shows farmland created by the North Sea Protection Works. Floodwalls keep surges of water from flooding the land during storms. Other areas could not be dammed. More dams would hurt the country's shipping industry. They would hurt wildlife habitats. So the builders made a floodwall unlike any other. The wall was built with giant gates. The gates stay open when the sea is calm. Open gates allow ships to come and go. They keep the wildlife safe. During storms, the gates can be closed. Closed gates prevent flooding. The North Sea Protection Works gave the Dutch a huge gift of land. The gift was over one-half million acres. The land is used for farming. It is used for livestock. It is used for homes. Flood protection was another gain for the people.

4The Canadian National Tower is the next wonder. Cross the Atlantic Ocean from the Netherlands to Toronto, Canada. Visitors can stand on an observation deck of the Canadian National Tower. People also call it the CN Tower. From there they can see Niagara Falls. The falls are about 85 miles away, which is 137 kilometers. The tower is over 1,800 feet high, which is 548 meters. It is one of the tallest freestanding structures in the world. Toronto already had many tall buildings by the 1960s. Many were so tall they blocked radio signals. They blocked television signals. The city needed a tower tall enough for a clear send. No building could block signals coming from it. Drawings and plans were made for the CN Tower. Building something so tall was not easy. Workers used instruments on planes. The planes flew over the CN Tower. The instruments made sure the tower was straight. Builders used a helicopter to place the antenna. The antenna went at the tower's top. Around the tower's base, they constructed a four-level observation deck. The deck was lifted into place high above the ground when it was finished. The top level is called the Skypod. It is one of the highest public observation decks in the world. Tourists flock to the tower. On the bottom observation level, visitors find the Glass Floor. They walk on a see-through surface. They look down at the city below. A view from the Glass Floor of the CN Tower shows that drop.

5The Empire State Building stands southeast of the CN Tower, in the United States. Work started in 1930. It was the tallest building of its time. It rose in the New York City skyline in one year and forty-five days. The Great Depression was underway when construction began. Many people were looking for jobs. They did not mind the danger. They did not mind the hard work of building it so quickly. They built four and one-half floors a week. They put together the 58,000-ton frame in less than a month. The building is 1,250 feet tall, which is 381 meters. It has 102 stories. It became a New York City landmark. It has 73 elevators. It has 1,860 steps. It has 6,500 windows. People come from around the world to see the city. They look from the observation deck. Travel west to the Golden Gate Bridge in San Francisco, on the west coast of the United States. Local residents wanted a bridge across a narrow waterway. The waterway lies between San Francisco Bay and the Pacific Ocean. Planning took 65 years. Then construction started in 1933. The work provided jobs during the Great Depression. Men worked on towers 746 feet above the water. That height is 227 meters. That is a little more than half the height of the Empire State Building. The men worked with thick cables. The cables sat in bundles a yard wide. They worked in the cold. They worked in the fog. They worked in the wind. They worked with the constant danger of falling. Eleven men fell and died during the work on the bridge. The entrance to San Francisco Bay is crossed by the Golden Gate Bridge.

6A suspension bridge is built in a set order. Workers first had to construct tall towers. Strong, thick cables were then strung from tower to tower. Cables held up the floor, also called the deck, of the bridge. The cables were secured at each end of the bridge. Secured means held in place. A picture shows thousands of wires inside a cable. A worker walks on them. A cross-section shows the same cable. On the day the Golden Gate Bridge opened in 1937, people walked its length. The length is 4,200 feet, which is 1,280 meters. That is almost a mile. Cars crossed for the first time on the following day. Since then, a huge number of vehicles have used the bridge. The number is over a billion and a half. Once it was the longest suspension bridge in the world. It was the tallest too. It is still one of the biggest. It is still one of the most spectacular. A major earthquake did not bring it down. The Panama Canal is the next stop, south of the United States in the country of Panama. A lake there almost connects the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. As early as 1534, people talked about digging through the land. They wanted to extend the lake to the oceans. Work started on the Panama Canal in 1904. It took 10 years to finish. Before the canal, ships had a long route. People had to sail around South America to get from one ocean to the other. During digging, disease caused problems. Landslides caused problems. Mudslides caused problems. After they finished digging, they built a system of chambers. The chambers raise and lower ships from the oceans to the lake. Ships enter chambers on one side of the canal. Those chambers take them to the lake. The ships make their way across the lake. Chambers on the other side take them down to the ocean. One ship is shown getting ready to enter the Panama Canal. Today, the canal can handle about 50 ships a day. It averages about 14,000 ships a year.

7Here is how the Panama Canal works. Each side of the lake has three chambers. Water flows from one chamber to the next three times. That flow raises and lowers the ships on each side. First, a ship enters the canal chamber. There it is raised from sea level to lake level. Second, water flows into the chamber from the lake. The flow makes the water the same height on both sides of the gate. Third, the gate opens. The ship moves into the lake. The Itaipú Dam is the next wonder. Head south from Panama to the countries of Brazil and Paraguay. In 1975, the two countries teamed up. They built a hydroelectric plant. They wanted to produce more electricity for their people. They would build it on the Paraná River. The river runs on the border between the two countries. A hydroelectric plant needs water. It needs a dam to create electricity. Builders overcame big challenges. They changed the course of the Paraná. It is the seventh largest river in the world. They dug up more than 50 million tons of dirt and rocks. They removed that earth. They used enough concrete to build a city for four million people. They used enough iron and steel to build 380 Eiffel Towers. The result was a series of dams. It was also a power plant one-half mile long, which is 0.8 kilometers. Records for power produced have been broken by this power plant. It now supplies most of the power for Paraguay. It supplies about a quarter of the power for Brazil.

8A diagram shows how a hydroelectric plant works. The labels are powerhouse, power lines, reservoir, transformer, dam, intake, generator, penstock, outflow, control gate, and turbine. The Itaipú Dam is a giant wall with gates. The gates hold back water from the Paraná River. When the gates of the dam are opened, water goes through a pipe. The pipe leads to a turbine. The turbine has blades. The blades are like a fan, only much larger. Turning blades are driven by the water. The blades cause powerful magnets in the generator to turn. A generator is something like a motor. Electrons are moved when the magnets pass copper coils inside the generator. Energy comes in tiny bits called electrons. Electricity is what these electrons become. Tourists visit the Itaipú Dam. Someday, new lists of wonders will be made. Even greater works are already under construction. These Seven Wonders of the Modern World still stand as proof. They prove the power of human beings in the 1900s. They prove the courage of human beings in that century.

9These words help with the book. Engineers are people trained to design buildings or bridges. Habitats are places where plants and animals live in their natural environment. A hydroelectric plant is a factory that uses water to make electricity. A landmark is a building important to the history of a place. An observation deck is a place for looking at what is around a building. A power plant is a factory that makes electricity. Radio and television signals are electromagnetic signals. They transmit pictures and sounds. Scholars are educated people. The shipping industry is the business of using ships to transport goods. A skyline is the outline against the sky that buildings make. A suspension bridge hangs the part people walk or drive on from cables. A waterway is a body of water ships can use. A word list points back to the main topics. It includes the Atlantic Ocean and Brazil. It includes the Channel Tunnel, also called the Chunnel, and the CN Tower. It includes dams, deaths, and digging. It includes electricity and the Empire State Building. It includes England and the English Channel. It includes farmland, floods, and France. It includes the Golden Gate Bridge and the Great Depression. It includes the Great Pyramid and the hydroelectric plant. It includes the Itaipú Dam and the Netherlands North Sea Protection Works. It includes New York City and the observation deck. It includes the Pacific Ocean, Panama, and the Panama Canal. It includes Paraguay and the Paraná River. It includes radio and television signals and San Francisco. It includes the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World and the Seven Wonders of the Modern World. It includes the suspension bridge, the tallest structures, and Toronto. It includes the underwater tunnel and the waterway.

54. Shadows on the Sun and the Moon

1In Bangladesh, a girl sets up to watch the Moon slide across the Sun. This book takes the topics in this order. Darkness in the middle of the day, or in the middle of the night, comes first. History comes next. Giant shadows come after that. The red color of the Moon comes next. A covered Sun follows. Forecasts follow that. Safe watching comes after the forecasts. A closing follows. A list of words is last. Another picture catches the Moon crossing part of a Sun that is setting. Imagine noon, full sun, and open air. Darkness falls on everything around you. The sky holds no cloud at all. Or imagine the full moon starting milky white. Bit by bit it shifts. It ends a spooky blood-red. Eclipses are the name for strange events like these. Wonder has followed them through history. Fear has followed them too. Excitement has followed them too. One kind is solar. In that kind, the Moon covers the Sun. Another kind is lunar. In that kind, Earth's shadow sweeps over the Moon. The Moon's color changes while that happens.

2Not knowing the cause can make an eclipse scary. People long ago were afraid. They read these events as bad omens. Ancient China had one explanation for a solar eclipse. People there said a dragon was swallowing the Sun. Drums were their answer. Pots were their answer too. They hoped loud banging would drive the dragon away. Ancient Greece held a different guess. Some people there thought quakes in the ground and eclipses might go together. Those two events are not connected. A picture shows China's daytime sky growing dark as the Sun is covered. History itself may have turned because of some eclipses. The Middle East gives one example. The century was the sixth bc. The Lydians were one group in a war. The Medes were the other group. Five years of fighting had already passed. The date of the battle was May 28, 585 bc. The fighting was fierce. Then a total eclipse swapped day for night. The armies were so afraid that they set their weapons down. Peace was the agreement they made. Study of eclipses began among ancient peoples. China was one of those peoples. Greece was another. Babylonia was another. Egypt was another. They came to see eclipses as natural events. Dragons were not part of the cause. Other monsters were not part of the cause. Even so, the true explanation traveled slowly from one land to another.

3A diagram places the Sun, Earth, and the Moon for a lunar eclipse. The cause is known now. Earth, the Moon, and the Sun must stand in a line in space. What follows is a huge shadow, and nothing more. Your own body throws a shadow on the ground if you stand in sun. Earth does the same thing out in space. The Moon does the same thing out in space. The view changes with the place you watch from. From the Moon's surface during a lunar eclipse, Earth would hide the Sun. Red light would ring that Earth. Earth's view is not like that. From here, the full moon fades slowly. Earth's shadow is what it is crossing. Moonlight is only sunlight bounced back. Earth in the way stops that bounce. Next comes the red color. Strip away Earth's atmosphere and a total lunar eclipse would leave the Moon black. The atmosphere is there, though. Sunlight travels through it. Most of those rays strike the ground. The ground stops them. Other rays cross the air and never touch the ground. Filtering is one thing the air does to that sunlight. Scattering is another.

4Labels on a diagram name Earth's shadow, the Sun, the Moon, and the atmosphere. Red light that the air has scattered is part of the picture. Some of the Sun's red light bends on its path through the air. It then arrives at the Moon. Red is the color the Moon takes on. Many colors mix to make the Sun's white light. Blue is the color the air takes in most strongly from those rays. Red gets through. Scattering spreads that red. Some of it leaves again, outward, into space. A share of it lands on the Moon. The Moon then looks spooky. Reddish is the common result. Orange is possible too. Yellow is possible too. Brown is possible too. Dust floating in the air helps pick the color. Clouds help pick the color too. Dramatic red is what a total lunar eclipse can paint on the Moon. Eight views show the change, and the order matters. View one: light still covers most of the Moon, while darkness sits on the lower left. View two: darkness has grown to one third. View three: darkness reaches halfway, while the upper right half stays bright. View four: brightness is down to one third, and darkness has everything else. View five: darkness has taken most of the Moon. View six: a last bright spot sits at the upper right, and darkness has nearly the whole Moon. View seven: the entire round Moon glows a dark purplish-red. View eight: the entire round Moon glows a light orangish-red.

5Full lunar eclipses are not rare. One year can hold as many as three. Another year can hold zero. Shifting places of the Moon and of Earth decide it. Night covers one whole face of Earth. Anyone on that face can see a lunar eclipse. Near your home, chances will probably come many times. A lunar eclipse is safe to watch. Binoculars do not make it unsafe. A telescope does not make it unsafe. Full shadow on the Moon does not last one fixed time. About thirty minutes is possible. More than an hour is possible. A telescope can show a lunar eclipse clearly. Block the Sun with the Moon and the corona's hot gases stand out. Solar is the other eclipse type. Moon and Earth trade places relative to where they sit in a lunar eclipse. Size is one comparison. The Sun is roughly four hundred times the Moon's size. Distance is another comparison. The Sun sits roughly four hundred times farther from Earth than the Moon does. Nature's lucky match follows from those two facts. From Earth, the Moon's round face is sized just right to hide the Sun. Cover the Sun's main light and the outer layer appears. Corona is the name of that outer layer. Bright glow comes from the corona's hot gases. The glow rings the Sun's hidden disk.

6A solar eclipse sends two shadows from the Moon onto Earth. The inner shadow is the dark one. People standing there see a total eclipse. For a brief time, none of the Sun's disk shows. The outer shadow is lighter. People there can still see a piece of the Sun. That view is a partial eclipse. Step outside the lighter shadow and the eclipse is gone for you. An annular eclipse leaves a bright ring around the Moon. Earth is not circled by the Moon in a perfect circle. Distance from Earth to the Moon therefore changes. Farther away, the Moon looks slightly smaller. It then fails to hide the whole Sun. A thin ring of the Sun shows around the Moon. Annular is the name for that eclipse. The word comes from Latin. In Latin it means ring. A total solar eclipse does not last the same length every time. Your viewing place changes the length too. The longest full darkening anyone can watch lasts seven minutes plus half a minute.

7Solar eclipses are much harder to catch than lunar ones. About every eighteen months, some form of solar eclipse occurs somewhere on Earth. Open ocean is the site of many of them. Polar regions are the site of many others. Almost nobody is there to watch. Width is the next limit. The darker inner shadow never stretches more than 269 kilometers across Earth. In miles, that width is 167. Your hometown therefore has a tiny chance of lying under a total eclipse. Average the wait for one spot on Earth and you get 370 years. Travel is the better plan for catching the Sun fully covered. Go where one is already expected. Hoping one visits you is the weaker plan. The next question is how anyone knows the time and the place. From space, that lunar shadow can be watched as it crosses Earth in a solar eclipse. Forecasting eclipses is an old goal. Sky watchers in ancient times tried it. Careful records were kept by many of them. A long cycle showed up in those records. They also tracked the Moon's path around Earth. Lunar eclipses could then be forecast with some accuracy. Solar eclipses stayed much harder. About 1,800 years ago, the skill reached China. It reached Greece as well. Ptolemy was one famous Greek who could do it. Say his name TAWL-uh-mee. He and the others of his age could get only within about a month. Ptolemy's fame was in mathematics. His fame was also in astronomy. His life was around ad 90 to 168.

8Accurate solar-eclipse forecasts began with an English astronomer. Edmond Halley was his name. His lifetime was the early ad 1700s. By his day, people knew Earth traveled around the Sun. True positions for Sun, Earth, and Moon made the math simpler. Hard work remained. A second English scientist eased that work. Isaac Newton was his name. He worked out the motion of solar-system objects. Gravity got a very detailed theory from him. Halley took those findings and calculated eclipses that had not happened yet. Newton's gravity laws can be put into computers now. Those machines let scientists forecast eclipses a long way ahead. Our picture of the universe changed because of Newton's gravity ideas. It changed because of his mathematics too. A picture shows a boy who herds animals, plus his goat. They are in Lebanon, watching the Sun go dark. Finding the right place is not the last task. Safety steps still have to be taken. Eyes can be harmed by a direct look at the Sun. On an ordinary day the Sun is too bright for a long look. Pain turns your face away. An eclipse lowers that brightness. A look can feel painless. Serious eye damage can still happen. So never aim your eyes straight at the Sun while an eclipse is on. Never aim them straight at the Sun at any other time.

9Indirect viewing is safest, and a pinhole projector does that job. The Sun's rays are focused by this simple tool. They land on a flat surface. That patch of light is safe to look at. Heed this warning. Bare eyes are not safe for a solar eclipse. Ordinary sunglasses are not safe either. A telescope is never the right tool for looking at one. Binoculars are never the right tool either. Magnifying the sight also magnifies the injury to your eyes. Special light filters offer another safe path. Cheap glasses made for eclipse watching are an example. Even those glasses should be used in short looks. A few seconds of looking is enough. Then look away for a few seconds. An adult should be with you when you use them. Care around the Sun can never be too great. The year 1999 brought a practice session in the United Kingdom. A crowd there tried protective glasses before an eclipse.

10Jupiter, a giant planet, has a small moon. That moon casts a shadow on Jupiter while it orbits. Eclipses are powerful events out in the cosmos. Awe still hits people of all ages who see them. The feeling is worldwide. Causes are understood now, thanks to science. Timing can be forecast with amazing accuracy, thanks to science. Mystery will probably remain for the people who watch. Magic will probably remain too. Watchers thousands of years ago had that same feeling. One photo lines up the Moon at gaps of five minutes. The eclipse in that photo was lunar. The place was upstate New York.

11Word meanings come last. Accuracy means how exact, correct, and precise something is. An astronomer is a scientist who studies objects in space, including planets, stars, and galaxies. A coincidence is an unplanned meeting in time of things that seem related. Cosmic means belonging to space past Earth. A light filter is a see-through material that stops some wavelengths of light. Obscured means hidden or covered over. An omen is an event people take as a clue about what will come. Orbited means moved in a path around some other object. Partial means having to do with a piece, not the entire thing. Predict means to tell a future event by using what already happened or what is happening now. A theory is an explanation someone offers before it has been shown to be true.

55. Ships the Sea Has Kept

1A world map marks eight famous losses. North America, Europe, Africa, the Atlantic Ocean, and the Pacific Ocean frame them. Antikythera is one mark. HMS Victory is another. So are Mary Celeste, HMS Erebus, and HMS Terror. SS Valencia, USS Cyclops, and SS Edmund Fitzgerald complete the set. Some marks show where a wreck lies. Some show the last known spot of a ship that vanished. One mark notes a ghost ship that sailors claimed to see. Coastlines and seafloors, the United Nations estimates, hold more than three million shipwrecks. Specialists in marine archaeology examine wrecks hundreds of years old. Some are thousands of years old. Treasure hunters chase other wrecks because of riches said to have gone down with them. In some cases a ship simply vanished. No clue was left to suggest what happened. Questions hide inside each wreck. What cargo was aboard? Where did the remains settle? What became of the people? Curiosity locks hardest onto one puzzle: what truly doomed the ship. These stories are full of danger. So are death, sunken treasure, and schemes. A mystery can yield if the clues are good. Most of the time, though, the clues stay hidden for years. Sometimes they stay hidden forever. The sea does not give its answers on a schedule. That is why a single wreck can occupy searchers for a lifetime, and why a missing ship can leave only a blank on the chart.

2In 1708 a British warship sank a Spanish galleon. Gold was aboard, and so were emeralds. The treasure was meant to pay for Spain's war against Great Britain. Nobody knew where the wreck lay, until a recent find. Searchers located it in 2015, off Colombia's coast. Ownership of that wreck, and of its treasure, has been a long dispute between Spain and Colombia. Value of the goods may reach 17 billion dollars. Few wrecks anywhere would outrank it in value. Divers in 1900 found a wreck near a Greek island. It was partly buried. It lay 55 meters down, a depth of 180 ft. No one knew the cause of the sinking. Greek archaeologists soon cared more about the date. Artifacts brought up showed a ship older than two thousand years. Amazing art was in the cargo. Luxury goods were in it too. One object has been called the earliest computer anyone knows. Gears in the device calculated exact places of the stars and of the planets. Research teams are still at work, more than 120 years after the discovery. A fragment of that ancient computer is the picture. HMS Victory launched in 1737. It carried 110 cannons. Great Britain's powerful navy had no finer ship. Victory was leading the fleet back toward Britain early in October 1744. The English Channel threw a fierce storm at the fleet. The rest of the fleet lost sight of Victory. Some 1,150 people vanished with the ship. Islanders close by heard booming cannons that night. The sound was a call for help from the sea. Rescue was impossible. The water was far too dangerous. Days later, pieces of the vessel washed onto island shores. The hull was not among them. The decking was not among them either. A painting by Thomas Butterworth shows the ship in wild seas. A company that salvages wrecks located the remains in 2008. Valuables were raised with respect, in a joint effort by that company and Britain's government. Another ship, still in naval service, is the oldest of its kind afloat. It bears the name HMS Victory.

3The cat Emmy was kept aboard a liner called the Empress of Ireland. She left the vessel twice on the day before it sailed from Canada. People read that behavior as a bad sign. A collision with another ship came the following day. Fourteen minutes was all it took to sink. Deaths numbered more than one thousand. Canada has no deadlier wreck on record. Vanishing without a seabed grave is an even stranger fate for some ships. Mary Celeste, a cargo ship, departed New York on November 7, 1872. The planned port lay in Italy. The vessel measured 30.1 meters, or 100 ft. Seven crew sailed on it. The captain sailed too, and so did his family. A month afterward, a British ship saw a vessel drifting on the Atlantic Ocean. It was Mary Celeste. A boarding party found nobody. Gear for navigation was gone. A lifeboat was gone. Nothing suggested violence. Cargo remained. Other gear remained. The captain's log ended with no hint of trouble. Captain, family, and crew were never seen again. With no answers, people invented accounts. Treachery shows up in those tales. Murder shows up. Sea monsters show up too. A painting by François Etienne Musin shows HMS Erebus trapped in ice. In 1845 the British navy launched the Franklin Expedition. The goal was a shorter shipping route between Europe and Asia. Two ships carried 129 people. The ships were HMS Terror and HMS Erebus. Whaling crews, two ships of them, sighted the pair in Canada's Baffin Bay on July 26, 1845. Two years then went by, and the commander sent no word. Fear for the explorers spread among officials. The public feared for them too.

4Rescue ships later found gear that had been abandoned. They found graves. They found notes that desperate crew members left on empty islands. Pack ice had trapped both ships in September 1846. The expedition's commander died the next June. Sick sailors, many of them dying, waited two years for ice to free the ships. Survivors finally attempted a desperate southward march in April 1848. They hoped to reach the Canadian mainland. Local Inuit, in 1855, told investigators about Europeans who had starved along the coast. Evidence showed the group had turned to cannibalism in order to live. A sonar-equipped ship found the Erebus in 2014. The wreck was well preserved. It lay in Arctic water 12 meters deep, or 40 ft. September 2016 brought the partner ship to light, and it too was well preserved. About 72 kilometers, equal to 45 mi., separated the two finds. A diver is shown exploring what remains of the Erebus. SS Valencia was among the most terrifying wrecks of all. Seattle was the steamer's goal in January 1906. The head count aboard was 173. The iron hull struck ground near Vancouver Island close to midnight on January 22. Once trapped, the ship took a pounding from the waves. Crew lowered lifeboats. Churning water capsized most of those boats. Freezing water took the people who were thrown in, and they drowned. High winds and high waves blocked rescue. Shore witnesses, horror-struck, were watching once thirty-six hours had passed since the stranding. The upper deck was swept by a huge wave. Dozens of passengers there were clinging on for their lives. Out of 136 passengers, the living numbered only 37. A lifeboat from Valencia is shown escaping the violent water. A few of the survivors ride in it.

5San Francisco is the port in a photo of Valencia taken eight years before the tragedy. This wreck's puzzle was not the how, the why, or the where. Bad decisions by the captain and the crew were the investigators' conclusion. Those choices put the ship and its passengers in danger. Later mysteries fed tales of the supernatural. In 1910, papers reported a ghostly Valencia that sailors said was sailing near where the ship had been lost. Another story traveled as rumor. The claim was that skeletons filled a lifeboat inside a nearby cave. Confirmation never arrived. Twenty-seven years had passed since the loss when, during 1933, a lifeboat from Valencia showed up in a nearby bay. Visitors can now see the nameplate. The place is British Columbia's Maritime Museum. USS Cyclops, shown in a photo, was a huge supply ship of the U.S. Navy. No noncombat event in U.S. naval history cost more lives than this disappearance. A heavy ore cargo came aboard in Brazil while the ship served in World War I. Captain W. Worley, still in Brazil, reported to superiors that repairs were needed on one engine. It was not operational. He was ordered to have it fixed after he reached the United States. Departure from Brazil came on February 22, 1918. The destination was Baltimore. 309 crew were aboard. Somewhere in the Atlantic Ocean, Cyclops vanished. Searchers have never recovered a single piece of wreckage. People of that time wondered if a submarine from Germany had sent it down. Captain Worley's German birth made some naval officials suspicious. A secret handover to the enemy was the suspicion, and it was never proved. No proof of that exists.

6Some ships in the Bermuda Triangle were sunk on purpose. Sea life gains from the artificial reefs those hulls become. A different theory starts from the place where Cyclops was lost. Ships are said to be swallowed by the Bermuda Triangle, an Atlantic region with that reputation. Supernatural explanations do not convince most naval experts. They believe the ship lacked full engine power. They also believe it was overloaded and unstable. A violent storm on March 10, they think, may have capsized it. The Bermuda Triangle is a region of the Atlantic Ocean. Bermuda is one corner. Puerto Rico is another. Florida's tip is the third. Legend says a high number of ships and aircraft vanish there without explanation. Rumors follow, about supernatural powers that sink ships or snatch them. Researchers have decided otherwise. Busy lanes elsewhere lose ships just as often, researchers have found. Caribbean islands, Puerto Rico, Bermuda, and Florida of the United States all appear around the triangle on a map. On November 9, 1975, the huge freighter SS Edmund Fitzgerald left Superior, Wisconsin. Iron ore filled the hold. A storm was in the forecast. The captain was not worried. Every ship was told to find shelter that afternoon, November 10, by the U.S. Coast Guard. Whitefish Bay, Wisconsin, became the ship's heading. Water was coming aboard, the captain reported around 7:00 p.m. A radio message added that the crew was still holding on. Moments later, radar no longer showed the ship. No lifeboat was launched. None of the twenty-nine crew members was found. The lake floor yielded the wreck to the Coast Guard a few days afterward. Half the hull had broken away from the other half. Investigators suspect three rogue waves in a row. The ship may have gone down so fast that no distress call was even possible. Researchers blame rogue waves for some shipping disasters that otherwise make no sense. The danger is that they cannot be predicted. Their size is part of the danger. Their power is part of it. A rogue wave appears from nowhere. Nearby waves are much smaller. Far offshore, high winds and strong currents usually build such a wave. A sudden jump in wave height can flip a large freighter.

7Ships carrying enslaved people, as many as one thousand of them, went down between the sixteenth century and the nineteenth. Discovery has still not come for most of them. They are still undocumented. Finding those ships, and the history they hold, is work taken up by several groups. The Slave Wrecks Project is one of them. Founding year for the project: 2008. Its first major recovery came in 2014. South Africa's Cape Town coast was where a sunken ship came to light. Danger has always ridden with anyone who sails. Oceans cover vast distances. Weather can turn foul without warning. Reefs often hide along coasts. Rocks often hide there too. Shipping is safer now than in any earlier age, thanks to modern gear. About two thousand people still die yearly in dozens of wrecks. Shipboard work remains one of the world's most dangerous jobs. Sailors trust their knowledge. They trust their skills. They trust the ships they serve. Sometimes luck decides their fate anyway. Every wreck leaves mysteries behind. Some mysteries can be explored and, in time, explained. Older wrecks may offer a glimpse of the past. Secrets of the sea, much of the time, stay hidden. A few words close the account. To run aground is to strike a shore or a bottom in some body of water. Use maritime for matters of the sea, of sailing, or of jobs carried out on water. Artifacts are objects people made or used long ago. Navigational has to do with guiding a course to a chosen end point. A boat has capsized when it rolls and its underside, or its side, points upward. Salvage is property saved from damage or destruction, or the recovery of a wreck or its cargo. Ships or vehicles that travel as one group, under a single command, form a fleet. When a ship sinks or is destroyed, the result is a shipwreck. The hull means that central structure: the bottom, the sides, and the deck. If science and nature's laws cannot explain a thing, people call it supernatural. Investigators are people who examine details to learn the facts. Betrayal, or a dishonest act, is treachery.

56. Small Clues That Catch Criminals

1A man crossed a field in a hurry. He went into an old mill. Workers in a mill crush wheat to make flour. Inside the building, the man killed someone. He rushed away. No person saw him leave. Police questioned him later. He kept saying that he was innocent. He might have gone free. He only needed to wipe the tiny proof off his shoes. That tiny proof is called trace evidence. Trace evidence can be dust. It can be hairs. It can be threads. It can be other very small bits of material. People find these bits on a suspect. They also find them near a victim. Edmond Locard was a detective. He studied the man's shoes with a microscope. He saw flour on the heels. He saw flour on the soles. No other person had noticed that flour. The flour matched the flour at the mill. The victim was killed at that mill. The matching flour put the man at the crime scene. That proof helped a court convict him of murder. A picture shows flour on the shoes, seen through a microscope.

2Forensic science caught the killer from the flour mill. Forensic science means using science to solve crimes. Courts also use that science to convict criminals. Around 1900, detectives began to use science on crimes. Before that year, police used eyewitnesses. They also used informers. Today, crime scene investigators matter in many cases. People call them CSIs. These workers do their study in a crime lab. A crime lab is a room full of science tools. The tools help workers find forensic evidence. The tools also help workers study that evidence. The first crime lab in the world opened in 1910. The lab was in Lyons, France. Police detective Edmond Locard created it. Locard had also solved the case of the flour mill. Locard gave scientists a guiding rule. He called the rule the Exchange Principle. Forensic scientists still follow that rule today. The rule says that things which touch always trade tiny traces. A person who enters a crime scene carries something away. That person also leaves something behind. A picture shows a forensic scientist looking at samples. The first case file is set in Oregon, in the U.S.A. The date is October 11, 1923. The crime was an attempt to rob a train. People called that train the Gold Special. Men's overalls were the clue that was left. The place was a lonely stretch of track. The track ran through southern Oregon. The year of the robbery was 1923. Bandits robbed a Union Pacific freight train. They killed the engineer. They killed two other train workers. They used a homemade dynamite bomb. The bomb blew open the mail car. In those years, mail often held stock certificates. It also held bond certificates. Sometimes the mail held cash. Sometimes it held gold. Police searched the scene. They found only one piece of evidence. Stains covered those overalls. One bandit had left the overalls behind. A picture shows that Union Pacific freight trains carried many goods. Those goods included food. They also included raw materials.

3The bandits stole a detonator from a construction site. They used too much dynamite. If money was inside the mail car, the blast ruined it. The clerk who worked for the Railway Post Office died in the blast. The noise was huge. The damage was huge. Panic sent the bandits running. They left without robbing any person of anything. A picture shows two men in 1924. They are studying dynamite and other explosives. Police asked Edward Heinrich for help. He led the forensic science laboratory in Berkeley, California. He was famous for learning a lot from very little proof. He told police whom to watch for. The person was a lumberjack. The lumberjack was left-handed. He was in his early twenties. He weighed about 166 pounds (75 kg). His height came to 5 feet plus 10 inches, or 1.8 m. His hair was light brown. He rolled his own cigarettes. He was unusually neat about his looks. Heinrich explained each clue from the overalls. The pocket on the left showed deeper wear than the one on the right. Heinrich read the uneven wear as proof of a left-handed owner. Tree sap had stained the overalls. The sap came from trees in the forests of southern Oregon. Lumberjacks work in those forests. The size of the overalls told the owner's height. The size also told his weight. A light brown hair was caught on a button. Heinrich used that hair to judge the owner's age. Tobacco shreds sat in a pocket. Nail clippings were caught in a seam. Those last clues told him the rest. Heinrich showed police one more find. It was a piece of paper. A rolled paper lay in the lowest corner inside a pocket. Many washings had bleached the paper clean. He treated the paper with iodine. Words began to show. The paper was a post office receipt. The man named on the receipt lived in Eugene, Oregon. Police went to that man's house. They learned that he was missing. His two brothers were missing too. Neighbors described the man. Their description matched Heinrich's description exactly. Years later, police found the brothers. The brothers confessed to the robbery. They confessed to the murders. A court sent them to prison. Heinrich solved some two thousand cases in his career. The railroad case was only one of them.

4The second case file could be set in any place in the U.S.A. The time is any time after 1950. The crime was a series of burglaries. The evidence was dirty dishes. Police believed one gang had done all the burglaries. Detectives at last found the gang's apartment. They raided it. The apartment was empty. Someone had wiped the whole place clean. The thieves had forgotten one job. They had not run the dishwasher. Police still needed the thieves' names. Who the thieves were could be read from their hands. Give the tips of your fingers a careful look. Look at the tips of your thumbs too. Skin there rises into ridges. The ridges run in patterns of curving lines. Those patterns are your fingerprints. Each print is different from your other nine prints. Each print is unique. No other person on Earth has prints like yours. No future person will have them either. In 1896, an Englishman found a way to sort fingerprints. His name was Edward Henry. By 1901 he held the post of police commissioner. He used his sorting system to identify criminals. Every print has ridges. Ridges are the raised lines. Every print also has furrows. Furrows are the low spots between ridges. Arches show up in prints. Loops show up too. Whorls show up as well. An arch can be tented. A tented arch is pointed at the top. An arch can be plain. A plain arch is rounded. A loop can be radial. A radial loop runs toward the thumb. A loop can be ulnar. An ulnar loop runs toward the little finger. A whorl is circular. Henry added smaller marks to his system. Those marks are called forks. Others are called dots. Others are called islands. Others are called hooks. Others are called bridges. The type of these marks helps make each print unique. Their number helps too. Their position helps too. A picture shows three main kinds of prints. Type 1 is an arch. Type 2 is a loop. Type 3 is a whorl. People still use Henry's basic system today. The Federal Bureau of Investigation keeps a huge set of prints. People call that bureau the FBI. Its database holds more than seventy million fingerprints. That set is the largest in the world. Prints from a crime scene can be checked fast. Workers compare them with every print in the databases. A match gives police a useful piece of evidence. The match puts a person at the crime scene. Criminals try hard not to leave fingerprints. In this burglary case, CSIs found prints on the dishes. The dishes were inside the dishwasher. The prints matched prints in the database.

5DNA sits in each cell of your body. It carries instructions. One job of the instructions is to guide how you live. They also tell your body how to grow. All people share about 98 percent of those instructions. The other 2 percent are different. That small part makes your DNA unique. Your fingerprints are unique in the same way. Unique DNA can be shown in tiny pictures made by X-ray. They call those pictures DNA profiles. Police have built computer databases of DNA profiles. Fingerprint databases work in a similar way. Almost any cell you have can yield DNA. Cells in your hair can give DNA. Cells in saliva can give it. Cells in blood can give it. Cells in sweat can give it. Cells in tears can give it. The technology is very advanced. A single skin cell could be enough to build a DNA profile. Workers can also build profiles from animal DNA. A database of cat DNA began in Great Britain in 2013. It can help link a cat hair on a victim to one suspect's cat. Pictures of DNA show a ladder shape that twists. The third case file is set in Indiana, in the U.S.A. The date is February 29, 2016. An online sale turned into a murder. The evidence was a digital trail. Not all evidence is tangible. Tangible evidence is something a person can pick up. A person can examine it. A person can take it to a crime lab for testing. In many cases, the evidence is digital. A court can treat emails as proof. Web searches can be used that way. GPS tracking information can be used that way. Rito Llamas-Juarez replied to an ad on a winter evening. Family members answered it with him. The ad was in an app. In that app, people connect to buy belongings. They also connect to sell belongings. Llamas-Juarez found a listing for two cell phones. The price was $500. His family contacted the seller. The seller used the name Sports. The meeting place they picked was a parking lot. Three men walked up to Llamas-Juarez and his family. One man shot Llamas-Juarez. The shot killed him. The shooter fled the scene.

6Crime scene investigators searched the scene. They found a smoked cigarette. A box that had held a cell phone was also there. The box came from the failed sale. It was in the car of Llamas-Juarez. Investigators searched a phone. That phone was the one the family used to set up the sale. Police got a warrant. Using a warrant, police made the app identify who held the Sports account. The account linked to a social media account. That account belonged to Larry Thomas. Investigators now had a suspect. A second warrant opened his house to a search. They found ammunition. Those rounds were the same kind fired during the killing. A swab took DNA from Thomas. His DNA matched the DNA on the cigarette. Fingerprints on the box matched Thomas too. Investigators also had digital evidence. They searched the cell phone of Thomas. They found the password for the Sports account. Thomas had emails from other possible buyers. Another key piece was a photo. The photo showed Thomas posing with a gun. The gun was the type used in the shooting. Forensic digital investigators did a large part of this work. A court found Thomas guilty of his crimes. Scientists can build a DNA profile for a suspect who is still unknown. After that, the search is for a profile that matches. A match might take years. Police keep a database for this search. It holds DNA profiles of people tied to other crimes. If they wish, people may place their DNA on genealogy websites. They may want facts about their ancestors. They may want to find unknown family members. Some of those websites let law enforcement upload crime scene DNA. Officers search there for matches. This new field is called investigative genetic genealogy. A match is not always exact. A close match lets investigators move toward a family. That family has ties to the DNA sample. Investigators follow family trees linked to the DNA. They use age as a clue. They use gender as a clue. They use known locations as a clue. Those clues help them decide who the suspect is. To be sure, they need a DNA sample from that person. The sample often comes from a suspect who does not know. It might be a used straw from the suspect's trash. It might be a coffee cup from that trash. DNA can help convict a suspect. DNA can also free a person who was convicted by mistake. Investigators now see a hard truth. Many convicted people are not the real perpetrators. Some of them are serving long sentences. Some are serving life sentences. Many people work hard to use DNA in a new way. They use it to free people who were convicted wrongly.

7Every case here turns on its own sort of forensic evidence. Other kinds exist too. Footprints can be evidence. Shoe prints can be evidence. Palm prints can be evidence. Lip prints can be evidence. Bite marks can be evidence. Paint chips can be evidence. Tire tread marks can be evidence. Markings on a bullet can be evidence. More kinds exist as well.
