Any of these can link a suspect to a crime scene. Any of them can also show who is innocent. Officers and scientists gather this evidence. They study it together. Their work uses nearly all of the sciences. The range runs from anthropology to zoology. Each worker may specialize in one science. They still share one habit. They use what they know to notice what other people miss. These words appear in the book. Convict means to prove that a person is guilty of a crime. Forensic science means the sciences that are used in a court of law. Those sciences often help prove guilt. They also often help prove innocence. A crime lab is a place for studying crime materials. Microscopes are used there. Chemicals are used there. Informers are people who secretly give facts about a crime. They often do it for a reward. A crime scene investigator is a law officer. That officer searches a crime scene for forensic evidence. A microscope is a device for viewing tiny objects. A suspect is a person believed to be guilty of a crime. A victim is a person who has suffered harm. A crime can be that act. A war can be that condition. An eyewitness saw an event happen. The event might be a crime. The event might be an accident. Fingerprints are the unique patterns on the tips of fingers. The same kind of patterns are on the tips of thumbs. Those patterns are made of ridges and furrows.

57. South Korea Up Close

1A packed market fills a street in Seoul. Shoppers crowd the stalls, and the photo shows how busy the capital can be. The country's formal name is the Republic of Korea. It is a small nation in East Asia. Measured flat, the land covers 99,720 square kilometers. The same area is 38,502 square miles. Iceland is slightly bigger, which helps picture the size. The Korean peninsula is home ground, and this nation holds the southern portion. Water borders three sides of that portion. Only one neighbor shares a land line, and that neighbor is North Korea on the north. Japan is the closest country to the east. China lies both north and west, but the sea sits between. Tsushima is a Japanese island. The water between that island and the Korean shore is the thinner gap, tighter than the wider seas nearby. On a map, Seoul is marked in the country. North Korea is drawn above the border. China is drawn beyond the water. Japan and Tsushima are drawn to the east. Little insets of Asia and Africa show where this corner of the world sits. Three wet sides and one land border explain the shape of daily travel. A trip toward Japan crosses water. A trip toward China crosses water too. A trip north meets North Korea on solid ground. The market crowd in Seoul is the human face of this compact country. The peninsula's southern seat is what lines the neighbors up as they are. Size, sea, and that single land border are the facts a first look should hold.

2Seoul, the capital, holds more than nine million residents. No other South Korean city is larger. It also ranks among the biggest cities on Earth. The site is the northwest, beside the Han River. Trade and business make today's Seoul modern. History makes it important too. Walls that first went up over six centuries ago still ring the downtown. Inside them stand palaces centuries old. Shrines stand there. Fortress gates and royal gardens stand there too. A humbler building also survives: the hanok, a traditional house. Winters here are bitterly cold, so the hanok was planned for comfort. Hot air travels in channels under a stone floor. That warmth is the heating system. Modern apartments house more than 60 percent of Seoul's people. Their floors are warmed by a system borrowed from the hanok idea. A palace from the group known as the Five Grand Palaces occupies the middle of the city. Respect shows up in daily manners. A photo from 2007 shows a boy waiting to shake the president's hand. In older custom, people rise if an elder enters the room. A younger person who will shake hands waits. The older person must offer a hand first. The population stands above forty-nine million. Most of them are in urban places. Korean is the national language. Chinese is also heard. Japanese is heard. English is heard. Some areas use a dialect, with its own words, phrases, or sounds. Until not long ago, big communities of Korean speakers lived only in the North and the South. Hangul, pronounced HAHNG-gul, has been the alphabet since the fifteenth century. Each Hangul letter matches one sound. Chinese writing is different, because a symbol there can stand for a whole word. Jobs in South Korea take many forms. The nation leads the world in computer-related technologies and in goods sold abroad. Manufacturing employs many people. They build electronics, medical devices, cars, and further items bound for other countries.

3After the regular school day, lots of students continue at a hagwon, pronounced HAH-gwon. Languages are studied there. Math is studied there. Music is studied there. Family holds a high place in Korean society. Two generations sometimes share one home. Three generations sometimes do. That pattern is growing less common. Traditional practice honors elders. It honors the family. People keep written records of family history. Holidays bring special food and special ceremonies. Many South Koreans treat education as the path to success and to power. Home life often turns around the children's schooling. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development compares its member nations. Korean pupils rank with the best readers in the group. They rank with the best problem solvers too. Religious life is varied. Christianity is practiced. Buddhism is practiced. Confucianism, shamanism, and Islam are practiced too. Hills and mountains cover most of the land. Only a little ground is flat enough to farm. The Taebaek Mountains, pronounced TE-bek, follow the eastern coast. Other ranges split off and run roughly from east to west. Most summits stay under 1,219 meters, or 4,000 ft. The highest is Mount Halla, also called Hallasan, at 1,950 meters, or 6,398 ft. It is an extinct volcano. The peak stands on Jeju. Jeju belongs to a pair of volcanic islands lying off the southern tip. The Han River and the Bukhan River cross the mapped north. The east coast runs fairly straight. Elsewhere, rivers and streams cut the shore into countless inlets. Those waters hold over 3,500 little islands.

4Streams and rivers line the narrow lowlands. Some of the world's highest tides rise there. At Incheon, the port near Seoul, the water level shifts by about 9 meters, or 30 ft. A three-story house could disappear under a change that large. Most rural residents live on the coastal plains and the inland plains. Those plains lie in the west and the south. The soil is fertile. Rice grows there. Vegetables grow there. A temperate setting gives the country four seasons. Winter averages about −6°C, or 21°F. Summer highs reach about 27 to 32°C, or 80 to 90°F. The rainy season arrives in summer. More than half the year's rain falls then. Typhoons sometimes strike in that season. Heavy floods are common. Rice fields, called paddies, do well in this climate. Written records for the whole Korean region, North together with South, go back over two thousand years. Human settlement reaches back at least ten thousand years. For a long time the region sat apart from much of the wider world. Historians believe the earliest Koreans arrived from Mongolia. They also point to Siberia. Control was the prize of many kingdoms. Invasions came from China. They came from the Mongolian Empire. They came from Japan. A treaty in 1905 was pressed onto Korea by Japan. Under that treaty, Japanese control began. Colony status followed in 1910, again imposed by Japan. Speaking Korean was banned in those years. Practicing religion was banned too. Marching was one way people protested. Holding on to traditions was another. Control by Japan lasted until that empire gave up at the close of the Second World War. Each August 15, people celebrate the freedom that followed. Students mark the day by waving the nation's flag.

5Soldiers from the South patrol the border. Once World War II had finished, the United Nations planned to give Korea self-rule again. In that period, the United States military held the southern half of the peninsula. The Soviet Union held the northern half. Democratic elections were ordered by the United Nations. South Korea held them. North Korea set up a communist government instead. In 1948, the United Nations accepted the South's government as the sole lawful government for the Korean region. Invasion from the North came two years later. The aim was to force the split nation back together. The Korean War took 2.5 million lives. Both countries were left in ruins. A cease-fire was signed in 1953. What remained was a separation, a band 4 kilometers across, equal to 2.5 mi. No official peace treaty has ever been signed. More than 25,000 American troops remain stationed in the South. Until the middle of the twentieth century, the South was a farming society. Many holidays follow the moon calendar. The most important is New Year's Day, Seollal, pronounced SAHL-lahl. People eat tteokguk, pronounced DAWK-gook, a soup of rice cakes. Everyone is treated as one year older. Gifts, games, and fortune-telling fill the day. Chuseok is a harvest celebration, and it matters deeply. Families reunite. They visit family tombs. Food is left as an offering for the dead. A baby's first birthday is a large party. Parents set objects in front of the child and let the child pick a favorite. A book means the child will be smart. Money means the child will be wealthy. Plenty of food at the party stands for prosperity. Parents are shown holding their baby at that first birthday.

6There are probably hundreds of different kinds of kimchi. It is a pickled vegetable dish, and it is usually very spicy. Cabbage kimchi is among the favorites. Radish kimchi is another. Cucumber kimchi is another. Water kimchi is another. Squid kimchi is served as well. Some kind of kimchi accompanies nearly every traditional meal. South Korean cooking is bright and full of flavor. Kimchi, close to a spicy sauerkraut, shows up at nearly every traditional meal. Rice does too. Fish and other seafood matter in the cuisine. So do pounded rice cakes called tteok, pronounced DAWK. A local saying claims that food is the best medicine. The meaning is simple. Health can come from what people eat. Sickness can come from it too. Seaweed is a birthday food, and many people believe it improves health. Some women who are expecting a baby eat seaweed. They hope it will help the birth go well. Other foods are thought to bring luck, or a strong harvest. On the winter solstice, people eat porridge that mixes rice with red beans. The aim is to welcome spring. At night, the busy capital, Seoul, shines. From crowded cities to rough mountains and rich plains, South Koreans have shared one culture for centuries. That culture prizes hard work. It prizes respect for family and for elders. Today's industrial economy is worth a trillion dollars. Few economies anywhere are stronger. The country now counts as a modern power among nations. Its people face a bright future.

7Figures from 2021 list the population as 51,715,162. The land measures 99,720 square kilometers, or 38,502 sq. mi. Seoul is the capital. Korean is the primary language. Christianity and Buddhism are the primary religions. The currency is the won. A few words from this portrait are worth pinning down. A cease-fire is a deal to pause the fighting in a war for a time. Communist describes support for a system in which the state runs the economy. Culture means what a group believes and how that group usually lives. Democratic describes government by the people, using elections that are free and frequent. A dialect is a language form used in one region or by one group. Exported describes goods sold in some other country or area. Extinct, for a volcano, means it has not erupted for thousands of years and shows no sign it will. Generations are stretches of about twenty to thirty years between parents and their children. A harvest is the season when crops are picked and brought in. Inlets are narrow water fingers leading from a larger water into the land. Typhoons are violent rotating storms. Heavy rain comes with them. High winds come with them. They form near the Indian Ocean or the western Pacific. Urban describes cities or towns and the residents in them. South Korea's story ends on that mix of land, work, and family respect.

58. Strange Tales: Proof or a Trick?

1An amateur photographer took a picture in 1952. Many people thought it showed an alien spacecraft. Do you think the picture is real? Or do you think it is a fake? This book moves through these parts. An introduction comes first. Bigfoot comes next. Crop circles follow. The curse of the mummy comes after that. The Bermuda Triangle comes next. A conclusion and word meanings close the book. Would you believe a story about hairy giants in our wilderness? Would you believe that extraterrestrials make strange designs in wheat fields? What if a friend told you an ancient curse causes people to die? What if something in a part of the Atlantic Ocean makes ships disappear? What would tell you whether these stories were true? A young king's tomb raises a question. Was it protected by a curse? After reading this book, you will have evidence about four unsolved mysteries. You can decide whether you think they are real. What person or force has drawn such detailed designs across acres of fields? Is there an explanation for the mysterious losses of ships and planes?

2A map key uses one mark for each Bigfoot sighting. The map shows Washington. It shows Oregon. It shows the United States. Bigfoot stories come from remote areas of the Pacific Northwest. Native Americans have told stories about gigantic creatures for hundreds of years. The creatures are mysterious. They are apelike. The Salish peoples of Canada called them Sasquatch. That name means wild man of the woods. Bigfoot is the name English speakers use most often. Other people have reported encounters with this creature. Railway workers have reported them. Forest workers have reported them. Hikers, travelers, and people who live in remote areas have reported them. The Native American stories are unknown to most of them. A Bigfoot is reported to be as tall as 8 feet, which is 2.4 meters. It is covered with hair. Its weight is estimated from the depth of its tremendous footprints. The estimate is between 350 and 800 pounds. That range is 160 to 360 kilograms. People who see one frequently report a sound. They hear high-pitched screams. They also report a smell. The smell is a foul odor. Cryptozoologists have spent a lot of time on the question. A few other people have spent a lot of money too. Cryptozoologists are scientists who study animals that may or may not exist. They want to find out whether Bigfoot really exists. They have followed up on thousands of eyewitness reports. They have not yet found proof. A height chart compares three figures. A grizzly is 9 feet, or 2.74 meters. Bigfoot is shown at 8 feet, or 2.44 meters. A human is 6 feet, or 1.83 meters. Lower marks show 4 feet, or 1.22 meters, and 2 feet, or 0.61 meters. Bigfoot is believed to be smaller than a grizzly bear. Bigfoot is believed to be taller than the average human.

3In 1924, a lumberjack went into the mountains alone. He went to prospect for gold. During the third night of his trip, something huge carried him off. It was smelly. He was in his sleeping bag. Later, it dropped him in a clearing. Four other apelike creatures surrounded him. The group looked like a family. He escaped after nearly a week. He was badly shaken. He was unharmed. Only one Bigfoot encounter is described in this report. Roger Patterson took a picture in 1967. Is it a Bigfoot? Is it a bear? Is it a human in a gorilla suit? In the vast forests of the northwestern United States, nature works fast. Glaciers are there too. Nature quickly gets rid of dead bodies. Scientists still believe something. If Bigfoot does exist, someone should be able to find remains. A dead body would do. A skeleton would do. Fossil remains would do. Nothing has ever been found. In 1977, a Bigfoot sighting in northern Washington turned out to be a hoax. Three young men had planned it. This makes some people think other reports must have been faked as well. Do you think the Bigfoot sightings are real? Or do you think they are a hoax? Crop circles are the next mystery. Strange circles of flattened plants in fields were reported as early as 1590. Farmers thought the wind made them. In the 1980s, the number of circles increased. The circles changed to more intricate designs. A very large size is common among crop circles. One consisted of 149 circles. It appeared near Stonehenge. It appeared within 20 minutes. It appeared in broad daylight. Most crop circles form mysteriously at night. A few people report a different sight. They say they have seen circles being formed by spaceships. Others say whirlwinds formed them. Sometimes lights are seen in the sky. Humming is heard. Music is heard. Inside the circles, radiation is sometimes found. Crops inside the circles stay uncrushed. The bend is at the lowest node on the stalk. Plants outside the circles often grow less well than these bent crops. Experiments suggest a possible cause. Microwave beams might cause the circles. It is not clear where the beams would come from. Some people think the circles are messages from outer space. In areas where many circles are found, some people watch the fields at night. They watch for signs of activity. A few minutes, they say, is enough time for a complicated circle pattern to appear.

4Many crop circles are made by humans. The reasons vary. Some people just want to prove that it can be done. Others want to play tricks. In 1991, two Englishmen made a claim. Their names were Doug Bower and David Chorley. They claimed they had made every crop circle since 1978. Some people accepted the explanation of their hoax. Others doubted their skill. They doubted the men had the strength to create huge patterns at night. They doubted the men could do it without being seen. Seven years later, Doug took back his confession. Some people suggest that tornadoes create the circles. Crop circle designs are controlled. They are intricate. Tornadoes destroy a wide area. Another weather theory uses a type of whirlwind. It is called a plasma vortex. A plasma vortex can create the lights reported by eyewitnesses. It can create the sounds. It can hover in one place. It can move as if it is under remote control. That movement could make it look like a UFO. Some researchers have suggested a military test. They say the military is developing a high-energy weapon. The weapon is powered by microwaves. In this scenario, crop circles are produced by tests of this weapon. The weapon is top secret. Do you think crop circles are real? Or do you think they are a hoax? The curse of the mummy is the next mystery. In 1922, Howard Carter discovered a tomb. Egyptian workers helped him. The tomb belonged to the Egyptian pharaoh Tutankhamun. He is known today as King Tut. Incredibly valuable treasures filled the tomb. Newspapers circulated stories of a curse. They said the curse was painted on a tomb wall. The words said that they who enter this sacred tomb shall swiftly be visited by wings of death. Lord Carnarvon paid for Carter's search for the tomb. When Lord Carnarvon died in 1923, newspapers gave a cause. They said a pharaoh's curse killed him. The newspapers reported a count of deaths. Twenty-six people involved with finding the tomb died in the first ten years. Suspicious circumstances were suspected in many of these deaths. This mystery has been used as the theme for many movies. It has been used in books and games. A picture shows Howard Carter with Lord Carnarvon. Carnarvon funded the search for King Tut's tomb. The search was in an area of Egypt called the Valley of the Kings.

5In the early 1900s, reporters sometimes invented facts. They wanted to make stories more exciting. Before Lord Carnarvon died, he had in fact been sick for twenty years. His death may have come at that time by coincidence. Research shows a smaller count. Only six people involved with finding the tomb died in the first ten years. Howard Carter worked on the tomb for at least ten years. He lived for seventeen years after the discovery. No such curse was written in the tomb, despite the reports. Valuable treasures were packed inside King Tut's tomb. Dead bodies might produce bacteria. Those bacteria could cause illness and death. Might this have played a part in Lord Carnarvon's death? Tomb robbers of early times might have fallen ill for this reason. Stories of a curse may have begun in this way. Early Egyptians believed something about kings. Kings should be buried with riches to use in their next life. These Egyptians may have started legends of danger. The legends would keep people away from the tombs. Do you think the curse of the mummy is real? Or do you think it is a hoax? The Bermuda Triangle is the next mystery. A map shows Canada, the United States, Bermuda, the Bahamas, Miami, San Juan, Mexico, and Puerto Rico. Some people include a larger area when they describe strange events in the Atlantic Ocean. Strange things have been happening to ships in one part of that ocean. Planes have had trouble there too. The area lies between Florida, Bermuda, and Puerto Rico. In 1965, Vincent Gaddis wrote a book about these strange occurrences. The book was called Invisible Horizons. The name Bermuda Triangle was first used by him for this area. Triangle of Death was another name he used. Numerous planes disappear in this area. Ships disappear too. Crews vanish from ships. Dense fogs suddenly appear. Compasses stop working. Navigation equipment stops working. On a clear day in 1945, a group of planes was on a routine training mission. All of them lost their bearings. They disappeared. The airship sent to rescue them vanished as well.

6In 1918 the USS Cyclops vanished. It had 306 people on board. Among the earliest incidents tied to the Bermuda Triangle is this one. In 1881, the merchant ship Ellen Austin made a discovery. It found a ghost ship floating without a crew. A crew boarded to steer the ship to port. A thick fog surrounded both ships. By the next day, the second crew was gone from the ghost ship as well. In 1966, Captain Donald Henry was towing a cargo barge. His tug was the Good News. The barge was going from Puerto Rico to Florida. A dense fog suddenly swirled around the barge. The Good News lost the use of all of its instruments. It partially lost power. For five minutes, the ship struggled. It was in a tug-of-war with the fog bank. It finally managed to pull itself free. It pulled the barge free too. People claim that a mysterious power causes the many losses. Ships are lost in the Bermuda Triangle. Crews are lost there. A UFO capture is what some people blame for humans being taken away. Others say the unexplained losses come from severe weather. That weather is common in the area. A destroyed vessel would go down and leave no trace. After being rescued, some of the missing crews tell stories. They say they were forced to leave their storm-damaged ships. Some people insist that nothing unusual is going on in the area. They suggest a location error. Some of the losses blamed on the Bermuda Triangle actually happened several hundred miles away. Some vessels reported lost showed up again later. Do you think the Bermuda Triangle is real? Or do you think it is a hoax? In the vast ocean, violent weather could destroy a ship. It might not leave any evidence.

7Two more mysteries wait beyond the four in this book. Rapa Nui is also known as Easter Island. How were the moai statues carved? How were they moved? Stonehenge raises another pair of questions. Why were these structures built? How were they built? Mysteries will always exist. Some people will think they are nonsense. Others will claim they are real. You have now read evidence about four of them. It is time to consider what you have read. Decide what you believe. You can use the Internet to find more information. You can use the library too. Keep in mind that some sources can be trusted more than others. What do you think about these mysteries? What others can you find? These words help with the book. Encounters are unexpected meetings, conflicts, or experiences. Evidence is something that supports a theory or claim. Extraterrestrials are beings from outside Earth or its atmosphere. A hoax is something meant to mislead or trick. To hover is to stay in one place in the air. Intricate means very detailed or complicated. It means complex. A microwave is an electromagnetic energy wave. It is shorter than a radio wave. It is longer than infrared radiation. It is often used in heating and in radar devices. Mysteries are things that are unknown or difficult to understand. A node is the place on the stem of a plant from which a leaf or branch grows. A pharaoh is a ruler in ancient Egypt. Plasma is charged particles of gas that can conduct electricity. Retracted means took back or withdrew.

59. Sunday of the Championship Game

1History and the early games come before the modern game and its records. A weak beginning comes first. Growth of the game comes after that. A stunning score comes next. The fun around the game follows. Then comes the show. A closing comes last. The opening picture shows James Harrison in a Pittsburgh uniform. His team is the Steelers. He is taking the ball away inside the scoring area called the end zone. From there he begins a run that will set a record. The score he is chasing will cover 100 yards. Arizona's team, the Cardinals, is behind. The scoreboard reads 10 for Pittsburgh and 7 for Arizona. The first half has eighteen seconds left. Arizona holds the ball. Only one yard remains before a Pittsburgh score. The Steelers are the team defending that yard. The snap goes to Kurt Warner. He is an all-star at quarterback. He moves backward from the line. His throw goes to a teammate who is waiting for a catch that would mean a score. The play looks simple. A score seems sure. Wait. James Harrison, a Pittsburgh linebacker, pulls the ball from the air. He races along the sideline. He steps around some tacklers. He pulls free from others. He passes the 50-yard line. He reaches the 40. He reaches the 30. He reaches the 20. He reaches the 10. Touchdown!

2Harrison's run covered the whole field before he scored. The play is hard to believe. It was an interception returned 100 yards for a score. Inside the Tampa, Florida, stadium, 75,000 fans erupt. Across the country, 100 million Americans have just seen football history. That crowd is one-third of the nation. The date was Sunday, February 1, 2009. The game was Super Bowl 43. Anyone watching saw the longest touchdown ever in a Super Bowl. They also saw one of the finest Super Bowls ever played. Arizona was the underdog. That team trailed 17-7. Arizona fought back. Late in the fourth quarter, Arizona led 23-20. Then Pittsburgh scored. Only 35 seconds remained. The final score was 27-23 for the Steelers. No club had more of these championships than Pittsburgh did after that win. The total stood at six. Famous players are part of the day. Famous plays are part of the day. Famous clubs are part of the day. A giant crowd watches in the seats and on screens. Put those pieces together and you have this championship game. The Tampa stadium in the picture is full of fans.

3A lineup chart shows where players stand. A line called the line of scrimmage crosses the field. One side is the defense. That side has a defense end zone. The other side is the offense. A referee stands with them. Each short label has a longer name. CB means cornerback. WR means wide receiver. TE means tight end. DE means defensive end. S means safety. LB means linebacker. LT means left tackle. DL means defensive lineman. LG means left guard. C means center. QB means quarterback. TB means tailback. FB means fullback. RG means right guard. RT means right tackle. Only eleven players from a team may be on the field at one time. Fans mark Super Bowl Sunday with parties. They also mark it with barbecues. The Super Bowl is the year's biggest football game. It is more than a sports contest. People treat Super Bowl Sunday like a national holiday, though it is not an official one. Friends gather. Families gather. They watch the game. They cheer their team. They enjoy the day. Some parties last all day. In the city that hosts the game, the celebrating can last a week. Fans often wear team jerseys. Some fans paint team colors on their faces. On that Sunday, lots of fans travel by car to the place where the game is played. They go for tailgate parties. A tailgate party is a big outdoor barbecue. It is held in a parking lot.

4People all over the country get a reason to celebrate because of this game. Football is a game of the United States. It is also a way to show civic pride. People show that pride for a team's home city. People show that pride for a team's home state. One picture shows a fan of the Packers, the club from Green Bay. A cheesehead sits on his head at the game. Bruce Springsteen was the halftime performer in 2009. The Super Bowl is a show the whole world can watch. About 100 million people in the United States watch it. Millions more watch in almost every country. Some viewers do not care much about football. They still turn on the live halftime show. At Super Bowl 43, the famous performer was Bruce Springsteen. He is a legend of rock and roll. U2 has taken that stage. So has the band known as the Rolling Stones. So has Prince.

5Television ads are another reason people watch. Many of those ads are made to air for the first time on this game. A single ad of 30 seconds can cost an advertiser over $3 million. One commercial during this game showed Britney Spears. Pepsi was the product in that ad. The game did not always bring in so much money. The first game was in 1967. A commercial then cost just $40,000. The audience that day was just 24 million people. Nobody called the game the Super Bowl yet. Its name was the AFL-NFL World Championship. Halftime music that day came from marching bands. The first game had lots of action. It also had a marching band at halftime.

6The picture of the first game shows many empty seats. That game was at the Los Angeles Coliseum. The calendar said January 15 in the year 1967. Green Bay's Packers came out on top. Kansas City's Chiefs were the losers. The winners had 35 points. The losers had 10. Attendance was above 60,000. Even so, 40,000 seats stayed empty. Empty seats like that are hard to imagine now. Today, the cheapest Super Bowl seats can cost thousands of dollars. Big college games had drawn fans from the 1880s on. A pro league called the National Football League formed in 1920. People shorten that name to NFL. From 1960 until 1989, Pete Rozelle was the NFL's leader. Credit for inventing this championship game often goes to him. Near the end of the 1950s, twelve clubs made up the NFL. Fans seemed to want still more football. Two businessmen from Texas started another league in 1960. That league was the American Football League, or AFL. Eight clubs joined that new league. At the start, the NFL did not respect the AFL. Within a few years, the leagues were rivals. They both wanted players. They both wanted fans. In 1966, a plan took shape to join the leagues into one. A special game was set to stir interest in that coming mix. The top club from the NFL would meet the top club from the AFL. The meeting would come when the season was over. Until the next season started, fans would still have this game on their minds. The winning Super Bowl team receives the Vince Lombardi Trophy. The name honors a famous coach, Vince Lombardi. His club was the Packers from Green Bay. It is made of sterling silver. It weighs seven pounds.

7Pete Rozelle wanted a plain name for the AFL-NFL showdown. He wanted to call it The Big One. Hunt hoped for a name that felt more exciting. He wanted a name with more bounce. Hunt helped found the AFL. He owned the Kansas City Chiefs. He thought of Super Bowl after watching his children play. Their toy was a SuperBall. The maker of that toy was Wham-O. The word Bowl came from stadium shape. Many college football stadiums are rounded. One famous example is the Rose Bowl. It stands in Pasadena. That city is in California. An NFL team, the Green Bay Packers, won the first Super Bowl with ease. The Packers also won the second one with ease. Some people wondered if the AFL could not keep up. Joe Namath answered that doubt. People called him Broadway Joe. He was young, and he played quarterback. His club was the Jets from New York. He bragged about a Jets victory in championship game number three. The opponent was the Baltimore Colts. The Colts were the heavy favorites. Namath backed his words with a bet. The Jets beat the Colts in an upset. The score was 16-7. From then on, the Super Bowl was the place where football bragging rights were settled. Joe Namath led that famous win. A field is sometimes nicknamed a gridiron. The nickname fits because the lines look like a grate. That kind of grate is used for broiling food.

8Fans' interest in the Super Bowl rose fast. Super Bowl 5 was tense until the end. The winning play came in the last five seconds. The score was tied 13-13. Jim O'Brien, the placekicker for the Baltimore Colts, kicked a field goal. That kick won the game. During the 1970s, Pittsburgh's Steelers grew into a power. People call that run a dynasty. The team caught fans' imaginations. In a stretch of six seasons, that club took four of these titles. Today the NFL has thirty-two teams. News coverage of the playoff games adds excitement. Those games lead to the final showdown. In one picture, Jim O'Brien leaps with joy after the kick that won the game. A set of famous moments belongs in Super Bowl history. One moment is called the Steeltown dynasty. From 1975 through 1980, Pittsburgh's club collected four of these championships. That stretch covered six years. Another moment is a rushing record. The runner was Timmy Smith. He played for the Washington Redskins. He set the mark. He ran for 204 yards in 1988. Rushing yards means yards gained while running with the ball. Another moment is a receiving record. The receiver was Jerry Rice. His club was the San Francisco 49ers. He set the mark. He gained 215 receiving yards in 1989. Receiving yards means yards gained by catching passes. Another moment came down to the last moments. In 1991, New York's Giants edged Buffalo's Bills. The score was 20-19. The Buffalo Bills were a strong team in the early 1990s. Four times running, they took the AFC title. They lost every Super Bowl they played in those years. They played in four.

9The year's biggest football game comes with high hopes. The fun is that nobody knows what will happen. Game number 24 was one-sided. San Francisco's 49ers rolled past Denver's Broncos. The score was 55-10. A year later, the championship was about as close as this game gets. The New York Giants barely got past the Buffalo Bills. The score was 20-19. This year the lead might swing back and forth. The ending might come in the last seconds. This year might bring the first Super Bowl shutout. It might bring some other surprise no one can foresee. When the game arrives, sit by the TV. Sit with family. Sit with friends. Have favorite foods nearby. Get ready to mark Super Sunday in a big way. In the picture, a New England Patriots fan puts on a game face. These words have special meanings. Civic describes something about a city, about citizenship, or about community affairs. A dynasty is a line of rulers from one family in a country. Here the word is used as a figure of speech. Festivities are parties or festivals. An interception is a play in which a player from the other team catches a pass or takes it away. To merge is to join into one. To root is to cheer for someone or to show support. A spectacle is an unusual or striking public sight or event. Trounced means beaten by a wide margin. An underdog is the side expected to lose a contest.

60. The Biggest Birds Alive

1When an ostrich runs, it uses half as much energy as a human uses. A size chart can set an ostrich beside a person. Ostrich height on the chart is 9 feet, or 2.74 meters. Ostrich weight on the chart is 350 pounds, or 158.8 kilograms. Human height on the chart is 6 feet, or 1.8 meters. Human weight on the chart is 175 pounds, or 79.4 kilograms. The bird in front of you is huge. It is powerful. It acts like it has a job to do. That bird is an ostrich. It is the largest bird living in the world today. It is a far different creature from the delicate songbirds many people imagine. An ostrich can keep running for a very long distance. An ostrich can also deliver a heavy kick. Bother its feathers and you will land in serious trouble.

2Ostriches are the giants among birds. An adult male can reach 9 feet when his neck is stretched out. That height is 2.7 meters. He can weigh as much as 350 pounds. That weight is 160 kilograms. A female is slightly smaller than a male. She is still enormous. Color makes a grown male simple to separate from a grown female. A bold mix of black and white covers the males. Females are grayish-brown. Juveniles are grayish-brown too. Some ostriches have pink necks. Some have pink thighs. A male and a female take turns watching the chicks. They keep watch until the chicks are full grown. The main toe lets an ostrich run fast. A sharp claw grows on that toe. The claw measures 4 inches, which is 10 centimeters. Ostriches differ from most birds because they cannot fly. Even so, they are the fastest birds on foot. They can hold 30 miles per hour over a long distance. That speed is 48.2 kilometers per hour. They can sprint as fast as 45 miles per hour. That speed is 72.4 kilometers per hour. A large body does not stop them from being agile. They can spin in a very tight turn. Their wings help them balance in that turn. They are the only birds in the world with two toes. Each foot runs on its longer toe. The other toe is used for balance.

3An ostrich still counts as a bird for several reasons. Its eyes are five times bigger than a human's eyes. Nostrils on its bill help it breathe. It cannot fly, yet its feathers keep it warm. Its wings help it balance during a run. Its eggs are the largest eggs of any bird. They are also the thickest. Each foot carries only two toes. All birds share a set of traits. All birds have a backbone. All birds have feathers. All birds have wings. All birds have a bill. All birds lay eggs. All birds are warm-blooded. Ostrich feathers are unusual next to most other feathers. Most birds grow stiff feathers. A strong spine runs down the middle of those feathers. Ostrich feathers are soft and fluffy instead. By day the feathers protect these giants from sunlight. At night the feathers keep them warm. Most birds have a gland that helps when they clean themselves. The gland spreads oil over the feathers. The oil makes the feathers waterproof. Ostriches do not have this gland. A rainstorm can soak them all the way to the skin. Their eyes are enormous. The eyes are the largest of any land animal. Each eye measures almost 2 inches across, which is 5 centimeters. The brain is about the same size as one eye. That is quite small for such a huge animal. Dr. Carole Price is a veterinarian who cares for ostriches. She says these birds are as dumb as rocks in a box. She says they run or they fight. She says they do not think. They are curious about everything around them. They feel they must check a new thing out. A wrinkle in a person's T-shirt can draw that curiosity. Sparkly jewelry can draw it too. One of these big birds earned a nickname, The $10,000 Ostrich. It plucked a diamond earring from its owner and swallowed it.

4Ostriches live in the deserts of Africa. They also live on African savannas. A savanna is flat grassland with few trees. A range map places them in Africa near the equator. The Atlantic Ocean lies beside that part of the world. The Indian Ocean lies beside it too. A wider map shows Europe and Asia to the north. The places ostriches live are dry. Daytime heat there is extreme. Nighttime temperatures are cold. Ostriches live in herds. A herd usually holds fewer than twelve birds. Now and then a group of one hundred or more may gather. They gather near a watering hole. Life in a herd lets them use teamwork to stay safe. Good vision helps them notice danger from far away. Long necks help with that far look too. A rooster is the dominant male. The herd is under his command. He makes a roaring call that sounds like boo-boo-BOOhoo. The call warns the flock that danger is nearby. He also uses the call to intimidate other males. He uses it to impress the females, who are called hens. The dominant male performs an elaborate courtship dance for the main hen. He bows. He shakes one wing at a time. He moves his tail up and then down. Then he holds his wings out. He comes toward the female while he stamps his feet. Showing his feathers is part of that courtship dance.

5The legs of an ostrich do not bend the way human legs bend. Many other animals bend their legs in that human way too. An ostrich's legs bend forward. The forward bend produces a powerful kick. Ostriches can hold their own against predators. The kick is how they do it. The kick is so strong that one blow can kill a full-grown lion. If an ostrich cannot fight, and cannot flee, it has another defense. It lies down. It lays its long neck on the ground. It stays still in that position. Staying still makes it less visible. This defense gave rise to a myth. The myth claims that these birds push their heads under the sand. They do not do that. Ostriches do not need to drink water. The plants they eat give them enough water. Ostriches are omnivores. An omnivore eats both plants and animals. Their typical foods are leaves, seeds, and roots. They also eat lizards and snakes. They also eat rodents and insects. If they are hungry, they eat any other food they can find. Their diet changes through the year. Food is sometimes scarce. Their intestines have evolved to be extra long. The extra length helps them take as many nutrients as possible from their food. The intestines measure 46 feet, which is 14 meters. That is almost twice the length of human intestines. These giant birds swallow pebbles and sand. The pebbles and sand help grind food inside the gizzard. A gizzard is a special organ used for digestion.

6The dominant male digs a shallow pit in the dirt. The pit is for the main hen to lay her eggs. Six eggs or more go from one female into a low dip in the sand. Every female in the herd places her eggs in the main hen's nest. The main hen sits on the eggs during the day. The dominant male takes the night duty. About forty days pass before the eggs hatch. Grown ostriches are left alone by most other animals. The eggs can still be stolen by predators. Vultures may take the eggs. Jackals may take them. Hyenas may take them. Those same hunters may also take young ostriches. A chick is the size of a full-grown chicken when it hatches. Both the male and the female share the job of raising the chicks. The dominant male protects them by distracting predators. He also teaches the chicks which foods to eat. The young birds grow about 1 foot each month, which is 30 centimeters. By the age of six months they are close to adult size. Ostriches can live to age fifty or even older. Ostrich numbers dropped sharply in the 1700s. They dropped sharply in the 1800s as well. People hunted them for their feathers. Long ago those feathers were used in women's fashion. People also hunted them for food and for leather. People hunted them to make feather dusters. Ostrich farming began in 1838. After farming started, some wild herds recovered. Becoming endangered is not a present danger for wild ostriches. Ostriches are now farmed around the world. Farms raise them for meat, leather, feathers, and eggs. They lay the biggest eggs in the world. One ostrich egg weighs as much as two dozen eggs from a chicken. An ostrich egg measures about 6 inches long, which is 15 centimeters. It weighs about 3 pounds, which is 1.5 kilograms. Ostriches are among the closest living relatives of Tyrannosaurus rex. A scientist found a bone from Tyrannosaurus rex. He compared the cells in that bone with cells from twenty-one modern animals. The closest match was with ostriches and chickens.

7A female ostrich chases a rival away from her place. Unlike most other birds, ostriches are not timid. They are not delicate. They are not easily startled. These creatures are bold and sturdy. They hold their ground when they are challenged. They are agile runners. They are masterful fighters. They carry a whole set of fascinating adaptations. Put simply, they are the biggest and the toughest birds in the world. A few word meanings belong with their story. Adapted means changed so a living thing fits a certain place or a certain way of life. Dominant means more powerful, more effective, or more important than the others. Endangered means at risk of disappearing completely. A gizzard is a bird organ that grinds food and breaks it down. To intimidate is to frighten someone or to overwhelm that someone. Juveniles are young people, or young animals, that have not reached maturity yet. Omnivores are animals that eat plants and also eat other animals. Predators are animals that hunt other animals and eat them in order to live. Savannas are flat grasslands that have few trees.

61. The Boxer Who Took a New Name

1A 1963 photo shows Cassius Clay as a punch lands. Patrick Power, a British boy of six, is the one throwing it. Boxing lessons were Patrick's way to stand up to bullies. Another photo places Clay beside Sonny Liston before a championship bout. The place was Miami Beach, Florida. The day was February 24, 1964. In that year, Sonny Liston held the heavyweight crown. He was so hard to beat that some fighters feared stepping in with him. Cassius Clay was the latest man to challenge him. Almost nobody looked for a Clay victory. The usual boxer stayed planted and swung with power. Clay's method was different. His feet stayed busy, and his punches came in quick bursts. He wrote a poem of insults before they met. In it, a blow sends Liston flying off the planet. Fans, the poem suggested, would feel they had watched a person shot into orbit.

2Those insults left Liston too furious to stay calm once the bell rang. Because Clay was nimble, Liston's biggest swings missed. Quick jabs, meanwhile, drained Liston's strength. When the sixth round ended, Liston stopped the fight. Cassius Clay left the ring as heavyweight champion of the world. More of the story still lay ahead. He would soon answer to Muhammad Ali, a name history would keep. His body measured 6 feet 3 inches tall, which is 1.9 meters. He weighed 215 pounds, or 97.5 kilograms. Even at that size, blinding speed protected him. Landing a clean punch on him was difficult. The baby born in Louisville, Kentucky, in 1942 was named Cassius Clay. His family had a middle-class life. Segregation still shaped ordinary days for the Clays. In large parts of the South, a restaurant would turn Black Americans away. A store might do the same. Mobs of angry white people sometimes attacked Black people. Murder happened too. The target was often someone who insisted on equal treatment. Cassius began boxing lessons at twelve. A thief had taken his bike. He found Joe Martin, a local police officer, and said he wanted to thrash the thief. Martin pointed him toward a boxing ring instead. With Martin coaching, Cassius trained and won a bout before that year ended. The Golden Gloves beginner division was his at age fourteen. The Golden Gloves was the nation's leading tournament for amateurs. Matches were also held by his school. The principal started using a prediction. He called the boy the coming heavyweight champion of the world.

3Clay rose quickly toward the top of amateur boxing in the United States. At seventeen he won the Golden Gloves title. The national championship of the Amateur Athletic Union was his as well. Italy was next. Rome hosted the Olympic Games of 1960, and he went. He was eighteen. Air travel was new to him, and it scared him so much that a parachute went into his bag. Fear stayed outside the ring. The gold medal was his. Payment replaced medals once he came home from Rome. Each victory led to another. Rhymes became his way of mocking the next opponent. Before meeting Jim Robinson, Clay promised the fight would be short. He said he would end it in a single round. He did. Robinson fell in round one. A string of nineteen victories followed. One photo freezes Clay against a Polish boxer during the Summer Olympics of 1960. Islam had already entered his life two years before the Liston bout. He heard Malcolm X, a civil rights leader, talk about that faith, and he came away impressed. The two became friends. Malcolm guided him as a mentor. On the day the heavyweight crown became his, no name in boxing was better known. He no longer wanted to wear the old name. He entered Islam and adopted the name of the faith's prophet. Reporters heard his reason. Cassius Clay, he said, came from slavery. Nobody had let him choose it, and he rejected it. He would be called Muhammad Ali. That name was free, he said, and its sense is someone God loves. He demanded the new name whenever people addressed him or mentioned him. A photograph lines up two civil rights leaders. Martin Luther King Jr. is on the left side. Malcolm X is on the right. Each one left a deep mark on how the young fighter thought.

4Before his trial, Ali speaks to the press in one photo. Vietnam lies in Southeast Asia. During the middle years of the 1960s, American forces were fighting there. The army drafted young men and sent them to battle. Ali's turn came, and he said no. His new faith taught against war. He added another argument. He would not take up arms for a nation that denied him an equal citizen's place. A lifetime of racism had prepared him to resist. He put a question to reporters. Why, he asked, should he rain explosives and gunfire on people with brown skin? Back in Louisville, he said, people then labeled Negro were handled like dogs. Through much of the twentieth century, Negro named people whose heritage was African. By the late 1960s the word was widely seen as an insult. Black and African American mostly replaced it. May 10, 1967, found him at the University of Chicago. He was giving a speech at a gathering that opposed the war. Many people treated him as a hero because he challenged both war and American racism. Boxing's leaders wanted no trouble from their biggest star. Arrest for draft refusal came on a single day, and two blows followed at once. Officials stripped the heavyweight crown. They also banned him from the sport. College talks filled the years outside the ring. He discussed the war. He discussed civil rights. People came to know his moral case as well as they knew his fists. Respect grew because he set his career aside for conscience. Some of that respect came from listeners who still disagreed.

5The draft case was still unfinished after three years. Separately, a judge decided Ali had to be let back into boxing. Two tune-up bouts came first. He then went after Joe Frazier, who held the heavyweight title. Frazier was rugged. His record, like Ali's, showed no losses. Promoters named the challenge the Fight of the Century. The night matched the name. For Ali, the result flipped the old Liston pattern. Frazier's power beat Ali's speed. Ali went down more than once. The judges' decision favored Frazier. No professional loss had stood on Ali's record until then. One photo catches him crouched after his feet slipped in round eleven. The year was 1971, and the opponent was Joe Frazier. A greater win arrived three months later. Ali's right to reject the draft was upheld by the Supreme Court. The justices classed him as a conscientious objector. Religious objection to war, they said, deserved respect for Ali just as it did for other Americans. His stand pushed people from many walks of life to defend their own convictions. Apollo Creed had a real-life model. The 1976 film Rocky took its story from Chuck Wepner, a fighter ranked far down the list. Wepner earned a 1975 title shot against Ali and nearly pulled off a surprise win. Rocky's rival on screen, the magnetic champion Apollo Creed, was drawn straight from Ali.

6Three more years of fighting passed before Frazier and Ali met again. Ali won. The belt was no longer Frazier's. A young power puncher, George Foreman, had claimed it. Their title fight was set in Zaire, now known as the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Organizers called it the Rumble in the Jungle. Ali's plan was new. He rested on the ropes, blocked, and let Foreman spend energy on punches. The trick got the name rope-a-dope. Foreman took the bait and exhausted himself. Ali could then put him on the canvas more easily. The championship returned to Muhammad Ali. A 1974 photo from Zaire shows the moment. Ali tips backward into the ropes while he works the rope-a-dope. Frazier wanted the crown again the following year. Manila, in the Philippines, hosted the bout known as the Thrilla in Manila. The punishment was severe. Ali afterward called it the nearest he had come to dying. Frazier claimed his blows could have felled a building. Round fourteen brought Ali's last store of effort. He threw a violent flurry until his strength was gone. Frazier quit. The damage ran so deep that Ali summed it up later. Champions had flown to Manila, he said, and old men had flown home. In 1978 Ali met Leon Spinks a second time, and a photo records it. The contest ran fifteen rounds. Two and a half further years went by with Ali still champion. Leon Spinks then beat him. Months later they fought once more, and Ali won. Winning the heavyweight crown three times had never been done by anyone else. He stayed out of the ring for two years. His next fight handed the title to Larry Holmes for good. Ali was thirty-eight years old. The long run of bouts had finished.

7Out of the Ring, Still Battling. Retirement from boxing did not end his travel. He crossed the world speaking for human rights. Parkinson's was the diagnosis in 1984. Muscles become hard for the brain to steer when this illness takes hold. As Ali weakened, speech turned difficult. The Olympic Games of 1996 still brought him back. He was there to ignite the Olympic flame, in Atlanta, Georgia. Viewers could see the strain of raising the torch. Cheers rose, and he kept the flame lifted. A fighter's spirit lasted to the end. He died in 2016 at the age of seventy-four. Argument had once surrounded him. By then, affection for him was nearly universal. Courage was the quality President Obama chose to praise. Obama said Ali refused to yield, and that the win helped the country grow comfortable with the America people know now. Greatness in the ring was only part of him. Beliefs he was willing to fight for also helped remake his nation. One photo shows the torch in his hands, just before the flame is lit. It is the opening ceremony of the 1996 Games in Atlanta. Glossary. amateur (adjective), page 6: done for pleasure rather than as paid work. human rights (noun), page 15: claims such as justice, freedom, and equality that most societies say belong to every person from birth. banned (verb), page 10: officially forbade a person to take part. Islam (noun), page 8: the faith followed by Muslims, centered on one God and on what the prophet Muhammad taught. civil rights (noun), page 8: legal, social, and economic guarantees of freedom and equal standing for all citizens. racism (noun), page 9: a belief that ranks one race over another, plus mistreatment based on that belief. conscience (noun), page 10: the inner sense that tells right from wrong. conscientious objector (noun), page 12: someone who declines military service on religious or moral grounds. segregation (noun), page 6: a practice of keeping groups separate, often by race. diagnosed (verb), page 15: named as the illness, injury, or condition a person has. Supreme Court (noun), page 12: the top court of law in the United States. drafting (verb), page 9: calling a person into the armed forces, above all in wartime.

62. The Boy Who Learned the Night Sky

1A 2011 photo shows Neil deGrasse Tyson at a microphone. He talks about a telescope. The telescope is small and powerful. The event opens a new observatory. The school is Southern Illinois University. The town is Edwardsville. The state is Illinois. The summer felt fantastic. He attended his junior high graduation. He said goodbye to his family. He boarded the ship SS Canberra. Neil Armstrong was on the ship. Armstrong had walked on the Moon before any other man. Isaac Asimov was on the ship too. He was a famous writer of science fiction. Hundreds of top scientists were on the ship. The ship sailed toward West Africa and its coast. The goal was a solar eclipse. Most people never see an eclipse like that. A whole life can pass without one. It is that rare. Neil was fourteen. The ship was his way to Africa for the eclipse. Later that summer he took a bus. The ride lasted fifty-three hours. Home had been New York. The camp was in California. The camp taught astronomy. He was born in 1958. The city of his birth was New York City. Bright lights hid most stars there. Tall buildings hid them. Smog hid them. Darkness in the Mojave Desert changed the view. He saw thousands of stars in a clear sky. Never before had he seen them that way. He was only fourteen. Studying stars was his dream, and that dream had begun to happen. The later fame was hidden from him. He himself would be treated like a star.

2Young Neil came to love the earliest Hayden Planetarium more than other stops. A small photo shows him there. Neil deGrasse Tyson grew into an accomplished scientist. He is a Black scientist. The year 1996 put him in the history books. Directing Hayden Planetarium became his job. That building stands in New York City. No Black person had directed it before. His dream of life as an astrophysicist started in that building. He was nine. Stars and planets were projected above him. He found it hard to believe the show. He was not sure those lights stood for the real night sky. A wish to learn more stayed with him. Two years later he used binoculars on the night sky. That was his first real look. He saw planets. Craters on the Moon stood out clearly. A small telescope came as a gift from his parents. Hours of his nights went to sky study. A larger telescope became his next wish. All through junior high he walked dogs. The pay would buy that bigger telescope. Sports came easily to him. He won medals for swimming. He won medals for track. Baseball placed him on an all-star team. Teachers complained about class. He liked talking with friends more than they wished. His work in school was average. Change began with a sixth-grade teacher. That teacher pointed him to classes about astronomy. Hayden Planetarium was the meeting place. He signed up with no one pushing him. Each new star fact made him want another. Wrestling was his contest in high school. Wrestling was his contest in college too.

3Talents stack up in Tyson's life. During 2016 he spoke a character's lines in a movie. The movie was animated and made for children. Ice Age: Collision Course was the film's name. Astronomy was that character's specialty. Tyson was the model for that character. Secondary school for him was Bronx High School of Science. The wrestling team had him as captain. He still found time for talks at the Hayden Planetarium. He still found time to study stars. Family members heard about his astronomy skill. Friends heard about it too. In 1973 the news carried a comet that people seldom see. Someone invited him to give a talk about it. He agreed. City College of New York was where he spoke. He showed space photos from astronomy camp. He had taken those photos himself. He was fifteen. Speaking to adults did not make him nervous. The topic was stars, and he loved that topic. Fifty dollars was his pay for the talk. Walking many dogs had been harder work than earning this pay. A top college would require good grades. A statewide mathematics exam gave him the top mark. During that last school year he served as editor in chief. Each year the school produced a physical science journal. He led it. The United States Department of Education put a label on him. The label was gifted and talented. He did not like that label. He felt hard work had made his success. A mere gift had not. Carl Sagan, a scientist, made difficult ideas easy to follow. Tyson sent applications to top universities across the country. Cornell University was one of them. Carl Sagan himself wrote back about that application. Tyson met Sagan in person. Tyson was a kid of seventeen. Sagan's willingness to help impressed him. Even a complicated idea stayed clear for the public when Sagan spoke. That skill impressed him too. Tyson wanted to become a man like Sagan. He still chose Harvard University. Harvard completed his physics studies in 1980. He left with a bachelor's degree. University of Texas at Austin came next for him. Three years after that, his master's degree was in astronomy. At Harvard he was on the wrestling team and the rowing team. A dance group at University of Texas counted him as a performer. Popular magazines on astronomy printed articles he wrote. He gave talks. In 1991 Columbia University granted his doctorate. The childhood goal was met. He had become an astrophysicist.

4Princeton University, in the state of New Jersey, hired him after that. He researched supernovas. He researched galactic bulges. A bulge is a tight pack of stars at a galaxy's center. His observations were part of wider research. That research led to a method for measuring distance in space. It also led to the discovery of dark energy. Dark energy is a mysterious force. Much of the universe is filled by it. An offer came in 1995, and he took it. He would direct the Hayden Planetarium. He returned to the place where stars first won his love. The earliest Hayden Planetarium rose in 1935. Afterward, scientists gained a great deal of new knowledge about the universe. Tyson convinced people that a new planetarium was needed. Crews pulled the old building down. Work then started to raise another Hayden Planetarium. The new one would belong to the Rose Center. Earth and Space are the focus of that center. Visitors entered the rebuilt Hayden Planetarium in 2000. The build cost 210 million dollars. General readers kept getting books and articles from him. Television presented him as someone who knows space. What would make him famous might also make him infamous. The cause would be our solar system's smallest planet. Kids explore exhibits inside the Hayden Planetarium. Pluto was found in 1930. The International Astronomical Union classified it. People call that group the IAU. Counting out from the Sun put Pluto in the ninth planet spot. A moon of Pluto was discovered in 1978. Scientists then learned the old size for Pluto was far too high. It was smaller than the Moon of Earth. By the 1990s, scientists were finding objects similar to Pluto. The region is the Kuiper Belt. Icy debris orbits there. Neptune is the near edge of that belt. A common view said Pluto fit with those icy bodies. They thought it matched the other planets less well. Did the word planet fit Pluto? The IAU had not yet set down what a planet is. Nobody could settle the question. Tyson faced a serious problem over Pluto. His aim for the Rose Center was teaching science that was current. He did not want later changes to displays that cost a great deal and stay in place. Would the displays call tiny icy Pluto a planet? Or would they refuse that label?

5His choice favored the plan that would teach visitors more. Objects in space that are alike should be grouped. Visitors in 2000 found the rebuilt Rose Center open. Rocky planets shared a single display. Mercury was with them. Venus was with them. Earth was with them. Mars was with them. Giant gas planets shared another display. Jupiter was with them. Saturn was with them. Uranus was with them. Neptune was with them. Inside the Kuiper Belt display, Pluto stood beside bodies like itself. Mail soon flooded his box. People demanded that Pluto be shown as a planet. As many as two hundred emails arrived on some days. Affection for Pluto ran high. Letters came from schoolchildren in many parts of the country. The letters insisted Pluto was a planet. They said so even though it is small. A new label stuck to Tyson. He was the man who demoted Pluto. Anger grew once researchers suggested Pluto could lose the rank of planet. Chris Spurgeon answered with a bumper sticker. The sticker spoke against that decision. His job is computer programming. Los Angeles, California, is where he lives. Over the next few years, scientists found more solar system objects. Eris was one. It lies in the Kuiper Belt and is larger than Pluto. Could Eris count as a planet? Ceres raised the same kind of question. Ceres travels in the asteroid belt. Mars lies on one side of that belt. Jupiter lies on the other side. Similar objects had been called asteroids. Might Ceres be a planet as well? The IAU realized a risk. Leave the word undefined, and planets could soon number in the hundreds inside our solar system. A chart compares sizes. Earth's Moon outweighs many dwarf planets in size. Charon is the largest moon Pluto has. Say the name KARE-on. In 2006 the IAU set three tests for a planet. First, the object must orbit the Sun. Second, its mass must be great enough to pull it into a sphere. Third, its gravity must clear most other objects away from its path. Pluto failed the third test. It was not a planet. A new category received it. That category is the dwarf planet. Tyson's view had been unpopular. Later it proved correct.

6A comic page links Tyson with Superman. In Action Comics number 14, from November 2012, Tyson helped Superman. The help was finding Krypton. Krypton is the home planet of Superman. While people argued about Pluto, space science found a public face in Tyson. Knowledge draws audiences to him. Humor draws them. Enthusiasm for space draws them. News programs invite him often. Talk programs invite him often. Science commissions have included him. Some served NASA, the space agency of the United States. Some served the White House. The commissions help choose later goals for the country's space exploration. He still writes articles and books about science. Public television, known as PBS, has aired science shows with him as host. He has hosted shows for the History Channel. His popular radio show is called StarTalk. His page on Twitter ranks among the leading sites worldwide. The rank is inside the top 140. He has shown up in a Superman comic book. A television comedy called The Big Bang Theory has included him. Fame is a tool he uses for schools. He wants better science teaching. He wants better math teaching. His claim is plain. Kids are not the source of the trouble. A child starts life as a scientist. Adults are the source of the trouble. That is why adults are the main listeners he seeks. He asks leaders to put more money into space research. In his view, space makes people eager for science. He says research and technology drive the economy. From each tax dollar, the share for NASA is under half of one cent. He calls that share a small price. He says that small share helps this country lead the world in technology. A photo shows him talking with two young boys. The visit is on the campus of the University of Iowa.

7A photo lines up three people. Neil deGrasse Tyson stands on the right. Bill Nye stands on the left. People know Nye as The Science Guy. Barack Obama stands in the center. He was president of the United States. A fresh television series in 2014 had Tyson as the host. Its title was Cosmos: A Spacetime Odyssey. An earlier Cosmos series had been watched by more people than any other show on PBS. That series aired in 1980. Carl Sagan hosted it. Sagan was the man who inspired Tyson when Tyson was young. The new series included discoveries made after the first show. The discoveries were new and exciting. Viewers learned what we know. They also learned the way we know it. Twelve Emmy awards listed the show among their nominees. Neil deGrasse Tyson still looks ahead. More hours for research are what he wants. For now, public talk about science keeps him busy. Any direction could come later. One change is already complete. The boy who loved the stars grew up into a star of his own.

63. The Charter That Bound a King

1This book moves through these parts. A detested King John comes first. The barons organize next. Runnymede and a faithless king follow. The aftermath comes after that. Word meanings close the book. In the year 1199, England's king Richard I died in France. He died from an arrow wound. The wound became infected. Richard had been fighting to hold on to French lands. England's royal family had long claimed those lands. King Richard chose his brother John to take the throne after his death. Richard had taxed the people heavily. The tax paid for the war in France. It also paid for his participation in a Crusade. The people of England wanted one thing when John became king. They did not want to be taxed even more. That unwanted result is just what came next. John was the youngest of four boys. He was not expected to become king of England. He imposed excessive taxes on the barons. He also took much of their property. In almost every way, John ruled badly. To protect himself from rebellion, John took many prisoners. He took them from the nobility. The nobility were the leading families of England. The nobles had to pay to get their relatives released. John sometimes killed the prisoners even after being paid.

2A terrible crime inside his own family in 1203 added to John's offenses. He had a nephew in France. The boy was fifteen years old. His name was Arthur. King Philip II of France favored Arthur. Philip wanted Arthur to be the ruler of England. John wanted Arthur gone. His forces captured the lad. Then the boy disappeared. John probably ordered Arthur to be murdered. He may have killed the boy himself. In 1204, King Philip defeated an army of hired soldiers. John had raised that army for a war in France. This victory allowed Philip to reclaim most of a large territory. England's royal family had held that French land. King Philip II changed France in a deep way. He turned it from a small feudal state into one of the most powerful countries in Europe. John kept causing trouble in every place he could. In 1205, the archbishop of Canterbury died. England needed to replace him. Pope Innocent III wanted the position to go to an English cardinal. That cardinal was Stephen Langton. John had his own ideas. John demanded the post for an English bishop. When John did not get his way, he began taking church lands. John's actions brought a strong response from the pope. In 1208, Innocent put all of England under a ruling. That ruling was called an interdict. Under the interdict, England's church doors were shut to everyone. During the interdict, priests could not perform masses. They could not perform funerals. They could not perform other rituals. The pope cut John off from the church because John still refused to yield. People who were excommunicated were completely separated from the church. They were told they could not enter heaven. That did not worry John. He continued to anger Innocent. He seized more property belonging to the church. He seized more money belonging to the church. The pope then joined forces with the French king. They aimed to have Philip invade England. They aimed to replace John as king. Eighteen years was the length of Innocent III's time as pope.

3At this point John saw how serious his situation had become. So in 1213, he finally agreed to a change. He allowed Cardinal Langton to become archbishop. John did not stop there. Surprising everyone, he humbled himself to Innocent. He offered to become a servant of the pope. The delighted Innocent accepted the offer at once. He pardoned the king. That bold step by John was a very smart move. He went from being a cornered outcast to having a powerful friend. That friend was the Roman Catholic Church. In medieval England, a baron was a certain kind of noble. He had received land from a superior. In return he gave loyalty and military service. Higher-ranking barons received their land from the king. They could in turn give parcels of their land to lesser barons. In 1214, the barons swore an oath. They swore to achieve fair treatment from the king. The barons organize around a still-angry adviser. Archbishop Langton was still angry with King John. He was determined that John must go. Langton became an adviser to a group of barons. The group numbered some two hundred. Those barons also wanted to get rid of the king. Some of the barons did not oppose John. A few hoped to make relations with the king better. Those barons included a famous knight. His name was William Marshal. People respected Marshal for his good character. They respected his loyalty. He had served four kings. John was one of them. Marshal became a go-between. He stood between the barons and John. July 1213 was the first time the barons met together as a group. At this meeting, they decided to pressure John. They wanted him to uphold a document. The document was called King Henry I's Coronation Charter. More than a hundred years had passed since that agreement was approved. It spelled out the laws the king would follow. Those laws covered dealing with the nobles. They covered church officials. They covered the common people of England. The first earl of Pembroke was William Marshal's official title.

4John gave his word that the Coronation Charter's laws would guide him. When John broke his promise, the barons met again. The meeting was in November 1214. They discussed what to do next. Archbishop Langton spoke about the Coronation Charter. He said it provided a historical reason for the barons' challenge to John. One of the barons became a leader of the forces opposing John. His name was Robert Fitzwalter. He helped guide their plans. The 1214 meeting was when the barons started to show their strength. They decided to pay no further taxes to John. The taxes were for his wars in France. They went a step further. They drew up a list of demands. The list would be presented to the king. The list was based on the Coronation Charter. It also included other items. The additions stated a new rule. The king had to live by the same laws as all other people. A refusal from John would push the barons to rebel against him. In January 1215, Fitzwalter met with John. A few other barons came too. They presented their list. John told them he would give them a reply by Easter. He did not. The barons then moved forward with new plans. They would present John with a more formal list of their demands. They also began preparing for war. Runnymede was the place. The king was faithless. The Magna Carta, or the Great Charter, was the barons' final attempt. They hoped to stop John's excesses before going to war. The first version of the charter was a Latin document. It was known as the Articles of the Barons. It listed sixty-three demands. Among them were demands shielding the barons from royal abuse. Other demands shielded them from too many taxes. Protection for the rights of the English Church was another demand in the document. It further said something about free citizens. No free citizen would be put in jail without first being tried in a court of law. No free citizen would be punished without that trial. A group of twenty-five barons would see that the king obeyed the charter. They would use force if necessary. The barons grew stronger. In May 1215, a group of them seized London. London was the most important city in England. The seizure further weakened John's position. The king then agreed to meet with the barons. He would be presented with the charter. The meeting began on June 15, 1215. It was held in a large meadow at Runnymede. Runnymede is a town near London. A tent holding a small throne was prepared for the king. John said he accepted every part of the charter once he arrived. He put his royal seal on the document. He swore an oath that he would uphold it.

5In the days after the meeting, copies of the Great Charter were sent out. Those copies were also written in Latin. Few people believed the king would keep his oath. They doubted he would uphold the charter. Breaking an oath was easy for John. The barons feared a quick change. John would ignore the charter as soon as he could do so safely. The king proved to be just as faithless as everyone suspected. He wanted no part of the charter. He called on his friend Pope Innocent for help. Innocent took John's side. In August 1215, the pope nullified the charter. That act freed John from all its provisions. Most pictures of the meeting at Runnymede show King John with a quill pen. They show him signing the Magna Carta. That picture is inaccurate. The king's seal is what made the Magna Carta official. This was how almost every medieval document was made official. An engraved design sat on a handheld seal or a signet ring. The design was pressed into a blob of soft, warm wax. The wax then hardened. A seal could be applied to the document itself. More often it was placed on a ribbon or cord. That ribbon or cord was attached to the bottom of the document. That nullifying act was the final straw for the barons. Some barons remained loyal to the crown. Marshal was one of them. A large group of them launched a civil war anyway. Fitzwalter led that group. They invited Philip's son to join the fight. That son was Prince Louis of France. Their plan was to place Louis on the English throne after a victory. Louis raised an army. He invaded England. In late 1216, there was a completely unexpected development. Both Pope Innocent and King John died. John's nine-year-old son then became king. His name was Henry III. Marshal was now aged seventy. He became the administrator of the government. Henry was still too young to rule on his own. Marshal advised Henry to reissue the charter. The reissue would show the barons a promise. Henry would be a law-abiding king. Many paintings make Henry III look just like his father, John I.

6A timeline lists the events of the Great Charter. In April 1199, John becomes king of England. In July 1205, the archbishop of Canterbury dies. In March 1208, Pope Innocent III lays England under an interdict. In May 1213, King John bows to the pope. He allows Stephen Langton to become archbishop of Canterbury. In July 1213, the barons meet as a group for the first time. They meet in St. Albans. In November 1214, the barons meet as a group for the second time. They meet in Bury St. Edmunds. In January 1215, Robert Fitzwalter and a few other barons meet with King John. In May 1215, the barons seize London. In June 1215, King John seals the Great Charter.
