In August 1215, Pope Innocent III nullifies the charter. In July 1216, Pope Innocent III dies. In October 1216, King John dies. His son, Henry, becomes king of England. In September 1217, William Marshal defeats the barons. He ends the civil war. In November 1217, King Henry III reissues the charter. The aftermath shows Marshal's worth once again. In 1217, he defeated the rebel barons. He sent Prince Louis back to France. Henry reissued the Great Charter. That act satisfied the barons. They had worried that his reign would not be much different from John's reign. Henry turned eighteen in 1225. That year, he again reissued the Great Charter. The new issue reinforced his promise to be a good ruler. Henry accepted a big idea. Even the king of England must obey the law. The charter was reissued one more time, in 1297. That was during the reign of Henry's son, King Edward I. Edward I confirmed the charter for a reason. The barons believed he was not governing as a good king should.

7Four remaining copies of the Magna Carta were brought together in April 2015. It was the first time they were together. The gathering celebrated the 800th anniversary of the charter. The Great Charter became a powerful symbol of freedom. It also stood for the idea that no one is above the law. It served as the foundation for English Common Law. That is England's legal system. According to the charter, people charged with a crime must be treated as innocent. They stay innocent until proven guilty. The proof comes in a trial by jury. Many of the ideas in the charter deeply influenced political thinking in Europe. They also influenced the American colonies in the 1700s. In that century the colonies broke away from British rule. They created the United States. Many of those same ideas found new expression later. They appear in the U.S. Constitution. They appear in the Bill of Rights. These words help with the book. Barons were men holding low rank in European nobility. An interdict is a punishment within the Catholic Church. It prohibits a person or group from receiving holy sacraments. It also prohibits Christian burial. A charter is an official document. It defines the rights and responsibilities of a person or group. Nullified means made to have no effect, value, or legal power. A civil war is a war inside one country. Groups of people from that country fight against each other. An oath is a formal promise. A rebellion is a fight against authority or power. A Crusade was any of the military campaigns of European Christians. They traveled to Jerusalem, or the Holy Land. They tried to take control of it. A successor is a person who follows another in a job or elected position. Taxed means a fee was collected. The fee paid for government services, operations, or functions. Humbled means made lower in power or prestige. It can mean made to feel modest or less proud. Tried means judged in court following a legal investigation.

64. The Cold Green Forest of the North

1Almost nobody lives in this forest biome. A Wide Green Band A satellite high over the North Pole looks down on Earth. The Arctic Ocean is what that view shows first. Land makes a ring around the pole. No trees grow on that first ring. People call the ring the tundra region. After the tundra comes a broader band of deep green. Cities and roads are rare across most of the green band. The trees there are amazing in number. Some of the hardiest animals on Earth live among those trees. Modern life has left the region nearly alone. This place is called the taiga. The word taiga comes from Russian. Sources do not give the word one shared meaning. One meaning is a mountain covered with forest. Another meaning is a forest that is swampy and moist. A further meaning is forests of conifers. People in North America often use a second name. They call the taiga the boreal forest. Boreal means northern. The word goes back to Boreas. Greek stories say Boreas was the god of the north wind.

2For most of the year, the taiga can stay in winter. A Cold Forest Region Earth's surface holds many kinds of environments. Plants and animals live together in those regions. Scientists call each region, with its living communities, a biome. A desert is one kind of biome. A grassland is another. A rainforest is another. An ocean is another. The taiga belongs on that list too. Several factors work together to make Earth's biomes. One important factor is latitude. Latitude tells how far a spot is from the equator. Elevation is important as well. It means how high a place sits above the sea. Warmth or coolness depends in part on those two factors. Climate helps build a biome. So do land and water. So do the plants and the animals. Cold parts of the Northern Hemisphere are where the taiga lies. The main plants are conifers. A conifer puts its seeds in a cone, not in a flower. No other land biome on Earth is larger than the taiga. A wide band of it crosses the north of North America, of Europe, and of Asia. Canada is largely taiga. Alaska is largely taiga too. In Europe, only small patches grow in the Highlands of Scotland. The forest then runs on through Norway. It continues through Sweden and through Finland. After that it crosses all of Russia and reaches the Pacific Ocean. Parts of China have taiga. Parts of Mongolia have it too. Taiga covers about one-sixth of the land on Earth. East to west, Russia's share measures about 5,800 kilometers. In miles, that stretch is 3,600. A map of these regions names Russia, Alaska, and Canada. Europe, Asia, and North America are on the map as well. So are Africa, South America, Australia, and Antarctica. The Arctic Ocean, the Atlantic Ocean, and the Pacific Ocean are labeled too. North of the taiga is the tundra, where trees almost never grow. Where the two biomes meet, people speak of the tree line. South of the taiga, the next biome is not the same everywhere. Temperate forests fill some of those lands. Grasslands fill others.

3Weather and the Ground Cold is the usual climate of the taiga, though one place is not exactly like another. The forest sits a long way north of the equator. Sunlight therefore meets the ground at a low angle. Places closer to the equator receive more heat energy than this region does. Snow on the ground makes the cold worse. The snow sends sunlight back, rather than taking it in. Nights in winter are long, and that is a third cause. More heat leaks away into the air around Earth during those nights. A taiga winter lasts a long time. The air is cold, and the wind is strong. The coldest month is January. Readings then usually fall below −10°C, or 14°F. Eastern Siberia has seen winter cold as extreme as −50°C. That is −58°F. Snow that piles up generally stays for the whole winter. Southern parts of the taiga can keep that snow for five months or longer. Northern parts can keep it for as many as eight months. Glaciers and Land Bridges During the last ice age, glaciers lay over much of the taiga. A little less than twelve thousand years have passed since that ice age ended. A huge share of Earth's water was locked in ice, so the seas stayed lower. Islands that stand alone today were then joined to the mainland, still above the water. The British Isles were connected in that way. Far eastern Russia was linked by a land bridge to parts of Alaska and of Canada. Many kinds of animals crossed that bridge into North America. A foggy thunderstorm over the Canadian taiga can turn the sky a deep purple. July brings the warmest weather. The range then is 15 to 20°C, or 59–68°F. At the hottest hour of the day, the air may climb to 25°C, or 77°F. Thunderstorms are frequent while the months are warmer. Lightning comes with them, but rain is light. Fires can break out in the forest under those conditions. A fire can help. It clears away trees that are old or sick, and young trees get space to grow. Eastern North America gets the most precipitation in a year, and northern Europe does too. Lakes, streams, and wetlands are common in those areas. More than 100 centimeters of precipitation may fall there each year. That is 39 inches.

4Taiga soil is usually cold. It is also shallow, rocky, and short of nutrients. Only certain plants can grow in many of these places. Where the taiga is warmer, the soil holds more nutrients. Living material breaks down faster in that warmer ground. Glaciers scraped large parts of Canada. What soil remains is too thin for a full-grown forest. Boggy ground supports spruce and tamarack, plus mosses and other plants. Permafrost is ground that never thaws. In many spots it sits just under the top soil. Solid rock sits just under the top soil in other spots. Water cannot drain well through either one. Shallow bogs are common in the taiga because of that. Melting permafrost, driven by climate change, is making still more bogs. Permafrost in the Taiga If the average temperature for a whole year stays below freezing, permafrost may be present. A great many kinds of trees cannot grow on that frozen ground. Tamarack can still do well when enough loose soil lies above the ice. Black spruce can do well in that same deep top layer. Northern Canada has a lot of permafrost. The Asian part of Russia has a lot of it too. It shows up most where the sun is weaker. A mountain's north-facing slope is a typical place. Plants of the Cold Forest A plant here must get through a growing season that is short. It must also handle cold, frozen ground, and soil with few nutrients. Biomes closer to the equator have more species than the taiga does. Conifers lead the plant life, and pine, fir, and spruce are among them. Lots of these trees are evergreens, so their leaves stay on all year. Tamarack is a common conifer of a different kind. It is deciduous, and its leaves fall off in winter. A few deciduous trees that make flowers grow here as well. Poplar is one of them. Birch is another. They do not spread as widely as the conifers. Among the trees you will meet most often is Scotch pine. Mosses, lichens, and mushrooms make up much of the cover on the ground. Their roots stay shallow. Sunlight and water are things they need only in small amounts. Cold does not stop them. Grasses grow here, and so do ferns and other plants that stay low. In summer, Calypso orchids appear in the damp parts of the taiga.

5Several adaptations help these plants last in the taiga. An evergreen keeps its leaves through every season. Energy and nutrients are saved that way. A fresh crop of leaves each spring would demand extra sunlight. It would also demand extra food from the soil. Neither sunlight nor soil nutrients are plentiful. The needles on a Scotch pine hold water in. Heavy snow can load a Norway spruce, and the tree still stands. Pines and many other cone-bearing trees here grow leaves that look like needles. Wax coats those needles. The shape helps the tree keep its water. Rain may be too light to supply much water. Frozen water may be out of reach as well. Because needles hold little sap, they are less likely to freeze the tree. Leaves of a dark green color soak up more heat. That helps the tree take in energy from the Sun and use it for photosynthesis. A cone is the shape of many of these trees. Snow slides off the branches quickly, so its weight does not snap them. Animals of the Cold Forest Few kinds of animals can make a home here, because the climate is cold and the plants are limited. The ones that do live here are tough. Their bodies fit the hard conditions. Thick fur is common on the mammals, and the fur works as insulation. Long legs and big feet are common on the larger kinds. Deep snow is easier to cross with feet like that. One large animal of this biome is the moose. Deer, elk, moose, and caribou are the big plant-eaters. Another name for caribou is reindeer. Hunters include black bears and grizzly bears. Wolves, wolverines, and lynxes hunt here too. So do martens, animals much like weasels. In eastern Russia, Siberian tigers are hunters as well. Squirrels live here, and so do snowshoe hares and lemmings. From the trees, birds of prey hunt those smaller mammals. Eagles take part in that hunt, and so do hawks and owls. A pine marten and a lynx appear among these animals.

6Summer brings huge numbers of insects, breeding in the bogs, the lakes, and the ponds. Waterfowl fly in to use that rich supply of food. Many other birds arrive for the same reason, and they raise their young. Those travelers head south again when winter turns long and cold. Warmer lands are where they spend that season. Woodpeckers remain all year. Ravens, loons, and chickadees remain too. Reptiles have a hard time in this biome, and amphibians do as well. They cannot set their body temperature from the inside. Spring and summer warm some parts of the taiga enough for them. Winter cold is met by hibernating. Some sleep through it on land. Turtles, and certain frogs, sleep at the bottom of a lake or a pond. Frozen Frogs An odd adaptation lets the wood frog last through taiga cold. As it hibernates, the blood freezes, and the body tissues freeze too. Breathing stops in that state. The heart stops beating. Blood no longer moves. Crystals of ice form beneath the skin. Proteins of a special kind, together with sugars, keep the cells from being harmed. More than half the frog's body can freeze, and the frog can stand it. People Who Live in the Forest Thousands of years of human life have already passed in the taiga. Today, traditional communities there number more than six hundred. Herding reindeer is one way they make a living. Fishing, hunting, and crafts are other ways. Many of them work to keep the forests standing. They also work to keep their old way of life. One photograph shows a woman who is an elder. She is part of the Cree First Nation at Waswanipi, a community in Quebec. In Canada, few native groups work harder than her tribe to guard the taiga. Forest covers this biome, so trees are a main natural resource. Logging goes on widely. Mining goes on too. So does the search for oil and gas. So does the building of roads. Visitors come to boat, to fish, and to hike. They ski, ride snowmobiles, and travel by dogsled. They rest in cabins that feel cozy. People are fairly scarce across most of the taiga. Two cities stand out as the largest. One is Toronto, in Canada. The other is Moscow, in Russia.

7Russia holds one of the biggest stretches of taiga on Earth. Where Cone Trees Cover the Land Across the northern lands, the taiga covers nearly 13 million square kilometers. That is about 5 million square miles. In this cold country, conifers are the trees in charge. Russia's Siberia contains huge tracts of taiga. Anton Chekhov, a Russian writer of plays, rode into that Siberian forest in the late 1800s. He went on horseback. Green conifers seemed to run on without end, and he wondered whether he would ever find a way out. People can leave the taiga. Anyone fortunate enough to see it will remember it for a long time. An adaptation is a change in a living thing. The change lets that living thing last in the place where it lives. A bog is wet land with a spongy feel. A conifer is a tree that makes cones. Needle-shaped leaves are common on a conifer. Hardiest means best able to last when conditions are difficult. Industrial describes the making of goods, above all when machines and technology do the work. Insulation is a material that blocks the passage of heat, of sound, or of electricity. To migrate is to travel from one region to another. The trip happens at a set time each year. A nutrient is a substance a living thing must have so it can live and grow. Organic describes what comes from a living organism, or what has to do with one. Photosynthesis is a process inside plant cells. Chlorophyll uses light from the Sun, plus water, air, and nutrients, and makes food. Precipitation is water that comes down to the ground. Rain is one form, and snow is another. The taiga is a cold region of the Northern Hemisphere. Forests of conifers cover it.

65. The Fight That Built a Nation

1A time line sits at the front of this book. Europe's Seven Years' War took in the French and Indian War as one piece. That war began in 1754. It ended in 1763 with the Treaty of Paris. The Sugar Act passed in 1764. The Stamp Act passed in 1765. The Quartering Act passed in 1765. The Townshend Acts passed in 1767. The Boston Massacre happened in 1770. The Boston Tea Party happened in 1773. The Coercive Acts passed in 1774. Colonists called them the Intolerable Acts. The Boston Port Act was one of those laws. It also dates to 1774. The First Continental Congress met in 1774. On April 19, 1775, fighting started at Lexington and Concord. People gave that first shot a famous title: shot heard round the world. That day, the Revolutionary War began. This book opens with how the war started. Then it tells about a second meeting of colonial delegates. Next, Patriot fighters take a fort called Ticonderoga. The hills that come next are Breed's Hill, followed by Bunker Hill. After that, the colonies declare independence. The middle of the book follows the long fight for freedom. Southern battles come next. A word list closes the book. Country status did not always belong to the United States. It began as thirteen colonies. Great Britain ruled them. The mother country started taxing the colonists. It also made new laws that people disliked. The colonists objected. Their demand rejected taxation while representation was missing. They wanted that voice in the British Parliament. As time passed, the disagreements grew worse. Bad feelings increased. Violence increased. King George III of Britain made control over the colonists his aim. He failed. A chain of events reached a clash. The day was April 19, 1775. British soldiers met colonists at two Massachusetts towns. The towns were Lexington and Concord. Lexington's village green was where the shots rang out. Which side fired first remains unknown. A famous title stuck to that first shot: shot heard round the world. Britain and the thirteen colonies went to war from that moment. Already a third group had homes on the land in that fight. The region had held Native peoples through thousands of years. By 1775, millions of Native people had died after Europeans arrived. In the next century, millions more would die. More land would be taken from them. That land ran from coast to coast.

2The taxes stayed, because King George would not cancel them. A fight was clearly the colonies' only remaining path. They would fight for their independence. Patrick Henry returned to Virginia once the First Continental Congress ended. He gave a speech there. He cried out for liberty. He said he would rather die than live without liberty. During the war, Patriots shouted a battle cry. The cry paired liberty with death. The Second Continental Congress opened its meeting on May 10, 1775. The meeting was at Independence Hall. That hall is in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. Command of the troops went to George Washington by the delegates' choice. Virginia had sent Washington as one delegate. He had been an officer in the British army. The Congress voted to name the troops the Continental Army. The army would be volunteer soldiers. Each of the thirteen colonies would send some. Washington's job as commander would not be easy. His soldiers were a rough mix of workers. Some were farmers. Some were carpenters. Some were blacksmiths. They had few weapons. They had little training, or none. They would fight powerful Britain. Britain had a well-trained army. It had a well-supplied army. It had a strong navy too. Washington expected to fail. He told Patrick Henry about that fear. He said that the day he took command would mark his fall. He said that same day would ruin his reputation. He still believed strongly in American independence. He took the job as army commander. Pay for the work was something he refused. Not every colonist wanted to leave Britain. Washington headed toward Concord and Lexington, near Boston. He went there to lead his new troops. The Continental Congress kept trying to make peace. Making amends with the Parliament of Britain was the delegates' hope. King George III was sent a petition by them. Once more they asked that rights be given to the colonists. They asked him to call the colonists loyal English subjects. King George refused even to read the petition. He said the colonists had gone into open rebellion. He said they had declared that rebellion in the open.

3The Revolutionary War hit Native peoples hard. Separation of Native peoples from colonists had been King George III's aim. He hoped that separation would prevent violence between them. Some lands were reserved by Great Britain for Native peoples. The colonists did not like that decision. As time passed, the Patriot side gained some Native peoples. Others joined the British. Sometimes a Native nation was split between the two sides. Alliances were split in the same way. Defeat cost Great Britain a huge stretch of land, which went to the United States. Native peoples had lived on that land for centuries. Land was not the only loss these Native peoples suffered. They lost cultures. They lost countless lives. Native peoples had also resisted the British before the American fight. A picture shows the Ottawa leader Pontiac. He visits the British in 1763. Soon after that visit, Pontiac tried to drive the British out. Support came from nearly every tribe around the Great Lakes. Pontiac's War lasted from 1763 to 1766. The war was named for him. Colonist soldiers won a fight on the day the Second Continental Congress first met. They beat the British at Fort Ticonderoga. Ethan Allen was a rough, tough farmer. He and other farmers formed a group. They called it the Green Mountain Boys. Capture of a British fort was the task the Congress gave the Green Mountain Boys. Lake Champlain in New York was where the fort stood. Another soldier was also ordered to attack that fort. His name was Benedict Arnold. Leadership of the attack was wanted by both Arnold and Allen. They argued during the whole trip to Ticonderoga. They still took the fort together. The date was May 10, 1775. A picture shows Ethan Allen at Fort Ticonderoga. The victory lifted the soldiers' morale. It also announced that war had truly begun. Colonists now had to pick a side. Staying inside Britain was what Loyalists wanted. Patriots wanted independence from Britain.

4First among the battles of the American Revolution was the one at Lexington. After it, British soldiers retreated to Boston. Major John Pitcairn led them. Colonist soldiers camped outside Boston. They gathered more forces there. About 16,000 Patriot troops finally surrounded Boston. They cut off supplies to the British. British General Thomas Gage had a worry. Gage feared enemy troops on the hills that faced Boston across the Charles River. Bunker Hill was one of those hills. Breed's Hill was the other. They are in Charlestown. A map shows the British retreat. It marks Charlestown, Lexington, Boston, and Concord. After the defeats at Lexington and Concord, British troops went to Charlestown. They crossed the river into Boston. The Atlantic Ocean is on that map of North America. Trenches were dug by Patriot soldiers through the dark hours of June 16, 1775. The trenches went into Breed's Hill. The soldiers worked all night. By morning, soldiers covered the hill. Trenches covered it too. British soldiers crossed the Charles River by ship. Their cannons blasted as they came. The Patriots were not well trained. Britain's professional soldiers were the force facing them. Gunpowder on the Patriot side was very scarce. They needed to save ammunition. Officers on the Patriot side ordered each shot to matter. They told them to wait until the enemy was very close. They said to fire only when each enemy eye showed its white. Up the hill rushed the British soldiers. Fire from the Americans waited until safety was almost gone. The plan worked. Many British soldiers died. More British troops landed. They attacked again. The Americans kept waiting. Then they shot. The Americans' gunpowder was gone at last. They had to retreat. Breed's Hill fell into British hands. They captured Bunker Hill too. A picture shows the kind of muskets used in the Revolutionary War. People also called those guns rifles. Gunpowder was kept inside a powder horn.

5A battle map marks Bunker Hill. The same map marks Breed's Hill. The Mystic River is on it. The Charles River is on it. Charlestown and Boston are on it. Copp's Hill is on it. The map shows where Patriot soldiers stood. It shows where British soldiers stood. The British took control of the two hills. The cost in British lives was high. British wounded and dead together numbered more than 1,000. The Patriots lost 441 men. Patriot morale still rose by a large amount. They had lost a battle. They had shown they could fight professional soldiers. They believed they could win a war against them. Most of the action was on Breed's Hill. Even so, people call the fight the Battle of Bunker Hill. General George Washington's troops kept the British stuck in Boston. That hold lasted nearly a year. Canada was also the target of forces he sent. He wanted to stop the British from landing there. He did not want them to send forces south into New York. The Patriots captured Montreal. Quebec did not fall to their attack. Winter brought Patriot use of cannons seized earlier from the British. They turned those cannons on British soldiers in Boston. Boston was emptied of British soldiers on March 17, 1776. Leaving beside them were thousands of colonists who stayed loyal to Britain. Washington's troops marched into the city in triumph. A picture shows cannons the Continental Army used against the British.

6People sometimes say to put your John Hancock on a paper. That saying means please sign this. The saying goes back to 1776. That year, John Hancock signed the Declaration of Independence in a bold hand. Seeing his large signature pushed the rest of the signers to sign. There were 53 other signers. If Britain had won, every signer could have been hanged. They would have been hanged as traitors. Common Sense is the pamphlet written by Patriot Thomas Paine. In it, he said independence was the only right choice for the colonists. Within a few months, buyers had taken 150,000 copies. It moved many Loyalist colonists toward independence. A committee was chosen by the Continental Congress in June 1776. The committee was to write a statement. Self-governing was the colonial right the statement described. Thomas Jefferson was chosen to do the actual writing. July 4, 1776, brought a yes vote for the Declaration of Independence. The Continental Congress cast that vote. Each of the thirteen colonies then passed it. The United States of America came into being with that approval. Dark days lay ahead for the Patriots. They lost battle after battle. A month after the Declaration was signed, a huge British force arrived. General William Howe led it. New York Harbor filled with ships carrying 30,000 soldiers. The Patriots were outnumbered. The Battle of Long Island went against them. New Jersey was the land they crossed while falling back south. They went to Philadelphia. New York City passed into British hands. They won another battle there. In that battle, Patriots surrendered Fort Washington. A statue honors the sacrifice of Nathan Hale. Nathan Hale was a teacher. He was 21 years old. Spying on British troops inside New York City was the job he volunteered to do. Hale was caught. He was hanged. His last words expressed one regret. He said his single life was all he could offer his country.

7Bravery marked the general named Benedict Arnold. He felt that Congress had mistreated him. Mistreatment by the Continental Army was something he also felt. In 1779, Washington gave Arnold a command. The command was a fort called West Point. West Point stands on the lower Hudson River. Selling that fort to the British was Arnold's plan. His plan was revealed. He then joined the British army. In October 1776, gunboats under Patriot Benedict Arnold lost a fight. The fight was at Lake Champlain in Canada. The Patriots fought so hard that the British grew worried. The rebels might be harder to beat than the British had expected. George Washington took his men over a river on December 24, 1776. The river was the Delaware. They crossed to Trenton, New Jersey. Victory in a battle there went to the Patriots. The fight lasted less than an hour. A few days later, Washington beat the British again. That fight was at Princeton, New Jersey. These wins lifted Patriot morale again. A picture shows George Washington in 1776. The picture shows him accepting a surrender at Trenton, New Jersey. The men giving up are British troops. Britain struck back in June 1777. A large army moved south from Canada. General John Burgoyne led it. Burgoyne planned to take the Hudson River area. That move would cut New England off from the other colonies. It would cut New York off too. On the way, Burgoyne took Fort Ticonderoga again. Patriot soldiers stopped his push at the Battle of Saratoga. The battle was in October. Burgoyne surrendered about 6,000 men. Burgoyne's southward march out of Canada is drawn on a map. It marks Burgoyne, Lake Champlain, and Fort Ticonderoga. It marks the leaders Riedesel, St. Clair, and Phillips. It shows British troops. It shows British military leaders.

8Saratoga turned the direction of the war. It showed France that the Patriots might win. It showed other European countries the same thing. France joined the fight against Great Britain. Great Britain had long been France's enemy. France sent supplies to the Continental Army. Spain soon entered a war against Britain. The Continental Army found supplies harder and harder to get. Soldiers often lacked food. They often lacked clothing. They often lacked shelter. The Continental Congress needed allies. France was one ally that could help supply the troops. George Washington's troops spent a hard winter at Valley Forge. Valley Forge is in Pennsylvania. The winter was cold. The soldiers were hungry. Supplies reached them only after that winter. In June 1778, Washington attacked the British army. The fight was the Battle of Monmouth. General Henry Clinton now commanded the British. Neither side won the fight. No later major battle was fought in the northern colonies. The National Memorial Arch stands at Valley Forge. It carries words from Washington. He praised soldiers who stayed patient and faithful. He said this even though they lacked clothes and were starving. Women could not serve in the army. Other kinds of service still let them aid the war. One way was making cloth at home. Many women backed the revolution once Britain's Stamp Act of 1765 was law. They boycotted British goods. They made their own goods instead. That choice was an act of protest. It was also an act of rebellion. Daughters of Liberty was the name a group of women chose. They even held public spinning demonstrations. Women made bullets. Women sewed blankets. Women sewed uniforms. Women raised funds. Women joined the battle camps. There they cooked. They cleaned. They nursed people who were hurt. They nursed people who were ill. They even searched the land for food. Some women risked their lives. Water reached troops in the field because these women carried it. Mary Ludwick Hays took her husband's place when he was wounded. His name was William Hays. He was wounded in action. Molly Pitcher is the name history uses for her. At the Battle of Monmouth, water for the soldiers was carried by Mary Hays. She carried water for the cannon too. Molly Pitcher became her nickname because of that work.

9Savannah, Georgia, fell to British forces in December 1778. They attacked Charleston, South Carolina. They captured it in May 1780. August 1780 brought them another win, this time at Camden, South Carolina. Loyalists made up a large share of colonists in the southern colonies. Britain was winning in the South. The Patriots still would not give up. The war's direction started to change in October. King's Mountain in South Carolina was the site of a Patriot win. The fight took only sixty-five minutes. They won again at Camden. They won at Cowpens. Next they pushed British General Charles Cornwallis north. He was pushed into Virginia. Cornwallis had helped the British win at Long Island. British troops in the South had come under his command. Real help began once the Patriots and the French were allied. Holding the British back was work French soldiers shared. They also fought beside colonists. Washington's march into Virginia included those French soldiers. A picture shows Charles Cornwallis. The war's fighters included thousands of Black people. They did not all fight on the same side. Most of them were enslaved at this time. Freedom looked more likely on one side. Most joined that side. Great Britain had more than 20,000 Black fighters. The Patriot side had somewhere from 5,000 to 8,000 of these fighters. Decades would pass before many enslaved Black people gained freedom. James Armistead stands as one American hero. Before the war, Virginia was where he lived in slavery. He became a double agent. He was a good one. His disguise was a runaway loyal to the British. Spying on the Patriots became the job the British gave him. They did not know the truth. At the same time the Patriots had him watching the British. General Lafayette received British battle plans from Armistead. The plans included details the Patriots needed. Those details helped them win at Yorktown. That win helped them win the war. The Act of 1783, passed once the war ended, set some people free. It freed enslaved soldiers who had fought for the Revolution. Armistead was a spy, so he did not get that benefit. He went back to life as a slave. His French commander later helped him become free. Lafayette became an added part of Armistead's name. He did it to show his thanks. He also did it to show the bond they shared. A painting from 1824 shows James Armistead Lafayette.

10A picture shows Cornwallis giving up to Washington at Yorktown. The war's most important battle was ready to begin. French ships drove off British ships. Those British ships had been sent to rescue Cornwallis. Yorktown sits on Virginia's coast. That was the place. Extra soldiers came with the French as well. Those soldiers would help the fight on land. Yorktown was entered by French troops together with Patriot troops. They surrounded the British army. Three weeks of fighting followed for the British. They surrendered on October 19, 1781. The Revolutionary War was over. Victory in the war belonged to the Patriots. They were now independent from Britain. The colonies were used to being supported by another country. Now they had to come together. They had to build a brand new nation. These people played major parts in the Revolutionary War. George Washington commanded the Continental Army. The country's first president was a later role of his. Thomas Gage commanded British troops in the colonies. After Lexington and Concord, Boston became a trap for his army. John Burgoyne commanded the British northern army. He captured Fort Ticonderoga. He was defeated at Saratoga. King George III became king of Great Britain. He became king at the age of twenty-two. Keeping the colonies mattered to him no matter the cost. The Declaration of Independence came from Thomas Jefferson's pen. A pamphlet by Thomas Paine carries the name Common Sense. Many colonists chose independence because that pamphlet moved them. William Howe led Britain's forces in North America across the years 1775 to 1778. In 1778 Henry Clinton took Howe's place as British commander. Pictures show George Washington and King George III.

11Charles Cornwallis was a British general under Henry Clinton. The South was the region under his command. October 19, 1781, was the day he gave up at Yorktown. The Marquis de Lafayette was a young Frenchman. Washington was the leader he served under as a commander. He played a key part in getting French military help. That help won the war. A picture shows the Marquis de Lafayette. A map marks important sites of the Revolutionary War. The sites include Quebec and Ticonderoga. They include Boston and Concord. They include Long Island and Valley Forge. They include Yorktown and King's Mountain. They include Camden, Charleston, and Savannah. The Atlantic Ocean is on the map. Allies are people or groups that join others for a shared cause. Morale is the level of confidence a person feels. It can also be the enthusiasm of a group. The feeling can rise during a project. It can also rise while a goal is pursued. Amends are acts meant to make up for a bad situation. They can also make up for a loss. Patriots were people who supported independence for the thirteen colonies. They did this during the American Revolution. Colonies are areas or countries ruled by another country. A colony can also belong to another country. A petition is a formal written request. It usually comes with the signatures of many citizens. Delegates are chosen or elected people. They represent others and act for them. Rebellion means fighting authority. It can also mean fighting power. Gunpowder is a dry material that can explode. People use it in guns. They use it in fireworks. They use it for blasting. Representation is the act of speaking for another person. It can also mean acting for a group. Independence is freedom from the control of others. It is also freedom from their influence, support, or help. Retaliated means attacked back after being attacked. Loyalists were people in the thirteen colonies who kept faith with Great Britain. They stayed loyal during the American Revolution. Self-governing means having the right to create laws. It also means having the right to enforce those laws. No outside power interferes. Momentum is the strength that keeps something moving. It can also be the force that keeps something growing over time.

66. The Frame Under Your Skin

1A lion, a cow, a seal, an elephant, and a monkey appear together in the opening picture. The book moves through these topics in order. First comes the way bones shape a body. Next comes the head. Then comes the back. Arms and legs follow. Joints come after that. The inside of a bone is next. Care of bones comes near the end. A word list finishes the book. A lizard's body has a bony frame inside it. An elephant's body has one. So does a fish that swims in the ocean. Your body has one as well. The shared thing is a skeleton. That word means the full set of bones an animal keeps inside. Picture those bones as a frame. Muscle lies wrapped on the frame. Blood vessels lie wrapped there too. Skin is the outer wrap. People belong to the group called vertebrates. Plenty of other animals belong to that group. The frame is what gives a vertebrate its outline. The frame is also what gives a vertebrate its form. Take the skin away and the bones still tell a story. You can often guess the animal from the bones alone. The lion's outline depends on its frame. The cow's outline depends on its frame. The seal's outline depends on its frame. The elephant's outline depends on its frame. The monkey's outline depends on its frame. A person's outline depends on a human frame. Bones gathered into one set are what we call the skeleton. They sit under the softer parts. Those softer parts are muscle, blood vessels, and skin. The wrap hides the frame, but the frame decides the shape. A bare set of bones can still look like the animal it came from. A fish skeleton can give the fish away. An elephant skeleton can give the elephant away. A human skeleton can give a person away.

2Count the bones in a grown person's skeleton and the total is 206. The count begins with the skull. The count ends with the bones of the toes. Movement uses some of those bones. Muscles join them by means of tendons. Other bones act as guards for organs that are easy to hurt. The heart is one organ under that guard. The brain is another. A special center sits inside many of the big bones. Blood cells are made in that center. Bands of tissue called ligaments tie bone to bone. The tied bones are the skeleton. Looking at one body region at a time makes the work of bone clearer. In the hand, ligaments keep the many bones from falling apart. In the foot, ligaments do the same job. Bicycle riders in the picture wear helmets. The helmets are there to guard the skull. Now look at the forehead, the face above the eyebrows. Would you call it soft, the way a pillow is soft? Would you call it hard, the way a desk is hard? It is hard. Right beneath the skin sits the skull. Cranium is another name for that skull. The cranium is one bone set in the body. Its job is to guard the brain. The brain matters a great deal. The brain is also easy to injure. A crash helmet and the cranium do similar work. The cranium cannot take as much of a hit as a crash helmet can. Extra protection is a good idea. Wear a helmet on a bike. Wear a helmet for in-line skating. Wear a helmet for some other sports. Football is one sport that calls for a helmet.

3Run a hand over your head and the skull can feel like a single piece. It is not a single piece. Many bones make it up. They meet along joints named sutures. Most joints shift a lot. Sutures hardly shift at all. The forehead region has its own name, the frontal bone. Above the eyes, a bony ridge is called the supraorbital ridge. Two bones called the parietal bones form the biggest share of the skull. Say parietal like puh-RY-eh-tul. They lie over the top of the head. They also lie over the back of the head. Low at the back, just over the neck, is the occipital bone. Say occipital like awk-SIP-ih-tul. On the sides, over the ears, sit the temporal bones. A chart of the main skull bones can point to each of these. The chart can mark the frontal bone. It can mark a parietal bone. It can mark the supraorbital ridge. It can mark the sutures. It can mark the occipital bone. It can mark a temporal bone. Add up the skull bones and the sum is twenty-two. Leave the six middle-ear bones out of that sum. Leave out the one bone that sits in the throat. Press the cheeks and you can feel the cheekbones. Zygomatic bones is another name for them. Two bones build the jaw. Maxilla is the name of the upper jaw. Mandible is the name of the lower jaw. On its own, the lower jaw is able to move. Very few other skull bones can move alone like that. A close picture can point to the cheekbone. It can point to the lower jaw bone. It can point to the upper jaw bone. An extra note is about the ears. Bones live in the ears as well. Their names are hammer, anvil, and stirrup. Each one is fixed to the eardrum. No bones in the body are smaller. Sound reaches the eardrum. The eardrum starts to shake. That shaking shifts the hammer. The hammer shakes next. The anvil shakes because of the hammer. The stirrup is pushed by the anvil. Nerves notice the shaking. They carry it to the brain. The brain turns that signal into meaning. Some people cannot hear. Some people hear only a little. A hearing aid works as an amplifier for them. It helps the brain catch the shaking that starts at the hammer. A tiny diagram can show anvil, hammer, eardrum, and stirrup.

4Bone is harder than cartilage. Bone is softer than a tooth. Look at a skeleton's face and the nose may seem to be gone. The sticking-out part of a nose is not bone. It is cartilage. Say cartilage like CAR-tih-ledj. A finger can touch a nose. A finger can shift a nose. A finger can bend a nose. Bone will not bend that way. Cartilage also sits at bone ends. It stops one hard bone from scraping another. Teeth show up on a skeleton. They still are not bones. They outlast bone because they are harder. Enamel covers the outside of a tooth. Nothing in the body is harder than enamel. The skull joins a major bone system called the spinal column. Backbone is the everyday name. The column's first pieces begin behind the neck. They run down the back. They reach the hips. Each ridge is a vertebra. The plural is vertebrae, said VER-teh-bray. Each vertebra is its own bone. Thirty-three vertebrae make the whole column. Seven of them are cervical vertebrae. Those seven sit in the neck. Twelve of them are thoracic vertebrae. Say thoracic like thor-AH-sik. They begin high on the back. They reach about halfway down the back. Five lumbar vertebrae sit behind the waist. Five sacral vertebrae come next, and they are fused. They rest between the hips. What is left forms the coccyx, said KOK-siks. The coccyx is the column's bottom end. Neck vertebrae are what let a person tip the face upward. An extra note names the highest two vertebrae. One is the atlas. The other is the axis. Nodding uses them. Shaking the head uses them too.

5A spinal-column drawing can show a side view and a front view. Labels on it name the cervical vertebrae. They name the thoracic vertebrae. They name the lumbar vertebrae. They name the sacrum. They name the coccyx. The column does two big jobs. Job one is guarding the spinal cord, which is easy to hurt. The cord travels inside the vertebrae. Every nerve in the body meets there. From that meeting place, news travels to the brain. Job two is letting the body move. Bending uses the column. Twisting uses the column. Rolling uses the column. Flipping uses the column. The backbone is a chain, not one stiff piece. A chain can flex. It can shift several ways. Other bone sets also fasten to the backbone, not only the skull. Ribs attach there. Pelvic bones attach there. The chest gets its shape from the ribs. The lungs get protection from the ribs. The heart gets protection from the ribs. Both organs sit inside the rib cage. Someone can thump a chest. The lungs stay uncrushed. The heart stays uncrushed. Ribs form a strong wall around them. Twelve rib bones stand on the left side. Twelve rib bones stand on the right side. Each rib meets one thoracic vertebra. Twelve thoracic vertebrae match those ribs. Another pair of views, front and side, can label the clavicle. They can label the scapula. They can label the ribs. They can label the spinal column. They can label the pelvis.

6High on the spinal column, a scapula sits on each side. A clavicle sits on each side too. Shoulder blade is the everyday name for scapula. Collarbone is the everyday name for clavicle. Together, scapula and clavicle build the shoulder. The sacrum is marked lower down. Two hip bones near the column's lower end build the pelvis. Seen from the side, one hip bone has a shallow dish shape. It can also look like a bowl. Intestines rest in that bowl. Other organs of the lower body rest there too. A newborn's skeleton does not match an adult's. Before a baby is born, cartilage is there instead of bone. Growth changes that. Development changes that. The cartilage grows hard. It becomes bone. At birth, most of that cartilage has already turned to bone. A baby grows into a child. A child grows into an adult. Bones keep getting harder. Some bones join. Skull bones do this. The pelvis is among the last groups to join. Those bones become one solid piece. The change comes in the late teens. It can come in the early twenties. Arms, hands, legs, and feet are the body's appendages. People use them for many activities. Lifting uses arms and hands. Holding uses arms and hands. Getting from place to place uses legs and feet. Bones inside the appendages make part of that possible. A diagram can mark three arm bones by name. One name is humerus. One name is ulna. One name is radius. Three bones build each arm. Humerus is the bone of the upper arm. Its top end meets the shoulder. Radius and ulna fill the lower arm. They run from elbow to wrist. More labels mark wrist bones, palm bones, and the bones of thumb and fingers. In the playground picture, children push up with their arms.

7A hand X-ray is crowded with bones. No other body region has more bones than the wrist plus the hand. The number there is twenty-seven. Two hands add up to fifty-four. So many bones make the wrist and hand very flexible. They also make them dexterous. Small, careful work becomes possible. Writing is that kind of work. Piano playing is that kind of work. Tying a shoelace is that kind of work. A comparison chart is about bones used for handling things. A finger is smaller than an arm. A finger still has more bones. The chart compares the counts this way. One arm: 3 bones. One wrist: 8 carpals. One palm: 5 metacarpals. One finger: 3 phalanges, said fuh-LAN-jeez. One thumb: 2 phalanges. Fingers plus thumb: 14 phalanges in all. Leg and foot follow a plan you can set beside arm and hand. The upper leg is a single solid bone. Its names are thighbone and femur. The lower leg has two bones. Their names are shinbone, or tibia, and fibula. Between upper leg and lower leg sits one more bone. Its names are kneecap and patella. The patella rests over the knee joint. Under it are tendons. The patella guards those tendons. The tendons let the leg bend. Draw a runner and the leg bones can be shown. An extra note names the body's longest bone. It is also the strongest. It is also the largest. It lives in the leg. It is the thighbone, also called the femur. It runs from pelvis to knee. Only a large force will break a femur. A fall from a great height could do it. A high-speed crash while skiing could do it. A high-speed crash while skating could do it.

8A foot, like a hand, is a crowded set of bones. One foot has twenty-six bones. A hand has one more than that. Two feet add up to fifty-two. Seven tarsal bones fill the ankle and the heel. Five metatarsal bones fill the ball of the foot. Fourteen phalanges fill the toes, the same count as in a hand. The big toe gets two of them. Every other toe gets three. Soles are the bottoms of the feet. Skin and tissue there guard the bones when someone jumps. They guard the bones when someone runs. A leg-and-foot diagram can mark femur, patella, fibula, and tibia. It can mark ankle bones, the ball, and toe bones. Skin and tissue cushion the foot bones. The cushion is why those bones need not break during a run. The cushion helps during a jump. The cushion helps during a hop. Joints are what let a person bend into many poses. Joints are what let a person twist into many poses. A grown body has those 206 bones. It also has over 100 joints. A joint is a meeting place of bones. Bone itself is hard. Bone itself will not bend. The meetings let the body bend anyway. The meetings let the body twist anyway. People sometimes say someone is double-jointed. That phrase does not mean two joints sit where one joint should. It means the person flexes more than average. The ligaments at those joints are looser. Loose ligaments allow bends that look unusual.

9One picture marks a ball and a socket. An X-ray of the hip shows the joint there. That joint links pelvis and femur. People call this kind of joint a ball-and-socket. Joints do not all work the same way. The humerus meets the shoulder bone in a ball-and-socket joint. The femur meets the pelvis bone in a ball-and-socket joint. The humerus has a ball at its top end. The femur has a ball at its top end. Each ball sits snugly in a round socket. The shoulder holds one of those sockets. The pelvis holds the other. Elbow and knee are hinge joints. A hinge joint bends one way only. Joints between spinal vertebrae are swivel joints. A swivel joint lets the body tilt. A swivel joint lets the body turn. Sutures are the last joint type. They are the skull's joints. They link skull bones. They allow little movement. A bone can look like a dead rock, only hard. That idea is wrong. Bone is alive. Millions of bone cells live in it. Those cells must have oxygen. Those cells must have food. Other cells in the body need the same things. The outer layer is compact bone. Compact bone is hard. Compact bone is solid. Under it lies spongy bone. Tiny holes fill the spongy bone. The holes keep a bone from being too heavy. Muscles can lift a lighter bone. Marrow fills the space under the spongy bone. Marrow also fills spaces inside the spongy bone. Marrow matters because blood cells are made there. In most adults, marrow turns out more than 50 billion red cells for the blood each day. A cutaway drawing can mark bone marrow, compact bone, and spongy bone.

10Bone is strong, yet a hard enough strike can break it. A doctor gives a little of the help a break needs. Bone cells give a great deal of the help. Proper healing means the pieces go back as they were. How bad the break is can change the doctor's work. The doctor may have to shift the pieces. The goal is to set them in position again. A cast then wraps the hurt body part. The part cannot move inside the cast. The bone gets time to mend. Repair by bone cells starts the moment a bone breaks. The cast keeps the break still. Stillness lets the cells do their work. A picture can show a cast holding a break so healing can happen. Strong bones are healthy bones. Moving your body on a regular schedule does the most to keep them working well. A balanced diet helps marrow make healthy blood cells. Legumes help bones. A pinto bean is a legume. A pea is a legume. Other vegetables help bones. Fruit helps bones. Calcium-rich foods help bones grow. Dairy foods are rich in calcium. Fortified soy milk is rich in calcium. Fortified rice milk is rich in calcium. Fortified orange juice is rich in calcium. Shape is one gift bones give a body. They give more than shape. Moving is one of those gifts. Sitting is one of those gifts. Standing is one of those gifts. Writing is one of those gifts. A human body would not be the same if the bones were gone. Fun activities depend on bones. Soccer with friends is one of those activities.

11Here are meanings for special words. An appendage is an outer body part that juts out, like an arm or a leg. A ball-and-socket joint fits the way a ball fits in a glove. Bone marrow is the spongy center material that makes blood cells. Cartilage is stretchy tissue. Humans have it. Other vertebrates have it. Dexterous describes someone who can do tricky motions with grace. Fused describes parts that have joined. A hinge joint opens the way a door opens. A legume is a plant that bears seed pods. Beans, lentils, and peas are legumes. A ligament is tissue that ties one bone to another bone. The spinal cord is a nerve bundle. Vertebrae shield it. A suture is a joint, or a seam, between skull bones. A swivel joint can tip. A swivel joint can rotate. A tendon is tough tissue that fastens muscle onto bone. A vertebrate is an animal that has a backbone. A full-body bone map can name the parts one by one. The map shows the cranium. The map shows the clavicle. The map shows the humerus. The map shows the rib cage. The map shows the spinal column. The map shows the radius. The map shows the ulna. The map shows the wrist bones. The map shows the hand bones. The map shows the pelvis. The map shows the femur. The map shows the patella. The map shows the fibula. The map shows the tibia. The map shows the ankle bones. The map shows the foot bones.

67. The Island People Who Vanished

1A map shows Crete in the Mediterranean Sea. Italy, Greece, and Turkey are nearby. The Aegean Sea is marked. The Black Sea is marked too. This book begins with the island of Crete. Then it tells about the first people who lived there. Next it tells about Minoan culture. Then a volcano on Thera explodes. The book asks whether that blast ended the Minoans. A Greek invasion comes next. Then the book asks whether Crete was Atlantis. A word list and a topic list close the book. South of Greece lies a large island. The island is called Crete. Crete has many mountains. The Mediterranean Sea around it is a beautiful part of that sea. That part is called the Aegean Sea. The name sounds like ih-JEE-uhn. Greece is the country that includes Crete today. In earlier times Crete stood as a nation by itself. A great people lived there. Their culture is known as the Minoan civilization.

2From about 2600 bc to about 1450 bc, the Minoans did well on Crete. For hundreds of years they traded with other countries. Those countries lay around the Mediterranean Sea. Trade made the Minoans rich. Then the Minoan civilization seemed to vanish overnight. A mystery began. How could a rich nation disappear so fast? That nation had been a leader among other nations. Greek myths tell about Minos. The Greek god Zeus had a son named Minos. He ruled the island of Crete. His palace was at Knossos. Minoan is a word that points back to Minos. An early student of old Crete chose the culture's name. He called it Minoan after King Minos. Some research says Greek myths may hold some truth. A title, not only one man, is what some researchers see in Minos. They think every ruler of Crete used that title. That span runs from about 3000 bc until 1000 bc. People call that time the Bronze Age. King Minos has a throne room in one picture. It is in the palace at Knossos. Ships used by Crete's people appear in Minoan art. Settlement on Crete probably began about 8,000 years ago. Researchers believe they came from a place known today as Turkey. Crete is an island, so settlers needed ships. Those people would have brought farming knowledge with them. They would have brought knowledge of the sea.

3Researchers have learned something about Crete's soil. It was good for growing food. The Minoans raised sheep. They grew olives. They grew grapes. They got better at making goods. The goods included olive oil, wine, and wool. As those skills grew, the civilization grew too. Forests on the island were full of trees. People cut the trees down for wood. Ships were built by the Minoans from that wood. Goods traveled on those ships. They traded those goods with other nations. A picture shows that farmland on Crete is still excellent for food. Great trading was a Minoan skill by about 3000 bc. They traded their goods with neighbors around the Mediterranean. They received gemstones in return. They received ivory. They received silver. They received gold. They received copper. Crete itself did not have those materials. The people valued them for that reason. Trade was the path that made the Minoans rich. As years passed, Minoan life grew more advanced. Writing was a system they already had. They made many fine works of art. The art included frescoes. It included pottery. It included jewelry. They built more towns. They linked the towns with paved roads. They built storehouses. The storehouses held goods that would be traded. They built fine houses. They built large palaces. Society gathered around the palaces. A theory is the form of much Minoan knowledge we hold. A theory is an idea based on evidence. It can also be a group of ideas. Evidence can be an object such as a building. It can be a work of art. Researchers can study those objects. A picture shows a Minoan ring.

4Researchers studied the kinds of gems in Minoan jewelry. Then they found the mountains where those gems were mined. They also studied the clay used in the pottery. Frescoes are important evidence. Pottery is important evidence too. These works often show how people lived. Many Minoan artworks show daily life. Frescoes and pottery show people farming. They show people sailing. They show people celebrating. They show how Minoans dressed. They show how Minoans wore their hair. Another clue matters just as much. The frescoes and pottery show few battle scenes. Researchers read that as a sign. Peace was the usual way of the Minoan people. Few enemies rose up to test their power. A drinking cup shows three activities. The activities are boxing, bull-leaping, and wrestling. Researchers have studied palace ruins at Malia. They use those ruins to learn about Minoan culture. The Minoan civilization reached its high point after about 1700 bc. Collapse of the civilization began about 1450 bc. Evidence shows that many of its cities burned. Many of its palaces burned too. About 1100 bc marks a time with no Minoan civilization left. The mystery has drawn researchers who want an answer. They study the evidence. A volcano was the cause many historians named for a long time.

5An island called Thera lay near the Minoan home. People now call that island Santorini. North of Crete, the distance to Thera was about 70 miles, or 40 km. For many thousands of years, a volcano on Thera kept waking. It was active off and on. Then the volcano stayed quiet for a long time. Safety was what people started to expect on the island. They built cities there. A large store of magma was gathering far beneath the island. Melted rock plus hot gases is what magma is. The growing magma caused great pressure inside the mountain island. The pressure made the land shake. Those shakes were earthquakes. After several earthquakes, a day came when Thera exploded. A picture shows a statue from Thera. A map places Thera and Crete in the Aegean Sea. Greece and Turkey are on the map. The Mediterranean Sea is on it too. Other pictures show Mount Saint Helens. One picture shows the mountain before the 1980 eruption. One shows it after that eruption. One shows the mountain blowing its top. The blast at Thera was among the strongest eruptions in history. Pictures of Mount Saint Helens may be familiar. Washington State saw that volcano erupt in 1980. That eruption was big. It was tiny beside Thera. The Thera blast was about twelve times larger than the Mount Saint Helens blast. Huge amounts of rock blew out of the volcano. Hot gases blew out. Ashes blew out. All of it went into the sky above the volcano. Rocks and ash fell on islands across the Aegean Sea. A gigantic dark cloud formed from small rocks, gases, and ash.

6The Thera blast was so large that it made a tsunami. The word sounds like tsoo-NOM-ee. A tsunami is a large sea wave. Its height may have reached 100 feet. It may have been even higher. Shores all around the Mediterranean were struck by the tsunami. Water covered the land on many islands. Farms were lost. Whole cities were lost. After the eruption, the middle of Thera was gone. A large hole was all that remained there. A hole left when a volcano falls in is called a caldera. The word sounds like call-DARE-uh. Sea water filled the caldera. Thera took the shape of a crescent. A picture shows that collapse. The island's center was left as a huge hole. Two smaller islands remained where one large island had been. For a long time, researchers blamed Thera for a bigger loss. They thought the eruption made the Minoans of Crete disappear. In their view, both events shared one moment in time. Later evidence showed a gap in time. About 180 years separate that eruption from the later loss. The Minoans vanished after that gap. Did researchers then throw out the volcano idea? Not exactly. Some researchers now think the eruption played a part. It may have weakened the Minoans. The tsunami would have wrecked many Minoan ships. It would have wrecked ports along the shores of Crete. It would have ruined crops as well. The Minoans would have had few goods left to trade. They would have had few ships left for trade. Quakes before the eruption could have wrecked the cities of Crete too. Survivors would have felt deep sadness after so much loss. They would have needed lots of money to rebuild Crete. They would have needed lots of energy too. These losses left Crete open to enemies. Crete had never been that open before.

7Beginning about 1450 bc, people from Greece invaded Crete. They were called the Mycenaeans. The name sounds like my-suh-NEE-unz. The Mycenaeans probably struck the last blow. That blow ended the Minoan civilization. The eruption at Thera had left the Minoans weak. They could not gather enough strength to stay safe. They could not hold off the Mycenaeans. The Mycenaeans were fighters. They took over cities. Researchers know this from written tales of their fights. People can still read those writings today. A Mycenaean vase is decorated with warriors. It shows spears. It shows an early kind of armor. Many people know the Mycenaeans through a tale by a man named Homer. Some researchers think Homer lived around 1200 bc. Troy is the city Homer put in his tale. He wrote about a fight to win a woman back. Her name was Helen. The fighters in that tale were the Mycenaeans. People once believed Homer's tale was made up. A very old city turned up in Turkey under researchers' study. The city seemed to match the Troy in Homer's tale. Ruins in Turkey pointed to a new idea. Homer's words about Troy may have been true.

8Many people are starting to think that Homer told real stories. Real cities may be hiding inside those tales. Real people may be hiding inside those tales too. Their lives were lived very far back in time. They also think other ancient writers may have told the truth. That idea follows if Homer's stories hold some truth. An old Greek philosopher told a very interesting story. A philosopher is a deep thinker. His name was Plato. He said a great island country once existed. Then that country disappeared. He called the country Atlantis. Plato said a terrible disaster destroyed Atlantis. The disaster made the country sink under the sea. People never saw it again. Plato wrote about Atlantis two times. He wrote those pages about a decade before he died. He died in 348 bc. He described an ideal civilization. It had existed millions of years before he wrote. Plato said Atlantis was huge. Libya and Asia together were still smaller than Atlantis. That size is bigger than the continental United States. Plato wrote about the kings of Atlantis. Those kings were descended from the god Poseidon. Poseidon was god of the sea. He was also god of earthquakes. Those kings had power over the whole known world. Minoan Crete had been great. Then it seemed to vanish. Because of that pair of facts, some people link Crete to Atlantis. Some people read Plato's Atlantis stories for another reason. They hope to learn more about the fall of Minoan civilization. A picture shows Plato. Crete may have been Atlantis, or it may not. Both mysteries leave many people deeply curious. Solving the two mysteries is a pleasure for them. Researchers study the evidence with a hope. They hope to fit one more piece into the puzzle. One part of the puzzle is Atlantis. The other part is the loss of Minoan Crete. Maybe no one will ever learn what really happened. One thing is certain. The hunt for answers will go on. A picture shows a work called Timaeus. Atlantis is the subject of Plato's writing called Timaeus.

9A civilization is a culture with developed ways of living. Those ways include government and religion. They include sciences and language. They include art and learning. Collapsed means fell apart. Descended means linked by blood to an ancestor. A disaster is a sudden, terrible event. An eruption is a sudden push of material out of a volcano. Evidence is something that shows a claim is real. It can show that a claim is true. Fictional means made up. It means not true. Frescoes are paintings on walls or ceilings. The surface is plaster. Intrigued means made very curious. Invaded means went into another country to take control. It can also mean went in to make war. A mystery is something unknown. It can also be something hard to understand. A philosopher wants to understand every part of life. That person also wants to explain those parts. Pressure is force from one thing pushing hard on another. It can also be a build-up of energy. Researchers are people who study a topic with care. They look for facts. They try to find out what is true. A theory is an idea that explains events. It can be a set of ideas. Those ideas rest on evidence. Topics in this book include the Aegean Sea. They include Atlantis and the word caldera. They include Greece, Homer, and King Minos. They include the Mediterranean Sea. Minoan topics cover farming. They cover art and building. They cover the civilization, the land, and the people. They cover trade. The Mycenaeans are a topic. Plato is a topic. Thera, the tsunami, and Turkey are topics. The volcano is a topic too.

68. The Monday That Honors Work

1Marchers in a New York City parade for Labor Day carry a banner that honors union workers. In the United States, the holiday falls on September's first Monday. For many American children it is a final burst of summer fun before school begins. Many businesses close. Every government office closes. Some people have the day free and may hold a party. Rest is not the only purpose. The U.S. government also set the day aside to honor what workers in America have achieved, in the past and in the present. To understand that honor, learn about the labor movement. In it, workers joined together so their work and their lives could improve.

2From the late 1700s into the early 1800s, the Industrial Revolution brought many new kinds of machines. Jobs once done by hand could be finished much faster by machines. They could also be finished with less strain. Farmers began using machines to put crops in the ground and to bring them in. Buying the machines was beyond many small farmers. Their work disappeared. Factories could also produce goods far more cheaply than small businesses run from homes. Because of these shifts, many people left farming towns for cities. They took factory jobs. Many factory bosses paid as little as possible, so the business would earn more. Low wages came with work that was often dangerous. Recent immigrants were very open to harm from such bosses. So were people who had formerly been enslaved. They were more likely to face unsafe conditions for low pay. A 1925 picture shows a farmer guiding a tractor as it plows a field. Free time was scarce for many workers in the 1800s. No rule in the United States limited how many hours a person could work. Employers used that gap. A typical factory hand worked 100 hours in a week. Anyone who disliked the hours could be fired with ease. A replacement was hired. A 1911 picture shows women and children working as spinners inside a Mississippi factory.

3Family farms used child workers before the Industrial Revolution. Factories did too. So did jobs as assistants. The revolution, though, raised the amount of child labor in factories. Children could run most of the machines. Pay for a child could sit below an adult's pay. They were easier to direct. Around two million children, by the early 1800s, held jobs in mills or in factories inside the United States. Some family businesses had been closed by the new factory age. Jobs often began before age ten. Sometimes a child was six or seven. The week ran six days, and a day could last eighteen hours. Those children often supported the family. Rest was rare. School and play had no room. Many grew ill from danger on the job and from the long hours. A 1917 picture shows four children inside a tobacco factory. Over time, workers started joining together to force change. They formed labor unions, groups built to protect workers' rights. A union bargains with an employer. It asks for better hours, better wages, safer conditions, and stronger benefits. A strike is one tool a union may use. Refusing work can strengthen its side of a negotiation. During a strike, workers refuse all further work until changes come. In 1869, President Ulysses S. Grant announced that government workers needed to work only eight hours a day. Soon an effort began to win a similar law for people employed by private organizations. Many unions keep a seal of their own. They place it on things they make or work on. The seal is a mark of pride. It also tells a shopper which goods came from union labor.

4A picture shows workers marching through New York City in 1872, on strike for a workday of eight hours. Women were mostly shut out of the early labor movement. Women's rights took a large step in New York City. Textile workers there formed the Ladies Garment Workers Union. They joined with the men who worked beside them. They proved women mattered to the movement. Across the country, membership in unions has fallen since the 1980s. From 2020 onward, though, strikes and drives to form unions have been rising. Unions of government workers keep growing at a steady pace. Teachers have strong unions. Mail carriers have them. Firefighters have them. Police officers have them. About 10.3 percent of the country's workers belonged to a union as of 2021. Help from Congress arrived slowly. The year 1938 marked a turn. Labor activists found a listener in President Franklin Delano Roosevelt. The result was a law from Congress, the Fair Labor Standards Act. People shorten that name to FLSA. Its aim was to stop employers from using low wages and poor conditions against workers. The act capped the workweek at forty-four hours. In 1940 the cap became forty hours. It also created the minimum wage, the lowest pay an employer was allowed to give. In a picture from 1935, President Franklin D. Roosevelt signs the Social Security Act. That law was one of several steps meant to give American workers better lives. When the 1938 act passed, the minimum wage stood at $0.25 per hour. The same wage, in later money, equals $5.03. By 2022 a nationwide floor of $7.25 an hour was in place. A state may set a higher floor. Thirty states, and Washington, D.C., have done so.

5The act also required extra pay when someone works longer than usual. The extra time is called overtime. For each of those hours, the worker earns one and a half times the usual hourly rate. Overtime is every hour past forty in a workweek. The added pay was meant to stop bosses from forcing overly long weeks. It was also meant to push bosses to hire more people. The act set safety rules on the job as well. It banned many forms of child labor. During school hours, the youngest allowed age was sixteen. A fourteen-year-old could hold certain jobs after school. Dangerous jobs required the worker to be eighteen. One pay example uses a rate of $15.00 an hour. A week of forty hours brings that worker $600. A week that adds ten overtime hours brings $825. Long strikes had already shown why pay rules mattered. In the Pullman Strike of 1894, railroad workers halted work for more than two months. Cuts in wages were hurting their families. Several people stood at the center of the labor movement. Mother Jones was Mary Harris Jones, and she lived from 1837 to 1930. In the early 1900s she helped coal miners. Members of the union called her Mother because she worked so hard on their behalf. She crossed the United States to aid miners on strike and to stop child labor. A. Philip Randolph lived from 1889 to 1979. He was widely known for speaking up for Black working-class interests in the United States. Organizing the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters took a drive that he led for ten years. Those workers cared for passengers' needs on train trips. He urged people to march on Washington. The protest targeted unfair hiring inside the armed forces. He trusted protest that stayed nonviolent. He trusted action by great numbers of people. That trust helped spark the civil rights movement during the 1950s and the 1960s. Eugene Debs lived from 1855 to 1926. He helped found major unions for railroad workers and for industrial workers. Between 1900 and 1920 he ran for president five times. Trips across the nation let him help workers in their talks with bosses. Dolores Huerta was born in 1930. She co-founded the United Farm Workers Association. Her activist work centered on families with low incomes, on women, and on children. Grape farmers walked out in 1965, and the strike she helped organize counted 5,000 of them. A contract came out of those talks. It made conditions on the job safer. Now she travels the country, backing campaigns and urging laws and policies that support equal rights.

6Workers march in an 1882 Labor Day celebration in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. New York City held the earliest celebration. The year of that celebration was also 1882. A state law in 1887 made the day official, and Oregon was the state that passed it first. Similar laws then passed in thirty more states. In 1894 the national government added it to the federal calendar. Canada marks the same Monday in September. More than sixty other countries instead mark International Workers' Day on May 1. Like the American holiday, that day celebrates people who work. Activists use it to teach rights. They also work to stop practices that treat labor unfairly. Canadian ironworkers march together in a parade in Toronto, Ontario.

7The American Welding Society began in 1919. Safety gear is required for welders. Thick gloves of leather are part of it. A helmet made for the job is part of it. The gear keeps injury away. Movements for labor still try to improve treatment and pay. The COVID-19 pandemic reached the United States early in 2020. It drew notice to people in healthcare, in food service, and in retail. Support for them has included calls for a higher federal minimum wage. In 2022 the United States lifted pay for federal workers to a minimum of $15 an hour. Workers outside the federal workforce stayed at a minimum of $7.25 an hour. On the holiday, pause to honor the people whose work builds better lives for themselves and for their communities. A minimum wage is the lowest hourly pay the law allows. Federal refers to a central government. That government divides power with states, or with regions, that stay separate. A rate is an amount measured against some other unit, such as dollars for each hour. The Industrial Revolution was a change in making goods and in transport, from the power of people and animals to the power of machines, beginning late in the eighteenth century. Rights are freedoms or powers a person can justly claim. A strike is a protest in which workers stop. They show unhappiness with conditions, or they press employers to change. Labor can mean hard physical work, or the people who do it. The labor movement is workers acting together, through bargaining, to improve conditions. Wages are the regular pay a worker earns, based on time spent working.

69. The Moving Plates of Earth

1An introduction opens this book. Earth's structure comes next. The fragile crust comes after that. Tectonic plates come next. Pangaea comes after the plates. Ocean ridges and trenches follow. A conclusion follows them. A glossary ends the book. A globe can make you ask why Earth has this shape. Why do oceans split the big lands? Why is there not one single mass of land? Why do separate continents exist? This book hunts for answers. You will learn how Earth is built. You will learn how that build has changed. A possible future shape of Earth is part of the lesson. Earth never stops changing. The change is happening now. The build comes before the reasons for the look and the change. Knowing the build makes the change easier to grasp. An earthquake arrives every 11 seconds. Active volcanoes in the world number more than 600. Each quake is one way Earth changes. Each eruption is another way.

2Earth measures about 12,742 kilometers from side to side. That is 7,918 miles. Ancient Greeks already knew that size. Earth is made of three main layers. Their names are crust, mantle, and core. A drawing shows the inside. It is drawn to scale, so each layer keeps its share of the size, only much smaller. The crust is the outside. It is rigid. Next to the other layers it is thin. Thickness is not the same everywhere. Under oceans it is only about 4.8 kilometers. That is 3 miles. Under a mountain range it can reach 100 kilometers. That is 62 miles.
