The Swiss Alps are one such range. Another example is the Cascades. They stand in the northwest of the United States. Great pressure can snap the crust because the crust is brittle. The mantle sits under the crust. It is dense. It is hot. It is semi-solid rock about 2,800 kilometers thick. That is 1,750 miles. Heat is why it is only semi-solid. Heat in the mantle far exceeds heat in the crust.

3Deep inside Earth, pressure is far above the pressure at the surface. The deepest mantle is hotter because of that pressure. It is also denser. The core sits under the mantle, at Earth's center. Density there is almost double the mantle. Pressure is higher still. Metal, not rock, makes up most of the core. Two layers fill the center. The outer core is liquid and about 2,080 kilometers thick. That is 1,300 miles. A solid inner core is the true middle. Iron makes up almost all of it. Earth turns, and the liquid outer core turns with it. That spin makes Earth's magnetic field. Picture the pieces in order. A thin crust is stiff and able to break. A hotter mantle in the middle is not fully solid. A core in the center has a solid heart and a liquid-like outside. Some people picture a hard-boiled egg. Shell stands for crust. White stands for mantle. Yolk stands for core. The picture can help you remember. One difference matters. A yolk is a single layer. Earth's core has two. Heat is the first thing to remember about the mantle. Hot rock softens. Hot metal softens. Either one can move toward liquid. A blacksmith heats a horseshoe until the metal glows red. Soft metal can then be hammered to the hoof. The mantle stays that hot all the time, so it never turns fully solid. Think of a soft dough. It can feel firm. A push changes its shape. The mantle behaves that way. It is solid-ish, and also not. Rigid crust is above it. A spinning liquid outer core is below it. Stress builds because it is squeezed in the middle. Two strong forces never let go. Motion in the mantle never stops. Crust rides on that moving mantle. Usually the crust holds together as solid rock. The same stress can shift huge slabs of crust. Cracks can open. Those cracks are fault lines. Quakes are known to strike along them.

4Fault lines often sit where big slabs of crust meet. The next section explains that motion. Enough pressure makes enough heat to melt mantle rock into magma. Hot magma swells. It presses the crust above. Cracks become paths for the magma. The melt can climb close to the surface. If the push is strong enough, magma breaks out and a volcano forms. A still stronger push makes an explosion. Dust flies. Ash flies. Steam flies. Liquid rock called lava flies. Volcanoes, like quakes, usually sit where two or more slabs meet. A picture shows lava bursting out. About fifteen huge slabs, called plates, make the crust. Some plates pull apart. Some plates push together. Some plates slide past one another. Land covers some plates. Ocean covers others. A plate under land is a continental plate. A plate under ocean is an oceanic plate. A plate can vanish over time. A new plate can appear. The count can change. Your lifetime will not see that change. Millions of years are required. Forming and moving of plates is called plate tectonics. The Greek root of tectonic means to build. The name means Earth is built of rock plates. The plates likely formed early in a history about five billion years long. Long ago every continental plate was joined. One continent existed. Its name is Pangaea. Greek gives that name the sense of all lands.

5Drawings on the following page show seven continents once locked in one giant land. Hundreds of millions of years passed. Forces inside Earth shoved the continental plates. The plates spread. Continents arrived where we find them now. Move from picture to picture and the lands look like puzzle pieces. South America once nestled into Africa's coast. Nobody knows the map hundreds of millions of years ahead. Separation to today's spots took 225 million years. Some scientists think most continents will join again someday. Continental drift is the name for this slow shift. What force inside Earth is strong enough to shove such huge slabs? A label on the page reads Movement of Continental Plates.

6An odd chain of mountains turned up under the Atlantic, near its center. Later work showed the chain runs between all the continents. It winds around Earth. The name is the global mid-ocean ridge. Hot magma leaks up fault lines along that ridge. It spreads on the sea floor and cools. Oceanic plates grow from that buildup. They press outward against other plates. Underwater eruptions happen at some spots on the ridge. Enough magma has piled up to make islands. Iceland formed that way. Deep trenches ring the Pacific Ocean. Older crust is shoved into those trenches while new crust is made. One plate dives under another there. Quakes cluster at those spots. Volcanoes cluster there too. That rim of Pacific land earned the name Ring of Fire. Western shores of North America hold ranges built when ocean plates dove under land plates. Western shores of South America hold such ranges. Eastern shores of Asia hold them too. Many volcanoes sit in those ranges. Colliding plates drove the crust upward. A drawing shows an oceanic plate sliding under a continental plate.

7A drawing tracks India moving north across the last 80 million years. Other drawings show the Indian plate's tip forced upward. Colliding plates built the Himalayas that way. When Pangaea split, India was an island off Australia. Northward speed was about 9.1 meters each century. That is 30 feet. The crash into Asia slowed India. Northward motion still went on. India's coastal edge rose against the Eurasian continent, which did not move aside. That edge became the Himalaya Mountains. Fossils of water animals sit in sandstone and other Himalayan rock. Those fossils show a salty sea once covered that ground. The Indian plate has not stopped. The Himalayas have not stopped growing. Yearly growth is 1 centimeter. That is 0.39 inches. A million years of that rate adds 9.66 kilometers. That is 6 miles.

8Plate tectonics explains a great deal about past change on Earth. It also points to change still ahead. The science is still young. More insight into Earth's make-up will come. Several major quakes will strike during your life. A few serious eruptions will strike too. Each event adds clues about how Earth fits together. Daily tracking is possible now. Some pages on the internet log quakes around the world. They log eruptions too. The past grows clearer through this study. A possible future grows clearer too. Many scientists expect Los Angeles to end up beside San Francisco. Los Angeles rides an oceanic plate headed north. San Francisco sits safely on a continental plate. A drawing shows two plates. One is the Pacific Plate. One is the North American Plate. Living long enough to watch would be fun. The wait is huge for a person. For Earth it is only a blink.

9Continental drift means continents creep as plates shift. Continental plates are crust plates that carry the continents. The core is Earth's innermost layer. A liquid outer part and a solid inner part make it up. The crust is Earth's solid outside. A fault is a crack in the crust where movement happens. The global mid-ocean ridge is an undersea mountain chain that zigzags between the continents. Lava is melted rock that has reached open air. Magma is melted rock from the mantle that is still underground. The mantle is the semi-solid layer between crust and outer core. Oceanic plates are the plates under the oceans. Pangaea was the single continent that once held all the land. Plate tectonics is the moving of crust plates. Plates are the great rock slabs of the crust. The Ring of Fire is the volcano ring on continent edges that face the Pacific Ocean. A trench is a very deep place where one plate slides beneath another. A volcano is an opening in a planet's crust. Melted rock exits there. Steam exits too. The hill or mountain built from that material is a volcano too.

70. The Normandy Landing Called D-Day

1This book moves through these parts. An introduction comes first. Background comes next. Operation Overlord follows. The beaches come after that. Utah Beach, Omaha Beach, Gold Beach, Juno Beach, and Sword Beach each get a turn. A conclusion comes near the end. Word meanings close the book. Hundreds of men huddled in dozens of small landing craft. They thought about their families far away. The men were just off the coast of France. German forces occupied that coast. Most of them were not trained soldiers. They had not spent their whole lives in the military. They were teachers. They were store clerks. They were housepainters. They were other people from the United States. They came from the United Kingdom too. They came from Canada too. They were fighting in World War II. The landing craft were rocking in the rough waters. Many of the men were seasick. All of them were scared. To begin their mission, they needed to jump into the cold water. Then they needed to run across the beaches. Members of the German army shot at them. Those German fighters had not been soldiers before the war either. Soon the world these men knew would not be the same. This mission had a code name. The name was Operation Overlord. It was a must-win for the Allies. This is the story of the day called D-Day. In military terminology, the D in D-Day stands for day. Any important military operation could use this special code for its chosen day. The days before a particular D-Day used a minus sign. The days after it used a plus sign. In this case the day was June 6, 1944. D minus 3 meant three days before D-Day. That date was June 3. D plus 3 meant three days after D-Day. That date was June 9.

2A map of Europe in 1942 shows who held the land. Ireland is on the map. Prussia is marked. England is marked. The Netherlands is marked. Poland is marked. Germany is marked. Belgium is marked. Czechoslovakia is marked. Luxembourg is marked. The Atlantic Ocean is marked. France is marked. Austria is marked. Switzerland is marked. Hungary is marked. Romania is marked. Portugal is marked. Yugoslavia is marked. Bulgaria is marked. Spain is marked. Italy is marked. Albania is marked. Greece is marked. The Mediterranean Sea is marked. A key sorts the land into German control, neutral country, and Allied control. World War II was the biggest war in modern history. It began when German troops invaded Poland in September 1939. German troops quickly captured Poland. Then they invaded France in June 1940. Over the next four years, Germany took over most of Europe. The other Axis powers did too. Those powers were Italy and Japan. They also took many Pacific islands. The Allies were trying to stop the Axis powers. The Allies included the United Kingdom. They included the United States. They included Canada. They included the Soviet Union. They included other nations. If Allied forces could free France, German troops would be trapped. Allied-occupied France would stand on one side. The Soviet Union would stand on the other. A map of the Normandy beach landing points shows Great Britain. Southampton is marked. Portsmouth is marked. Shoreham-by-Sea is marked. Portland is marked. Dartmouth is marked. The English Channel is marked. Utah beach is marked. Omaha beach is marked. Gold beach is marked. Juno beach is marked. Sword beach is marked. U.S. forces, British forces, and Canadian forces are shown. France is shown too. The D-Day invasion on June 6, 1944, was one of the most important days for Allied forces during World War II. The Allies had to move more than 156,000 men across the English Channel. They had to move all their gear too. They had to do it without the Axis powers learning the plan too far in advance. The plan called for Allied air forces to parachute into zones across the north of France. That drop was set for the morning of June 6. Other troops would then leave the landing craft. They would storm across five beaches. The beaches were Utah, Omaha, Gold, Juno, and Sword. The Allies hoped to gain a foothold along the French coast. Then they hoped to move forward into German-occupied France.

3Utah Beach is shown with a key. German positions are marked. U.S. positions as of midnight are marked. Omaha Beach sits beside it on the map. The numbers for Utah Beach are these. The number of U.S. troops landed was 20,000. The number of military vehicles landed was 1,700. The number of U.S. casualties was 589. The United States 4th Infantry Division planned to land on Utah beach. The 82nd Airborne Division was part of the plan. The 101st Airborne Division was part of it too. The landing time was 6:30 am. Five hours earlier, paratroopers were dropped at many points inland. Those points were 2 to 5 miles inland. That distance is 3.2 to 8.0 kilometers. The paratroopers had to secure the main road from Valognes to Carentan. Say those names vah-LOHN-yuh and kah-rohn-TOHN. The Germans used searchlights to find the Allied planes. Those planes were dropping paratroopers. German troops did not know the role of the paratroopers. They might be the main attack force. They might be a distraction. The beach troops were supposed to use that distraction. They landed at 6:30 am. They were supposed to push inland. They were supposed to meet up with the paratroopers. The strong tide changed the landing. Their craft landed 2,200 yards from the beach targets. That distance is 2 kilometers. Wading was the only way for the soldiers to reach shore. General Theodore Roosevelt Jr. told his men they would start the war from right there. He ordered them to advance. Luckily, that part of the beach was not heavily defended. American casualties were few compared with the other beaches. By afternoon, the U.S. 4th Infantry had met up with American paratroopers. The German troops were defeated quickly. The mission was a success. The Americans advanced 4 miles inland. That distance is 6.4 kilometers.

4Omaha Beach is shown with Utah Beach, Gold Beach, and a key. German resistance is marked. U.S. positions as of midnight are marked. The numbers for Omaha Beach are these. The number of U.S. troops landed was 34,000. The number of military vehicles lost was 136. The number of U.S. casualties was 3,686. The United States 1st Army was at a disadvantage from the start. All around Omaha Beach were cliffs 100 feet high. That height is 30.5 meters. The cliffs made it very difficult for the Americans to attack. The Germans had also placed armed dragon's teeth around the beach. Those forms were 3 to 4 feet tall. That height is 0.9 to 1.2 meters. They looked like teeth. They were meant to take out any landing craft. German troops were firing from the cliffs too. The attack was planned for 6:30 am. The tide would be low then. The dragon's teeth could be seen. The plan was to land infantry troops. Twenty-nine tanks would land with them. Allied troops would have gained a huge advantage from those tanks. The tanks were released from their landing craft too far from the beach. All but two tanks flooded. They sank to the bottom of the ocean. Nothing could be done to save the tanks. Nothing could be done to save their crews. The troops did not get their armored cover from the tanks. Bad weather made the Allies' trouble even worse. Many landing craft were blown far from their targets by powerful winds. The troops fell into mass confusion because of this. German fire easily cut down the Americans. General Omar Bradley thought about calling off the mission because the losses were so great. The only way through was a hard run. Soldiers had to run across the beach toward the cliffs. They had to dodge heavy German gunfire. Anyone who reached the cliffs still had to climb them. U.S. ships got as close as they could. They attacked the German troops. The ships brought important relief. They distracted the Germans. Those Germans had been focused on the Americans on the beach. Night came with the Americans holding a piece of Omaha Beach.

5Gold Beach is shown with Juno Beach and a key. German resistance is marked. British positions as of midnight are marked. The numbers for Gold Beach are these. The number of British troops landed was 24,970. The number of military vehicles landed was 2,100. The number of British casualties was 1,023. British forces of the 50th Infantry Division faced a huge problem at Gold Beach. Strong winds covered the German mines on the beach with water. The troops could not go in and disable the mines as planned. These hidden mines damaged twenty armored cars. The situation could have been worse. Many of the German troops had been taken out by sea attacks. Air attacks had taken out many too. By afternoon, the British had taken control of most of Gold Beach. They quickly pushed inland. They also successfully captured the fishing village of Arromanches. Say ar-roh-MAHNSH. Later the Allies unloaded supplies in this town. Juno Beach is shown with Gold Beach, Sword Beach, and a key. German resistance is marked. Canadian positions as of midnight are marked. The numbers for Juno Beach are these. The number of Canadian troops landed was 21,400. The number of military vehicles landed was 3,200. The number of Canadian casualties was 961. The Canadian 3rd Infantry was tasked with taking Juno Beach. They were to move inland. They were to form a link between two British-held beaches. Those beaches were Gold and Sword. Bad weather and a rising tide covered the German mines. The mines were difficult to destroy. Almost one-third of the landing craft were damaged or destroyed by the mines. Wading to shore was a struggle for many Canadian soldiers. About half of the first Canadian wave on the beaches could expect to stay alive. The Canadians were not going to give up. No troops on the other four beaches pushed as far inland as they did.

6Sword Beach is shown with Juno Beach and a key. German resistance is marked. British positions as of midnight are marked. The numbers for Sword Beach are these. The number of British troops landed was 29,000. The number of military vehicles landed was 2,603. The number of British casualties was 630. Sword Beach was the other beach attacked by British forces. The British 3rd Infantry Division made that attack. The main goal of this mission was to capture the town of Caen. Say KAHN. Caen lay 9.3 miles inland, which is 15 kilometers. All the main roads in the area ran through the city. Control of those roads was important for the Allies. The raid began at 7:25 am. Troops stormed the beaches. Paratroopers landed inland. They joined the British troops on the beach. There was little German opposition compared with the other beaches. Most of the fighting had ended by 8:00 am. British troops and the paratroopers had joined by 1:00 pm. The British troops had things going well. Sword Beach was not safe for long. The Germans launched a counterattack. The counterattack failed. Even so, it stopped British troops from linking up with Canadian troops from Juno Beach that day. The mission was a huge victory for the Allies. The British forces did not reach Caen. Allied forces were still able to secure the beach. They advanced 4 miles inland, which is 6.4 kilometers. The next day they joined the Canadians. Caen fell to Allied troops later, on July 20, 1944. Bad weather delayed the D-Day invasion. The D-Day invasion date was first scheduled for June 5. The Allies chose that date for three reasons. They wanted to land when visibility was good. They wanted winds from the northwest to be light. They wanted the tides to be low. June 5, June 6, and June 7 were the best dates because of the tides. Otherwise they would have to wait two more weeks. Ideal conditions would return only then. June 5 brought weather full of storms. Strong winds would ruin any chance of a naval landing. High waves would ruin it too. Low-level clouds would prevent pilots from seeing targets. They needed to see in order to drop paratroopers. They needed to see in order to attack enemy positions. The poor weather pushed the operation back to June 6. The weather was not much better that day.

7The conclusion is both proud and sad. The cost in Allied soldiers' lives was high. The cost in Axis soldiers' lives was high too. Even so, Operation Overlord was a big success. A foothold in France was what the Allied forces managed to gain. They could then begin to push back the Germans. They could free occupied France. This operation was a huge military victory for the Allies. It was also a day of sadness. Owing to the action on D-Day, numbers were hard to record. Casualties on either side were hard to count. The term casualties refers to several groups. It means troops who were killed. It means troops who were wounded. It means troops missing in action. It means prisoners of war. Historians think German casualties fell in a range. The range was between four thousand and nine thousand. They think Allied casualties were more than six thousand. The war dragged on for about another year. Allied troops continued to capture zones in Europe that Germany occupied. On May 8, 1945, Germany at last gave up. Japan surrendered on August 15, 1945. That surrender finally ended the war. D-Day was an important turning point in World War II. The liberation of France was a turning point too. The war may have finished another way if Allied soldiers had not fought on D-Day. In Rheims, France, German military officers put their names on the surrender papers. These words help with the book. The Allies were the countries that aided each other against Germany, Italy, and Japan in World War II. Great Britain, the United States, France, and the Soviet Union were among them. Infantry are soldiers trained and given weapons and gear to fight on foot. Invaded means entered aggressively to conquer, weaken, or injure. Liberation is the act of setting free. The Axis powers were the countries that fought against the Allies in World War II. Germany, Italy, and Japan were among them. Mines are bombs hidden underground or underwater. They explode when touched or moved. Captured means caught, or taken control of by force. A mission is a set purpose for doing something. It is a special task or assignment. Casualties are people injured, killed, or missing during a war, accident, or disaster. Paratroopers are soldiers trained to jump out of airplanes and fight behind enemy lines. To disable is to make something unusable. A foothold is a position from which a person can advance toward a goal.

71. The Painter Who Faked a Master

1The parts of this book are Great Masters, Van Meegeren's First Paintings, Copying a Master, Master of Success, Forgery Uncovered, The Real Vermeer, and a glossary. View of Delft is a painting by Jan Vermeer from 1661. It shows the city two hundred years before Han lived. When Han Van Meegeren was a young child in Holland, he loved to draw. He enjoyed visiting museums and gazing at pictures by Dutch artists. Rembrandt and Vermeer had died more than two hundred years earlier. Even so, their paintings lived in his mind.

2Early work comes next. The year was 1908, and Han was nineteen when architecture study began. A few buildings were designed by him. Love of pictures, of paint, and of the famous Dutch painters remained. Architecture was dropped so that art study could begin. Scenes of Delft from 1904 show buildings a student of architecture might have studied. The early results were strong. Art school ended with his graduation. A job teaching other students followed. Awards for painting skill came as well. Later, his effort dropped. Many critics disliked the work. They said it stayed too close to the old masters. They said talent was missing. Those bad reviews left Han sad. They also left him very angry. Techniques from the Dutch Golden Age fed his own pictures.

3Han could not stop thinking about the critics. He wrote angry letters, but that was not enough. There had to be some way to get back at them. He wanted to fool and embarrass them the way they had embarrassed him. An idea formed in his mind. What if he painted a picture and said Johannes Vermeer had painted it? Could he fool the critics into thinking the forgery was a genuine Vermeer? Would they praise it as they praised Vermeer's other work? He imagined what they would say when they found out he had painted it. Copying a master came next. Han knew a great deal about art and life in the years Vermeer was painting. He knew a convincing forgery required many things. The subjects had to fit the time Vermeer lived in. The paint and canvas had to look old. Above all, the technique had to carry Vermeer's style.

4The work began with an old painting from the seventeenth century. It had to be more than two hundred years old. After he found one, the canvas was cleaned. He left the old cracks that sat in the white layer underneath. Tiny crack lines are normal on old paintings. The new picture took a very long time. Subjects were chosen to match what critics might expect from Vermeer. Life in the late 1600s was what Vermeer painted. A forger of his pictures would need deep knowledge of that life. Dress was one thing to learn. Hair was another. Humble clothing on a servant is the subject of The Milkmaid. Details in The Disciples at Emmaus seem to point to Vermeer. The painter was actually the forger Han Van Meegeren. Brushes and paints were chosen with great care. Only colors and brushes matching those of Vermeer were used. Sometimes Han ground paints himself. He did that for blues that, two hundred years earlier, were made only in a certain way. Real paint needs many years to harden. A chemical was probably added so his paint would dry fast. Varnish was added too. It made the whole picture look a bit old and dusty. The finished picture was named The Disciples at Emmaus.

5Success followed the first forgery. Everyone believed Vermeer had painted it. A sale brought a great deal of money. Best of all, praise came from the critics. Han had planned to tell them he was the painter. He changed that plan. Greed was part of his character. The pay was far above what he had expected. More forgeries were the next decision. Great riches were the aim. Forgeries based on Dutch Golden Age masters made Han Van Meegeren rich. Pieter de Hooch was one master he faked. Frans Hals was another. Real Vermeer pictures were studied with care while new fakes were made. Every detail had to be right. Otherwise critics would see the fakes. Several pictures sold under the Vermeer name. Wealth did follow.

6Like many criminals, Han became lazy. One forgery was sold to a high-ranking Nazi official during World War II. The Dutch and the Nazis were enemies. After the war, Han was nearly jailed for life for selling a Dutch national treasure to the enemy. He confessed that the painting was a forgery. He painted a new picture in the Vermeer manner to prove what he said. He was punished with just two years in jail. Before he could go to jail, he died. At his trial he painted Teaching in the Temple to show how he forged the pictures. The forgery in the Vermeer style is the one that got him caught. Vermeer's style and technique took Han many years to master. Vermeer was a genius at using light. In his paintings, light often comes through a window and shines on tiny details. He was also a genius at showing mood and creating a feeling.

7Mood is the question in The Guitar Player. Her look upward seems shy. A reader may guess her thoughts. The picture dates from about 1672. The medium is oil on canvas. The size is 53 by 46.3 centimeters. Kenwood is where it is kept. The real Vermeer is the next question. In 1993 a man brought a painting to a famous art house. The title was A Young Woman Seated at the Virginal. He asked if Vermeer had truly painted it. He also asked if Han Van Meegeren, the famous forger, might be the painter. An investigation was accepted by the art house. A virginal is an instrument much like a modern piano. Experts, like Han before them, studied paints Vermeer had used elsewhere. Brushes were studied too. Microscopes and X-rays revealed brush strokes. The small canvas interested them most. The picture sat on that canvas. Its coarse weave matched the canvas of The Lacemaker. A reader may ask if A Young Woman Seated at the Virginal is genuine or a forgery.

8The Lacemaker dates from about 1669 to 1670. It is oil on canvas that was later moved onto a panel. The size is 23.9 by 20.5 centimeters, or 9 and 13/32 by 8 and 1/2 inches. The Louvre in Paris holds it. A Young Woman Seated at the Virginal dates from about 1670. Its size is 9 and 7/8 by 7 and 7/8 inches, or 25.2 by 20 centimeters. An art gallery in Las Vegas, Nevada, has shown it. Folds in the lady's dress in Mistress and Maid showed experts more examples of how Vermeer painted. When the experts finished with technique, they turned to style. They compared the painting with other Vermeer paintings of girls playing musical instruments. They compared skirt folds and other details with paintings such as The Guitar Player. Then they cleaned the painting. They found their answer in the cool lighting, the shadows, the wall, and the mood.

9Famous forgeries like those painted by Van Meegeren changed the way art experts examine a painting. Experts have determined that Vermeer painted about thirty-five known works. No one but Vermeer could have painted A Young Woman Seated at the Virginal. Johannes Vermeer used light brilliantly. His colors were soft and gentle. He chose them to create a mood or to show a moment in time. He enjoyed painting the people he saw every day. He was a genius at expressing their feelings. What feelings do you see in his paintings? Girl at the Window Reading a Letter is one place to look. Convincing means appearing worthy of belief. Critics are people who find faults or carefully judge work for review. Embarrass means to make someone feel awkward, uneasy, or self-conscious. A forgery is an illegal copy made so that it will look genuine.

72. The Real Cost of Fresh Water

1Tadpoles race against time while their rock puddle shrinks. The book begins with water that seems to be everywhere. A drop in the bucket comes next. Then come the impacts of pollution, of population, and of climate change. Solving the problem follows. A word list ends the book. Russia's Lake Baikal is the deepest freshwater lake on Earth. It is also the oldest. By volume it is the largest, but not by surface area. Lake Superior holds the surface-area record. Many people around the world take water for granted. Water is all around, so the habit is easy to understand. It comes out of faucets. Rain leaves it in sidewalk puddles. Lakes brim with it. Rivers brim with it. Bottles of it are bought. Drinking fountains are slurped from. Imagine the United States shaped as one huge drinking glass. Every drop of water on the planet goes inside. The glass would need to stand 145 kilometers tall, or 90 miles, to hold it all. So much water makes a fair supply seem certain. It is not.

2Gold and oil are losing ground. Water is becoming the more precious substance. Usable water for everyone is something the planet simply does not have. Salt water is most of what Earth holds. People cannot drink it. Crops cannot be watered with it. Fresh water makes up only about 3 percent of the water on Earth. Most of that fresh share is locked away. Polar ice caps hold a great deal. Glaciers hold a great deal. Aquifers, the underground rock layers, hold a great deal too. A chart splits the water. Oceans, the salt water, are 97 percent. Fresh water is 3 percent. Of the fresh water, ice caps and glaciers hold 68.7 percent. Groundwater holds 30.1 percent. Surface water holds 0.3 percent. Of fresh surface water, lakes hold 87 percent. Rivers hold 2 percent. Swamps hold 11 percent. Groundwater supplies 25 percent to 40 percent of the world's drinking water. Food crops take an even larger share from it. Those groundwater supplies are shrinking. Saudi Arabia is a water-starved region. Access remains possible there, since the country has a high income. Fresh water is richer in some countries than in others. Most countries still have enough to meet people's needs. The means to deliver that water are what they sometimes lack. Hard-to-get sources are easier for high-income countries to tap. In low-income countries, money is often too short for wells. It is often too short for dams that would create reservoirs. Humans today can reach and use only 1 percent of Earth's freshwater. Three problems put that 1 percent under stress. Pollution is one. Demand is rising because population keeps growing. Climate change is the third.

3Brazil's Amazon River receives many kinds of polluting waste. On many continents, water pollution is a huge problem. South America's Amazon rainforest spans 7 million square kilometers, or 2.7 million square miles. About 30 million people live there. More than 30,000 plant species live there. For years, untreated human waste has been dumped into the Amazon River. Toxic chemicals have been dumped there too. Oil drilling has made some sections toxic. Gold mining has done the same. In other low-income areas, fresh water often goes untreated. Pollution then makes people sick in further ways. Running water is missing. Indoor plumbing is missing. Human waste ends up outside. More people worldwide have a mobile phone than have a toilet. Bacteria fill that waste. The waste then flows into rivers and streams. People drink from those toxic waterways. They cook with the water. They bathe in it. The United Nations Development Program reports a stark fact. Half the world's hospital beds hold patients made sick by unclean drinking water. Most people in a high-income country like the United States can drink clean water. Other pollution troubles remain. Agriculture is the most common source. Rain washes farm chemicals into waterways. It washes animal waste in too. An aging sewage system threatens U.S. waters. Oil threatens them. Other pollution does too. In 2014 a Pennsylvania resident held up a jug of polluted water. An official in Washington, D.C., was shown that jug. He and other residents wanted nearby fracking for oil and gas to stop.

4The year 2011 brought a milestone for the human species. The Philippines was the birthplace of a baby girl on October 30. She was the world's 7 billionth person. By 2050, experts expect the planet to hold 9.7 billion people. Each one will look for food, for energy, for land, and for water. Less water per person follows when populations grow. In 1950, 2.5 billion people used only a third of the fresh water used today. Safe drinking water is missing for 1 person out of every 9, research shows. Many live on less than 8 liters a day, or 2 gallons. By 2050, more than half the world's people will live where water is scarce. Polluted drinking water is far less likely in high-income countries than in low-income countries. Surging populations still hit some richer places. Shortages can follow, partly because people there use more water. A comparison sets daily use side by side. An American figure is 100 gallons, or 379 liters. A figure for many low-income people is 2 gallons, or 8 liters. An average family of four in the United States uses 1,514 liters each day. That is about 400 gallons. Each person uses about 379 liters, or 100 gallons. A few users could keep up that pace. More and more people instead rely on limited sources. Los Angeles County is expected to reach 13 million people by 2050. Its own water can support only 1 million. Los Angeles pulls water from distant rivers. The same distant-river supply serves many more cities in the American West. That river water is running out. Growing populations are one cause. Climate change is another. A chart titled around big population and big water demand tracks human water use in trillion cubic meters per year. One cubic meter equals 264 gallons. Human population is shown in billions.

5People around the world already feel climate change through extreme weather. Storms are one form. Floods are another. Nothing else may threaten the world's water supply as badly. By 2050, scientists say, climate change may leave more than 5 billion people with severe water shortages. The cause is an overload of carbon dioxide, plus other greenhouse gases, in the air. Burning fossil fuels produces a large part of those gases. The gases trap the Sun's heat close to Earth's surface, much as a greenhouse does. Earth's temperature rises overall. That warming leads to climate change. The water cycle is disrupted by the warmer temperatures. Evaporation and precipitation normally stay in a delicate balance. Warmer air speeds evaporation of surface water into the atmosphere. Different parts of the world then feel different effects. Some areas may dry out from the extra evaporation. Other areas may face droughts. A drought is a long spell of precipitation below normal. A water shortage is the result. The Mediterranean sits among the regions at highest drought risk. The Middle East does too. Most scientists in the United States say climate change is behind an extreme drought in the Southwest and in California. Problems from the Southwest drought have continued since 1999. The water line has plunged at Lake Mead, which sits on the Nevada-Arizona border. The Colorado River feeds that lake. Fresh water for 25 million people comes from it. If rains do not increase soon, desert residents will likely have to start rationing water. Dependence on the Colorado River reaches nearly 40 million people. The sea is no longer reached. The river fades to a trickle first.

6A boy fishes in the Daning River. The Himalayas feed that river and many others. Melting glaciers high in the Himalaya mountains are also tied to climate change. Fresh water for 1.5 billion people comes with help from those glaciers. The people live in India, in Pakistan, and in six other Asian countries. In the past, meltwater entered the rivers below at a slow pace. Rapid melt is the pattern now. The long-term water supply is shrinking. Severe flooding along these rivers has come from the faster melt at the same time. Less water remains for ranching as climate change worsens. Less remains for growing crops. Less remains for producing energy. Nature suffers. Wildlife suffers. Fights start when two groups claim a stronger right to one shared supply. Cities argue. States argue. Countries argue. Both Pakistan and India hurry to dam the upstream waters of one shared river. Tensions between the two countries run high. The growing water crisis has not helped. Each person's effort to conserve water can help. States can conserve too. Much of the American West draws water from the Colorado River. Cities there are growing rapidly. More than 70 percent of this river is still taken by farms and ranches. Some of that water might go to cities instead. Countries need solutions of their own. Workers in Saudi Arabia turn salt water into fresh water. The process is called desalination. The cost is high. Many countries cannot afford desalination plants. Personal steps can help. Cut shower time. A bath is fine if you prefer to stay longer in the water. Buy used or recycled things when you can, instead of new things. Ride a bike, walk, or use public transit to help slow climate change. Turn off the water while you brush your teeth. Buy a rain barrel so plants can be watered from stored rain. Fix leaks and drips. Eat less meat. The same weight of beef needs, on average, 125 times the water that potatoes need.

7A chart compares competing uses of water. The groups are high-income countries, the world, and low- and middle-income countries. The uses are domestic, industrial, and agricultural. The figures come from the World Water Development Report of UNESCO. In high-income countries, agriculture takes about 30 percent, industry about 59 percent, and home use about 11 percent. For the world, agriculture takes about 70 percent, industry about 22 percent, and home use about 8 percent. In low- and middle-income countries, agriculture takes about 82 percent, industry about 10 percent, and home use about 8 percent. Singapore has tried cleaning wastewater. The water comes from washing dishes, from flushing toilets, and from baths and showers. Some other countries do this too. One-third of Singapore's water is obtained this way. Cities are growing rapidly. Agriculture still uses about 70 percent of the world's water. Some farmers and ranchers are trying more efficient ways. Water saved that way could go to cities instead. The planet's water problem is hard to solve. Ways to conserve this valuable resource still have to be found. The need belongs to our generation. It belongs to the generations yet to come. Words in this book include the following. Carbon dioxide is an invisible gas often formed when fossil fuels burn. Climate change means the long-term, lasting shifts in Earth's weather patterns. To conserve is to protect a natural place or a resource so it lasts longer. A crisis is a dangerous or unstable time that demands attention. Evaporation is water changing from liquid to gas when temperature rises. Fossil fuels are energy sources taken from the ground, such as coal, oil, and natural gas. Fresh water is water that is not salty. Pollution is the act or the result of putting harmful substances into air, water, or soil. A population is every member of one species in a particular area. Precipitation is falling water. Hail counts. Sleet counts. Rain counts. Snow counts. Rationing means controlling how goods are portioned when supply is short. A resource is a stock of a thing that is valuable or that people truly need.

73. The Soil Scientist George Washington Carver

1Topics run in this order. A ruined landscape comes first. Birth in slavery comes next. Learning without a school comes after that. Making a change follows. Free ideas follow that. A message that lasted follows. Word meanings come last. From a train window in Alabama, cotton seemed to be the only crop. George Washington Carver was the man looking out. The year was 1896. Farmland was eroded. It was cracked. Shacks were crumbling. Cotton plants drooped. They reached all the way to the porch. The Civil War ran from 1861 to 1865. Many old plantations in the South were destroyed in that war. Deaths in the fighting passed six hundred thousand. Farms were left empty or uncared for. The North won. In time, freedom reached over four million people who had been enslaved.

2Life after the war was hard for Black Americans. Skills were many. Formal schooling had been forbidden. Cruel treatment from white people was common. Acceptance was refused. Jobs were blocked in white communities. Home buying was blocked there too. Thirty years on, many freed people could barely feed a family. Carver left a good teaching post to come to Alabama. The post was at a college in Iowa. Struggling farmers were the people he meant to help. His lesson was simple. A good thing, taken too far, turns harmful. Cotton, grown without rest, was what ruined the farms. A soft fiber grows around cotton seeds. During slavery and after it, bands of men roamed the countryside. They terrified people. They robbed people. They murdered people. Their wish was that Black people stay enslaved. Fear was a tool. Punishment was a tool. Targets were people trying to escape or to build a better life. Sheets covered the men so they would look like ghosts. Night was when they attacked. Night riders became their name. George's birth year was 1864. The place was Missouri. The Civil War was still going. His mother was enslaved, so George was born enslaved. An older brother, Jim, was born enslaved too. Their father, also enslaved, died before George was born. Night riders stole the baby and his mother. Moses Carver and Susan Carver had held them in slavery. Those two sent a man to search. George was found. Nobody ever found his mother. A photo from the 1870s shows George with Jim.

3A map marks the states of his life and his work. Iowa appears. Ohio is one. Nebraska is one. Indiana is one. Illinois is one. Colorado is one. Kansas is one. Kentucky is one. Missouri is one. Tennessee is one. Arkansas is one. Oklahoma is one. Mississippi is one. Georgia is one. Alabama is one. Texas is one. Louisiana is one. Florida is one. Freedom came when the war ended in 1865. The boys did not leave. Both parents were dead. Jim was six. George was one. They kept living with the Carvers, their former enslavers. Slavery had ended for them. Work was still forced as they grew. Jim worked the fields with Moses. George was often ill. He stayed home and helped Susan. Reading came from her teaching. Writing came from her teaching. Sewing came from her teaching. Gardens and nature were what he liked best. The Carver house stood in Diamond, Missouri. George taught himself the local plants. He taught himself the local animals. School was still his wish. Segregated schools were common. White students and Black students could not share a school. The nearby school barred Black students. At age twelve, George left the Carver home for school. A couple named the Watkins took him in. Meals and a bed were earned by work. Kansas became the next home when he was thirteen. A 1916 photo shows a segregated school in Kentucky. His mother chose his first name. People called him Carver's George. At twelve, when he moved, Mariah Watkins spoke to him. She said he was nobody's property. She told him to use the name George Carver. Another George Carver lived in town later. He added the initial W so mail and names would not mix. Years afterward, someone asked what the W meant. He answered, "Washington." From then on, the full name was George Washington Carver.

4Skin color kept him out of college in Kansas. He worked for several Kansas families. High school graduation came during those years. A scholarship offered Highland University, a Kansas college. Arrival brought a refusal. The college would not take Black students. He was unhappy. He did not quit learning. He farmed. He taught himself to paint. Friends urged a different college. Simpson College, in Iowa, was for art study. This time the college said yes. He was happy there. He believed farming science would let him help more people. Agriculture is that science. He moved on to Iowa State Agricultural College. He became its first Black graduate. He also became its first Black professor. The year 1896 took him to Alabama. He began teaching at the Tuskegee Institute. He stayed forty-seven years. One photo is the diploma that Iowa State's farm college gave him.

5The cotton problem was clear soon after he reached Alabama. Only cotton, year after year, had worn the soil out. Food money was almost all the farmers earned. Fertilizer money did not exist. Each crop came in smaller. The struggle grew. One photo shows a chunk of tired field soil in his hand. Another shows Southern crops at work in his lab. Dead leaves could go back into the soil. Swamp muck could go back too. The effect was like fertilizer. The cost was nothing. After cotton was picked, other plants helped the soil. Sweet potatoes were one. Peas were one. Peanuts were one. Those plants returned nitrogen. Nitrogen is a nutrient cotton uses up. The new crops were also food. Farmers could eat them. Carver mailed growing advice. He mailed recipes for new dishes that tasted good. Store food then cost the farmers less.

6Sales still mattered. Farmers needed buyers for the new crops. Carver turned inventor. Sweet-potato uses from his work passed one hundred. Peanut uses passed three hundred. He also saw that oil would run out someday. Plant fuel was one of his experiments. He told farmers to choose natural fertilizers. He warned against costly chemicals that were unsafe. Those chemicals polluted land and water. Recycling was another lesson. He told students to keep every scrap. He told them to build what they needed from things already on hand. A note corrects a peanut-butter story. His three hundred peanut uses include pavement. They include grease. They include medicines. They include peanut coffee. They include peanut mayonnaise. They include peanut flour. They include peanut milk. They include shoe polish. They include bleach. They include sandpaper. They include more. He did not invent peanut butter, despite what many people think. The Aztecs, in central Mexico, ate a peanut paste hundreds of years ago. The Incas of Peru did so even earlier. Creamy peanut butter as people eat it now was first made by companies. Peter Pan was one. Skippy came after it. By 1921, listeners were ready for Carver's ideas. Congress asked him to speak. Some members from the South had not expected a Black speaker. The sight shocked them. They laughed. They mocked him. He started listing what a tiny peanut could become. The room went quiet. His ten minutes ended. They gave him more time. A law followed. It helped peanut farmers in the United States. Other countries had to pay more to sell goods, peanuts included, inside the country. Fame grew over the years. Crowds came to hear him. Thomas Edison, the inventor, offered a high-paying lab job. Carver refused. Helping people mattered more to him than money. Ideas, he believed, were free. Free things should be given freely. Around 1936 he greeted President Franklin Delano Roosevelt.

7Not long before death, the Tuskegee Institute received $33,000 from him. The gift was to continue the farm work he had started. In today's money, that sum is about $450,000. Death came in 1943. He was seventy-eight. The legacy outlasted him. He earned the country's respect in an era when respect for Black people was scarce. Franklin D. Roosevelt, as president, signed a law to raise a monument honoring Carver. A national hall that honors inventors later added his name. People remember the revolutionary ideas. Among Black scientists of that era, his influence ranks with the greatest. Word meanings finish the book. Agriculture is the science of farming and of raising livestock. The Civil War divided the United States. Northern states fought southern states. The years were 1861 to 1865. Congress writes the highest laws in the country. It includes the Senate. It includes the House of Representatives. Fertilizer helps plants grow. It may come from nature. It may be made as a chemical. An inventor brings a new thing into being by making it, planning it, or constructing it. A nutrient is matter a living body must have for life, for health, and for growth. A professor is a college or university teacher in a specialized field. A resource is a supply of something valuable or very useful. Segregated means kept apart because of group differences, such as race.

74. Trains That Carried Children to Safety

1A 1939 map of Europe names the North Sea and the Baltic Sea. England and Germany are labeled, with the English Channel between them. Prague sits inside Czechoslovakia on the map. The Mediterranean Sea is labeled too. German troops entered Prague that year. People in Czechoslovakia watched them arrive. The watchers stayed silent. Vera Gissing later described the morning her mother and father sent her out of the country. They hoped the trip would keep her alive. July 1939 was the month. Her eleventh birthday had not yet arrived. Dozens of Jewish children waited with her. Each child wore fine clothes. A tag bearing a number hung at each child's neck. The gathering place was Prague's main railway station. Prague is Czechoslovakia's capital. Vapor from the locomotives drifted among the families. Parents pulled their children close. Kisses followed. Soft words carried love. Soft words carried hope. Speaking in 2002, Gissing said her parents' faces that morning would stay with her always. Grief and pain filled those faces. A face full of grief or pain is called anguished.

2The Eberstark girls left that Prague station on the same day. They never again saw their parents. An England-bound train then took the children. As it moved off, Gissing tried to keep sight of her parents' faces. She did not know the parting was final. She did not know those parents would soon be taken away to be killed. Most of the mothers and fathers waiting there would be taken too. A man from Great Britain was unknown to her. His open heart would be why she lived. Nicholas Winton's part begins in 1938. He worked in London as a banker. His age was twenty-nine. A skiing holiday in the Alps was already planned, and he was set to depart England. A friend asked him to come to Prague instead. That friend was there with aid groups. Thousands of Jewish families were receiving their help. The families had run from their homes. Germany had seized the Sudetenland, a region of Czechoslovakia. Helpers from Christian groups and helpers from Jewish groups worked as partners. Winton later said a job was the last thing on his mind. Even so, the task mattered deeply to him. His family roots were German and Jewish. His parents had made England their home. They had also joined the Christian faith. Without both changes, danger would have reached his family too. A 1938 map of Central Europe labels Germany, Poland, the Sudetenland, Prague, Czechoslovakia, Austria, and Hungary. Germany took those Czechoslovak borderlands in 1938.

3The Sudetenland seizure belonged to a secret plan. Adolf Hitler, Germany's leader, made that plan. He had served earlier as a soldier. Germany's loss in World War I still angered him. The year of that loss was 1918. He placed part of the blame on Jewish people. Black people, disabled people, LGBTQ+ people, and Roma people were blamed as well. After the fighting, he helped create the Nazi Party. The party wanted Germany powerful in the world once more. Hitler and the Nazis, meaning his followers, later grew strong enough that Germany named him leader. Control passed into his hands. He then enlarged the military. He also meant to reclaim land Germany had been compelled to surrender after World War I. One picture catches him in Austria in 1938, shouting before a crowd. His opening move, in 1936, reclaimed land that had been handed to France. Two years on, Austria came under his control. The Sudetenland followed. His next command covered Jewish residents whose birthplace was Poland or Russia. The army had to remove them from Germany. Trucks held some of them. Wagons held others. Drivers took them as far as the border. Then the people were abandoned. Not long after, the army kidnapped 30,000 Jewish people of Germany and removed them. Nazi concentration camps received them. Those camps worked like prisons. People sent there had to live and labor in terrible conditions. Hitler later ordered that they be killed. One picture shows a wagon taking a Jewish family out of Krakow, Poland. Armbands on the family mark them as Jewish.

4Jewish people across Europe grew so frightened that many left home. They were trying to get away from danger. Inside Prague, camps held Jewish citizens of Czechoslovakia. Winton walked into those camps. Conditions there were terrible, and he saw it. Some aid groups were searching out new homes for Jewish people. He noticed that elderly people received the attention. Sick people received it too. Czechoslovakia's Jewish children were getting almost no help. He decided the children would be his task. A picture shows a Czechoslovak school housing refugee families from the Sudetenland. In 2002 a film telling his story records his judgment. He called the situation bad. The refugees felt few days remained. His own group felt the same. They expected German forces to reach the rest of Czechoslovakia. The refugees could see no way to save themselves. They could see nothing useful to do. They could see nowhere to go. They were stuck. Wartime photographs often show Jewish men, women, and children with a six-pointed star on their clothes. Two triangles locked together often form that star. People also call it the Star of David. For thousands of years it has stood as a sign of Judaism. Nazi rulers ordered every Jewish person to wear one. People who were not Jewish could then recognize them at once. The badge was meant to bring shame. It was also meant to stir discrimination. The order covered every Jewish person older than six. It covered every land under German rule. A refugee is someone fleeing war, famine, persecution, or a natural disaster. Often that person has no settled destination.

5Winton aimed to place the children in safe family homes beyond Czechoslovakia. Czech families arrived by the hundreds, all seeking help. He hired two assistants to work with them. Then he went back to England. Living places for the children were still required. Money for the journey was still required. From London he wrote to leaders of nations around the world. Each letter asked that the children be accepted. Many nations refused. Their laws blocked any child who came without parents. Sweden alone said yes, together with Great Britain. A 1938 picture shows a German Jewish girl reaching England. Britain's rules for letting the children in were still strict. A host family had to be found for every child. British leaders also required Winton to pay a fee. The fee would cover a later journey home, once a return to Czechoslovakia was possible. The charge was fifty pounds for each child. In those days the sum was enormous. Britain's money is called the pound. A country's money can also be called its currency. In 1939 people treated fifty pounds as a small fortune. The sum was then worth more than 3,400 dollars of the United States. Newspaper notices were one search method he used. Conversations with churches were another. He had the children's pictures printed. He had those pictures sent across the country. He believed a family, once it saw a child's face, would want to help. At the same time he pressed German leaders for entry permission. British leaders had to agree as well. When the paperwork moved too slowly, he and a few helpers sometimes produced permits that were fake. He said the group had only hurried things a little. A permit is an official paper allowing a person to do something.

6A route map for the trains labels the North Sea, the Baltic Sea, and England. London and a ferry appear. Poland, the English Channel, and Germany appear. Czechoslovakia, Prague, France, Austria, Hungary, and Italy are labeled too. In 1939, children traveled in seven train groups from Prague toward London. Holland's coast was where they changed to a ferry. The ferry took them across the English Channel. A second train, after the water, carried them on to London. The hard work first succeeded on March 14, 1939. Fifteen children, the earliest group, flew from Prague to Great Britain. During the half year that followed, seven trains left Prague full of children. At a London station the journey ended in the arms of new families. Winton stood watching, and a smile was on his face. Safety was reached by 669 children altogether. Family homes took most of them. Many of the others lived at a boarding school for Czech children, located in Wales. An eighth train was still in his plans. It was due to depart Prague on September 3, 1939. Another 250 children would have been aboard. On that date Hitler sent his army into Poland. The borders were closed. The train vanished. Those children were never seen again. A horrible struggle among armies followed. It lasted close to six years. Nations around the world were pulled in. People later called that struggle World War II. A 1939 picture places Winton beside one child he had brought out of Czechoslovakia.

7Barbed wire splits the men from the women inside a camp run by Germany. Off to the right, a guard keeps watch. Hitler's war plans led him, in 1941, to rule that every Jewish person must be killed. Millions were forced into the camps. They had to labor until weakness brought death. Nazi leaders later judged that dying in the camps took too long. Murder replaced the wait. Hitler's drive to wipe out the Jewish people is called the Holocaust. The camps took six million Jewish lives. Children accounted for more than a million of them. People who were not Jewish were killed there in the millions too. Among crimes in human history, the Holocaust ranks with the worst. The war stopped Winton's rescues all at once. He searched for different kinds of useful work. His first role was with the Red Cross, a relief group. Later he entered the Royal Air Force. He learned to fly. Peace brought him back to banking. Marriage came next. A family came after that. He never talked about the children he had labored to save. In 1988 his wife, Grete, stumbled onto the secret. A dusty leather briefcase turned up in the attic. She opened it and found an old worn scrapbook. Pictures of the children filled the book. Letters lay inside as well. Other papers described the work he had done. She urged him until he told the story. A newspaper soon printed an account. Also in 1988, Britain's television program That's Life made a show about him. The surprise was the rescued children in the audience. More than two dozen had come to offer thanks. Vera Gissing was among them at that emotional reunion. A reunion gathers people again after a time apart. She later wrote a biography of Winton. She also wrote a book about her own childhood in the war.

8Gissing says Winton saved most of the Jewish children of her generation in Czechoslovakia. A generation is everyone born and living around the same time. The word can apply to animals as well. Almost none of those children met their parents again. The parents perished inside concentration camps. To perish is to die, especially in a sudden, violent, or unexpected way. Had the children not been spirited away, Gissing says, they would have been killed beside their parents. Spirited means carried off in secret. As many as 5,000 descendants now come from those 669 children. The children had reached safety on his trains in 1939. Descendants are the later offspring of a person or a group from the past. The children themselves are old now. Many still use the name Winton's Children. Leaders in Great Britain have given him many honors. Leaders in the Czech Republic have honored him too. Queen Elizabeth II made him a knight in 2002. The award recognizes bravery. It also recognizes service. It also recognizes success. One picture shows some of Winton's Children arriving in London. They were meeting the man who saved them, seventy years after the evacuation. A 2009 journey copied the old route linking Prague and London. The train used the same path. It marked seventy years since his final train. Many of the people he had saved rode aboard. In London he welcomed them in person. His arms were spread wide. Only a few months had passed since his hundredth birthday. Another picture shows him next to that train. The train had repeated the closing stretch of the historic run from Prague to London.

9One picture shows Winton laughing beside a boy. The boy is a grandson of a girl saved seventy years before. Once the secret was known, he often explained why he had helped the Czech children. He insisted the work was not special. He insisted he was no hero. His account was plain. He saw what was happening around him. Then he gave whatever help he could. A ring reached him as thanks from several whom he had rescued. Cut into the ring is a saying taken from Jewish legal writing. The line teaches that saving a single life is like saving the world. Sir Nicholas Winton's death came on July 1, 2015. That date fell 76 years after a train left Prague with the largest group of children. The group numbered 241. Jewish refers to a people's race, culture, or religion. A concentration camp confines people who do not choose to be there. Conditions are usually cruel. The reason is membership in an ethnic group, a minority, or a political group. The Holocaust names the Nazis' organized killing during World War II, directed above all at Jewish people.

75. Two Probes Beyond the Planets

1Voyager 1 photographed Saturn and one of its moons on November 3, 1980. The moon's shadow falls on the planet's cloud tops. The book moves from a tough job to planning and the main task. Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune each get a turn. The Golden Record follows, then the final task, a conclusion, and a word list. Florida's Kennedy Space Center was the launch site for Voyager 2 on August 20, 1977. A Titan/Centaur rocket carried it into space. The two Voyager spacecraft launched in 1977 with a tough job ahead. Jupiter and Saturn were the worlds this mission set out to explore. Those are two giant outer planets of the solar system. Freezing temperatures waited on the journey. Powerful radiation waited too. A broken part could not be fixed by a visit. Whatever was already on board would have to be enough for the space probes.

2Tough design was the scientists' answer. Radiation shields protected the instruments. Computer-controlled heaters protected them too. Important equipment had backups, including the thrusters used for steering. Problems that might happen were built into the computer programs. Computers of 1977 were very different from machines of today. A modern smartphone has about 7,500 times more computing power. It has 240,000 times more memory than the computers running the Voyager spacecraft. Scientists guessed the Voyagers would last about five years. By 2014, thirty-seven years after launch, information was still arriving from the twin craft. In that year the distance to Voyager 1 was about eleven billion miles. Its link to Earth is a 22.4-watt transmitter, about as strong as a refrigerator lightbulb. About seventeen hours pass before a signal arrives. By then the signal has faded to about 0.2 billion-billionths of a watt. That tiny amount is written 0.0000000000000000002. Dish antennas 70 meters across, or 230 feet, belong to NASA's Deep Space Network. They stand around the globe and catch the faint signal. A diagram shows how gravity assist can add speed or take speed away. Jupiter's orbit around the Sun is marked, along with Jupiter and a Voyager spacecraft. A planet's gravity can bend a spacecraft's path. Speed can change at the same time. Passing just ahead of a planet slows the craft. Passing just behind it speeds the craft up. Careful timing set the Voyager launches. In the late 1970s the orbits of the four outer planets put them nearly in a straight line. Several planets could be visited on one trip because they sat so close together. Billions of miles still had to be crossed. The rockets could only push the craft as far as Jupiter. That was about halfway to Saturn. Jupiter's strong gravity became the fix. A boost came as each craft passed by. The technique is called a gravity assist.

3A flight diagram lists the dates. Voyager 2 launched on August 20, 1977. Voyager 1 launched on September 5, 1977. Jupiter flyby dates shown are March 5, 1979, and July 9, 1979. Saturn dates shown are November 12, 1980, and August 25, 1981. Uranus is marked January 24, 1986. Neptune is marked August 25, 1989. The Sun is marked as well. The planet lineup at launch was extremely rare. A clock can show why. Its hands mark hours, minutes, and seconds. Each hand circles at its own rate. One trip around takes a minute, an hour, or twelve hours. Two hands line up whenever one passes the other. All three line up much less often. Planet orbits take far longer than those clock trips, so lineup is even rarer. The four-planet arrangement of the Voyager missions happens only once every 175 years. Gear on board can be listed. There are electromagnetic sensors and a plasma sensor. There are TV cameras. There is a low-energy charged particle sensor and a cosmic ray sensor. There is a low-gain antenna, a power supply, and a high-gain antenna. A Golden Record rides along. A boom measures magnetic fields. A radio antenna is carried too. At first the main task was Jupiter and Saturn. Their larger moons were included. Saturn's rings were included. Cameras rode on the craft. So did scientific instruments, with sensors for radiation, for magnetic fields, and for plasma. Information from those tools changed how we understand our solar system.

4Jupiter, the solar system's largest planet, was the first target. Telescopes had already been used to study it. New information still came back from the Voyagers. The Great Red Spot was shown to be a huge storm. The storm rotated counterclockwise all the time. A faint ring was discovered around Jupiter. It is similar to the rings that orbit Saturn. Counting out from the Sun, Jupiter comes fifth. It is the first of the outer planets. Its moons differ from one another. They differ from the moons of other planets. Europa, for example, is covered by a sheet of ice. Scientists think an ocean might hide under that ice. Io, another moon, is covered with volcanoes. Gas and dust shoot 306 kilometers, or 190 miles, above the surface. Until these missions, active volcanoes were known only on Earth inside our solar system. Volcanic action on Io is now known to be ten times all of Earth's put together. Saturn has the largest ring system of any planet in our solar system. Discoveries continued at Saturn. The two craft arrived nine months apart, in 1980 and in 1981. Close-up pictures showed new rings around the second-largest planet. Those rings could not be seen from Earth. Unexpected kinks appear in the rings. Spokes appear too, like the spokes of bicycle wheels. Time-lapse photos let scientists watch spokes form. The spokes then dissolved again. Several small moons act like shepherds. They keep orbiting ice and dust in separate rings. Titan, the largest moon, wore a thick haze. That haze was an atmosphere. The discovery was so shocking that Voyager 1's flight path was changed for a closer look. Some scientists think Titan could support life.

5Once Saturn was behind it, Voyager 1 flew out of the zone where most planets circle the Sun. Its path led toward interstellar space. That is the region beyond the Sun's magnetic field. Voyager 2's position still allowed a trip onward to Uranus. Every instrument was still working. NASA decided to extend the mission. Uranus was a mystery. Uranus looks strange because it lies tipped onto its side. A collision with something the size of a planet may explain that tip. January 1986 was the month Voyager 2 went by Uranus. Measurements showed a twist in the magnetic field. The sideways planet pulls that field into a corkscrew tail that follows behind it. Until then, scientists did not know Uranus had a magnetic field at all. Rings around Uranus make the sideways tip easy to see. Methane gas in the atmosphere of Neptune gives that planet its deep blue color. A successful Uranus flyby led NASA to send Voyager 2 on to Neptune. Arrival came in August 1989. Five new moons were discovered there. Triton, the largest moon, had eruptions of dust and gas that looked like geysers. Voyager 2 then began its own journey toward interstellar space, as Voyager 1 had done.

6Carrying a message is the other half of the Voyager mission, beyond gathering information. The message is for life that is not from Earth, also called aliens. Each craft carries a twelve-inch Golden Record on its side. Music is on the record. Art is on it. Spoken greetings from around the world are on it. Sounds from nature are on it too. A map on the outside shows where Earth sits in the universe. Aliens could use that map to find Earth. A close pass is not likely anytime soon. At least forty thousand years will pass before Voyager 1 comes near another star. Millions of years will pass before either craft comes near another planet. Famous American astronomer Dr. Carl Sagan led the committee that chose the record's contents. Humans had sent messages into space before the Golden Record. Pioneer 10 and Pioneer 11 are the only other objects made by humans that are now headed out of the solar system. Each carries a metal plaque. Drawings show a man, a woman, and Earth's position in the universe. These are the first probes sent to study space beyond our solar system. A diagram names interstellar space. One marked bubble is strong solar wind that pours out of our sun. It shows our sun, Voyager 1, and a larger bubble of weak solar wind trailing behind our sun. Voyager 2 is marked. Neptune's path is marked too.

7A time line lists important dates for the Voyager missions. In 1977, Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 launched 16 days apart. In 1979, the Jupiter flybys brought discovery of volcanoes and of ice on Jupiter's moons. In 1980, the Saturn flybys brought discovery of an atmosphere on Titan, and Voyager 1 began its trip out of the solar system. In 1986, Voyager 2 reached Uranus. In 1989, Voyager 2 reached Neptune and began its trip out of the solar system. In 1990, the Voyager Interstellar Mission began. Voyager 1 moved past Pioneer 10 in 1998. No object made by humans was farther out. In 2012, Voyager 1 entered interstellar space. Voyager project scientist Dr. Edward Stone has summed up the work. He says the mission opened our solar system in a way the years before the Space Age could not. All of the giant outer planets were explored by the two craft. Forty-eight of their moons were explored too. A glimpse of interstellar space is what the Voyagers give us now. They are like two small bottles in the universe's immense ocean. Words in this book include the following. Exploring means traveling across an area, or through it, in order to watch and learn. Gravity is the natural pull of objects toward one another, as when things are pulled toward Earth's center. Instruments are tools, especially tools that make or record measurements. Interstellar describes the deep space between stars, or something that happens there. A mission is a spacecraft or aircraft flight meant to finish a special assignment. Orbits are the paths of objects in space as they circle larger objects. Plasma is charged gas particles that can conduct electricity. Probes are devices that send back information from places that are hard or dangerous to reach. Objects that circle a star, taken together, make a solar system.

76. Washington Leads a New Country

1One painting catches the 1776 night of the Delaware crossing, with Washington among his soldiers. On April 30, 1789, George Washington swore the oath and became the first president of America. Before that day he had owned a plantation. He had served as a military officer. He had led an army as a general. The inauguration was about to make him president of the United States. The room was Federal Hall. The city around it was New York City. New York's top judge was Robert Livingston. He came forward carrying a Bible. Washington laid a hand on the book and gave his word. He promised to carry out the president's office with faith. He promised to guard the Constitution of the United States, to keep it safe, and to stand up for it, as far as his ability reached. The crowd watching cheered with enthusiasm. The oath made the office his. He now stood as America's president in full.

2February 22, 1732, was the day George Washington was born. His parents were Augustine Washington and Mary Ball Washington. From age three, George and the family lived at Mount Vernon, a plantation in Virginia. The older Washington died when George was only eleven. Luck was with the boy. Lawrence, an older half brother, looked after him and raised him. Formal schooling was not especially strong. Doing tasks taught him more, above all the daily work at Mount Vernon. Practical lessons included the care of a crop field. By age twenty he ran Mount Vernon. Farming was how he described his own role. Many enslaved people did the field labor he oversaw. Military life drew his interest as well. Events of the time would give him a chance to serve. Through the 1700s, Britain ruled each of thirteen colonies. Each colony kept its own militia. The Virginia militia made him an officer starting in 1752. A conflict called the French and Indian War, which was part of Europe's Seven Years' War, would soon test him. Fighting on Britain's side, he became known as a commander both brave and demanding. Britain was upset that France was pushing its reach farther in North America. Talks with the French were the errand a general gave him. War broke out with them anyway. Native peoples joined the French and added to their strength. Washington commanded Virginia's militia for Britain and gained experience of great worth. A major battle ended in a win he had helped earn. Retirement at Mount Vernon followed. He married Martha Dandridge Custis, a wealthy widow of Virginia. Martha added thousands of acres, and more enslaved people, to his estate. Wealth for the family came from work done by enslaved people on that plantation. Near the end of his life, George ordered that the 123 people he himself had enslaved be freed when Martha died. The year 1799 brought his death. Martha then feared that her own life was in danger. She felt forced to free them at once. People enslaved through her own estate were not freed. At her death in 1802, those people were divided among her grandchildren.

3Life in the British colonies late in the 1700s was hard. Laws from Britain forced high payments on colonial goods. Tea was one of those goods. Paper was another. Washington and other colonial leaders felt frustrated. They began to plan resistance. Delegates were picked from the colonies in 1774. Their secret gathering met in Philadelphia, a city in Pennsylvania. The meeting was the First Continental Congress. Washington backed a proposal at that meeting. If Britain kept its course, the colonies would answer with armed force. A hunger for revolution was already rumbling. April 1775 brought the first gunfire of the American Revolution, and colonial troops fired it. One month later, delegates gathered again. That meeting was the Second Continental Congress. Washington and the other delegates reached one conclusion there. Fighting could no longer wait. July 3, 1775, was the day of his appointment. He would lead the new Continental Army as its chief. He began his work as leader against the British. In March 1776 he took his first major military action. Boston was cleared of Britain's army by his push. Those troops fell back toward New York. July 4, 1776, made the separation from Britain official. That was the day the Declaration of Independence received its signatures. Fighting in New Jersey, and close to it, fills one map. The dates run through 1776 and into the following year. Labels include New York, Connecticut, New Jersey, New York City, Morristown, Pennsylvania, Valley Forge, the Atlantic Ocean, Philadelphia, Maryland, and Delaware. Long Island is dated August 27, 1776. White Plains is dated October 28, 1776. Trenton is dated December 26, 1776. Princeton is dated January 3, 1777. Brandywine is dated September 11, 1777. Germantown is dated October 4, 1777. Monmouth is dated June 28, 1778. A move from Halifax is dated June 29, 1776. British troops left New York City on August 25, 1777. The map marks both colonial troops and British troops. A scale reads 50 miles. That summer, the army under Washington suffered a humiliating defeat at Long Island, in New York. British forces killed three hundred men. They captured more than a thousand others. Washington had to retreat. Trenton, New Jersey, held an enemy camp late in 1776. Washington answered with an attack they did not expect. Christmas night was pitch black. In its middle hours the Continental Army crossed the Delaware by boat. A victory of real weight followed.
