Retreat then belonged to the other side. The pullback reached New York. Another turning point came in 1777. At Saratoga the colonial side won a clear run of fights against Britain. That city lies about 180 miles north of New York City. The distance is 290 km. France, wanting revenge after its loss in the Seven Years' War, had been watching the conflict.

4France had lost that earlier war to Britain. French leaders chose to join the colonists. Their help would matter greatly to the war's outcome. Farther south, Washington still faced pressure. General Howe took Philadelphia, the colonial capital, on September 26, 1777. Washington and his men could only fall back to Valley Forge nearby. Winter there was cold and harsh. Food ran short. Other supplies ran short too. Some three thousand men deserted the army. The colonists' final victory waited until 1781. France sent both soldiers and ships to help. With that help, the colonists closed around Britain's forces at Yorktown, in Virginia. The British had no choice except surrender. At Valley Forge, weak support from the government left few supplies and brought the men near starvation. A picture of the 1787 Constitutional Convention shows George Washington standing at the right. He presided over that meeting. After the victory, the colonists started building a lasting government for the United States. George Washington, newly famous from the war, was someone they wanted involved. James Madison, a friend from Virginia like himself, invited him. The government meeting would be held in Philadelphia. More than fifty other delegates would attend. At the Constitutional Convention, America's Founding Fathers worked toward a plan for a new government. Someone still had to lead it. Unsurprisingly, they turned to George Washington. Leading the nation as its opening president was not a role he desired. He felt duty required him to accept. Congress voted in February 1789. Every member agreed on Washington. That spring he traveled from Mount Vernon to New York City. There, on April 30, he took the oath of office.

5President Washington had a great deal to do. No one had held the office before. It fell to him to set many precedents. He began establishing three branches of government. The executive branch is overseen by the president. The legislative branch is Congress. The judicial branch is the Supreme Court. His manner as president had been shaped by his military career. Making a decision did not frighten him. Sticking to it did not frighten him either. The presidency included several firsts. His swearing-in included a speech read aloud for Congress. Presidents today deliver that address before a crowd gathered to listen. A speech to Congress once each year began with him. People know that speech as the State of the Union. A president still delivers that yearly address in front of Congress. He served only two terms. Stopping after two terms stayed the custom through 1940. The limit became law in 1951. A picture shows President Barack Obama giving an inaugural address in 2013. A second term came by election in 1792. The next four years held more conflict. One major fight of that term was the Whiskey Rebellion. The new government taxed people in the colonies who made whiskey, and the tax felt unfair. Revolt started among a group inside Pennsylvania. As president, he told that state's militia to quiet the trouble. The Pennsylvania militia was the force he used in 1794. The uprising was stopped. That same term brought a fresh danger. Britain and France looked ready to fight one another again. He believed military action should be used only when it was necessary. He refused to let the United States be dragged into that quarrel. He held to the idea that the country would stay neutral. The choice was not well liked. Unpopularity arrived, something new in his public life. Ordinary people turned away. Newspapers did too.

6He ended the presidency after two terms. That choice set a precedent which remained for nearly 150 years. Before the office ended, he offered advice to the young nation he loved so much. The Farewell Address shows a mind always alert to military matters. Foreign alliances, he said, called for caution. Those bonds, in his view, could drag a country into war. He also warned against an army grown too large, which might encourage military conflicts. What mattered most, he felt, was that the American people stand united as one nation. Returning to Mount Vernon brought relief. A tired Washington began retirement in 1797. Late in 1799 a bad sore throat made him ill. Death came on the fourteenth day of December in that year. Public duties were finished. Hours with family at Mount Vernon could increase. The record is astonishing. A military career of high rank is part of it. Help in building a new nation is part of it too. Command of the Continental Army was his. Under it, the United States broke free from Britain. Later presidents have tried to copy the pattern he set while holding the office first. Courage and confidence marked the way he led, and the nation admired him. A congressman of that time called him foremost in war and foremost in peace, and said his countrymen held him first in their hearts. Out of that regard came a name people gave him: Father of His Country. Historical figures are often reduced to simple labels. In truth, those figures are fully as complex, and fully as flawed, as people living now. A dollar bill first carried his portrait in 1869. By then the Civil War had ended. The design still familiar first appeared in 1963.

7A timeline of George Washington runs through these years. In 1732 he was born in Westmoreland County, Virginia. In 1735 the family moved to Mount Vernon, Virginia. Fighting in 1754 placed him inside the French and Indian War. That struggle belonged to the larger Seven Years' War. The American Revolution was underway in 1775 when command arrived. He would stand as chief over the Continental Army. In 1787 he presided over the Constitutional Convention. In 1789 he was elected the first president of the United States. The year 1794 brought the Whiskey Rebellion. In 1797 retirement began at Mount Vernon. In 1799 he died on December 14. A precedent is an act or a situation later used as an example. An alliance is a close tie between countries, or between other groups, that work together. To preserve something is to care for it and save it for later. Colonies looked to the Continental Congress as their chief governing group before the Revolution. It kept that role through the fighting, and for a while after peace returned. To revolt is to fight a government or another authority. A revolution removes a government by force and puts another in its place. Delegates are people chosen or elected to represent others and to act for them. A term is a set or limited time in an official post. To be inaugurated is to enter office through a formal ceremony. A militia is an army of ordinary citizens rather than trained soldiers. Unanimously means with complete agreement from everyone. Neutral means taking neither side in a conflict, and not stating an opinion on a subject.

77. Water Hidden Under the Ground

1In August 2014, ten days after a well went dry, a woman in California received 300 gallons, or 1,136 L, of water fit to drink. Picture a morning when the faucet is turned and nothing comes but a gurgle. That scene happened in 2014, in a California region famous for fruit and for vegetables. Years of drought had brought little rain. Crops needed water, so farmers drew enormous volumes from stores lying under the fields. Some two thousand wells went dry. Experts warn that even rainfall will not end the shortage there soon. California is not alone in facing a water crisis. Water held below ground is called groundwater. It fills spaces and cracks among rocks, sand, and soil.

2A chart of usable water splits all the water on Earth. Salt water is 97 percent. Fresh water is 3 percent. Of the fresh share, ground ice and permafrost lock away 70 percent. Surface water is 0.3 percent. The U.S. Geological Survey is the source. Globes fool many viewers. The planet looks as if it holds all the water anyone could need. Most of it, though, sits in the oceans. Salt makes that water unfit to drink and useless on crops. Fresh water keeps us alive, yet it is under 3 percent of the total. Nearly 70 percent of the fresh share sits locked in polar ice and in glaciers. Rivers, lakes, and ponds hold surface water equal to just 0.3 percent of the fresh supply. Scientists estimate that a striking 99 percent of fresh liquid water is groundwater. It is fresh water moving slowly beneath the surface. Aquifers store most of it. Those layers are rock, gravel, and sand. They keep water the way a giant sponge keeps liquid. Rain and melting snow sink very slowly through surface soil and rock, feeding those layers. An aquifer may reach thousands of feet down. Rivers, lakes, and wetlands draw from it. Its fresh water also waters the world's best farming regions. For more than a hundred years, people have pumped billions of gallons from below. The uses include drinking, growing crops, and other needs. Even during drought, towns and farms sitting over an aquifer can draw water, survive, and thrive. This supply keeps much of humanity from hunger and from thirst. The trouble is a fast drop in the level. Crises over water threaten food. They threaten peace. People nearby and far away must conserve a resource that gives life. Center-pivot irrigation lets farms succeed in many dry regions.

3Research now shows pumping running ahead of nature's ability to refill the supply. Since 1995, experts say, levels have dropped in almost two-thirds of wells across the United States. They expect the Ogallala Aquifer, beneath the Great Plains, to be 70 percent used up by 2060. A chart of rises and mostly falls covers that aquifer, also called the High Plains Aquifer. It waters the nation's wheat fields, yet the store cannot last forever. State-by-state shifts appear for a span of about sixty years, from 1950 to 2010. The U.S. Geological Survey supplied the map. Some places are largely unchanged. Others have crashed. Wyoming shifted by -0.4 feet, or -0.12 m. South Dakota shifted by 0 feet, or 0 m. Nebraska shifted by -0.9 feet, or -0.27 m. Colorado shifted by -13.2 feet, or -4.02 m. Kansas shifted by -22.8 feet, or -6.95 m. New Mexico shifted by -15.1 feet, or -4.6 m. Oklahoma shifted by -12.3 feet, or -3.75 m. Texas shifted by -36.7 feet, or -11.19 m. Depth below the surface is marked in feet. The marks run 0, then 20, then 40, then 60, then 80, then 100, then 120, then 140. One well in Texas has dropped more than 120 feet, or 36.6 m. Vineyards made Sonoma Valley, a place in California, widely known. In some farm regions, competition for the underground supply is stirring conflict. In Northern California, winemakers grow acres of grapes. Those plants need a great deal of water. Deep wells are the choice of many growers who want a sure supply. Without it, the business might fail. Smaller farmers and homeowners nearby often blame the vineyards. They say the vines take too much of a shared supply, while shallower wells run dry. In many cases the smaller owners cannot pay to drill deeper. It is like too many straws in one drink. Some farms and businesses can buy extra straws and longer ones. Large questions follow. Who owns this water? What amount of use is fair?

4A chart compares yearly water use for each person in India, in China, in the United States, and in Pakistan. A single cubic kilometer holds one trillion liters. In gallons, that volume is 264,172,052,358. That volume would fill about 400,000 swimming pools of Olympic size. India has 1,225 million people. Its yearly total is 251 cubic kilometers. Each person there uses 205,000 liters a year. China has 1,341 million people. Its yearly total is 112 cubic kilometers. Each person there uses 83,500 liters a year. The United States has 310 million people. Its yearly total is 112 cubic kilometers. Each person there uses 361,300 liters a year. Pakistan has 174 million people. Its yearly total is 65 cubic kilometers. Each person there uses 373,600 liters a year. Population size can raise a country's overall use. Even so, the amount each person uses is not the same from country to country. Halfway around the world, water available in Pakistan has fallen by almost 75 percent across the last sixty years. Many people there blame India, the neighbor to the south. Their charge is that dams inside India stop river water. Without the dams, that water would flow onward to Pakistan. They say the blockage has pushed Pakistani farmers to pump more from underground. Officials in India answer that Pakistan alone is at fault. They say Pakistan has handled its water poorly. Four wars already stand in the history between these neighbors. Today both face shortages and rising competition for fresh supplies. The United Nations expects fights over water to grow worse. If nothing changes, the world, by its estimate, will miss 40 percent of the water it needs in the year 2030. Nearly two billion people could face severe shortages. Food shortages and famine could follow. Experts warn that such shortages can, in time, lead even to war. In some places, missing water has already pushed large numbers of people from their homes. Drought in Syria, for example, sent rural people into cities. Evidence suggests that movement helped set off a civil war in 2011. Many Syrians died as a result. Two children from Syria stand outside a shelter in a camp for refugees. In many regions this hidden water is that important. It divides green farms from fields of dust. It is a question of life or of death. Where people cannot rely on a supply, violence and deep suffering may spread as they struggle over what remains.

5An old saying claims that staying clear of trouble is easier than escaping it later. The saying fits the world's underground supply. Facing the crisis now will be far easier than facing it after the aquifers go dry. A response, though, means planning ahead. Climate change is one growing threat. Almost every scientist who studies Earth now agrees the planet is getting hotter. Weather patterns may shift as well. A region may depend on rain that comes in a regular season. Climate shifts may move the timing of that season. The moisture those seasons bring may change. Fresh water may grow harder to obtain. California's long dry spell fed a chain of wildfires. The year was 2015. Population growth is another huge test. The planet's people now number above seven billion. The figure is expected to hit eleven billion by the year 2100. Every person will need a drink and water for food. The underground store must be managed now, and management is possible. The best hope is conservation, meaning ways to use less and to leave more in the ground. No step matters more than a change in farming methods. Experts put the share near 65 percent. That is how much of the fresh groundwater pumped up in America is poured onto crops. Many watering methods waste it. They spray and sprinkle on the top, where evaporation carries much of it off. More farmers now accept that such heavy pumping cannot continue. New methods try to make each drop count. Meters now watch how moist the soil is. They start and stop the flow on their own, so less is wasted. Many orchards of fruit and of nuts bury the pipes. Water then arrives closer to the roots, and less is lost. A picture shows almond trees in bloom.

6A view from space labels Europe, Asia, the Indian Ocean, Africa, and the Atlantic Ocean. Some aquifers are losing water quickly. Others are gaining it. Since 2002, NASA has watched groundwater changes from orbit. Its name is GRACE, short for Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment. Two satellites respond to Earth's field of gravity. Changes in how much water sits above ground can be measured by them. Changes under the ground can be measured too. Data gathered across ten years, from 2003 to 2013, show trends for the planet's largest aquifers. About one-third of those aquifers are depleted to a dangerous degree. Choosing different crops can also save water. In Kansas and in Iowa, some farms are leaving corn for other plants, because corn drinks heavily. Corn still earns more money, so many farmers resist the switch. New farming methods are needed. Refusal to save water by choice leaves another teacher. Aquifers that run dry will compel the change. A 2016 study found that toilets use more household water than any other device. Researchers looked inside 23,749 homes spread across the United States. Household use per day in the study includes 33.1 gallons, equal to 125.3 L. Another figure is 31.7 gallons, or 120 L. Another is 26.3 gallons, or 99.6 L. Another is 23.9 gallons, or 90.5 L. The last is 22.7 gallons, or 86 L. The uses listed are a clothes washer, a dishwasher along with leaks and other draws, a faucet, a shower and a bath, and a toilet. A similar study in 1999 recorded higher use. Newer toilets that waste less send less water down the sewer. Some families practice selective flushing, meaning they do not flush after every use. The numbers are gallons for a household in a day. Record drought pushed California to cut back. At one point, a city there could charge a fine of five hundred dollars each day when people broke limits on washing cars or on watering lawns. Use fell because of those rules. Within only six months, average daily use dropped from a high of 140 gallons, or 530 L, for each person to 67 gallons, or 254 L.

7Households that depend on underground water make up 57 percent of homes in the country. In rural places the share is above 90 percent. Small shifts in pipes and in habits can save hundreds of gallons each week in a typical home. Toilets that flush with less water, and showers that are shorter, lower the draw. Owners can also save by trading thirsty grass for yards that need little water. California's catchy line for letting a lawn die says that brown has taken the place of green. Saving the underground supply is not simple. People must drink. Farmers must water crops if food is to grow. Even so, smarter use is possible, now and far ahead. Summer in 2014 was dry. Some Los Angeles homeowners replaced grass with plants that live on little water. Climate change means lasting, long-term shifts in weather for Earth, or for one region. Conservation means using a resource with care so it is not wasted, finished off, or destroyed. A crisis is a dangerous or unsteady time that calls for attention. Depleted means emptied, or mostly used up. Drought names a long stretch of dry weather. Rain is scarce, or it does not come at all. To irrigate is to bring water onto land, especially so crops can grow. To monitor is to watch how something progresses. To percolate is to trickle, or to spread slowly, through a material full of small openings. Something kept in supply, and valued or strongly useful, is a resource. The United Nations is an international body working to promote peace and economic development.

78. Westward with Magellan

1page 16. Rivals on the Ocean. Explorers of earlier centuries set out on very long trips. They understood little about the lands ahead. No modern tools helped them find the way. Wide oceans were full of danger. They were mysterious, and they did not behave in a steady way. People sailed anyway. Their aims were not all the same. In the sixteenth century, one European aim was a water path for trade linking Europe with Asia. Spices and other luxury goods moved by land in those years. The overland trip took a long time and cost a great deal. Goods passed through many hands along the way. Each hand raised the price, so Europeans paid heavily. Merchants wanted ships that could reach Asia. A sea path would let them stop paying the people on the land route. More of the money would stay with the merchants. Spain and Portugal turned into fierce rivals. Each wanted to assert command of the oceans. Each wanted fresh trade routes into Asia. Christopher Columbus crossed the Atlantic in 1492. That voyage opened a time of planned Spanish growth in the West. It also sharpened the contest with Portugal. Both kingdoms raced to locate new trading paths. Both tried to seize new territory in the Americas, in Africa, and in Asia.

2By 1514, Portuguese ships controlled the sea from Africa across to India. Important ports had been planted near the Spice Islands. African peoples and Asian peoples already lived on those lands. Portugal took the lands over. That occupation blocked Spain from doing the same. A map of the Maluku Islands shows the Pacific Ocean, Indonesia, and Papua New Guinea. Australia is marked as well. A key points to nutmeg and mace. The scale runs from 0 miles and 0 kilometers out to 750. The Trade in Spices. In Europe of the sixteenth century, spices were a huge business. A trader who imported sweet-smelling herbs and powders could grow very rich. Asia supplied most of those spices. The richest source was a region then called the Spice Islands. Today those islands are the Maluku Islands, in Indonesia. Distance and scarcity made the goods costly. Cinnamon was precious. So were clove, nutmeg, and black pepper. People even spent them the way they spent money. Ferdinand Magellan. Among the leading navigators of that age of European voyages was Ferdinand Magellan. He was not a simple man. Courage and cruelty both belonged to him. Portugal was his homeland, yet he sailed at last for Spain, Portugal's rival. Memory often names him the first person to circumnavigate Earth. He died, in fact, before any return to Spain. The tale can feel confusing. One point is clear. His voyage changed the world in a large way. The year of his birth was 1480. His family belonged to the nobility of Portugal. While still a child, he worked at court in the role of a page. Stories of far-off lands filled that court, and he listened. When he was old enough, he entered the Portuguese navy. A portrait shows Ferdinand Magellan.

3An early picture shows Magellan leaving port near the start of his career. Between 1506 and 1512 he fought in many sea battles. The battles mattered, and his side won them. Their goal was to grab spice routes and trade routes that brought profit. India was one target. The Spice Islands were another. Those islands are known today as Malaysia and Indonesia. People came to see him as a skilled sailor and a skilled fighter. They also saw a man who was rowdy and who disobeyed. His captain removed him from the post. He was sent home to Portugal in disgrace because he had ignored orders of the fleet. The year 1512 took him to North Africa. His mission was to seize the port city of Azzamur. The fighting was fierce, and a battle wounded his leg. King Manuel I was not pleased when Magellan came back to Portugal. A charge said Magellan had made secret trading deals with the Moors. The Portuguese navy dismissed him, and this time the break was final. Anger and bitterness followed. In 1517 he left Portugal to meet Spain's King Charles I. Helping Spain meant turning against his own country. Even so, he offered King Charles a plan. Spanish ships, he said, could reach the riches of the Far East. The king already knew the reputation. Magellan was spoken of as a fine navigator and a fighter. Charles was hungry for more land, more wealth, and more resources for Spain. Eastward routes were already in Portuguese hands. His answer pointed the ships west. First they would cross the Atlantic Ocean. After that, he thought a channel through South America would open the way to the Far East. Earlier explorers had searched for that passage and failed. Magellan still felt sure of success. He won King Charles over. The fleet left Spain on September 20, 1519. A picture shows him offering to help the king locate new paths for trade.

4A world map follows the voyage. The map names Asia and also Spain. Europe is marked. Both the Pacific Ocean and the Atlantic Ocean are marked. Viewers can find Africa. They can find the Spice Islands. South America and Australia are on the map as well. Ten dated points mark the route. In September 1519 the ships left Spain. April 1520 brought a mutiny against Magellan. May 1520 wrecked the Santiago. In October 1520 the San Antonio deserted. October and November 1520 carried the fleet through the Strait of Magellan and out to the Pacific Ocean. March 1521 brought Guam. April 1521 brought Cebu, and Magellan was killed. Also in April 1521, the Concepción was burned. November 1521 brought the Spice Islands. In September 1522 the Victoria reached Spain again. Five old ships made up the fleet. Trinidad was the flagship. Four ships sailed as escorts. Their names were San Antonio and Victoria. Santiago was another. The last was Concepción, a name said kohn-sep-SYOHN. Sailors were hard to recruit. Magellan's reputation was not fully honorable, and that hurt the search. Spanish crew did not want a Portuguese captain over them. Portuguese crew looked on Magellan as a traitor. Many who did sign on did not trust him. Trouble from that mistrust came later. The Atlantic had been crossed by the end of November. South America's coast then led the ships south. Along the way they gathered notes on geography and climate. They noted plants, animals, and the Native people they met. Each time a river mouth appeared, Magellan sent ships to learn where the river went. He was hunting a water link from the Atlantic to the South Sea. The Spice Islands, he believed, lay on that sea. The hunt brought no success. Frustration grew, and so did disorder. Months at sea had left many men weary. Sickness spread. In April 1520, Spanish captains rose in mutiny against the Portuguese commander. Magellan crushed the revolt. Punishment for the traitors was harsh. Some were killed. Some were put ashore. Others were forced into hard labor. The voyage went on, but not for long without loss. One ship was wrecked. Another quit and turned back toward Spain. Later in that year only two ships were left, and Magellan was close to quitting. He was about to head for Spain when news arrived. One of the vessels had found a strait. The opening was in a place they had mistaken for a bay.

5A picture shows Magellan's crew moving through the strait. The Pacific Ocean fills their view, a sight they had never had. People now call that passage the Strait of Magellan. Through the Strait and onto the Sea. The last two ships were the Concepción and the Victoria. Magellan led them into the strait. Rough water lasted thirty-eight days. In November 1520 they came out on the South Sea. He gave that sea a new name, the Pacific Ocean, because the water seemed peaceful. He badly misjudged how far South America stood from Asia. He counted on islands along the way. Those stops were supposed to refill supplies and fresh food. What the crew met instead was rotten food. Illness followed, and so did poor sanitation. Three months passed in that condition. Nineteen sailors were dead by the time Guam appeared, in March 1521. Worse than a Sick Stomach. Sailors of that era could spend months with no land and no fresh food. Scurvy struck many of them. The cause is too little vitamin C. Joints ached. Spots of blood showed under the skin. A sick person could grow too weak to walk. Eating could become impossible. Without treatment, death followed. About half of Magellan's crew died of scurvy. Beriberi was another sailor's illness. It attacks the nervous system. The missing mineral is thiamine. The name comes from a language of Asia. It means I cannot, I cannot. Nerves grew so damaged that simple tasks became impossible, and then the person died. A picture shows sailors collecting oranges and lemons. Both fruits cure scurvy.

6Taking the Philippines. A month after Guam, the ships reached a group of islands Europeans had not known. Native people already lived on them. Magellan still claimed the islands for Spain at once. He renamed them the Philippines, for Spain's King Philip II. He ordered the Native people to convert to Catholicism. He ordered them to accept Spanish rule. Some agreed. Many refused. He attacked the people who refused. Confidence that was not deserved led him to the Island of Mactan. Only a few dozen men went with him. More than 1,500 Mactan fighters were waiting. The Mactan force defeated the European sailors with ease. Magellan died in that battle on April 27, 1521. Who Circled the World First? April 1521, in the Philippines, brought Magellan a surprise. One member of his crew could speak the local language. The man's name was Enrique, and he was enslaved. Magellan had brought him on the voyage. Skill in the language of the islands' Native people suggests a past life there, before enslavement. If that reading is right, Enrique completed a full circle of the globe before Magellan did. No European in the crew would hold that first place either. After the Leader Died. The few crew still alive kept going once Magellan was dead. September 1522 brought them back to Spain. One ship remained. A few dozen men remained. Magellan was not among them. The voyage had been grueling, and the suffering was severe. Even so, navigation gained a major achievement. Asia, the trip showed, could be reached by sailing west instead of east. The true size of Earth, and its true scope, stood clearer. Europeans met a strait they had not known. They met an ocean they had not known. The world, it was proved, could be circled by ship. The path also grew smoother for European colonization of the lands called the New World. Life changed for the Native people of Mactan and of the islands around it. No gold was ever found there. No spices were found there either. Spaniards came back after this voyage and took control of the Philippines. Many Native people were converted to Catholicism. Spanish laws were put in place, and a Spanish government ruled. Spanish speech and Spanish customs spread widely among Native people. From that mix, Filipino culture was born.

7A timeline of Ferdinand Magellan's life lists these years. In 1480 he was born in Sabrosa, Portugal. By 1493 he was serving Lisbon's Royal Court, and the job was a page's job. In 1506 he joined the Portuguese navy. In 1518 he gave up his loyalty to Portugal and pledged it to Spain. In 1519 the expedition left Spain, sailing west to seek the Spice Islands. The year 1520 brought him to the passage that would carry his name. From that passage he entered the Pacific Ocean. In 1521 he died in battle in the Philippines. Native Filipino people did not accept Spanish rule as enough. They fought it. The struggle ran longer than three hundred years. Freedom was won in 1896. Major changes in the world followed this expedition. Some of the changes brought progress. Others brought harm. Magellan stays an important figure, and a complicated one, in the historical record. Glossary. assert (verb), page 16: to press others to notice something, such as one's authority, by acting with force or with confidence. navigation (noun), page 6: steering a course that leads toward a chosen place. circumnavigate (verb), page 2: to travel all the way around, especially in a ship. prominent (adjective), page 2: easy to notice, standing out, or important. recruit (verb), page 4: to bring a person in so that person will join. expedition (noun), page 7: a journey, or a voyage, made for one clear purpose. sanitation (noun), page 11: keeping a site clean, and moving waste out of it, including the methods and the tools for that work. flagship (noun), page 9: the ship that carries a fleet's commander and flies that commander's flag. scope (noun), page 14: how wide something reaches, or how far it extends. grueling (adjective), page 14: extremely hard, and exhausting. trade routes (noun), page 4: paths on sea or on land that traders use again and again. mutiny (noun), page 10: a refusal to obey orders from a government or from another authority, a rebellion.

79. When the Black Death Swept Europe

1A map tracks the Black Plague year by year. Dates on it run 1347 CE, 1348 CE, 1349 CE, 1350 CE, and 1351 CE. Some places are marked mostly unaffected. Waters shown include the Atlantic Ocean, the Black Sea, and the Mediterranean Sea. Cities on the map include Lubeck, Amsterdam, and London. Danzig, Paris, and Kiev are marked too. So are Vienna, Nuremberg, and Venice. Bordeaux and Marseille appear. Genoa, Ragusa, and Barcelona appear. Valencia, Naples, Rome, and Constantinople appear as well. The scene, and the smell, must have been overwhelming. October 1347 brought a dozen trading ships into Messina's port. Sicily holds Messina, and Sicily is part of today's Italy. Their long voyage had taken them across the Black Sea. Dockside excitement was likely. News often arrived on such ships, and so did exotic goods from distant lands. What met the greeters was a shock none of them had known. The same meeting may have handed them the thing that would kill them. Death had already taken most of the crew. Those still hauling ropes and sails were themselves dying. Their skin oozed from open sores. Rumors of a terrible Asian disease had already reached Europe. The plague entered Europe aboard these ships, carried by these sailors. It was extremely infectious. It raced across Europe. It raced across North Africa. Strangers passed it to strangers without knowing. Friends passed it to friends. New ports received it by ship, and fresh victims were waiting. Tens of millions died. Later the outbreak was named the Black Death. Europe has never suffered a worse wave of disease.

2During the 1300s, nobody had yet linked germs to illness. No one yet knew a cold could come from bacteria or from viruses. The flu was a mystery in the same way. So were other sicknesses. Disease, for many people, seemed to belong to the supernatural. A line-up of planets took the blame from professors working at the University of Paris. Magic was how one doctor described the way it spread. He claimed a healthy person could die at once if a spirit leaving a sick man's eyes struck someone standing close and looking at the patient. Nobody had connected the plague to the fleas that were truly carrying it. Scientists named Yersinia pestis only in 1894, almost 550 years later. The plague was probably this bacterium's work. It enters the digestive system of a flea. The flea normally feeds on blood from black rats and other rodents. Rat colonies that hosted the fleas died from the plague. Fleas then had to hunt other warm-blooded animals, humans included. Medieval towns were filthy and crowded, so the plague moved very fast. Sanitation and hygiene were poor in the 1300s, and that made things worse. Overcrowded city streets often received human waste. Trash was dumped there as well. Bugs were regular guests in houses. Flea bites, and bites from other pests, were an unpleasant fact of daily life.

3Fleas may not have been the sole source, and not every researcher is convinced they were. Huge deadly outbreaks can also come from cholera. Typhus can do the same. Speed is the objection some researchers raise. The 1347 wave spread too quickly, they say, and it killed too fast, to match Yersinia pestis. A deadlier microbe, they suggest, might have been the true cause. Yersinia pestis is still the leading suspect, because the symptoms match old descriptions. Archaeologists have also found this bacterium's DNA in mass graves from the time. Person-to-person spread, though, does seem clear. Pus from a person could infect someone else. Blood could. Saliva could. A simple cough could pass the sickness on. A handshake could too. After that, almost nothing could stop it. A five-step picture shows the path. A rodent is infected first. A flea bites that rodent. Plague bacteria multiply in the flea's gut. The flea bites a person. The person is infected. No effective treatment existed then for a disease this serious. After infection, several days passed before the bacteria showed themselves. As the illness ran on, victims had headaches. They had fever. They vomited. They swelled. They felt intense pain. Death could come quickly. A victim might instead live a few more days. Of people who showed symptoms, historians think just one in five lived. Part of the deadliness was that plague could take different forms. Bubonic plague bacteria begin by attacking lymph nodes in the neck, the groin, and the underarms. Inside the immune system, lymph nodes are vital organs. Fighting disease is the help they give the body. Plague makes those nodes swell. Poisoned blood and pus turn them black. The boils go by the name buboes. Lungs can be infected too, and then they bleed. Others can catch it from nothing more than a cough. Once it enters the blood, the victim is poisoned from within. Europe's spread was underway by 1348. New districts received it from travelers. Traders did too. Weeks often passed before an infected place knew something was horribly wrong. Useful action was no longer possible.

4Once a community realized the plague had arrived, many people panicked. Frightened families left sick relatives behind. Shopkeepers shut their doors. Doctors fled the places and the people they served. Priests fled too. Safety seemed more likely out in the country, so city dwellers ran there. Leaving town often carried the disease along. Useful ideas for fighting or controlling it were scarce. Desperate people tried useless cures. One was strapping a skinned chicken onto the buboes. Potions sold as unicorn horn fooled other buyers. Incense was burned by some. Some wore flowers, hoping to purify the air. Many turned to faith and hoped to be rescued. Christians called flagellants traveled in bands between towns. Spiked whips cut their backs until they bled. The prayer was that God would see their sorrow for sin, forgive them, and spare them. Jews were wrongly accused, in some places, by Christian groups who said they had caused the plague. Attacks fell on Jewish communities. People were driven off or killed. Pope Clement VI, head of the Catholic Church, issued a declaration. Jews, the statement made plain, were innocent and must not be harmed. Jewish villages destroyed in the middle of the 1300s numbered over two hundred. Common sense guided a few cities. Visiting ships, port cities realized, were spreading the contagion. Entry was refused to ships that came from infected places. Some port authorities made ships wait forty days before docking. That wait, called quarantine, was meant to show the crew was free of plague before they met local residents. Holding people in place, some officials learned, was the strongest chance to slow the advance. A family already sick could not leave home. Cities put limits on who could come and go. Trade was limited too. Work crews rushed to bury victims at once. They feared corpses could infect others. Enforcing such rules was difficult where public order had collapsed.

5Imagine your town, or your city, with half its people missing. The shops have shut. Stores have no food. Many who lived through the worst of the Black Death knew that experience. Historians can only estimate the dead. About eighty million Europeans lived before the Black Death struck. The share who died is placed somewhere from 40 percent up to 60 percent. Place changed the rate a great deal. Spain may have lost 75 to 80 percent. Southern France may have lost that share too. Germany's rate may have sat nearer 20 percent. England's may have too. The hardest blows usually fell on cities. Crowded, dirty neighborhoods let the disease spread easily. London lost nearly 60 percent of its people. Paris lost half its people. A chart of Europe's population, counted in millions, shows a crash and a long recovery. Recovery of the population took two hundred years. The chart labels the year 1000. It also labels 1100. Further labels are 1200 and then 1300. Later labels are 1400 and then 1500. The final labels are 1600 and 1700. Easing came after 1351. Researchers still cannot fully say why. Immunity may have grown in those who lived. The bacteria may have changed into a less deadly form. Over the following five hundred years, plague came back many times. No later return was as deadly. The health catastrophe left Europe deeply changed. Workers became hugely scarce. Craft skill was scarce too. Laborers were scarce. Manufacturing fell into crisis. Workers could demand better pay. They could demand better treatment.

6Fields went unplanted. They went unharvested. Peasants were not there to work them. Untended animals died. Many parts of Europe then suffered food shortages and starvation. Views of society shifted among survivors. So did views of what life meant. Church belief came into question for many. Rulers faced challenges from some of the people. Powerful people had failed to protect those they controlled. Progress still appeared in many places. Farmers tried better practices and better equipment so fewer hands could grow more food. Public health improved. Medicine improved. More communities saw that sanitation and cleanliness mattered. They set up better ways to handle outbreaks. A heavy plow helped end the food shortages that followed the plague years. Horses, rather than oxen, pulled it, so farmers could till fields much faster. Another outbreak on the scale of the Black Death is all but impossible under modern medicine. Flea-borne plague bacteria still survive on some rodent colonies. Most outbreaks can be halted quickly by medicines used today. Public sanitation helps control the spread of most disease. Health programs help too. Antibiotics are a recent step in human history. Some healers, earlier than the mid-1800s, already saw plant molds attack bacteria. Other fungi did the same. The 1800s brought clearer research on how microbes connect to disease. Accident led Scottish biologist Alexander Fleming, during the 1920s, to a plant mold. A dangerous kind of bacteria died when that mold touched it. Penicillin grew out of that research. The drug can kill many bacterial infections, and people called it a wonder. In 1945 he received the Nobel Prize. The field was Medicine.

7Europe in the mid-1300s lived in mystery and in horror under the Black Death. The end of the world felt real to many who lived there. No event in European history destroyed more lives, if death rates are the measure. Some historians also link the disaster to improvements that came afterward. Europe's Renaissance ran from the late 1300s into the 1600s. Gains came in medicine. Science advanced. Art advanced. Renaissance means rebirth in French. Rebirth was the very thing Europe required once the Black Death had passed. England suffered an economic shock after the Black Plague. Demand for farmers and for laborers was so high that pay went up. Pay climbed by as much as 40 percent. One end of that span is the 1340s. The other end is the 1380s. Alarm among the upper classes and the nobility pushed royal officials to pass a law. Peasant pay was supposed to be locked at pre-plague levels. Another law tried to stop peasants from leaving home villages to seek better jobs. A major rising followed the crackdowns. People call it the Peasants' Revolt. The year was 1381. King Richard II is shown that year, standing before the peasant army. A few terms close the story. Antibodies travel in the immune system so the body can fight infection. A bacterium is a tiny organism made of one cell, and some of them cause infection or disease. A disease is infectious when it can move from organism to organism. Contagion names an illness passed by contact, direct or indirect. It also names that passing itself. Without a tool to magnify it, a microbe cannot be seen. It is still a living thing. Digestive describes breaking food down so the body can use it. Keeping a place clean, or taking waste away, is sanitation. The word covers the work and the tools. DNA works like a code. It stores what a living thing inherits. Spelled out, the letters stand for deoxyribonucleic acid. A symptom is a definite sign that someone is ill or hurt. Call a thing exotic when it seems mysterious, when it seems unusual, or when it comes from far away. Viruses are tiny organisms that infect the body, and also the diseases they cause. Hygiene is cleanliness kept up so a person can stay healthy.

80. When the Ground Shakes and the Sea Rises

1The parts of this book are an introduction, the deep Earth, earthquakes, the Richter scale, volcanoes, tsunamis, a conclusion, and a word list. Smoke can rise from a volcano that looks calm. Ground and sea often seem steady. They often seem peaceful. Under our feet, the ground seems quiet. At the shore, the ocean seems to lap gently. Forces far below can break loose without warning. That peace ends when they do. Earthquakes are the violent shaking those forces cause. Volcanoes throw out ash, gases, and hot rock. Tsunamis (tsoo-NOM-ees) are the huge waves they raise. This book explains those events. It also explains the forces underneath them.

2Under the surface cover of soil, stone, and water, change never stops. Giant slabs of rock, like puzzle pieces, form the top layer. Those slabs are tectonic plates. Continents and ocean floors are made of them. Fourteen major plates, plus many smaller ones, form the outer crust. Each plate is around 100 km thick, about 60 miles. Where edges meet, cracks and gaps are common. Those openings are faults. Most quakes and most volcanic activity happen near faults on plate edges. A map can name the Eurasian Plate and the North American Plate. The Pacific Plate is on it too. So are the African Plate, the Indian Plate, and the Nazca Plate. The South American Plate, the Australian Plate, the Antarctic Plate, and the Scotia Plate can be marked as well. A line for the equator crosses the map. Dotted lines trace plate edges. Below the plates, heat is extreme. Typical temperatures run from 700 degrees Celsius to 1,300 degrees Celsius. In Fahrenheit, that is 1,292 to 2,372. Rock melts into liquid magma at that heat. Plates float on the magma. The magma keeps moving, and the plates ride with it. In a typical year a plate shifts somewhere from 0.65 centimeters up to 8.50 centimeters. That span is 0.25 to 3.35 inches. Three things can happen where moving plates meet. When two plates push together, one rides above the second, or the second rides above the first. If they slide past each other, the edges grind. If they pull apart, a gap opens and magma seeps out. Pictures can show mountains, magma, and these three motions.

3Buildings can be damaged by a quake. A strong quake can bring them down. Plate edges usually creep forward very slowly. Sometimes big pieces catch on one another. The plates still try to move. The hold comes from huge blocks of stone. Pressure and energy collect. Then the rocks give way all at once. The stored pressure and energy burst free. Plates jerk ahead. The ground shakes. People far above feel the quake. Some quakes are small and do no harm. The ground only trembles a little. Hanging objects may swing. Branches move as they would in a light breeze. Some quakes are so slight that nobody notices. In some regions, small quakes are common. Two regions inside the United States are California and Alaska. Chile, Greece, and Japan are others. A powerful shake can crumble buildings. Bridges can fall. Wide cracks can open in the ground. A picture can show earth split open by a quake.

4Strength is measured with a seismograph (SIZE-moh-graf). A number on the Richter (RICK-ter) scale is given to each quake. Strength decides the number. A chart can show how each level feels. On that scale, each whole step is ten times the strength of the step below. A 6.0 is ten times a 5.0. A 6.0 is one hundred times a 4.0. The biggest quake ever measured reached 9.5. Chile, on the South American coast, was the site. Scientists are still studying these dangers. A day may come when people can be warned before the shaking starts. The levels can be described this way. At 1, people feel nothing. Only sensitive instruments detect it. At 2, most people still feel nothing. Someone in a tall building may notice a slight sway. At 3, the shaking is noticed by many people close to where it starts. Damage does not occur. At 4, people at the origin certainly feel it. Hanging objects sway. Pool water sloshes. A weak building may be harmed. At 5, a wider area feels it. Weak buildings at the center, and around it, usually take heavy harm. Stronger buildings may take some harm. At 6, weak buildings take heavy harm. Strong buildings take some harm. Harm can reach across 160 kilometers, or 100 miles. At 7, the event is very major. Destruction takes most buildings around the middle. Cracks form in the earth. Pipes underground break. Large landslides can occur. At 8, buildings and bridges are destroyed. Big cracks open in the ground. Large landslides occur. At 9, the ground seems to roll in waves. Whole rivers may shift. Airborne objects are possible. Buildings and other structures can be totally destroyed. The scale has no highest number. The record remains 9.5.

5A picture can show a building ruined by a quake. On October 17, 1989, a major quake hit the San Francisco Bay Area in California. Its name is the Loma Prieta Earthquake. The Richter reading was 6.9 to 7.1. Shaking lasted only fifteen seconds. More than sixty people were killed. Several thousand more were hurt. Damage was estimated at 6 billion dollars. The losses covered structures, streets, spans, and further property. Not since 1906 had California seen a larger quake on the fault called San Andreas. That earlier quake was even stronger. Fires after it destroyed much of San Francisco. A volcano is the next subject. It forms where magma from deep inside comes out through a surface crack. Plate edges are the usual places, because cracks and thin spots let magma leak. Magma that pours out then hardens. Often it piles into a mountain. Sometimes the liquid rock flows calmly across the land. Many volcanoes in the Hawaiian Islands behave this way. Runny rock there can move as smoothly as a quiet river.

6A plug can form, and then a violent blast follows. In a very powerful volcano, hot magma may cool before it reaches the surface. It hardens into solid rock. That rock blocks the crack or hole where magma had been seeping. The block works like a cork in a bottle. Magma keeps pushing up. Hot gases inside it press on the block. Pressure climbs and climbs. Then the volcano explodes. Huge chunks of rock fly out. Whole mountainsides can be torn away. Hot poisonous gas shoots skyward. Ash and melted rock shoot with it. The power of the eruption is hard to believe. A picture can show dust, ash, gas, a lava flow, and a giant ash cloud. Eruptions bring many dangers. When a mountain explodes, masses of stone tumble down its sides. Those falling masses are landslides. A landslide can bury a whole city. It can block a river, and the blocked river can flood. Ash and dust rise in clouds. Ash then falls like snow. It is heavy enough to collapse house roofs. An ash cloud can travel around the world. A large one can even block sunlight. After a large eruption, the temperature of the whole Earth can drop.

7A picture can show trees knocked flat by a volcanic blast. Extremely hot poisonous gas can explode outward. The blast can be strong enough to knock down whole forests. It can be hot enough to start destructive fires. Snow and ice sit on some large volcanoes. Hot gas can melt all of that snow and ice at one time. Water then rushes down the mountain. The dirty flood is a mudslide. Think of it as a landslide made of liquid. Scientists collect clues from a volcanic fissure. Quakes still cannot be predicted. Large eruptions, however, can now be predicted quite well. In 1991, scientists warned people who lived near a volcano in the Philippines. They said an eruption was close. Many people left. They reached safety before the huge volcano blew.

8On May 18, 1980, Mount St. Helens, a very large volcano in Washington State, erupted. It belongs to a chain called the Cascade Mountain Range. That range runs through the Pacific Northwest. That is where two plates come together. One is the Juan de Fuca plate. The other is the North American plate. The blast destroyed the upper part of the mountain completely. Forests for miles around were flattened. Ash in the air turned daylight dim across much of the country. For several hours the ash fell like snow. Ten states received it. In the history of the United States, this was the deadliest eruption. Fifty-seven people died. Homes, bridges, railroads, and highways were destroyed. Pictures can show the mountain before the 1980 blast and the mountain after it. Tsunamis are the largest waves on Earth. They are huge waves raised by quakes or by volcanoes. People used to call them tidal waves. Tidal refers to the ordinary tides of the ocean. These waves have no link to the tides. The length of a football field is a fair picture of how tall one can stand.

9Ocean margins are the usual home of those plate borders. Quakes and volcanoes cluster there. A quake can shake loose a large landslide. A volcanic blast can do the same. Whole hills can collapse. A collapse into the ocean can raise enormous waves. Quakes and volcanoes also occur under the sea. An underwater quake makes the sea floor jerk. An undersea volcano blasts beneath the water. Either event builds huge waves that spread over the ocean surface. A picture can show steam rising from a volcano beside the sea. The waves race out from their source in every direction. One wave can cross a whole ocean. Speed can reach 320 kilometers per hour, or 200 miles per hour. Far from land, the wave may not stand very high. It is still very deep. Near land, the water grows shallow. The raised sea floor pushes the wave up. The pace drops. About 70 kilometers each hour is the new speed. That equals 45 miles each hour. The floor keeps lifting the wave. At the shore it can be tall enough to wreck almost anything in its path. Height near shore may be 10 to 100 feet. In open water, most of the wave stays below the surface. At the shore, the waves break as giants.

10A picture can show what a tsunami leaves behind. The largest one ever recorded was in 1958. A quake set off a landslide in a small bay in Alaska. Water was splashed 524 meters, or 1,720 feet, into the air. A giant wave then raced down the bay. Most tsunamis are smaller. At the shore they are usually one to ten stories high. That may not sound tall. The power of so much moving water is still hard to picture. Most coastal towns and villages sit well under 30 meters, or 100 feet, above the sea. Even a smaller tsunami can wreck houses, streets, and whole towns. In 1883, a volcano in Indonesia raised a tsunami that killed 36,000 people. In 2004, a large tsunami struck countries along the Indian Ocean. The start was a seabed quake. The site was off the west side of Indonesia. A ring of waves sped out from that point. Open water in their path measured in the hundreds of kilometers. Some paths measured in the thousands. Distant countries were hit. More than 225,000 people died in eleven countries that border that ocean. Later satellite data showed the deep-ocean height. It was only 60 centimeters, or 2 feet. In shallow water by the beaches, the waves often grew past 24 meters, or 78 feet. After that disaster, many countries began working together on a warning system for that region. A map can name Bangladesh, Myanmar, India, Thailand, and Somalia. Malaysia, Sri Lanka, the Maldives, Kenya, and the Seychelles can be named too. Tanzania, Indonesia, Madagascar, and South Africa can be marked as well. The origin sits in the Indian Ocean.

11Prediction of tsunamis, like prediction of volcanoes, is getting easier. The wave usually reaches shore minutes to hours after the quake or eruption that starts it. Instruments can detect volcanoes and quakes. After a large eruption or quake, scientists have time to warn that a tsunami may be on the way. Homes and belongings cannot be saved in that time. Lives can. Saving lives matters most. Our quiet planet sometimes turns violent. In a large quake, the ground shakes. Homes and property are wrecked. In a violent eruption, liquid rock can bury cities. Poisonous gas, ash, and landslides can bury them too. Along coasts, tsunami damage can cost billions of dollars. Scientists are working to learn all they can about these events. Better knowledge lets them predict volcanoes, quakes, and tsunamis. Those warnings can save thousands of lives. Words in this book can be explained this way. An earthquake is shaking of the crust caused by vibrations underground. Faults are cracks in the crust where movement happens. Landslides are masses of soil and rock moving down slopes. Magma is melted rock under the surface. A mudslide is a flood packed with dirt and debris. The Richter scale is the measure of quake strength. Tectonic plates are the huge rocky sheets, soil included, that build the crust. Tsunamis are enormous ocean waves raised by underwater quakes, landslides, or volcanoes. Volcanoes are openings where gas, ash, and lava pour out on top of the ground.

81. Where a Flush Really Goes

1A plant pond is there so bacteria can multiply. Sewage comes apart because those bacteria do the work. A flush finishes with a swoosh. That noise shows up whenever a toilet is used. Where does everything you send down the drain actually travel? The handle is only a starting move. A community needs a complex process to carry waste away. That process may stretch across many miles. It may also run below the streets. Four pieces do the toilet's work. They are the tank, the valve, the bowl, and the trap. At rest, the tank holds water up to its top mark. The bowl is filled to its top mark as well. Flushing opens the valve. Clean water stored in the tank flows into the bowl. Used water exits by way of the trap. The tank is left with nothing in it. Then the valve shuts. Fresh water starts returning to the tank. The bowl fills again at the same time. Both end full, back at those top marks. Think of the flush as four moments. Moment one is a full tank beside a full bowl. Moment two opens the way for clean tank water to enter, while the trap takes the used water out. Moment three closes the valve after the tank has run dry, and refilling starts. Moment four puts both water levels back at the top. The swoosh never tells you how many miles still lie ahead. Those miles stay out of sight under the community.

2People's waste does not look the same every time. It does not all start in one spot either. The shared name for it is sewage. Ordinary home life creates a lot of it. Using the toilet dirties water. So does taking a shower. So does cleaning plates. So does laundering clothes. Any other job that soils water adds more. In one day, a typical American dirties about 100 gallons, or 380 L. Chemicals help factories make their goods. A number of those chemicals are toxic. What the factory cannot keep becomes sewage. A restaurant can add to the flow by cleaning dishes with chemicals. Grease tipped into a drain counts as waste too. Rivers might receive that waste later on. Reservoirs might receive it. Groundwater might receive it. Daily life depends on that fresh water. Drinking it would be unsafe if sewage got in. Homes in a 2016 study numbered 23,749, spread through the United States. Of the water they used, 24 percent went through toilets. Showers used 20 percent. Faucets used 19 percent. Clothes washers used 17 percent. Leaks used 12 percent. Uses grouped as other came to 4 percent. Baths used 3 percent. Dishwashers used 1 percent. Flush toilets are missing for more than two billion people worldwide. Sewerage systems are missing for them too. Their waste mostly stacks up on open land. A great deal of it also flows into lakes and rivers. Terrible diseases thrive in those conditions. Each year, untreated sewage leads to the deaths of millions. Specialists are pushing hard for a fix. Even so, the challenge stays enormous. One river carries a warning sign that tells people to stay back. Sewage, along with other waste, has fouled it. Drinking-water sources are not where home pipes simply dump their load. School pipes and store pipes do not do that either. In lots of cities and towns, dirty water spins away down the drains. The local sewerage system is where it collects. Narrow pipes meet and form wider ones. A few of those wider pipes leave enough room for a human to walk inside.

3Under the ground, two pipe networks do different jobs. Household sewage from toilets, sinks, and the like travels in one of them. Rain can enter through a catch basin and a storm sewer pipe. Waste rides the sewer pipes until it reaches a sewage treatment plant. Rainwater shares that trip in some storm pipes. In others, rain runs straight out to creeks, ponds, and further waterways. All of that wastewater arrives at the plant through a large pipe network. Cleaning happens there so the water can be reused. After the breakdown, most of what was in the sewage is safe to return to the environment. Fertilizers are part of what remains. Methane is part of it. Water is part of it too. Living things that spread disease have to come out before any reuse. Other pollutants have to come out as well. No two treatment setups match in every way. Location helps decide the method. The number of people nearby helps decide it too. Crowded areas often use one familiar kind of plant. Its cleaning follows a series of steps. A giant screen does the first step. You can picture a huge kitchen strainer. Rocks, sticks, and garbage are among the big items it catches. Plant machines would jam if those items stayed in. Thick, dirty water is what remains, and it is called sludge. Air is pumped into that sludge for the second step. Helpful bacteria multiply because of the air. The name for this step is aeration. Sludge is what those bacteria consume, and they break it apart. The tanks a city plant needs are enormous. San Francisco, California, has a plant that treats 60 million gallons, equal to 227 million L, on an ordinary day. Rainy days push the load to 250 million gallons, equal to 946 million L.

4Aeration has to finish before the third step. Broken-down sludge then moves into a clarifier. Solid waste drops to the bottom inside that machine. Water sitting on top is sent through one more filter. Further cleaning happens there. Safe water may be released into a nearby waterway after that. A stream could receive it. A lake could receive it. The sea could receive it. Crops can be watered with it too. Solids take a different route in the fourth step. They enter a huge sealed tank known as a digester. Inside, another group of helpful bacteria feeds on much of the sludge. Digesting is what those bacteria do. Because no oxygen is present, the process is called anaerobic digestion. Solid sludge breaks down still further in the digester. More water is pulled out of it there as well. Carbon dioxide is one result. Methane gas is another. These gases account for about half the sludge. Drying is the fate of the other half. What remains feels similar to soil. Methane becomes a fuel for the plant. Machines there draw power from it. Farm fields often receive the sludge that is left. Poor soils gain organic matter from it. They gain fertilizer from it too. A landfill is the destination at other times. Country homes may stand a long way from one another. Linking them with a full sewerage system would be too costly. It would be impractical as well. Those households need a different plan for human waste. Waste from each house goes to its own septic system. That system is a mini treatment plant serving only that house. A septic tank is one part. A drainage field is the other. Soil receives the liquid and strains it. The tank holds on to the solids.

5Both the tank and the drainage field lie in the yard. Concrete forms the tank, and it is buried. Everything the house sends out runs directly into that tank. Solids sink and part from the liquids. Effluent is the name of those liquids. A run of buried pipes carries the effluent into the drainage field. From there it spreads through the soil. Filtering happens as the effluent percolates downward. Harmful pollutants are taken out by the soil itself. Groundwater is reached only after that cleaning. Solid sludge gathers in the tank. More of it collects as time passes. Too much sludge means the owners must call for help. A septic company then pumps the tank empty. Water that gathers below the surface on its own is groundwater. Rain and melted snow supply much of it. The water slips downward and rests in gaps among soil particles. A hard rock layer finally stops the downward trip. Enough water below ground can climb back up. Springs may form. Streams, lakes, and wetlands may form too. A large share of drinking water comes from groundwater. Sewage can escape a sewer pipe that has cracked. Soil takes it in, and groundwater can take it in later. Very harmful microorganisms fill that sewage. People can become very sick from them. Death is possible as well. Modern Greece still has an ancient sewer canal. The earliest sewerage systems go back thousands of years. The Indus Valley, now Pakistan, was one place that built them. Persia was another. Egypt was another. Pipes and canals, kept simple, made up those systems. Human waste left the cities through them. Storm water left too. Nearby waterways were where it all went.

6Pipes were a huge step forward. Earlier, people hurled buckets of waste from windows. Streets caught it. People in the street sometimes caught it too. The old canals still did harm. Nearby water picked up harmful bacteria. Deadly diseases traveled with those bacteria. Sickness followed for anyone who used that water. Century by century, handling sewage got a little better. Large cities kept struggling anyway. New York was among them. Waste was still hard to manage there in the 1800s. Growth in New York City was very fast. Sewage treatment plants did not exist yet. Waste heaped up across the city. People were too numerous. Waste was too plentiful. A privy, also called an outhouse, served many homes. Sometimes the privy was nothing but a hole. No one could flush. Waste kept filling the hole. A full privy brought a visit from the night-soil man. He worked after dark so residents would not watch. Buckets went from the privy out to the street. A horse-drawn cart received them. The cart hauled the load off. A full cart was usually emptied in the closest river. Shores sometimes grew so packed with waste that crews had to dig them clear. Until that digging, ships could not come alongside. Around 1870, a night-soil crew in Rochdale, England, was pictured hauling waste. River dumping was already bad. Street dumping happened too. Some privies were allowed to spill over. Their waste washed out where people walked. Storm sewers did not exist yet to carry it off. Children played in the same spots. The smell was more than anyone could stand. The 1880s brought New York City more than human waste. Pigs wandered loose, and so did cows and sheep. Street manure grew by huge amounts because of them. Horses caused the worst animal mess. Cars had not arrived, and thousands of horses used the streets. Each day, a single horse left about 24 pounds, or 11 kg, of manure.

7Maryland workers in 1915 were putting a sewerage system in place. Around the middle of the 1800s, experts made a grim connection. Deadly diseases moved through streets that were already flowing with waste. New York started sewers so waste would have somewhere to travel. Nearly 850 miles of sewers, a reach of 1,368 km, existed in New York City by 1914. Modern treatment systems rest on that early network. Most people in the United States barely notice the sewerage system now. Toilets and sinks seem to swallow waste on their own. It can feel like a trick. The real route is the one you have just followed. Next time the swoosh sounds, take a second to be glad for it. A modern sewerage system is a wonder. A few words help name the steps. Aeration means oxygen is forced into sewage so the waste can come apart. A liquid percolates when it seeps slowly through tiny openings. A clarifier is a tank where solid sewage sinks. A septic system treats sewage for one home with a tank and a drainage field. A digester is a big plant tank in which microorganisms break solid waste apart. Sewage is human waste moved away from buildings inside pipes. A drainage field is open ground that receives liquid from a septic tank. A sewage treatment plant is where sewage is cleaned and made safer for the world around it. Effluent is waste in liquid form. Sewerage systems are joined drains, pipes, and pumps that gather sewage and move it off. Methane is a gas you cannot see or smell, and it can catch fire. People also call it natural gas. Organisms are things that are alive.

82. Women Who Changed Sports in America

1Julie Chu lets a shot go. Her team is Team USA. The year of the match is 2014. The event is the Olympic Games. Canada is the opponent. The opening of this book is an introduction. Serena Williams is the first athlete after that. Allysa Seely is the next athlete. Chloe Kim follows Seely. Diana Taurasi follows Kim. Carli Lloyd follows Taurasi. The book then closes with a conclusion. A glossary of words comes after the conclusion. A tennis match was broadcast on September 20, 1973. Viewers around the world numbered ninety million. One player was Billie Jean King. The other player was Bobby Riggs. King ranked with the leading women in tennis. Riggs had earlier ranked as the top man. His age at the match was fifty-five. His playing career had already ended. Riggs dared King to face him. His claim was that men played tennis far better than women. He said even a man of his age could beat the top woman then playing. King came out the winner. She took every set, and there were three. People still rank that match among the key moments in sports in the United States. Women and girls across the country began joining sports because of it. Today, standout women play the full range of sports found in the United States. Tennis is one of those sports. Snowboarding is another. Soccer is another. They play at the top level when countries meet. They set records for the world. They make history. Billie Jean King raises the trophy. The win over Bobby Riggs is hers.

2The ball is just out of Williams's reach. She is playing at the French Open. A new tennis star was on the way twenty years after King's famous match. Compton, California, is where Serena Williams grew up. Courts open to everyone sat near the house her family lived in. She learned tennis there. Her first contest came when she was four. Paid tennis began for her at age fourteen. A Grand Slam win by a Black woman had happened only once before Williams. That first winner was Althea Gibson. Gibson's French Open title came in 1956. Gibson was also first among Black athletes to win at Wimbledon. The year was 1958. The U.S. Open gave her the same first in 1958. Williams was eighteen in 1999. She took the U.S. Open title that year. No Grand Slam tournament had been hers before that. Four events each year count as the Grand Slam. The Australian Open is one. The U.S. Open is one. The French Open is one. Wimbledon is one. From 1999 on, her singles titles at those events number more than twenty. No athlete from the United States has more singles wins at the Grand Slam. Olympic gold medals for Williams number four. Singles gold came in 2012. Three more golds came beside her sister, Venus Williams. The team years were 2000, 2008, and 2012. Outside of training, a large share of her time goes to work that is nonprofit. Schools have been built with her help. She has pushed to make education better. Girls are a special focus of that help. Kenya is one place. Uganda is another. Zimbabwe is another. Jamaica is another. A partner group helps students in the United States who come from communities with low incomes. The goal is college. Patsy T. Mink was a representative in the U.S. Congress. In 1972 she brought a bill forward. People know the bill by the name Title IX. One effect was a ban on gender discrimination in school sports. Public schools had to give girls the same chance to play that boys had. Girls' teams had been badly short of money before 1972. After the bill, funding for teams rose a great deal. College scholarships rose too. In 1972, high school sports counted about 300,000 girls. By 2019 the count was past three million. Many paths opened for women who wanted to play. Equal standing for women in sports is still unfinished work.

3Children are the usual starters in a pro athlete's sport. Allysa Seely waited. She was nineteen at her first triathlon. That race showed her she had found her sport. Three stages make up a triathlon, and the race is long. A swim is the usual first stage. A bike ride is the usual second. A run is the usual third. Arizona State University is where Seely went to school. The triathlon team there took her in. A national ranking followed. Doctors in 2010 found three illnesses in Seely. Brain and spine are what those illnesses affect. Surgery became necessary. She feared running would have to stop. Walking without an aid was uncertain, her doctors said. Months of treatment passed. Then she could walk by herself. A photo catches Seely in a race at the Paralympic Games of 2020. Below-the-knee loss of her leg came in 2013. Complications from the illnesses were the cause. Five gold medals came the next year. The events were international triathlons for athletes who have disabilities. A first world title came in 2015. A second world title came the year after. International triathlon golds since 2014 number more than fifteen. The Paralympic Games of 2016 added one of those golds. Severe pain can come with her illness. Weak muscles can come with it too. Training still reaches thirty-five hours in a week. A service dog helps with that training. She also tells people what an illness that continues is like to live with. Seely is in the center of a celebration photo. Hailey Danz stands on the left. Melissa Stockwell stands on the right. The medal they celebrate is gold.

4Snowboarding started for Chloe Kim at age four. Contests started at age six. Her first X Games came in 2014. Extreme sports fill that yearly event. Superpipe silver was hers. Her age was only thirteen. No younger medalist had ever stood at the X Games. Gold came the following year. The Winter Youth Olympic Games of 2016 were her next stage. Her snowboard score topped every earlier score in that meet. A photo shows her jumping in the half-pipe final. Those Games are the Winter Olympics of 2018. Gold is around her neck in the center of another photo. Bronze belongs to Arielle Gold, an athlete from the United States. She stands on the left. Silver belongs to Jiayu Liu of China, on the right. South Korea hosted the Winter Olympic Games of 2018, and Kim was seventeen. Two 1080 jumps, one right after the other, had never been landed by a woman in an Olympic contest before her. A 1080 means the boarder spins three complete times and then lands. Gold came from those jumps. Her parents left South Korea for the United States before her birth. She felt both countries were hers to stand for at the Games. Halfpipe gold came again at the Winter Olympics of 2022. No one before her had taken that event's gold at two Winter Games in a row. Speaking up about bullying has been part of her life as a pro. Climate change has been part of that work too. The year 2019 brought a partnership with Protect Our Winters. Young people become climate advocates through that nonprofit.

5A balance beam routine is what Lee is doing. History at the Olympic Games of 2021 belongs to eighteen-year-old Sunisa Lee. Team USA had never had a Hmong American before her. The word Hmong sounds like MAWNG. All-around gold had never gone to an Asian American gymnast before her. Four events make up the all-around. Vault is one. Uneven bars is one. Balance beam is one. Floor exercise is one. Those Games were the first Olympics for Lee. Team silver was also hers. Uneven bars brought her a bronze. Basketball filled Diana Taurasi's childhood in Chino, California. Three national championships came while she was at the University of Connecticut. Graduation year was 2004. Pro basketball then began with the Phoenix Mercury. Three championships for that club came with her on the roster. The league is the Women's National Basketball Association, called the WNBA. Olympic gold also came with the national women's basketball side of the United States. The gold years were 2004, 2008, 2012, and 2016. Four times she has been named Female Athlete of the Year by USA Basketball. Career points in the WNBA reached 8,000 with her before any other player. The total now is past 8,900. That sum is the league record. Argentina is where her parents lived before they moved to the United States. She gives them credit for teaching determination. She gives them credit for teaching hard work. Effort on the court is constant. Effort off the court is constant too. Volunteer time fills the hours away from training. Money is raised for nonprofit groups. The WNBA Community Assist Award came to her in 2018. It goes to players whose help reaches people facing hard times. Play spaces for children are built by one group she joins. The communities have too little funding. A three-point shot is leaving her hands in a photo.

6Hockey was one childhood sport for Carli Lloyd. Football was another. Basketball was another. Softball was another. Volleyball was another. Soccer began at age six. It soon became the favorite. High school soccer filled the next years. Rutgers University then put her on its soccer team. Several pro clubs came after college. Two World Cup championships came while she played for the women's national soccer side of the United States. The years were 2015 and 2019. Women's Player of the Year was her title both of those years. Three goals in the 2015 World Cup final were hers. Fifteen minutes held all three. Japan fell, and the United States won. That year voters gave her a Golden Ball from the Women's World Cup. Voters pick the player they see as best. A photo shows Lloyd shooting toward the goal. Costa Rica is the other side. Co-captain has also been her role for the women's national soccer side. Two Olympic golds came with her help in that role. The years were 2008 and 2012. The winning goal was hers both times. Charity work off the field includes Habitat for Humanity. Houses for people who lack homes are what that group builds. A soccer camp for children is hers to run. New Jersey is the state she calls home. December 2020 is when Sarah Fuller made football history. A score by a woman in a big-conference college football game had never happened before. Vanderbilt University used her as kicker. The extra point after the first touchdown was her kick. The game was tied by that kick. Soccer at Vanderbilt came before football. A national championship for that soccer side had her help. Her football uniform now sits on display. College Football Hall of Fame is where that uniform can be seen. Fuller is shown getting ready before play begins.

7Alana Nichols. Melissa Gonzalez. Ibtihaj Muhammad. Amanda Bingson. A fight was required before women in the United States could play sports. Most sports once turned women away. Some sports barred them outright. Many people thought sports were not proper for women. They also thought sports harmed women's health. Women built teams of their own anyway.
