They built clubs of their own. They played in spite of the ban. A road opened for the athletes who came later. Williams is one of those athletes. Seely is one. Kim is one. Taurasi is one. Lloyd is one. They compete. They stir young players to try. They give their sports a wider meaning. Amputated means a part of the body was removed. Banned means an official rule says a person may not do a thing. Challenged means one person dared another into a contest. Nonprofit means the aim is not profit. Perform means to carry out an action, or several actions in a row. Professionally means the person is paid, rather than playing only for fun. Redefine means to set a new meaning, or a wider one. Representing means acting or speaking for someone else, or for a group. A score is the total a game records, whether that total is points, runs, or goals. A tournament is a run of games or contests that names a final champion. A triathlon joins three sports in one athletic event. Underfunded means the money on hand is not enough.

83. Worlds That Travel around Our Sun

1Our Solar System holds the Sun at its center. Eight planets are the official ones. Several dwarf planets belong as well. Hundreds of moons belong. Another name for a moon is a planetary satellite. Comets belong. Asteroids belong. Clouds of gas belong. Everything other than the Sun travels around it. That travel is an orbit. Four inner planets come first. They are Mercury, then Venus, then Earth, then Mars. They are rocky. Hard materials make them. Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune are the outer planets. People know them as the gas giants. Gases make up most of what they are. Set beside Earth, each outer planet is enormous. The difference is hundreds of times in size. A labeled drawing can show the Sun and the worlds around it. Saturn, Uranus, Jupiter, Neptune, Mars, Pluto, Earth, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon can appear. A comet can appear. Asteroids can appear.

2A size game can make the Solar System easier to picture. Let Earth be a grape. The Moon then matches a green pea. The Sun matches a ball so large that a grown man could stand inside it. Jupiter is the largest planet, so it matches a grapefruit. Saturn is second in size, so it matches an orange. Uranus matches a lemon. Neptune matches a lemon too. The diameter of Earth is about 13,000 kilometers. That is about 8,100 miles. The diameter of the Sun is about 1.4 million kilometers. That is about 870,000 miles. Try a question. How many times would the Sun's diameter cover Earth's diameter? The Sun's diameter would cover Earth's diameter about 108 times. Heat on the Sun's surface is about 6,000 degrees Celsius. That is about 10,832 degrees Fahrenheit. Heat in the Sun's core is about 15,000,000 degrees Celsius. That is about 27,000,032 degrees Fahrenheit. Picture the Sun as a vast ball. Burning gas is what forms it. Its energy streams far out through the Solar System. Daily life gives the Sun a very important part. All life on Earth depends on that energy. Seasons are one effect of the Sun. It causes climate. It causes ocean currents. It causes air to circulate. It causes weather. Plants could not grow if that energy stopped. They could not make food. There would be no gas. There would be no oil. There would be no coal. Those three are fossil fuels of Earth. Dead plant life helps form them. Dead animal life helps form them. Formation takes millions of years.

3The Sun is a star, and stars exist by the billions. About 4.6 billion years have passed since this star began. For 5 billion years more, energy will still pour from it. Before the end, it will swell. Many inner planets will be swallowed. After that swell, it will shrink into a far smaller ball. A chart can compare object sizes in our Solar System. The chart can show the Sun. After it come Mercury, then Venus, then Earth, then Mars, then Jupiter, then Saturn, then Uranus, then Neptune, and finally Pluto. A close image of Mercury comes from 2008. The flight was the NASA Discovery mission. The image shows the Caloris Impact Basin, and the basin is huge. Mercury lies nearer the Sun than any other planet. No planet in our Solar System is smaller than Mercury. A full loop around the Sun takes Mercury only 88 days of Earth time. Earth needs 365 days for its own loop. That Earth loop is one year. Like every planet, Mercury spins while it orbits. Picture the spin as a top. The spin is very slow. People on that planet would call one full spin a day. Mercury's day is 59 times an Earth day in length. Because the spin is so slow, daytime grows very hot. Nighttime grows very cold.

4Scientists found two hard facts about Venus. The air is too heavy for a person to breathe. Venus also turns in a backward direction. Sunrise there happens in the west. Sunset happens in the east. Colors on a picture from the Magellan mission are a code. Each color marks a different elevation of the ground. Venus and Earth are close in size. They are still very different worlds. Thick cloud layers wrap Venus. The clouds there are much thicker than clouds around Earth. Those clouds hold in most heat from the Sun. The temperature becomes very, very hot. It passes four times the heat of water at a boil. The clouds also throw sunlight back. That bounced light is why Venus looks so bright. Few sights in the sky outshine it. Air pressure there is ninety times what Earth has. Space probes are able to land. Within a few hours, the probes quit. Turning on Venus is even slower than turning on Mercury. One Venus day matches 243 days on Earth. Maat Mons is a volcano there. The height is 8 kilometers, or 5 miles. Hawaii has volcanoes of this type. Maat Mons is very much like those Hawaii volcanoes.

5Earth is special because it is our home. It is special for a second reason too. Life can continue here. No other planet in our Solar System can support life. The biggest difference is liquid water, and Earth has it in abundance. Close to 70 percent of the ground is under water. Earth turns once in about 24 hours. People call that turn one day. One trip around the Sun takes about 365 days. People call that trip one year. Gases form Earth's atmosphere. Living things need those gases in order to stay alive. The atmosphere is a shield. It blocks most harmful rays from the Sun. It also meets meteors. It makes them burn. The burning happens before they can hit the ground. Earth has one natural satellite. That satellite is the Moon. A note explains the thin air. Think of Earth as an apple. Only the skin of that apple would match the atmosphere's thickness.

6Compared with Earth, the Moon is about a fourth as large. Light from the Sun bounces off the Moon and reaches us. Many scientists think the Moon began as a piece of our planet. A huge crash in space broke that piece free. Tests have found ice made of water. It lies on the lunar surface. Ocean tides on Earth have a cause. The Moon's gravitational pull is that cause. Mars comes fourth when you count out from the Sun. People call Mars the red planet. Dust the color of rust lies on it in large amounts. That dust gives the color. Of every planet around our Sun, Mars is the one most like Earth. Its seasons resemble seasons here. Its soil resembles soil here. Its air does not. Oxygen is very scarce. Water vapor is very scarce. Climate swings widely as the seasons change. Summer on the surface can reach 30 degrees Celsius, which is 86 degrees Fahrenheit. Winter can drop to minus 130 degrees Celsius, which is minus 202 degrees Fahrenheit.

7Mars often has strong winds. They can blow at 200 kilometers an hour, or 120 miles an hour. Those winds raise great storms of dust. The dust turns the air of Mars pink. Ice caps sit on both poles. The northern cap is mostly water, and that water never melts. The southern pole is carbon dioxide. In the summer of Mars, the southern ice changes from a solid into a gas. Two small moons belong to Mars. Their names are Phobos and Deimos. One Mars year nearly matches two years on Earth. Add about thirty minutes, and a Mars day matches one day here. Gullies at Hale Crater are under study. Shapes on that surface keep changing. The question is whether moving liquid water makes the new shapes. A picture dated April 9, 2007, shows Jupiter and the moon Ganymede. The Hubble Space Telescope took it. No planet in our Solar System is larger than Jupiter. In several ways it resembles a star. Most of it is clouds of gas. The clouds line up in bands. Winds in the bands are very high. Storms never really stop. One storm is gigantic and turns counterclockwise. Speed stays at 360 kilometers an hour, or 225 miles an hour. The storm behaves much like a hurricane. Its name is the Great Red Spot. People can see it without much trouble. Three Earths could sit across its width. Cloud tops there are very cold. Deep at the core, heat passes the heat of the Sun's outer layer.

8Size and company make Jupiter seem like a little system of its own. Four moons are large. Dozens of smaller moons travel around it. Several thin rings circle the equator. Some scientists think a larger Jupiter might have turned into a star. That change would have needed more growth while the planet was forming. The spin is quite fast for a world this big. One day lasts roughly ten hours. One loop around the Sun takes almost twelve years of Earth time. A caption names the dust storm that does not end. The caption calls it the Great Red Spot. Viewers can see it clearly. Four moons can be lined up from larger view to smaller view. From the top of that line to the bottom, the names run Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto. Rings around Saturn make a spectacular show. Most of each ring is water ice. A usual ring is about 30 feet deep. Some bumps and sharp points stand taller than two miles. Count out from the Sun and Saturn is world number six. People know it at once because the ring system is large and visible. Millions of chunks form those rings. Some chunks are ice. Some chunks are frozen gas. Dozens of small moons travel around Saturn as well.

9Saturn stands out for a second reason. Its weight is low for such a large body. Build a swimming pool huge enough to hold it, and Saturn would float. The planet spins very fast. A day there lasts ten hours and an extra half hour. Four moons can cross in front of Saturn together. Enceladus and Dione sit at the far left, and both cast shadows. Titan is the larger moon at the far right. Mimas is the small moon there. Those two cast no shadow. A Hubble Telescope picture shows moons of Uranus and some rings. The picture is very clear. On the far right, bright spots mark clouds that ride high. Count outward and Uranus is world number seven. Only two planets are bigger. Methane in the air gives a blue-green color. The planet seems to roll on its path around the Sun. The cause is a strong tilt. Scientists think it may have struck another body long ago. That body would have been about as big as a planet. Moons around Uranus number at least twenty-seven. Five of them are large. Rings have been tallied as well. That ring tally is at least thirteen. One loop around the Sun takes eighty-one years as Earth counts years.

10High on Neptune is a storm that runs in a backward way. Scientists named it Dark Spot One. Dark Spot Two sits lower. Their winds resemble a cyclone. The spin goes against the way Neptune itself orbits. Neptune is world number eight from the Sun. People sometimes call Neptune and Uranus the twin giants because the two are so much alike. Size nearly matches. Color nearly matches. Thick clouds cover both worlds. Winds there outrun every other wind in the Solar System. They hit 2,000 kilometers an hour. That speed is over 1,242 miles an hour. One moon is large. Many moons are smaller. Several dust rings can be seen. One loop around the Sun takes about 165 years of Earth time. Before 2006, the object Pluto counted as planet number nine. Scientists debated the old rank and then voted. The vote created dwarf planets as a new category. Pluto is the sort of object that category describes. A dwarf planet must travel around the Sun. Its shape must be nearly round. Its brightness must meet a minimum level. It must not be a moon. Its pull of gravity is too small to clear other objects off its path. Scientists first named six official dwarf planets. Some scientists hoped to place dozens of similar objects in that class. New tools make dim objects easier to find. Many more could join the dwarf planets. Gravity changes from world to world, and gravity sets your weight. Begin at 70 pounds here on Earth. Other places would change the reading. Mercury would show 27 pounds. Venus would show 63 pounds. The Moon would show 12 pounds. Mars would show 27 pounds. Jupiter would show 165 pounds. Saturn would show 65 pounds. Uranus would show 62 pounds. Neptune would show 79 pounds. Pluto would show 5 pounds. In outer space the scale would show nothing.

11Satellites watch tests of impacts. The tests study how to keep asteroids from hitting Earth. Asteroids are rocky and they are metallic. They travel around the Sun. Width can be only a few feet. Width can also be hundreds of miles. Diameter means a straight measure through the middle of an object. Most asteroids keep to the space between Mars and Jupiter. Some paths cut across the path of Earth. In earlier ages, some of them even slammed into Earth. When an asteroid or a smaller object enters Earth's atmosphere, it is called a meteoroid. If it lasts and reaches the ground, it is called a meteorite. If it burns away before the ground, it is called a meteor. A strong clue that an asteroid once hit Earth is the Barringer Crater. The crater lies near Winslow, Arizona. A photo shows the comet called NEAT. The WIYN telescope made the photo. The site is Kitt Peak National Observatory. Arizona is the state. The year 2001 was the year of the find. Near Earth Asteroid Tracking was the system behind that find. A comet is ice mixed with dust. Picture a large snowball that dust has made dirty, flying through space. The orbit is a long oval. For a while the comet comes near the Sun. Then it swings far outward. Some comets finish a loop in under 200 years. Halley's Comet is the famous one in that group. Seventy-six years pass, and then it comes back. Other comets need thousands of years for one loop. In 1996, Comet Hyakutake came near Earth. About 9,000 years must pass before that comet comes back.

12People have always asked what is going on far out in space. For centuries, guessing was the only method. Rockets changed that. Space probes changed it. Satellites changed it. Telescopes changed it. Each day these tools reveal events in our Solar System. With them, scientists discover planets that are new to us. They count moons over again. They watch a star being born. They watch a star being swallowed. The tools produced the first map that surveys every part of our universe's sky. They also let us look straight at the Sun. What they show next, in our Solar System or past it, is still ahead. In July 2010 the Planck Telescope sent its first sky-wide survey. The telescope orbits Earth for the European Space Agency, known as ESA. Mapping had gone on for a year. Planck measures radiation that remains from the universe's ancient start. Scientists use those measures to study how the universe came to be. As the telescope sweeps the sky, it records temperatures. It records how dense matter is. It records speed. It records the way galaxies move.

84. Writing That Began as Pictures

1A piece of Egyptian cloth in the opening picture is covered with hieroglyphs. One picture shows a crosswalk signal. A red hand on it is lit up. Walkers are being told to halt, which means they should not step into the street. If that signal stood in front of you, would its meaning be plain? No words are required. The pictures on the traffic signal are enough. Drawing came first in human history. Written words arrived much later. Languages made of pictures have passed along stories. They have also passed along facts people needed. When the images are familiar, most viewers can follow the message. The goal, in most cases, is to reach as many people as possible. Two picture languages rank among the most famous ever practiced. Egypt's hieroglyphs are one. The glyphs of the Maya are the other.

2Speech of the Gods. Visitors to today's Egypt can see the old picture writing without a long search. People call that writing hieroglyphic. Famous ruins carry the carved symbols. Monuments carry them, and temples do too. The marks can feel as if they cover everything. A belief explains the abundance. From 3100 bce until 332 ce, a span of almost three thousand years, Egyptians treated writing as sacred. Their kings said the gods had given language as a gift. A ruler had a holy job: to use the gift. Thoth would be angry if the job was skipped. Thoth was heaven's scribe. Scribes on Earth, employed by the king, had to do the work. Egyptians called the king a pharaoh. Learning the system was hard. More than seven hundred hieroglyphs had to be mastered. Boys were the usual students, and they were usually the sons of working scribes. A special school for scribes took them in at six or seven. Years of study passed before a student could serve as a full scribe at court. Placement mattered as much as the shapes. A young scribe had to set each glyph in the proper spot. Word Wise. The English word hieroglyph grew from Greek hieroglyphikos. In Greek, the meaning is a carving that is sacred. Two Kinds of Egyptian Signs. Hieroglyphs fell into two main types. One type was the logogram, a unit of meaning. Logograms made up most of the system. A single logogram could stand for a full word. Duck, walk, and Sun are examples. The other type was the phonogram, a unit of sound. Phonograms resemble the letters of most alphabets used in the modern West, yet they are not the same. No sign stood for the vowel e. None stood for the vowel u. Some signs stood for a pair or group of letters, and sh is one example. Egypt's hieroglyphic script used twenty-four phonograms. A scroll made in modern times lays out that alphabet. Each character sits beside the sound it represents.

3Temple walls in ancient Egypt often showed these signs to anyone who looked. A message might run in a horizontal row. It might run in a vertical column instead. Reading began at the right and moved left. Periods never troubled a scribe. Question marks never did either. The script had no punctuation at all. Blank spaces between words were missing too. Royalty did receive one special mark. Words about the pharaoh, and words about his family, were enclosed. The frame might be a rectangle. It might be an oval. The name for that frame is a cartouche. Its meaning joined two images: Earth drawn flat, and the Sun's arc traveling above it. The frame announced that the pharaoh's power reached over all things. A picture presents the cartouche of Niuserra, a pharaoh linked to Memphis. From Clay to Stone to Paper. The earliest hieroglyphs known go back to about 3100 bce. Finders located them in a tomb at Abydos, an old city. Abydos lies about 48 kilometers from Cairo, a distance of 30 miles. The objects were small clay tags. Each tag was roughly as big as a stamp used on mail. Glyphs were cut into the clay. Researchers who study ancient remains think the tags named the contents of boxes and jars. Stone came later. Carved hieroglyphs announced important decisions. Large upright slabs, called stelae, often carried them. So did obelisks, which are tall stones with a point. Graves and headstones of people who had died carried the signs as well. Stone carving was slow. The labor was heavy. Scribes eventually picked up reed pens and ink. Papyrus became their surface. Glyphs written this way were a plainer version of the carved signs. Speed improved, and the work grew easier. A photo captures the stela of Unis. He was a pharaoh at Saqqara during the Fifth Dynasty.

4Use of hieroglyphs shrank as time moved on. Roman forces took Egypt around 30 bce. After that conquest, stone hieroglyphs mostly decorated buildings. Sending a message was no longer their main job. One object, the Cup of Immortality, came from the tomb of Tutankhamun, a pharaoh. Real hieroglyphs can be viewed without a trip to Egypt. Big museums display Egyptian writing. New York's Metropolitan Museum of Art is one. London's British Museum is another. Some cities offer the signs on an ordinary street. In Paris, France, the square called the Place de la Concorde holds the Luxor Obelisk. Three thousand years have passed since that stone was made. Its glyphs declare the years when Ramses II ruled. France received the obelisk from Egypt in 1833. In Paris the Luxor Obelisk rises 23 meters, which is 75 feet. Egypt's government was the giver. Picture Writing in Mesoamerica. While Egypt's hieroglyphs declined, another picture script was spreading far away. The Maya are a people of southern Mexico. They also belong to the northern countries of Central America: Guatemala, Belize, Honduras, and El Salvador. They lived in those lands long ago, and they live there now. Specialists rank their picture language among the most complex of this kind. Palenque, in Mexico, is a Mayan city that remains in good condition. One wall there is covered with glyphs from edge to edge. The start of Mayan writing, archaeologists think, falls near 1000 bce. Clues point to the Olmecs as the first developers. The Olmecs were ancestors of the Maya. Surviving Mayan glyphs, though, go back only to 300 bce. Writing, for the Maya as for Egyptians, was something the gods had given. Itzamna stood as the supreme deity. He was a shaman, and writing was his creation. A sacred script could not be open to everyone. Only chosen scribes could read and write it, along with members of the royal family.

5Rich and Hard to Read. Mayan writing of long ago shared a plan with Egypt's system. About 800 glyphs existed, and they split into two sets. Logograms were the larger set. Each one stood for an entire word. Roughly 150 other glyphs were syllables. A syllable could be attached at the front of a word, as a prefix, or at the end, as a suffix. There was no alphabet of separate signs for separate sounds. Mayan Numbers. Three marks made up Mayan numerals. A shell shape was one mark. Dots were another. Bars were the third. To spell a word, scribes packed glyphs into a square frame, also called a cartouche. In Mayan use, that frame was only a bunch of glyphs that belonged as a group. You might compare the bunch to words sitting inside a sentence. Grids then held the squares. Columns came in pairs. The eye traveled left, then right, then downward, following a zigzag. At Palenque, Mexico, a temple yielded a cartouche filled with calendar glyphs. Beauty was a serious goal. Each frame was a source of pride, and scribes labored over the look. They wanted viewers to notice their work. Inside the frame, glyphs went wherever the scribe judged best. The result was a message with its own beauty. Reading grew harder for a related reason. One idea might be drawn in several different layouts. A further twist added trouble. Some logograms did double duty and could be read as syllables. A Mayan urn shows Itzamna. He was the god who created things.

6How Mayan Scribes Lived. A pharaoh depended on Egyptian scribes. A Mayan tribal king depended on his scribes in much the same way. Ceremony in religion needed written text, and scribes supplied it. Most of the books did not survive. Spanish conquerors destroyed them while taking the region in the sixteenth century. One stone carving shows a Mayan scribe kneeling as he writes. Battle victories of a king were a frequent subject. Stone walls of monuments and temples received the carved glyphs. Obelisks received them too. The texts worked as propaganda. Their aim was to brag about a ruler's deeds. By putting the deeds on display, a ruler could show who held authority. He could also press his power on others. A Matter of Time. Timekeeping filled many Mayan documents. Astronomy was a Mayan strength. Their calendar system was complex. One calendar followed the Sun and contained 365 days. Eighteen months divided those days, and each month had 20 days. Five days remained. People called the extra days wayeb and believed they brought bad luck. Public posting of these messages fell to the scribes. A scribe whose king had won found the task easy, and safe. A scribe on the defeated side did not. Winners thought the contest of words had a clear tactic. Deny the losers any chance to speak in writing. Hands of captured scribes were often injured for that reason. The hurt was supposed to end their writing forever. Preparing art was part of the job as well. Together, the art and the words praised the king. Fine Mayan glyphs still stand at places all through the Yucatan Peninsula. Palenque has them. Teotihuacan has them. Tikal has them. The stone work is ornate and lovely, cut by scribes of long ago. Egypt's hieroglyphs retell old human stories. Mayan glyphs do the same for people who lived very far in the past.

7Closing. Nobody still writes in the lovely picture languages of the old Maya or of old Egypt. Other ancient picture scripts remain alive. Chinese is one, and so are Japanese and Korean. Each uses thousands of symbols built from pictures. Newer picture signs exist too. Block-shaped glyphs show up on signs made for travel across borders. A traveler from any region can see where bags are collected. The same signs point toward a bus. One set of glyphs beats a stack of signs in language after language. A single picture, today as before, can sometimes replace a dozen words. Shared symbols of this kind let travelers around the world understand one another. Glossary. cartouche (noun), page 7: a box or an oval drawn around hieroglyphs or glyphs. Egyptian writers and Mayan writers used it to mark one ruler or one idea. phonograms (noun), page 6: signs that stand for sounds. pictographic (adjective), page 10: describing a picture, or a symbol, that stands in for a word or an idea. propaganda (noun), page 13: claims that are untrue or overstated, spread in order to move people's opinions. glyphs (noun), page 4: pictures, or other marks, that hold a special meaning and are often cut into a surface. scribe (noun), page 5: someone who copies writing by hand, or who sets information down in writing. hieroglyphs (noun), page 4: picture signs used as writing, especially by people in ancient Egypt. shaman (noun), page 10: in a tribal community, a person who heals or who leads in spiritual matters. logograms (noun), page 6: signs that stand for whole words or for phrases. stelae (noun), page 8: more than one stela. Each is a big stone slab or column set upright, usually carved with pictures or with words. papyrus (noun), page 8: a writing surface made from a plant with grasslike leaves, used by cultures of long ago. pharaoh (noun), page 5: the title of a ruler in ancient Egypt.

85. Young Mushers on the Snow Trail

1What this book covers comes first. The opening explains the junior race. Later parts tell how racers prepare, how the start works, what the trail is like, and how the finish feels. A word list and a topic list close the book. Late February is the season for a special gathering. The racers are young people from fourteen through seventeen years old. Alaska is the setting, beside a lake called Knik (kuh-NIK). Dogs come with them. In this race, a racer is called a musher. The musher rides at the back end of a sled. Snow and ice lie under the runners while a dog team pulls. Hard terrain stretches for roughly 150 miles, equal to 241 km. Blizzards, severe winds, and temperatures below zero are part of the test. The finish line is the aim. The name of the race is the Jr. Iditarod. It asks a great deal of every team. The year 1978 was the first time it was held. Every year after that, the race has returned. Here is a related fact. The longer Iditarod is the model for this junior race. Its length is more than 1,000 miles, which is about 1,600 km. Fifteen days is as long as it may last. During the Alaska Gold Rush, part of this route carried gold. Ships could not reach those inland places. Centuries earlier, Native Alaskans already used the route. Hunting was one use. Travel between villages was another. The year 1973 was the start of the highly competitive Iditarod Race. Remembering the old trail was one reason it was created. Remembering how important sled dogs were in Alaska history was the other reason. Young mushers use the Jr. Iditarod as preparation. A later entry in the Iditarod is what that preparation supports.

2Preparation starts long before a racer is old enough to enter. Training together is the first big idea. For some mushers, practice toward the Jr. Iditarod begins at age five. Supplies and warm clothing go into the pack. Parents go along. Snowy trails and a dog team are the classroom. Staying safe in the cold is one of the earliest lessons. Special clothing covers hands and faces. Dangerous winds are one threat. Temperatures below freezing are another. Mushers cannot do without proper equipment. Commands form another major lesson. The dogs learn a set of orders from the musher. Daily practice is the rule. Understanding each order matters. Obeying each order matters too. Healthy food is a lesson mushers learn very young. Success at dogsledding depends on it. Dogsledding means driving dogs that pull a sled. Strength has to last the whole distance. Muscles grow with proper nutrition. Best performance depends on that nutrition too. The command list works like this. A right turn is gee. A left turn is haw. A 180-degree turn to the right is come gee. A 180-degree turn to the left is come haw. A stop is whoa. A slower pace is easy. The signal to get going is mush. Line out is the order for the lead dog to place every dog in one straight row.

3Daily feeding gets careful attention from the musher. Dog care comes next. Alaskan huskies make up most sled teams. Speed is one trait they are known for. Strength is another. Stamina is another. A love of snow is another. Friendly dogs are what mushers want, along with those traits. A positive attitude is wanted too. Everyday dog food is not enough for dogs like these. Proper nutrition matters for the dogs, just as it does for the musher. Energy for the Jr. Iditarod has to come from that food. Morning feeding starts early. Rice is cooked in big pots. Fish goes into the rice. A vitamin mix goes in as well. This is the special food. The same strict routine happens every morning. It starts when the dogs are still puppies. Choosing the leader is a major decision during training. No two dogs share one personality. The leader is the dog that shows the rest which way to go. Humans differ from one another, and so do the dogs. High energy marks some dogs. A quieter manner marks others. Some dogs get along with teammates more easily. Less cooperation marks the rest.

4Practice puts a different dog in the front spot each time. The musher watches how the team runs. The following day brings a new arrangement. A smooth team that can run as fast as possible is the goal. The search continues until that arrangement appears. Front place belongs to the lead dog. Double file is the line behind the leader. Daily practice of that same line continues until race day. Here is another fact. Evidence of dog sledding goes back as far as 1000 CE, according to archaeologists. Inuit people invented the practice. Their home was the northernmost part of what is now Canada. The practice then spread quickly across the region. Before Europeans arrived, nomadic Alaskan natives already used dogs to carry supplies. Summer was one season for that work. Winter was the other. As years passed, breeding by Native people produced dogs fit for sled pulling. Among mushers today, the Alaskan husky is a favorite. Strength, energy, and agility are the traits behind that favor. A picture for this part shows the dogs lining up. The check-in comes when the big day finally arrives. Mushers come into the area of Wasilla. Anchorage lies to the south. That area is where the race begins. Warm clothing goes on first. The danger is frostbite, a condition in which skin freezes from the cold. Dog booties go on next. Ice and extreme cold are what the booties guard against. Leads, which are long ropes of strong material, fasten at the sled front. High tension from pulling is what those ropes can withstand. A harness wraps the chest of each dog. The musher joins each harness to the leads until the dogs form one team. Harnesses and booties are on, and the dogs are ready.

5A picture shows adults checking the supplies on a sled. Those supplies are the payload, and adults use a checklist for them. Every item has to be in the sled. Neat packing is required. Secure packing is required too. A hard race means a lost item is a serious problem. A wet item is a serious problem too. After the check, a jersey with an official race number goes on the musher. The start itself comes next. Teams reach the starting line one after another. Spectators stand along the course to watch and to cheer. The grueling miles ahead fill the mushers with excitement. Hearts pound during the wait. Two minutes separate each departure. Years of diligent preparation have led to this moment. The dogs are excited as well. They pull forward before the signal. A snow hook appears in a picture of the wait. The musher stands on a brake, a pedal like the brake of a car. Extra holding power comes from the snow hook. It serves as a backup brake for emergencies. The snow grips both the pedal and the hook. That grip holds the sled still. At the start signal, the brake is released and the snow hook is pulled. Yelps and barks come from the dogs as they strain forward. Cheers follow the teams down the trail. A minute is enough for a team to pass out of sight. A picture shows that takeoff.

6A picture of the 2006 Jr. Iditarod trail can sit beside the gear list. Essential equipment includes all of the following. A cold-weather sleeping bag is required. Food for one day for the musher is required. Emergency rations must add up to 3,000 calories. The hand axe must be at least 22 inches long. Snowshoes must be 28 inches long and 9 inches wide. Five cables for staking dogs out, each fitted with snaps, are required. Reflective tape is required. Eight booties for each dog are required. Matches or a lighter are required. A head lamp is required. A cooker for dog food is required. A second light is required. Three pairs of socks are required. A restraint that can hold a dog in the sled is required. Rain gear is required. Two pounds of dog food for each dog are required. Three pairs of gloves are required. Once the teams are racing, the path itself has to be followed. Years of training do not make the race easy. Markers in the ground, set every few yards, show where the trail is. Each marker is a wooden stick with a bright orange tip. The whole route has them. Headlamps on the sleds light the trail. Snowstorms are one time those lamps matter. Night is the other. A picture shows one of those markers. Straight, flat stretches fill much of the course. A sharp turn can appear without warning. A very steep hill can appear the same way. Soft snow is one surface the sled must cross. Hard snow is another. Frozen rivers, rocky ground, and forests are part of the route too. Commands are shouted the whole time. The musher watches what is ahead and stays alert enough to answer quickly.

7Dogs do not carry the whole job. On flat ground, the musher kicks to help the sled move. On a hill, the musher steps off and pushes. A loss of focus can send the sled off the trail. Lost time is the cost. Brutal weather is possible. The temperature can fall to minus 50 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 46 degrees Celsius). Wind can sting the face of a musher. Mushers and dogs can endure this because of long practice, solid meals, and training made for the work. A picture shows a musher pushing uphill. Another picture shows one team about to pass another. Winning is what each musher wants. Each team is pushed toward the greatest speed it can reach. The Jr. Iditarod is about more than a win. A shout of trail from a musher coming up behind has a clear meaning. The team in front must move aside and let the other team pass. Giving trail is the name of that duty. Refusal means automatic disqualification. Safety and well-being of other mushers stay on every mind. A musher in danger will be helped, even if the helper loses the race. Among mushers, the code of ethics ranks help above victory. Help has the higher priority.

8Stations along the trail are called checkpoints, and teams stop at them from time to time. Adults called checkers look over the mushers. Health is one thing they check. Supplies are the other. Veterinarians at those stations check the health of the dogs. The musher has a routine too. Booties are inspected. A walk around the sled confirms that leads and harnesses are sound. Jackets, gloves, and hats are checked. Wet or torn ones are replaced. Only the needed time is spent there. The trail is calling. A picture shows a musher at a checkpoint. Friendship is part of the layover that follows. Yentna Station is the halfway point, and every musher must stop there. Ten hours is the required break, called a layover. Rest, good meals, and dog care fill those hours. The musher in first place arrives and lights a bonfire. That fire is a tradition. Later arrivals sit around it together. Food is shared. Stories are shared too. Each musher can describe something from the trail. A funny story about the dogs is another choice.

9Ten hours later, the first-place musher leaves Yentna Station on the sled. The others leave in the same order they arrived. The return follows the same trail back to the starting point. The same checkpoints appear again. Often the only life in sight is the musher and the dogs. Success is the home stretch after the last checkpoint. This last part is the most exciting. A sign comes into view with the word Finish. All the training has pointed to this moment. Every bit of energy the musher can muster goes into a mad dash. The win belongs to the first musher across the finish line. Spectators waiting at the end cheer each team that appears. A picture shows a 2007 Jr. Iditarod team at that line.

10A picture shows Conway Seavey, the 2014 winner, with his lead dogs at the finish. Awards come after the final team crosses. Every musher gathers for them. Congratulations go around no matter the order of finish. Everyone knows how hard the Jr. Iditarod is for each participant. Pride in self and in the dogs follows many hours spent in practice and in hard effort. Each team worked as a unit to finish this incredible race. The mushers also worked beside one another. Pride comes from meeting a challenge that was set before them. That is why every participant can be called a winner. The winners, year by year, are these. Division I in 1978 was Joe Good. Division II in 1978 was Mike Newman. The 1979 winner was Clint Mayeur. The 1980 winner was Gary Baumgartner. The 1981 winner was Christine Delia. The 1982 winner was Tim Osmar. The 1983 winner was Tim Osmar. The 1984 winner was Tim Osmar. The 1985 winner was Lance Barve. The 1986 winner was Lance Barve. The 1987 winner was Dustin VanMeter. The 1988 winner was Dan Flodin. The 1989 winner was Jarad Jones. The 1990 winner was Jarad Jones. The 1991 winner was Brian Hanson. The 1992 winner was Ramey Smyth. The 1993 winner was Ramey Smyth. The 1994 winner was Cim Smyth. The 1995 winner was Dusty Whittemore. The 1996 winner was Dusty Whittemore. The 1997 winner was Tony Willis. The 1998 winner was Charlie Jordan. The 1999 winner was Ryan Redington. The 2000 winner was Ryan Redington. The 2001 winner was Tyrell Seavey. The 2002 winner was Cali King. The 2003 winner was Ellie Claus. The 2004 winner was Nicole Osmar. The 2005 winner was Melissa Owens. The 2006 winner was Micah T. Degerlund. The 2007 winner was Rohn Buser. The 2008 winner was Jessica Klejka. The 2009 winner was Cain Carter. The 2010 winner was Merissa Osmar. The 2011 winner was Jeremiah Klejka. The 2012 winner was Dallas Seavey. The 2013 winner was Noah Pereira. The 2014 winner was Conway Seavey. The 2015 winner was Kevin Harper. Which musher has the most wins? The 2016 winner was Kevin Harper. The 2017 winner was Andrew Nolan. The 2018 winner was Bailey Shaeffer. The 2019 winner was Anna Stephan. The 2020 winner was Nicholas Sousa. The 2021 winner was Morgan Martens. The 2022 winner was Emily Robinson. The 2023 winner was Emily Robinson. The 2024 winner was Emily Robinson. The 2025 winner was Emily Robinson.

11Words used in this book can be explained this way. To think about something before it happens is to anticipate. Extremely hard to cope with is the meaning of brutal. Willing to work with others is the meaning of cooperative. Hard, thorough work is what diligently describes. To live through a hard challenge is to endure. Moral principles that guide how a person acts are ethics. Very difficult and exhausting is the meaning of grueling. To summon or bring something forth is to muster. Importance is the meaning of priority. Energy that lasts a long time is stamina. Land or ground is terrain. One of a kind, unlike the others, is unique. To stay undamaged by something is to withstand. Topics a reader can look up include these. Anchorage is the city north of the starting area. Conditions are the weather and the trail tests. Distance is the length the teams must cover. The finish line is the goal at the end. The halfway point is Yentna Station. Participants are the young racers who earn awards. Sled dogs are the huskies on each team. Spectators are the people who cheer at the start and at the finish. The starting line is where teams leave at timed gaps. Training is the practice of commands, feeding, and choosing a leader.
